19 read sites in shard-keeper is the cutover surface — you're right to flag this isn't "hot path plus cleanup." The shape of risk:

- Routing reads are tested by traffic. Admin/validation reads are tested by whoever happens to exercise that code path, which in a small service often means a single on-call poking at a debug endpoint six weeks after the cutover.
- Backfill / shard-assignment reads sit in the danger zone — they run on replay, against stored shape, and a "weird" label_map value that would have been filtered or coerced at the loader is still sitting there in the source data.
- Validation paths are similar — they're exercised by lint-style inputs, not the live traffic mix, so they're the most likely to have been written against an older assumption and never re-tested when the loader was touched last time.

The "blast radius if missed" column is the one I think earns its keep in a touch matrix — it makes the cutover reviewable. A read that's "load full map and iterate" in a backfill tool has very different consequences from a "single key lookup" in an admin endpoint, and putting that next to each other on a single page forces the conversation about ordering and grouping before you're already mid-PR.

Want me to sketch a touch matrix template (columns + classification taxonomy) so when you sit down to fill it in, the shape is already there? Or do you want to keep that part in your own head and have me stay out until you've got the matrix drafted?

The discriminator is whether rollup-service is behind on volume (it will catch up if you give it time and stop feeding it) or behind on label shape (it will never catch up because it's filtering on the old map). Three questions that force a non-vague answer from Roman:

1. With replay paused or stopped on that shard, does rollup-service's lag on it drain to zero within a window, hold flat, or keep growing? Because backlog math is monotone-decreasing once input stops, and a parity defect does not drain — it stays at whatever level the filter mismatch leaves it at.

2. Of the events shard-keeper emitted on that shard during the replay window that rollup-service has not yet ingested, what label shape are they carrying — the old one or the new one? Because if the missing events are concentrated on the new shape, rollup-service is filtering on the pre-cutover map and this is the April 18 pattern, not throughput.

3. Does any other comparably low-volume shard show comparable lag during its own replay window, or is the lag specific to this one shard? Because cold-shard catch-up lag would repeat across low-volume shards under similar replay load, and a label-parity defect is bound to the diff, not to the shard's traffic profile.

If Roman's answers land on (1) drains, (2) mixed or old-shape only, (3) repeats elsewhere — it's backlog, and the path is throughput/time, not a config fix. If they land on (1) holds or grows, (2) new-shape concentrated, (3) unique to this shard — it's parity and you stop holding at 92% until the consumer map is reconciled.

# Query-volume delta event envelope (experimental, dogfood only)

Stability: `experimental`. Out of scope for the PM-facing v0 contract. Dogfood surfaces may read this type; PM-facing v0 consumers must filter it out by the routing rule below.

## Worked example — `query_volume_delta`

```json
{
  "id": "8c1a7f5e-3b2d-4d1a-9f0e-2c5b8a4e1d6f",
  "occurred_at": "2023-07-11T11:05:00Z",
  "type": "query_volume_delta",
  "schema_version": "0.1.0",
  "subject": {
    "service": "ingest-edge",
    "kind": "service"
  },
  "provenance": {
    "source_system": "metrics-router",
    "extractor": "lantern-ingest/query-volume-delta@<git-sha>",
    "extracted_at": "2023-07-11T11:05:00Z",
    "extraction_method": "sum_over_window_minus_trailing_baseline",
    "labels_propagated_from": ["service", "env"],
    "known_dropped_labels": ["shard"],
    "notes": "metrics-router does not currently propagate shard label into the query-volume pipeline; per-shard breakdown is not available from this source."
  },
  "data_quality": {
    "level": "partial",
    "reasons": ["shard_label_dropped"],
    "coverage_ratio": 0.984,
    "evaluated_at": "2023-07-11T11:05:00Z",
    "evaluated_by": "lantern-ingest/coverage-check@<git-sha>",
    "honest_unavailable": false
  },
  "stability": "experimental",
  "payload": {
    "window": {
      "start": "2023-07-11T10:00:00Z",
      "end":   "2023-07-11T11:00:00Z",
      "granularity": "1h"
    },
    "baseline": {
      "window_start": "2023-07-04T10:00:00Z",
      "window_end":   "2023-07-11T10:00:00Z",
      "method": "trailing_7d_same_hour"
    },
    "delta": {
      "absolute": -0.18,
      "relative": -0.04,
      "unit": "queries_per_second"
    }
  }
}
```

## Stable vs. experimental fields

Stable at v0 (consumer contract):

- `id`, `occurred_at`, `type`, `schema_version`
- `subject`
- `provenance` — shape is stable; per-source contents may grow
- `data_quality` — always present, evaluated per source per window
- `stability` — one of `stable` | `experimental`

Experimental at v0:

- All `payload.*` fields for `query_volume_delta`: `payload.window`, `payload.baseline`, `payload.delta`. Consumers must not rely on payload shape for this type until it is reclassified `stable` in a later schema version.
- `known_dropped_labels` is per-source and may change as upstream labels propagate; treat as informational, not contractual.

## Routing rule for v0 consumers

- PM-facing v0 surfaces: must ignore any event whose `stability` is not `stable`. `query_volume_delta` is therefore invisible to PM-facing v0 by construction, not by per-type policy alone.
- Internal dogfood surfaces: may render `query_volume_delta`, but must surface the `experimental` label and `data_quality.level` in the same view as the value. A delta rendered without its quality block is a bug in the dogfood UI, not an acceptable demo.

## Honest-unavailable path (exclusion)

If a source cannot honestly produce a `data_quality` block for a given window — no coverage check ran, extractor version missing, baseline window incomplete — the extractor must emit:

```json
"data_quality": {
  "level": "excluded",
  "reasons": ["coverage_check_not_run"],
  "honest_unavailable": true
}
```

Dogfood surfaces must drop these events from the rendered delta view. This is the rule that lets us say "this signal can be in the demo" without ever shipping a number we can't characterize.

## v0 promise vs. v1 revisit

- v0 promise: none to PMs about `query_volume_delta`. Internal dogfood only.
- v1 revisit: reclassify after dogfood reveals coverage gaps and label drift, and after Hema's permissions model determines who can see the values. Reclassification to `stable` requires an explicit `schema_version` bump and a contract addendum, not a quiet flag flip.

query_volume_delta — Lantern v0 event spec (proposed)

Purpose: surface change in service query volume between a current window and a baseline window, for internal dogfood review only. v0 ships as experimental; no PM-facing surface is promised.

Scope guardrails (v0):
  - visibility: "internal_only" — never rendered into PM-facing views
  - experimental: true — UI must render the experimental badge
  - When a source cannot honestly supply data_quality metadata for a window, exclude that source's deltas from dogfood entirely rather than emit "partial" as a fig leaf. (Per Alex's earlier rule.)

Envelope placement:
  - event_type: "query_volume_delta"
  - This spec defines the body fields. The envelope itself carries event_id, observed_at, and the standard provenance pair (source_system, emitting_adapter) — both already part of your field list.

Fields:

  event_id
    Type: string (ULID recommended)
    Required: yes
    Semantics: stable unique id for the delta event itself, not the underlying query. ULID keeps it time-orderable for the append-only store.

  event_type
    Type: string (enum constant)
    Required: yes
    Value: "query_volume_delta" (constant)

  observed_at
    Type: string (RFC3339 timestamp, UTC)
    Required: yes
    Semantics: when the delta was computed — i.e., the time the window closed and the rollup ran. Not the time of the queries themselves.

  service
    Type: string
    Required: yes
    Semantics: which Lantern-tracked service this query volume pertains to (e.g., metrics-router, ingest-edge, shard-keeper). Must match a service in the Lantern service registry; unknown services reject at ingest.

  source_system
    Type: string
    Required: yes
    Semantics: the underlying system that produced the measurement (e.g., prometheus, metrics-pipeline, rollup-service). Per Iris: must remain distinct from emitting_adapter so we can tell who computed vs who published.

  emitting_adapter
    Type: string
    Required: yes
    Semantics: the Lantern adapter that put this fact on the stream (e.g., lantern.metrics-adapter.v0).

  provenance_url
    Type: string (URL)
    Required: yes
    Semantics: link to the source query / dashboard / pipeline run that produced the delta. Must be dereferenceable by the on-call reviewing the number. If provenance_url cannot be honestly produced, the event must not be emitted. (Iris's "show your work" requirement.)

  window_start
    Type: string (RFC3339 timestamp, UTC)
    Required: yes
    Semantics: start of the current measurement window.

  window_end
    Type: string (RFC3339 timestamp, UTC)
    Required: yes
    Semantics: end of the current measurement window.

  baseline_window
    Type: object
    Required: yes
    Fields:
      start    — string (RFC3339 timestamp, UTC)
      end      — string (RFC3339 timestamp, UTC)
      label    — string (e.g., "previous_7d_same_hours", "trailing_28d_excluding_incidents")
    Semantics: the reference window against which delta_percent was computed. Must be explicit so the UI never has to guess "vs what."

  delta_percent
    Type: number (signed, two decimals)
    Required: yes
    Semantics: signed percent change of current window vs baseline_window. Positive = up, negative = down.
    Edge case: if baseline volume is zero, delta_percent is undefined; omit and set data_quality to "partial" with a provenance note rather than emitting infinity or NaN.

  data_quality
    Type: string (enum)
    Required: yes
    Allowed values: "complete" | "estimated" | "partial"
    Semantics (per Iris):
      complete  — full coverage of the service's query stream for both windows, no exclusions.
      estimated — coverage has known gaps, filled with documented estimation (e.g., partial shard sampling).
      partial   — coverage is incomplete and the number must not be used as ground truth.
    The UI styles each value distinctly; "partial" should look visibly weaker than the other two.

  visibility
    Type: string (enum)
    Required: yes
    v0 value: "internal_only"
    Allowed in v0: "internal_only" only ("pm_facing" reserved for v1).
    Semantics: scopes where this event is allowed to render. v0 forces internal_only so Iris's UI can hard-default dogfood rendering without risk of leakage.

  experimental
    Type: boolean
    Required: yes
    v0 value: true
    Semantics: when true, UI must render an experimental badge and any summary aggregation must not include this event in PM-facing rollups. Marking must be visible to the dogfood audience, not just stored.

Example event:

    {
      "event_id": "01HXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX",
      "event_type": "query_volume_delta",
      "observed_at": "2023-07-11T15:00:00Z",
      "service": "metrics-router",
      "source_system": "metrics-pipeline",
      "emitting_adapter": "lantern.metrics-adapter.v0",

    experimental in the same schema, and the UI treats experimental fields as
    non-load-bearing. We do not ship a giant schema dump for v0; we ship a thin

    deploy_completed, owner_changed) and grow from there.

Here's a skeleton you can hand her. It's a one-page structure for a design-lead thinking exercise, tuned to make her sound like a designer who can own a system without slipping into management-voice. Sections first, then what each is for, then what to watch out for in each. No sample sentences — she wants to write the words herself.

The structure

1. Read of the prompt (top of page, 3–4 sentences)
2. What I'd want to know first (4–5 sentences)
3. Shape of the work (4–6 sentences)
4. How I'd work with the people around it (3–4 sentences)
5. What "done" looks like (3–5 sentences)
6. What I'd want to talk about next (closing, 2–3 sentences)

What each section accomplishes

1. Read of the prompt. Shows she listened and can reframe the question precisely. Grounds everything that follows in the actual ask.
2. What I'd want to know first. Shows her instinct to investigate before designing. The questions a systems-thinker asks (who uses it, what's already there, what's load-bearing, what breaks if you change it) are the strongest evidence she thinks in systems, not screens.
3. Shape of the work. Light sketch of how the work would actually unfold — explore, define, build, ship, keep alive. This is where the "own a system" signal lands hardest, because a system is something that exists after launch day.
4. How I'd work with the people around it. Shows she's a collaborator who respects engineering and listens to PM/research. Names the craft partners she'd loop in.
5. What "done" looks like. Shows she thinks in outcomes a system produces over time — adoption, clarity for the next person, speed of future work, what's deliberately not in.
6. What I'd want to talk about next. Signals she's a thinking partner and leaves room for a real conversation. Gives the design lead something specific to respond to.

What not to overdo, per section

1. Don't restate the prompt verbatim. Don't write a thesis statement or a "my understanding is..." preamble. A few lines, then move.
2. Don't list ten questions. Pick the two or three that would actually shape the early work. Don't pretend she has answers yet — that's the agency-voice leak.
3. Don't write a project plan. No timelines, milestones, phases with dates, or RACI. A paragraph that names the shape of the work is enough. Don't claim to know how long anything takes.
4. Don't say "stakeholders," "alignment," "drive consensus," "lead cross-functional," or anything that sounds like a Director of Design job description. Name the actual people (engineering, PM, research) and what she'd be doing with them, not at them.
5. No OKRs, no metrics she can't know yet, no "we'll know we succeeded when…" theatre. Talk about what the system does for the next person and the next quarter. If a sentence could fit any designer's response to any prompt, cut it.
6. Don't summarize. Don't pitch herself again. Don't ask five questions at the end. Two or three lines, one real question, done.

Two cross-cutting notes

- Write in short paragraphs, not bullets. A bullet list reads like a deck slide or a kickoff agenda — that's the voice she's trying to leave behind. Prose reads like a designer thinking out loud on the page.
- One page is roughly 350–500 words; aim for the lower end. Density beats length. If she goes over, she's either being too general or adding a section she doesn't need.

The single best tell of "management manifesto" is the word "stakeholders." The second-best tell is "alignment." If those don't appear and the shape of the work has a keep-alive phase, she's landed the tone.

If the prompt turns out to be more concrete than "how would you approach X" — say, it's asking her to think through a specific edge case or a specific subsystem — she can compress sections 2 and 3 and let section 5 do more of the work. The skeleton holds either way; just shift the weight.

Hi Mara,

The short version: v1 of a pattern is the team's best guess about what the product needs. The hard part isn't shipping it — it's the handoff from "we built this" to "this belongs to a community of users." Most patterns don't fail because the design is wrong; they fail because the people who actually use them can't influence them.

Three things I'd try to put in place after v1 lands.

First, pull the first two or three real product teams in before launch, not after. Not to get consensus on every detail — that just creates committee design — but to surface where the pattern will break under realistic constraints. A pattern that looks good in a Figma library and a pattern that survives contact with a shipping roadmap are usually different artifacts.

Second, set up a lightweight contribution path. The minimum that tends to work: an issue template for friction, a channel for questions, and a documented way to propose changes — usually a short RFC with one or two reviewers, not a design-system committee. The goal is to make it easier for a team to extend the pattern than to fork it locally and ship their own variant.

Third, be explicit about what's flexible and what isn't. Token-level decisions (color, spacing, type) usually need to be locked, with a documented upgrade path. Component variants can be flexible within guardrails — blessed variants vs. opt-in. Composition patterns are the most flexible and should usually be documented as examples, not prescriptions. A lot of "rigid system" complaints are really a confusion of levels — someone treating a usage example as a hard rule.

On cadence: I'd plan a quarterly review window for the first year, plus an immediate-revisit trigger when adoption drops, override rates climb, or a team proposes a change that doesn't fit. The trap is over-measuring — a dashboard nobody reads is worse than nothing. A small set of signals (adoption, override rate, friction issue count) at a known cadence is usually enough.

The honest answer is that I don't think there's a stable version of this. The right ownership model at three teams is different from the right model at ten, and from fifty. The pattern owner's job is to keep adjusting what "correctly" means as the teams using the pattern change, and to make the system easier to use correctly than to misuse.

Anya

BUG: Lantern v0 — deploy-movement card shows stale "last refreshed" after worker restart

Reported:   2023-08-24 09:40 EDT by Iris
Surface:    Lantern v0 deploy-movement card (live internal)
Reproduced: Once. Manual worker action restored freshness. No incorrect
            ownership or incident-load card rendered. No data loss.
Window:     ~18 minutes. Card showed 10:42; the underlying store had
            deploy events through 11:00.

Severity: Sev3 (v0 freshness / credibility)

The card looked more current than it was for roughly eighteen minutes. No
wrong data rendered, but this directly contradicts the v0 promise of honest
provenance and freshness — a stale timestamp presented as current is exactly
the false confidence Lantern is supposed to avoid.

Likely failure mode (v0 freshness, NOT permissions or data contract)

The card's "last refreshed" stamp is sourced from the producer side — the
worker's last-processed-event cursor or the derived read model's own update
time — rather than from the store's actual max(event_time) for the deploy
stream at read time. After the worker restart, the worker was replaying from
a checkpoint and had not yet caught up to the store tail; the read model had
not yet been refreshed; the UI continued to show the pre-restart timestamp
(10:42) as if it were current. Once the worker caught up, the stamp moved
forward — but only because the worker emitted catch-up events, not because
the UI ever asked the store. Freshness is being asked of the producer, not
of the data. This is a backend / derived-model issue, not a permissions or
contract issue.

Acceptance criteria for the v0 fix

1.  The card's freshness timestamp reflects the store's max(event_time) for
    the deploy stream at read time, framed as "last seen" — not the worker
    cursor and not the derived read model's own update time. The UI must not
    be able to display a timestamp older than the store's actual newest
    deploy event.

2.  During a worker catch-up window after a restart, the card visibly
    indicates that freshness is stale (e.g., a catching-up / warming
    affordance, plus the actual store-side last-seen), rather than presenting
    a pre-restart timestamp as current.

3.  A regression test reproduces the exact scenario: worker restart with N
    newer events already in the store beyond the checkpoint; the UI must
    surface the staleness within that restart window, not silently display
    the pre-restart timestamp.

Owners

-   Freshness source (backend / derived read model): infra (Alex's lane)
-   UI interpretation of stale / warming state: Iris

Scope guardrails for the fix (carried over from v0 contract)

-   Do not introduce a "blocked" or "stale" backend status; the catch-up /
    stale UI affordance stays derived and permission-safe.
-   Do not broaden the v0 event types to carry freshness metadata; pull
    freshness from the store, not from the event envelope.
-   Do not infer a deeper system behind an absent freshness stamp on any
    other card.

If you want, I can file this as a follow-up on lantern#3 (or in a fresh
Lantern v0 bugs doc) and tag Iris + infra — just say where.

Acceptance criteria — Lantern v0 deploy-movement refresh-staleness fix

1. Worker heartbeat persists separately from latest source-event time.
   - The v0 worker writes a heartbeat on each processing tick, distinct from any source-event timestamps it persists.
   - The derived read model exposes two fields per relevant stream: source_last_event_at and worker_heartbeat_at. Both retain the v0 envelope's source_system and actor provenance.
   - A tick that processes no new source events still updates worker_heartbeat_at and leaves source_last_event_at unchanged.

2. Stale warning appears on the deploy-movement card when worker heartbeat lag exceeds five minutes.
   - The card displays "last source event at" using source_last_event_at.
   - When worker_heartbeat_at is more than five minutes behind wall-clock now, the card shows a visible stale indicator. Copy uses "last seen" wording; it does not imply the deploy is complete, current, or healthy.
   - source_last_event_at continues to render its actual value (possibly hours old). Stale is a worker-liveness signal, not a data-age assertion.

3. No inferred ownership changes.
   - Heartbeat presence, heartbeat staleness, and absence of recent source events do not change any card's owner field or feed into the blocked derivation.
   - blocked continues to derive only from permission-safe events (open deploy past expected window, open incident without matching resolution).
   - Existing ownership rows are not rewritten, backfilled, or re-attributed as a side effect of the fix.

4. No raw incident details.
   - The heartbeat field, the stale-state rendering, and any new copy introduced by this fix contain no incident bodies, notes, or unpermissioned text.
   - The deploy-movement card remains a permission-safe summary; the stale indicator is a system-level liveness signal, not a derived incident summary.

5. Paused-worker test proves the stale state appears.
   - An automated test pauses the v0 worker, advances time past the five-minute threshold, and asserts the card renders the stale indicator while source_last_event_at holds its pre-pause value.
   - The test resumes the worker, runs one tick, and asserts the stale indicator clears and worker_heartbeat_at advances.
   - The test cleans up its injected fixtures so staging data is not polluted.

Three prompts for systems-design loops:

1. Ownership: "Who is on the hook for this at 3 AM, and what are they actually looking at?"
2. Handoff: "How does this move to the next person without losing context?"
3. Rollback: "What specific signal causes you to roll this back, and have you tested the path?"

Strong-signal answers:
- Names a primary, names a backup, names paging criteria, names what the on-call sees first
- Runbook or handoff doc with concrete structure; a recent transfer that actually happened; paired shadow or documented walkthrough
- Explicit rollback criteria tied to user-visible signals; rollback path tested in staging; understands rollback has its own dependencies

Weak-signal answers (probe, don't auto-disqualify on these alone):
- "The team owns it" with no current primary, or ownership only framed as the team that built it
- "We'll onboard them" / "the runbook" / "they can ping me" — no concrete artifact or ceremony
- "We'd just revert" with no defined trigger; rollback untested because "we haven't needed it yet"

Caveat — don't over-index on Sphere-specific scars. The lesson here is reasoning about ownership, handoff, and rollback thresholds, not the particular shape of our April incident. A candidate who happened to live through a similar Sev2 isn't automatically stronger than one who reasons correctly about the failure mode when prompted. Reward the reasoning, not the war story.

Two notes: (1) restructured the three questions as a numbered sequence with explicit ordering so interviewers don't bounce around; (2) added a short probe ladder for shallow answers, since the original "why" said the candidate needed repeated prompting. Kept it portable — no stack-specific language.

  OPERATIONAL OWNERSHIP AND ROLLBACK SIGNAL IN SYSTEMS DESIGN

  Use after the candidate has walked through a system design. Goal: test whether operational ownership and rollback criteria are part of how they design, separate from whether the architecture itself is correct.

  Three questions, in order:

  1. Ownership. After this ships, who owns the alert, owns the deploy, and owns the rollback decision? Names or team names — even a hypothetical org chart — are fine.

  2. Rollback criteria. What measurable condition makes you stop or roll back, and what condition makes you keep watching? Give concrete thresholds — error rate, lag, dropped writes, customer-visible symptoms.

  3. Environment progression. What changes between staging, canary, and full production? What are you checking at each step before you widen the rollout?

  Probes if the answer stays shallow:

    - "Who specifically gets paged at 2 a.m., and what do they do first?"
    - "What's a number that, if it moved, you'd roll back without debating?"
    - "What could pass staging and still fail at 100%?"

  Strong signals (look for at least three):

    - Names an operator or owning team, even a hypothetical one.
    - Defines rollback and hold thresholds in user-visible impact or data-safety terms, not "things look bad."
    - Names the artifact left behind for the next person: runbook, dashboard, alert owner, paging path, escalation rule.
    - Describes something genuinely different about staging vs. canary vs. production — real traffic, blast radius, soak time, rollback cost.
    - Distinguishes "the code works" from "we're confident enough to keep it at 100%."

  Weak signals (any one is a hold):

    - Rollback equals "redeploy the previous version" with no criteria.
    - "Whoever wrote it owns it," or no clear handoff to operations.
    - Talks only about architecture diagrams and not about who responds at 2 a.m.
    - Staging success equals production confidence; can't name what could pass staging and still fail in production.
    - Treats ownership and rollback as someone else's problem.

  Calibration note for interviewers:

  A strong architectural answer with weak ownership/rollback answers is a signal, not an automatic no-hire. Note it for the loop and let the next interviewer probe in their own context. The reverse — fluent ownership/rollback language with a fuzzy design — also warrants a probe; the candidate may be performing the operational vocabulary without grounding it.

Nothing dramatic, but also not nothing. The pivot tenderness is the signal worth respecting, because that's the motion the stretched ligament hates.

Next 24 hours:

Three pieces, matching the three questions.

1. Where token ownership ends and implementation ownership begins

Design owns:
  - token names and semantic intent (what --color-action-primary means, when it applies)
  - the primitive to semantic to component relationships
  - criteria for adding, renaming, or deprecating a token
  - usage rules and do/don't examples

Engineering owns:
  - implementation (CSS vars, JS exports, build tooling)
  - distribution (how tokens ship — npm package, CDN, design-tokens artifact)
  - platform mapping (web, iOS, Android specifics)
  - migration mechanics (codemods, deprecation windows, version bumps)

The seam: design documents what a token means and when to use it; engineering decides how it's exposed and how teams move to it.

2. What belongs in the handoff doc

In:
  - token names plus semantic intent (link to the token source, do not paste values)
  - usage guidance: when this component applies, when it does not
  - short do/don't list, 3-5 examples
  - stable vs product-decided: which slots are fixed, which can vary by context
  - owner plus review process
  - known gaps or open questions

Out:
  - implementation specifics (which CSS property, which event handler)
  - codemods or migration scripts
  - performance or bundle-size claims
  - full token tables (link instead of pasting)

3. How to claim semantics plus usage without claiming migration

Cleanest framing: design owns the contract; engineering implements and migrates against the contract.

Specifically:
  - design owns: name, meaning, usage rules, do/don't examples, governance criteria
  - engineering owns: codemods, deprecation windows in code, version bump timing, platform-specific mapping
  - design does NOT specify: which CSS-in-JS library, the migration script, the npm release cadence

One sentence that captures the whole boundary: design writes what the token means and where it applies; engineering decides how it's shipped and how teams migrate to it.

Worth saying that last sentence out loud in the exercise so the engineer reading it knows exactly where their call starts and design's stops.

Here is a practical checklist for today and a calm text to Devika. Plain text so it copies cleanly into a notes app or message.

  1. KIBO INSPECTION (next 1–2 hours, on a non-slip surface)

    Hands-on, treats for cooperation:
      - Run fingers through the fur on the chest and just behind the front legs where the harness sat. Look and feel for rub marks, raw spots, pulled fur, or swelling.
      - Gently press along the ribcage, then the shoulders, then down each front leg to the paw pads. He should tolerate all of it; flinch, yelp, or pulling away is a flag.
      - Check all four paw pads and between the toes for cuts, gravel, or a torn nail. Curb clips often show up there, not on the legs.
      - Tail base and lower back — hand down the spine, watch for guarding.

    Movement, on a flat floor:
      - Walk away from you and back at a normal pace. Watch for head-bob, shortened stride on any leg, or a hip-hitch.
      - Sit-to-down and down-to-stand. A slow sit is more sensitive than a limp at a walk.
      - A step or two on stairs if you have them. Same logic as your own stair checks.

    Over the next 24 hours, just keep notes — no alarm unless you see one:
      - Appetite, water intake, stool.
      - Any limp that appears after rest (soft-tissue soreness often shows up the next morning, not immediately).
      - Repeated licking or chewing at one spot.
      - Behavior change: hiding, panting at rest, reluctance to be touched.

    Vet threshold, not Dr. Google: any of the above flags, or a limp that worsens over 24h rather than improves. One bad stair moment tomorrow morning does not need a same-day panic; three do.

  2. HARNESS FIT CHECK (why it slipped)

    Quick diagnosis on the current harness:
      - Clip type: side-release buckle? Buckles lose spring tension with age and pop under sudden load — the most common failure.
      - Webbing: fraying near the buckle or D-ring? Stretched webbing that no longer lies flat is the second.
      - Sliders: do the chest and girth straps hold their position, or has the loop slipped under load? If sliders no longer bite, refitting won't fix it.
      - Geometry: is the chest piece sitting high on the chest (good) or sliding back toward the shoulders (girth too loose or wrong shape for his build)?

    Re-fit rule of thumb even if you keep this harness one more walk:
      - Two flat fingers under each strap at the chest and behind the front legs. Tighter and he coughs; looser and a lunge creates slack to slip.
      - Chest piece sits above the sternum, not across it, not pressing into the armpits.
      - Back-clip only is what failed you. If you keep the harness, add a front-clip D-ring at the chest so a future surprise has two anchor points.

  3. REPLACEMENT BEFORE THE NEXT WALK

    Replace (don't repair) if: the buckle popped, the webbing is stretched, or the sliders no longer hold. A harness that slipped once under sudden load will slip again, and the next surprise may not be a curb.
    Repair/re-fit only if: the hardware is sound and the slip was purely a fit error.

    What to order today, fit tonight or tomorrow:
      - Y-front or H-style harness with a padded chest plate. The Y keeps the strap off the trachea and reduces shoulder slip.
      - Both a front D-ring (steering/control) and a back D-ring (casual walks). For the park entrance and delivery-bike territory, the front clip is the one you actually want.
      - Measure chest girth just behind the front legs and use the manufacturer's size chart, not weight alone.
      - Backup: a simple slip-on mesh harness as a just-in-case for the next 48 hours if the old one is being retired.

    Until the new one is fitted: short leash, busy-street side, no flexi. Treat the next walk as a fit verification, not exercise.

  4. TEXT TO DEVIKA

    Drop-in ready, factual, acknowledges the scare without inventing one or minimizing it:

      "Hey — Kibo's fine. Caught the leash the second the harness slipped, no contact with the bike, no limp, no sore spots when I checked him over. The harness is the issue, not him — it's stretched and the buckle gave under the surprise load. I'm replacing it today with a front-clip fit before his next walk. Wanted you to know before your week kicks in so it's not sitting in your head. Love you."

The harness is the problem (stretched buckle), not him — replacing it today with a front-clip fit before his next walk. Wanted you to know so it's not sitting in your head this week. Love you."

Slightly fuller variant if the card needs the service named:

Shorter alternative that makes the bounded-source framing even more explicit:

Why this beats "No recent deploy activity":

- "No deploy events" is the only thing Lantern can actually assert is absent. It does not say no deploys happened, only that none were recorded from sources Lantern can see.
- "from permissioned sources" bounds the claim to the v0 contract. It is not a claim about the service or the team — just about the slice of the world Lantern can read. A reader who knows the contract lands on "Lantern doesn't see this"; a reader who doesn't lands on "Lantern doesn't see this either."
- "in this window" scopes the claim to the user's filter, so it cannot be read as a global quiet or healthy statement.
- It avoids "no activity" (reads as health), "no recent work" (reads as inactivity), and "broaden the window" framing entirely.

What I deliberately left out:

- No "yet" — Lantern cannot claim future events.
- No "... check the deploy pipeline" — that belongs to a pointer/link on the card, not the empty-state line. Mixing it in turns a one-line claim into a suggestion and re-introduces the false-confidence tone.
- No freshness timestamp inside the copy itself — keep the empty-state line to one clause. The card's existing last-refreshed / last-seen marker stays separate so it can do its freshness job without crowding the absence claim.

Short reply to your note.

The "same button = equivalent rollback" framing is mostly right about the mechanism and wrong about the decision. Three places it overreaches:

1.  The decision to press it. Staging rollback is a clean rehearsal under no pressure. Prod rollback is during an active incident, with imperfect information, and sometimes with the cost of being wrong already accumulating. The button is the smallest part of that risk.

2.  Pre-conditions on what you're rolling back to. The prior version still has to have intact config — label map, downstream consumer acknowledgments, no paired-service asymmetry. Same button still gets you the bad state if rollback target is wrong.

3.  Decision criteria, not post-conditions. The checks (error rate, replay, collector health, smoke test) verify the rollback worked. They don't authorize pressing it. Authorization needs pre-defined symptom + threshold + elapsed-time rules, not improvisation at 2 a.m.

"Same button, same code path" — true and worth keeping. "Therefore first-pass prod rollback is equivalent" — overreach. Treat the decision as out-of-scope for solo until pre-conditions and decision criteria are explicit.

WHY WE'RE OPENING THIS WAY (about 1 minute)

Lantern v0 is in a limited internal audience, and this is the first real round of feedback on the live internal product. Hema asked us to spend ten minutes at the front so the session lands on signal rather than on the boundary. That's the only reason for the intro. It's not a defensive posture -- just a way to use the time well, and to make sure the feedback we get this hour is feedback we can actually act on inside v0.

WHAT LANTERN V0 ACTUALLY SHOWS (about 3 minutes)

Three signal types are in scope for v0: deploy movement, ownership changes, and permission-safe incident-load summaries. That's the whole surface.

Every event carries provenance -- a source_system and an actor. Every card in the UI is traceable back to what system recorded it and who recorded it. If you can't trace a card, that's a bug, and we want to hear about it. If a card is empty because no event exists yet, that's provenance, not UI.

The status model is a small, stable enum on the backend: pending, active, resolved, unknown. There is no `blocked` status on the backend. The `blocked` chip you may see is derived in the UI -- it shows up when an open deploy has passed its expected window, or when an open incident has no matching resolution. It's a permission-safe affordance, not hidden state. The UI reads from a derived read model, not from raw events -- that's the permission boundary in practice, and it's why summaries and raw notes are different surfaces.

The store is append-only. Corrections are new events that reference the prior event's ID. This is why historical ownership transitions render correctly -- we don't backfill or rewrite. The first real owner-map import exposed an actual historical delta instead of just current state, and that's the same mechanism at work.

THREE PATTERNS WE'D LIKE TO HEAD OFF (about 4 minutes)

1. Empty owner cards look like a bug. They aren't. An empty card means we don't yet have a provenanced ownership-change event for that service -- either the source system hasn't emitted one, or the actor wasn't in the v0 import set. It's a provenance signal, not a UI gap. Useful feedback in this category: "I expected to see X for service Y -- can someone trace whether the import actually fired?" Less useful: "why is this card blank?" The blank card is the system telling you something true.

2. Asking for raw incident notes behind the incident-load card. The card is a permission-safe summary because the permissions model hasn't decided who can see raw incident bodies yet. Surfacing raw notes inside v0 would bypass that decision. Useful feedback in this category: "tell me what decision you'd actually make with the raw note, and whether a permissioned summary already covers it." If a summary genuinely doesn't cover a real decision you're trying to make, that's a v1 scope question, not a v0 tweak. We'll collect those.

3. Reading Lantern as readiness scoring. v0 does not tell you whether a service is ready to ship, healthy, or trustworthy. The status enum is operational state from upstream systems -- pending, active, resolved -- not a quality grade. Useful feedback in this category: "does the operational state shown here line up with what I know about this service from elsewhere?" Less useful: asking for an overall "this service looks good" signal. That's a product question, not a data question, and it lives in v1.

HOW TO FILE FEEDBACK IN THIS SESSION (about 1 minute)

In v0 scope: signal clarity, schema fit, provenance traces -- "I expected X and got Y, here's why."
v1 candidates: surface the question, mark it scope expansion, and we'll collect them in a shared doc and revisit when v0 closes.

The omissions are part of the contract. We're not defending them out of rigidity -- any of them can be revisited with evidence, including the ones we just walked through. We just don't want to silently expand scope in the middle of a feedback round, because that turns the signal into noise for everyone in the room.

CLOSE (about 30 seconds)

Two asks. Tell us when the operational state matches what you know. Tell us when it doesn't. Both are useful, and both are exactly what v0 is for. Everything else -- readiness scores, raw incident bodies, code-movement inference -- park it as a v1 candidate and we'll get to it with the rest.

Here are four checks you can run on it yourself. Not a rewrite, and no reason to send anything on to North Pier — just a legibility test:

1. After handoff, who owns the seam? The piece should make it obvious that engineering owns implementation, migration sequencing, and rollout, while design owns semantics, usage rules, and acceptance criteria. If your role blurs into "we shipped it," that's where it starts to sound borrowed.

2. Is engineering a co-owner of the seam, or a downstream recipient? Watch for "we documented and handed off" vs. "we agreed with engineering that…" — the first reads like a deck, the second reads like collaboration. The handoff section is strongest when engineering is in the room while the contract is being defined, not just on the receiving end.

3. Where does design's ownership actually stop? The case study shouldn't claim design ownership of things that are genuinely engineering: deprecation policy, breaking-change mechanics, migration order, rollout sequencing. If any of those sit under your column, either pull them out or reframe them as "the question design raised" rather than "the decision design made."

4. Does it use engineering vocabulary it can't actually back? Words like API contract, schema, versioning, rollout — if they appear without a concrete example of what design owned within them, they read borrowed. Either the example shows what design decided (the semantics, the usage rules, the acceptance bar) or the term should go.

If it passes all four cleanly, it reads legible. If any of them feel borrowed, the answer is usually to tighten, not to add more engineering words.

Cardinality Guardrails — First Control Slice: PR/Review Checklist
================================================================

Scope of this checklist
-----------------------
Three controls, applied to metrics-router and shard-keeper PRs (and any change
that affects what those services emit to downstream consumers):

  A. Label-cardinality preflight
  B. Alert-source classification (live vs replay/mirror)
  C. Rollup-service parity before any label-name or label-semantics change
     crosses a service boundary

This is a first cut, not a mature program. It does not replace the existing
label-change preflight runbook entry; it gives reviewers concrete pass/fail
lines to apply against an open PR.

Non-goals (do not expand the slice inside this checklist)
---------------------------------------------------------
- Not a legacy-aggregator retirement effort. legacy-aggregator stays out of
  production rollback and is retired on a separate evidence basis.
- Not a broad telemetry rewrite. This checklist does not reword existing
  alerts, rename dashboards, or rehome panels.
- No customer-facing dashboard work in this slice.
- No fourth control. The three above are the slice. New controls wait until
  these are clear.
- Cost-model work is advisory only (Cyrus). This checklist does not set
  pricing, enforcement, or a deploy gate on cost.
- This checklist does not define cardinality limits as hard thresholds. It
  flags risky patterns and requires sampling before promotion; it does not
  declare any high-cardinality label forbidden by category.

Framing for reviewers
---------------------
High cardinality alone is not a fail. The preflight fails when a new
high-cardinality pattern is added without being identified, sampled, and
reasoned about. customer_id is high-cardinality and expected; this checklist
does not flag it, and reviewers should not treat it as a fail either.


Control A — Label-cardinality preflight (metrics-router / shard-keeper)
-----------------------------------------------------------------------
[ ] PASS  PR description names every new label key and every change to an
         existing label's value shape (new enum values, new cardinality
         source, changed semantics).
[ ] PASS  For any new label in a flagged risky family — unbounded or
         one-off experiment_id, raw-path route_pattern, noisy joins with
         deployment_sha — the PR attaches a sample distinct-count with the
         window and sample method called out.
[ ] PASS  No raw error_detail (or comparable free-form text) is introduced
         as a label.
[ ] FAIL  PR adds a new label key without identifying it in the description.
[ ] FAIL  PR adds a new label in a risky family without an attached
         distinct-count sample.
[ ] FAIL  PR introduces raw error_detail or similar free-form text as a
         label.

Control B — Alert-source classification (live vs replay/mirror)
---------------------------------------------------------------
[ ] PASS  Every new or modified dashboard panel and alert that surfaces
         metrics-router or shard-keeper data is labeled with its source:
         live, canary, replay, or mirror.
[ ] PASS  Alert text and runbook links distinguish live-path movement from
         replay/mirror movement. "Replay moved" or "mirror moved" is not
         written as if it were a live rollback signal.
[ ] PASS  No "safe to ignore" or equivalent phrasing that collapses the
         live/validation boundary.
[ ] FAIL  A panel or alert can be read as a live rollback trigger when its
         underlying signal is replay or mirror.
[ ] FAIL  Alert text or runbook language treats replay/mirror movement as
         rollback evidence.
[RULE]  Only live-path movement can start a rollback discussion. Replay or

Three signals Theo can read from the narrow PE feedback ring next week. Each one is a behavior to watch for (or against); none require expanding the Lantern surface, opening incident bodies, scoring release readiness, or letting anyone edit owner cards by hand.

1. Provenance — the follow-up goes to the source system, not back to Lantern.
When a PE user looks at a card and wants more, watch where their next question goes. If they click through to the underlying work system (deploy pipeline, owner-map thread, runbook) and ask there, they understand the pointer. If they ask Lantern to surface the underlying event, show a longer history, or add a field the source does not provide, the contract has not landed. The signal is the path of the follow-up, not the volume of clicks.

2. Permission wording — missing detail is attributed to permission, not to a bug.
When a card shows a summary-with-pointer and the underlying notes are not visible, listen to how users describe the gap. The right reading is "I do not have access at the source" or "this is permissioned elsewhere." The wrong reading is "Lantern is missing data" or "this is broken," and the worse reading is asking Lantern to bypass the permission model. The signal is whether users can name the boundary correctly without prompting, and whether their requests for more go to the source-system owner rather than to Lantern.

3. Empty states — empty cards do not generate panicked escalations.
When a card is empty — no recent deploy movement, no recent ownership change, no incident-load summary — users should not treat it as evidence of a problem. They should ask the question that matches the empty state's actual meaning: has there been a deploy in this window; is this service in the owner-map import; is this service in the incident-load summary scope. If empty states trigger escalations to owners or pings to on-call, the wording is being misread as "no data" when it means "no event yet" or "not yet imported" or "out of permissioned scope."

Why these avoid the traps. The first measures whether users use the pointer, not how often they mention Lantern in release review (and it goes red on requests to widen the surface, which is exactly the failure mode Iris's instinct would have rewarded). The second measures whether they read the permission marker, not whether they want raw incident notes surfaced; it goes red on requests to loosen permission wording. The third measures whether they interpret silence correctly, not whether they are filling gaps by hand; it goes red on owner-card overrides and on escalations that the empty-state wording should have prevented. None of the three require new ingestion, new UI affordances, or a wider audience to score.

Verdict on the two options, then the plan.

Bike vs walk, both reasonable if kept easy — neither is wrong, but they're different probes:
  - Easy bike spin (seated, easy gear, ~85-90 rpm, flat, 20-30 min) is the gentler probe. Peak calf load per stroke is small and controllable. The risk is that "easy" drifts: a headwind, a slight rise, dropping a gear, or going out of the saddle all silently turn it into calf work.
  - Flat walk is more grounding but the calf is genuinely loaded every step. The trick is keeping your stride below the lengthened-stride threshold on purpose, not finding it by accident. Duration is also cumulative load — keep it under ~45 min the first time.

I'd do one today, the other tomorrow, not both same day. If you want a single recommendation: bike first (lower peak load, easier to keep sub-symptomatic), walk tomorrow if the bike was clean.

Weekend plan (Sat 10/28 → Sun 10/29)

Sat: skip pickup (already decided, good). Optional easy bike spin, ~20-30 min, seated, easy gear, flat route, no headwind grind. Or skip the spin entirely and just walk Kibo normally — that's also a valid Saturday. Do not stack bike + walk + errands that involve hills or stairs.

Sun (only if Sat was clean, no during/after tightness): flat walk, deliberately shorter stride than feels natural, 30-45 min, no hills, no "let me test the long stride" detours. After: calf should feel like it did this morning, not tighter.

Mon-Tue: rest days, normal life. Reassess Wed/Thu. If mid-week is quiet, you're cleared to think about next steps — not before.

Next weekend (11/4): if the whole week stays sub-symptomatic, one short low-intensity pickup game with a hard stop rule (e.g., one game, off if any tightening, no second game) is reasonable. Still no bouldering on a soccer day.

Week after (11/11-ish): bouldering returns, separate day from any running/soccer, easy problems only first session.

What to avoid until the faint lengthened-stride tightness is gone for a full week
  - Sprinting in any form — soccer sprint, running sprint, dynamic bouldering move
  - Hills, loaded stairs, stair machines
  - Plyometrics, jumping, bounding
  - Overstriding — the symptom you described IS the ceiling; reaching for it is testing, not training
  - "Easy" bouldering this weekend. Even easy problems involve loaded plantarflexion and unpredictable foot positions
  - Two loading sessions in one day
  - Anything that masks the warning signal: deep calf massage, foam rolling the calf aggressively, hot tub before activity, NSAIDs taken pre-activity so you "feel fine"
  - The "it doesn't hurt, so push it" loop. The faint tightness is the signal, not noise

Back-off signals during or after a session — stop, cool down, treat today as a rest day
  - Sharp pain, catch, grab, or "something moved" feeling
  - Tightness that comes on earlier in the session than last time (threshold is shortening)
  - Tightness that doesn't ease within 10-15 min of stopping
  - Gait change — limping, walking flat-footed to spare the calf
  - First-step pain getting out of bed the next morning
  - Visible swelling, warmth, or redness
  - Post-activity soreness that's worse than during-activity discomfort

Escalate-if signals (these are not "back off," they're "get it checked")
  - Sudden sharp pain during a small movement, inability to bear weight
  - Calf swelling that's clearly one-sided and not just post-exercise, especially if it shows up without a clear exertion trigger
  - Tenderness along the back of the calf with warmth, particularly after any period of relative immobility — that's the DVT shape to watch for, not because it's likely here, but because "wait and see" is the wrong call on that one
  - Numbness, tingling, color change in the foot
  - Pain that's trending worse day-over-day across a full week of conservative care, not better

The framing, since you named it: improvement is the bar to be allowed to probe at the next rung down, not clearance to test the current rung. The faint tightness on a lengthened stride is the current ceiling. The plan is to load below it for a week and see if the ceiling moves up on its own — not to poke the ceiling and see if it holds.

WALK TIMING
- Take the main walk at about 4:00 PM — an hour before the trick-or-treat rush starts. You want him tired and emptied out before the hallways get loud, not during.
- Keep it 20-25 minutes, not a long loop. This is decompression, not exercise training. Kibo's already showing reactive edges; you don't need him working through new smells and stimulus tonight.
- Plan a short relief-only outing around 7:15-7:30 if he needs one — two blocks, tree, home. Skip this entirely if he's calm.

ROUTE
- 7th Avenue side, like you've already noted works. Skip the Prospect Park entrances completely — bike + costume + crowd density at the corners is exactly the combo that gets him jumpy.
- Stay off blocks where you know brownstones are doing the big stoop setups with crowds on the stairs. Side streets away from the candy hotspots are quieter even at peak.
- Short leash and front-clip harness the whole walk. You already know that combo resets him quickly after a close pass. Don't extend to the long leash even on the "quiet" blocks tonight.

DOOR AND CANDY SETUP (this is the main lever)
- Put the candy bowl outside the apartment door, not inside. Small table or basket, a "please take one" sign, done. This is the single biggest fix — no doorbell, no door opening, no door-rehearsal barking from Kibo for every group.
- If you want to greet kids, leave the door propped with the chain so you can wave without a full open-and-react cycle. But honestly, the unattended bowl is the whole move.
- Keep Kibo in the back room with a stuffed Kong, a lick mat, or a long-lasting chew starting around 4:30. The point is to give him a settled job during the peak, not a "watch the door" job. If he drifts to the door anyway, redirect quietly and don't scold — you don't want him rehearsing arousal.
- Skip the costume on him. Tonight is not the night. Even a bandana changes his silhouette and the inflatable kids he already spooked at today are exactly the kind of visual his brain is primed to over-read.

WHAT TO SKIP IF THE HALLWAY GETS LOUD
- Skip answering the door at all. The bowl handles it. You don't need to be the host tonight.
- Skip laundry, dishwasher, blender, vacuum. Apartment needs to be quiet for Devika by 7:45 so when she walks in at 8 it's a calm room, not a buzzer-and-machine one.
- Skip a second long walk. A relief-only trip is fine if he really needs it, but don't try to "wear him out" with a longer one — overstimulation reads as more barking, not less.
- Skip group-texting from the stoop. If neighbors are outside, that's fine, but don't linger with Kibo at the front of the building where the foot traffic is thickest.
- Skip TV at high volume to mask the hallway noise. Kibo hears the door better than you do; louder background just adds to his arousal budget. Low light, quiet room, chew in mouth — that's the setup.

If Kibo does bark at the door a few times despite the bowl, don't make it a correction moment. He's going to hear kids yelling in the hall regardless. Just keep him out of sight of the door and let the Kong do its job. By 7:30 most of Park Slope has cleared the rounds, and you should have a quiet apartment waiting for Devika by 8.

Skipping 7v7 is the right call. Sprinting and hard cutting is exactly the acceleration work you haven't tested, and "just filling in" tends to flatten the conservative re-entry you've been running since the 14th.

The "dull tightness with longer stride / thinking about push-off" pattern is residual irritability, almost certainly in the gastrocnemius. Soleus is usually quiet by the time stairs are fine, but the gastroc is more involved in long-length/long-stride work since it crosses both joints. The fact that even *imagining* explosive push-off fires the symptom means the neural readiness for rapid plantarflexion under stretch isn't fully back. Two weekends ago was acute; now it's subacute and load-tolerant for walking and raises. Bouldering can fit in that envelope, but the session has to stay in the "controlled low-grade load" band, not the "explore power" band.

DECISION RULE (pick before you leave the house)
- Go if: warmup is fully quiet, and you commit to the avoid list below without negotiating mid-session.
- Skip if: any tightness in the first 5 min of easy walking warmup, or you can already feel the social pull toward "just one more try."

WARMUP (15-20 min, on-site, before touching a wall)
1. 5 min flat easy walking.
2. 3 x 20 air squats + 3 x 10 lunges, short stride, knee tracking over the toes.
3. Single-leg calf raises, both legs: 2 x 15 easy, then 1 x 8 slow and full ROM on the injured leg. Stop if dull tightness sharpens to a grab.
4. 30 sec passive hang from a jug — calves under stretch, fully unloaded. Diagnostic.
5. 2-3 easy traverses on large feet, no heel hooks, no high reaches. Just checking.

WHAT TO CLIMB
- Vertical to slightly overhanging terrain, foot size at least a quarter pad.
- Static movement only: place foot -> shift weight slowly -> pull with hands.
- Cap at ~3-5 attempts per problem, 4-5 problems, 60 min total on the wall.

WHAT TO AVOID (non-negotiable)
- Dynos, jump moves, any campus-style sequence, drop-offs, rollovers.
- Heel hooks — heavily loads the soleus at end-range.
- Toe hooks, aggressive smears where you're driving off the front of the foot under tension.
- Long lunges or high reaches from a high foot — that stride-lengthening geometry is exactly your symptom.
- "Just one more try" once the tightness returns. It will still be there Tuesday.

STOP SIGNALS — pack it in if any of these show up
- Tightness sharpens to a grab or pinch mid-climb.
- Localized hot spot, swelling, or any limp on the walk back.
- Pain that persists more than 24 hours after the session. Today decides Tuesday; Tuesday decides next week.

SAFER ALTERNATIVE IF YOU SKIP
Top-rope easy routes (if the gym has them) on juggy feet — same social session, no dynamic moves, calves stay in the walking-raise envelope. If you'd rather not climb at all: 30 min easy walk + 2 x 15 single-leg raises + 10 min open-hand hangboarding on a large edge is a "still showed up" dose that keeps rehab moving and lets you hang with your friend without sitting on the bench the whole time. Cleanest substitute, if you don't go at all: 45 min flat walk + the raises.

If the tightness keeps re-surfacing over the next 1-2 weeks, that's worth a real PT eval — recurring gastroc irritability this often is usually a load-management or biomechanics thing, not bad luck.

Reviewing Roman's shape before Cyrus samples it:

The label fails Cardinality Guardrails the same way `error_detail` did. `replay_source_id` is a raw per-source identifier — the replay stream explicitly includes one-off backfills and validation chunks, so the value space is effectively unbounded. Putting it on a counter is the same anti-pattern as putting raw error strings on a metric: bounded label families only, or the metric becomes a cardinality sink and a slow dashboard.

The debugging need is real, but it doesn't justify unbounded labels. Two paths that preserve the need:

Option A — bounded source-class label, raw ID in logs.
  Replace `replay_source_id` with a small fixed enum that reflects what the
  source actually IS, not which specific source instance produced this run.
  Concretely:
    replay_source_class = "nightly_replay"
                        | "manual_backfill"
                        | "validation_chunk"
                        | "mirror_continuous"
                        | "fixture_replay"
  On mismatch, also emit a structured log carrying the raw `replay_source_id`
  plus `replay_run_id` and the window timestamp. Dashboards group by class;
  the actual source ID lives in logs, joinable by `replay_run_id` or the
  minute bucket. This mirrors the live/replay/mirror split we just locked
  for dashboards — bounded on the metric, raw detail where the data system
  can carry it.

Option B — no label, raw ID only in the mismatch log line.
  Keep the existing counter (`validation_result="match|mismatch"`) as-is.
  On mismatch, the structured log line carries `replay_source_id`. Dashboards
  group by `validation_result`. Log search resolves "which source produced
  this." No metric cardinality cost, no preflight needed, no alert-semantics
  change. This is the right answer if source-class breakdown doesn't earn
  its keep on a dashboard.

Explicit checks required before this lands, regardless of which option:

  1. Cardinality preflight on the current shape. A real count of distinct
     `replay_source_id` values over a representative window — at least a
     week, and it must include any one-off backfills and validation chunks
     that ran in that window. The proposed shape fails review if the count
     is unbounded or visibly growing. This is the preflight rule, applied
     to rollup-service here the same way it applies to metrics-router and
     shard-keeper.

  2. Rollup-service parity BEFORE sampling. The label crosses service
     boundaries — rollup-service emits it, dashboards consume it. The name
     and semantics have to be agreed on the consumer side first. A green
     metrics-router or rollup-service canary does not substitute for that
     check; it's the same rule we wrote into the label-parity guidance.

  3. Replay/mirror classification in alerts and dashboards. This metric is
     validation-only, not live. Dashboards and alert text must continue to
     treat `validation_result` mismatches as investigation evidence and Q4
     controls input, not as rollback criteria. The label change cannot be
     allowed to make a validation mismatch look like a live signal on a
     panel.

  4. Bounded enum, not free text. Whatever enum replaces the raw ID, every
     value must be defined up front. No `other` / `unknown` bucket that
     quietly grows. If a new source class shows up, it gets added to the
     enum deliberately, not by emission.

Iris's read is right. An AI digest of the raw incident note is still raw-note-derived — same boundary applies. The reason isn't about form (raw text vs. prose summary), it's about where the incident content lives and whose eyes are supposed to be on it.

The distinction that already exists in the Lantern contract is useful here:

- In scope (v0): service-level incident-load summaries. Aggregate signals — "service X had N Sev3 in the last 7d" — permission-safe by construction. No incident-specific content, no names, no narrative.
- Out of scope (v0): anything derived from the content of a specific incident note, including an AI digest of that note. The underlying incident content lives in the incident tracker with role-based visibility, and any representation of that content inherits the same scope. A digest isn't permission-laundered by being shorter.

Two extra reasons an AI digest specifically is a bad fit for v0, even setting aside the permission question:

1. Provenance drift. A digest is generated text that paraphrases the source. The audit chain now has to cover "did the digest accurately represent what the on-call actually saw?" That's an editorial liability Lantern shouldn't pick up.
2. Boundary creep. Once a digest is allowed, the question becomes how much: five bullets, one sentence, just keywords, named systems, named people. That spectrum slowly re-introduces the raw surface in a form that's harder to police than the original.

The constructive path Iris can offer:

- Improve the pointer language on the incident-load card so the click-through lands somewhere useful in the source system in one hop. That's a real fix to the "save people from clicking" friction and it's the right place for it.
- If digests become a real need later, the source system produces a permissioned digest as a first-class artifact (its own visibility settings, its own provenance), and Lantern ingests that as a bounded typed event. The digest has to be created where the permissions live, not generated inside Lantern.

Quick read on the signal
  Faint pull on a quickly lengthened stride = end-range / lengthened-position reactivity under quick load.
  Short lever, moderate load, slow tempo = probably fine.
  Long lever, sudden load, fast tempo = the stuff that still talks back.

Warmup is the decision gate. Do these in order; stop and call it at the first one that doesn't pass.
  1.  5 min easy walking / step-ups, easy pace.
  2.  Slow walking lunges with a long stride, both sides, just to end-range. No bounce. Stretch, not pull.
  3.  Single-leg calf raises, slow, both sides. 15 reps each, full ROM. Any grab = skip.
  4.  10 min of easy traversing or a V0/V1 jog on a juggy warmup wall. Literally just moving, not "trying problems."

  Green = all four clean and the calf feels like yesterday's walk.
  Yellow = mild tightness in steps 2-4 that doesn't get worse. Don't climb. Walk or spin instead.
  Red = any sharp pain, grab, swelling, or anything that doesn't match yesterday. Skip.

If green, conservative session
  Grade ceiling: V2. If you're asking whether a problem is V2, it's not V2.
  Holds: jugs and big edges only. Fingertip pulls to stay on = off.
  Tempo: static. Feet, then hands, then move. No momentum, no campus sequencing.
  Leg position: bent knee where you can. Don't lock out a standing leg at full extension for long.
  Feet: smears and flat edges. No standing on tiny sharp footholds that put the heel high.
  Between problems: sit down, shake out the calves, drink water. Don't keep the calf loaded while you rest.

Moves to avoid (explicit)
  - Dynos. None, regardless of size.
  - Hard heel hooks. If a problem needs one to fix a barn door, walk off.
  - Repeated jump-downs. Downclimb or step down every time. One or two controlled drops at the very end of the session, max.
  - Any move where the back foot is the only thing keeping you on and has to push explosively.
  - Long reaches from low feet (long lever into the calf).
  - Sprinting anywhere — across the gym, onto the mat, between problems.
  - "One more try" once a problem starts requiring any of the above.

Hard stop conditions
  - Sharp or sudden pain anywhere in the calf.
  - The "faint pull" gets louder, sharper, or more localized.
  - Pain or weakness on a single-leg calf raise at any point mid-session.
  - Any swelling, hot spot, or "something is wrong" gut signal.
  - Limping on the walk out, even subtly.
  - Three problems in and the calf feels different from how it started. Cumulative load counts too.

Soft caps (regardless of how it feels)
  - 60 minutes total in the gym.
  - 6-8 problems, max. Fewer problems with longer rest beats more problems chained together.
  - No "one more for the send" once you've hit the cap. The send isn't worth it today.

Safer alternative if you skip
  Option A (best for today): easy flat walk, 30-45 min, Prospect Park loop or similar. Brisk enough to feel like a session, no quick stride changes, no hills. Gets you out of the apartment so Devika's recovery day stays quiet.
  Option B: easy bike spin on the flat, 20-30 min, easy gear, no standing climbs. Zero eccentric load on the calf.
  Option C: mobility work and a slow walk with Kibo. Treat the calf as the test, not the activity.

Frame for your friend and for yourself
  "Easy session" only works if easy is what actually happens. If the warmup isn't clean, the line is "I came out, but my calf isn't actually ready — going to walk instead." Climbers hear this all the time; it doesn't have to be weird.
  "Better than last weekend" and "ready for heel hooks and dynos" are different thresholds. Improvement is data, not a green light.

Thanks for surfacing this in the planning room — we want Lantern to stay useful here, and we want to be specific about why a manager-or-chain rollup is not in v0.

The incident-load and deploy-movement cards aggregate by service. That is the dimension the incident source emits, the dimension the v0 read model groups on, and the unit the permission boundary covers. There is no manager or management-chain field on the incident event, on the deploy-movement event, or on the ownership-provenance record. To produce the rollup you are describing, we would have to change at least one of three things, each of which is out of v0 scope for a structural reason:

1. Schema. Add a manager or chain key to incident events, or build a derived join in the read model against a separate people or owner-map source. The v0 envelope deliberately keeps the event set narrow — deploy movement, ownership changes, bounded incident-load summaries — so Lantern is not maintaining a second attribution pipeline. Code-movement inference was excluded from v0 for the same reason, and a manager rollup would reintroduce that cost under a different name.

2. Source-of-truth. Manager identity does not live in the incident source. Pulling it in from owner-map means Lantern is responsible for keeping a people-to-service join current, and any drift in that join shows up as incorrect incident attribution in a planning room.

3. Permissions. A service-level incident-load summary is scoped to the audience that can already see that service's operational state. A manager rollup exposes incident volume attributable to specific people to viewers who do not necessarily hold that permission. That is a different permission profile, and v0 does not cover it.

What v0 does give the planning room, today: each card carries its service and an ownership-provenance pointer — owner, last owner change, source_system, actor. The cards stay observed operational signals anchored to services, ownership provenance, and system state. From that you can read which service is in scope, who owns it, and what its operational posture looks like. The unit of analysis stays the service and the system state, not a person or a chain. If a manager-level view becomes a real Product Engineering need, that is a separate proposal — new source, new permissions review, new contract pass — and we can scope it as such rather than folding it into v0.

— Alex & Iris

A live reference, for this gate, is anything that could route traffic to legacy-aggregator from the live metrics-router path or the rollup-service read path, or that a responder under pressure could reasonably read as a current operational signal from legacy-aggregator. Concretely: routing predicates, consumer configs, dashboard panels labeled as production traffic, alert definitions or alert text, and runbook steps that say "do X against legacy-aggregator" without an explicit "mirror/replay only" qualifier.

Stale annotations are a different category. A comment in retired code, a dashboard panel that hasn't been touched since the cut, a note buried in a deprecated alert description — these don't create reintroduction risk on their own because nothing reads them as authoritative at runtime. The name appearing in a search hit is not the same as the name being on a live path.

That said, I don't want this gate to degrade into "search returned nothing scary." Two reasons:

1. The bar the criteria set is *no* live references — meaning none of the things in the first list above, even an unintentional one. A responder under pressure who reads an untagged stale annotation as a hint that legacy-aggregator is still authoritative is exactly the reintroduction risk the gate is meant to close. We've been here before with the paired rollback footnote on the rollup-service fallback read.
2. Cleanup or explicit tagging is part of the same hygiene that lets us stand behind "live references absent" later. If we accept the gate against a codebase full of ambiguous mentions, the next reviewer has to redo the judgment work from scratch, and the next responder has no signal that the mention is stale.

Proposed path for these two: delete the ones that are easy to delete (drop the comment, retire the panel, prune the description). For anything worth keeping as historical context, tag it in place — something like "historical reference; legacy-aggregator is not in the live path, mirrored writes and replay validation only" — so a future reader can't mistake it for an active instruction.

Once both are either gone or explicitly tagged, the gate holds. If either turns out to actually be reading from a live path when you look closer, that's a different finding and I'd want it back before we close the criteria discussion.

Plan for Kibo's front paw tonight and tomorrow morning.

Quick frame: this is common-sense dog first aid, not a diagnosis. The job is (a) to confirm the rinse already handled a salt/grit issue, and (b) to catch a real injury early without turning the apartment into an ER.

Tonight, under good light (bathroom or a desk lamp):

  - Lift the paw and look at the pad, between every toe, and around the nail bed on all four feet. Asymmetry matters: salt irritation usually hits all four paws; a single-paw focus suggests a foreign body, cut, or bruise on that one.
  - Look specifically for a small cut or puncture, a cracked or torn nail, a swollen single toe, a dark or blistered pad, salt crusted between toes, or a stone or ice ball lodged in a pad fold.
  - Gently palpate the paw and lower leg. A flinch, snap, or withdrawal is a pain signal, not drama.
  - Watch him walk a few steps on a flat floor. Note any head bob, shortened stride, toe-touching only, or weight shift off that paw.
  - A second lukewarm rinse to dissolve any remaining salt, then pat dry. Don't rub.
  - If he licks again tonight, a light sock wrap or an e-collar can break the cycle, but only after you've actually inspected. Licking that gets more frantic rather than less is itself a signal.

Tonight's house rules: avoid stairs if you can, keep the walk short, don't repeat the park route.

Tomorrow morning:

  - Re-inspect before the walk. Any of the above findings worse than tonight = vet call.
  - Apply Musher's wax or paw balm to pads and between toes before going out. Boots only if he's used to them; a first-time boot walk in December is its own problem.
  - Route: stay on the less-treated side streets near the park, or shorten the walk. Avoid the freshest grit.
  - Post-walk rinse and pat-dry becomes the routine for the cold snap.
  - Re-check gait before and after the walk on a flat surface.

Clear signs that justify a vet call (any one is enough):

  - A visible limp that persists after rest: head bob, toe-touching, refusal to bear weight.
  - A cut, puncture, or bleeding that doesn't stop with gentle pressure within a few minutes.
  - A single swollen toe or pad that's visibly larger or warmer than the others.
  - A torn, cracked, or loose nail, or any exposed quick.
  - A pad that looks discolored (deep red, purple, black) or blistered.
  - Pain on gentle palpation: flinch, growl, snap, withdrawal.
  - Licking that escalates or becomes frantic despite rinsing.
  - Lameness still present tomorrow morning after a night of rest.
  - Behavior change: off food, reluctance to move, panting at rest, hiding.

What's probably fine and does not need a vet tonight, as long as the above stay absent: symmetric salt irritation across all paws, mild intermittent licking that responds to rinsing and paw balm, no limp, no swelling, normal behavior. That profile matches what you've described so far, and the rinse was the right first move.

If anything in the vet-call list shows up, call. Your judgment, not a checklist, is the threshold. If you're stuck between "wait" and "go," a quick phone call to your regular vet is cheap and faster than guessing.

Slide 3 — Four readiness dimensions

- Scope clarity — does everyone agree on what's in/out of this cut?
- Asset readiness — what does each side actually have, what's still missing?
- Decision ownership — who decides when to move, and on what signal?
- Blocker visibility — what's still in the way, named honestly?

- Engineering owns: implementation approach, technical sequencing, code-level decisions
