Tomorrow plan — left calf, Sunday bouldering

Note up front: flat-walking tolerance is not bouldering clearance. Walking tests slow concentric/eccentric load. Bouldering tests quick push-off, dynamic catch, awkward landings, and controlled drops — none of which you have a clean read on yet. So this is a yes-but-very-bounded plan, not a green light.

RECOMMENDED DEFAULT: skip or arrive late and downgrade to traverse-only. If you go, treat it as a probe, not a session.

1. Morning check (in apartment, before you commit to going)
   - Single-leg calf raises on the floor, slow, 10 reps each side. No sharp sensation, no grabbing.
   - 6–8 small two-foot hops in place. Any calf grab or hesitation = skip.
   - One bodyweight step-down off the bottom stair on the left. Clean = continue. Any tightness = skip.
   - Walk to subway at normal pace. If anything in that 10–15 min walk reminds you the calf is there, downgrade or skip before you arrive.

2. At the gym, before any rope/wall
   - 8–10 min easy traverse, flat feet, no heel hooks, no high left steps.
   - On the warmup wall, one easy low-percentage route (V0-ish, jugs). Stop after the route, not after a number of moves.
   - First downclimb off any wall = a proper downclimb hold, not a drop. If the downclimb feels sketchy, the answer for the day is "downclimb clean, no jumping down."

3. Probe question (one and only one)
   - On the first easy route, take one quick push-off with the left on a defined foot, low height, controlled. If it produces any pull, tightness, or a moment of doubt — done for the day, traverse-only or leave.

4. Routes to avoid today, no exceptions
   - Dynos. Any reach where missing means a sudden load.
   - Heel hooks.
   - High left foot steps or any move that loads the left calf in a stretched position.
   - Slopey/smeary feet where a slip equals surprise load.
   - Long tension moves where a fall would be uncontrolled.
   - Jumping down from anything taller than ~1 m. Today is feet-down controlled, or you don't do it.
   - Awkward downclimbs. Use the proper downclimb wall only.

5. Hard caps if you climb
   - Total: 3 problems maximum, all sub-max.
   - Total time on wall: ~30 min. Then leave even if you feel fine.
   - No second attempt on anything. First try is the only data point you need.

6. Stop conditions (any one = done for the day, no debate)
   - Any sharp calf sensation, even a flicker.
   - Tightening during a route that doesn't loosen within one minute of rest.
   - Calf awareness that wasn't there at the start of the session.
   - Hesitation or distrust on a downclimb or push-off.
   - A stumble, slip, or jump-down that loads the calf unexpectedly.
   - Anything you find yourself "pushing through." That is not a data point, that is a warning.

7. What a clean day looks like (so you don't misremember later)
   - Morning check clean, warmup clean, one push-off probe clean, 2–3 easy problems, no jumps, no dynos, calf feels the same at the end as at the start. That is a "calf tolerated easy bouldering," not "calf cleared." Write that down mentally before you leave so next weekend's memory is honest.

Kibo acting normal right now is the most reassuring fact you have. A 1-2 inch piece of curling ribbon in a dog who is eating, drinking, and behaving normally is not a panic scenario — it's a measured-watch scenario. But string-like objects are their own category for a real reason: a linear object can anchor at one end (often under the tongue, around a tooth, or at the pylorus) while the intestine tries to advance the rest, which can plicate and eventually compromise the bowel wall. So a watch window matters, and the timing is on your side right now.

Two framings worth holding at once:
  - Most small linear pieces pass without incident.
  - The window where a vet can intervene cheaply — before obstruction or perforation — is exactly the window you're in now.

If you do one thing in the next hour, make it a phone call to your regular vet or an urgent-care vet describing what happened and asking whether they want to see him today. Many will say "watch at home" if the exam is clean, but some will want an X-ray now because linear objects don't always read clearly on a plain film and barium contrast or ultrasound changes the picture. That's a triage call, not an escalation. If your regular vet is closed for the holiday weekend, the nearest 24-hour ER or ASPCA Animal Poison Control (888-426-4435; fee may apply) can do the same triage over the phone.

Practical 24-48 hour watch plan:

Things to actively watch for — these are the signals that matter:
  - Vomiting more than once, especially repeated episodes over a few hours. One isolated vomit is a yellow flag, not a red one.
  - Repeated retching or gagging that produces nothing, or the classic "prayer position" — front end down, back end up, unable to settle. That posture is an acute-abdomen signal and is urgent.
  - New or excessive drooling — can mean something is caught in the esophagus or at the back of the mouth.
  - Refusing or being slow about his next meal when he's normally enthusiastic.
  - Tender or tense belly. A calm hand rested on his abdomen should be tolerated. Flinching, guarding, or a hard belly is a signal.
  - Stool changes: black tarry stool (digested blood), bright red blood, or no stool at all for 24+ hours when he normally poops regularly.
  - Lethargy that goes past "tired after a walk" into "won't get up, won't engage with you."
  - Gums: pink and moist is normal. Pale, tacky, or grey is urgent.
  - Any piece of ribbon visible at the mouth or the rectum.

One useful at-home exam you can do calmly once, today: lift his lips and look along the gumline and around the upper molars, and gently lift the tongue to look underneath near the base. If a ribbon end is caught on a tooth or tucked under the tongue, you'll sometimes see it. If you do — don't pull. Cut it short and go to the vet.

What not to do (these matter specifically with linear objects):
  - Don't induce vomiting. A linear object anchored anywhere along the GI tract can tear tissue on the way back up. This is the single most important "don't."
  - Don't pull on a visible ribbon end from either direction. Cut it short at the mouth or rectum and go in.
  - Don't give a laxative, mineral oil, or hydrogen peroxide without the vet's say-so.
  - Don't change his diet. Don't withhold food. Don't bulk him up with bread or pumpkin on your own initiative — those are reasonable ideas in some linear-object cases but they should be the vet's call, not yours at 10 a.m. on a holiday morning.
  - Don't re-examine him every 20 minutes. That elevates his stress and yours. Two or three calm check-ins through the day is plenty — eating, drinking, a relaxed belly, normal posture.

Things that are actually fine and worth knowing:
  - Normal eating and drinking tonight is reassuring.
  - Walking normally and engaging normally is reassuring.
  - One normal bowel movement that contains the ribbon is the cleanest resolution. Pick up after him for the next ~48 hours and look carefully through the stool — a damp red ribbon against a brown background is easy to miss. Gloves and a quick visual scan, not a forensic exercise.
  - He may pass it overnight without you ever seeing it. That's a common outcome.

Phone numbers worth having ready in case the day shifts:
  - Your regular vet's after-hours line (most route to an ER partner on the message).
  - The nearest 24-hour ER — worth knowing the drive time tonight, not tomorrow morning.
  - ASPCA Animal Poison Control: 888-426-4435. They triage foreign-body calls regularly and can tell you whether tonight needs an exam or a watch.

The summary version: phone call now, calm watch through the next 48 hours, stool checks, call back or go in if any of the signals above show up. You're not in a panic scenario. You're in a timing-on-your-side scenario, and the main job today is to keep the timing on your side.

APARTMENT SETUP (next 20–30 min)
  - Close windows and curtains in any room where bangs or flashes are reaching him. He is already telling you the window is the bad room — respect that.
  - Pick a "den" room: interior bathroom, the back of the hallway, or the spot behind the couch farthest from exterior walls. Put his bed, water bowl, and a worn t-shirt (yours or Devika's) there. Soft, enclosed, smells like you.

  - Yes: do one trip now, while the early bangs are still short and the gaps are long. On-leash, short loop, no park or open lot.

  - One good walk now buys you a much quieter night than a heroic midnight outing during peak bangs.

WHAT TO AVOID
  - Do not drag him to the window to "show him it's nothing." It isn't nothing to him.
  - Do not hover or over-comfort — fussing rewards the panic. Calm presence, treats tossed away from the window (you already know this works), normal voice.

  - Do not let your own tension spike — he reads you. Slow exhale, low voice, normal movements.

ESCALATION SIGNS (these are vet/ER territory, not noise anxiety)
  - Repeated vomiting or retching — not just a single spit-up
  - Heavy drooling that's clearly different from panting
  - Pale, grey, or tacky gums
  - Collapse, wobbly gait, or sudden weakness
  - Bloating or hard abdomen

The 6-worker result is a clear signal at that worker count, but it's one data point on two curves you actually care about: runtime scaling and memory scaling. Both could be linear, sublinear, or cliff-shaped. The 28s gain tells you the speedup slope is shallow; the memory blowout tells you the ceiling is somewhere ≤ 6 workers. Neither tells you whether 4 workers is a clean fit or a tight one.

Worth running 4 if:
- You're genuinely uncertain whether 2→4 is operationally viable as a permanent default, not just whether the experiment is interesting.
- The benchmark is cheap relative to making the wrong call on a long-lived production setting. One more replay run is much cheaper than discovering six months from now that 4 workers would have been a clean 15s win and you walked away from it.
- You can pre-commit to: a 4-worker memory blowout = drop the experiment. Don't let "let's also try 5" become the next ask.

Worth stopping at 6 if:
- The absolute baseline at 2 workers is short enough that 28s isn't material — in which case 4 workers likely isn't either, and you're just gathering a data point to delay closing out a question that's already answered.
- "Tuning has no value" is your working conclusion and the 4-worker run would just make the experiment feel more real (which is exactly the dynamic that turns one-off probes into inherited defaults).

One thing the 6-worker number doesn't tell you is how much of the 28s you'd lose going from 6→4. If speedup is roughly linear in worker count, 4 workers gives you ~19s and 6 workers gives you 28s — most of the gain is already captured below 6. If speedup is sublinear (which is typical when workers contend for shared resources like the compactor's I/O or the storage layer), 4 workers might capture most of the 28s anyway. Either way, the speedup at 4 is going to be smaller than 28s, not larger. So the question collapses to: is there a workers count between 2 and 6 that fits memory with a speedup worth the operational complexity of changing the production default? That's exactly what the 4-worker run answers.

Two things would sharpen the call:
- Absolute baseline time at 2 workers. "28s only" reads very differently if the baseline is 3 minutes vs 30 minutes.
- Where 6 workers landed vs the memory budget. "Blew past" could mean 10% over or 2x over. If 6 was 10% over, 4 likely fits cleanly. If 6 was 2x over, 4 might still be tight and not obviously safer than the existing config.

If you do run it, set the decision criteria before Roman kicks it off — what speedup at what memory utilization actually justifies taking 4 workers to staging and prod validation, and what combination means drop the experiment on the spot. Otherwise the 4-worker result becomes "interesting data" instead of a verdict, and the experiment stays open another week.

The 6-worker run fails the budget.

  Peak memory 86% vs 75% ceiling — over by 11 points.
  Completion 14m12s vs 14m40s — 28s saved, about 3.2%.
  No correctness or starvation failures in either run.

  Budget is a guardrail, not a target. The proposed experiment violates it and shouldn't be promoted on these numbers. Clean correctness and starvation don't rescue a memory-budget miss.

  If a real speedup is the goal, the next useful run is somewhere between 2 and 6 workers. The curve from (2, 68%) to (6, 86%) is roughly 4.5 points per worker, so 3 or 4 is the interesting range to probe. Linear guess, not a measurement — the actual scaling depends on per-worker buffers and GC, which the two given points don't pin down.

Short version: yes, run one four-worker comparison — but frame it as the closing data point, not the start of a sweep. The pre-commit on the bar is the whole point.

The four-worker run is worth it because two workers (current baseline) and six workers (failed memory) don't tell you whether a middle-ground worker count recovers most of the 28s without blowing memory. Four sits between them; it's the right closing point. If four fails the bar, the curve has no viable middle, and "tuning has no value" is the actual answer — which is still a useful answer.

What justifies changing the baseline:

What does NOT justify changing the baseline:

  - Smaller speedup (<14s)
  - Single-run numbers without reproducibility

The shape of "I see my batch twice" looks like a data-duplication symptom, but the pieces you have describe a duplicated batch attempt, not duplicated stored data. The two things can be told apart from what you've already checked.

What each piece of evidence does and doesn't establish:

- Two rows in the received-batches panel: two batch attempts, not two stored batches. The panel counts attempts, so a retried batch produces a second row by design. The panel alone says nothing about storage.

- First attempt reached upstream write acknowledgement before the client saw the 504: the upstream ack arrived back at the server before the server's response reached the client. That's consistent with the upstream write having landed; it doesn't by itself prove durable commit, but combined with the dedup behavior below it fits a write-then-late-failure pattern rather than a write-that-failed.

- Retry hit dedup and accepted zero new points: this is the load-bearing signal. When the retried batch arrived, the dedup layer recognized it and rejected it as already-known. Zero new points accepted on the retry means the retry did not write a second copy.

- Stored-point check at sampled timestamps shows one point per timestamp: a sample, not an enumeration. With the dedup result above, the sample is consistent with no duplication in storage at the timestamps you checked.

So what's duplicated is the attempt (which the panel is designed to show), not the stored data (which dedup prevented and which the sample is consistent with). The 504 caused an unnecessary retry; the retry was correctly absorbed.

What the evidence does NOT support, and shouldn't be claimed without further checking:

- That every timestamp in the batch — not just the sampled ones — is exactly one point. The sample supports "no observed duplication at sampled timestamps"; it doesn't establish "no duplication anywhere in the batch."
- That the 504's root cause isn't worth investigating. The retry path absorbed this incident correctly, but the underlying 504 is a separate question about the write response path.
- Anything about other batches, other tenants, or other time windows.

If support or the customer needs a stronger statement than "no observed duplication at sampled timestamps," the next step is a full point enumeration over the batch's actual timestamp range — not a different reading of the same evidence.

No — the points were not stored twice. The "2" in the received-batches panel reflects ingress attempts, not stored batches. Three lines of evidence agree:

1. Attempt 1 (10:14:02): upstream_write_ack=true, client_status=504. The upstream accepted the write, but the client saw a timeout, so it retried. Classic at-least-once delivery — the client can't tell from a 504 whether the write actually landed.

2. Attempt 2 (10:14:09): dedup_result=duplicate, accepted_points=0. Server-side dedup caught the retry and stored nothing new. The second attempt is a no-op for storage.

3. Stored-point samples for the three timestamps in the batch (10:13:00, 10:13:10, 10:13:20) each show count=1. If points had been double-stored, those counts would be 2.

The system behaved correctly. The customer-facing confusion is a naming issue: "received-batches" is per its definition an attempt counter, so "2 = two batches stored" is a reasonable but wrong read. Two things worth raising with whoever owns the panel:

  - A tooltip or clarifier on the panel header noting it counts ingress attempts (including retried attempts) and is not an accepted-points metric.
  - Pointing the customer at the accepted-points panel, which for b-771 will show accepted_points=1 from attempt 1, and 0 from attempt 2.

Suggested customer reply:

  "No — your points were stored exactly once. The received-batches panel shows 2 because it counts every time the batch reached our edge, including the retry you sent after the 504. Our dedup caught the duplicate on the retry and stored nothing from it. The authoritative count for batch b-771 is in the accepted-points panel: 1 point accepted, 0 from the duplicate. No double storage occurred."

Evidence

  - First batch attempt reached upstream write acknowledgement before the client received the 504, so the original batch was actually accepted.
  - The client's retry was deduplicated server-side; it accepted zero new points.
  - The received-batches panel counts batch ATTEMPTS, not stored/accepted points. A retried batch showing twice there is expected, not evidence of duplicate storage.
  - Spot-check of stored data at sampled timestamps in the affected window: one stored point per timestamp, no duplicates.

The first attempt was acknowledged upstream before the client received the 504, so when the client retried the batch, our server-side deduplication recognized the points and accepted zero new ones. The received-batches panel counts batch attempts, not stored points, which is why a retried batch can show twice there even when nothing was stored twice.

Concretely: the row count for that window should equal the unique-timestamp count of the original batch, not double it. If they see one value per timestamp matching their original batch, there are no duplicates despite the panel showing two attempts.

Scope: local fixture endpoint only. Production is unaffected; do not extend this checklist to prod trust stores.

 3. Install the new managed root. Add `Sphere Dev Root 2024` to the local keychain via the managed install path (not by downloading from the endpoint on first contact and not by importing whatever the client just presented).
 4. VERIFICATION CHECKPOINT — required before removing the old root:
    a. Confirm `Sphere Dev Root 2024` is present in the keychain and marked trusted.
    b. Confirm the fixture endpoint's presented chain validates against the new root.
    c. Confirm a fixture pull succeeds with the new root installed and the old root still present.
    Only proceed to step 5 if all three pass. If any fails, stop. Do not remove `Sphere Dev Root 2023`; the snapshot in step 2 is still your working state.
 5. WARNING — do not disable TLS checks. Do not pass `--insecure` / `-k` / `NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0` or equivalent. Do not add a permanent trust exception for the endpoint hostname. Do not skip certificate verification in the client, proxy, or container. The new root is the fix; bypassing verification is not.
 6. Remove `Sphere Dev Root 2023` from the local keychain. This step is gated on step 4 passing. Removing the old root before verification is what creates an unrecoverable state if the new root turns out to be wrong.
 7. Restart Docker so daemons and any in-process TLS caches pick up the updated trust store.
 8. Run `sphere-dev doctor` and confirm it reports a clean trust state with no certificate warnings.
 9. Final confirmation: re-run the fixture pull. Expect success, no certificate warning, and no TLS-bypass flag in effect.

Drop-in review comment:

The `quantile="0.99"` series is a summary computed per-instance from that instance's own observations, so each value reflects only that instance's distribution. `avg by (route)` then averages N independent quantiles, and quantiles are not linear — the mean of N per-instance p99s is not the p99 of the combined fleet. Concrete failure mode: one instance with a single slow outlier reports a high per-instance p99 that doesn't represent 1% of total fleet traffic; averaging its p99 with the rest of the fleet gives a number that matches neither the per-instance p99 nor the fleet p99. metrics-router also emits the histogram form (`_bucket` series with `le` labels) carrying the raw cumulative bucket counts. Summing the bucket rates across instances first, then running `histogram_quantile`, computes the p99 over the combined observations — which is what the panel is trying to show. This is a panel-query correction only; alert thresholds and rule definitions are unchanged.

Thresholds for the full-jitter [0, 2s] rerun vs. the fixed-1s sawtooth baseline (100 simulated clients, single injected 503):

Smoothing (must improve):
- Peak concurrent retries ≤ 50% of the fixed-1s sawtooth peak. Baseline stacks ~100 clients into one second; jitter should spread peak across [0, 2s] and drop it to ≤50 in any 100ms window.
- Peak / mean concurrent retry ratio ≤ 2.0. Catches residual clustering that the absolute number can miss.

Completion-time (allow modest regression, block big):
- Staging p99 completion time (request → accepted) ≤ 1.3x the fixed-1s baseline p99. Absorbs clients landing near the 2s ceiling.
- Mean completion time ≤ 1.1x baseline. Past 10% means jitter is shifting load, not just spreading it.

Hard zero (no negotiation):
- Dropped points = 0.
- Duplicate-accepted points = 0. Idempotency must hold across the retry.

Fail conditions, not just missed thresholds:
- Peak retries didn't drop below baseline → experiment didn't demonstrate smoothing; treat as inconclusive, not a pass.
- Any retry attempt with gap > 2.0s → jitter ceiling wasn't enforced; fix config before rerun.
- Dropped or duplicate-accepted > 0 → hard fail regardless of how good the smoothing looks.

Read. Quick take:

The 94/100 peak concurrency and the one-second sawtooth are the same artifact — fixed delay synchronizes every retry onto the same wall-clock tick. Full jitter [0, 2s] will break the synchronization; that's well-trodden (AWS exponential-backoff post, etc.). Mean delay stays at 1s, so average time-to-eventual-success is unchanged. What changes is variance and peak concurrency. Math: with uniform [0, 2s], expected retry rate is ~50/s, so any 100ms slice sees ~5 retries instead of 94. Peak should drop roughly an order of magnitude; sawtooth should be gone.

Before approving the rerun, three things I'd pin down first so the report doesn't pick its own goalposts:

1. **Pre-register success criteria.** Concretely: peak concurrent retries < ~15 (rough order-of-magnitude target, not a hard SLA). Sawtooth pattern absent. Dropped points = 0, duplicate-accepted points = 0 (invariant, not a goal). p99 I'd *not* pre-commit on — direction is genuinely uncertain because some clients will draw near-zero delays and re-hit the 503 storm before downstream recovers. Report it, don't promise it.

2. **Worst-case delay doubles.** A client drawing near 2s waits 2x as long as today. Worth a quick check that no client-side timeout on this path sits near 1.5s. If there's anything tight, full jitter changes the failure mode even though it doesn't change the mean.

3. **Is this a one-shot retry, or does the client retry again on a second 503?** If one-shot, full jitter [0, 2s] is fine as stated. If multi-shot, the policy needs to be specified per attempt. Equal jitter (`base/2 + random(0, base/2)`) would keep a 1s floor on every attempt and eliminate the near-zero re-hit case — at the cost of somewhat weaker de-synchronization. Worth asking Wes which behavior the client actually has.

Things worth reporting from the rerun even if they go right:

- 503 rate over time — does it clear on first retry, or do we see clients needing multiple attempts?
- First-retry success rate — under fixed 1s, everyone retries after downstream recovery; under full jitter [0,2s], they're spread across the recovery window.
- Worst observed retry delay — confirm the cap is near 2s and not higher.
- Retry-log volume vs. the 1s-fixed baseline. Yuki's adjacent-staging work earlier showed ~27-29% reduction just from config tightening; this is a different mechanism but a useful comparison number.

The 0 dropped / 0 duplicate-accepted on the current run is a good baseline — it tells me the dedup path is real and working, which is the main reason jitter is low-risk here. Jitter changes timing, not semantics, so duplicates should still be 0.

Platform Systems Interview Rubric
Multi-Tenant Metrics Ingestion Under Bursty Load
45 minutes total

Opening (5 min)
  Hand the prompt verbatim. Do not add framing. Listen for what they
  ask before they draw.
    Strong: surface 3+ of {tenant count and size mix, payload/series
            profile, SLO and loss budget, downstream consumers and
            their owners, retention, what "bursty" means in numbers,
            who owns the system after launch}
    Weak:   jump to architecture, or ask only one question

Criteria (35 min, ~5 min each)
  Score 0-3 per row. No trivia. Multiple architectures are acceptable.
  Score on judgment, grounding, and explicit tradeoffs, not on the
  specific stack or product chosen.

  1. Requirement clarification
     3 = names what they'd lock down vs. leave open; pulls non-functional
         constraints (retention, loss budget, replay need, cost ceiling)
         without prompting
     2 = asks most key questions with light prompting
     1 = asks one or two questions, then defaults to generic assumptions
     0 = no clarification; dives into design

  2. Bounded backpressure
     3 = explicit policy for what fills and what sheds; distinguishes edge
         vs. downstream pressure; names who pays the cost (latency, drop,
         throttle); finite buffer/queue with a concrete shedding rule
     2 = bounded queues and shedding exist, but boundary or who absorbs
         pressure is vague
     1 = mentions backpressure but no concrete policy
     0 = unbounded queues, "add capacity," or no discussion

  3. Tenant fairness
     3 = per-tenant or weighted fair queuing; explicit noisy-neighbor
         handling; defines what a tenant gets under contention
     2 = per-tenant quotas exist but coarse (only at ingest edge, or only
         a global cap)
     1 = global rate limit only, fairness as a footnote
     0 = first-come-first-served with no fairness treatment

  4. Idempotency and retries
     3 = explicit dedup/idempotency key; retry policy bounded (count and
         window); chooses at-least-once vs. at-most-once by sink capability;
         surfaces duplicate cost on downstream consumers
     2 = idempotency mentioned with concrete key, retry policy partial
     1 = retries mentioned but not bounded, or assumes exactly-once
     0 = retries and dedup not addressed

  5. Cardinality control
     3 = bounded label/value set with owner and budget; preflight or drop
         rule for unknown labels; pre-aggregation where it pays; separates
         control-plane governance from runtime enforcement
     2 = cardinality cap exists but enforcement point or owner unclear
     1 = "we'll cap cardinality" with no bounded value shape or owner
     0 = not discussed, or assumed clean

  6. Rollout and observability
     3 = staged rollout with canary and soak; dashboards and SLOs that
         distinguish cause from symptom; replay/validation path; readiness
         and rollback criteria named before deploy
     2 = staged rollout + dashboards present; rollback criteria vague
     1 = "deploy and monitor"
     0 = no rollout or observability plan

  7. Explicit service ownership
     3 = names primary and backup owners per stage; on-call handoff
         defined; runbook expectations surfaced; escalation path with
         thresholds
     2 = ownership named for the system as a whole, but per-stage or
         backup unclear
     1 = "the team will handle it" or only the on-call rotation mentioned
     0 = ownership not addressed

Closing probe (5 min)
  "Walk me through who owns this on day 30 after launch, and what would
   make you roll it back."
    Strong: per-stage owners with backups; on-call expectation; runbook
            reference; rollback trigger tied to a metric, not a feeling
            (e.g., "if ingest p99 > X for Y minutes AND drop rate > Z")
    Weak:   "the team," or "if it's broken"

Scoring (max 21)
  18-21  strong hire signal for the role level
  13-17  calibrated hire; lean on other loops for the missing areas
   8-12  weak signal; missing critical judgment
   0-7   no-hire for this role level

Notes template
  Two sentences per criterion: one concrete signal they showed, one gap.
  Calibrate against other loops. Flag any place they reached a good answer
  only after heavy prompting — that is a different signal than reaching it
  on their own.

Things to ignore
  - Specific protocol, queue, or library names
  - Whether they remembered a number
  - Stack or vendor preference
  - Nerves on the first 60 seconds
  - Whether their sketch matches your whiteboard

Things to actively probe
  - Whether they treat rollback thresholds as something they own and
    define, or something on-call decides during an incident
  - Whether per-stage owners and backups are concrete names/roles or
    "the team"
  - Whether their idempotency story breaks under a retry burst larger
    than their dedup window

Both questions land inside the lane. Neither has to be territorial if asked as a working-relationship question rather than a boundary-defense question. Pressure-test notes:

Question 1 — "how design-system ownership is divided between design and product engineering once a component enters the codebase"

Territorial risk: low to medium. "Divided...once a component enters" can be heard as "where does design's claim end and engineering's begin," which can read like someone preparing to defend ground. The fix is a single word that signals she's asking about the post-handoff working relationship, not the handoff moment itself.

What it can reveal:

  - Whether the org has a real model for the seam between intent (semantics, usage guidance, "why") and implementation (code, refactor, migration). A healthy answer names both sides and the seam — design keeps authority over intent and usage, engineering keeps authority over implementation, and there is a named moment when one needs the other.
  - Whether a component in the codebase is treated as a living artifact or a delivered artifact. "We hand it off, then engineering owns the code" usually means design loses the system over time. "Design keeps updating specs, engineering implements them" usually means engineering is being used as a build service.
  - Whether drift gets surfaced. A useful answer explains how engineering handles a usage or semantic change after handoff and how design gets pulled back in.
  - Whether there is a quiet default owner for "weird" cases — i.e. who decides when a component is used in a way neither side anticipated.

Small wording tweak: add "ongoing" so the question points clearly at the living-artifact phase, not the handoff moment.

  "after a component lands in the codebase, how is ongoing ownership split between design and product engineering?"

Question 2 — "when a product deadline requires an exception to the system, who documents that exception and who owns removing it later"

Territorial risk: low if it lands around artifacts and ownership. Medium if it lands as "do you have a process" — that can read either as bureaucratic or as accusatory ("do you ever actually clean these up?"). The fix is to make the two time points visible (at creation, at removal) so the question lands as mechanics, not policy.

What it can reveal:

  - Whether exceptions are real artifacts or folklore. A good answer names a specific surface — a ticket type, a design-system debt log, an ADR, a Figma note inside the pattern itself — and a standing rule for who can raise one.
  - Whether ownership is named at creation or only at removal. Strong answers name the owner when the exception is raised. Weak answers push ownership to "design cleans up later," which is how design systems quietly rot.
  - Whether deadline pressure actually holds. A useful signal is whether they have a count or review surface for outstanding exceptions, or whether it is all memory.
  - Who defaults if the original requester moves on. A good answer names a default (design-systems owner, component owner, the next person to touch it). A bad answer is "we'll figure it out."
  - Whether visual debt gets the same operational discipline as code debt. If "tech debt" has a tracker but design-system debt does not, that is itself a signal.

Small wording tweak: disambiguate "the system" so it cannot be heard as the product, and split the two ownership moments so the question lands as mechanics rather than policy.

Yes, the read is right — the draft is conflating four distinct guarantees that belong to four different owners, and the conflation is doing real work in the document. Pulling them apart:

Client retry behavior. "Every client retries for at least 15 minutes" is not a property of clients in this system — it's a description of ingest-edge's local dedup window that happened to be sized against observed client behavior. The platform cannot assert it; it's an empirical observation that may already be false for any client outside the metrics pipeline, and even for pipeline clients it's a measurement, not a guarantee. If it goes into the invariant as a premise, any client that retries for less becomes an "invariant violation" rather than a service-specific choice.

Ingress acknowledgement. A 2xx from the receiver says "the receiver accepted the request for processing." It does not say the request was processed, was persisted, or will be persisted if the receiver crashes between ack and write. The b-771 case from earlier this month is the proof on the other side: upstream had already acknowledged the write, then the client received a 504, and the only thing that prevented a duplicate was the dedup window catching the retry. So 2xx and durable are not the same word, and treating them as one word makes the invariant wrong in both directions.

Dedup ownership. Bounded backpressure is exactly the condition under which a 5-minute server-side dedup window is unsafe — the receiver is signaling clients to slow down, which extends the time before retry, which means a client retrying past the dedup window now produces a duplicate. The 15-minute window wasn't a preference; it was the floor that kept b-771-style cases from creating double writes. Shortening it required evidence the safety case doesn't appear to cover: what's the worst-case client retry interval under the bounded-backpressure regime, and where's the gap between that and 5 minutes?

Downstream durability. Owned by rollup-service / the storage layer, not by the receiver's ack and not by platform. The only proofs are downstream acknowledgement or storage-side evidence (replay validation, mirrored writes, end-to-end counts). The draft can't substitute ingress acks for that proof without inventing a guarantee that doesn't exist.

The platform-as-exception-owner failure mode is then mechanical. If the invariant asserts "client retries ≥ 15 min, server dedups ≥ 5 min, 2xx means durable," then when something breaks, the investigation goes: client retried 8 minutes → invariant violated; server dedup expired → invariant violated; receiver acked then crashed → invariant violated. Three different owners' bugs all become "the invariant was wrong," and the draft's actual scope — which is presumably one or two of those four boundaries — gets buried under the others. Platform ends up holding the policy for failures it can't detect and can't enforce.

What the draft would need to do instead is treat the invariant as a per-boundary contract: at each boundary, name the owner, name the signal, name what the signal proves, and name what it doesn't. Backpressure signaling needs to be made explicit so dedup windows can be sized against it, and durability needs to point at downstream evidence rather than ingress acks. The "15-minute" number survives as ingest-edge's local window sized against observed client behavior, not as a global assumption.

I haven't read the draft itself, only your assessment — if anything above mischaracterizes what's actually in it, the framing would shift. If useful, I can sketch what the per-boundary contract would look like for the metrics pipeline specifically.

The load-bearing problem in this draft is a safety hole, not just an ownership problem.

Client retry budget is 15 minutes. Server dedup window is 5 minutes. After minute 5, a retry from the same client carrying the same idempotency key arrives at a receiver that has already aged out its dedup state. The receiver treats the request as new. Depending on what the request does, that produces duplicate downstream effects — duplicate stored points, duplicate side effects, duplicate charges. The whole point of an idempotency contract is that the sender's retry budget and the receiver's dedup window must match, or the receiver's window must exceed the sender's budget. The current draft inverts that.

This is also exactly the asymmetry you flagged in the ingest-edge retry-dedup benchmark. The draft reproduces it: it asserts "backpressure is bounded" as the justification for a shorter receiver window without proving that no client crosses the 5-minute boundary in those conditions. The benchmark failed the same safety case the same way.

Other issues, briefly:

  1. "Globally unique idempotency key" — unique across what scope, for how long? In practice this is "unique per (sender, receiver) within the dedup retention window." Otherwise you're asking receivers to retain state forever, which contradicts the 5-minute window on the same line.

  2. "Downstream services may treat any 2xx response as durable" — too permissive as written. A 2xx commonly means "accepted for processing," not "durably committed." The contract should distinguish: a bare 2xx = accepted; a separate durability marker (header, status, or commit timestamp) = durably committed to the receiver's primary store under its documented replication factor. Otherwise downstream services reason about durability from response codes and get it wrong.

  3. "Backpressure is bounded" — undefined. This is the loophole that swallows the exception. If the contract doesn't enumerate the thresholds (queue depth, in-flight count, retry-arrival rate, p99 latency, I/O wait), every receiver defines "bounded" locally and the exception becomes meaningless. The thresholds belong in the contract.

  4. No retry pattern specified. "Retry for at least 15 minutes" without requiring jittered exponential backoff is a fixed-loop hammer. The contract should require jittered exponential with a documented starting delay, or it will amplify load during the very backpressure it claims to bound.

  5. "The platform team owns exceptions" — exactly the structural problem the review goal targets. "Platform team" plus an open-ended exceptions bucket is how invariants stop being invariants. Exceptions have to be typed and assigned to specific teams. Worth noting: in the metrics-pipeline work, platform ownership was drawn around primitives and metric contracts, not around every service's implementation choices. The draft conflates those two layers.

Structural proposal — distribute ownership by exception type, not by team bucket:

  Retry behavior (clients): each service team that emits requests owns the retry implementation in their client. Contract: jittered exponential backoff for at least 15 minutes, same idempotency key reused across retries.

  Idempotency contract (receivers): each receiving service team owns its dedup implementation. Platform team owns the contract itself (the rule). The dedup window MUST match or exceed the maximum client retry budget the receiver is exposed to. A shorter window is permitted only when the receiver publishes the bounded-backpressure thresholds it meets AND proves — not asserts — that no client retries across the boundary in those conditions.

  Durability boundary: each receiving service owns what its 2xx responses mean. Bare 2xx = accepted. A separate durability marker = durably committed. Downstream services consume the marker, not the bare code.

  Backpressure definition: platform team owns the metric contract (which signals every receiver must expose). Each service team owns its own dashboards, alerts, and the question of whether its service is currently inside the bounded envelope.

  Exceptions, typed:
    - Tenant-specific quota/throughput exceptions: tenant-facing service team.
    - Cross-service invariant relaxations: the proposing team, with written sign-off from every affected receiver and a documented sunset.
    - Service-local implementation choices (e.g., a cost-driven shorter window on a non-critical path): the service team, documented in their runbook, scoped to their own boundary.
    - Emergency capacity relaxations under sustained pressure: the affected service team in the moment, with mandatory incident review and post-incident justification.
  No "exceptions" bucket belongs to one team.

That gets you a cross-service invariant that fixes the safety hole and doesn't make any single team the owner of every problem.

Contradictions and ownership gaps in the current draft:

1. Retry horizon vs. dedup window. The draft assumes every client retries for at least 15 minutes, then lets receivers keep dedup state for only 5. Anything retrying between minute 5 and 15 produces a duplicate the receiver thought was already once-and-done. The two clauses are directly inconsistent.

2. Backpressure-coupled retention. The 5-minute retention is qualified "when backpressure is bounded." Dedup retention cannot be conditional on a condition the client cannot observe. If backpressure relaxes mid-retry, the dedup window collapses and clients have no signal to stop retrying. Coupling retention to backpressure is a hidden invariant in the wrong place.

3. 2xx = durable. Treating any 2xx as durable conflates ingress acknowledgement with downstream durability. Ingress can ack and fail before the durable handoff completes; a client retrying on a lost 2xx duplicates work the receiver has no way to recognize.

4. Layer conflation in a single sentence. The draft governs client behavior, ingress ack, dedup ownership, and downstream persistence together. These are four layers with different owners and different failure modes. One invariant across all four will misroute ownership and hide boundary failures.

5. Silent ownership. The draft names no owner for dedup state, no owner for retry identity, no on-call path when dedup eviction lets a duplicate through, and no owner of the retry horizon contract.

Tighter invariant structure:

1. Documented supported retry horizon (per ingress, not universal). Each ingress publishes a supported retry horizon: the longest client retry interval after which at-most-once processing is still guaranteed at the receiver. Versioned, runbook-referenced, contract-visible. Clients retrying outside the horizon get an explicit "retry-unsafe" line, not a silent assumption. If two ingresses feed the same receiver, the receiver's horizon is the max.

2. Stable retry identity. Producer emits a stable identity (idempotency key) at emission. That identity is the unit of dedup at every layer: client, ingress, receiver, downstream. No layer may regenerate or transform the identity without an explicit lineage rule. The identity is what makes "already seen" decidable.

3. Dedup retention with a named safety margin. Receiver dedup retention must be greater than the max documented supported retry horizon across all ingresses feeding it, plus a named margin (e.g., 1.5x the longest horizon, or aligned to the slowest profiling window — pick one and write it down). If retention cannot meet that bar, the supported retry horizon shortens; the draft cannot silently compress dedup to fit a memory budget. Backpressure does not enter this equation.

4. Acknowledgement boundary. Two named ack semantics:
   - Ingress ack = "received, dedup-registered, durably buffered at ingress."
   - Downstream ack = "durably persisted at the receiver."
   2xx at ingress does not imply downstream ack. Clients retrying on ingress-timeout must understand which boundary they crossed; the runbook states which.

5. Service ownership for implementation and operations.
   - Retry identity creation: producer (primary), ingress (backup).
   - Supported retry horizon documentation and contract: ingress owner (primary), platform/reliability (backup).
   - Dedup state and retention: receiver (primary), ingress (backup).
   - Durability and downstream persistence: receiver (primary), storage owner (backup).
   - Incident response when dedup eviction lets a duplicate through: receiver on-call (primary), ingress on-call (backup). Runbook names both, not just "the on-call."

Evidence needed before settling the dedup window:

- Profiled client retry interval histograms per ingress (p50, p95, p99, max). The 15-minute number is currently an assumption.
- Memory cost of dedup retention at candidate windows (5, 15, 30 min) under realistic load.
- Duplicate rate observed at the 5-minute boundary in any current replay or staging fixture.
- Failure-mode profile for dedup eviction: how often it happens, what the duplicate blast radius is.

If profiling is not yet available, the safe default is the longer documented horizon (15 min) plus margin, with an explicit revisit date once the histograms exist. The 5-minute default in the draft is unsafe absent that evidence, and it must not be approved on the back-pressure rationale alone.

Short answer for Cyrus: this is a distribution shift inside a bounded label space, not a cardinality event. Don't touch the metric.

Why: cardinality is the count of unique series, which is the count of unique (label-name, label-value) combinations. The label inventory is still {small, medium, large, unknown}, total series count is unchanged, and no new label name has appeared — so by definition nothing has gone cardinality-bad. What changed is the *proportion* of tenants landing in `unknown`: roughly 735 more of them. The bounded enum is doing exactly what it was designed to do — `unknown` is the safety valve for un-classifiable inputs, and it absorbed the spike. The metric is correct. The problem is upstream of it.

Most likely causes, in rough order of how often this shows up right after a nightly fixture refresh:

1. Fixture join degraded. The size-class lookup table changed shape, lost rows, or normalized keys differently. Denominator held at 5,000, so it's not a population growth — the resolution rate fell.
2. New cohort with no size-class record yet. The fixture (or an upstream sync) added tenants whose account/billing-tier data hasn't propagated. `unknown` is the right answer for them at this instant.
3. Upstream classification source went stale or partially failed. A sync job to the source-of-truth for size class fell behind or skipped a partition.
4. Schema / key drift. Tenant_id format in the metric pipeline no longer matches the fixture keys (whitespace, prefix, case, int-vs-string).

Fastest checks, in order — these are all reads, no metric changes:

1. Fixture refresh job log. Did it complete clean? Any skipped rows, failed joins, or schema-validation warnings? First thing to check because it's the closest causal neighbor in time.
2. Diff the fixture snapshot before vs after the refresh. Which specific tenants moved into `unknown`? Contiguous cohort (one tier / one region / one creation-date band) points to a fixture or classification-source issue. Scattered across all dates and tiers points to a key-normalization issue.
3. Upstream size-class source freshness. If a sync job populates the classification table, did it run on schedule, and is it behind?
4. Grep debug logs for recent `unknown` tenant hashes. Raw hash is debug-log-only by design, so this is a safe sample. Look for a shared pattern (newly created, specific tier, specific region).
5. Cross-check creation timestamps. If the new `unknown` tenants are all newer than the last successful upstream sync, that's the "cohort not yet classified" hypothesis confirmed.
6. Confirm the denominator. Is 5,000 the fixture size, or the size of a separate join input? If they come from different sources, the ratio can drift with no input change at all.

What not to do yet:

- Don't change the metric. The bounded enum is working.
- Don't add a label to "explain" the unknown. That's the trap the original `tenant_id_hash` proposal fell into and the reason the enum exists.
- Don't call this a cardinality incident. Series count + label inventory are the cardinality signal, and neither moved.

Decision point after the checks: if the fixture diff shows a clean cohort shift (e.g., all 735 are tenants added in the last 24h), this is expected behavior during a sync lag — leave the metric alone, wait for the upstream sync to catch up, re-check in one cycle. If the diff shows scattered tenants across all creation dates and tiers, it's a join or schema problem and the fix lives in the fixture pipeline or the key normalization, not in the metric.

Cross-service retry invariant (draft, for review — not adopted policy):

Each receiving service owns the durability boundary that its acknowledgement represents, and a successful response must not be assumed to carry the same durability meaning across services — one service may acknowledge that a unit of work is durably accepted while downstream processing is still pending, while another may acknowledge only after its own durable commit. Failures occurring before a service's stated acknowledgement boundary remain retryable by the client. Each service must publish a discoverable retry horizon during which a retry bearing a stable retry identity will be recognized and de-duplicated, and must retain deduplication state for at least that horizon plus an explicit safety margin. Work that has crossed a service's acknowledgement boundary must not be lost within the published horizon and is that service's responsibility to make recoverable.

What this intentionally does not hard-code, so neither owner's implementation leaks into the invariant: the specific HTTP status codes (202 vs 200), the storage primitives behind the boundary (local WAL, aggregate commit, object storage), and any per-service window values. The "durably accepted / downstream pending" and "own durable commit" phrases are the two boundary archetypes the design pass landed on, written generically so a third service adopting the invariant can pick either or describe a third without the language breaking.

Short version: this is not a server-side regression on our side. The change is on the client histogram, and the right fix is to keep request_id in logs and traces rather than as a metric label.

What we saw
  The client histogram now carries a `request_id` label with a unique value per request. Over twelve minutes this produced 42,318 active series for that one metric in this tenant. ingest-edge enforces a per-tenant active-series cap; once the tenant crossed it, new series were rejected at the edge. Shared-service error rate, latency, and queue depth stayed flat through the window. That is what distinguishes cardinality capping from a real ingest or backend problem.

Why this is not a regression
  A real ingest or backend regression moves the shared-service health signals. Those did not move. The rejections are the cap doing its job: protecting this tenant and the shared path from a label set that grew without bound.

Immediate safe mitigation
  Remove `request_id` from the histogram's metric labels, or replace it with a bounded classification (fixed enum or short hash bucket) if a metric dimension is genuinely needed. Once the unbounded label stops being emitted, ingest-edge will accept new series again as the rejected set drains.

Preserving request-level debugging
  The need to look up a specific request is real; putting a unique-per-request identifier into a metric label is the problem. Keep `request_id` in application logs and distributed-trace span attributes. Logs and traces are looked up by id with bounded retention; metric labels aggregate per unique combination and are paid for in active series. To go from a metric series to a specific request, join on `timestamp + trace_id` (already bounded), then pull `request_id` from the trace or log. That gives per-request debugging without unbounded cardinality.

Optional guardrail for next time
  Cardinality Guardrails require a label-cardinality preflight on label changes touching ingest-edge, metrics-router, shard-keeper, or rollup-service. Sharing the planned label set before shipping lets us flag unbounded labels ahead of the cap rather than at it.

Let us know once the label is removed and we will watch the tenant return to a normal active-series count.

Diagnosis is consistent with the change. request_id is unbounded by construction — one series per UUID per histogram bucket. Raw route multiplies that by every unique path the handler serves. 42,318 active series after 12 minutes is what you'd expect from a histogram with two unbounded labels at non-trivial QPS. New-series rejects at the tenant series cap (not a global limit), with shared ingest-edge flat on error rate, latency, and queue depth, confirms this is a per-tenant cardinality problem, not a platform-wide ingestion issue. Live path and downstream rollup-service are not affected.

Proposed fix is the right shape:

- Drop request_id from the metric. UUIDs don't belong in histogram labels; logs and traces are the right home for per-request correlation.
- Replace raw route with a bounded route-template. The bounded set has to actually be bounded — if the customer's handlers emit raw paths today, a template/normalization pass has to land first, or this just relocates the cardinality.
- Keep request_id in logs and traces. Worth verifying that path actually carries it, not just asserting.

2. Consumer check on the new label shape. Alert definitions and dashboard panels referencing the old raw route need to be updated or they'll silently break. Downstream rollup-service consumers need to recognize the new label — Nadia will want label-name parity so this doesn't become a separate cleanup effort.

Quick verdict: Yuki's design avoids log thrash and, assuming the hash check is event-driven rather than timer-driven, doesn't add meaningful recovery delay. Worth landing, with one detail pinned down and a few small additions.

Review
  - Log thrash: gone. From ~10 attempts/sec/replica to a 30s ceiling is roughly a 300x drop in parse attempts, which more than absorbs the 9pp CPU bump. Replacing per-attempt log lines with a consecutive-fail counter is the right shape — counters are cheap and queryable, log lines are not.
  - Recovery delay: hinges on what "immediate retry when the config content hash changes" actually means. If a fsnotify/inotify-style watcher fires the hash comparison, fix-to-pickup is effectively instant. If the hash check rides on the same backoff timer, worst-case is ~30s. Both are acceptable for a config file, but the PR needs to be explicit about which it is. If there's no watcher today, adding one is in-scope for this fix; otherwise "immediate" should be reworded.

Small additions before this lands
  - Add modest jitter (e.g., ±10%) so multiple metrics-router replicas don't synchronize retry bursts against the same bad file.
  - Counter must reset to 0 on a *successful* parse, not just on file change — otherwise a stale-but-valid attempt leaves the streak elevated.
  - State-transition logs (first failure WARN, recovery INFO with the streak count) preserve the signal that the old per-attempt lines used to provide; debug-level per-attempt line is fine for the staging soak but should not be on by default in prod.

Acceptance criteria
  1. Per-replica parse-error log volume for an unchanged malformed config drops to ≤1 line per state transition (first failure WARN, recovery INFO); intermediate failures are counter increments only. Verified in staging against the same fixture that produced the original ~600/min.
  2. Process CPU returns to pre-thrash baseline within one backoff window of the fix being live.
  3. Recovery latency on operator fix: ≤5s if a file-change watcher is in place, otherwise bounded by one backoff window (~30s). Trigger mechanism stated explicitly in the PR description.
  4. Hash-change → immediate retry is covered by a test: mutate file content in place, observe the next parse attempt firing before the backoff timer expires.
  5. Counter `metrics_router_config_consecutive_failures` increments per failed parse, resets to 0 on successful parse, is exposed as a Prometheus metric, and is alertable on a sustained nonzero streak (existing paging or a small new alert — Yuki's call, but pick one before merge).
  6. Live traffic serving is unchanged during the bad-config window. True today; the fix must not regress it.
  7. Rollback path tested in staging: reverting the change restores the original rapid-retry / verbose-log behavior cleanly.
  8. Scope is config-retry only — no incidental parser, schema, or config-loader changes in the same PR.
  9. Per-replica independence: no global lock or cross-replica coordination added.
 10. Rollout: staging soak ≥24h, then production canary through the deploy pipeline. Not deployed Friday afternoon.

Recommendation: HOLD at the 5% cohort, do not advance, do not clear the slice. The shape
in evidence is bounded-warm-up-plausible but not yet bounded-warm-up-confirmed, and
tearing the cohort down loses the only window we have to watch it plateau. The
first-pass hold by Wes was correct; the escalation was warranted because a monotone
+18 percentage-point memory slope over 20 minutes with a co-rising queue age is not
a safe-proceed signal even with error rate, dropped, and duplicate-accepted all clean.

Why this is not yet a "safe proceed":
  - Memory is monotonic over a 20-minute window. Warm-up signatures flatten; leaks
    do not. The slope is the primary evidence, not the level.
  - Queue age moved with memory. Co-movement means memory pressure is slowing the
    pipeline, not just occupying it. That argues against a one-shot warm spike and
    toward something still allocating or holding.
  - 0.08% error rate, zero drops, zero duplicate-accepted tell us correctness is
    intact. They do not exonerate a leak; they just say we have time to look.
  - 5% synthetic is light load. If memory is climbing at 5%, the growth is largely
    input-shape-driven (cache fills, allocations per item, retained state), not
    load-driven. That is exactly the cache/allocation surface we need to inspect
    before another bump.

Hold disposition:
  - Leave the 5% slice in place. Stop the clock on advancing the cohort; do not
    roll back the version yet. We need plateau evidence or slope-flat evidence
    before either decision.
  - Capture a snapshot now: process RSS, heap in-use, GC stats, each cache size
    and hit/miss counter, each queue depth and age, allocations/sec by subsystem
    if exposed. This is the t=0 baseline for the plateau test.
  - Pre-declare an abort before any further attempt: if memory does not plateau
    within 30 minutes of observation at 5%, or crosses 85%, treat as leak-shaped,
    halt, and roll back v2.18.3. No silent re-attempt.

Minimum checks to distinguish bounded warm-up from a leak:

CACHE
  - Identify every in-process cache on the ingest-edge path: label-set cache,
    routing-rule cache, auth-token cache, regex/glob compilation cache,
    request-coalesce key cache, dedup cache. For each, record size, cap, hit
    ratio, eviction counter, and oldest-entry age.
  - Bounded warm-up signature: size approaches a known cap, hit ratio climbs and
    stabilizes, evictions begin, oldest-entry age stops growing. Unbounded
    signature: size keeps climbing with no cap hit, evictions flat or absent,
    oldest-entry age keeps growing.
  - Compare to the same 5% cohort on the last green build. If the previous build
    plateaued around 65-70% at this cohort, today's 82% and still climbing is
    not the same warm-up curve and is investigation, not proceed.
  - Any cache without a hard cap is, by definition, the leak candidate until
    proven otherwise.

ALLOCATION

Spiced chickpeas and spinach with garlicky yogurt sauce and warm pita. Everything in one pan plus a foil packet in the oven for the pita so it lands hot at the same time.

Order of operations (about 30 min, mostly hands-off)

0:00 — Sauce first, it just sits.
  In a small bowl stir together:
  - most of the Greek yogurt (save a couple spoonfuls for plating if you like)
  - juice of half the lemon
  - 1 small clove garlic, grated or very finely minced
  - 1 tbsp olive oil
  - pinch of salt, pinch of cumin
  Taste, adjust lemon and salt. Cover and leave on the counter.

0:02 — Heat oven to 350°F. Stack the pitas, wrap loosely in foil, slide into the oven. They will be ready in 6–8 min and stay warm in the foil for the rest of cook time.

0:05 — Chickpeas, the only real cooking.
  Large skillet, medium heat, about 2 tbsp olive oil. Add 2 cloves of garlic sliced thin, stir 60 seconds until just fragrant and not browned.

0:07 — Add 1 tsp cumin and 1 tsp smoked paprika to the oil, stir 30 seconds to bloom. This is where the warm, smoky flavor comes from, do not skip.

0:08 — Add both cans of chickpeas, drained, and a generous handful of cherry tomatoes halved (about 1 cup). Big pinch of salt. Stir. Cook 8–10 minutes, stirring now and then, pressing a few chickpeas against the pan with the back of a spoon so they break down and make a light sauce.

0:18 — Add the spinach in a few handfuls, stirring just until wilted, 2–3 minutes. Squeeze in the other half of the lemon. Taste for salt. If it looks dry, a small glug of olive oil or a spoon of pasta water if you have it.

0:22 — Plate.
  - Spoon chickpeas into two bowls
  - Big dollop of yogurt sauce on top or alongside
  - Warm pita cut into wedges
  - Optional finish that costs nothing: drizzle of olive oil, tiny extra sprinkle of smoked paprika, lemon wedge

Heads-up first: 62°F is uncomfortable but safe for healthy adults in layered clothes for a couple of hours. The risk in a short heat outage isn't cold itself — it's the improvised heat sources people reach for. Most of the danger here is CO and fire, not the temperature.

Plan for ~2h20m until the 10:30 tech window:

Stay warm — do
- Layer: base layer + fleece/sweater + socks. One warm layer beats one thick layer for trapping heat.
- Hunker in one room (smallest comfortable one), close the others, drape a blanket over a doorway if there's a gap.
- Hot drinks and a warm meal. Digestion generates real body heat — a warm breakfast helps more than people expect.
- Move around every 30–40 min for a few minutes, then rest. Don't sit still the whole time.
- If you have a hot-water bottle or can warm a sock full of rice in the oven (then OFF, out of the oven), it makes a good foot warmer.
- Sun: if any window gets direct light, open the curtain on that side during the day.

Stay warm — do NOT
- Oven left on for heat. Fire hazard, and on a gas range it's a CO source.
- Gas stove burners for heat. Same CO problem. This is the big one — NYC has CO deaths from this every year.
- Kerosene/propane heater indoors. Unvented combustion = CO.
- Charcoal or "campfire" anything indoors.
- Space heater on an extension cord or power strip, or two heaters on one outlet. If you use a space heater, plug it directly into a wall outlet, keep it 3 ft from anything, and turn it off when you leave the room.
- Generator indoors or in a garage. CO.

Thresholds — leave or escalate before 10:30
- Indoor temp drops below ~58°F and still falling: text the super back, ask if the tech can come sooner or whether neighboring units have heat. If nothing moves, plan to leave to a warm place (coffee shop, library, friend's place).
- Indoor temp drops below ~55°F: leave, regardless of tech ETA. Not an emergency yet, but no reason to sit in it.
- Any of these symptoms in either of you — leave immediately and call 911:
  - shivering you can't stop
  - confusion, slurred speech, drowsiness that's unusual
  - bluish lips or fingertips
  - chest pain, rapid breathing, or a headache plus nausea (think CO)
- Any gas smell or the CO alarm goes off: leave now, doors/windows open on the way out if you can do it safely, call 911 from outside. Do not stay to investigate.

Kibo
- He's fine at 62°F for a couple hours with a blanket or sweater and a person nearby. Smaller space + a dog bed + a blanket over him holds his heat well.
- Watch for sustained shivering, hunching, lethargy, or whining — that's his "I'm cold" threshold. If the apartment drops into the 50s, take him with you when you leave.

Notes worth flagging if the tech asks
- The living-room radiator has been quiet since the November vent-cap reseat, no current leak from your unit.
- This looks building-wide (no heat anywhere, super resetting the boiler), not a unit issue.

Background
- NYC Heat Law requires the landlord to maintain ≥68°F daytime during heating season (Oct 1–May 31) when outdoor temp is below 55°F. 62°F is below that. Worth a 311 complaint later for the record, but 311 is not an emergency line — won't speed the tech up.

You're both home, you've got ~2h, and the path is: stay layered in one room, avoid every combustion-heat shortcut, and watch for the thresholds above. The tech window is reasonable — you should be able to ride this out.

DIAGNOSIS — Clock skew on one collector host

Every rejected sample in this case is coming from a single collector host, with timestamps about 11 minutes 42 seconds in the future. Two pieces of evidence point clearly to clock skew on that host rather than an ingest or service-side issue:

  1. The rejects are isolated to one collector host — your other collector hosts are ingesting normally.
  2. On our side, shared ingest-edge error rate, latency, and queue depth are all normal across this window. There is no service-side cause we can find.

The 11m 42s offset is the giveaway — that is roughly the drift between that host's local clock and our accepted time reference. Ingestion rejects samples whose timestamps fall too far in the future, and this host has been doing exactly that on every sample it sent during the window.

WHAT WE NEED YOU TO DO

Please correct time synchronization on the affected collector host before sending more samples. The usual culprits, in roughly descending order of frequency we see:

  - NTP / chrony daemon not running, not configured, or not reachable to a time source
  - A VM whose clock has drifted because the hypervisor time source is misconfigured
  - A containerized collector that was started without an injected host time source

Use whatever time-sync mechanism is standard in your environment, bring the host's clock back to within a few seconds of true time, and confirm it is staying there before resuming sample send. If you can identify which one of the above it is on this host, that helps us rule out anything systemic on your side.

HOW TO VERIFY RECOVERY

Once the host's clock is corrected, please send a small batch (a handful of samples is enough) and check:

  - The timestamps on those samples, as visible in your dashboard or query results, are within a couple of seconds of current wall-clock time.
  - No new rejects appear in the collector's rejected-sample log for that host.
  - The same metric series that was rejecting earlier now accepts and stores normally.

If you can share one accepted sample's stored timestamp relative to wall-clock time from your side, we can confirm on our side as well. We will also watch our ingest reject counts for that host over the next window.

WHAT WE DO NOT RECOMMEND

Please do not work around this by rewriting timestamps — neither client-side (substituting server time for the host clock) nor anywhere in a pipeline you control. Hiding the drift would (a) leave the underlying time-sync problem in place, (b) distort timestamps for any future samples that host sends, and (c) make the next incident much harder to diagnose because the offsets would no longer match reality. We would rather see the host's clock fixed than see clean-looking timestamps that mean the wrong thing.

If the host's clock comes back into line and rejects do not stop, or if you see any drift on the other collector hosts, please send us what you are seeing and we will keep digging on our side.

Diagnosis

The +11m42s offset on a single collector host is the root cause. The ingest-edge validator's "timestamp too far in future" rejection window is doing its job — it's rejecting samples whose `time` field sits too far ahead of the validator's own clock. With shared ingest-edge error rate, latency, and queue depth all normal, and the other hosts' timestamps and ingestion normal, the failure surface is one host, not the pipeline. The other hosts are a control, not a co-conspirator.

Why not rewrite timestamps

Rewriting here would mask the actual fault, leave the host's clock wrong, and put false times into the store. Any later replay from that host, or any mirror/replay comparison against corrected-but-now-incorrect samples, would produce inconsistent or duplicate points relative to real wall time. The boundary you set is the right one: fix the host clock first; only then decide what to do with the rejected batch, and the answer is unlikely to be "rewrite."

Remediation order (conservative)

  1. Confirm the drift is current, not a stale reading. From the host, check the time-sync daemon's status and current offset vs. its configured source (e.g. `chronyc tracking` / `chronyc sources -v` / `timedatectl status`, or the ntpd equivalent). The +11m42s should reproduce live.

  2. Find why this one host drifted while siblings didn't. In rough order of likelihood:
     - time-sync daemon not running on this host
     - NTP/chrony source unreachable from this host only (ACL, firewall, route, instance-metadata, leap-second handling)
     - daemon running but unsynchronized (no reachable source, stratum 16, "not synced")
     - VM suspend/resume without a resume-time resync
     - tz misconfiguration (unlikely at this magnitude, but cheap to rule out)

  3. Step, do not slew. At ~12 minutes, slew is too slow and the validator will keep rejecting for the duration of the catch-up. Force a step (e.g. `chronyc makestep` after enabling `makestep` in chrony.conf, or the daemon's equivalent). Then let normal sync resume.

  4. Verify ingestion immediately on that host. The rejection counter on the offending collector should drop to zero within seconds; the shared ingest-edge error rate should stay flat.

  5. Confirm no live-path impact. You said shared error rate / latency / queue depth are normal — keep that watch up for at least one full validator window after the step. Movement on the live path is what would justify a rollback discussion. This is host-side clock drift with a clean live path, so it doesn't.

Rejected batch — what to do with it

After the host clock is correct, the rejected samples' original timestamps are now in the past, not the future. Two cases, and neither is "rewrite":

  - If the client retried automatically and the now-corrected host is sending the same real-time samples with current timestamps, the originals are duplicates — let the rejection stand or drop them at the host. No rewriting.
  - If the batch was lost client-side (no retry, no WAL), it's already lost. Don't paper over it with timestamp edits.

Follow-ups

  - Runbook: add a short clock-drift entry — either on rb_ingest_edge (validator-side symptom + guardrail) or on the collector-host runbook (host-side remediation). Cross-link both. The entry should explicitly carry the "do not rewrite timestamps" guardrail so the next on-call doesn't reach for it under pressure.

Minimal ordered diagnostic plan — staging compaction rehearsal, 3 manifest checksum mismatches, prod untouched.

Premise / boundary
  - Rehearsal is staging-only. Replay/mirror movement is investigation evidence, not a rollback criterion. Live-path movement would start a rollback discussion; we are not there.
  - Wes stopping and not self-repairing was correct. shard-keeper stays outside his solo scope. You drive; Cyrus-team backup is in the loop.
  - Three manifests is a bounded scope. Do not let the investigation expand to other manifests mid-flight.

Step 1 — Freeze the failure surface (determinism first)
  a. Capture, verbatim: the exact rehearsal command, the fixture ID/version, the staging build SHA, the restore target ID, the three manifest paths, and the expected vs actual checksum values printed by restore verification.
  b. Record the reported shard count (128 matches) and which manifest indices failed.
  c. If the rehearsal is rerun before these are captured, the rest of this plan is noise. Hard stop here until captured.

Step 2 — Rule out stale fixture artifacts (the cheap path)
  a. For each of the three manifests, read its provenance metadata (whatever the writer stamps: source version, builder version, compaction epoch, fixture-id). Compare to the current staging shard-keeper build's expected manifest schema and compaction rules.
  b. If any of the three stamps predate the current build or were produced by a different compaction pass, the "mismatch" is fixture drift, not a restore defect. Refresh that part of the fixture from a known-good source, rerun the rehearsal once. If clean, document provenance and close.
  c. If stamps match, fixture is not the cause. Move to step 3.

Step 3 — Rule out checksum-library version skew
  a. Pin the checksum library + version used by the restore-verification tool in this rehearsal.
  b. Pin the checksum library + version used when each manifest was written (from build provenance or fixture metadata).
  c. If they differ, the candidate failure modes are: different hash algorithm, different canonical encoding (key ordering, whitespace, line endings), or different compression framing (hash-then-decompress vs decompress-then-hash).
  d. Cheapest test: rebuild one manifest locally with the writer's library version and compare the resulting checksum to the stored value. If it matches, skew is the cause. Pin the version in the rehearsal harness, rerun once, document.
  e. If the checksum still doesn't match with the writer's library, move to step 4.

Step 4 — Isolate an actual restore defect
  a. Pick one of the three manifests and run the restore path on it with verbose logging around the verify step: log the exact bytes read, the canonicalization applied, and the checksum computed at verify time.
  b. Independently confirm the bytes-on-disk match what the manifest claims (size, header, body) before any checksum is computed.
  c. Run the same restore code path on a known-good manifest from the same fixture to confirm the path produces correct checksums on good inputs.
  d. If the good manifest verifies cleanly and the failing ones diverge only at the checksum step, the restore code is hashing different bytes than the writer did. Capture the exact divergence (encoding, framing, key ordering). Do not patch — write up the defect.
  e. Hard stop at the first reproducible defect. Do NOT rerun the rehearsal against an unknown restore path. Hand the code fix to the Cyrus-team backup under your oversight.

Step 5 — Gate before rerun
  - Stale fixture confirmed  → refresh fixture, no code change, record provenance, rerun once.
  - Skew confirmed           → pin library version, record, rerun once.
  - Restore defect confirmed → pause. No rerun. Open a defect, document evidence, schedule fix under pairing.
  - If steps 2–4 are inconclusive, do not rerun. Stop and escalate.

Pairing posture throughout
  - You drive diagnostic authority. Wes can take keyboard on read-only inspection (manifest reads, version pins, log capture) but does not modify fixture, library pins, or restore code solo.
  - Cyrus-team backup owns the actual restore-code fix path if step 4 confirms a defect.
  - No laptop deploys. Scope stays at the three named manifests.
  - Record each step's evidence (inputs, outputs, stamps, versions) before moving to the next.

One framing note: ordering matters because each step is cheaper and safer than the next. Step 2 costs a fixture diff. Step 3 costs a library pin + one local rebuild. Step 4 is the only one that touches the restore code path, and it's the only one that can produce a real defect. Don't skip ahead — the temptation to jump straight to "is the restore broken" is exactly how rehearsal diagnoses turn into scope creep.
