Spinach-feta baked eggs with warm pita and a yogurt-lemon sauce. One skillet, eggs go in last, pita warms during the egg set, sauce sits and gets better while everything else happens.

T-minus 25 min (start ~6:35, serve ~7:00):

6:35 — Yogurt sauce (do first, it rests): small bowl, ~3/4 cup yogurt, squeeze of half a lemon, one grated garlic clove (microplane if you have it, otherwise crush to a paste with the side of a knife + pinch salt), pinch of salt, a glug of olive oil on top. Stir, leave on the counter. 2 min.

6:37 — Wilt the spinach. Same oven-safe skillet, olive oil over medium heat. Thinly slice 2 garlic cloves, soft-sweat 30–45 sec (don't brown). Add spinach in handfuls with a pinch of salt, stirring until just collapsed and any liquid is mostly gone, 3–4 min. Squeeze in a little lemon. Push it into an even layer.

6:42 — Make 4 shallow wells in the spinach. Crack 4 eggs into the wells (crack each on the counter, not the edge). Crumble a generous handful of feta (~1/2 cup) over and around — not on top of the yolks. Salt the yolks lightly, pepper.

6:44 — Into a 400°F oven (or cover the skillet, lowest possible heat, if you want to skip the oven). Timer for 7 min. This is also when you start the pita: stack, wrapped in foil or a towel, into the oven for the last 4 min, or straight on a gas burner flame one at a time for ~20 sec/side, or a hot dry skillet.

6:51 — Check eggs. Whites just set, yolks still soft = done. If whites are still translucent on top, give it 60–90 sec more. Pull the skillet and the pita at the same time.

6:54 — Skillet goes on a trivet on the table. Pita in a pile next to it (or torn into quarters). Yogurt sauce in a bowl with a spoon. Done.

Why the order works: the sauce is the only thing that improves by sitting, so it goes first and you never think about it again. Spinach is forgiving — it can sit in the pan while you crack eggs without overcooking. Eggs are the only thing that punishes waiting, so they're last and finish at minute 7. Pita shares the oven time with the eggs so nothing's competing for a burner at the end.

If you want a green thing on the side without effort: a quick lemon-and-oil dressed handful of whatever raw crunchy green you have (arugula, romaine, whatever) — not necessary, but it's 90 seconds if you have it.

Don't cut into the eggs before she sits down; the yolks staying intact is half the appeal and you'll just be standing there waiting if you plate them early.

DIAGNOSIS — your read is correct. Aerator clog is the most common cause of
"both sides weak at one fixture, everything else fine." Grit + mineral flakes is
exactly what scale and sediment look like. Kitchen normal rules out building-side
pressure. Aerator-off flow normal confirms the bottleneck is at the spout
outlet, not at the cartridge or supply lines. You don't need to touch the
shutoffs for this job.

TOOLS / WHAT TO GATHER
  - Old soft toothbrush (best tool for the screen)
  - Small bowl for soaking parts
  - White vinegar (cheap, gentle, dissolves calcium carbonate)
  - Clean rag or paper towels
  - Wooden toothpick or plastic pick for stubborn holes
  - Flashlight or headlamp (handy under the spout)
  - Phone camera — photograph the aerator and the part stack before disassembly
  - Optional: food-safe silicone plumber's grease ONLY if a rubber washer feels
    dry after cleaning (do not use petroleum jelly / Vaseline on rubber seals)
  - Optional: PTFE tape only if you find damaged threads
  - Keep Kibo away from the vinegar bowl and any small parts on the floor

DISASSEMBLY
  - Aerators are typically: housing (outer ring) -> flow restrictor disc ->
    rubber washer/gasket -> fine screen -> sometimes a flow-straightener
  - Most unscrew by hand, gently clockwise from your view looking at the
    spout. Hand-tight is all that was used at the factory.
  - If it won't budge by hand: wrap the spout chrome with a rag or two layers
    of masking tape before using pliers/channel-lock, so the finish isn't
    chewed up. Adjustable pliers with a rag works; a proper aerator wrench is
    cheaper than refinishing the faucet.
  - Lay parts out on a clean towel IN ORDER. Take the phone photo first.
    The order matters on reassembly.
  - Do NOT force anything that feels stuck. Stop signs below.

CLEANING — DO
  - Soak the screen and housing in white vinegar for 30-60 minutes. Heavy
    scale can go a few hours. Warm vinegar works faster than cold.
  - After soaking, scrub the screen gently with the old toothbrush, both
    sides, in the direction of the mesh (not across it).
  - Use a wooden toothpick or plastic pick to clear individual holes — the
    point is to push scale out, not to widen the holes.
  - Rinse thoroughly under running water so no grit is redeposited.

CLEANING — DO NOT
  - No metal tools on the screen. Pins, needles, screwdrivers, wire — they
    stretch or tear the fine mesh and the aerator is ruined. A picked screen
    sprays sideways forever.
  - No abrasive pads. No Scotch-Brite, no steel wool. They scratch the chrome
    and the housing.
  - No harsh acids (muriatic, hydrochloric). Overkill, dangerous in a
    bathroom, and they will damage rubber seals and finishes.
  - No bleach on the rubber washer — it degrades EPDM/nitrile over time.
  - No CLR on rubber or plastic parts without checking the label; CLR is
    fine on the metal screen but can attack seals. Vinegar is the safer
    default and is sufficient for typical scale.
  - Don't soak the rubber washer for hours — a few minutes is fine; overnight
    in vinegar can swell some rubbers.
  - Don't use Vaseline/petroleum jelly on the rubber gasket. If you want to
    re-lubricate, use a silicone-based plumber's grease sparingly.

REASSEMBLY
  - Dry-fit all parts in the order you removed them. Confirm orientation of
    the restrictor disc (notched side usually faces the screen).
  - Hand-tighten the housing only. Snug, not forced. Overtightening cracks
    the housing or deforms the seal and you'll get a persistent drip from
    the seam that's much worse than the original problem.
  - If the threads feel gritty or cross-thread slightly, back it off and
    retry. Never force a misaligned start.
  - The rubber washer/gasket belongs between the housing and the spout face
    to seal. If it's missing or pinched, the aerator will leak.

TEST
  - Run both hot and cold, low and high. Flow should be restored and roughly
    equal between sides.
  - Watch the aerator seam for any drip, even a slow one.
  - Check under the sink again with a dry paper towel — you didn't disturb
    the supply lines, but a quick dry check after the work is cheap.
  - Run for a minute or two, then recheck under the sink. Some drips only
    show up after the lines are flowing and warm.

STOP AND CALL THE BUILDING SUPER IF ANY OF THESE APPEAR
  - The aerator housing is stuck hard and you can't free it without risking
    damage to the spout finish or the housing itself. The super has the right
    tools; forcing it now risks a cracked spout that becomes a leak.
  - Threads on the spout or inside the housing look stripped, corroded, or
    deformed. Don't tape over damage and force it; that's a future leak.
  - When you run water with the aerator off, water appears anywhere it
    shouldn't: around the base of the spout, around the handle, under the
    handle trim. That's the valve/cartridge, not the aerator — different job.
  - The rubber washer is missing or crumbled — don't substitute without the
    correct replacement; mismatched seals leak.
  - After reassembly, the aerator seam drips and re-seating doesn't fix it.
    Stop, take it apart, inspect. If the housing is warped, that's a
    replacement part, not a force-it-tighter situation.
  - Any new moisture under the sink appears, even small. Given the packing-
    nut history on the cold shutoff, do not assume it's the same thing — get
    it looked at.
  - The supply shutoffs under the sink don't fully close when you test them.
    If a real shutoff is ever needed (it shouldn't be for this job), you
    need working valves. The super should know.
  - Flow is still weak with the aerator fully removed and the screen cleaned.
    That's a different problem — possibly the cartridge or a supply-line
    restriction — and not an aerator job anymore.

PRACTICAL NOTES FOR TODAY
  - Saturday morning is fine to do this. The work is at the spout, no water
    needs to be shut off, and a slow vinegar soak doesn't require attention.
  - Don't run the dishwasher or washing machine until you're sure nothing
    else is going on with the supply side — not because of the aerator, but
    as a habit when any plumbing question is in flight.
  - If everything goes clean and reassembly seals, this is a 20-30 minute
    job plus soak time. No need to call the super preemptively.
  - If you do need to call, lead with "bathroom faucet aerator is clogged,
    cleaned it, flow is back / not back" rather than the longer history —
    the super has seen this exact thing dozens of times.

Good signal that your diagnostic was already on the right track. Send the
parts to the vinegar soak and reassemble in the same order they came out.

Clean resolution. Vinegar + brushing is exactly the right chemistry for mineral-clogged aerator screens, and the ten-minute dry check covering both the faucet and the shutoffs was the right scope — that confirms nothing upstream got disturbed while you had the aerator out.

One small forward note: if the flow drops again within a few weeks, the grit source is probably deeper than the screen (building-side supply lines) rather than another aerator clog, and a super check would be the better call than another disassembly.

Failure mechanism

Expiration is computed correctly in process: time.Now().Add(30 * time.Minute) produces a time.Time with both an absolute instant and a location. The bug is the persist/parse round-trip on that field.

The shape consistent with your "persist and parse, not math" framing and with the immediate-expiry-after-restart symptom is:

  Write:  expiresAt.Format("2006-01-02T15:04:05")      // layout has no zone
  Read:   t, _ := time.Parse("2006-01-02T15:04:05", s) // defaults to UTC

A Format call with a layout lacking Z07:00 drops the timezone designator and emits a bare wall-clock string. Parse on the same layout returns UTC. The absolute instant is silently shifted by ±(local offset) on the round-trip.

Why this fires only "after restart" and only in the DST replay:

Steady-state recovery uses in-memory monotonic time, so the bug never surfaces in normal operation. The round-trip only happens across restart, which is the whole point of the replay harness.

The DST replay is the first test that required staging to run with TZ=America/New_York instead of TZ=UTC. With UTC the round-trip was correct by accident — both sides agreed the value was UTC. With America/New_York the offset between written wall clock and parsed-back UTC is -5h (EST) or -4h (EDT). A lease acquired at 2024-03-10T01:30:00 EST (06:30 UTC) is written as "2024-03-10T01:30:00", reads back as 01:30 UTC, and trails the original by five hours. After restart, time.Now() > parsedExpiry evaluates against the current EDT clock, which is well past the trailing parsed instant. A 30-minute lease reads as "expired ~5h ago" — i.e., immediately expired. A post-DST lease (acquired at 03:30 EDT, 07:30 UTC) writes as "2024-03-10T03:30:00", reads as 03:30 UTC, and trails by four hours — same outcome, just a different absolute offset.

Smallest unambiguous storage fix

Replace the lossy string format with an absolute-integer encoding. Two options, in preference order:

1.  Unix-epoch integer (preferred). No string, no tz, no parser, bit-exact round-trip:

      Write:  strconv.AppendInt(buf, expiresAt.UnixNano(), 10)
      Read:   n, _ := strconv.ParseInt(s, 10, 64)
              expiresAt := time.Unix(0, n)

    Hot-path comparison becomes time.Now().UnixNano() > expiresAtUnixNano with no parse step. If the lease record is binary, use binary.BigEndian.PutUint64 for the same effect.

2.  RFC3339Nano with explicit UTC (minimum-surgery fallback if the field's wire format can't change without a schema migration):

      Write:  expiresAt.UTC().Format(time.RFC3339Nano)
      Read:   time.Parse(time.RFC3339Nano, s)

    Forcing .UTC() on write makes the offset unambiguous regardless of time.Local. Still relies on a layout string, so it's slightly more fragile than option 1, but it's a one-line diff per side.

I'd recommend option 1. The reason: option 2 fails in the same layout-drift shape as the original bug; epoch eliminates the string-format variable entirely.

Focused tests

Table-driven, gofmt-strict, TZ=America/New_York set inside the test (not the process env) so the test is self-contained. Each row: acquireAt, reloadAt, expected validity and remaining duration. Use time.Time.Equal (compares absolute instant, ignores location) for round-trip assertions.

Spring-forward boundary:

  Row 1 — acquired 30 real min before the jump, reloaded just after acquire:
    acquireAt:  2024-03-10T01:30:00-05:00   (06:30 UTC)
    reloadAt:   2024-03-10T01:45:00-05:00   (15 real min later)
    expect:     lease valid, ~15 min remaining

  Row 2 — same lease, reloaded across the DST jump (60 real min later):
    acquireAt:  2024-03-10T01:30:00-05:00
    reloadAt:   2024-03-10T03:30:00-04:00
    expect:     lease expired

  Row 3 — acquired just after the jump:
    acquireAt:  2024-03-10T03:30:00-04:00   (07:30 UTC)
    reloadAt:   2024-03-10T03:45:00-04:00   (15 real min later)
    expect:     lease valid, ~15 min remaining

Ordinary date (baseline regression, same TZ):

  Row 4 — non-DST day, neutral hour:
    acquireAt:  2024-02-15T14:30:00-05:00   (19:30 UTC)
    reloadAt:   2024-02-15T14:45:00-05:00
    expect:     lease valid, ~15 min remaining

  Row 5 — exact round-trip, no clock advance:
    acquireAt:  2024-02-15T14:30:00-05:00
    reloadAt:   same as acquireAt
    expect:     reloaded.Equal(acquireAt) == true
    expect:     lease duration == 30 min exactly

Two extra assertions worth adding to the table:

  - The serialized form must not contain -05:00, -04:00, EST, or EDT substrings. That fails the test if anyone later swaps the format back to one that emits a zone, re-introducing the original class of bug.
  - A row asserting that acquireAt.Add(30*time.Minute) lands on a valid instant in time.Local even when the math crosses 02:00 on March 10. This guards against any future "wall-clock arithmetic" refactor — e.g., time.Date(..., now.Hour(), now.Minute()+30, ..., time.Local) — which would silently produce a 90-minute lease across the gap.

---
**Fail-closed behavior required for Lantern importer (permission snapshots are not safe to reuse)**

Surfacing this as a failure-mode exception because the current draft is unsafe, not because it's an ordinary admission issue.

The draft snapshots source permissions at job start and lets a retry resume under that old snapshot. That's wrong: if access is revoked mid-run, a retry would happily continue fetching and then publish before the next permission sweep, which means we'd publish imported material we no longer have authority to read.

Required behavior, fail-closed:

- **Reauthorize before each source-page fetch.** No page is fetched under a stale snapshot, including on retry. If the reauthorization check fails or is unavailable, the fetch does not happen and any in-flight partial material is treated as untrusted.
- **Reauthorize again immediately before publication.** This is a separate check from the per-page one, run as late as possible in the job. Publication must not proceed if this check fails or cannot be completed.
- **Invalidate partial imported material on denial.** If any authorization check fails at any point — per-page, pre-publish, or via an external revocation signal — every partially-imported artifact for that job must be invalidated: discard the in-memory buffer, drop any staged-but-unpublished records, and mark the job so no downstream consumer can resurrect the material (no "promote on next successful run," no retained staging table). Invalidation must be observable, not just an internal flag.
- **Retries must start with a fresh authorization context.** A retry must not reuse the original job's permission snapshot, token cache, or any derived "still authorized" state. It must perform a fresh authorization pass before its first fetch, and is subject to the same per-fetch and pre-publish reauthorization as a first run. There is no "resume under previous auth" path.

In addition to the above, please add explicit test coverage in this failure-modes doc for:

- Revocation between job start and first retry → partial material discarded, no publication.
- Revocation between last successful page fetch and pre-publish check → publication blocked, partial material invalidated.
- Revocation during a retry that began with a fresh authorization context → that retry fails closed; a subsequent retry must re-authorize again.
- A retry that, for any reason, attempts to reuse the original snapshot → treated as a failure, not as a successful re-auth.

This should be treated as a contract change, not a tuning item: the current snapshot-and-resume design is the bug.

The current draft snapshots permissions at job start and lets the retry resume under that snapshot. That permits a publish-before-sweep window: pages can be fetched and the room can be published under an authorization that was revoked mid-job, with cleanup deferred to the next permission sweep. The concrete failure sequence makes the issue concrete:

  - Job starts with 10 source pages. Snapshot taken.
  - Pages 1–4 fetched under the snapshot.
  - Source access revoked. The snapshot is now stale at exactly the moment it matters.
  - Worker fails before page 5.
  - Retry resumes at page 5 under the original snapshot — pages 5–10 fetch under an authorization that no longer exists.
  - Current draft publishes once page 10 lands, before any sweep runs.

The snapshot is load-bearing in exactly the wrong way: it converts a real-time authorization check into a stale-cache read at the two moments that matter (each fetch and the publish). "Rely on the next permission sweep to hide the room" is not a containment story — it's a window where the importer is the system that publishes content the source no longer authorizes, and a downstream sweep is the only thing standing between that and a visible artifact.

Required changes:

  1. Reauthorize immediately before every source-page fetch. No fetch may run against a snapshot taken at job start. The snapshot, if retained at all, is informational — it cannot gate an actual fetch or a publish.

  2. Reauthorize immediately before publication, against the same identity and target room the job will publish to. The publish path needs its own current authorization check, not "we got pages earlier so we must still be allowed."

  3. On any denial — at fetch or at the publish gate — fail closed. Abort the job. Discard any partial imported material held in working state; do not park it for a sweep, do not queue it for reconciliation. Do not create or publish the room. This is the same posture we took on the metrics-router label-name parity check: a partial or stale authorization must not become a publish path.

  4. A retry is a new job, not a continuation under the prior snapshot. It re-checks current authorization at every fetch and at publish. There is no "resume under original authorization" mode.

If the retry is meant to be cheaper than a from-scratch run, the efficiency story is durable progress markers + re-fetched content + reauthorization on every fetch — not a cached authorization that survives revocation.

Before approving, I'd want the diff to make two things explicit:

  - Where the publish gate performs its authorization check, and that it reads current state, not a stored snapshot.
  - What happens to partial imported material on a denial — deleted, not quarantined for later reconciliation.

One framing note, since it tends to come up: "reauthorize on every fetch" sounds expensive until you remember the alternative is publishing content under a revoked authorization and depending on a separate sweep to clean it up. The check is cheap; the publish is not.

Diagnosis confirms: averaging queue_age across the whole service weights the canary slice by its share of the population. At a typical 1-2% canary, a bad canary moves the mean by 1-2% of its regression, which won't cross a reasonable threshold until the regression is severe enough to move the whole service. By that point it's a whole-service incident, not a canary signal.

Smallest alert correction that preserves rollout separation:

Scope the existing rule to the canary slice only. Add the canary marker as a label selector on the queue_age series. If the current rule is roughly:

  avg(queue_age{service="metrics-router"}) > T for 10m

the smallest fix is:

  avg(queue_age{service="metrics-router", canary="true"}) > T for 10m

(substitute whatever the actual canary-marker label name is on queue_age — most likely `canary="true"` or `canary_source="..."`, but verify against a current canary window).

This preserves rollout separation because canary and stable become independent populations with independent alerts. A canary regression fires the canary alert; a stable regression is no longer caught by this rule and either needs a separate canary="false" rule or is accepted as out of scope for this fix.

Before Nadia ships, three things to verify:

1. The canary marker label actually exists on the queue_age series in Prometheus today. If it doesn't, the rule evaluates against an empty series and never fires — the fix silently becomes a no-op. This is the highest-risk assumption. One PromQL query against a current canary window confirms it.

2. The label name on the canary hosts is what we expect. The April 17 lesson applies: if the label name differs between the emitter (metrics-router) and the alert evaluator, the fix won't catch what it should. Confirm the label round-trips through the pipeline.

3. Empty-series handling. With no canary hosts routed, avg() of an empty series is NaN. The `for` window usually absorbs this, but verify the alert doesn't fire spuriously or get stuck in a pending state when the canary slice is at 0%.

Out of scope for this fix (flag, don't expand):

The existing rule is doing two jobs — canary monitoring and stable monitoring — with one rule. After the fix it does one. A canary-vs-stable ratio rule (alert when canary queue_age > N× stable) is a stronger signal in some respects, but it's a derived metric and not the smallest correction. Mention only.

Synthetic test expectations:

Positive (alert MUST fire):

1. Canary queue_age at 2× threshold for 10+ minutes, stable at 0. Old rule: silent (masked). New rule: fires within the `for` window.
2. Canary queue_age at threshold + 50%, sustained for the full 10m. Fires at the 10m mark.
3. Both slices above threshold simultaneously. Canary rule fires. If a stable-side rule is added later, it also fires — verify both behave independently.
4. Canary queue_age oscillating across threshold for the full 10m (e.g. 5m above, 5m below, repeating). Fires — the `for` window evaluates against the pending condition, not against continuous presence.

Negative (alert MUST NOT fire):

1. Stable queue_age at 2× threshold, canary at 0. Old rule: fires. New rule: silent. This is the headline behavior change — Nadia should be explicit that the canary-only rule will not catch a stable-only regression and either add a stable-side rule or accept that gap deliberately.
2. Canary queue_age stays at 0 for the full synthetic window. Silent.
3. Stable briefly spikes under the `for` window then recovers. Silent on both rules.
4. Single brief canary spike under the `for` window then recovers. Silent. Transient blips are not canary alerts; this is correct behavior.

Edge cases worth pinning in the test:

5. Empty canary slice (no canary hosts routed). Silent — no NaN-induced fire, no stuck pending state.
6. Mixed population where some metrics-router hosts emit the canary label and others don't. Those hosts' queue_age is excluded from the canary alert. Confirm Nadia wants this — almost certainly yes, but worth being explicit, because it means hosts with the label missing are unmonitored by the canary rule and a misconfigured emitter could silently fall off the alert.

Test scaffolding (Nadia's call, not a directive):

Drive a fixed queue_age series into the synthetic eval rather than depending on prod load. Use a synthetic instance or label set tagged with a deterministic marker so each case is hermetic. Each case is its own eval window with an expected `alertstate` outcome — one row per case, one assertion per row, no shared state between rows.

Verdict: the current rule does NOT produce the expected behavior. The canary slice is invisible to it.

Why, by the math:
  canary pods:   4 * ~24s = ~96
  stable pods:  36 * ~1.5s = ~54
  service-wide avg: 150 / 40 = ~3.75s (matches the stated 3.4)
  threshold: 15s
  3.75 < 15, so for the entire 12-minute window the predicate never becomes true even once. With `for: 5m` requiring the predicate to hold continuously, a rule that never satisfies the predicate cannot fire. Zero pages.

Root cause is aggregation masking. `avg by (service)` collapses every pod in the service into one bucket. Canary pods are a small fraction of the population by construction (low traffic share, low pod count), so their elevated queue age is diluted by the larger stable pool. This is the exact failure shape that matters most: a bad change at 10% rollout is the scenario you most want to catch early, and the current rule makes it structurally invisible.

Note for the record that this is not a `for` duration problem and not a threshold problem. The breach never reaches the threshold at all in the service-wide view.

Proposed fix: put `rollout` into the grouping so canary and stable are evaluated as independent series.

  avg by (service, rollout) (queue_age_seconds) > 15
  for: 5m

Behavior under the same synthetic:
  canary series:  4 pods, ~24s avg -> above 15 -> predicate true at T+0, alert fires at T+5m and is still firing through minute 12 (alert active for ~7m before the test ends). Matches expected.
  stable series:  4 pods... wait, 36 pods, ~1.5s avg -> below 15 -> never fires. Matches expected.

Cardinality cost of adding `rollout` is small: `rollout` takes a fixed, small enum (canary / stable in practice, occasionally baseline), so this does not introduce a label-explosion risk and is consistent with the Cardinality Guardrails posture for label changes touching metrics-router, shard-keeper, or rollup-service.

Two alternatives worth naming, with why I would not pick them as the default:
  max by (service, rollout) (queue_age_seconds) > 15
    Would also separate the slices, and would fire slightly earlier because a single canary pod at 26s alone exceeds the threshold. More sensitive, but also more prone to single-pod noise if pods are heterogeneously loaded. For queue age specifically, average over the rollout slice is usually the right grain.
  quantile_over_time(0.95, queue_age_seconds[5m]) by (service, rollout) > 15
    Strictly more sensitive than avg, but heavier and rarely needed once the masking is removed. Reconsider only if avg turns out to be too forgiving at the per-pod level.

Recommendation: ship the grouping fix (`avg by (service, rollout)`) as the minimal correct change. Verify in staging that the new series evaluate independently before promoting the rule, and confirm that any existing alert routing or silencing keyed on the service label still resolves the new canary series correctly.

DIFFERENCE: PRESENT-BUT-FLAT vs ABSENT

A counter that exists but is not increasing means the exporter is still scraping, but the nightly job has stopped making progress — this is the "stuck" state.

A series that has gone away means the exporter has stopped reporting entirely. Prometheus has no sample at all to evaluate.

`rate(metric[5m])` returns the literal value 0 when the counter is present but not advancing. When the series is absent, `rate()` has fewer samples in its window than it needs and returns no vector at all — there is nothing to compare to zero. That is why `rate(...) == 0 for: 15m` cannot enter pending once the exporter disappears; the comparison is over an empty result, not a zero.

THE RIGHT 15-MINUTE `absent_over_time` EXPRESSION

    expr: absent_over_time(batch_completed_total{job="nightly"}[15m])
    for: 0m

`absent_over_time` emits a single sample with value 1 and no labels when no samples of the metric exist in the window, and emits nothing when samples are present. The 15-minute window already encodes the duration, so `for: 0m` is correct (any non-zero `for:` would delay firing on top of the window and lengthen the detection time beyond 15 minutes).

Two things to carry into the rule definition explicitly:
  - The output has no labels. Add the `job="nightly"` context in the alert's `summary` and `description` annotations, otherwise the page will read as if it came from nowhere.
  - This rule catches only the absent case. A continuously scraped counter that is simply not advancing will not fire it. If the customer also wants to alert on "stuck but alive", keep the existing `rate(...)[5m] == 0` rule alongside this one as a separate alert — the two failure modes need separate signals.

TEST EXPECTATIONS

  Case A — no samples in the last 15 minutes (exporter gone, series absent)
    Expression evaluates to: {}=1
    Alert state: FIRES (positive — this is the case the original rule misses)
    Sanity check on the old rule: rate(...)==0 returns no vector and never enters pending — confirms the bug.

  Case B — a recent sample exists (younger than 15 minutes)
    Expression evaluates to: empty vector
    Alert state: does NOT fire (negative — exporter is alive, even if quiet between batches)

  Case C — continuously scraped counter with a flat value (samples present on every scrape, value not changing)
    Expression evaluates to: empty vector
    Alert state: does NOT fire (negative — series is present and being scraped)
    Note: by design. Coverage of this case is the job of the kept `rate(...)[5m] == 0` rule, not this one.

A clean test run produces: A fires, B silent, C silent — in that order. If A is silent, the range vector still contains a sample and the 15-minute absence window has not elapsed; if B or C fires, the rule is matching on label presence rather than sample absence and needs to be re-checked.

The right frame for the proposal isn't "Figma or the repo" — it's "what's the contract that holds regardless of which surface is canonical."

That contract has four pieces:

1. One machine-readable canonical source. Whichever surface owns token semantics — name, value, semantic role, deprecation state — that's the source of truth. The other surface is a consumer, not a co-author.

2. Downstream representations are generated, not edited. Figma variables, the engineering JSON, any CSS / Swift / Tailwind bindings, docs — all produced from the canonical source by a build step. No hand-copying.

3. Changes are versioned. Every change to the canonical source has a reviewable history with ownership, so consumers can pin to a known version and migrations are explicit rather than implicit.

4. Drift is checked in CI, not by humans noticing. A job that compares the canonical source to every generated artifact fails the build the moment they diverge. The fix is always to regenerate — never to hand-edit an artifact back into sync.

Anya's proposal should commit to that contract. The choice of which surface is canonical is a decision for her and her team, driven by who owns semantic intent and which tool supports machine-readable exports with versioned history. The proposal's job is to lock the contract; the team's job is to pick the surface inside it.

Hi [name],

Quick clarification on the 413 you saw against ingest-edge, because the limit works a bit differently than the assumption in your bug report.

What we enforce. The 10 MiB cap applies to the *decoded* request body, not the compressed bytes you put on the wire. We have to decode before we can process the payload, so the cap exists to bound decompression and downstream memory on our side — not to restrict how much you can send over the network.

Why gzip doesn't get you a larger logical request. If anything, the opposite. A 1.86 MiB gzipped upload that expands to ~14.9 MiB costs us strictly more than a 10 MiB uncompressed upload — we have to allocate and decompress the full expanded body before we can do anything with it. So gzip shrinks your network usage and our ingress bandwidth, but it doesn't change (and slightly increases) the resource budget we apply on the decoded side. Your batch is a single logical request either way.

Recommended batching and retry procedure. Until we have a different conversation about limits, please keep each *decoded* batch comfortably under 10 MiB. A conservative target is roughly 8–9 MiB of decoded payload per request to leave headroom for OTLP framing, retries, and any small growth between flushes.

  2. If it's over 8 MiB, split into N chunks by record count so each chunk's decoded size lands around 6–8 MiB. Don't split below ~4 MiB decoded per chunk — smaller chunks waste compression ratio and inflate your wire size without buying anything on our side.
  3. Send each chunk as its own gzip-compressed request. Use distinct idempotency keys per chunk so a retry of one chunk doesn't duplicate the whole window.
  4. On 413, don't retry the same payload. Halve the chunk's decoded size and retry the chunk with a new idempotency key. The 10 MiB cap is a hard ceiling, not a soft one, so a retry of an oversized payload will just 413 again.
  5. On a 5xx or a connection drop after the body was sent, retry the same chunk with the *same* idempotency key — those are the cases where the server may not have durably accepted what you sent.

  wire (compressed):   1,950,351 B  (~1.86 MB)
  decoded:            14,889,779 B (~14.2 MB)
  limit:              10,485,760 B (10 MB)
  expansion ratio:    ~7.6x
  overage:            ~4.4 MB / ~42% over limit

Why the limit is on decoded size:
  - the gateway holds the full decoded body in memory while it parses and routes
  - decoded size is the natural place to bound it; wire size is enforced separately at the LB / TLS layer for different reasons
  - the design protects against the classic "tiny zip bomb blows up the parser" shape — wire and decoded are intentionally not interchangeable

For the customer:
  - the 413 is correct, not a misconfiguration on our side
  - retrying the same payload will get another 413 — they should NOT retry until they shrink the decoded body
  - their retry buffer is at risk if they don't act; the failed payload is sitting on their side, not ours, and we have not accepted or buffered anything
  - concrete options, in order:
    1. split the batch into multiple requests, each comfortably under 10 MB decoded. If they're sending OTLP metrics, this is usually the right answer.
    2. reduce points-per-request (fewer points, more frequent sends).
    3. try snappy instead of gzip — same route, advertised, and the ratio may be friendlier for their data shape. Decoded size still rules either way.

For us:
  - no service change needed
  - no limit increase without a capacity review and a concrete answer to "why does this customer need 14+ MB decoded payloads, and is the workload pattern safe at a higher cap?"
  - watch for whether this becomes a pattern across customers before treating it as anything other than a single-account sizing question

Suggested relay text for Support → customer (short, technical, no hand-holding):

  "The 10 MB request limit on ingest-edge is enforced against the decoded body, not the wire size. Your 1.86 MB gzipped request decompressed to ~14.2 MB, which exceeds the limit. The 413 is expected behavior. To resume, split each batch into requests that decompress to under 10 MB (fewer points per request, or multiple smaller requests). The same route accepts Content-Encoding: snappy if you'd like to try a different codec. The rejected payload is on your side; we did not retain it. Please confirm when your client has been adjusted and we can re-check ingress."

If you want this turned into a runbook note (the "decoded vs wire" framing tends to come up repeatedly with customers new to OTLP/protobuf+gzip), I can draft a short entry for rb_ingest_edge — but I'd hold off until I see whether this is one customer or a pattern. One case isn't evidence.

Limit the search to places she can reach without going back into the hospital:

PHASE 3 — NOTIFY THE CHARGE NURSE (FYI, after she has facts)

PRE-REPAIR CHECKLIST — UNLOCKED PHONE, 2:00 PM SLOT

Your current state (no swelling, no heat, no odor, no exposed battery, no frame bend, intact glass near the charge port, all functions working) is fine to keep powered on for handoff. The triggers to power down instead are in section 5.

  - Belt-and-suspenders: AirDrop / USB-copy the photo library and any must-not-lose folders (notes, message exports, authenticator app backup codes screenshot) to a second device or laptop. Backups fail quietly; this is your real proof.
  - Sanity check: backup size should be non-trivial (GB-scale, not 0 MB). If it shows 0 MB or a stale date, the backup is not actually running.

2. ACCOUNTS & PAYMENT — TIGHTEN BEFORE HANDOFF
  - Remove all cards from Apple Pay / Google Pay / Samsung Wallet before leaving home.
  - Sign out of anything that doesn't need to be on the device for a screen swap: banking apps, password manager, work SSO / email, crypto, health, Venmo, anything with stored credentials. Re-login when you get it back.
  - "Find My" / Find My Device: leave ON. It does not block the repair, and it is your recovery path if the device is lost in transit. Confirm you know the Apple ID / Google password and 2FA method, otherwise you can get locked out post-repair.
  - Revoke active sessions on email and banking from another device if you want a tighter posture (optional, conservative).
  - Unpair Apple Watch / Galaxy Watch / earbuds if you want them off the device, but this is optional.

3. MAINTENANCE / REPAIR MODE
  - Samsung (Android 13+): Settings → Battery and device care → Maintenance Mode → turn on. This creates a separate guest profile; your data is hidden.
  - Pixel (Android 14+): similar Maintenance Mode exists on Pixels running current builds — check Settings → System → Maintenance Mode.
  - iPhone: no equivalent. The practical substitute is signing out of sensitive apps (section 2) and trusting the work-order scope.
  - If your phone supports Maintenance Mode, enable it before you leave; it is the single best privacy control available.

4. DOCUMENT BEFORE HANDOFF
  - Photos of: top-left spidering, the rest of the frame, the back, the corners. Same for any pre-existing dings/scratches elsewhere, so they aren't attributed to the repair.
  - Confirm the serial number / IMEI on the work order matches the device (Settings → General → About, or on the SIM tray).
  - Confirm the work order says "screen replacement only" — not a vague "display repair." If it says anything about battery, frame, or "as needed," ask them to specify.
  - Ask: OEM / genuine part or aftermarket? Will the IP68 water-resistance rating be preserved or voided?
  - Note handoff time and the promised return time on the receipt.
  - Keep the receipt. Photograph it.

5. POWER-DOWN TRIGGERS — DO NOT HAND OFF IF YOU SEE
Your current phone does not show any of these. But before you leave (and again in the next ~3 hours before the slot), power down and skip the screen swap if you observe any of:
  - Case separation — back glass or screen lifting away from the frame (battery swell).
  - Sweet chemical or burning odor.
  - Heat during normal use or while charging, beyond what you'd expect.
  - Visible battery exposure through any crack, or bulging you can feel when you run a fingertip around the inside edge of the spidering.
  - Screen flickering, vertical lines, or touch dead zones that weren't there this morning.
  - A dark / discolored patch spreading from the impact site.
  - Device rocks when placed flat on a table (press a corner; lift opposite corner — gap = swell).
  - Crack running from the impact toward the bottom edge (where the battery sits) or the frame visibly twisted.
  - Loose glass fragments at the charge-port edge that could enter the port when a cable is plugged in.

Any one of these → power down, do not charge, the repair becomes a battery-and-frame assessment first, not a screen swap. Phone the shop before you leave and explain; a good shop will reschedule rather than press on a swollen pack.

LAST-MINUTE BEFORE YOU LEAVE
  - Charge to roughly 60–80%. Lithium prefers partial state; a full-to-100% handoff is unnecessary.
  - SIM and SD card: take them if you want to reduce exposure, but they are not required.
  - Confirm you can get back into the phone after the repair (know the passcode; if Face ID / fingerprint will need re-enrollment, that's normal).

Hand-off is fine to proceed as planned. Good luck with the repair.

Review answer for Wes — request-buffer pool in metrics-router

Verdict: reject this shape. The underlying optimization is sound, accept it conditionally once bounded and proven.

Why the current shape fails:

  910 MiB retained against a 1 GiB pod limit is 89% of the budget consumed by one structure. That leaves no room for Go runtime, in-flight batches, OTel collector baseline plus its ~5% post-bump delta, queue depth under burst, or GC headroom, before OOMKill.

  Retained heap that does not fall back after traffic goes idle is the leak signature, not a warm-up curve. A pool with no eviction is a one-way valve; in the long run its retained set equals the high-water mark of buffers ever allocated, which on any non-trivial workload will reach the pod limit.

  The 34% allocation cut is real but it is a short-window measurement. On a long-lived pool the relevant cost is retained-set times concurrent in-flight, not allocation count. Steady-load at 90 minutes is also too short to call bounded; we have not seen warm-up complete, only a slice of it.

Smallest safe bound I would accept:

  High-water mark: 32 buffers at 8 MiB = 256 MiB hard cap. 25% of the pod limit.
  Low-water mark: 16 buffers at 8 MiB = 128 MiB, target after sustained idle. 50% of HWM.
  Warm floor: 2 buffers retained across idle, so the first request after idle does not pay allocator plus GC cost.
  Trim policy: drop one buffer per minute back toward LWM once utilization stays below 50% of LWM for 5 consecutive minutes. Anything more aggressive will thrash on bursty traffic; anything less will not actually return memory.
  Reasoning: 25% leaves roughly 750 MiB for runtime, queues, OTel, GC, and one unplanned spike. If we ever need more pool capacity the right move is a larger pod, not a larger pool, because that keeps the failure mode legible.

One number to push back on before locking the HWM. The 90-minute soak peaked around 910 MiB retained, which is roughly 113 concurrent buffers. If that represents realistic peak in-flight, then HWM at 32 means under burst 80+ requests per moment fall through to heap allocation and the 34% win degrades sharply. If the soak was a steady-rate stress that does not match actual bursty production, the peak is overstated. Either way, get the real production-traffic concurrent-in-flight number, from metrics or a canary replay, before the bound is final. Do not let the 34% headline drive the HWM; the retained-set story does.

Required tests before this moves forward. Each one needs explicit pass/fail thresholds in the PR, not "looks good."

  Steady-load soak. Sustained production p50 for at least 4 hours, not 90 minutes. Pass: retained heap stabilizes below HWM within 30 minutes of warm-up; RSS tracks retained within roughly 10%; zero GC-induced p99 latency tail spikes above current baseline; zero OOMs. The test must surface a monotonic-rise vs plateau signal so warm-up and a leak are not confused. If retained climbs continuously past HWM the test fails immediately; do not wait for OOM.

  Burst-and-idle. Ramp from idle to 3x peak production rate for 30 minutes, then drop to idle for 15. Pass: during burst the pool grows to HWM and stays there with no eviction; after idle begins, retained returns to within 5% of pre-burst baseline within 5 minutes. This is the test the current shape fails outright. Secondary check: the trim policy must not evict a buffer that is still checked out from the burst tail; in-flight buffers cannot be forcibly reclaimed.

  Concurrency. Drive concurrent in-flight where N is meaningfully larger than HWM, say 4x. Pass: pool stays at HWM, never exceeds it. Excess requests either wait on a bounded queue with an explicit wait counter, or fall through to heap allocation with an explicit counter; both counters are visible. No unbounded growth path. p99 latency stays within current baseline. The 34% allocation reduction still holds at sustained concurrency below HWM, which is the regime we actually run in. Failure mode the test must catch: a slow consumer holding one buffer for an unusual duration. Pool must not block behind it; new requests must continue to allocate, and the slow consumer must not stall the eviction timer.

Process gating:

  All three tests pass in staging with the numbers above written into the PR, not described verbally.
  Staging pass must hold clean for two consecutive weekdays. Tuesday and Wednesday staging; production cutover Thursday morning at the earliest, never Friday per the existing rule.
  Rollback is a single config flip reverting pool size to the previous bounded default; that path must be tested in staging before the canary, not after.
  Cache-key uniqueness and allocation-site checks remain on the pre-rollout checklist. Wes added those after the February cohort incident; they apply here too.

One framing point for the design review itself. If Wes leads with "34% fewer allocations" the room will underweight the memory risk. The right comparison is not "current code allocates X per op" but "at production concurrency for a full day, what is the retained-set footprint and does it return to baseline overnight." Make him produce that number before the review closes.

Looks like textbook seasonal allergic rhinitis after outdoor pollen exposure (late March in Brooklyn = early tree pollen, juniper/elm/maple). Symptom pattern fits and the negatives rule out the obvious look-alikes. Conservative plan below.

TONIGHT
- Shower and wash your hair before bed. Pollen sticks to hair and you transfer it to the pillow, then dose yourself all night.
- Saline nasal rinse (Neti pot or squeeze bottle with distilled/cooled-boiled water). Clears pollen from the nasal mucosa; cheap, no drug interaction, often surprisingly effective on its own. One rinse now, one in the morning.
- Cold compress or clean cool washcloth over closed eyes for the itch. Limit to ~10 min at a time.
- Keep bedroom window closed. If you run a fan, point it away from your face.
- Avoid rubbing your eyes. Worsens itch and can scratch the cornea.
- Skip alcohol tonight if you're going to take an oral antihistamine — they amplify sedation.

TOMORROW MORNING (before work)
- Saline rinse before leaving.
- Take your chosen oral antihistamine 30–60 min before any outdoor exposure for the steady blood level.
- If you'll be outside for a while, sunglasses and a hat reduce pollen contact with eyes/scalp.
- Continue the nasal rinse once midday if symptoms climb.

OTC OPTIONS — sedation-conscious for a workday
Picking from least to most sedating:

- Fexofenadine 180 mg (Allegra). Non-drowsy for most adults, 24-hr coverage. Best default if you want zero sedation risk. Take on an empty stomach — fruit juice and food can cut absorption.
- Loratadine 10 mg (Claritin). Also non-drowsy for most, 24-hr coverage. Slightly slower onset than cetirizine but very steady.
- Cetirizine 10 mg (Zyrtec). Effective, 24-hr coverage, but ~10–15% of people feel real sedation from it. If you've never tried it on a workday, don't debut it the morning of a meeting-heavy day.
- Intranasal fluticasone (Flonase) or triamcinolone (Nasacort). Most effective single agent for nasal symptoms. Not sedating. Caveat: takes 12+ hours to start helping and 3–7 days for full effect, so it's a "start now, expect relief tomorrow/two days out" tool, not an emergency one. Two sprays each nostril daily.
- Antihistamine eye drops — ketotifen 0.025% (Zaditor, Alaway). OTC, directly targets the itchy-watery-eye component. Wait 10 min after the drop before putting contacts back in, and don't use it while wearing contacts. Non-sedating.

What to AVOID on a workday:
- Diphenhydramine (Benadryl) — sedation + dry mouth + cognitive impairment. Don't.
- First-generation combo sleep-aid products that contain doxylamine or diphenhydramine.
- "Allergy plus decongestant" combos (e.g., Claritin-D, Allegra-D, Zyrtec-D) — the pseudoephedrine can cause jitteriness, insomnia, and raise heart rate. Not needed here; your symptom list doesn't include congestion.

Redundancy note: it's fine to combine a non-sedating oral antihistamine + a nasal steroid + a ketotifen eye drop. They're different drug classes and target different symptom clusters.

WARNING SIGNS — more than a routine allergy flare, seek prompt care
Respiratory
- Wheezing, chest tightness, or shortness of breath (asthma or early anaphylaxis — same-day eval).
- Trouble speaking in full sentences, lips or fingertips turning bluish, or a high-pitched noise on inhale (stridor). This is the ER.
- Cough that produces colored sputum and doesn't clear, or cough that wakes you at night repeatedly.

Sinus / infectious
- Fever ≥ 38°C / 100.4°F, chills, or body aches (rules out simple allergy — think URI, flu, COVID).
- Facial pain/pressure, thick yellow or green nasal discharge, or tooth pain in the upper teeth — possible bacterial sinusitis.
- Symptoms that improve and then noticeably worsen 5–7 days in ("double-sick" pattern) — classic bacterial superinfection.
- Symptoms persisting beyond 10–14 days without a clear improvement trajectory.

Eye
- Eye pain (not itching), especially with light sensitivity or a foreign-body sensation — could be keratitis or abrasion from rubbing.
- Any change in vision: blur, halos around lights, loss of part of the visual field.
- Marked eye redness with thick yellow/green discharge (infectious conjunctivitis needs assessment, often antibiotic).
- Swelling around the eye with tenderness and warmth.

Systemic / allergic escalation
- Hives or rash spreading beyond the face/neck.
- Swelling of lips, tongue, throat, or face (anaphylaxis — ER, epinephrine).
- Dizziness, faintness, or a feeling of "impending doom" — get help now.
- Vomiting or significant abdominal pain soon after the sneezing started.

Minimal deterministic parser behavior

The nondeterminism comes from copying values via `for k, v := range rawMap`. Stop iterating the map. Instead, unmarshal into a struct where both keys are pointers, then make the dual-key case a hard error before any effective-value assignment:

    type rawConfig struct {
        MaxBatchBytes   *int64 `yaml:"max_batch_bytes"`
        MaxRequestBytes *int64 `yaml:"max_request_bytes"`
    }

    // after unmarshal, in this exact order:
    switch {
    case r.MaxBatchBytes != nil && r.MaxRequestBytes != nil:
        return fmt.Errorf("config sets both max_batch_bytes and max_request_bytes; remove the legacy key")
    case r.MaxRequestBytes != nil:
        eff.MaxRequestBytes = *r.MaxRequestBytes
    case r.MaxBatchBytes != nil:
        log.Deprecation("max_batch_bytes is deprecated, rename to max_request_bytes")
        eff.MaxRequestBytes = *r.MaxBatchBytes
    default:
        return fmt.Errorf("config missing required max_request_bytes")
    }

Field binding from YAML/JSON is deterministic; the map is never iterated; the only outcome for "both keys" is the explicit error. That is the minimum.

Why fail closed rather than picking a precedence

Picking "replacement wins" silently fixes the symptom but keeps the bug latent: a future change that introduces another shared key would reintroduce it, and the legacy key would never get cleaned out of configs. Production configs only contain `max_request_bytes`, so a dual-key config in the wild is always either a developer mistake or an in-progress migration that should fail loudly. The error message names both keys so the operator knows exactly what to delete.

Startup tests (table-driven, next to the existing parser tests)

1. replacement_only — `{max_request_bytes: 12582912}` — effective == 12582912, no deprecation log.
2. legacy_only — `{max_batch_bytes: 8388608}` — effective == 8388608, one deprecation log line.
3. both_keys — `{max_batch_bytes: 8388608, max_request_bytes: 12582912}` — load returns an error whose message contains both `max_batch_bytes` and `max_request_bytes`.
4. neither_key — `{}` — load returns an error mentioning `max_request_bytes`.
5. both_keys_determinism — run case 3 ten times back-to-back; assert the error message string and error type are byte-identical each time. Catches any accidental map-iteration that survives on the error path.
6. startup_failure_exits — boot the binary with the dual-key fixture and assert non-zero exit, error in stderr/logs. Startup failure should not silently fall back to defaults.

These four cases plus the determinism soak and the startup exit check cover the "rejected / legacy-only / replacement-only" requirements.

Live-reload tests

The reload path must parse the new bytes in isolation, validate fully, and only then atomically swap the live config pointer (`atomic.StorePointer` or `atomic.Value.Store`). Tests:

1. reload_replacement_increase — start V1 = 8 MiB, reload V2 = 12 MiB; assert active pointer changed and effective reads 12 MiB.
2. reload_replacement_decrease — same shape, opposite direction.
3. reload_legacy_only — reload legacy-only config; active pointer changed, effective matches legacy value, one deprecation log line.
4. reload_both_keys_rejected_and_preserved — start V1 = 8 MiB; attempt reload with dual-key fixture; assert all four of:
     - reload call returns the dual-key error
     - active pointer identity is unchanged (capture the pointer before, compare after — do not just compare values)
     - effective reads 8 MiB
     - one error log line names both keys
5. reload_malformed_yaml — same shape as 4: active pointer unchanged, error returned, no swap.
6. reload_recovery_after_failure — after a failed reload, a subsequent valid reload succeeds and updates effective normally. Proves the failed attempt did not poison internal state.
7. concurrent_reload_during_request — hold a goroutine continuously reading effective; in parallel fire a failing reload; assert every read returns the pre-reload value. Catches torn writes on a non-atomic `active = newCfg` style.

Failed-reload preservation, specifically

The single thing worth asserting is pointer-identity preservation, not just value equality. If the reload code does `active = newCfg` on a plain variable, the value can read correctly by accident while a half-written struct is in flight. Capture the `unsafe.Pointer` (or `atomic.Value` snapshot) before the failing reload and assert it is byte-equal after. That is the assertion that catches "swap happened even though we returned an error" bugs.

Startup and reload failure handling differ on purpose and the tests should pin that: a bad-config boot exits non-zero (do not run with a config you did not ask for); a reload failure leaves the process running on the existing active config and logs the error. The reload tests above cover the second half; the startup exit test in case 6 covers the first.

Two small follow-ons worth flagging in Nadia's PR description so reviewers do not have to ask

The deprecation log should include the config file path and the legacy key name, so operators grepping logs know which file to edit. And since production configs only contain `max_request_bytes`, the legacy branch is a transitional concession — worth a `TODO(deprecation)` comment with a removal date or trigger so this does not quietly become permanent.

Kibo is currently stable — alert, breathing normally, ambulating, no swelling, no vomiting. The licking and single drool are the expected localized oral irritation from calcium oxalate crystals in pothos. A small crescent bite is a low-dose exposure; this is a triage call, not an automatic ER rush. Call now for guidance, monitor closely for the next 4 hours, escalate on clear signals.

ORDERED IMMEDIATE RESPONSE

1. MOUTH DECONTAMINATION (next ~5 minutes)
   - Wipe the outside of his lips, gum-line, and the visible part of his tongue gently with a cool, damp cloth or paper towel. Goal: lift residual sap and loose crystals off the mucosa, do not grind them in.
   - Offer a small bowl of cool water. Let him choose to drink; do not syringe or pour into his mouth.
   - Optional, only if he takes it voluntarily: a small spoonful of plain yogurt, milk, or xylitol-free peanut butter. Dairy binds residual oxalate and soothes mucosa. Offer, never force.
   - Do not scrub. Do not probe inside the mouth. Do not try to fish out anything you cannot clearly see.

2. CALL NOW
   - First call: your regular vet. Saturday-morning hours or the answering service can triage based on Kibo's record.
   - If you can't reach your vet quickly, call ASPCA Animal Poison Control at 888-426-4435 (24/7, fee applies, roughly $95). They specialize in plant toxicology and will tell you whether ER is warranted. Pet Poison Helpline 855-764-7661 is equivalent.
   - This call is for guidance, not necessarily transport.

3. INFORMATION TO HAVE READY
   - Plant: pothos (Epipremnum aureum; also sold as Devil's Ivy / golden pothos). If you know the exact cultivar, say so.
   - Estimated dose: one small crescent bite from a single leaf; no larger piece observed swallowed.
   - Time of exposure: approximately 09:22 today, Saturday 3/30.
   - Signs observed so far: brief licking, one drool episode, no swallowing distress.
   - Current status: alert, normal breathing, ambulating normally, no visible swelling, no vomiting, no pawing at the face.
   - Kibo's age, weight, breed, current medications, and any chronic conditions.
   - First aid already done: plant moved out of reach, mouth wiped, water offered.
   - Have the plant available but bagged — do not bring the live plant into the clinic; APCC or your vet may want the species confirmed from a photo.

4. WHAT NOT TO DO
   - Do NOT induce vomiting. Calcium oxalate crystals damage tissue on the way back up too; this toxin is not a vomiting indication.
   - Do NOT force food or water into his mouth. Risk of aspiration if his throat is already irritated, and it can drive crystals further into mucosa.
   - Do NOT give hydrogen peroxide, activated charcoal, Benadryl, or any other medication without vet/APCC direction.
   - Do NOT assume "he looks fine" means he is fine. Oral and lingual swelling from calcium oxalate can develop over 1–4 hours.
   - Do NOT scrub the mouth aggressively.
   - Do NOT put the plant back in reach "to see if he does it again."

5. SYMPTOMS THAT MEAN EMERGENCY VET (go now, do not wait for a callback)
   - Any visible swelling of the face, lips, or tongue
   - Stridor, noisy breathing, or any change in breathing effort
   - Gagging, repeated retching, or apparent inability to swallow
   - Drooling that does not settle within 30 minutes, or drooling that increases rather than decreases
   - Repeated vomiting within an hour (one isolated vomit is less urgent; sustained vomiting is not)
   - Sustained pawing at the face or rubbing the face on the floor for more than a few minutes
   - Restlessness, agitation, or unusual withdrawal/quietness
   - Pale gums, weakness, stumbling, or collapse
   - Refusal of water for more than 4–6 hours
   - Any sign of airway compromise, even subtle

6. MONITORING PLAN (next 24 hours)
   - Closest watch: the first 4 hours. Most pothos signs appear in this window.
   - Gentle lip-lift checks at the 2-hour and 4-hour marks: look for swelling, redness, or small ulcers on the gums and tongue. Stop if he resists; do not force.
   - Normal meals on his regular schedule. Skipping one meal is a yellow flag, not yet emergency. Skipping two consecutive meals → call your vet.
   - Keep water available; let him self-regulate. Do not push intake.
   - Normal walks and activity are fine unless symptoms appear.
   - Expect mild, transient oral discomfort. Some dogs eat slightly less for one meal — that is normal.
   - If 24 hours pass with no escalation, he is fine.

If APCC or your vet says go in, head to your nearest 24-hour veterinary ER — in NYC that is BluePearl, Animal Medical Center, or NYC Veterinary Specialists depending on borough.

        - Form 1040 line 25d (estimated tax payments, which now includes your $2,000)
        - Form 1040 line 33 (total payments)
        - Form 1040 line 37 (amount you owe) OR line 34 (refund)

    The expected delta from the pre-entry version is exactly $2,000 on the right side of the balance: balance-due goes down by $2,000, OR refund goes up by $2,000, OR some combination if state withholding changed shape (it should not, but check). If the delta is not $2,000 within rounding, something else moved and you want to know what before you file.

    While you are on the return, also check:

        - Whether the software computed an underpayment penalty on Form 2210.  If so, the $2,000 likely reduces or eliminates it; if it does not, that is a small inconsistency worth understanding (penalty is usually waived if withholding + estimated >= safe-harbor: 90% of 2023 tax, or 100% of 2022 tax / 110% if 2022 AGI > $150K).
        - State return:  estimated federal payments do not carry to state; verify the state side still balances independently.

5.  Build a single documentation packet, even if filing e-file.

    Keep a folder named "2023 return - estimated tax proof" containing, in this order:

        a. The Direct Pay confirmation page (PDF or screenshot of the final confirmation screen, with the confirmation number visible).
        b. The bank statement or bank-side transaction detail showing the ACH debit on January 15, 2024 for the same amount.
        c. A one-line written summary:  "$2,000 IRS Direct Pay, paid 01/15/2024, confirmation [number], applied to 2023 Form 1040 line 26 via Schedule 3 line 8."
        d. A copy or screenshot of the filed return's summary page showing the $2,000 on Schedule 3 line 8 and the resulting refund or balance-due.

    Items (a), (b), and (c) are your evidence. Item (d) is what you actually filed. If the IRS later asks, you hand them the whole folder. Retention: at least 7 years (6-year substantial-omission window plus a margin).

6.  What to do if the IRS account transcript later does not show the payment.

    This is a normal lag, not a sign of a problem. The sequence on the IRS side is:

        - Direct Pay ACH debit clears your bank  -> ~1-2 business days.
        - IRS posts the payment to your tax account -> typically 1-3 weeks.
        - Account transcript reflects the payment  -> typically another 1-3 weeks.
        - Total:  anywhere from "already there" to ~6 weeks after January 15.

    So the test is not "does the transcript show it now," it is "does the transcript show it six weeks after the payment date." If you file before then, which you probably will, expect the transcript to still be empty for the payment when you first look.

    Specific scenarios and what to do in each:

        - Transcript shows zero payments for 2023, but your bank and Direct Pay both show the debit:  this is the lag above.  Wait, do not act.  Re-check the transcript at the 6-week mark.  The IRS also has a separate "view what you owe / payments" page that updates a little faster than the formal transcript; check that as well.
        - Transcript still shows zero at the 6-week mark:  call the IRS (the number on the "Payments" page of irs.gov for individual taxpayers, not the general 800 line if you can avoid it).  Have items (a), (b), (c) in front of you.  Ask the agent to trace the confirmation number.
        - Transcript shows zero but IRS sends a notice ("you underpaid by $2,000 / balance due / penalty notice"):  do not pay the notice yet.  Respond with a copy of (a) and (b) by the notice's response date, citing the confirmation number.  The IRS Payment Trace process (Form 3911) is the formal path for a missing payment, but you only need to file it if the regular phone trace cannot locate the payment after several weeks.
        - Transcript eventually shows $2,000 posted correctly:  no action needed; close the folder in your records.

7.  Things to deliberately NOT do.

        - Do not send another $2,000.  You have bank evidence and a confirmation number; a duplicate payment would create a real problem instead of a paper one.
        - Do not file an amended return (Form 1040-X).  You have not filed the original; you are entering the payment on the original.  1040-X is the wrong tool here.
        - Do not enter the payment as "paid with return" or "additional payment" on the filing screen.  That is a separate mechanism, and layering it on top of a missing estimated payment would double-count.
        - Do not trust the import's "zero" without checking the schedule.  Most importers look for matching 1099-ES forms or a payroll W-2 withholding line; Direct Pay is intentionally not linked to either, so a zero import is common, not an error.

If the recompute in step 4 produces exactly a $2,000 swing on the right side of your balance and Form 2210 reflects the larger payment, you are done; file the return and put the packet from step 5 in your tax archive. The transcript will catch up on its own schedule.

PART 1 — Customer-facing language (safe to send):

The HTTP 200 status only means the server received and processed the export request. It does not mean every data point was accepted. The OTLP export protocol reports per-point outcomes in the response body, and a `partialSuccess` object means the receiver accepted some data points in the batch and rejected others. Your batch fell into that case: the receiver accepted the rest of the points and rejected 487 of them.

The reason for the rejection is permanent at the receiver: "exponential histogram scale 25 exceeds supported range [-10,20]." The exponential histogram bucket-scale parameter on those 487 points is outside the range the receiver accepts, so they were not stored. The receiver cannot rewrite a scale of 25 into 20; the fix has to happen on the client side before the points are exported.

Do NOT resend the entire batch. The accepted points are already stored, so resending would duplicate them. The 487 rejected points would be rejected again for the same reason.

To recover those points, do this:
  1. Adjust the exporter (or the source producing the histograms) so exponential histogram scale is within [-10, 20] for any affected series. Values at or below 20 are accepted; values above 20 are not.
  2. After the fix, resend only the rejected points, not the full batch.

Verification: in your own query results, confirm that timestamps belonging to the previously accepted set still appear exactly once (not duplicated), and that timestamps from the originally rejected set appear after the corrected resend.

If you want to confirm the count, the response body itself shows 487 rejected for this export; the other points in that batch should already be visible in your query results.

PART 2 — Internal note for Support (for the ticket, do not send to customer verbatim):

  - The 200 is transport-level acceptance, not a per-point success signal. Do not characterize the export as "successful" without addressing the `partialSuccess` body.
  - Resend guidance is resend-rejected-only after a client-side fix. Resend-the-whole-batch is wrong because it duplicates the already-accepted points and replays the same 487 rejections.
  - The fix lives on the client: clamp/reduce exponential histogram scale to ≤20 (and ≥-10). The receiver does not coerce.
  - Verification Support can ask the customer for: pick a small set of timestamps from the originally-accepted portion and confirm each appears once in query results; pick a small set from the originally-rejected portion and confirm corrected resends now appear.
  - Do not promise the fix will be lossless until the customer's own query results confirm both conditions.

Couscous is the right call — it steams off the heat in 5 minutes while the chickpea-tomato-spinach pan builds the warm bowl, and the yogurt-garlic-lemon sauce keeps it from tipping heavy.

Quantities (for 2, with leftover sauce):
- Couscous: 1 cup dry + 1 1/4 cups water or broth + 1 tbsp olive oil + pinch salt + 1 smashed garlic clove
- Chickpeas: 1 can (15 oz), drained and rinsed
- Spinach: about 4 oz / 4 packed cups
- Cherry tomatoes: 1 cup, halved
- Garlic: 3 cloves total — 1 in the couscous, 2 minced in the pan, 1 grated into the sauce
- Lemon: 1 — zest and juice split between sauce and finishing
- Yogurt sauce: 3/4 cup plain yogurt + the grated garlic clove + zest of half the lemon + 1 tbsp lemon juice + pinch salt + small drizzle olive oil
- Spices: 1 tsp ground cumin, 1/2 tsp smoked paprika, salt, black pepper, optional pinch of red pepper flakes
- Olive oil for the pan: about 2 tbsp

Equipment: one 2-quart pot for the couscous, one 10-inch skillet for the chickpea mixture. That's it.

Sequencing, target finish around 9:35 PM so it lands warm when she walks in:

T+0  Put the water on to boil in the pot. While it heats: drain and rinse the chickpeas, halve the tomatoes, mince 2 garlic cloves, zest and juice the lemon.

T+3  Water boils. Stir in couscous, olive oil, salt, and the smashed garlic clove. Cover, remove from heat. Set a 5-minute timer.

T+3  Same minute — heat 2 tbsp olive oil in the skillet over medium. Add the minced garlic, cook 30 to 45 seconds until fragrant but not browned.

T+4  Add chickpeas, cumin, smoked paprika, salt, pepper. Stir to coat and warm through, about 2 minutes.

T+6  Push chickpeas to one side, add tomatoes cut-side down. Let them sit 2 minutes so they soften and just begin to burst. Then stir together.

T+8  Stir in the spinach in two handfuls. It wilts in 60 to 90 seconds. Pull the pan off the heat — residual heat keeps cooking it.

T+8  Make the sauce: in a small bowl stir yogurt, grated garlic, lemon zest, lemon juice, salt, drizzle of olive oil. Taste, adjust.

T+10 Uncover couscous, fluff with a fork. Grains should be tender and separate. If any clumps remain, re-cover for another minute.

T+12 Plate: couscous on the bottom, chickpea-tomato-spinach on top, yogurt sauce spooned over or served on the side. Finish with a squeeze of lemon and a pinch of smoked paprika.

If her departure slips and you're holding dinner:

Safe to pause, covered:
- Couscous holds covered off-heat for 15 to 20 minutes. When she arrives, splash 1 to 2 tbsp of hot water over it, re-cover for 2 minutes, then fluff. Texture comes right back.
- Chickpea-tomato-spinach holds covered on LOW heat for 10 to 15 minutes. The spinach darkens a little; that's fine. A squeeze of lemon at the end brightens it back up.
- Yogurt sauce made at T+8 keeps covered in the fridge, and the garlic actually mellows while it waits.

Do not do early:
- Do not wilt the spinach until you're within about 5 minutes of plating. It goes from wilted to grey-mushy faster than you'd expect, and the green is half the point.
- Do not dress the couscous with the sauce or lemon until plating. Plain couscous holds better and reheats cleaner.

The long-slip case (20+ minutes late): turn off the chickpea pan and cover it. When she texts, splash the couscous with hot water and re-cover for 2 minutes, then re-warm the chickpea pan over low for 1 to 2 minutes while you plate. Sauce comes straight from the fridge — it's meant to be cool against the warm bowl.

One last note: the bowl is forgiving if your portions end up a bit off. The real timing risk is the spinach, so save it for last and don't worry if everything else is done 4 minutes early — just keep the pan off heat with a lid on until you're ready to plate.

DIAGNOSIS: attestation-subject mismatch, not artifact substitution.

The two digests are not competing claims about the same object — they are a parent/child pair in the OCI layout:

  - 9f41d8c0  registry manifest list  (the multi-arch index tagged v3.8.2)
  - 21b77a6e  linux/amd64 image manifest  (the per-platform child that actually runs)

What happened:

  - The build pipeline produced a provenance attestation bound to the per-platform image manifest (the SLSA/Sigstore default — attest to what was built).
  - The verifier policy is comparing the attestation subject against the manifest list digest instead of the per-platform image manifest digest.
  - That is a category error in the policy: a leaf artifact compared against its parent index.

It is not substitution because there is no competing linux/amd64 image. Substitution would require 9f41d8c0's linux/amd64 descriptor to point at some *third* digest (say aabbccdd) while the attestation names 21b77a6e. Nothing in the error indicates that.

SAFE CORRECTION (no bypass):

  1. Resolve the relationship first. Pull 9f41d8c0 and read its linux/amd64 descriptor. If that descriptor equals 21b77a6e, the attestation subject is correct and the build is honest.
  2. Re-run the verifier against the per-platform image manifest digest for the deploy target (21b77a6e for linux/amd64). It should now match the attestation subject and clear.
  3. If 9f41d8c0's linux/amd64 descriptor points to a different digest, STOP. That is a real substitution — full provenance investigation, no promotion.

Do NOT:

  - Bypass the verifier. Same discipline as the Cardinality Guardrails gate; skipping it leaves no auditable reason the release proceeded.
  - Re-pull / re-tag hoping digests change. The artifact pair is fixed; the same mismatch will reproduce.
  - Re-sign against the manifest list to make the existing check pass. That attests to an index pointer rather than the artifact that runs — weaker provenance, and it papers over the policy bug instead of fixing it.

Hardening follow-up (after release): have the build emit an index-level attestation that references the per-platform attestations, so the manifest list is also bound. But for unblocking v3.8.2 staging today, fix the comparison, not the artifact.

To Support — diagnosis for the HTTP 400 on series_index=17:

What's failing
The 400 is from ingest-edge's EXEMPLAR validator, not the sample/series validator. Exemplars are a separate object attached to a sample — they carry their own label set (typically trace_id, span_id) and have an independent per-label-value limit of 128 bytes (OpenMetrics exemplar spec). The limit is enforced per exemplar label, not summed across labels, and is not shared with series labels.

Series labels and timestamps passed validation (otherwise the error would name a series-side field). The exemplar's trace_id measured 142 bytes, exceeding the 128-byte limit by 14, so ingest-edge rejects the whole request with HTTP 400 and writes nothing for the series.

Direct answers to the customer's two questions

Q: "Can we shorten a normal metric label instead?"
A: No. Sample/series labels and exemplar labels are validated by separate paths with separate limits. The 142-byte value lives on the EXEMPLAR, not the series. Shortening any series-side label will not change the exemplar label-value length check, will not turn the 400 into a 2xx, and is the wrong change to make — the series labels are not the cause.

Q: "Can we resend this payload unchanged?"
A: No. The validation is deterministic on the exemplar label-value length. The same payload will produce the same 400. Retrying unchanged just costs another rejected request and another backoff cycle. Do not retry until the exemplar is changed.

What the customer must change before retrying
The exemplar's own trace_id label value must be ≤ 128 bytes (UTF-8 byte length). Other exemplar label values are subject to the same limit, but only trace_id is over in this payload.

  - Identify the source of the 142-byte trace_id. Standard OpenTelemetry/W3C tracecontext trace_id is 32 hex chars (32 bytes); a 142-byte value is non-standard — likely concatenated IDs (trace+span+parent), a vendor format with extra metadata, a binary ID that isn't being hex-encoded, or padding. Have the customer confirm what their tracing library/agent is actually emitting as the exemplar's trace_id.
  - Preferred fix: reconfigure the tracing library/agent so the exemplar's trace_id is ≤ 128 bytes. W3C tracecontext IDs (32 hex chars) fit comfortably and keep full trace↔metric correlation.
  - Workaround if the ID format cannot be changed at the source: truncate the value fed into the exemplar's trace_id to ≤ 128 bytes before remote-write. This weakens correlation back to the trace backend, so treat it as a workaround, not a clean fix — the root cause should still be investigated.
  - Fallback if neither is feasible immediately: disable exemplar export on the remote-write path. This removes the 400 but also removes the trace↔metric link; treat as temporary, not a steady state.
  - After any of the above, retry the same payload. Series labels, timestamps, and the rest of the batch can stay as-is — only the exemplar label value needs to change.

What the customer does NOT need to change

  - Series labels on series_index=17 — valid; do not retouch.
  - Sample timestamps — valid; do not retouch.
  - Other exemplars in the batch that are within 128 bytes — no change needed.

Escalation
If, after shortening trace_id, ingest-edge still rejects with an exemplar-related 400, ask for the new error string and series_index. The next failure is unlikely to be on the same field, and a global exemplar limit bump is not the right answer.
