Decision: keep admission rejection (429) as the primary mechanism under queue saturation. Do not adopt evict-oldest as the default behavior.

Reasons, anchored to existing principles:

  - Acceptance contract. Once a request has been enqueued, the system has implicitly accepted responsibility for it. Silently discarding already-admitted work breaks the "if I got 202, my data is durable" invariant that downstream consumers (rollup-service, shard-keeper, dashboards) rely on. 429 is a protocol-level refusal, not a contract violation.

  - Bounded mechanism. The 429 + Retry-After path is standard, observable, and already covered by the ingest-edge v2.19.4 production behavior. Eviction is a new mechanism with its own failure modes; the memory-limiter / buffer-pool precedents do not transfer automatically. Any new mechanism here has to earn its own boundaries, observability, and rollback test.

  - Cardinality and fairness risk. Eviction that is tenant-blind preferentially drops whichever tenant happened to be admitted first; eviction that is tenant-aware needs a fairness policy that does not yet exist (and would conflict with the Cardinality Guardrails if it adds a per-request label to the eviction path). Either path is a new cardinality surface for a feature that is supposed to be pressure relief.

  - Recovery. With 429, the dropped work has a recovery path: the client retries with Retry-After. With eviction, the dropped work is gone — there is no automatic way for the client to know what was lost, and any reconciliation becomes owner-by-owner detective work. The April 18 Sev2 lesson was that gaps in admitted-but-undelivered state are exactly the failure mode we cannot afford.

  - Observability. 429 emits a structured refusal. Eviction needs to emit something equivalent (drop reason, request_id, original enqueue time, tenant) or it becomes a silent data-loss path.

Narrow exception worth flagging for Wes: if there is a freshness-tier contract documented end-to-end (specific tenants, specific downstream consumers sign off in writing, and eviction is part of the published contract), eviction inside that tier is defensible. That is not the current state, so it is not the v0.

Focused tests required for the kept 429 path:

  Retry signaling
    - 429 response carries a Retry-After header that tracks observed drain rate, not a static value; bounded randomized jitter (1–3s window, mirroring ingest-edge v2.19.4) so synchronized retry bursts do not reform after refusal.
    - 429 body carries a stable request_id and a reason code (e.g., queue_full) for client-side correlation and for matching against later successful retries.
    - No 5xx under sustained overload; saturation only converts offered load into 429, never into errors.
    - p99 latency of admitted requests does not degrade while the queue is at or near the 20,000 cap; admitted requests must not pay the cost of refusal.
    - Client conformance: a stub client that honors Retry-After eventually drains its backlog with zero loss; the same client that retries immediately does not improve its acceptance rate (anti-amplification check).

  Ordering
    - FIFO position is preserved for requests already enqueued when a new request arrives at a full queue and is refused.
    - Per-tenant in-flight ordering is stable across fill/drain cycles; no reorder across the refusal boundary — a retried request from tenant X lands behind any tenant-X request that was admitted earlier and is still pending, not interleaved.
    - Cross-tenant ordering is best-effort and is not asserted as a guarantee; a test documents this explicitly so a future bug report does not get framed as a regression.
    - Admitted request order at the downstream sink (rollup-service, shard-keeper) matches enqueue order modulo the above.

  Accounting
    - A dedicated rejection counter increments once per 429, with bounded cardinality (per `tenant_size_class`, not per raw tenant_id; the existing `small` / `medium` / `large` / `unknown` taxonomy is the right grain).
    - Total offered = admitted + refused + in-flight, reconciled continuously under load; the equation must close within the metric flush interval.
    - Refused is distinct from failed; a refused request must never appear in the failed counter or in any drop-equivalent counter that downstream alerting could mistake for data loss.
    - Rejection rate has a written alert threshold tied to expected pressure (e.g., page at >2% sustained 5m; warn at >0.5%), not a single hard number, with the threshold derived from the load-test envelope.
    - Per-tenant rejection breakdown is exposed but not auto-paged; a tenant that exceeds its share becomes an investigation signal, not an incident.

  Recovery after the queue falls below the cap
    - When queue depth drops below the 20,000 cap, the next offered request is admitted within one drain interval; no zombie saturation state where admission stays latched.
    - p99 returns to baseline within a documented window after load subsides (e.g., 60s); the exact number comes from the load-test plateau.
    - 429 rate returns to zero under nominal offered load; any residual 429 at nominal load is a regression and a stop condition.
    - Memory returns to pre-saturation baseline; gauge the resident set size and any pool (request-buffer pool cap-64 is adjacent — observe, do not transfer the precedent).
    - No goroutine, connection-pool, or open-file-descriptor leak after a saturation cycle; a soak of N fill/drain cycles holds the same resident-set envelope as a single saturation event.
    - Refused-but-retried requests are matchable end-to-end: request_id from the 429 appears in the eventual 202 log line for the same payload, proving no silent drop in the refused-and-recovered path.

Rollout posture, if any behavior change is later proposed:

  - Keep Wes's solo scope for metrics-router non-production and staging canary; an admission-control change that affects the contract with every client is a paired-review item before any production cohort.
  - Reuse the cutover playbook pattern: explicit gate plan, gate maxima, paired routing/service rollback, first-pass monitor identified by name, and a 48-hour production read with a documented close-out date.
  - Written stop conditions before staging: 5xx up, p99 over threshold sustained, retry bursts reforming, rejection cardinality growing unexpectedly, or any silent-drop path appearing in accounting.
  - Owner: Wes drives the implementation and the load test; Alex owns the production go decision and the contract wording with downstream consumers.

Reply to Wes in that shape: decision, the four test buckets above, and the offer to revisit eviction only if a freshness-tier contract is proposed in writing with named downstream signoff.

The skate is mechanical, not a confidence issue. When you pull the shallow right sidepull, the force vector rotates your hips away from the wall and unloads the left smear — the foot loses pressure right when you need it most. So every cue below targets keeping pressure on the smear while the sidepull does its job.

Concrete cues to try on the next few attempts (one per attempt is fine):

1. Row the sidepull, don't yank it. Pull the right hold DOWN toward your right hip with the elbow bent around 90 degrees. Shoulder stays low — don't shrug it up to your ear. The body stays closer to the wall and the smear stays loaded. Think "row" not "pull-up."

2. Drive the toes through the smear, don't just stand on it. Push the left toes DOWN and INTO the wall through the rubber. The cue is "scrape down toward your heel." On a polished smear, direction of force is everything — flat-footed standing or letting the heel drop kills friction.

3. Step the right foot up FIRST, before reaching. Even a small edge or a higher smear changes the geometry a lot. Right foot up = hips rise, the reach to the high left edge shortens, and your weight centers between both feet instead of cantilevering left over the polished smear.

4. Counter-rotate. Point your belt buckle slightly LEFT, toward the wall the high edge sits on. Fights the peel the sidepull wants to put on your torso and keeps your chest closer to the wall.

5. Stick the left edge with a straight arm, then commit. Touch the high left hold with a straight left arm — don't grab and try to pull immediately. Once the left hand is on, step up on the right foot and pull the right sidepull DOWN simultaneously. Bend the left arm and bring the body in only after your weight is over the right foot.

6. Reset before the move. Shake out the right arm, chalk, look at the hold, exhale, then move. Skatiness spikes with tension — a clean reset is part of the sequence, not a pause.

If the reach still feels too big after the right-foot-up step, flag the right foot out to the right when you commit to the left hand — it counterbalances and keeps your hips centered over the smear for that last instant.

Best one to try first: the row + drive the toes through the smear together, on the same attempt. Those two fix the skate directly. If those land, add the right-foot-up step on the attempt after.

Here is the customer-facing guidance for Support to send.

Direct answers

1. Can the client cache the first Retry-After value for all later retries? No. Each 429 response carries its own Retry-After value intended for that response. The 1-3s window is randomized per response on the server side to spread retry traffic; treating any one value as constant across the retry chain re-creates the synchronization the randomization exists to prevent.

2. Should the client add its own jitter? The server is already randomizing each response's Retry-After across a 1-3s window, which is the primary mechanism for spreading retry traffic. The client should treat the header as the minimum delay for that specific retry and add only enough additional spread to avoid all clients retrying at the head of the same window simultaneously. A fixed offset that every instance applies identically is no better than the synchronization the server is already breaking up; a wide additional distribution is unnecessary and can push retries past the server's pacing intent.

3. Does a successful retry mean later 429 responses can be ignored? No. Each response reflects current server state (queue depth, tenant quota, backpressure). A 202 on one request does not entitle the client to assume future requests will succeed without honoring Retry-After. The 429 / 202 decision is made per request.

Operating principles the client should follow

  - Treat each Retry-After value as the minimum delay before that retry, not as a global constant.
  - Read the header on every 429 response; do not cache it across responses.
  - Cap total retries with an overall retry budget (a bounded attempt count, or a bounded cumulative retry delay) so the client does not retry indefinitely against a degraded endpoint.
  - Avoid synchronized immediate retries: do not retry at exactly t = Retry-After with zero additional spread, and do not apply a fixed offset that all instances apply in lockstep.
  - When the retry budget is exhausted, stop retrying and surface the failure to the caller.

What Support should not say

  - Do not promise that a retry will succeed. The 429 indicates the server asked the client to slow down; the next attempt may still be 429, 5xx, or another error depending on server state.
  - Do not characterize the server-side randomized Retry-After change as removing the need for client backoff. The change reduces synchronized retry bursts at the boundary, but per-response Retry-After compliance, an overall retry budget, and avoidance of immediate-retry synchronization are still required of the client.

DIAGNOSIS

Traffic did NOT switch configurations. The four log lines are consistent with a correct validate-then-swap path: at 10:12:01.204Z a reload attempt for candidate 442 began; 15 ms later (10:12:01.219Z) validation rejected it for flush_interval=0s; 1 ms after that (10:12:01.220Z) the reload path held the active generation at 441. The 1 ms gap between validation_failed and reload_kept_active is the expected ordering — validate fully, then swap, swap never reached on rejection. Live traffic continued on generation 441 from 10:12:01.220Z through the /healthz read at 10:12:04.008Z, and presumably until the next successful reload. So no customer request was served by generation 442.

WHAT THE HEALTHZ ACTUALLY SAID

  2024-04-08T10:12:04.008Z GET /healthz 200 {"status":"healthy","config_generation":442}

The healthz payload reports config_generation=442, but the truth at that instant was active_generation=441. The endpoint is not reporting the active generation. It is reporting the candidate / last-attempted generation. From an operator or downstream consumer's perspective, this is a quiet lie: a 200 + status:healthy + a numeric generation that advances on every attempted reload regardless of whether the swap actually happened.

THE OBSERVABILITY DEFECT

The defect is a single field name (config_generation) carrying two semantically different values depending on success:

  - On a successful reload, it equals the active generation (truthful)
  - On a failed reload, it equals the candidate generation that was just rejected (misleading)

This collapses three distinct states into one label:

  1. attempted   — the candidate parsed off disk or pushed by config-loader (442 here)
  2. validated   — the candidate that passed schema and semantic checks and is eligible to swap (still 441 in this window)
  3. active      — the generation currently serving live traffic (441)

Because healthz exposes only one of these and updates it on attempt rather than on swap, every rejected reload silently advances the reported number. An on-call engineer, a dashboard panel, or a "did the new config go live?" check that reads healthz will see 442 and infer a swap that never happened. That is exactly how Support produced the report you are investigating.

This is the same shape of defect the earlier reload fixes were designed to prevent at the reload layer — preserving the active configuration and watcher on failed reload, and treating swap as a separate step from validation. The reload path here is doing the right thing (kept 441 active). The health surface is undoing it by reporting the attempted value as if it were active.

RECOMMENDED HEALTH-ENDPOINT SEMANTICS

The fix belongs on the health surface, not on the reload path. The reload path must remain: validate candidate fully, then atomic swap, never swap on failure. The healthz must expose the three generations as separate fields, each updated on the event that justifies the update. Concretely:

  status:                       "healthy" | "degraded" | "unhealthy"
  active_generation:            <int>     // updates only on successful swap
  candidate_generation:         <int|null> // updates on reload_start
  last_validated_generation:    <int>     // last candidate that passed validation
  last_reload_status:           "applied" | "rejected" | "in_progress" | "idle"
  last_reload_at:               <rfc3339>
  last_reload_error:            { field, value, error } | null
  last_successful_reload_at:    <rfc3339>
  last_validation_failure_at:   <rfc3339> | null
  generation_in_flight:         bool      // true between reload_start and a terminal event

Properties the new shape must hold:

  - active_generation is read from the same atomic pointer the live serving path uses. If traffic is on 441, active_generation is 441 by construction, not by convention.
  - candidate_generation and last_reload_status advance on reload_start, not on validation outcome. The attempt is observable even when it fails.
  - last_reload_status is "rejected" with a structured error whenever validation fails, so the rejection is visible at the health surface without log correlation.
  - status:"healthy" does not imply a successful reload in the current window. It means the live serving path is responsive on the active generation. Decouple liveness from reload success.
  - generation_in_flight is true between reload_start and a terminal event, so a wedged or stuck reload attempt shows as a flat healthz with generation_in_flight:true for longer than the expected validate-then-swap window.
  - The active configuration is not changed on a failed reload. This is non-load-bearing for the live path — it only restructures what is observable.

What healthz would have said at 10:12:04.008Z under the new schema:

  {
    "status": "healthy",
    "active_generation": 441,
    "candidate_generation": 442,
    "last_validated_generation": 441,
    "last_reload_status": "rejected",
    "last_reload_error": {"field":"flush_interval","value":"0s","error":"must be greater than zero"},
    "last_reload_at": "2024-04-08T10:12:01.204Z",
    "last_successful_reload_at": "<previous apply timestamp>",
    "last_validation_failure_at": "2024-04-08T10:12:01.219Z",
    "generation_in_flight": false
  }

Support sees the truth directly: live traffic on 441, candidate 442 rejected, active configuration unchanged. No log correlation required.

WHAT TO TELL SUPPORT

1. Traffic did not switch. Active generation remained 441 throughout the attempted reload and the healthz read. No request was served by generation 442.

2. The reload path is behaving correctly — validate-then-swap, swap skipped on rejection, active and watcher preserved on failure.

3. The defect is in /healthz reporting the attempted generation as if it were the active one. That is why their report described generation 442 as healthy even though 442 never served traffic.

4. The recommended healthz change is observability-only. It does not modify the active configuration, the reload path, or the validation logic. It only separates the three generations into distinct fields and updates each on the event that justifies the update, so the rejection is visible at the health surface instead of being silently absorbed into the active-generation number.

Reading: Anya is asking for a 20-min call to walk through three things — whether you agree with the proposed package, where the current handoff causes trouble, and whether you'd use it.

Quick read: the three questions answer cleanly in writing; a meeting is overkill unless she actually wants dialogue. Given your pattern with Anya — give her what's useful, don't turn it into a project — a written reply is probably the right move. Offer the meeting as available, not as the default.

Draft to send Anya:

Hey — happy to give you notes now; I'd lean toward writing it out instead of a 20-min call, unless you actually want to talk it through. If you do, the structure I'd ask for is: you walk me through what you're proposing, then I push on the weakest part, then we agree on what changes.

Three direct answers.

1.  Where the current handoff causes trouble (in order of severity):
    -  Two sources of truth. Figma is editable and the JSON is editable and people copy between them. They will drift. Not a discipline problem, structural.
    -  No provenance on a token. Rename or deprecation leaves no record, so the engineer holding the JSON can't tell what's current.
    -  Examples are missing or stale. Without generated examples of correct use, every engineer reinvents the pattern and the UI drifts.
    -  Ownership is fuzzy. Designers think they've handed off implementation guidance; engineers think they've been handed design specs. The boundary leaks both ways.
    -  No test. Nothing catches a deprecated token in code or Figma-vs-JSON drift until it shows up in production.

2.  Whether I agree with the proposed package:
    Instinct is right — a single approved package with examples is much better than what's there now. But by itself it doesn't fix the drift; it moves it. For it to actually be the answer, three things have to be true:
    -  Single source of truth. Either Figma generates the JSON, or the JSON is canonical and Figma is a read-only view. Not both editable.
    -  CI check that fails on drift — code uses a missing token, JSON drifts from Figma, etc.
    -  Ownership boundary written into the package: design owns semantic naming, intended behavior, examples of correct use. Engineering owns framework choice, migration sequence, code-level refactors. Anything ambiguous goes in a "non-goals" or "still unsettled" section, not guessed at.
    If those three are in place, the package is real. If not, it's a rebrand.

3.  Would I use it:
    Conditional yes. Same way I use any well-defined contract — I'd consume it as source of truth if it's enforced (CI, single source, ownership lines). If it's just "here's the JSON plus some screenshots," I'd treat it as advisory and keep making my own calls. Which means the package didn't actually standardize anything; it just added a layer.

One thing I'd add: a "non-goals" section and a "still unsettled" section. Future-you will be glad she wrote down what the package is not.

Send me the draft when it's ready and I'll read it.

   For each fact type, list the source-system audience that can read it today. The Lantern audience for the room has to be a subset of that, not a superset. Side-by-side comparison, not a vibe.

   If the source has a deletion obligation (GDPR right to erasure, CCPA, contract-level), the room inherits it. Name the obligation and the propagation path. Don't let the room become a place where deletion is harder than in the source.

   What does the room render when the source is down or hasn't emitted in N hours? Facts with their original timestamps plus a "last seen" marker, or empty? Empty without a provenance-gap signal is a misleading read and isn't admissible.

EXPLANATION OF THE DRY-RUN DEFECT

  has("env") && label("env") != "dev"
       ^^^^^^^
       short-circuits here

When `env` is absent, `has("env")` is false, so the entire `&&` expression is false regardless of the second clause. The rule never gets to compare anything for series without an `env` label, so all 6,772 of them fall through to "not routed" — exactly opposite to the customer's intent.

The 41,208 prod-routed and 2,109 dev-excluded numbers are correct because both clauses are evaluated for those series. The defect only surfaces on the missing-label branch.

CORRECTED EXPRESSION

  !has("env") || label("env") != "dev"

Read as: route if the label is missing, OR if it is present and not equal to "dev". The `has` check is moved into the positive (route) branch instead of guarding the comparison. This does not depend on what `label()` returns for a missing key — the two halves are independent.

If your DSL guarantees `label("env") == ""` when the label is absent, the shorter form is equivalent:

  label("env") != "dev"

Prefer the explicit `!has("env") || …` form unless that empty-string convention is documented and covered by tests.

TRUTH TABLE FOR THE CUSTOMER

  env present | env value | current rule      | corrected rule    | matches intent?
  ----------- | --------- | ----------------- | ----------------- | ---------------
  no          | (absent)  | NOT routed  <-- BUG | routed           | yes
  yes         | "dev"     | NOT routed        | NOT routed       | yes
  yes         | "prod"    | routed            | routed           | yes
  yes         | "staging" | routed            | routed           | yes
  yes         | "qa"      | routed            | routed           | yes
  yes         | ""        | routed            | routed           | yes (empty != dev)

EXPECTED POST-FIX DRY RUN

  env="prod":    41,208 routed     (unchanged)
  env="dev":      2,109 not routed (unchanged)
  env absent:     6,772 routed     (was NOT routed — now fixed)
  env="staging", "qa", etc.:      routed     (unchanged)
  total routed:                  47,980     (up from 41,208)

The only behavioral change is the 6,772 missing-env series flipping from excluded to included, which is exactly the customer's stated intent. Series counts for every other branch are preserved, so nothing currently routed is dropped and nothing currently excluded (the 2,109 dev series) is newly admitted.

NOTES BEFORE PROMOTING

The split outer shell with no quick exposure, no pain, normal gait, and no persistent licking is consistent with a low-risk distal claw crack. The claw husk can split from snagging and usually resolves as the sheath grows out.

TONIGHT
  - Wipe the paw once with a damp cloth to clear any debris, then pat dry. Do not apply ointments, peroxide, or anything he'll need to lick off.
  - Prevent another snag. A loose baby or dog sock over just that paw (other toes exposed, secured gently above the wrist, not tight) can help if he tolerates it. If he tries to chew it off, skip it — chewing is worse than the snag risk.
  - No need to restrict activity or walks. If he starts limping or favoring the paw, shorten them.

TRIMMING
  - The cautious default is no. The piece can extend further up than it looks, a sudden pull can extend the split toward the quick, and self-trim trauma is one of the more common reasons these turn into vet visits.
  - Trimming is reasonable only if all of these hold:
      (1) the cracked piece is clearly dangling and not bearing weight when he stands
      (2) you can see no pink/red inside the cracked end
      (3) he is calm and you have a second person to gently hold/distract
      (4) you use clean clippers and stop the instant he pulls or you see pink
    In that case, snip only the loose flapping portion, flush with the intact shell. Otherwise leave it and let a vet handle it at a routine visit.
  - Do not pull, twist, or peel any piece off.

ROUTINE VET VISIT (within a few days, not urgent)
  - Crack does not improve over 3–5 days or visibly extends toward the base
  - Claw becomes looser or wobbly in its bed
  - Color change in or under the claw (darkening can mean blood pooling under the husk)
  - Mild licking that increases in frequency or duration
  - Any change in gait even if subtle

URGENT VET VISIT (tonight or tomorrow morning)
  - Active bleeding from the claw that does not stop with 5–10 minutes of gentle pressure
  - Pink/red center (the quick) becomes exposed
  - Swelling, heat, or tenderness in the toe or paw
  - Limping or favoring the paw
  - Pus or foul-smelling discharge
  - Persistent licking, chewing, or guarding of the paw
  - Lethargy, appetite loss, or any sign of systemic illness
  - Crack propagates up toward the claw base

If something borderline shows up and you are unsure whether to go in, an after-hours vet telehealth consult is a reasonable middle step before committing to an ER trip. Most plain cracked sheaths without quick exposure do not become vet visits, but the early signs above are the ones that change that.

Verdict: the lease guard behaved correctly, no process restart is warranted, and the alert can be closed after a short, defined set of post-event checks.

1. Did the safety mechanism behave correctly?

Yes. The guard observed 740 ms of clock skew against a 500 ms threshold and relinquished shard 17 about 8 ms later — the relinquish preceded the actual chronyd backstep (-711 ms at 10:02:16.403Z) by roughly 2.3 s. That ordering is exactly what the guard is designed for: a host whose clock is about to be stepped backwards must drop leadership before the step lands, otherwise it could re-issue a lease interval it has already lived through and collide with whichever replica picked up the partition in the meantime. The four supporting signals all line up:

  - skew exceeded threshold → relinquish (correct trigger)
  - chronyd backstep landed shortly after, not before (correct ordering)
  - fencing held: no duplicate leadership signal
  - lease reacquired cleanly ~3 s after relinquish, with the host now within 20 ms

A peak replication lag of 1.8 s during a ~3 s leadership gap is consistent with a clean handoff rather than a partition fight. Write availability holding with no drop is the strongest single signal that no client ever saw two leaders.

2. Is a process restart warranted?

No. Nothing in the trace points at a process fault:

  - The skew came from the host clock, not from shard-keeper internals.
  - After the step, the process reacquired its lease on the first attempt and continued.
  - There is no duplicate leadership, no fencing violation, no retry storm, no error-rate movement.
  - Restarting would force a second, unnecessary leadership transition without addressing any actual defect. The guard already did the right thing.

3. Proportionate short-window checks before closing

Aim for ~10–15 minutes of observation, not an open-ended watch. Pull these from the existing shard-keeper lease-convergence runbook entry rather than inventing new ones:

  a. Confirm lease epochs for shard 17 (and its peers) are monotonic across the relinquish/reacquire boundary. Two contiguous lease IDs with strictly increasing epochs is the minimum acceptable; a non-monotonic or duplicate epoch is the only thing that should re-open the alert.
  b. Verify every partition has exactly one owner. The guard protects the shard you saw relinquish, but the host clock was drifting broadly enough to trigger it, so check the other shards on the same replica for any brief dual-ownership window.
  c. Confirm no "stale-owner" or fence-rejection messages for two full lease-renewal intervals after reacquire — this is the standard post-failover quiet-period check.
  d. Read the replication-lag panel for shard 17 specifically and confirm lag returned to baseline within one renewal interval of the reacquire (i.e. no residual tail).
  e. Check the host's chrony tracking for the prior 30 minutes: one step is fine; a second step, or sustained offset oscillation above ~100 ms, would suggest the NTP source itself is unstable and warrants a separate NTF/hardware ticket, but does not change the shard-keeper verdict.
  f. Skim shard-keeper error-rate, leadership-change, and fence-rejection counters for any movement outside the 10:02:14–10:02:20Z window.

If (a)–(f) are clean, close the alert with a one-line note: "lease guard exercised correctly during host clock step; fencing held; no process action required." If any of them is not clean, that is a separate finding and should be escalated on its own evidence rather than folded into this one.

Optional follow-up worth flagging but not blocking the close: a -711 ms chronyd step is on the larger side for a healthy NTP path. If the same host produces a second skew-triggered relinquish inside, say, 30 days, that's the moment to file an NTP/host-clock investigation; one occurrence is just noise.

The test pins one happy-path transition: full → 429 → free one slot → 202 → still at cap. That's the only thing it actually proves. Below is what's missing, ordered by what I'd want Wes to add before merge. Group 5 (the cap-1 race) is the one I'd block on; the rest can land in the same PR but aren't blockers individually.

1. IDENTITY OF QUEUED REQUESTS

The test never proves the request admitted by submit(retryRequest) is the one that lives in the queue, nor that the rejected nextRequest stayed out. After the 202:

    require.True(t, q.Contains(retryRequest.ID), "accepted request must be present in the queue")
    require.False(t, q.Contains(nextRequest.ID), "rejected request must not be present")

This catches the failure modes where the implementation drops accepted requests or admits rejected ones — both would otherwise pass the current assertions because Len() == 20000 is true in either case.

2. ACCEPTED / REJECTED ACCOUNTING

The service needs counters (Accepted, Rejected, Dropped). If they don't exist yet, this PR should add them — they're cheap and every other assertion below depends on them. Then around the test body:

    before := metrics.Snapshot()
    // ... existing fill / 429 / completeOne / 202 ...
    after := metrics.Snapshot()
    require.Equal(t, before.Accepted + 1, after.Accepted)
    require.Equal(t, before.Rejected + 1, after.Rejected)
    require.Equal(t, before.Dropped, after.Dropped)   // no silent loss

The Dropped invariant is the one that catches double-admission or a missing rejection path under the concurrency tests below.

3. RETRY-AFTER HEADER

The 429 must carry Retry-After in the 1–3 second jitter band that the rest of ingest-edge uses, and it must remain jittered under load — otherwise the synchronized-retry burst that motivated the whole change comes back:

    ra, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"))
    require.NoError(t, err)
    require.GreaterOrEqual(t, ra, 1)
    require.LessOrEqual(t, ra, 3)

Run the at-cap scenario with N concurrent submitters and assert the observed Retry-After values are not all identical:

    require.Greater(t, len(uniqueRetryAfters), 1, "Retry-After must stay jittered under concurrent rejection")

4. CONCURRENT SUBMITTERS

Same scenario, N goroutines hammering an at-cap queue, then a second wave after completeOne opens one slot:

    var wg sync.WaitGroup
    codes := make([]int, N)
    for i := 0; i < N; i++ {
        wg.Add(1)
        go func(i int) {
            defer wg.Done()
            codes[i] = submit(requests[i]).StatusCode
        }(i)
    }
    wg.Wait()

    acc := count(codes, 202)
    rej := count(codes, 429)
    oth := N - acc - rej
    require.Equal(t, 0, oth, "every submit must terminate with 202 or 429")
    require.Equal(t, 1, acc, "at most one slot opened by completeOne")
    require.Equal(t, before.Accepted + acc, after.Accepted)
    require.Equal(t, before.Rejected + rej, after.Rejected)

This is also where an over-admission or under-admission bug at the boundary would first surface, which leads into the next one.

5. RACE-SENSITIVE CHECK AROUND THE TRANSITION BELOW THE CAP

This is the gap I'd most want closed. The classic check-then-act race sits at cap-1: two submitters both read Len() == cap-1, both decide "admit", both enqueue, queue goes to cap+1. Or both read Len() == cap while a slot opened between the read and the enqueue, and both reject. Pin the boundary by hammering at cap-1 with K >> 1 concurrent submitters while a separate goroutine calls completeOne:

    // Drive queue to exactly cap-1, then fire K submitters concurrently with one completion.
    for i := 0; i < K; i++ {
        wg.Add(1)
        go func() {
            defer wg.Done()
            r := submit(reqs[i])
            require.Contains(t, []int{202, 429}, r.StatusCode)
        }()
    }
    go completeOne(q)
    wg.Wait()

    require.LessOrEqual(t, q.Len(), cap, "queue must never exceed cap")
    require.Equal(t, before.Dropped, after.Dropped, "no silent loss across the race")
    require.Equal(t, K, (after.Accepted - before.Accepted) + (after.Rejected - before.Rejected),
        "every submission must be accounted for")

A simpler version if Wes wants to keep it tight: no concurrent completion, just hammer at cap-1 with K submitters and assert accepted <= 1. If admission reads Len() outside the enqueue lock, that one assertion will fail.

OPTIONAL BUT CHEAP

- Boundary at exactly cap and cap-1, one line each: at cap → 429, at cap-1 → 202.
- Recovery latency: after completeOne, the next submit should succeed within a small bounded window (e.g., eventually up to ~50ms), not require a long sleep.
- Clock check: Retry-After must not be in the past relative to test time if the framework exposes a clock.

OUT OF SCOPE FOR THIS PR

End-to-end staging load (the Jan 18 100-client jitter test belongs with the rollout, not this unit). Dropped-counter coverage at multiples of cap. These can wait.

The separation matters because a leading invitation generates agreement data ("yes, this would help"), which is the weakest form of evidence for a proposal. Five neutral interviews produce observational data about how the handoff actually works and where it strains. The risk now is that the proposal's frame colors interpretation — a designer with a token-versioning hypothesis will hear "versioning pain" more loudly than unrelated friction she didn't anticipate.

Below is a structure Anya can fill in directly. It is deliberately restrictive in places; that is the point.

THREE BUCKETS

1. OBSERVED THEMES — what was said across the five interviews
   Each theme is a discrete observation, not a synthesis. Tag every entry with:
     - how many of 5 raised it
     - unprompted vs only in response to a question
     - the interviewee's own phrasing when it is sharp ("I just rebuild it locally" beats "inconsistency between environments")
     - whether a concrete example is attached (a specific token, a specific rollback, a specific moment)
   Sub-categories that usually emerge in this kind of interview:
     - handoff friction (where design→eng transfer breaks or slows)
     - uncertainty (moments when people do not know what is authoritative)
     - workarounds (the unofficial paths people actually take)
     - concrete failures (the specific incidents that crystallize a problem)
     - variation by surface area (web vs iOS vs Android; product vs marketing)
     - variation by team (who copes well, who does not, and what seems to explain it)
   Hard rule: no theme in this section contains "should," "need," or "must." Themes describe the current state.

2. OPEN QUESTIONS — things surfaced but unresolved
     - Single-signal items that could be outliers (flag as "1 of 5, follow-up needed before treating as pattern")
     - Contradictions between interviewees — record both positions, do not resolve
     - Statements that need operational evidence to confirm ("feels slow" needs a measured number; "we always rerun CI" needs an actual rerun rate)
     - Gaps the neutral invitation did not cover but the themes now suggest matter
     - Sampling caveats (the 5 may under-represent some surface area or team)
   Hard rule: no hypothesis language here. This section is what she does not know.

3. SOLUTION HYPOTHESES — what Anya might propose
   This section is deliberately separate from the other two. Each hypothesis is its own entry with:
     - the proposal in one plain sentence
     - which observed theme numbers it claims to address
     - the kind of support the interviews actually provide:
         direct — interviewee named this need unprompted
         indirect — interviewee named the underlying friction, not this solution
         tangential — related but not the same thing
         none — engineering instinct, interviews neither confirm nor deny
     - what evidence is still missing (acceptance criteria, feasibility, alternatives considered, cost)
     - alternative explanations for the same themes (the same observed friction motivates several different proposals; the interviews do not select among them)
     - what would need to be true for this hypothesis to be right
   Hard rule: hypotheses are framed as "the interviews motivate asking whether X," not "the interviews show X is needed."

ANTI-PATTERNS — how the original proposal sneaks back in
     - Cherry-picking: only citing the 2 of 5 whose direction matched
     - Up-weighting: treating one mention of "versioning pain" as more important than three mentions of an unrelated problem
     - Causality creep: "engineers described friction" quietly becomes "engineers said my proposal would fix it" when they did not
     - Solution leakage in the themes section: a theme that already contains the answer
     - Counting weak support as strong: an interviewee saying "yeah, that could help" after being shown a proposal is weaker evidence than them describing the friction unprompted. Both get recorded, with different tags.

PRESENTATION SKELETON
   1. What I did and did not ask (one paragraph): five neutral interviews on current handoff, uncertainty, workarounds, and concrete examples. The interviews were not structured to validate any specific proposal.
   2. Observed themes — the evidence, with the tags above
   3. Open questions — the honest gaps
   4. What the themes suggest worth investigating next — hypotheses as next questions, not findings
   5. What I am not claiming — one sentence each: that any specific solution is validated; that the themes are exhaustive; that five engineers represent all of engineering at North Pier; that absence of a theme means absence of a problem.

The discipline the structure enforces is the same one Alex uses everywhere: each claim has a citation, each gap is named, each hypothesis is marked as a hypothesis. If a stakeholder pushes that "the interviews did not show X is needed," Anya either points to the specific theme that does show it, or moves X into the open-questions section and concedes it. That is the move.

Wes's proposal has three specific failures against the invariant. Naming them first, then the corrected state model.

Three failures in Wes's patch:

  1. "validated_generation changes after schema validation but before dynamic validation" — this is the exact shape of last week's mismatch. While dynamic validation is still in flight (or has just failed), the endpoint cannot claim the generation is validated. If dynamic validation then fails, validated_generation has already moved, and anything that read the endpoint in that window saw a green field where there was a pending failure. validated_generation must mean "this generation passed every check we run before fan-out". It must advance only after BOTH schema and dynamic validation have completed successfully. From the endpoint's perspective, validation is a single predicate; the endpoint never observes an intermediate state.

  2. "active_generation changes before the configuration is fanned out to workers" — violates the invariant directly. From the moment fan-out starts until the moment every worker has accepted, the generation is in-flight, not active. active_generation == X must mean X is the configuration in use on every worker, full stop.

  3. "If any worker rejects the apply, the old configuration remains in use even though active_generation already shows the requested generation" — this is a contradiction the endpoint can't paper over with a footnote. If active_generation == X and the running config is Y != X, the endpoint is reporting a generation that is not active. There is no recovery here; the invariant itself is broken.

Corrected state model:

Each of the three generations is monotonically non-decreasing within a process lifetime. None of them move on a failed path.

  attempted_generation
    Advances only after the configuration parses successfully and we have a structurally valid configuration object in hand.
    On syntax/parse failure: does not advance. The endpoint surfaces the failure separately (last_failed_generation, last_error.stage = "parse") so operators can see something was attempted and rejected without attempted_generation lying about it.

  validated_generation
    Advances only after BOTH schema validation and dynamic validation have completed successfully. Validation is atomic from the endpoint's view.
    On schema failure: does not advance.
    On dynamic failure: does not advance. The window between "schema passed" and "dynamic completed" is a black box to the endpoint; validated_generation stays at its prior value throughout.

  active_generation
    Advances only after every worker has acknowledged acceptance of the new configuration.
    On any worker rejection (partial or full): does not advance. Previous active_generation remains the truth.
    Fan-out in progress is a distinct state. If we want the endpoint to surface that a generation is being applied, it belongs in a separate field (pending_apply_generation), not in active_generation.

State transitions by failure path:

  Path                          attempted  validated  active
  syntax / parse failure        unchanged  unchanged  unchanged
  schema validation failure     advances   unchanged  unchanged
  dynamic validation failure    advances   unchanged  unchanged
  partial worker-apply failure  advances   advances   unchanged
  full activation (all accept)  advances   advances   advances

Supporting fields the endpoint must also expose, or it will lie by omission:

  pending_apply_generation
    The generation currently being fanned out, if any. Unset when no apply is in flight. Set when fan-out starts. Cleared on full accept (and active_generation then advances); cleared on any reject (active_generation stays put). Without this, an operator reading active_generation == X cannot distinguish "fan-out done" from "fan-out mid-flight" from "a different generation actually got accepted on one worker" — three very different situations.

  last_failed_generation
    The most recent generation that failed at any stage. Without this, attempted_generation > validated_generation leaves the operator guessing why; the endpoint must surface what happened.

  last_error
    Structured failure with stage tagged (parse / schema / dynamic / apply), generation number, and enough context to identify the failure. Stage is mandatory because the operator's response differs by stage — fix the config, fix a worker, or escalate.

What this buys Wes:

  - attempted and validated remain useful leading indicators but no longer over-claim. Operators can still see "we're working on N (attempted = N) and validated up to M (validated = M)" and infer the gap, but the endpoint does not claim validated == N while validation is mid-flight.
  - active_generation stays consistent with what is actually running everywhere. Fan-out gets its own honest signal (pending_apply_generation), not a fake active_generation that may revert.
  - The failure path is observable. last_failed_generation + last_error.stage means a "stuck" reload is debuggable from the endpoint rather than a mystery that requires log-diving.

Suggested review note back to Wes, short version: validated_generation must require both schema and dynamic validation; active_generation must require all-worker accept; add pending_apply_generation, last_failed_generation, and last_error.stage; active_generation never moves on a failed path.

Short version: the 400 is deterministic and content-driven, not congestion-driven. Retrying the same bytes (with or without a `Retry-After` delay) produces the same gzip-decode failure every time. The fix is on the wire shape, not on the schedule.

1. What the server is actually saying

The collector received bytes with `Content-Encoding: gzip` set, then handed the body to its gzip decoder. A gzip stream must begin with the two-byte magic `1f 8b`. The captured body is protobuf field tags (e.g. `0a ...` for OTLP `ExportTraceServiceRequest`), so the magic-number check fails immediately and the decoder raises an "invalid gzip header" / "not a gzip stream" error. The server returns 400 because it cannot parse a body it has been told is gzip-encoded.

Key point: this is a content-encoding contract violation, not a malformed protobuf. If the client had not set `Content-Encoding`, the same protobuf bytes would parse fine.

2. The two valid corrections

Exactly one of the following is correct per request; mixing them is the bug:

  A. Compress, then keep the header.
       - gzip the serialized protobuf bytes,
       - set `Content-Encoding: gzip`,
       - keep `Content-Type: application/x-protobuf` (or the variant their exporter uses).
       - This is the path the OTLP/HTTP spec intends when gzip is advertised.

  B. Don't compress; drop the header.
       - send the protobuf bytes verbatim,
       - set only `Content-Type: application/x-protobuf`,
       - do NOT set `Content-Encoding`.
       - Yes, simply removing the `Content-Encoding: gzip` header is sufficient *provided the body really is uncompressed protobuf*, which the capture here shows is the case.

Both options are valid; the choice depends on what the client code path actually produces. The customer should pick the one that matches their existing serialization, not switch encodings on the fly per request.

Things that are NOT valid fixes:
  - retrying the same body (see #3),
  - adding a `Retry-After` delay before resending the same body,
  - changing the value of `Content-Encoding` to something else (e.g. `identity`, `deflate`, `zstd`) without also changing the bytes — the header must describe the actual bytes.

3. Why retrying the unchanged request cannot recover

The 400 here is a deterministic function of the bytes and the header:

  gzip_decode(claimed_gzip_bytes) -> failure, every time.

There is no server-side state (quota window, inflight slot, queue position) that, given more time, would make those bytes suddenly parse as gzip. After one second, one minute, or one hour, the magic-number check still fails. So:

  - the retry guidance that applies to 5xx ("transient, back off, retry") does NOT apply,
  - the retry guidance that applies to 429 ("you exceeded quota, wait `Retry-After` and try again") does NOT apply,
  - and re-sending the same bytes is, in support-case language, a "permanent failure for that request shape."

This is the same shape as the exemplar/trace_id 400 case: a validation rule is being violated, so the unchanged payload deterministically fails again. The customer's exporter needs to produce a different request, not a delayed copy of the same one.

4. Why the production 429 / `Retry-After` behavior does not apply

The randomized 1-3s `Retry-After` on ingest-edge 429s is a backpressure mechanism. It exists because:

  - 429 means "I received your request, I understood it, and I'm choosing to slow you down."
  - The request shape is valid; the server state is the problem.
  - After a bounded delay, the same request with the same headers will be accepted.

A 400 with `invalid-gzip-header` is in a different category entirely:

  - the server cannot even reach the part of the pipeline that would consult backpressure,
  - `Retry-After` is not part of the 400 contract (per RFC 9110, `Retry-After` is defined for 503 and 429, with 3xx as a courtesy; it is not meaningful on 4xx other than 429),
  - waiting longer does not change the byte stream,
  - so the ingest-edge retry-dedup / randomized-backoff machinery has nothing to act on.

The two error families are not interchangeable. Customers sometimes assume "4xx means try again with a delay," but only 429 carries that semantic; other 4xx are "fix the request."

5. Recommended Support response, condensed

A short, customer-facing version they can paste into the ticket:

  The 400 with "invalid gzip header" means the request body is not actually gzip-compressed even though `Content-Encoding: gzip` is set. The collector's gzip decoder rejects the body on the magic-number check (gzip streams start with bytes `1f 8b`; the captured body starts with protobuf field tags, not those bytes).

  Please pick one of the following and apply it consistently:

    - If you want compressed transport: gzip the serialized protobuf body before sending, and keep `Content-Encoding: gzip`. The exporter should compress, then send.
    - If you want uncompressed transport: send the protobuf bytes as-is, set only `Content-Type: application/x-protobuf`, and remove the `Content-Encoding` header.

  Retrying the same body will reproduce the same 400 every time, because the failure is in the bytes, not in server load. `Retry-After` (which applies to 429 / 503) does not help here; this 400 will not become a 200 after a delay. The fix is to change what is sent, not when it is sent.

  If you can share the exporter/library name and version, we can point at the specific configuration flag that controls whether the body is compressed before the `Content-Encoding` header is set — most OTLP exporters expose this as a compression option that is off-by-default or wired separately from the header.

If you want, I can also draft a one-paragraph variant for the public status-page / docs FAQ entry, or pull together a tiny reproduction snippet (Python `requests` with both the broken and the fixed shape) that Support can attach so the customer can confirm against their own capture.

RECOMMENDATION: Cap the tenant backfill at roughly 50% of its current compaction-read share. Do not pause it. Do not roll back the service.

WHY THIS IS THE PROPORTIONATE CHOICE

  The live write path is intact: ingestion p99 is 92 ms (unchanged), no batches are being rejected, and disk utilization is 71% with headroom remaining. The degradation is bounded, identifiable, and originates from a single planned background task that is now consuming 43% of compaction reads. That is a resource-contention symptom on a non-critical background job, not a live-path regression.

  Pausing discards the completed backfill work and forces a full restart later. Backfill is idempotent and keyed by (tenant, batch, segment), so it can resume safely, but throwing away progress is a larger intervention than the symptoms justify. Capping preserves forward progress while relieving the specific load competing with live-path compaction. This matches the standing rule that background work throttles before live-path rollback is considered.

WHAT TO CAP, AND BY HOW MUCH

  Target: reduce the backfill's share of compaction reads from the current 43% to roughly 20%. In practice, that is approximately a 50% throttle on the backfill worker's read concurrency or per-tenant scan rate, depending on which knob is exposed. The exact number can be tuned once the cap is in place; the goal is to halve the attributable compaction-read load.

  Ingestion priority is preserved: if the cap does not produce visible recovery, the cap deepens (for example, to 75%) before any pause is considered. Pause is the fallback only if capping fails to bring metrics back into the recovery band, which would imply the cause is not solely the backfill.

MEASURABLE RECOVERY THRESHOLDS FOR LIFTING THE CAP

  All of the following must hold simultaneously for a sustained window of at least 30 minutes before the cap is removed:

    1. Compaction backlog age at or below 30 minutes. The baseline was 18 minutes; 30 leaves margin against the 64-minute observed peak and gives early warning if the underlying load shifts.
    2. Query p99 at or below 350 ms. Baseline is 240 ms; 350 is the recovery band, not the steady-state target.
    3. Ingestion write p99 unchanged from the 92 ms baseline. Any drift above roughly 100 ms is an early signal that contention is spreading to the live path.
    4. Object-store SlowDown rate below 0.1%. This is well under the 0.74% observed during the March 6 worker-doubling event and keeps read pressure on the store inside nominal bounds.
    5. Zero batches rejected; error rate unchanged from the current baseline.

  If compaction backlog age climbs past 90 minutes, query p99 exceeds 800 ms, or ingestion p99 begins to rise while the cap is in place, deepen the cap before considering pause. If a deepened cap does not bring metrics back into the band within 15 minutes, escalate to a pause and open a postmortem, because that pattern indicates a different cause than the backfill alone.

WHAT THIS IS NOT

  This is not a service rollback. Ingestion, query serving, and storage are all within nominal bounds. The live label set and rollup pipeline are unchanged. No tenant-visible behavior is being modified. The cap is a temporary throttle on a background task with written recovery conditions, not a configuration change to rollup-service or its consumer graph.

VERIFICATION CADENCE WHILE THE CAP IS IN PLACE

  Check compaction backlog age and query p99 every 5 minutes. Watch ingestion write p99 for drift above 100 ms as the canary for broader contention. If any recovery threshold is breached, deepen the cap first; if deepening does not recover within 15 minutes, escalate to pause plus investigation rather than treating this as a live-path incident.

  When the 30-minute sustained recovery holds, lift the cap in a single step back to the prior setting and continue watching the same metrics for the next hour. If they remain inside the recovery band, the backfill returns to its scheduled pace and this episode closes with a written note recording the cap level, the duration held, and the recovery readings.

Decision: null-to-basic coercion is NOT safe. It is a semantic collapse, not a default. The 8% of rows whose `account_tier` is unknown would be promoted into an affirmative low-touch classification that the renewal workflow acts on, which silently misroutes a real cohort. Once coerced at the source, the original "unknown" fact is gone — append-only corrections cannot restore it. This is the same shape as the billing-triage and renewal-risk-review cases: the upstream transformation destroys a distinction the downstream treats as load-bearing.

Minimum schema requirements
- `account_tier` MUST remain nullable OR carry a distinct sentinel value (e.g. `unknown` / `missing`) that is not equal to any named tier. "basic" cannot be used as a placeholder for missing data.
- `account_tier_source` / `account_tier_provenance` is required for every row, naming the system that supplied the value (vendor / internal / not_supplied). This aligns with the Lantern v0 `source_system` discipline.
- `account_tier_as_of` timestamp is required so the downstream can distinguish "stale basic" from "current basic" and reason about cohort freshness.
- The existing v0 envelope field `data_quality` MUST be set per row (e.g. `tier_missing=true`) when `account_tier` is not supplied. The room's contract should name which `data_quality` flags are emitted and what they mean.
- Status enums and field stability must be declared explicitly: which tier values are stable, which are experimental, and which (`unknown`) is a first-class state — not a transient.

Minimum validation requirements
- A contract assertion that source-row count for `account_tier = basic` equals downstream-row count for `account_tier = basic`. If the downstream `basic` count exceeds the source `basic` count, that is a hard failure of the contract.
- The null/unknown rate is a monitored metric with a tracked baseline (~8%). Sudden drift in either direction is an alertable condition: a drop indicates coercion has been reintroduced; a rise indicates an upstream regression.
- CI/lint guard rejecting transforms that coerce null to a named tier in the weekly model output. Treat such a transform as a contract change, not a fix.
- Provenance completeness check: every row with a non-null `account_tier` must have a populated `account_tier_source` and `account_tier_as_of`.

Minimum downstream-handling requirements
- The renewal workflow MUST treat missing/unknown `account_tier` as its own branch — for example, hold the renewal decision, route to manual review, or apply a conservative default that is explicitly labeled as "tier unknown" in any output. It MUST NOT silently treat missing rows as `basic`.
- The room contract documents the downstream null policy in writing, naming which branch is taken and who owns it. The renewal-workflow owner signs off on that wording.
- Any downstream report or UI that surfaces tier counts must show the unknown/missing bucket alongside the named tiers. Hiding it re-creates the same erasure at the read surface.

Admission posture (Iris's call)
- Admissible IF the upstream preserves null/unknown with provenance AND the renewal workflow handles it on an explicit branch.
- Not admissible if the weekly model output coerces nulls to `basic`, OR if the renewal workflow has no documented null branch.
- This stays Iris's ordinary admission decision once the contract shape above is met. Alex is not taking the admission lane — only the data-contract exception.

Suggested private Slack reply to Iris

> The null-to-basic coercion isn't safe as proposed — it collapses "unknown" into an affirmative low-touch tier the renewal workflow acts on, which would silently misroute ~8% of the cohort. To admit this room, the weekly model output needs to keep `account_tier` nullable (or use a distinct `unknown` value), carry `account_tier_source` and `account_tier_as_of` provenance, and set `data_quality` on the missing rows. On the downstream side, the renewal workflow needs an explicit branch for missing tier — hold, manual review, or a clearly labeled conservative default — and the renewal-workflow owner needs to sign off on that wording in the room contract. Once those are in place, the admission is yours to make through the ordinary workflow. I'm staying out of the room-admission lane; this is just the contract exception.

No memory write needed — this sits inside the already-recorded pattern of refusing upstream transformations that destroy distinctions the downstream treats as load-bearing (cf. billing-triage 2/28, renewal-risk-review 4/9–4/11).

Draft is sound in direction but leaves three things underspecified: (a) what counts as a generator failure, (b) what counts as partial output, and (c) what "publishing" actually is and where it writes. Walked through below.

GENERATOR FAILURE

  Could this publish? No (draft blocks on non-zero exit; previously published package unchanged).
  Could this silently rewrite? No (no commit/publish on failure path). 

  Gaps that could let a related scenario through:

  - "Unsuccessfully" needs an explicit definition. Exit code alone misses hangs (no exit), SIGKILL/OOM, generator crashes after writing some output, and generators that exit 0 with garbage output. The drift check would only catch the last case by accident.
  - CI timeout. A hung generator blocks the job until it times out. What's the timeout? Who is notified?
  - Non-deterministic generators. If output depends on timestamps, sort order, or environment, every run diffs against the committed representation. Drift check is permanently red, or operators learn to bypass it. Critical to address.
  - Logs and diagnostics. "Exit unsuccessfully" is silent without logs. Stdout/stderr should be a CI artifact on every failure path.
  - Temp directory lifecycle. Who creates/cleans it? Stale files from a prior partial run could be picked up by a later run. On failure, is it cleaned or leaked?

PARTIAL OUTPUT

  Could this publish? No. Drift check would catch partial output via diff (missing keys show up as differences). The drift check is doing more work than the exit-code check; worth making that explicit.
  Could this silently rewrite? No (no commit/publish).

  Gaps:

  - Atomic write. Does the generator write the output file directly, or write to a temp file and rename? A direct write that crashes halfway could leave a half-written file that the drift check then observes as the "result."
  - Schema vs. structural diff. A generator could produce output where every key matches the committed representation but a value's type or semantics changed (number-as-string, hex vs. rgb, px vs. rem). Key-level text diff may not surface this. Need schema-aware validation, not just text diff.
  - Completeness signal. Drift check tells you "something differs." It doesn't say whether the issue is missing tokens, renamed tokens, or value drift. Worth distinguishing for triage.
  - Generator-environment determinism. If the generator depends on Python/Node version, env vars, or a remote service, the same canonical input can produce different output across CI and local runs. Need a pinned generator environment and a reproducible build.

UNEXPECTED DIFF

  Could this publish? No (draft blocks on diff).
  Could this silently rewrite? No (no commit/publish).

  Gaps:

  - "Committed representation" is ambiguous. Same-PR committed representation (i.e., the PR may include regenerated files alongside the canonical-package update), or main-branch tip? If same-PR, the check protects against PRs that change the canonical but forget to regenerate. If main-tip, it also protects against a stale main. The choice should be explicit.
  - Diff scope and reporting. What does "key-level diff" mean exactly: per-token value comparison, structural diff, or whole-file text diff? Where is the diff uploaded (PR comment, artifact, both), and for how long?
  - False positives. Same root cause as the non-determinism issue above. Without determinism or canonicalization, the check is flaky.
  - TOCTOU between CI green and publish. "Publishing is permitted only when the drift check is clean" — but if publishing reads from a different source than CI (e.g., branch tip vs. pinned SHA), the published version may not be the one CI validated. The draft doesn't say what publishing reads from.
  - Manual override. Can a human publish without the check? If yes, the check is bypassable and the failure behavior is partly aspirational.

SILENT REWRITES THE DRAFT DOESN'T COVER

  The draft protects CI-mediated rewrites of the generated representations. It doesn't directly protect:

  - The canonical package itself. A direct commit to the canonical-package repo bypasses everything in this draft. Typical safeguards are branch protection, required reviewers, and the drift check running on PRs against the canonical repo. The most dangerous silent rewrite is upstream of the generator.
  - The published package. Where does "publishing" write? If it writes to a registry, CDN, package manager, or Figma library, that's a separate artifact store. A bad publish silently overwrites that store.
  - Local caches in downstream tools. A bad version that gets cached could persist after the fix. Need an invalidation story.

PUBLISHING IS UNDEFINED

  The draft talks about "publishing is blocked" but doesn't say what publishing is. This is the largest gap. Specifically:

  - What artifact is published? A versioned engineering JSON, a Figma library update, both, something else?
  - Where does publishing write: npm/internal registry, Figma library, documentation site, multiple destinations?
  - Manual or automated? If automated, what's the trigger (merge to main, tag push, scheduled)?
  - Who has permission to publish manually, and is that audited?
  - Rollback story. If a bad version is published, how is it reverted? Are consumers notified?

OTHER ITEMS WORTH RAISING

  - Figma round-trip direction. The draft assumes canonical -> Figma one-way. If designers can also publish back into the canonical package from Figma (a common workflow), the canonical-source property is at risk and the drift check needs to handle Figma-side divergence too. Pilot scope should say which direction is allowed.
  - Generator version pinning. Is the generator itself versioned and pinned? A generator update can change output even with the same canonical input. This is a separate axis of drift.
  - Audit trail retention. Where do key-level diffs live and for how long? Useful for postmortems and for understanding drift patterns over time.
  - Pilot stop conditions. If the drift check flaks or is bypassed repeatedly, what are the exit criteria? Worth defining before the pilot starts.
  - Backup owner. Anya owns the proposal and rollout. Is there a named backup for the CI on-call rotation during the pilot?

QUESTIONS FOR ANYA

  Specific things I'd want answered before the failure behavior is considered complete:

  1. What is "publishing" in concrete terms: what artifact, where does it write, who triggers it?
  2. What counts as "generator exits unsuccessfully": exit code only, or also timeout/OOM/signal? What's the CI timeout?
  3. How is generator determinism guaranteed: same canonical input + same generator version = same output across CI and local?
  4. Is the canonical-package repo protected (branch protection, required reviewers, drift check on PRs)?
  5. Is the generator itself versioned and pinned independently of the canonical package?
  6. Does the drift check compare against the same-PR committed representation or main-branch tip? Where is the key-level diff uploaded?
  7. Is the diff schema-aware (catches value-type changes) or text-only (catches only structural changes)?
  8. Can a human publish without the check passing? If yes, what's the audit trail?
  9. Is Figma round-tripping in or out of pilot scope?
  10. Is there a backup owner for the CI on-call rotation during the pilot?

If Anya can answer these, the draft becomes defensible. The three that most directly answer your question (could it ever publish or silently rewrite) are #1 (publishing), #2 (failure definition), and #4 (canonical-package protection). The other seven are about whether the failure behavior is complete enough to be the actual contract, rather than just a description of intent.

Contract review of Wes's semaphore swap

Contract 1 — overload rejected before admission. Preserved. tryAcquire is atomic; on permit exhaustion it returns false without any queue interaction, so rejection happens strictly before accepted_work++ and queue <- request.

Contract 2 — already queued work is never evicted. Preserved, conditional on the release being exact-once per admission. The permit is acquired before enqueue and only released on the natural exit path. No goroutine evicts an in-flight request.

Contract 3 — every rejection carries retry guidance. Preserved at the only admission-rejection point (the tryAcquire branch returns retryable429(), same as the original length-check branch). Worth asserting that no future rejection path bypasses retryable429().

Contract 4 — rejected work is not counted as accepted. Preserved. accepted_work++ sits after the rejection branch; a failed tryAcquire returns without incrementing.

Three things to nail down before merge

1. Release-site decision. "Released only when a queued request leaves the system" implies release at processing completion, not at dequeue. That is stricter than the original len(queue) check (which bounded only the queue, leaving worker concurrency uncapped) — the new code caps total admitted + in-flight at 20,000 across queue plus workers. Pick that interpretation explicitly and document it on the PR, because the assertion set differs: permits_in_use == len(queue) + active_workers at quiescence, not permits_in_use == len(queue).

2. Error path between admit and enqueue. The proposed order is tryAcquire -> accepted_work++ -> queue <- request. If the send is non-blocking (select with default, or send on a channel that returns ok==false) or plumbed to context cancellation, the permit can be held with no queue entry and accepted_work is inflated. Either (a) make the enqueue unconditional and synchronous with no failure mode, or (b) wrap the admit path in defer release() that fires on any early return. Add an assertion that a forced enqueue failure does not leak permits or accepted_work.

3. Panic safety. If the worker panics between admit and release, the permit leaks and the steady-state cap shrinks permanently. The release site must use defer and survive recover(). Add a test that injects a panic mid-processing and asserts permits_in_use returns to zero after recovery.

Required assertions before merge

Concurrency
- Race at boundary: N concurrent admission goroutines targeting queue length 19,999 over M trials; observed len(queue) + active_workers never exceeds 20,000. This is the exact race Wes found.
- Linearizability of permits: permits_in_use is a step function, monotonically +1 on admit and -1 on release, never +2 or -2 within a single step.
- No deadlock: fuzzed schedule of admit and release calls runs to completion under both fast and slow consumer configurations.
- No starvation: under sustained overload with one consumer, every accepted request eventually completes.
- No permit loss: 1,000,000 admit/release cycles end with permits_in_use == 0.
- Synchronous burst: 100,000 arrivals with zero consumers cap in-flight at exactly 20,000; the remaining 80,000 are rejected without enqueueing.

Accounting
- Rejections never increment accepted_work: 1,000,000 forced rejections leave accepted_work == 0.
- accepted_work == permits_in_use at every quiescent observation.
- accepted_work is monotonically non-decreasing across the test lifetime.
- accepted_work is read coherently under concurrent observation (no torn reads if 64-bit on 32-bit platforms; explicit atomic if not).
- Force-enqueue-failure test: simulated send failure leaves permits_in_use and accepted_work both unchanged.
- Panic-injection test: simulated panic in worker leaves permits_in_use == 0 after recovery and accepted_work equal to the number of permits that were acquired (no double-count).

Retry-After / 429 contract
- Every rejection returns HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header. The test should fail if retryable429() ever omits the header.
- Retry-After is in the documented range. If metrics-router adopts the same randomized 1-3 second policy as ingest-edge, the assertion is 1 <= Retry-After <= 3; if it has its own range, define it in the test.
- Retry-After > 0 always; never zero, never negative.
- Status code is exactly 429 on every rejection; no 503 fallback, no silent 200.
- Body content stable enough that downstream clients can distinguish 429-from-admission from other 429s if needed.

Recovery
- Saturation-then-drain: fill in-flight to 20,000, next admission returns 429, complete one request, the next admission succeeds.
- Full drain: after all admitted requests complete, permits_in_use == 0 and accepted_work holds at the peak.
- Recovery after processing error: worker errors mid-handling still release the permit; the next admission succeeds.
- Recovery after panic: worker panics mid-handling with recover() in place still release the permit; the next admission succeeds.
- Recovery after enqueue failure: forced enqueue failure releases the permit; the next admission succeeds.
- No permanent capacity shrink: 100 fill-then-drain cycles leave the steady-state cap at 20,000; cycle N+1 behaves identically to cycle 1.
- Graceful shutdown: all in-flight requests complete with permits released; cold restart yields permits_available == 20,000.

INVERSION ANKLE — SUNDAY PLAN
April 21, 2024

Mechanism (landing on another player's foot + inversion + lateral swelling) plus the negatives you reported — able to bear weight >4 steps, no bony tenderness, no deformity, no numbness, no open wound — are consistent with a low-grade lateral ankle ligament sprain (most often the anterior talofibular ligament). By the Ottawa Ankle Rules, none of the criteria for an X-ray are met on the exam you described, so urgent imaging is not indicated by what you've told me.

REST OF SUNDAY — POLICE approach

  P — Protection. Avoid inversion-prone movement (pivoting, cutting, stairs without a railing, uneven ground). Don't tape or brace tightly.
  OL — Optimal Loading. Keep weight bearing as tolerated — the goal is a near-normal gait, not protective limping. While icing, do gentle non-inversion motion: ankle pumps (plantar/dorsiflexion) and toe curls.
  I — Ice. 15–20 min every 2–3 h while awake, with a thin cloth between ice and skin. Stop if skin gets numb or blotchy.
  C — Compression. Elastic wrap or ankle sleeve from the ball of the foot to just above the malleoli. Snug, not tight — normal toe color, easy to wiggle toes, no tingling. Recheck in 20 min.
  E — Elevation. Above the level of the heart when sitting/lying.

Pain control, if needed: ibuprofen 400–600 mg with food every 6 h, OR naproxen 220–440 mg every 12 h, OR acetaminophen 500–1000 mg every 6 h (max 3 g/day). With any GI or kidney history, default to acetaminophen or topical diclofenac. Don't ask Devika to be the diagnostician; she's your partner, not your resident.

Do NOT (next 48–72 h): heat, alcohol, massage directly over the lateral malleolus, "testing it" with a hard pivot, or a tight circumferential bandage.

TODAY / TONIGHT

  - Normal apartment gait; skip uneven-sidewalk Kibo walks — a short leashed bathroom trip only
  - Skip bouldering and any cutting sport

GENTLE MOVEMENT TIMELINE (graded, same posture as the calf re-entry)

  0–48 h:    pain-free ROM only — ankle pumps, ankle alphabet (letters with the foot, no aggressive inversion), seated towel scrunches with the toes
  Day 3–5:   stationary bike with zero resistance if pain-free; seated heel raises; weight-shifting while standing near support; non-inversion band work (eversion, dorsiflexion only — NOT inversion)
  Day 5–7:   single-leg balance holding a doorway, working toward 30 s; short toe-walking; walking progression to full gait

RED FLAGS — SEEK URGENT / ER EVALUATION
