Bottom line: yes, this morning-after picture still fits a low-grade lateral ankle sprain, most likely a grade I–II ATFL (anterior talofibular ligament) injury. The overnight changes you describe are on the expected timeline, and the negatives you rechecked still rule out the things that would change management.

Why this still reads as a mild sprain
- The bruise tracking distally below the lateral malleolus is the classic signature of a lateral-ligament bleed. Gravity pulls even a small extravasation downward overnight, so a small patch under the outside ankle bone is what you expect to see 12–18 hours after an inversion injury, not a sign of something new.
- Swelling commonly gets worse before it gets better. Soft-tissue swelling typically peaks 24–72 hours after the mechanism, so a Monday-morning increase over a Sunday-evening roll is normal and not a red flag on its own. Overnight you are also not elevating or compressing, so it accumulates.
- The things that would change this picture are still absent: focal bony tenderness at either malleolus, tenderness at the base of the 5th metatarsal or the navicular, inability to bear weight even four steps, deformity, numbness/tingling, color change in the toes, or pain at rest that is getting worse rather than better. You have none of those, so the Ottawa Ankle Rule criteria for imaging are not met on what you have described.

Compression today
- Use a compression sleeve or an elastic wrap. A sleeve is simpler; if you use an ACE wrap, apply it in a figure-8 starting at the ball of the foot and working up the ankle, overlapping each pass by about half the wrap width. Snug, not tight.
- Correct tightness test: you should still have normal color and sensation in the toes, no new tingling, and pain should not increase. If the toes go pale, blue, cool, or numb, or the wrap starts to throb, unwrap and reapply more loosely.
- Wear it during the day when you are up and around. Take it off at night and when you elevate. Recheck the toes every couple of hours the first day.
- Ice is still useful in the first 48–72 hours, especially after you have been on it: 15–20 minutes on, at least 40 minutes off, with a barrier between the skin and the pack. Elevation matters more than people give it credit for: above heart level when you can, especially in the first 48 hours.
- It is fine to skip compression entirely if the wrap is uncomfortable; gentle motion and elevation do more work than compression alone for a grade I–II sprain.

Gentle motion today
- Non-weight-bearing ankle range of motion is the most useful thing you can do today. It keeps the joint from stiffening, helps the inflammatory fluid clear, and does not load the ligament.
  - Ankle pumps: slow dorsiflexion and plantarflexion, full comfortable range, 1–2 sets of 10–15.
  - Ankle alphabet: trace slow letters of the alphabet in the air with the toes, moving only the ankle. This is the single best home exercise for an acute lateral sprain.
  - Towel or band dorsiflexion stretch: leg out, loop around the forefoot, gently pull the foot toward you until you feel a calf stretch, no ankle pain. Hold 20–30 seconds, repeat a few times.
- Walking around the house as tolerated is fine. Limp if you need to, but do not push through sharp pain. Use a shoe with a slightly stiff sole if you have one; going barefoot on hard floors tends to aggravate lateral sprains.
- Do not test today: inversion (rolling the ankle inward on purpose), single-leg balance on that foot, hopping, cutting, pivoting, running, bouldering, or soccer. None of those are probe questions worth answering on day 1–2 of a lateral sprain; they risk re-tearing a healing ligament or extending the bruise.
- Tomorrow (Tuesday) and Wednesday, if swelling is receding and walking is more comfortable, you can add a standing calf stretch against a wall and easy heel raises, still avoiding inversion. Soccer return is not a question for this week regardless of how it feels.

What would make an in-person assessment appropriate
- Urgent (same day, ideally within hours):
  - Deformity at the ankle or foot
  - Open wound over the swelling or bruising
  - Numbness, tingling, or color change (pale, blue, mottled) in the toes that does not resolve after loosening any wrap and elevating
  - Pain at rest that is getting worse rather than better, especially if the foot feels tense or pain spikes with passive toe movement (concerning for compartment syndrome, which is rare but real)
  - Sudden calf pain, swelling, or warmth, particularly if the calf becomes tender to squeeze (DVT risk is low in your situation but not zero after a soft-tissue leg injury and reduced ambulation)
  - Inability to bear any weight at all, or weight-bearing becomes meaningfully worse compared with yesterday
- Routine but timely (within a few days):
  - New focal bony tenderness directly over either malleolus, the navicular, or the base of the 5th metatarsal that was not there before
  - Bruising that expands significantly, especially onto the sole of the foot or the heel, or bruising that appears under the toenails
  - A feeling of true instability — the ankle giving way during normal walking, not just discomfort
  - Swelling that has not started to recede by day 4–5, or pain that has not begun to improve at all by day 5–7
  - Locking, catching, or a sense that something is blocking motion

Practical note
- Devika is an internal-medicine resident and is in the apartment; an in-person exam by her this evening or tomorrow morning is a perfectly reasonable backstop if any of the borderline signs appear, before deciding whether formal evaluation is needed. None of what you described today crosses that line on its own.

Net plan for today: compression as tolerated during the day, ice and elevation as the main anti-swelling work, ankle alphabet and pumps for motion, walk normally but skip all loading probes, and recheck the red-flag list above tonight and tomorrow morning. If the picture stays as it is now or improves, this should track like the September 2023 inversion did.

Direct answer to the customer: no, 8,800 + 10,000 is not 18,800 unique points delivered. The 8,800 in the first response are the same 8,800 that appear in the second response — the replay almost certainly created duplicates on the server.

What the first response actually said

  HTTP 429 with Retry-After: 2 is normally read as "whole request rejected, back off." But the response also carried an OTLP partial_success body reporting rejected_data_points: 1,200 with the error "rate limit exceeded for a subset of points." An OTLP partial_success with a non-zero rejected count is the server reporting partial acceptance of the export, not partial failure of the export. Read together, the first response meant:

    - 8,800 of the 10,000 points were accepted and stored.
    - 1,200 were rejected (rate-limited).
    - The 429 + Retry-After was telling the client to back off before sending more.

  The two signals together mean "I accepted most of this, throttled the rest, and want you to wait before sending again" — not "nothing landed, retry the whole thing."

What the second response actually means

  The client waited 2 seconds and resent the original 10,000-point batch unchanged. The server returned HTTP 200 with 10,000 accepted. But those 10,000 are the same payload as before. OTLP does not define a standard batch-level idempotency key, and ingest-edge does not require one. The server has no in-protocol way to know that 8,800 of the resent points are duplicates of points it just accepted. Unless the customer's SDK is sending a batch ID that ingest-edge is using for dedup, those 8,800 were stored a second time.

Why honoring Retry-After does not make the replay safe

  Retry-After governs WHEN to retry, not WHAT to retry. The header tells the client the minimum backoff before the next send; it does not retroactively change which points the server already accepted. The accepted 8,800 are committed on the server from the moment the partial_success was emitted. A later successful replay of the full batch cannot make them un-committed or un-counted. The two responses are not additive — the second is largely a superset of the first.

What the client should do instead

  When a 429 carries an OTLP partial_success body (or a 200 carries one), the client should:

    1. Parse the partial_success and record how many points were rejected and why.
    2. Treat Retry-After as the minimum backoff for THIS response only. ingest-edge returns randomized 1-3 second Retry-After values across responses, so do not cache the value from one response and apply it to later ones.
    3. Fix the cause for the rejected points before resending. For a rate-limit cause, reduce export rate or batch size; for a scale cause, fix the value range.
    4. After the backoff, resend ONLY the rejected points. Not the full batch.
    5. Keep request IDs / batch IDs stable if the SDK supports them, so any further retries are observable as retries rather than new attempts.

For this specific batch, the right sequence was:

    - First response: 8,800 accepted and stored.
    - Wait >= 2 seconds (Retry-After from THIS response).
    - Resend ONLY the 1,200 rejected points (ideally after reducing rate to avoid another throttling).
    - Unique total: 8,800 + 1,200 = 10,000.

What the customer actually has

  Best case (server deduped by batch ID): 10,000 unique points, and the replay attempt was a no-op for the 8,800.
  Likely case (no dedup): 18,800 stored entries, of which 8,800 are duplicates of the first response's accepted points.

The customer should not claim 18,800 successfully delivered. They should assume duplicates were created unless they can show ingest-edge deduplicated by a stable batch identifier, and they should audit the affected series for the duplicated 8,800.

Sanity-check on the failure-path exercise.

What happened, in plain terms: the generator wrote a fresh CSS file into the canonical/normal output directory before the platform-JSON semantic-validation step failed. Registry publication did not run, which is the part that held. The damage is on disk: the workspace now contains a pre-existing set plus one freshly-written file, and a later manual commit could lift that mixed set into the repo. This is "fail-closed at publish, fail-open at the writer" - the publish guard was correct, but it was guarding the wrong layer.

Fail-closed invariant

The canonical output paths are read-only except for the single atomic promotion step. The active generation does not change on any failed path: not on syntax failure, not on semantic-validation failure, not on partial worker-apply failure, and not on a successful run before promotion completes.

Why the original design didn't catch it

The proposal already had "publish only when both generators complete and the drift check is clean", and that guard held. The gap is that the generator was allowed to write into the normal output directory during the run. The temp-directory intent was in the CI description but not enforced in the writer's contract. Publish was fail-closed at the registry; the workspace below it was fail-open.

Minimal redesign, sanity-check only

1. Scratch isolation, enforced at the writer, not at CI orchestration:
   - Each CI run creates a fresh _build/<run-id>/ directory.
   - Every generator is configured with that scratch directory as its output root. No generator is invoked with the canonical path. If a generator doesn't accept an output-root argument, wrap it: have it write to a temp dir, then move outputs into the scratch dir.
   - _build/ is gitignored. That alone makes "later manual commit captures partial output" physically impossible - there is nothing in tracked paths to commit.

2. Validate against the scratch only:
   - Syntax check, semantic check, and drift check all read from _build/<run-id>/. Never from canonical.
   - Drift-check baseline: the currently active generation, or the source package if no generation is active yet.

3. Promotion is the only step that touches canonical:
   - On validation pass, atomically rename _build/<run-id>/ to published/<generation-id>/.
   - Update a single active pointer (symlink or pointer file) to the new generation. Stable consumer URLs (tokens.engineering.json, tokens.figma.json, tokens.css) resolve through that pointer.
   - The pointer update is one filesystem operation, atomic on the same filesystem as published/.

4. Cleanup on failure:
   - On any failure before promotion, delete _build/<run-id>/. Canonical and active pointer are untouched. There is no in-between state for a human to encounter.

State semantics, per your earlier ask

  attempted    CI run starts; _build/<run-id>/ created.   Canonical effect: none.
  validated    All generators done; syntax/semantic/      Canonical effect: none.
               drift checks all pass.                    (scratch only)
  active       _build/<run-id>/ renamed to               Canonical effect:
               published/<generation-id>/ and            pointer updated;
               pointer updated in one step.              old gen becomes
                                                         previous; consumers
                                                         see new content.

Failure paths and active-generation effect:

  syntax failure (platform JSON doesn't parse)         active unchanged
  semantic-validation failure                          active unchanged
  partial worker-apply failure                         active unchanged
  drift check finds divergence                         active unchanged
  successful activation                               active = new generation

What this changes for Anya's pilot

  - Six-week scope, source-package-as-canonical, drift-check semantics, and the publishing rule ("only when validated and promoted") all stay the same.
  - It is purely a writer-side constraint plus a one-step promotion. No new service, no new infra, no new owner.

Things I'd flag before she ships it

  1. Pick the atomic-promotion primitive deliberately. A directory rename is atomic on the same filesystem. A symlink swap is atomic on POSIX but not on Windows; if any consumer path is Windows-served, prefer a pointer-file approach. Test against the Figma tokens plugin's caching if it re-fetches by URL.
  2. Generation-id should be derived from the source-package version, not the CI timestamp. Two CI runs of the same source package should produce the same generation id and be safe to dedupe.
  3. If the canonical artifacts are committed to the repo today, the fail-closed property still holds (canonical is touched only by CI's atomic promotion), but humans can see mixed state in `git status` between promotion and the next commit. Long-term, move artifacts out of the repo into build outputs served by CI/CD.
  4. Add a CI assertion: after the run, _build/<run-id>/ must either be promoted (i.e., empty or absent) or deleted. Its presence in a final state is itself a failure signal - it means a step after promotion tried to write somewhere it shouldn't.
  5. Don't add a retry that re-runs promotion on transient errors. If the atomic rename fails, treat the run as failed and investigate; retrying promotion can race and produce two active generations.

Tests before this is rolled out beyond the pilot

  - Each of the four failure modes exercised end-to-end in CI. After each, the active pointer's generation id is unchanged. (Read it before and after.)
  - Platform JSON intentionally broken: registry publication does not run, canonical paths untouched, _build/ is gone.
  - One generator intentionally killed mid-run: same three assertions.
  - Drift check forced to fail: same three assertions.
  - Happy path: pointer moves, old generation still in published/, new generation resolvable through stable URLs.

What stays with Anya

  - She owns the writer contract (how generators are invoked, where scratch lives, how the pointer is updated).
  - She owns the rollback story (the previous generation is still in published/, just not pointed to).
  - She owns the CI assertion in (4) and the cleanup-on-failure deletion.
  - She owns any decision about moving artifacts out of the repo (3).

Net

The publish guard held; the bug is below it. Fix is writer-side: scratch isolation, atomic promotion, and a single writer for canonical. Pilot design and rollout stay with her.

## Diagnosis

The histogram is exported in **seconds** (`router_request_duration_seconds_bucket`), so `histogram_quantile(0.99, …)` returns a value in **seconds**. The dashboard renders 470 ms by multiplying by 1000; the alert does not. The expression compares seconds against a raw scalar of `300`, so:

- 300 seconds = 300,000 ms — the threshold is effectively ~600× too high.
- Staging result 0.47 s (= 470 ms) is below 300, → alert stays inactive.

Two equivalent fixes:

1. **Scale the RHS** to seconds: `… > 0.3`
2. **Scale the LHS** to milliseconds: `(histogram_quantile(…) * 1000) > 300`

Option 1 is the conventional choice in PromQL: keep the histogram's native unit end-to-end and put the unit on the threshold constant.

## Corrected alert

```
- alert: MetricsRouterP99LatencyHigh
  expr: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(router_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))) > 0.3
  for: 2m
  labels:
    severity: page
    service: metrics-router
  annotations:
    summary: "metrics-router p99 exceeds 300 ms"
    description: "p99 = {{ $value | humanizeDuration }} over the last 5m (threshold 300 ms)."
```

Two small extra defenses worth adding now:

- `for: 2m` — a one-shot 5-minute rate sample over 0.3 s is enough to fire once; gating on `for` keeps it from flapping on a single bucket-edge spike. Keep it short; the staging exercise showed real excursions that should page.
- `humanizeDuration` in the annotation — Prometheus renders 0.32 as `320ms`, which matches how the dashboard already speaks. The alert and dashboard then agree to the unit instead of disagreeing silently.

If you want me to leave the right-hand side in milliseconds for readability in the rule source, that's fine too — the *expression* just has to agree with itself. Pick one and don't mix.

DECISION ON THE METRICS-ROUTER ENCODED-SLASH DIVERGENCE

This is the same shape as the October 30, 2023 live-path label-value-shape problem, just inverted: the shadow decodes, the active path doesn't, and a 97% mismatch concentrated on one encoding class is a real rule-semantics divergence, not noise. Active-path counters are clean, no drops, downstream is happy — but "happy" here can mean "lucky": if the encoded-slash labels are only being caught by the catchall, and the catchall happens to share a destination with the specific rule, the divergence is latent. It will bite the first time a customer writes a rule whose catchall destination differs from the specific destination.

1. TREATMENT OF THE CANARY

   Hold. Do not promote. The comparator is doing its job — it has found a rule-semantics divergence that must be resolved before promotion. Continuing the canary without alignment is the metrics-router equivalent of the October 30th mistake: replay/mirror validation cannot substitute for live canary judgment on a label value-shape change. The clean canary numbers (no drops, no consumer complaint, baseline mismatch on non-encoded-slash labels) are evidence that the divergence is bounded today, not evidence that it is safe to advance.

   Steps before promotion:
   - Stop the staged movement at the current slice; do not increase traffic share.
   - Preserve the comparator output (which values diverged, what the shadow chose, what the active chose, what was actually delivered) as evidence — do not let the canary expire without a snapshot.
   - Decide which path is correct (next section), fix the wrong path, and rerun the canary. Mismatch rate on encoded-slash labels should drop to baseline. If it does not, the fix did not land and promotion remains blocked.

2. WHICH PATH OWNS PRODUCTION RULE SEMANTICS

   Default answer: the SHADOW comparator's semantics — decode the label value before applying the rule, decode only once at ingress, and propagate the decoded form downstream — should be the production rule semantics. Reasons:
   - Customers author rules in the natural human-readable form (literal `/`). Encoding is an artifact of transport, not data.
   - The mismatch is concentrated entirely on encoded slashes; non-encoded-slash labels behave identically. That localizes the divergence to the decode order, not to the rule set.
   - "Active decision agrees with final destination" is consistent with the latent-bug reading: the active path falls through to catchall on encoded values, and catchall happens to route to the same destination as the specific rule. It is not consistent with the rules-actually-contain-`%2F` reading, because customers virtually never author rules in encoded form.
   - Decode-at-ingress is the durable mechanism: it gives one canonical view of every label value, removes the encoded/decoded dichotomy, and prevents a future rule author from being surprised when their literal-`/` rule does not match.

   The active path's current behavior (apply rule to raw value, decode only for downstream presentation) should be changed. Decode should happen exactly once, before rule selection, and the decoded form should be what rules see, what gets logged, and what is presented downstream.

   Verification gate before applying the fix:
   - Open the rule set currently applied by this canary slice. Confirm whether any rule predicate contains a literal `%2F`. If any do, the conclusion flips: the active path's "apply-to-raw" is then the production semantics for those rules, and the shadow's decoder needs to be removed (or, better, both paths stop decoding and rules are migrated). I would be surprised to find `%2F` in authored rules, but the call should be made on the rule content, not on convention. If this verification is not done, do not promote the fix either.

3. REGRESSION TESTS

   Three categories, each as a table-driven test. Every case must assert: (a) the rule that fires, (b) the destination it produces, (c) the downstream-presented label value, (d) zero series dropped, (e) mismatch counter delta = 0 against the comparator.

   ENCODED SLASH (input contains `%2F`)
   - `team%2Fapi` — rule "team/api" → destination D1 fires; presented as `team/api`; mismatch = 0.
   - `%2Fteam` — rule "/team" → destination D2 fires; presented as `/team`; mismatch = 0.
   - `team%2F` — rule "team/" → destination D3 fires; presented as `team/`; mismatch = 0.
   - `team%2Fapi%2Fv2` — rule "team/api/v2" → destination D4 fires; presented as `team/api/v2`; mismatch = 0.
   - `team%2F%2Fapi` — two encoded slashes decode to `team//api`; rule "team//api" fires; mismatch = 0. (Confirms decoder is not just "first %2F wins.")
   - `team%252Fapi` — double-encoded; decoder leaves as `team%2Fapi` (single decoding pass); rule does NOT match a literal-`/` predicate. This case documents the boundary: only single-encoding is decoded, and rules must not silently match double-encoded values. If a customer wants double-encoded to match, they author the predicate accordingly.
   - `%2F` alone — decoder yields `/`; catchall/rule behavior as authored.
   - Adversarial: label value that is ONLY `%2F` repeated, very long encoded strings, and a label that decodes to empty string. Each must produce a defined rule decision (not a panic, not a silent drop).

   DECODED SLASH (input already contains literal `/`)
   - `team/api` — rule "team/api" → D1 fires; presented as `team/api`; mismatch = 0.
   - `/team` — rule "/team" → D2 fires; presented as `/team`; mismatch = 0.
   - `team/` — rule "team/" → D3 fires; presented as `team/`; mismatch = 0.
   - `team/api/v2` — rule "team/api/v2" → D4 fires; presented as `team/api/v2`; mismatch = 0.
   - Round-trip stability: a value that arrives already decoded passes through the decoder unchanged and matches the same rule it matched before. This is the "baseline" case that should never move when the fix lands.

   LITERAL SLASH / NO-SLASH BASELINE (the "no encoding involved" sanity set)
   - `teamapi` — decoder is a no-op; rule "teamapi" fires; presented as `teamapi`; mismatch = 0.
   - `team` — decoder is a no-op; rule "team" fires; presented as `team`; mismatch = 0.
   - Empty label value — defined behavior (catchall); no drop.
   - High-cardinality literal value with no slash — same as pre-fix behavior, mismatch counter must stay at baseline. This is the regression guard that proves the fix did not disturb non-encoded traffic.

   CROSS-CUTTING (run against ALL of the above)
   - Decoder idempotency: decoding a value twice yields the same result as decoding once.
   - Active-path-vs-shadow mismatch counter is zero for every test input. This is the direct check that the divergence is gone.
   - No-series-dropped counter is zero for every test input. Decoder must never reject a value that the previous path accepted.
   - Downstream presentation: the value delivered to the destination is the decoded form, and it matches what the rule author would expect to see in logs.
   - Latent-bug detector: a synthetic rule pair where the specific rule sends to D1 and the catchall sends to D2. For every encoded-slash input, the specific rule must fire (proving the active path is no longer relying on catchall coincidence). Without this test, the "active decision agrees with final destination" condition can be satisfied by the bug rather than by correct routing.
   - Comparator parity: re-run the canary's comparator against the fixed path; the 97% mismatch concentration on `%2F` should disappear entirely. If any encoded-slash mismatch remains, the fix is incomplete.

4. ONE LINE TO THE TEAM

   The shadow comparator is right; the active path needs to decode before rule application. Hold the canary, fix the active path, prove it with the latent-bug detector test (specific vs. catchall destination divergence on encoded slashes), then rerun. Promotion stays blocked until the 97% mismatch drops to baseline and the rule-content verification gate is passed.

The minimum safe floor for this room is: no zone-less wall-clock text as the dedup-bearing key. That is the same class of bug Yuki's shard-keeper DST replay fix addressed on 2024-03-11 — a round-trip through a zone-free layout that discards the absolute instant. The current producer shape reproduces that bug exactly, and the downstream `(account_id, event_time)` dedup is the consumer half of it.

Below is the contract gate I'd want Iris to clear before admission. The admission call stays with her; this is the data-contract floor.

1. Schema (canonical representation)
   - `event_time` MUST NOT be a zone-less local string. One of the following is acceptable:
     a. RFC3339 string with explicit offset, e.g. `2024-11-03T01:24:00-04:00`. Preferred.
     b. Two fields: `event_time_local` (e.g. `2024-11-03 01:24:00`) + IANA zone `event_timezone` (`America/New_York`).
   - Canonical storage: absolute instant in UTC RFC3339Nano. Local text + zone are retained as provenance/display only.
   - `event_id` (globally unique, stable) stays the idempotency key for retried replays; the absolute instant is what disambiguates two real events that share local text on the fall-back hour.

2. Producer-side DST policy (documented in the contract, attested by the producer)
   - The producer must declare how it emits on the fall-back ambiguous hour (1:00–1:59 local). Either:
     a. Always emit with explicit offset (preferred — makes the question moot), or
     b. Emit a marker (`occurrence: "first" | "second"`) under a stated ordering rule so the room resolves the instant deterministically.
   - The producer must never emit on the spring-forward gap (2:00–2:59 local does not exist). If a business event genuinely occurs in that window, the source system must apply a documented mapping (e.g., shift to 3:00) and the producer must attest it.

3. Admission-time validation
   - Reject any row whose canonical instant cannot be resolved: zone-less text, missing/empty zone, missing offset, non-existent local time on spring-forward, ambiguous local time on fall-back without a disambiguator.
   - Validate the resolved instant falls within the producer-attested range and that the local text round-trips back to the same instant.
   - Quarantine rejected rows; do not silently coerce. Silent coercion is exactly how the Yuki fix class of bug reappears.

4. Backfill
   - For any week already admitted or staged, the producer must re-emit under the new schema. Re-emit is the only safe path; in-place text→instant coercion is the failure mode we're guarding against.
   - Records the producer cannot re-emit are dropped from the dedup-bearing key and flagged for owner review — never silently coerced.
   - The first batch after the contract change should be the DST-transition week itself, so the room proves it can disambiguate before the cycle crosses the boundary again.

5. Downstream deduplication
   - Dedup key for retries: `(account_id, event_id)`. `event_time_instant` is ordering only, never a uniqueness test.

Direction: approve — caching compiled matchers is the right move; compile cost is real and the work is redundant across reloads. The headline bug is that the cache key is wrong, and the rest of the structure follows from fixing it.

Correctness risks (must-fix before merge)

1. Semantic divergence per generation is the actual bug. The matcher captures gen.MissingLabelMode and gen.Normalizer, but the cache key is only rule.Expr. Two generations with identical expression strings but different missing-label policy or normalizer will share one matcher, baked from whichever generation compiled first. A generation that flips MissingLabelMode from Allow to Reject (or swaps normalizer) will silently keep the old semantics. This is a correctness violation, not just stale-data.

2. No eviction. Process-global, unbounded, no hook on generation replacement. Every distinct expression ever observed is retained forever. Operationally: cardinality drift across reloads grows the cache without bound.

3. Failed reload leaks partial work. If a reload compiles some rules before failing, those entries persist even though the active generation never advanced. The active config stays correct only because the new generation never becomes active — but the cache still grows, and a later successful reload of the same expression under different defaults will hit the stale entry.

4. Mutation hazard on the shared *Matcher. If any caller mutates matcher state after construction (per-instance buffers, lazily computed fields written from outside NewMatcher), sharing across goroutines and across generations is a data race. Need *Matcher to be read-only after NewMatcher returns. Document the invariant or assert it.

Safe cache identity

Cache key must include every input that affects matcher semantics. Two viable shapes:

  - (expr, missingLabelMode, normalizerID). normalizerID should be a pointer or stable handle, not a stringified function — two distinct normalizers hashing equal would silently alias.
  - (generationID, expr). Simpler. Re-compiles on every generation even when defaults are identical; usually fine, and compile is cheaper than debugging a stale semantic.

I would use the generation-scoped shape. It makes lifetime and failed-reload behavior trivially correct.

Generation lifetime

Cache is per-generation. On swap, the previous generation's entries become unreachable from any current compile path, and its matcher pointers can be dropped — Go GC handles the release once no active snapshot holds them. No explicit Clear() is needed if the key includes generation ID.

If you keep one global cache for memory-bookkeeping reasons, you still need a sweep hook on generation replacement — otherwise entries from retired generations pin matchers and any future dedup-by-expr key shape re-introduces the semantic bug.

Concurrency

  - sync.Map is fine for read-mostly access.
  - Two goroutines compiling the same expression under the same generation is wasted work, not unsafe. If reloads land on a hot path, wrap NewMatcher in a singleflight.Group keyed on (generationID, expr) — losers receive the winner's *Matcher. This is the right place to dedupe; do not use a compile-then-Store placeholder, since that re-introduces a race on the placeholder itself.

Failed-reload behavior

  - The new (failed) generation never becomes active, so nothing observable changes.
  - Cache entries it created are unreachable if the key includes the failed generation's ID.
  - After the failed reload returns, the active generation's cache state must be byte-identical to its state before the attempt. A test should assert this explicitly.

Focused tests before merge

Add to the existing table-driven matcher tests:

1. Same expr, different MissingLabelMode → distinct matchers, expected behavior change. Concretely: a rule that requires tenant="acme" with a missing env label must accept under Allow and reject under Reject. Compile under one mode, swap, recompile, verify behavior.

2. Same expr, different Normalizer → distinct matchers. Two normalizers that disagree on case folding or whitespace; verify the matcher respects the current generation's normalizer on a probe input.

3. Generation swap evicts (or at minimum: gen B does not reuse gen A's matcher). Compile R under gen A, advance to gen B with same expr but different defaults, verify gen B uses gen B's semantics.

4. Failed reload leaves cache clean. Snapshot cache size and contents, run a reload that fails partway through compilation, assert post-state equals pre-state.

5. Concurrent compile under same gen. N goroutines call compileRule with the same expr; assert all return the same *Matcher and NewMatcher is invoked once. Run under -race.

6. *Matcher is read-only after construction. Doc comment plus a -race run of the full suite; ideally a small assertion in NewMatcher's tests that no exported field is written after return.

7. Bounded growth under repeated reloads. Reload the same config N times; assert cache size is O(rules) per active generation, not O(rules × reloads). This is the leak-vs-warmup test you already use in shape, just applied here.

Growth note: fold cache-key dimensions (here: generation ID + expr) and whether each is bounded into the pre-rollout checklist you maintain for metrics-router canaries. You already distinguish bounded warmup from monotonic growth in the parser canary stop rule — same shape applies to this cache.

DECISION — TODAY'S EASY BOULDERING

Recommendation: SKIP today's bouldering session.

  - Inversion 3x15

  - Single-leg 3x8 each side

Pass criteria: single-leg heel raise 3x8 pain-free, no compensation, no after-session swelling, two-foot hop trending toward 0/10.

PHASE B — BALANCE (overlap with A; same days)

B1. Single-leg stance, firm ground, eyes open, 3x30 sec each side — you have this.
B2. Single-leg stance, eyes closed, 3x30 sec each side.
B3. Single-leg stance on folded towel or foam pad, 3x30 sec each side.
B4. Single-leg stance with head turns and arm reaches.

PHASE C — HOPPING (only after A + B pass AND two-foot hop at 0/10)

C1. Two-foot forward hop — your current test; the 0/10 gate.
C2. Two-foot side-to-side hop x10.
C3. Two-foot-to-single-leg landing on involved side, from small step height.
C4. Single-leg forward hop, involved side.
C5. Single-leg side hop, involved side.
C6. Single-leg triple hop for distance, involved side.
C7. Single-leg crossover hop, involved side.
C8. Single-leg vertical hop with 5-second stabilization hold on landing.

Pass criteria: triple hop distance within 90% of uninvolved side; crossover hop within 90%; no pain or instability; symmetric landing without compensation or hesitation.

PHASE D — BOULDERING-SPECIFIC (only after Phase C passes)

For each stage: stop if any pain, instability, or sense of apprehension emerges; 24h wait between new stages; do not advance a stage on "probably fine."

D-B1. Easy slab and low traversing only. Downclimb everything. No heel hooks, no toe hooks, no smearing on small footing with weight on outside of foot. 10–15 min. Stop while it still feels boring.
D-B2. Re-attempt easy slab/traversing 24h after D-B1 if no flare. Confirm morning-after status before progressing.
D-B3. Easy vertical problems with normal foot positions. Still no heel/toe hooks.
D-B4. One gentle single heel hook, brief, on a low-consequence move.
D-B5. One gentle single toe hook, brief.
D-B6. Small controlled dynamic moves to a nearby hold, on a wall where falling is safe onto pads.
D-B7. Downclimb small step-offs (~1–2 ft) — NOT jump-downs yet.
D-B8. Actual jump-downs to pads, low heights first, then build.
D-B9. Dynamic moves on steeper walls with a safe fall zone.
D-B10. Projecting at grade.

Per-stage record what you do and the morning-after status. Probe tolerance at one stage does not unlock the next — clean 24h after-image does.

PHASE D — SOCCER-SPECIFIC (only after at least one bouldering probe tolerated cleanly AND Phase C holds)

D-S2. 3x20 m lateral shuffles each direction. This was the recurrent trigger pattern through November–December with the calf; same caution applies to the lateral ankle.
D-S3. Progressive push-offs capped ~80%.
D-S4. 8-min jog + 4x10-sec accelerations capped ~85%.
D-S5. 10 min easy ball touches at jogging pace.
D-S6. Capped pickup — 8 min warm-up, 22 min easy play, 5 min cool-down, no all-out sprints or hard tackles (matches the 2024-02-04 pattern you used for the calf return).
D-S7. Full pickup.

Per-stage stop conditions: calf/ankle grab, altered gait, swelling, sense of lateral-ankle giving way, or apprehension on cuts/push-offs. Morning-after report.

- Any sense of giving way or frank instability during a test
- Inability to bear weight at any point
- Numbness, color change, or pain out of proportion
- Focal bony tenderness over the lateral malleolus, fifth metatarsal base, or talar dome
- Locking, catching, or a feeling of something out of place

- Pain at rest or pain that wakes you at night

- Two-foot hop at 0/10 ≠ single-leg triple hop within 90%

- Bouldering tolerance ≠ soccer clearance
- Easy controlled slab ≠ projecting at grade
- Capped easy jog ≠ soccer return
- Per-stage "tolerated" is not the same as the next stage unlocked

Day 7–8: if two-foot hop 0/10, begin Phase C. If still 2/10, give it another 2–3 days.

Bottom line: Day 8 with all the closed checks clean and no swelling is a good signal, but it's a low- to moderate-load profile. The untested items — hard cuts, deceleration, single-leg landing from height, dynamic movement — are exactly the loads that re-injure lateral ankles, and both Thursday bouldering and Sunday soccer contain versions of those loads. So Thursday and Sunday should each be a probe, not a clearance session; the first real full-speed test comes after you add the intermediate checks below on flat ground.

What's closed (low/moderate axial + frontal-plane control):
  - Walking, stairs, single-leg calf raises x10, single-leg balance 30s
  - Two-foot hops (axial, controlled)
  - Short easy jog (running gait, low intensity)
  - 5 controlled lateral bounds (frontal-plane plyometric, controlled landing)
  - No swelling; the day-4 2/10 lateral ache at hop has not been reproduced

What's still untested (the gaps that matter for both sports):
  - Single-leg landing from any height (step-down / downclimb / jump-down)
  - Deceleration under load (stopping a sprint, braking into a change of direction)
  - Hard / reactive cutting (50/50 balls, contested direction changes)
  - Max-effort acceleration
  - Ankle under fatigue (repeated calf raises to fatigue, late-session bounding)
  - Dynamic upper-body loading while standing on the ankle (dyno / deadpoint / catch)

Intermediate checks before Thursday (Tuesday or Wednesday, on flat ground, after a normal warmup):

  1. Single-leg hop for distance, 4 trials each side. Compare sides — should be roughly symmetric (within ~10%) and pain-free on landing. If the right side is meaningfully shorter, or landing reproduces the lateral ache, do not boulder Thursday.

  2. Single-leg step-down from a low box (~6-8"), 6-8 reps each side, slow and controlled. You're watching for any give-way, pinch on the lateral ankle, or sharp pain on landing. Stop the set at the first reproduction.

  3. Single-leg calf raises to fatigue on the right side.  Note the rep count and compare to the left; large asymmetry (>20%) means the ankle is still protecting itself and Thursday is too early.

  4. Deceleration drill: 4-6 easy accelerations to ~80% over ~15 m, then a controlled stop on command (straight-ahead brake, then brake into a 45-degree cut). No pain, no instability, no "the ankle feels weird" feeling. If braking reproduces anything, hold Thursday and Sunday.

  Treat each of these as a probe: stop the moment anything reproduces; the rest of that day's checks are off. If all four are clean Wednesday evening, Thursday is reasonable as a graded bouldering probe.

Thursday bouldering (probe, not a session):

  - Same template as the December 24 bouldering re-entry: easy slab and low traversing only, no dynos, no dynamic moves, no heel hooks, downclimb everything, stop while it still feels boring.
  - Avoid problems where falling means landing on the right foot or stepping down off anything higher than a few inches.
  - Avoid problems that need a high right foot smear or a twist-and-drop finish — both load the lateral ligaments.
  - Warm up first on the wall (easy traverses, easy low angles) before touching anything that matters. Don't start cold on a real problem.
  - Time-box it: 20-25 minutes total is plenty. The point is a single clean exposure, not volume.

Between Thursday and Sunday (if Thursday went clean and the next morning is clean):

  - Add one set of repeated single-leg hops to fatigue on each side, and one set of bounding at higher than your previous effort.
  - Add a slow T-drill or pro-agility at ~70% — the goal is to expose the ankle to cutting without sprinting yet.
  - If any of these reproduce the lateral ache, Sunday becomes a long flat walk, not pickup.

Sunday pickup (probe, capped, no sprints):

  - Same template as the February 4 capped pickup: ~35 min total, ~8 min warmup, easy play only, ~5 min cooldown, walk home.
  - No all-out sprints, no contested 50/50 balls, no hard tackles, no goalie/diving. These are the four moves that combine deceleration + reactive change of direction, which you still haven't cleanly tested.
  - Self-position conservatively (e.g., play a touch-and-pass role rather than chasing through the middle).
  - If at any point the right ankle feels off — even just "different" — come off immediately. Do not push through to see if it settles.

Stop criteria, written explicitly:

  During any session (intermediate checks, bouldering, or pickup) — stop the activity:
    - Any reproduction of the lateral ankle ache (the same spot as the day-4 hop)
    - Any sensation of giving way, instability, or "the ankle isn't tracking"
    - Any sharp pain on landing, cutting, or braking

Short answer: fix the generator (deterministic key ordering at generation time) AND keep the byte/hash gate, AND add a semantic comparator that produces a human-readable diff. Don't replace the byte gate with semantic comparison; don't try to fix this by loosening the publish gate either.

Why both, in that order:

1. The generator is a pure function of the canonical package. Producing different bytes from the same input is a bug, not a stylistic choice. The fix at the source is to serialize the offending map with sorted keys (or build an ordered structure upstream so iteration order is irrelevant). Once the generator is deterministic, the byte gate stops producing false positives — which is what was eroding confidence in it.

2. The byte/hash gate is doing real work beyond "are the tokens equal." It catches: hand-edits to the committed generated file, generator regressions (someone re-introduces nondeterminism, an upstream library changes encoding defaults, a debug timestamp leaks in, a comment block gets reordered), and stale-cache outputs that happen to be semantically equivalent. If you replace it with semantic comparison, those classes of failure pass silently.

3. Semantic comparison is the layer that makes the byte gate useful to humans. When the byte gate fails on a real change, the publish is blocked — but the reviewer needs to see "color.brand.hover added; spacing.lg changed 16px → 24px" rather than a raw hash mismatch. Semantic comparison produces that diff. It's the explanation, not the gate.

So: generator deterministic → byte gate strict → semantic comparator produces the diff → publish only when both generators exit 0 and byte gate passes.

Tests that distinguish meaningful drift from formatting churn without weakening the gate:

Determinism (regression for the original bug)
- Run the generator 1000x from the same pinned canonical package. All 1000 outputs must be byte-identical (sha256 match).
- Construct a canonical package with the offending map populated by insertions in an order known to vary (Go map iteration is intentionally randomized). Confirm output is stable across runs.
- Edge cases: empty map, single-key map, map with non-ASCII keys, deeply nested maps, large map (>10k keys).

Byte gate behavior
- Regenerate from canonical → byte-identical → gate passes.
- Manually edit one byte in the committed generated file (whitespace, comment) → gate fails.
- Manually edit one token value in canonical, regenerate → gate fails with semantic diff naming the token.

Semantic comparator behavior
- Two outputs that differ only in key ordering of a single map → semantic comparator reports "equivalent" (key-ordering-only difference is not meaningful).
- Same canonical with one token renamed → semantic reports "color.foo renamed to color.bar."
- Same canonical with one value changed → semantic reports "spacing.lg 16 → 24."
- Same canonical with one token added → semantic reports "added: motion.fade.in."
- Same canonical with one token removed → semantic reports "removed: motion.fade.out."

Cross-check between the two layers
- A case where byte gate says "equal" but semantic says "different" is a comparator bug → test must fail, never publish.
- A case where byte gate says "different" and semantic says "equivalent" is exactly the formatting-churn case → test asserts that this state is detected and reported as "formatting only, no semantic drift," and that publication is still blocked until the canonical is regenerated and committed (i.e., the churn is acknowledged, not silently accepted).

Publication safety (these must already pass — confirm they still do after the change)
- Generator exits non-zero → no artifact written, previously published package unchanged.
- Drift check fails → no artifact written, previously published package unchanged.
- Generator produces partial output then crashes → no artifact written.
- Two concurrent runs against the same canonical → no torn writes; only one set of artifacts lands in the publish target.
- Stale cache returning a previously-good output that no longer matches current canonical → gate must fail (this is why byte comparison against the committed canonical, not against a cached "last good," is the right anchor).

One operational note: the fail-closed staging-directory behavior is what kept this from being an incident. Don't trade it away. The fix is to eliminate false positives at the source (deterministic generator) so the gate stops firing spuriously — not to make the gate easier to satisfy.

WHY THIS POINTS TO THE SENDER, NOT THE SERVICE

  - One traffic pattern accounted for the large majority of

This is exactly the scenario the protective 429 is meant to catch:
one sender with a synchronized cadence and oversized post-
decompression payloads, against a healthy fleet.

CONCRETE RECOMMENDATIONS

  1. Add jitter to the flush / release cadence.
     If the sender flushes on a fixed timer (every N seconds),
     randomize the interval. A uniform "full jitter" of 0–N seconds,
     or "decorrelated jitter" where the next interval is random
     between base and roughly 3x base, is the single highest-
     leverage change.

  2. Add per-instance jitter if multiple instances are running.
     Even with per-flush jitter, instances that all start on the
     same minute boundary will co-flush. Each instance should
     pick its own independent jitter window.

  3. Shorten the flush interval modestly and keep the jitter.
     A 100-client staging test on this service showed that adding
     full 0–2s flush jitter dropped peak concurrent retries from
     94 to 19 and staging p99 from 470 ms to 205 ms. Total batch
     completion moved from 2.4 s to 2.7 s — a small tradeoff for
     a much smoother arrival curve. The same pattern (per-instance
     jitter + shorter flush interval) closed a similar
     customer-side flush-burst case on 2024-03-14 with no quota
     change.

  4. Reduce the per-batch payload size after decompression.
     The combination of "synchronized bursts" and "unusually large
     after decompression" is the tell: the sender is batching at
     the wire level in a way that doesn't reflect the post-
     decompression budget. Either lower the per-batch point count
     or pick a wire representation whose post-decompression size
     stays well under the per-request limit.

  5. Honor Retry-After on every 429.
     The 1–3 second randomized value is the mechanism that breaks
     synchronization. A client that retries on a fixed 1-second
     timer will keep recreating the wave the service is trying to
     dampen. If the sender's local backoff would otherwise retry
     sooner than Retry-After, take the larger of the two.

  6. Apply the same jitter treatment to background workers.
     Any telemetry forwarder, retry sweeper, or batcher that fires
     on a fixed cadence will recreate the wave after the main
     flush is fixed. This is where bursts often reappear.

The negative value does not prove data loss.

A monotonic counter reset is the expected behavior when a non-persisted counter restarts. Pre-restart = 18,442 and post-restart = 37 is exactly the signature of an in-memory counter that started fresh in the new process. Two pieces of evidence point away from data loss: ingest-edge reported no rejection, so the post-restart samples are being accepted normally, and timestamped samples continue to arrive, so the pipeline is still carrying traffic. What the dashboard is showing is an arithmetic artifact of naive delta math on a counter that reset. At the boundary the dashboard's window contains a small post-restart value (37) and a larger pre-restart value (18,442), and the raw delta subtracts them and gets a large negative number. That is a presentation / metric-type mismatch, not evidence that requests were dropped.

What actually cannot be recovered from this counter is what happened during the restart gap itself, when no collector process was running to emit samples. Any requests in that interval were not counted because the counter is in-memory and the prior running total is gone. But that is true regardless of what the dashboard shows, and it is true whether the dashboard reads naive delta or reset-aware math. The requests that did reach the collector before and after the restart are present in the cumulative values on either side of the boundary; the pipeline did not drop them.

The customer should be told the negative spike is a counter-reset artifact, not data loss. ingest-edge not rejecting and samples continuing to arrive are the direct evidence that the request stream is intact.

Adding a manual offset in the collector is unsafe.

If the collector starts up and reports 37, that genuinely is "37 requests since this process started." Adding a constant to make the line continuous lies about what the process actually counted. There are four reasons not to do it.

  1. It hides the reset from the consumers that are designed to handle it. Prometheus `rate()`, `increase()`, and `resets()` work by detecting a sample where the value decreases and treating that as a reset boundary. If the collector is configured to inject a fixed offset on startup, the reset becomes invisible to those functions, and any consumer using reset-aware math silently gets the wrong answer.

  2. It creates a new class of breakage. The offset has to be coordinated across every restart, every config change, and every rollback. The first restart where someone forgets to apply it, applies the wrong constant, or applies it after a config change is missed becomes a counter that lies about a reset it didn't actually have. The collector cannot verify the offset is correct because the prior running total is gone; it has nothing to validate against.

  3. It violates the OTel and Prometheus semantic convention for monotonic sums. The convention is that monotonic counters reset on process restart and consumers are expected to use reset-aware functions. A counter that does not reset on restart is non-interoperable with every other tool that follows the convention.

  4. It conflates two different things. "What my process counted" and "what the system saw" are not the same after a restart. A manual offset papers over the gap without changing which process was actually running. If continuity across restart is the real requirement, the durable fixes are to persist the running total across restart, or to accept the reset and fix the consumer math. A manual offset is a workaround that trades one correctness problem for a worse one.

How Prometheus-style reset-aware rate and increase should behave.

`rate(checkout.requests[5m])` and `increase(checkout.requests[5m])` scan the samples in the window and detect a reset whenever a sample's value is less than the previous sample's value. When they detect one, they partition the window into epochs around the reset boundary. For each epoch they compute `(last - first) / elapsed` as a per-second rate and sum the contributions across epochs in the window, weighted by the time each epoch occupied.

Concretely, with samples roughly:
    t=0    18,442
    t=60s  18,500
    t=120s 37     (reset)
    t=180s 80
    t=240s 130
    t=300s 200

a naive 5-minute delta returns 200 - 18,442 = -18,242, which is what the dashboard is plotting.

A reset-aware `increase()` over the same 5-minute window returns approximately:
    epoch 1 (pre-reset):  18,500 - 18,442 = 58 over ~60s
    epoch 2 (post-reset): 200 - 37 = 163 over ~180s
    total ~ 221 requests across the 5-minute window

A reset-aware `rate()` returns a positive per-second rate on the order of 0.7-0.8 req/s, derived from the per-epoch rates weighted by epoch duration. The result is positive, not negative, and reflects the actual observed request rate across the window.

There is one known under-count caveat: requests that occurred during the restart gap itself, when no collector was running, are not represented in either epoch. Reset-aware math cannot recover that gap because no samples exist for it, and that is also true of the naive delta. But reset-aware math does not go negative, and it does not require any collector-side workaround.

The fix for the customer is therefore: switch the dashboard panel from raw 5-minute delta to `rate(checkout.requests[5m])` or `increase(checkout.requests[5m])`, and change nothing in the collector.

Quantities (3 adults, generous):
  12 oz dried pasta (a short shape — ditalini, small shells, or broken spaghetti all work; something that holds the chickpeas)
  1 large bunch kale, ribs stripped, leaves torn into bite pieces
  1 large can (28 oz) or 2 regular cans chickpeas, drained
  4–5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced
  1/3 cup good olive oil, plus more for finishing
  1 lemon
  Big handful of Parmesan, grated on a microplane (zester works)
  Red pepper flakes, generous pinch + more at the table
  Salt for the pasta water

Timing from now (Anya at ~17:30, ~40 min):

  T-40  NOW
        Large pot of water on high heat to boil. Get out a large skillet, a small saucepan, a colander, and a microplane/zester.

  T-33  Water heating; start the base
        In the large skillet over medium heat, warm 1/3 cup olive oil with the sliced garlic and a generous pinch of red pepper flakes. Cook 2–3 min, just until the garlic is pale gold and fragrant. Do not brown it.
        Add the drained chickpeas and a small pinch of salt. Stir and warm 2 min, then mash about a third of them against the spoon — this is what makes the sauce cling to the pasta instead of sliding off.

  T-25  Water should be at a hard boil
        Salt the water heavily (it should taste like sea water — pasta water is your only real seasoning).
        Drop the pasta. Set a timer for 1 minute less than the package says.

  T-22  While pasta cooks, finish the veg
        Add the torn kale to the chickpea skillet with a small splash of the boiling pasta water. Stir until wilted and silky, 2–3 min. Taste; it should be well-salted and a little spicy.

  T-13  Pasta timer goes off
        Reserve about 1 cup of pasta water, then drain.
        Add pasta to the chickpea-kale skillet. Splash in 1/2 cup of the reserved pasta water and toss vigorously over low heat for about 1 minute until everything is glossy and loose. Taste for salt. Kill the heat.

  T-12  Split for Devika — this is the key step
        Scoop roughly one-third of the pasta into the small saucepan. (The chickpeas-and-kale sauce should split roughly proportionally; if you got more noodles than veg in her share, top it up with a ladle of sauce from the main pan.)
        To her saucepan add: a generous drizzle of olive oil and another 1/4 cup of the reserved pasta water. Swirl to coat everything.
        Cover her saucepan and set it on the smallest back burner on the lowest possible flame (or, better, just leave it covered off the heat — it will hold 20–30 minutes that way because the olive oil + starch water coat protects the pasta).
        Cover the main skillet too. Wipe counters, slice bread, set the table.

  T-0  Anya walks in (~17:30)
        Put the main skillet back over low heat for 60 seconds, tossing, with another small splash of water if it looks tight.
        Off the heat: zest the whole lemon over the pan, squeeze in about half the juice, toss again.

        Plate two bowls. Bread on the table.

When Devika arrives (the hold):

  Put her small saucepan over low heat. Add another small splash of water. Stir gently for 2–3 minutes until loosened, glossy, and hot through. The starch-water + olive oil coating will have kept the pasta from gumming; if it tightens up, water is the fix, not more heat.
  Off the heat: zest the remaining lemon over her portion, squeeze in the rest of the juice, add Parmesan, one last drizzle of olive oil, toss, plate.

Rules that keep this from going wrong:

  - Cook the pasta 1 minute shy of the package time. It finishes in the sauce and survives the hold.
  - Never add lemon or cheese while the pan is sitting hot and idle — the acid and dairy will make the starch seize and turn gluey. Both go in at the moment of serving, off heat.
  - The pasta water is your insurance. Salt it like sea water, reserve a cup before draining, and use it to re-loosen anything that tightens up — during the cook, the hold, or the reheat.
  - Olive oil is the second insurance. A generous final coat is what stops the pasta from drying out and clumping while it sits.
  - Hold Devika's portion in a separate pan, not on a plate. A lidded saucepan with a little water and oil is what lets you actually refresh the pasta instead of just rewarming a clump.
  - Bread does double duty: it rounds out the meal and is the right vehicle for any leftover chickpeas-and-kale sauce.

Bottom line
- This is host-local disk pressure on a single node, not a consensus-layer fault. Treat as a delayed-append / disk-bound catch-up event, not a failover.
- Immediate posture: hold the alert open, do not restart either replica, drain them from the follower-read path, and address the host.

Why this is not a failover (negative case)
All four failover markers from your negative-case rule are absent, and the remaining evidence is consistent with disk-bound catch-up rather than lease instability:
- Lease holder unchanged, lease epoch unchanged → no election occurred.
- No acquisition or relinquishment record → no replica volunteered to lead and none stepped down.
- No overlapping leader interval → no two replicas believed themselves leader for any overlapping term.
- No stale-owner messages → the two followers are not being told someone else owns their lease.
- No write failures → the leader is still committing and replicating normally.
- Both replicas are still making forward catch-up progress → they are appending entries, not stalled or rewinding.

The 16 followers that already returned below 1 s confirm the consensus path is healthy cluster-wide; only two replicas on one host with 6x baseline disk-write latency remain behind. The lag is fully explained by slow fsync / WAL append on that host slowing Raft persistence there. The other host's followers are unaffected, which is consistent with a host-local I/O problem and inconsistent with a leader, network, or quorum problem.

Follower-read recommendation
- Yes, remove (drain) both replicas from the follower-read path while they catch up. 34 to 41 s of lag is well past any reasonable read-staleness SLO, and serving reads from them would (a) hand callers stale data and (b) add load to a host whose disk is already saturated.
- Keep both replicas as voting/replicating members. Removing them from the replica set would be an over-reaction: their lease and epoch are intact, they are progressing, and pulling them out would force the leader to replicate to fewer followers and weaken quorum on that host. The right scope is read-path only.
- Do not re-add them to the read pool until each replica has held lag below your normal follower-read threshold (sub-second, matching the 16 that already recovered) for at least one full lease-renewal interval. This prevents flapping if disk latency blips again.
- Confirm the leader is not on the troubled host. If it is, that is a different and higher-severity case (leader commit/fsync pressure) and warrants paging the secondary immediately; the read-drain advice still applies but the rest of this response does not.

Exact checks required before closing the alert (no automatic restart)
All of the following must be true at the moment of close. Run them in this order; do not close on partial evidence.

1. Host disk write latency back to baseline. Confirm the 6x disk-write-latency condition on the affected host has cleared (sustained for at least 5 minutes at or near the pre-event baseline). This is the root cause; if it is not resolved, the lag will recur and closing the alert is premature.

2. Both lagging replicas back below the lag threshold. Each replica must have lag below your standard follower-lag warning threshold (the same threshold the 16 already crossed) for at least one full lease-renewal interval, with no re-crossing.

3. Forward catch-up progress was monotonic. Across the recovery window, lag for each replica must have been non-increasing on average (allow brief single-sample blips), with no flat period longer than roughly two lease-renewal intervals. A replica that stops progressing while still behind is a different failure mode and must not be closed under this checklist.

4. Lease holder and lease epoch unchanged throughout. Re-verify for both replicas across the full catch-up window (not just at the initial alert snapshot): epoch monotonic, holder identity unchanged, no second holder ever recorded for the same range.

5. No acquisition or relinquishment record at any point. Re-query the full window for either replica and the leader; both must remain empty.

6. No overlapping leader interval. Leader term must be strictly monotonic across the window for both lagging replicas' view and the leader's view; no term may appear twice.

7. No stale-owner messages. Across at least two full lease-renewal intervals after the lagging replicas return below threshold, confirm zero stale-owner messages on either replica.

8. No write failures anywhere. Write error rate stayed at zero across the cluster for the full window, including from the leader and from any client-side apply path. A non-zero write error rate invalidates the "not a failover" premise because it would mean the cluster briefly could not durably commit.

9. Apply and commit indexes monotonic on both replicas. Raft apply index advanced monotonically; no truncation, no snapshot-replay from index zero, no WAL reset. A replay-from-scratch would be evidence the replica lost local state, which is a different incident class and not closeable under this checklist.

10. Cluster quorum intact and stable. Quorum was never at risk during the window. If the troubled host had also held the leader or a quorum-critical voter at any point, that changes severity and this checklist is insufficient on its own.

11. No spillover. No additional replica on the troubled host crossed the lag threshold during the window, and no other host showed elevated disk-write latency.

12. Owner notification recorded. Page or notify the listed primary and backup for shard-keeper (per the runbook's owner pair); note the alert ID, the time the host's disk latency returned to baseline, and the time both replicas returned below threshold. The close record is auditable.

Why no automatic restart
- The replicas are making forward progress. A restart would interrupt that progress and force a snapshot replay, which under disk pressure is exactly the wrong workload to add.
- A restart on this host would generate cold-cache reads and a WAL replay at the same moment disk is already 6x baseline; this can convert a slow catch-up into a hard stall.
- No consensus-layer fault is present. Restart is the standard response to lease instability, split brain, or corrupted local state; none of those are indicated here (epoch unchanged, no overlap, no stale-owner, indexes monotonic).
- The disk problem is host-level, not replica-level. Restarting the replica process does not change disk latency; only resolving the host condition will.

Escalation triggers (change posture if any of these occur while the alert is open)
- Either replica's lag stops decreasing for more than ~2 lease-renewal intervals, or begins to grow → re-evaluate as a stalled-replica case; restart may then be warranted, but only after re-checking the negative-case markers at the moment of the stall.
- A second host shows elevated disk write latency or follower lag → cluster-wide storage problem, not host-local; page secondary, escalate to on-call storage owner.
- Any stale-owner message, acquisition/relinquishment record, overlapping leader term, write failure, or non-monotonic apply index → the negative case no longer holds; this is now a failover-class event and the close checklist above does not apply.
- Leader is on the troubled host → immediate secondary page; the leader's commit/fsync latency is now a quorum risk.

Operating rule (for the runbook)
A replication-lag alert with unchanged lease holder and epoch, no acquisition/relinquishment, no overlap, no stale-owner, no write failures, and forward catch-up progress is a delayed-append / disk-bound catch-up event, not a failover, and must not trigger an automatic replica restart. Follower-read removal during catch-up is permitted and recommended when lag exceeds the read-staleness SLO; replica-set membership must be preserved until the host condition is resolved and the close checklist above passes.

Review of `matcherFor` / `activate` (revised, generation-keyed).

1. Direct answer to your question
   - Yes. Keying by `(generation, expression)` now correctly prevents semantic reuse, because two generations can carry different `MissingLabelMode`/`Normalizer` and the same expression string must not collapse. Good fix on identity.
   - Yes, it also still creates unbounded retention. Every reload adds a new `(gen, expr)` entry that is never evicted. After N reloads the map holds N generations of matchers even though `active` only points at one. Correctness is bought at the cost of a memory leak that grows with reload frequency × rule count.

2. Cache identity — mostly right, one fragile spot
   - `cacheKey{generation uint64, expression string}` is a comparable value type, so `sync.Map` can use it directly. Good.
   - `defaults Defaults` is passed into `Compile` but is NOT part of the key. The caller is implicitly promising that `defaults` is a pure function of `gen`. That contract is not stated anywhere and is the next place this will silently bite. Either key on a `defaultsID` derived from the generation, or document and assert the invariant at the boundary.
   - `generation uint64` is fine for aliasing; no practical wrap risk. What it represents (monotonic counter? build id? hash of the parsed config?) is not stated and should be: two generations that produce identical matchers must still be distinct keys, and two that produce different matchers must collide only when intended.

3. Generation lifetime — the actual defect
   - Today: write-once, never removed. No reference from entry to its `*Generation`, so there is no way for Go's GC to reclaim old generations' matchers even after every goroutine has dropped its `*Matcher`.
   - There is no signaling between `activate` (which swaps the active pointer) and `compiled` (which retains every generation ever seen). The two data structures are unaware of each other.
   - Requirement: a matcher must remain reachable at least as long as any goroutine that has already obtained it from the cache. After that, its entry must be reclaimable. The current code over-satisfies the first half and entirely fails the second.

4. Failed-reload behavior — not specified, partially safe, partially risky
   - `Compile(expr, defaults)` is called inline; if it returns an error, no entry is stored. So a per-expression failure does not poison the cache for that `(gen, expr)` pair. Fine.
   - If `Compile` panics or partially succeeds across many expressions during a reload, there is no transactional cleanup. A failed reload can leave a half-populated generation in the cache, and `activate(next)` does not show a rollback path. If `activate` is called only on success, that protects correctness, but the failed generation's entries are then orphans that nobody will ever read — same leak as a successful reload, just less useful.
   - Requirement: a failed reload must leave the cache consistent with the prior active generation. No entries from the failed generation may be observable from the active path, and entries from the failed generation must be reclaimable on the same terms as any old generation.
   - Requirement: a successful reload must not leave entries from the prior generation reachable to the active path. (Already true by construction since keying includes `gen`, but worth stating.)

5. Concurrency — adequate, invariant not stated
   - `sync.Map` gives safe concurrent `Load`/`LoadOrStore`. Multiple readers racing to compile the same `(gen, expr)` will both call `Compile`; the loser's matcher is discarded by `LoadOrStore` and becomes unreachable. Wasted work, not a correctness bug, but it is allocation pressure on hot paths and should be either accepted explicitly or short-circuited with a single-flight wrapper.
   - Requirement: a returned `*Matcher` must be treated as immutable by all holders. If anything downstream mutates fields on it (e.g., caches of compiled normalizer state), the cache invariant breaks for every reader. State this in a doc comment on `Matcher` or at the cache boundary.
   - Requirement: if `Defaults` is copied by value into the matcher, document that callers must not mutate the `Defaults` they pass in after handing it to `matcherFor`.

6. Cleanup — explicit requirements
   - Pin entries to the generation they were compiled under. Concretely: the entry's lifetime is bounded by the lifetime of the `*Generation` it was compiled for, plus any `*Matcher` already handed out.
   - Eviction must be reference-based, not time-based. We do not know how long a goroutine will hold a `*Matcher`; a TTL or a "stale after N reloads" rule will eventually race a long-running reader.
   - Eviction must be safe under concurrent `Load`. Iterating a `sync.Map` and deleting is not safe with concurrent loads; the cache shape has to change to make eviction safe.

7. Suggested shape (one concrete option; others exist)
   - Move the cache off the process-global `sync.Map` and onto the `*Generation` itself: each `Generation` carries its own `compiled sync.Map` (or a `sync.RWMutex`+`map`). `matcherFor` reads `active` to find the current generation and uses that generation's map. `activate` swaps the atomic pointer to a fresh `*Generation` whose map is empty (or pre-warmed by a separate compile pass before activation). The prior generation's map becomes unreachable once no goroutine still holds a `*Matcher` from it, and Go's GC reclaims both the map and the matchers together.
   - This satisfies identity (key is per-generation by construction), lifetime (pinned to the generation pointer), cleanup (automatic via GC), concurrency (per-map `sync.Map` is still concurrent-safe), and failed-reload (a failed reload never constructs a new `*Generation`, so no swap occurs and no half-populated map exists). The compile-during-reload duplication is unchanged but bounded to one generation's worth of work.
   - If a process-global structure is required for some reason, the next-best shape is a generation-indexed map of `sync.Map`s with the same activation semantics; same correctness, slightly more bookkeeping.

8. Tests Wes should add before merge (matches the pre-rollout checklist item on cache-key shape and allocation)
   - Identity: same `expr`, different `Defaults` (e.g., `MissingLabelMode` toggle) across two generations, must yield two distinct `*Matcher` values, neither reused. This is the regression that motivated the revision; assert it directly.
   - Lifetime: after activating gen N+1, assert that the gen N cache is unreachable from the active path (e.g., via a generation-scoped handle or by inspecting the cache structure). Memory reclaim can be asserted with a finalizer or by exposing a debug-only counter; not required for merge, required for confidence.
   - Concurrency: hammer `matcherFor` for the same `(gen, expr)` from many goroutines; assert no panic, no data race (`go test -race`), and that the returned `*Matcher` is one of the actually-stored values. A short single-flight wrapper is acceptable to remove the duplicate-`Compile` waste.
   - Failed reload: drive `Compile` to fail for some expressions and succeed for others; assert no `(failedGen, expr)` entries remain reachable from the active path; assert that activating a partially-failed generation is either rejected outright or followed by an explicit rollback that removes its entries.
   - Immutability: assert that mutating a returned `*Matcher`'s fields is either forbidden by the type's API or is detected (this is more of a code-review line than a test, but state it explicitly).

Net: the revision fixes the semantic-reuse bug. It does not yet fix the unbounded-retention bug; those are independent and both have to hold before merge.
