This is a non-emergency. Half an inch of standing water + a drain-phase hum that stops is the classic signature of a clogged filter or sump debris jamming the drain pump. The hum means the pump is trying to start but is starved of flow or locked against a small object. The common cases resolve quietly without touching the pump housing.

BEFORE YOU TOUCH THE MACHINE

  Lay a dry towel at the base of the door to catch drips.
  Power off at the breaker before you lean into the tub. Restore it only after the filter is back in place. This is just to get a known safe state, not because anything is electrically wrong.
  Do NOT run a full cycle as a test. A no-drain cycle burns out the drain pump and wakes Devika. You don't need it.

  1. BAIL THE STANDING WATER (silent)
     Use a cup and a shallow baking dish. Ladle the half-inch out of the tub into the dish, dump it in the sink, repeat. This prevents the float switch from tripping mid-work and removes the sloshing noise if the door is opened later.

  2. PULL AND CLEAN THE FILTER (quiet, this is the actual fix ~80% of the time)
     Remove the lower rack.
     The filter is a cylindrical assembly, usually twist-out by hand, sitting at the bottom of the tub under where the lower spray arm rests. Some models have a flat coarse strainer underneath.
     Lift it out. Rinse under warm tap water. Use an old toothbrush on the mesh. Look for: food debris, glass shards, fruit pits, bone fragments, paper labels (they glue themselves to the mesh).
     While the filter is out, SHINE A FLASHLIGHT into the sump well. Look for a small object sitting at the bottom, e.g., a fork tine, glass chip, broken crockery. If you can see and reach it safely with your fingers, pull it out. If it is wedged or you cannot see clearly, STOP. Do not fish into the pump opening. That is past your stated scope.

  3. AIR GAP / DISPOSAL QUICK CHECKS (silent, optional)
     If your sink or countertop has a small chrome cylinder mounted on it (the "air gap"), unscrew the cap. If it is packed with grey slime, that is the choke point. Rinse it out. Many codes require this; the dishwasher cannot vent properly otherwise.
     If you have a garbage disposal and the dishwasher drains into it, run the disposal for about 10 seconds with water running. A common install mistake is leaving the knock-out plug in the disposal inlet; sludge builds up there. Do not put your hand in the disposal.

  4. QUIET DRAIN PROBE (not a cycle)
     With the filter reinstalled, pour about 1 quart of water from a pitcher into the bottom of the tub.
     Listen and watch:
       Pump hums briefly, water visibly drops in 30 to 60 seconds, ending with a whoosh — drain path is restored. Reinstall the rack and run a normal cycle later, ideally after Devika is up and the kitchen is not in quiet hours.
       Pump hums and water does not drop — blockage is past the filter (pump impeller, drain hose, or building drain). STOP. Call maintenance.
       Silence, water does not drop — pump is not getting power or has failed. STOP. Call maintenance.

STOP AND CALL BUILDING MAINTENANCE (or a licensed appliance tech) IF ANY OF THE FOLLOWING IS TRUE

  The 1-quart pour-drain probe does not drain, either silent or humming without water moving.
  Water appears under the dishwasher or near any electrical at any point.
  A burning or hot-plastic smell recurs, or the breaker trips when you restore power.
  Water backs up into the kitchen sink when the dishwasher drains (building drain blockage, not the appliance).
  You find a cracked hose, cracked sump, or water marks under the unit.

WHAT NOT TO DO (your stated scope, restated)

  No drain cleaner, CLR, or Drano. Will not clear a physical jam, attacks seals and gaskets, and is unsafe in standing water.
  No opening the pump housing. Past your stated scope; a stuck impeller needs a tech.
  No full test cycle. The 1-quart pour is the diagnostic; a cycle adds nothing and risks the pump.

If the filter/sump cleanup restores drain, wait until Devika is awake and the kitchen is not in quiet hours, then run one normal short/eco cycle as confirmation. If anything in the STOP list fires, hand off; the issue is past the filter and into the pump, hose, or building drain.

    Non-goals are stated, not merely omitted.

1. Purpose
    The preview exists to help a customer judge the operational risk of
    the Sphere services they rely on. It is an operational signal about
    services and system state. It is NOT a tool for evaluating Sphere
    employees, teams, managers, or organizational health.

2. Non-goals (explicit, written)
    The preview will NOT, in this version or in any version that shares
    its response shape:
        a. Break down incident load by internal owning team, squad, pod,
           or any internal organizational unit.
        b. Break down incident load by manager, management chain, or
           reporting line.
        c. Identify individual on-call responders, incident commanders,
           authors, reviewers, or any named person.
        d. Surface raw incident titles, summaries, postmortem excerpts,
           chat excerpts, or status messages.
        e. Surface incident IDs, page IDs, alert IDs, or any handle that
           resolves inside Sphere's internal incident or paging systems.
        f. Provide release-readiness, manager-readiness, "team health",
           "constrained team", "squad capacity", or "who is overloaded"
           interpretations.
        g. Compare Sphere organizational units against each other.
        h. Support period-over-period comparison at any interval finer
           than the window defined in section 4.
    These prohibitions are enforced at the API response shape. They are
    NOT enforced by UI convention, copy, or tooltip wording.

3. Service scope
    3.1 Eligible services are a fixed, engineering-owned, published list
        of customer-facing services. Internal-only services (for example:
        metrics-router, ingest-edge, shard-keeper, rollup-service,
        legacy-aggregator, metric-rollup, config-loader) are NOT in the
        customer-preview scope, regardless of any internal dependency.
        Customers cannot enumerate the eligible list beyond what is
        published; the list is not derived from internal taxonomy.
    3.2 A customer sees only services they have a contractual relationship
        with or that are exposed as part of their subscribed region.
        Cross-customer service comparisons are not provided.
    3.3 If a service the customer relies on is internal-only, the preview
        returns no row for it (see section 7) and does not signal its
        existence. The preview does not become a way to probe Sphere's
        internal architecture.

4. Window (fixed, not configurable)
    4.1 The customer-visible window is a FIXED rolling 30 days, ending at
        the most recent complete UTC day.
    4.2 The window is the same for every customer. Customers cannot
        narrow it, widen it, or choose a custom range. There is no
        `window`, `since`, `until`, or `interval` parameter on the
        preview endpoint.
    4.3 The window cannot be sliced into smaller sub-windows (week, day,
        hour, shift) in the customer response. Slicing is the mechanism
        by which small counts re-enable individual and team inference,
        because a small team on a quiet week looks identical to a small
        team on a quiet shift; slicing is therefore not exposed.
    4.4 The window anchor (the end date) is reported with each response
        so the customer can interpret trend direction. The anchor is a
        UTC date, not a timestamp.

5. Aggregation
    For each (service, severity_bucket) the preview returns ONE summary
    record containing:
        - service: the public service identifier (from the fixed list).
        - severity_bucket: one of {sev1, sev2, sev3, sev_unknown}. The
          internal sev0 / SEV-0 class is folded into sev1 for preview
          purposes; the internal classification is not exposed.
        - incident_count: a count of incidents in the window, subject to
          the suppression rules in section 6.
        - trend: one of {up, down, flat, insufficient_data} over the
          window, computed against the prior 30-day window. Trend is
          coarse-grained by design; customers do not receive a sparkline,
          per-week count, per-day count, or any sub-window series.
        - window_end: the UTC date the window ends (matches 4.4).
        - source_systems: public category names of the contributing
          internal systems (e.g., "incident-tracker", "page-router").
          Internal hostnames, schema names, and field names are not
          exposed.
        - generated_at: the UTC timestamp the summary was computed.
    The preview does NOT return:
        - incident timestamps, MTTR, time-to-detection, time-to-
          mitigation, or any duration field.
        - per-incident severity; only the bucket.
        - cause codes, root-cause taxonomy, remediation status, or
          action items.
        - on-call rotation names, page counts per responder, page
          volume, escalation counts.
        - any field that resolves to a Sphere employee, team, manager,
          owner-map record, or HR / org-chart attribute.
        - any pointer, deep link, or token that opens the underlying
          incident in Sphere's internal tooling.

6. Suppression
    6.1 Suppression threshold: any (service, severity_bucket) cell whose
        count is fewer than 5 incidents in the 30-day window is
        SUPPRESSED. The threshold is fixed and is not configurable by
        the customer.
    6.2 A suppressed cell is returned as a record with incident_count =
        null and a structured reason of "below_suppression_threshold".
        trend for that cell is "insufficient_data". The cell is NOT
        omitted from the response; suppressing by omission lets a
        customer distinguish "suppressed" from "no data", which is
        itself a leak.
    6.3 Suppression is also applied at the (service, ALL severities)
        aggregate so that a customer cannot recover a real count by
        summing sev1 + sev2 + sev3. The aggregate is suppressed if its
        total is below the threshold, even when the per-bucket counts
        would each be zero.
    6.4 Suppression is enforced at the API. The UI may render
        suppressed cells as "—" or omit them from a card body, but the
        API response always carries null + reason so suppression is
        auditable downstream and cannot be silently bypassed.
    6.5 The threshold value (5) is not advertised in customer-facing
        documentation. Advertising it would let a customer probe the
        boundary by repeated queries. The threshold may be raised by
        engineering; lowering it requires a contract amendment.

7. Zero, null, and denial semantics
    The API distinguishes three states. The UI is required to render
    them distinctly. The reason field is mandatory on every null
    record.

        a. ZERO.
            incident_count = 0
            trend          = "flat"
            reason         = (omitted; not a null record)
           Meaning: the (service, severity_bucket) had no incidents in
           the window. This is an actual observed zero. A customer who
           sees zero can rely on it.

        b. SUPPRESSED.
            incident_count = null
            trend          = "insufficient_data"
            reason         = "below_suppression_threshold"
           Meaning: incidents occurred, but the count did not clear the
           threshold. The customer cannot distinguish "1 incident" from
           "4 incidents". That ambiguity is intentional and is the
           point of suppression.

        c. NO DATA.
            The (service, severity_bucket) record is omitted from the
            response, OR returned with:
                incident_count = null
                trend          = "insufficient_data"
                reason         = "no_permissioned_source"
           Meaning: Sphere does not have a permissioned incident source
           for this service, OR the customer does not have visibility
           into this service, OR the service is out of customer-preview
           scope. The three sub-cases are NOT distinguishable by the
           customer, by design: an absence in the preview means "no
           permissioned summary is available", not "no incident load".

    Iris's earlier question - whether small-count cells could simply
    return an empty value to give the UI one branch - is rejected.
    Empty conflates zero with suppressed and with no-data, and the
    three states must remain distinct at the API. The UI is required
    to render the three states distinctly as well.

8. Attribution, provenance, and labeling
    8.1 The preview never returns owner-map IDs, employee IDs, employee
        names, team names, manager names, or any field that maps through
        Sphere's internal HR or org systems. This binds the customer
        preview regardless of what the internal preview carries.
    8.2 The provenance block on every record is limited to:
            source_systems (public category names),
            generated_at (UTC),
            window_end (UTC date).
        Provenance for the preview is not the same as provenance for
        the internal Lantern contract, and the two are not unified.
    8.3 The preview surfaces a pointer, not raw detail:
            "Summary generated from permissioned incident sources.
             For raw incident detail, refer to your internal incident
             system or your Sphere support contact."
        Raw incident detail is not rendered inside the preview surface
        and is not embedded in exports derived from it.

9. Customer-side use restriction (preview ToS, requires legal review)
    The preview summary is provided for the customer's internal
    evaluation of operational risk on services they use. The customer
    agrees not to:
        - use the summary to evaluate, score, rank, or compare Sphere
          employees, teams, managers, or organizational units;
        - redistribute the summary in any form that attributes incident
          load to a named Sphere employee or team;
        - combine the summary with other data to re-derive the
          prohibited breakdowns in section 2 or the prohibited fields
          in section 5;
        - use the summary as input to an automated decision about
          Sphere staffing, structure, or personnel.
    Violation is grounds for preview termination. This is a
    contractual clause, not a technical control; section 2 is the
    technical control that makes the clause enforceable.

10. Decisions still required from Theo (Thursday)
    These four items are isolated so they cannot be folded into UI copy
    or deferred to a follow-up review:

    a. SUPPRESSION THRESHOLD. Confirm or raise the value in 6.1. 5 is
       a starting proposal. The right value depends on the smallest
       internal team that owns a customer-facing service and on
       on-call rotation size; engineering should brief Theo on the
       smallest relevant team before the meeting. Lowering the
       threshold requires a contract amendment and is not on the
       table.

    b. WINDOW LENGTH. Confirm the fixed 30-day window in 4.1. 60 or
       90 days are alternatives if Theo wants a longer baseline for
       the trend computation. Shorter than 30 days is not on the
       table, because shorter windows are the inference vector this
       contract exists to remove.

    c. TEAM AXIS. Confirm that the customer preview NEVER carries
       the team axis, even as an opt-in or a future field. Iris's
       "responsible_team + last_verified_at" question applies to the
       internal preview only; the customer preview does not inherit
       that field, even with a staleness flag.

    d. ToS ENFORCEABILITY. Decide whether the language in section 9
       is enforceable as written or needs legal review before the
       preview is opened. The technical surface (sections 2, 5, 6, 8)
       is enforceable from day one; the contractual use restriction
       is not yet drafted.

11. What this contract does NOT resolve
    - Deploy-movement fields are out of scope here; they are governed
      by the deploy-movement contract draft.
    - External ownership labels are out of scope here; they are
      governed by the external-ownership-label contract draft.
    - The internal-only Lantern surface (with team, manager, and
      owner-map fields) is unchanged. This contract binds the customer
      preview only and does not constrain internal rooms.
    - The suppression in section 6 protects against team-size
      inference in the small-cell regime. It does NOT protect against
      a customer who infers team size from public Sphere engineering
      communications (blog posts, conference talks, OSS commits).
      That is an external-communications problem, not a preview-
      contract problem, and should be tracked separately if it
      matters.

End of draft.

DECISION: Reject the proposal as designed. Do not add `pod_uid` or `container_id` to `customer_request_errors_total`. The drill-down need is real; the unbounded labels are the wrong place for it. A bounded pattern with prior precedent (the `replay_source_id` review; the `request_id` customer case) already covers it.

CARDINALITY (rough):

Baseline today is bounded by customer × service × region × status_class × route_group — call it order-of-magnitude thousands of active series across the fleet, scaling with high-volume customers.

Add `pod_uid` (typical 40–120 live instances per service, ~80 mid-range):
  active series multiplier ≈ ×80 per emitting service × ~900 services ≈ +70k active series just from this one label.

Add `container_id` (often 1–3 per pod, correlated but still instance-level):
  smaller multiplier, but the same shape — every container is its own series.

The metric stops tracking "errors per customer/route" and starts tracking "errors per running workload instance." TSDB head count, query planner cost, and alerting rule evaluation cost all scale with active series.

CHURN:

`pod_uid` is per-pod, not per-deployment. New value on every deploy, every HPA scale event, every node restart, every crashloop. Across ~900 services at ~80 instances, churn is hundreds-to-low-thousands of new pod_uids per hour at a normal deploy posture.

Old pod_uids do not drop from the TSDB on redeploy. They persist for the retention window (days to weeks). So active series count grows over time even when error volume is flat — the inventory inflates with churn rather than tracking the thing the metric is supposed to track.

A pod that errors for 5 minutes, gets redeployed, then errors again 2 hours later looks like two unrelated instances contributing errors when it is one logical workload incident. The label actively obscures the answer the operator wants.

OPERATING-RULE CHECK:

Direct precedent in your own guidance: pod UIDs, request IDs, and other unbounded values are not recommended as metric labels. Raw identifiers belong in logs; bounded classification labels are acceptable when they serve a dashboard need. Same shape as `replay_source_id` (raw stays in logs; bounded classification on the metric) and the `request_id` customer case (label explosion, mitigation = drop the metric label, preserve request-level debugging in logs).

Cardinality Guardrails: this metric almost certainly flows metrics-router → rollup-service given the existing label set. Adding new labels is a cross-service label change. As written, it would require label-cardinality preflight, alert-source classification, the shared parity-fixture run with Roman's individual sign-off, and pre-push sync with Nadia — before it is treated as safe for production review. The proposal as written would fail that gate on cardinality alone; the preflight would block it.

SAFER DESIGN (preserves drill-down, keeps the broadly-queried metric bounded):

Option A — Logs + trace linkage (default recommendation):
  `pod_uid` and `container_id` are already on the request path in logs, and almost certainly in traces. Keep them there. From the dashboard's bounded view (customer × service × region × status_class × route_group × time window), pivot to logs using the same labels + approximate timestamp → `request_id` → `pod_uid`/`container_id`. If a click-through is needed, attach `trace_id` as an exemplar on the metric; exemplars are bounded per-scrape and trace_id ties back to logs without becoming a high-cardinality label.

Option B — Bounded grouping label:
  If the real question is "which workload version is failing" rather than "which pod right now," add a bounded `deployment_generation` or `instance_group` label — bounded by deploy cadence × retention window (e.g., last 100 generations per service). Operator gets "which generation is the source" without per-pod cardinality. This is the bounded-classification pattern from the `replay_source_id` precedent.

Option C — Separate drill-down metric on a non-broad path:
  Create a sibling metric (e.g., `customer_request_errors_by_instance_total`) carrying `pod_uid`/`container_id`. Route it only to drill-down consumers, not through rollup-service's broadly-queried path. ASSESSMENT

The prototype gets the shape right and the unit wrong.

Correct pieces (keep):
  - Double-bound semaphore (global cap of 4 active decompressions per pod, per-tenant cap of 2). This directly addresses the May 9 failure where two tenants pinned every worker.
  - Cancellation releases permits. Prevents permit leaks on client disconnect.
  - HTTP 429 with the existing randomized 1–3 s Retry-After for overflow. v2.19.4's retry-storm lever is the right tool here — no reason to fork it.
  - `decode_wait_seconds` exposed and folded into pressure accounting. Adds the visibility that the admission queue metric cannot give.

Broken pieces (the test is itself the evidence):
  - The semaphore is weighted only by compressed request bytes. The 9–13 s occupancy on tiny compressed bodies with large expanded payloads is exactly the failure this bound was supposed to prevent. The test reproduces the May 9 mode and then shows the bound did not catch it.
  - "Ordinary admission queues stayed responsive" is the wrong success criterion. It is the same lie the May 9 postmortem called out: admission-queue depth does not include pre-admission work. A worker pinned for 13 s by a single decompression looks like an idle queue from the queue metric's perspective.
  - No per-permit duration cap. A request that holds a permit for 9–13 s is not bounded at all; it just happens to terminate before someone escalates.
  - The 40-request test did not exercise the per-tenant fairness case (one tenant with high-ratio payloads vs. another tenant with normal traffic) or sustained saturation (global cap held full for >60 s). Without those, "stayed responsive" tells us nothing about the bound under the workload it most needs to bound.

WHY COMPRESSED-BYTE WEIGHTING IS INSUFFICIENT

Decompression cost is bounded by decompressed size, not compressed size:
  - CPU scales with the output stream (buffer fills, copies, CRCs, block parse).
  - Memory scales with the output buffer.
  - Wall time scales with decompressed bytes / CPU bandwidth.

A permit model whose unit is compressed bytes therefore underprices work in exactly the regime where work is highest: small wire size, large expanded size. A 100 KB gzipped body that expands to ~500 MB acquires roughly the same weight as a 100 KB body that expands to 200 KB, but the former holds a worker for orders of magnitude longer. Permit economics are inverted: the requests that should be most expensive are the cheapest to admit.

Concrete consequence in this test: tiny compressed bodies (low compressed-byte weight → low permit cost → admitted freely) then monopolize workers for 9–13 s. The per-tenant cap of 2 does not save you because each individual permit is "cheap" relative to actual work, so four such permits saturate the global cap while representing much more than 4 units of real work.

Compressed size is a wire-format detail. It is the right unit for the network, the TLS record layer, or the body-size limit on the wire — not for bounding CPU/memory work that has already crossed into decompression.

REVISED BOUNDS

1. Weight by decompressed bytes, with a per-permit ceiling equal to the existing 10 MiB decoded-body limit. Every permit represents up to one full body's worth of decompression work. Acquiring the permit at admission time uses the worst case (10 MiB); actual decompressed size cannot exceed it, so the bound is safe. No streaming estimate required.
  - Global cap: 4 permits × 10 MiB = 40 MiB of in-flight decompression per pod.
  - Per-tenant cap: 2 permits × 10 MiB = 20 MiB of in-flight decompression per tenant per pod.
2. Add a hard per-permit duration cap. A single decompression may not hold a permit beyond a defined maximum (proposal: 2× the p99 of normal decompression under the safe batching target, or a fixed ceiling such as 2 s — pick the larger of the two but make it explicit). On expiry: release the permit, fail the request with 429, log the compression-ratio and observed duration. This is the bound the prototype is missing today.
3. Keep the global cap aligned to actual decode-worker count. The cap of 4 must be ≤ decode_workers_per_pod. If decode_workers > 4, the cap is wasting capacity; if decode_workers < 4, the cap is fictional. Verify and document.
4. Keep cancellation behavior, 429 + 1–3 s Retry-After, and `decode_wait_seconds` exposure. These are correct.
5. Pressure-accounting signals (additive — do not retcon the existing queue metric, annotate it):
  - `decode_in_flight_global` and `decode_in_flight_per_tenant`
  - `decode_duration_seconds` (histogram)
  - `compression_ratio` (per request, histogram)
  - `decode_wait_seconds` measured from permit-acquire request, not from admission-queue entry
  - Alert: saturation-while-queue-low — if `decode_in_flight_global == global_cap` sustained for >X seconds while admission queue depth is below threshold, page. This is the alert that would have caught May 9 and will catch the prototype's current gap.

LOAD-TEST ASSERTIONS BEFORE THIS TEST COUNTS AS PROOF

Workload shape (must include, not optional):
  a. The May 9 reproduction: ~17 highly compressed requests from 2 tenants, compression ratio matching the incident. Pass: saturation duration bounded by per-permit timeout; no single request holds a worker past the cap.
  b. High-ratio asymmetry: one tenant submits small-compressed/large-decompressed payloads (compression ratio ≥ 50×, decompressed size near the body limit). Another tenant submits ordinary traffic simultaneously. Pass: the second tenant's admission p99 stays within threshold (proposal: ≤ 250 ms); its `decode_wait_seconds` p99 stays bounded (proposal: ≤ 500 ms); it is not starved past a defined bound.
  c. Sustained saturation: hold the global cap fully occupied for ≥ 60 s. Pass: no 5xx, no permit leak after the load drops, `decode_in_flight` returns to baseline, no orphan goroutines.
  d. Cancellation: client disconnects mid-decompression on ≥ 20% of in-flight requests. Pass: permits released within a defined window; subsequent requests are not blocked.
  e. Per-tenant cap: one tenant submits 10 simultaneous requests. Pass: at most 2 decompressing concurrently; the rest receive 429 with a Retry-After in [1 s, 3 s].
  f. Timeout path: a request engineered to exceed the per-permit duration cap. Pass: 429 returned, permit released, log contains compression ratio and observed duration, no worker stall afterward.

Observable metrics and thresholds (concrete, not ranges to be decided later):
  - Admission p99 latency (not queue depth) under saturation: ≤ 250 ms.
  - `decode_wait_seconds` p99: ≤ 500 ms.
  - `decode_duration_seconds` max: ≤ per-permit timeout ceiling (proposed 2 s).
  - 429 ratio under sustained overload: defined and bounded; synchronized-retry bursts (the v2.19.4 failure mode) must not reform — peak retry rate ≤ 130,000/s if reusing the existing canary envelope, or a new envelope defined and justified.
  - `decode_in_flight_global` p99 over the test window: must not exceed the cap by more than a defined tolerance (proposal: never — exceeding the cap means the semaphore is broken).
  - No single tenant's share of `decode_in_flight` may exceed its cap.

Pass/fail:
  - Any 5xx, any admission p99 above threshold, any `decode_in_flight` excursion above the cap, any permit observed past the duration ceiling, any worker pinned > 5 s after the load profile drops, or any saturation-while-queue-low alert firing during the test → fail. Roll back; do not reinterpret.

BOTTOM LINE

The architecture (double-bound semaphore, cancellation, 429 path, exposed wait) is the right shape and matches the May 9 recommendation. The weighting unit is the gap. The 40-request test as run is not proof — it is the failure mode being demonstrated against. Before accepting, fix the weight unit (decompressed bytes, per-permit ceiling at the 10 MiB body limit), add the per-permit duration cap, add the saturation-while-queue-low alert, and rerun with the workload shape and thresholds above. The compressed-byte weight is not a tunable knob — it is the wrong number.

Yes, this closes the original gap.

The original proof gap was two-part: (1) compressed bytes were treated as a proxy for decompression work — but a tiny compressed body can expand to gigabytes, as in the May 9 case where 17 requests from 2 tenants held every worker for 11-16 s while queue depth read 8%; and (2) pre-admission decode work was invisible to admission accounting. The revised prototype addresses both with specific architectural changes, not parameter tuning:

  - Compressed-body ceiling enforced BEFORE worker acquisition — fast rejection, no worker consumed by a request that will obviously overrun. The first prototype repeated the May 9 error because tiny compressed bodies that expanded large still occupied workers for 9-13 s.
  - Streamed decompressed bytes counted against the existing 10 MiB body limit; immediate abort on crossing — defense in depth. The compressed ceiling is a conservative gate; the streaming abort is the actual limit enforcer.
  - Count-bounded concurrency (4/pod, 2/tenant), not byte-bounded — work is time, not bytes. Per-tenant cap directly addresses the original symptom.
  - Permit release on cancellation and decode failure — no leaks under load.
  - Pressure metrics expose waiters AND active work as separate signals — closes the queue-depth blind spot by adding signals, not by relabeling the existing queue metric (the May 9 lesson holds).

The test design substantiates the architecture: bounded workers (≤4), per-tenant ≤2, baseline starvation guard (decode-wait p99 < 240 ms), early-rejection proof (oversized expansions rejected before admission), false-rejection guard (admitted points committed), and permit accounting (returns to 0 after cancel).

Test-coverage items I'd want explicit before calling this complete
(the description doesn't state them; they aren't architectural gaps, but they are claims I can't verify from what you've described):

  1. The per-tenant ≤2 bound is meaningful only with >2 tenants competing for 4 worker slots. If the test ran with only 2 tenants, the 2/tenant cap is trivially satisfied regardless of enforcement.
  2. Mid-decode streaming-abort tested as a separate code path from client cancellation — both must release the permit, but the trigger conditions are different.
  3. Compressed-ceiling threshold stated and defensible — either "no realistic input under this size can exceed 10 MiB decoded" or "conservative gate; streaming abort is the actual enforcer." Without the value, "rejected before admission" isn't falsifiable.
  4. Decode-failure paths (truncated gzip, CRC mismatch, decompressor error) verified to release permits, distinct from cancellation.
  5. Multi-pod behavior — 4/2 caps are per-pod. With consistent hashing, one tenant's traffic concentrating on one pod is bounded only by the per-tenant cap. The cluster-level guarantee is the weaker of the two.

Regression assertions that must remain
(ordered by drift risk):

  1. Compressed-body ceiling enforced BEFORE worker acquisition. This is the architectural fix. A future "optimization" that moves the check inside the worker pool silently re-opens the May 9 failure mode.
  2. Permit release on every exit path: success, streaming-abort, decode-error, client cancellation, timeout. A new error path added later that doesn't `defer releasePermit()` leaks under exactly the conditions where the prototype matters.
  3. Per-pod cap = 4 AND per-tenant cap = 2 enforced simultaneously. Either alone is insufficient.
  4. Body limit (10 MiB decoded) remains the upper bound on any admitted expansion. Streaming abort fires before this limit is crossed, not after.
  5. Pressure metric exposes waiters and active work as separate signals. Replacing either with a derived or composite metric re-creates the queue-depth blind spot.
  6. Queue-depth metric is not retconned. Add new signals, don't relabel the old. Decompression pressure is a new signal; queue depth is queue depth.
  7. Baseline decode-wait p99 stays < 240 ms under pathological load. This is the starvation guard — if it ever rises, the cap is no longer protecting baseline traffic.
  8. No 5xx, no dropped writes, no queue-depth regression in baseline traffic when the prototype is enabled vs disabled. Same shape as the v2.19.4 retry rollout hard-stops.
  9. Retry-After 1-3 s randomized behavior unchanged. Orthogonal lever (separate March 29 canary); decompression work must not be allowed to mask, retcon, or "improve" retry behavior.
  10. 7.5 MiB safe batching target still holds for customer-facing guidance. The prototype changes service behavior under pressure but does not change the customer's correct batching target — the March customer language stands.

Items 1 and 2 are the easiest to regress and the most important to pin. Item 1 is the architectural change itself; item 2 is the kind of bug that only surfaces under exactly the load the prototype is built to absorb.

Practical two-person checklist for installing the 58 lb window unit. The contractor's written note covers the new exterior bracket and the two new masonry anchors only — it does not cover the window sash, the sash hardware, side panels, drainage tilt, electrical path, or the unit itself. Treat each of those as an independent gate.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════
0. PRE-LIFT GATES (both people, before touching the unit)
═══════════════════════════════════════════════

  • Re-inspect the new bracket and both anchors with your own eyes:
      - Anchors are flush with the wall (the previous failure mode was ~3 mm proud).
      - Bracket shows no rust, no cracking, no movement when pressed laterally.
      - No gap between bracket back-plate and masonry.
  • Confirm the bracket is rated for the unit's weight. Written note confirms
    approval for 58 lb on this bracket — verify the label or spec sticker lists
    >=58 lb. If you cannot read a rating, do not proceed.
  • Confirm a grounded outlet is within reach of the unit's cord without an
    extension cord. No power strip. Outlet shows no scorch, no looseness, no
    buzzing. If it is a kitchen/bath/damp location, GFCI is required by code;
    test and reset.
  • Confirm the circuit can carry the unit's amps (nameplate on the side of the
    unit). A 58 lb window unit is typically 8-12A on a 115V circuit. Do not
    share with a space heater, hair dryer, or kitchen circuit that also feeds
    a fridge.
  • Open the window fully. Inspect both sash rails for cracks, rot, peeling
    paint that hides rot, and missing/damaged glazing. Lower the lower sash
    slowly and verify it travels smoothly and stops cleanly with no drift.
  • Verify the side accordion / filler panels match the opening height and
    width. A gap > ~1/4 inch between panel and frame is a stop.
  • Place a drop cloth directly below the window, inside. Clear a 6 ft path
    from where the unit sits on the floor to the window.
  • Decide who is INSIDE and who is OUTSIDE before lifting. Outside person is
    on stable ground (ladder or stoop) — not the window ledge.
  • Kibo and Devika are out of the room and the area below the window for the
    entire install.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════
1. THE LIFT (two-person, 58 lb)
═══════════════════════════════════════════════

  • Outside person grips the case at the chassis rails, not the fins, coil,
    or plastic end caps. Inside person grips the same rails from the room
    side.
  • Lift with legs. Communicate "ready - lift - stop - hold" before each
    phase. No one lets go until the unit is seated.
  • Inside person guides the bottom rail onto the bracket lip first. The
    bottom rail should sit flat against the bracket, with the chassis weight
    carried by the bracket — not by the lower sash or side panels.
  • Outside person steadies the unit from the top edge and confirms the
    bottom rail is fully captured by the bracket before any further movement.
  • Do not tilt the unit, swing it, or set it down on the sill until the
    bottom rail is confirmed on the bracket.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════
2. SASH RESTRAINT (the #1 injury mechanism)
═══════════════════════════════════════════════

  • Close the lower sash slowly onto the top rail of the unit until the top
    rail is firmly seated in the sash channel.
  • Engage the sash lock at both sides if your window has them. Lock must
    hold the sash at the chosen height with no audible click-loosening when
    the unit is gently pressed.
  • Install the L-bracket (or top-angle bracket supplied with the unit) that
    screws into the sash and hooks over the unit's top rail. This is the
    secondary restraint that catches the unit if the sash lock fails.
  • Verify by pressing UP on the lower sash with one hand while holding the
    unit's top edge with the other. The sash must not lift. The unit must
    not shift.
  • Fit the accordion / side panels and screw them into the sash and frame
    according to the unit's instructions. Panels are not structural but they
    keep the sash from sliding sideways.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════
3. OUTWARD TILT (drainage)
═══════════════════════════════════════════════

  • The unit must tilt slightly OUTWARD (about 1/4 to 1/2 inch lower at the
    back than at the front). Check the unit's instructions for the specified
    angle — typically "1/4 bubble toward the outside" on a small level set
    on the top rail.
  • The bracket's design usually provides this angle. If the bracket is flat
    and the unit sits level or tilts toward the room, do not shim with
    improvised materials — stop and call the contractor or management.
  • Pour ~1/2 cup of water into the unit's drain pan (or the base of the
    evaporator coil area) and confirm water drips to the OUTSIDE of the
    building. If it drips down the interior wall or pools inside the unit,
    the tilt is wrong — stop, recheck the bracket.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════
4. CORD PLACEMENT
═══════════════════════════════════════════════

  • Route the cord through the side panel's cord channel or notch, not over
    the back of the unit where condensate pools.
  • Make a drip loop in the cord just inside the window so any water tracking
    along the cord drips onto the sill, not into the outlet.
  • No kinks, no sharp bends, no pinching between sash and frame.
  • Plug directly into the wall outlet. Confirm the plug is fully seated and
    the cord is not under tension.
  • Cord must not contact the condenser coil or any hot surface on the rear
    of the unit.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════
5. POST-INSTALL CHECK (before sealing the panels)
═══════════════════════════════════════════════

  • Run the unit on FAN ONLY for 15 minutes. Listen for rattling, buzzing,
    scraping. Smell for burning, ozone, or melted plastic.
  • Check both masonry anchors are still flush. Any change from pre-install
    state is a stop.
  • Check the bracket is still seated with no movement when the running
    unit is gently pushed.
  • Run on COOL for 15 minutes. Confirm condensate drips outside, not
    inside.
  • Only after these pass: install remaining foam seals, screw side panels
    fully, and lower the window lock.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════
6. STOP CONDITIONS — call contractor or management, do not proceed
═══════════════════════════════════════════════

Stop and do not install if any of these are true:

  • Either masonry anchor is recessed, backed out, or no longer flush.
  • Any movement, creak, or visible deflection of the bracket or wall under
    the unit's weight.
  • Window sash will not lock firmly at the required height, sash travels
    with drift, or you see cracking / rot in the sash or frame.
  • Side panels cannot fill the opening to within ~1/4 inch.
  • No grounded outlet within cord reach, outlet is loose / scorched / not
    GFCI where required, or you would need an extension cord.
  • Unit tilt cannot be set outward, or condensate test drains inward.
  • Cord cannot be routed without kinking, blocking the drain path, or
    contacting hot surfaces.
  • During the 15-minute fan-only check: any rattle, buzz, scrape, smell,
    or any change in anchor flushness.
  • At any step, either person is not confident. Two-person means both
    people agree to continue.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════
7. POST-INSTALL MONITORING (next 48 hours)
═══════════════════════════════════════════════

  • T+15 min: anchor flushness, bracket seating, condensate direction.
  • T+2 hours: same checks while the unit has cycled.
  • T+next morning: wall below the bracket shows no new staining, no
    efflorescence, no rust streaks. Bracket still seated.
  • T+48 hours: same checks after multiple full cooling cycles. If anything
    has changed, take the unit out and call management.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════
SUMMARY
═══════════════════════════════════════════════

The contractor's written note gets you past the bracket gate. It does not
get you past the sash, the sash lock + L-bracket, the side panels, the
drainage tilt, the electrical path, or the cord routing. Each of those has
its own stop condition above, and any one of them is sufficient reason to
not install and to call back.

GENERATION-RETIREMENT REVIEW (metrics-router matcher cache revision)

The race you spotted is correct. Between
  g = active_generation.load()
and
  g.readers.fetch_add(1)
in Acquire(), Publish can swap, retire, observe readers == 1, and
free the old generation before Acquire reaches fetch_add. UAF on the
fetch_add and on every subsequent dereference of g.

Additional races in the same pseudocode:

  - TOCTOU in Publish. old.readers.load() == 0 then free(old) is
    check-then-act against any concurrent Acquire that has loaded
    active but not yet bumped readers. Even after fixing Acquire,
    Publish must not free until it can prove no in-flight Acquire can
    still reach old.readers.

  - Release underflow. fetch_sub(1) without a paired successful
    Acquire drives readers negative and breaks the last-reader-
    frees invariant. Treat Release as exactly-once. The retry path
    inside Acquire must decrement before retrying.

  - Ordering. Every atomic touching readers, retired, and
    active_generation needs explicit Acquire/Release. The pseudocode
    as written is not portable to weakly ordered targets; retire can
    be reordered with the readers count.

  - Retired without a checker. Publish sets retired = true but
    Acquire never consults it. A thread that holds an old pointer
    across a Publish must re-check retired (or the active pointer)
    before trusting the generation. The safe pattern below does both.

  - ReloadFailed. free(candidate) is correct only if candidate was
    never published and never shared with any thread outside the
    builder. If validation hands candidate to a worker, that worker
    must release its reference first.

SAFE PATTERN

The codebase's validate -> atomic-swap -> close-retired idiom fits
here. The missing piece is making close-retired safe against an in-
flight Acquire that has loaded active_generation but not yet
incremented readers. Two cooperating signals handle it:

  struct Gen {
      id       u64                // monotonic, never reused
      rules    []Rule
      matchers map[expr]*Matcher  // per-generation, see cache note
      readers  atomic.Int32       // includes the active reference
      retired  atomic.Bool
  }

  active          atomic.Pointer[Gen]
  in_flight       atomic.Int32   // Acquire()s between ticket-take and ticket-release
  swap_in_flight  atomic.Bool    // blocks new Acquire()s across the swap

  Acquire() *Gen:
      for {
          if swap_in_flight.Load(): continue        // publish mid-swap; retry
          in_flight.Add(1)
          g := active.Load()
          if g == nil {
              in_flight.Add(-1)
              return nil
          }
          g.readers.Add(1)                          // active ref counted in readers
          in_flight.Add(-1)
          if g.retired.Load() || active.Load() != g {
              prev := g.readers.Add(-1)
              if prev == 1 { free(g) }              // we held the only ref
              continue
          }
          return g
      }

  Release(g):
      prev := g.readers.Add(-1)
      if prev == 1 && g.retired.Load() { free(g) }

  Publish(candidate):
      // Validation step (existing pattern; out of scope here).
      swap_in_flight.Store(true)                    // block new Acquire()s
      for in_flight.Load() > 0 { /* yield */ }     // drain in-flight Acquires
      candidate.readers.Store(1)                   // the active reference
      old := active.Swap(candidate)
      old.retired.Store(true)
      prev := old.readers.Add(-1)                  // drop active reference
      if prev == 1 { free(old) }                   // no in-flight readers
      swap_in_flight.Store(false)

  ReloadFailed(candidate):
      if candidate.readers.Load() != 0 { /* bug: candidate was shared */ }
      free(candidate)

Why this closes the original race:

  Any Acquire that passes the swap_in_flight.Load check either ran
  entirely before swap_in_flight.Store(true) or entirely after
  swap_in_flight.Store(false). In the after case, active.Load() is
  sequenced-after the swap, so it cannot see the old pointer. In the
  before case, the Acquire took its in_flight ticket before
  Publish's swap, so Publish's in_flight spin waits for the matching
  readers.Add(1) before swapping. Either way, Publish's
  old.readers.Add(-1) is ordered after any Acquire's readers.Add(1)
  on the same generation. The verification
  (g.retired.Load() || active.Load() != g) catches any edge case
  where the in-flight bookkeeping happens to be quiescent at the
  wrong instant; the retry path drops the stale refcount.

  Without the swap_in_flight flag, an Acquire that takes its
  in_flight ticket after Publish's spin returns 0 can still race the
  swap. The flag closes that residual window without locking the
  Acquire hot path.

CACHE IDENTITY

Scoping identity to (generation, expression) is the right move away
from the earlier process-global sync.Map[expr]*Matcher, which would
have retained every expression forever.

  (a) Per-generation map. Each Gen carries its own matchers map; the
      map dies with Gen. No global structure, no eviction logic.
      Cold start on every config reload is the cost. Simplest, and
      removes the freed-pointer-aliasing risk that would arise from
      keying a global map by *Gen.

  (b) Global map keyed by (genID, expr), with eviction on Publish.
      Publish that installs gen N+1 walks the global map and drops
      entries with genID < N-K for some small K. Bounded retention
      and a warm cache across reloads, at the cost of an eviction
      step on every Publish.

Take (a) unless there is measured evidence that matcher build cost
dominates after a reload. Do NOT key the cache by *Gen directly:
freed pointers get reused, and a stale *Gen key will return the wrong
cached matcher once that address is recycled.

FAILED-RELOAD CLEANUP

ReloadFailed(candidate) -> free(candidate) is safe under one
precondition: no thread outside the builder holds a pointer to
candidate. If validation ever hands candidate to a worker for trial
evaluation, that worker must release its reference (or route through
Acquire/Release against candidate) before ReloadFailed is allowed
to free. Sanity-check candidate.readers == 0 before free and treat
a non-zero reading as a bug.

TESTS REQUIRED BEFORE MERGE

  - Concurrent Acquire/Release with a continuous Publish stream.
    Run with -race and an allocator that catches reads of freed
    memory. Assert no goroutine ever observes a freed *Gen as
    active.

  - Late Acquire that loaded active before Publish swapped. Park a
    goroutine between active.Load() and readers.Add(1) while another
    Publish swaps and (in a controlled variant) tries to free.
    Cover the case where the Acquire ultimately succeeds after
    retry with the new generation.

  - Publish during in-flight Acquire. Drive a continuous Acquire/
    Release stream and verify Publish observes in_flight == 0 before
    swapping.

  - swap_in_flight barrier. Verify no Acquire that returns a pointer
    ever sees a freed *Gen, even when an Acquire starts a few
    instructions after swap_in_flight.Store(true).

  - Release underflow. Assert Release without a prior successful
    Acquire, or two Releases for one Acquire, is a bug (panic in
    tests, fail-closed in prod).

  - ReloadFailed isolation. A build that fails validation must not
    leak any reference into active.

  - Cache identity. Swap N generations, retire all but the current,
    and assert the cache contains only matchers for live expressions
    in the active generation. With per-generation maps, assert each
    retired Gen's map is freed.

  - Matcher correctness across reload. A rule whose expression text
    is identical in generations N and N+1 must produce the same
    matcher modulo gen-specific fields (MissingLabelMode,
    Normalizer), which must be taken from the active gen, not from
    a cached one built under a different gen.

SCOPE NOTE

This is a review of the proposed pattern, not a statement about
ownership or rollout. The recommendations apply regardless of who
ends up merging it; the safe acquire/retire/cleanup pattern is
independent of who's on call for metrics-router.

DIRECT ANSWER

Foam alone is not adequate as the primary seal or restraint at a 1.25" gap. The accordion panels are not structural — they only fill the opening; the sash lock and the unit's bottom rail are what keep the unit from shifting or tipping outward. A 1.25" gap on the outer sash edge means the accordion is not fully seated against the frame, which (a) lets the unit creep sideways under vibration, (b) defeats the sash lock's bite on the rail, and (c) leaves a screen Kibo can push on with nothing behind it. Foam (spray or tape) is a gasket, not a structural element. Two specific pet-safety reasons to avoid foam as the sole fix: spray foam is toxic until fully cured (~24 h, off-gas isocyanates) and is attractive to chew, and open-cell foam tape will be chewed and ingested if Kibo reaches it. Your "door closed, unit unplugged" call is the right primary containment while you sort the gap.

PET-SAFE TEMPORARY CONTAINMENT PLAN (until the rigid panel is in and verified)

  1. Kibo stays out of the bedroom whenever the AC is mounted in the sash, full stop. The bedroom door stays closed. Do not rely on the screen — you already confirmed Kibo can reach it from the sill.
  2. No spray foam anywhere Kibo can reach, including cured foam. If you use spray foam at all, it is only as a gap-filler behind a rigid panel, and the room stays Kibo-free for the full 24 h cure window.
  3. No foam weatherstripping tape as the primary seal on a 1.25" gap. Foam tape is fine as a gasket around a rigid panel; it is not the panel.
  4. Power cord: route it so Kibo cannot reach it from the sill, the floor, or any furniture. The cord should not pass through the gap you are sealing, and it should not be pinched by the panel or the sash lock.
  5. While the unit is seated but the gap is unresolved, leave it unplugged and the door closed. The sash lock alone is not enough with a 1.25" gap — that is the situation you are trying to fix.

RIGID FILLER PANEL — MATERIAL, SIZE, HOW TO SECURE

Material (pick one):
  - Exterior-grade 1/2" plywood — easiest, cheapest, sturdy. Paint or seal the edges.
  - 1/2" or 3/4" XPS foam board — light, but it is a chew/ingestion hazard if Kibo ever reaches it; only acceptable because the panel sits behind the closed accordion and the door stays closed.
  - 1/4" acrylic or polycarbonate sheet — cleanest look, but you need to drill and fasten it; it is also the easiest for Kibo to see through and paw at, so avoid it unless you also add an opaque face.
Do not use cardboard, drywall, or Masonite. They will soften, bow, or delaminate from condensation and lose the seal.

Sizing:
  - Measure the gap at the outer sash edge, top to bottom and front to back. Do not assume the gap is uniform — accordion panels flare, and the opening is often wider at one corner.
  - Cut the panel ~1/8" proud of the largest measured dimension so it presses in and stays by friction.
  - The panel must bear against the window frame (jamb/header/sill), not just against the accordion. The accordion is not load-bearing.

How to secure (use all three, in order):
  1. Friction fit. The panel sits snugly between the sash stops or between the upper sash and the sill so it cannot slide. This is your primary restraint.
  2. Mechanical stop. Add a small wooden cleat or an L-bracket on the room-side of the panel so a push from inside (Kibo against the screen, or a person leaning) cannot dislodge it into the gap. A second cleat at the top stops upward migration if the sash shifts. Two short screws into the wood frame, not the vinyl, are enough.
  3. Closed-cell foam tape or caulk around the perimeter. This is the air seal only — it does no structural work. Foam tape (1/4"–1/2" wide, closed-cell) is easier to reverse than caulk.

After the panel is in, re-seat the accordion panel so its edge butts up to the rigid panel, not the bare sash. The accordion should not be the only thing spanning the gap.

PRE-USE / PRE-KIBO CHECKS — DO ALL OF THESE BEFORE PLUGGING IN OR REOPENING THE DOOR

  1. Visual seal. No daylight visible around the panel edges from inside. Daylight = the seal failed and Kibo can also get a claw in.
  2. Push test (inside). Press firmly on the panel and the accordion at hand pressure (~20–30 lb). No movement, no creak, no shift. If it moves, you are not done.
  3. Sash lock re-engaged with the panel in place. Lock the sash and confirm the bolt actually passes through the unit's upper rail (not just pressing on the accordion). Try to slide the unit sideways by hand — it should not move at all.
  4. Tilt/outward-lean test. With the sash locked, push up on the unit's front edge from inside. There should be no outward rotation. The bracket carries the weight; the sash lock and the rigid panel just keep the unit from sliding forward or sideways.
  5. Cord path. Power cord exits straight down or to the side, not across the panel, not through a gap, not over a sill edge where it can be snagged. Confirm the plug is fully seated before any power-on.
  6. Screen integrity. With the unit installed, check the screen for any pre-existing bow, tear, or popped spline. If the screen is the only thing between Kibo and a 1+ inch opening, it has to be intact and seated in the frame. A determined dog will push a loose screen.
  7. Vibration check. Plug the unit in, run it on fan-only for 10 minutes. Walk away and listen for any new rattle at the panel. If the panel buzzes, add a foam-tape shim or a second cleat. Do not ignore vibration — it is the early signal that the seal or the friction fit has slipped.

STOP CONDITIONS — DO NOT PLUG IN OR REOPEN THE DOOR IF ANY OF THESE ARE TRUE

  - Daylight visible around the panel
  - Panel shifts on the push test
  - Sash lock does not positively engage the unit's rail
  - Screen is loose, torn, or bowed
  - Power cord is routed through the gap, across the panel, or within Kibo's reach from the sill
  - Any new rattle from the panel during the fan-only run
  - Spray foam was used and is less than 24 h cured

If any stop condition trips, the unit stays unplugged and the bedroom door stays closed. Fix and re-run the checks. Once all seven pass, plug the unit in, run it for a final 5-minute listen, and only then reopen the bedroom door with Kibo supervised for the first hour so you can confirm he is not pawing at the panel or the screen.

ASSESSMENT

Consistent with a normal post-exercise tissue-load response, not a re-injury signal. What points that way:

- The symptom arrived after play, not during it, and you held out the high-risk moves (cuts).
- 1/10 stiffness only, no swelling, no focal tenderness. No specific ligament re-talking to you.
- Walking and stairs are normal — gait is not protecting the joint.
- The ankle has not been loaded like this in roughly four weeks; unfamiliar volume of weight-bearing soccer is a normal first-time irritant.

What is still pending and matters:

- How the ankle feels tonight and tomorrow morning.
- Whether the stiffness returns fully to baseline or worsens.
- Whether any swelling shows up later today or overnight.

This is one step in the progression, not a green light for unrestricted play. Same posture as the calf: today's tolerance is today's result, not full clearance.

THIS EVENING

- Relative rest. Normal walking is fine; don't avoid it.
- Gentle active ROM while seated or lying — ankle circles both directions, draw the alphabet with the toes, light calf pumps. Two or three short sets, stop before pain.
- If the stiffness is annoying: ice 10-15 minutes over the front/side of the ankle, optional, not required.
- Compression sleeve if you have one and it helps.
- Elevate briefly when sitting for a while. Not strict bed-rest elevation.
- Avoid tonight: heat, deep massage, aggressive rolling, hard stretching, hopping, jogging, or any new load.
- Sleep normal. No need to change position.
- Skip NSAIDs unless you want them for comfort — don't pre-emptively take them and then misread tomorrow's stiffness.

TOMORROW MORNING CHECK (before deciding anything for Monday)

- Stiffness gone or back to baseline.
- Walking and stairs still normal, no limp.
- No new swelling, no new bruising, no focal tenderness at the outside of the ankle where the original roll was.
- Bilateral calf raises comfortable, then single-leg calf raise on the right: comfortable.
- Two-foot hop comfortable, then single-leg hop on the right: comfortable and symmetric with the left.

If any of those are off, hold the progression and reassess; do not push into Monday soccer.

NEXT-SESSION CRITERIA (before the next soccer session, including Monday if one was planned)

1. Overnight and next-day stiffness has fully returned to baseline.
2. Walking, stairs, and single-leg calf raises are painless and stable.
3. Single-leg balance 30 seconds eyes open, then eyes closed: no wobble, no pain.
4. Single-leg hop (vertical and forward) on the right ankle: painless and symmetric with the left.
5. The day before the next session, a light continuous jog 5-10 minutes off the ankle: comfortable, no after-stiffness.
6. Direction-change progression in order: lateral shuffles, then controlled ~45° cuts, then easy 90° cuts, only then full-speed cuts. Each step clean before the next.
7. Next session: same warm-up; cap at 30-35 minutes or build by only ~5 minutes if everything above is clean. Stop early on any change.
8. Bouldering is fine in the meantime if grip, wrist, and forearm are not in play. Avoid using the right foot aggressively on volumes or heel hooks if you're protecting the lateral ankle.

STOP-PICKUP / NO FURTHER LOAD — any of these means don't push through, reassess the progression

- Stiffness that is worse the next morning than it is now, or doesn't return to baseline within 24-48 hours.
- Any swelling, even mild.
- Focal tenderness anywhere on the ankle, especially the outside.
- Pain with walking or stairs.
- Any feeling of instability, giving way, or "the ankle doesn't trust me."
- Pain during single-leg calf raise or single-leg hop.
- Limp of any kind.
- Pain that lingers more than 24-48 hours after the session.

PROMPT / SAME-DAY EVALUATION

- Rapidly developing swelling or any visible deformity.
- Bruising that spreads significantly.
- Inability to bear weight for four steps walking (Ottawa ankle rule positive).
- Numbness, tingling, or color change in the foot — pale, blue, mottled.
- Severe pain at rest (>5/10) or pain that wakes you.
- Locked or stuck joint, or a sensation of something moving that shouldn't.
- Calf pain, swelling, or tenderness — separate concern, do not conflate with the ankle.
- Fever with ankle pain or swelling (only if there's any skin break).

ROUTINE EVALUATION (within a few days if not improving)

- Stiffness, swelling, or pain that persists or worsens over 3-5 days.
- Recurrent feeling of giving way.
- Pain that limits walking or stairs after a week.
- Failure to clear any of the next-session criteria above.
- Limp that does not resolve.

This is the same conservative framework as the April 22, April 25, and May 5 progression — not a diagnosis and not clearance. If it helps, I can structure today's session, this evening's plan, and tomorrow-morning's check as a written record the way we did for the calf, so the next step has a clean starting point. Just tell me how you want it logged.

stop and re-plan, not to move the AC.

If the sash or the bracket shows any movement at any point, or the
contractor's note's scope appears insufficient for what the inspection
reveals, route the finding back to building management before any
further action. Do not improvise bracket or anchor work.

The kitchen cold tap clearing in about two minutes, with no sewage smell, no visible sediment, and no management boil notice, is consistent with the normal disturbance you get after a planned shutoff — air pockets in the lines plus loosened rust or scale from the work, not a contamination signal. The bathroom hot tap's faint yellow tint after only thirty seconds is not yet alarming on its own (hot-side lines almost always need more flushing than cold, both because the water heater holds a large reservoir of pre-shutdown water and because hot-side dead legs accumulate iron and manganese sediment), but it does need continued flushing before you treat the hot side as usable.

Practical flushing order (apartment context, no outside hose bib):

  1. Remove the aerators from every faucet you'll flush. Sediment clogs aerator screens and produces misleading "still dirty" readings, and the screen can also trap the last bits of grit you want out of the lines. Put aerator parts in a bowl so the rubber washer doesn't disappear down the drain.
  2. Toilet: flush once or twice to refill the tank and clear the supply stub. You are clearing the supply line, not the bowl.
  3. Cold lines, in this order:
     a. Bathroom cold tap: open fully, run 2–3 minutes, or until water is visually clear and free of sputtering for at least 30 seconds.
     b. Kitchen cold tap: same — 2–3 minutes fully open until clear.
     c. Shower cold, if you have one: run briefly to clear the dead leg.
  4. Hot lines:
     a. Pick one hot tap (bathroom is fine), open it fully, and let it run until you get a steady stream with no air sputtering. That refills the water heater.
     b. Then run each hot tap (bathroom, kitchen, shower) until visually clear. Hot commonly takes 3–5 minutes per fixture, longer than cold is normal.
     c. If the water heater rumbles or knocks during this, that is sediment shifting; not dangerous, but it confirms hot-side flushing was needed.
  5. Clean the aerator screens, reassemble, and reinstall.

Drinking water:

  Use only the kitchen cold tap for drinking, coffee, ice, and cooking until the cold side has been continuously clear for a full minute or two at the kitchen tap. Do not drink or cook with hot tap water regardless of how it looks — water-heater anode and dissolved-metal leaching is a separate concern from the disturbance, and it is a standing rule.

  Practical handling for today:
    - After the cold flush in step 3 is done, run the kitchen cold tap for another 30–60 seconds before filling any drinking container.
    - Discard the first gallon or so after clearing — plants, toilet refills, mopping.
    - A fridge pitcher is fine for the next 24 hours. Boiling is only necessary if management posts a notice; right now they have not, and nothing in the symptoms suggests one is warranted.

Appliance return to service:

  Dishwasher:
    - Do not run it until the kitchen hot tap has run clear for at least 2–3 minutes continuously and isn't sputtering.
    - First cycle: empty, no detergent, hottest setting. This flushes the inlet valve and the internal lines.
    - After the empty cycle, check the sump area for sediment. A small amount of fine material in the filter is normal for the first cycle after a disturbance; visible flakes or a lot of grit is not.
    - Only then resume normal cycles.

  Washing machine:
    - Same prerequisite: hot and cold at the machine's supply valves run clear. If you can reach the inlet hoses, briefly disconnect each and check the small screen filters at the hose ends — sediment collects there. Clean if visibly clogged.
    - First run: empty, hot setting, no detergent. Inspect the drum and the drain filter (if yours has one) afterward.
    - Then resume normal use.

When to report to management:

  Treat any of the following as a report-and-pause signal, not a "keep flushing" signal:
    - Yellow or brown tint in the cold tap persists beyond 5–10 minutes of continuous flushing, or returns after the tap has run clear.
    - Visible sediment — flakes, grit, or particles — comes out of any tap, especially if it continues after several minutes of flushing.
    - Sewage smell or rotten-egg smell at any fixture.
    - Pressure is abnormally low (trickle) or abnormally high (pulsing, water hammer) compared to your normal.
    - Any new leak appears, particularly under sinks, around the water heater, or at toilet bases.
    - The water heater does not refill (hot tap runs indefinitely with no steady flow) or makes sustained loud noises.
    - Discoloration appears only in hot and does not clear after 10–15 minutes of hot-side flushing.

  When you do report, the useful facts to give management are: which fixtures discolored, how long each took to clear (or did not), whether you saw sediment, whether you smell anything, your cold-versus-hot distinction, and confirmation that no boil notice was posted. Those map directly to whether the issue is on the building's riser (their problem) or your apartment's interior lines (yours).

Anya's sequence is mostly right but has gaps that will let a partial publication slip through and a few places where the comparison can pass for the wrong reasons. Walking through them so the second team patches the matrix before re-running.

Hidden partial-publication risks

1. Step 5 tests drift detection on CSS only. iOS, Android, and documentation are generated but never have their drift check triggered. If drift detection is per-target (different code paths for different formats), CSS passing proves nothing about Android. Either repeat step 5 once per target, or edit the canonical token and require ALL four targets to fail — that's what consumers actually hit.

2. Step 6 only proves the schema-validation-failure case. The North Pier pilot contract is "publishing is blocked if either generator exits unsuccessfully" — broader than schema validation. Add cases for: generator exit non-zero, generator crash mid-run producing partial output, drift mismatch, and a missing target. Each one needs to produce zero publication and leave 0.8.4 intact.

3. Step 7 states 0.8.4 stays published but never TESTS it. The invariant has to be a check, not a statement. After each failure injection in step 6, explicitly assert that the published artifact still resolves to 0.8.4 (registry tag, CDN object, whatever "published" means in their pipeline). Otherwise "we don't publish on failure" is a stated rule, not a tested one.

4. Step 1 bumps schema 2→3 before step 2 pins the generator. If the old generator silently accepts schema 3 input and produces 0.8.4-shaped output for new tokens, you have a quiet downgrade path from any unpinned consumer. The schema bump and the generator bump must be atomic from the consumer's view: old generator MUST reject schema 3, not accept-and-mangle.

5. "Pin consumer and shared CI generator at 0.9.0" — what about the documentation pipeline and any local dev path? If docs are generated by a separate pipeline with its own pin, or developers run a local copy, those are unverified surfaces. Enumerate every generator entry point and pin them all explicitly. The first mismatch came from exactly this kind of gap.

Misleading-comparison risks

1. Step 4's "20x byte stability" proves determinism, not correctness. A deterministically wrong output is stable across 20 runs and still wrong. The semantic fixture comparison covers it — but only for targets that HAVE semantic fixtures. Documentation is the target most likely to lack one because docs are usually free-form. Confirm explicitly.

2. Comparing 0.9.0 output to 0.8.4 fixtures after a schema bump is expected to produce SOME legitimate diffs. Without a known-good diff baseline, "passes the fixture comparison" can mean "correct" OR "matches a stale 0.8.4 view of the world." Decide which fixtures are pinned to 0.8.4 (must NOT match 0.9.0 — that's the upgrade proof) vs which are 0.9.0 expected output (must match exactly). Mixing the two in one check is the misleading case.

3. Step 5's "edit one generated CSS variable" tests the drift check from the wrong side. If the system compares generated output to committed fixtures, an uncommitted edit to a generated file may not be visible to the drift check at all. Edit the canonical source — the token in the machine-readable package — and let generation run normally. That's the path consumers actually exercise.

4. "Complete matrix passes" in step 7 is a goal, not a check. Spell out the matrix: targets × checks. At minimum, 4 targets × {schema validity, semantic fixture match, byte stability, drift-on-tamper, fail-closed behavior} = 20 cells, each with an explicit pass/fail signal. Without enumeration, "passes" can quietly drop a cell and nobody notices.

Suggested additions to make the sequence a real gate

- Make the matrix explicit and check every cell. Drift-on-tamper and fail-closed need per-target coverage, not CSS-only.
- Test the fail-closed invariant for at least four failure modes: schema invalid, generator exit non-zero, partial output, drift mismatch. Each must leave 0.8.4 verifiable.
- Move the schema bump to be atomic with the generator pin, OR ensure the old generator hard-rejects schema 3.
- Enumerate and pin every generator entry point (consumer, shared CI, docs pipeline, local dev), not just two.
- Separate the fixtures: legacy-pinned (must NOT match 0.9.0 — proves the upgrade actually changed something) from 0.9.0-expected (must match exactly — proves correctness). Don't mix.
- Edit the canonical source for the drift test, not the generated output.

If those land before the second team reruns, the sequence stops being a partial gate. Without them, it's likely to reproduce the original mismatch shape — just from a different direction.

        defer global.release()

    Global-first with leak fixed (keep only if global-first is load-bearing for a
    reason that isn't visible here, e.g. fairness between workers on the same pod):

        if err := global.acquire(ctx); err != nil {
            return backpressure(err)
        }
        defer global.release()

        if err := tenant.acquire(ctx); err != nil {
            return backpressure(err)
        }
        defer tenant.release()

    Either way: do not advertise Retry-After on a client cancel. Verify what canceled()
    actually emits today -- if it falls into the 429 path when ctx.Err() ==
    context.Canceled, fix that too. A canceled client is not coming back; Retry-After
    on a 499 is wrong.

Allocation-before-limit

    The loop allocates the chunk into output, THEN checks the limit:

        output = append(output, chunk...)
        decompressed += len(chunk)
        if decompressed > bodyLimit { return bodyTooLarge() }

    Two problems.

    (a) The overshoot bytes are resident in output before the check fires. The
        reject path holds up to one chunk of over-limit data. The chunk size is
        bounded by the decoder's internal buffer, not by bodyLimit. Against a
        gzip bomb that yields a single 4 MiB chunk on top of a 10 MiB body limit,
        you have 14 MiB resident before you return.

    (b) The decoder is never asked to stop. Its internal buffer drains the request
        body until the gzip reader is closed.

    Check before append:

        for chunk := range decoder {
            if decompressed + len(chunk) > bodyLimit {
                return bodyTooLarge()
            }
            output = append(output, chunk...)
            decompressed += len(chunk)
        }

    Belt-and-suspenders: on the reject path, call decoder.Close() (or equivalent)
    so the gzip reader's state is reset and the underlying request body is
    released for connection reuse.

Cancellation

    Three cases, all must release both permits (or zero, if acquired zero).

    - client cancels while waiting on tenant.acquire: with the fix above, no permits
      held; return 499 / close conn. No Retry-After.
    - client cancels mid-stream: drain-and-close the decoder, release both permits,
      return 499 / close conn.
    - server cancels (deadline, shutdown): same permit release; status is 503 or 504
      depending on cause. Do NOT emit Retry-After on server cancellation -- it would
      invite retries into a draining instance.

    The randomized 1-3s Retry-After stays for backpressure only (global or tenant
    pool full on a live request). Confirm the existing handler actually scopes the
    header that way; this PR shouldn't widen it.

Minimum regression tests (table-driven; one case per behavior)

    - cancel_during_tenant_acquire_releases_global: cancel ctx while tenant pool is
      saturated; assert global in-use count returns to baseline.
    - cancel_during_global_acquire_releases_nothing: cancel before global is taken;
      assert no permits held.
    - permit_order_is_tenant_then_global: instrument both semaphores; assert the
      acquire counter increments tenant→global, never global→tenant.
    - body_limit_exact_boundary: decompressed == bodyLimit succeeds; output.Len() == bodyLimit.
    - body_limit_one_byte_over: decompressed == bodyLimit+1 returns bodyTooLarge
      AND output.Len() stays <= bodyLimit (proves the check is pre-append).
    - single_chunk_overshoot_does_not_allocate_overshoot: feed one chunk that would
      exceed the limit; assert output is not extended past bodyLimit and no bodyTooLarge
      work is done after the check.
    - body_under_limit_succeeds: ordinary happy path.
    - retry_after_in_range_on_backpressure: pool full, 429 returned, Retry-After in
      [1.0, 3.0]s, randomized across many iterations.
    - retry_after_absent_on_client_cancel: ctx canceled by client; assert no
      Retry-After header.
    - retry_after_absent_on_server_cancel: deadline exceeded; assert no Retry-After.
    - decoder_closed_on_overflow: bodyTooLarge return path; assert decoder.Close()
      was called (mock the decoder or expose a flag).
    - invariant_soak: 10k iterations alternating full/empty pools; at quiescence,
      global in-use == 0 AND tenant in-use == 0 for every tenant.

    Plus the existing positive test that decompressed bodies under the limit still
    pass through unchanged -- this is the regression boundary for the bug class.

Net for the PR

    Block on: ordering fix, leak fix on cancellation, pre-append limit check,
    decoder-close-on-overflow, and the test set above. Randomized Retry-After
    behavior for overflow is preserved by the test suite, not by the code change;
    confirm the handler still emits it on the backpressure path before merging.
