For the left ring-finger skin flap:

1. CLEANING
  - You've already done the main thing — clean running water and gentle soap is enough.
  - Don't put hydrogen peroxide, rubbing alcohol, or undiluted iodine directly on the wound; they damage exposed tissue and slow healing.
  - If chalk dust or grit is still embedded, hold the finger under a slow trickle of water for a minute or two. Gentle irrigation, not scrubbing.
  - Pat dry with clean gauze or a paper towel. Don't rub the flap.

2. TRIM OR PRESERVE
  - Preserve it. A partially attached skin flap is your own biological dressing; it usually re-adheres, or at minimum protects the wound bed while new skin grows under it.
  - Do NOT cut it off yourself. Self-trim risks: turning a partial-thickness injury into a full-thickness wound, re-bleeding, infection.
  - A clinician may trim it later only if it turns clearly black/leathery and non-viable, or keeps folding back and contaminating the wound. Both are in-person decisions.

3. COVERING FOR THE EVENING
  - Thin layer of plain petroleum jelly (Vaseline) over the wound and flap — keeps it moist, which heals faster and with less scarring. A plain antibiotic ointment (bacitracin) is fine if you have it; either works.
  - Non-stick pad (Telfa-style) over that, so the dressing doesn't peel the flap off when you change it.
  - Soft gauze or self-adherent wrap (Coban) to hold the pad in place. Avoid a regular adhesive bandage stuck directly to the flap — it can lift the flap when removed.
  - Elevate the hand on a cushion while sitting or lying down to reduce throbbing.
  - For showering: waterproof cover (a finger cot, or cling wrap + tape at the base). Don't soak it.
  - Change the dressing once if it soaks through; otherwise leave it until tomorrow.

4. ACTIVITY LIMITS
  - No climbing or gripping/pulling with the left hand until the flap is clearly adherent and the wound is closed — typically about a week for this kind of injury, longer if still raw.
  - No submerging the finger (swimming, dish-soaking, hot-tub).
  - Normal daily use (typing, eating, light object handling) is fine; just avoid anything that snags the flap — pockets, gloves, rough towel drying.
  - Don't test the flap by pulling on it.

5. WHEN TO GET CARE

  Urgent (ER or urgent care tonight):
  - Bleeding that doesn't stop with 10–15 minutes of firm direct pressure.
  - Any loss of finger movement — can't fully bend or straighten at a joint, or feels "caught" — suggests tendon involvement.
  - Numbness, tingling, or color change (pale, blue, cold) in the fingertip — vascular or nerve concern.
  - Visible deep tissue (bone, tendon, fat) or a wound that gapes and won't close with gentle pressure.
  - Heavy contamination you can't clean (grease, animal bite, deep grit).
  - Rapidly spreading redness, red streaking up the finger or hand, fever, or pus — infection that's moving needs same-day treatment.

  Routine (clinician in the next 1–3 days):
  - Flap turns dusky/black or clearly dead.
  - Increasing pain, swelling, warmth, or pus after 24–48 hours.
  - Flap repeatedly flips back and won't stay in position.
  - You don't remember your last tetanus shot — climbing-gym chalk/dust counts as dirty enough that a booster may be indicated if it's been more than ~5 years (or more than 10 for a clean wound). A pharmacist or urgent-care clinician can sort that out quickly.
  - Wound not visibly improving after a week.

Pattern reminder: skin-flap injuries look dramatic on day one and usually settle with the right dressing. The two ways they go wrong are (a) the flap gets snagged and torn off, and (b) infection from moisture trapped under a too-thick dressing. So: petroleum jelly thin, non-stick pad on top, clean and dry on the outside, and don't pick at it.

WARM COUSCOUS BOWL WITH SPICED CHICKPEAS, PEAS, AND LEMON-YOGURT SAUCE
Serves 2. About 30 min active. Holds 10 min easily.

THE IDEA
  Warm couscous base, one-skillet chickpea + tomato + pea sauté,
  cold lemon-yogurt sauce on top, cucumber served raw on the side
  for crunch. The warm/cold contrast is the whole point.

TIMELINE (start ~30 min before she arrives)

  T-30  Put 1.5 cups water in a small pot on high. Get out:
          - a wide heatproof bowl (for couscous)
          - a skillet
          - a small bowl (for sauce)

  T-29  Make the sauce: ~1/2 cup yogurt, squeeze of half a lemon,
        pinch of salt. Stir with a fork. Cover; leave on counter.

  T-27  Drain chickpeas; pat briefly with a paper towel so they
        don't sputter. Halve cherry tomatoes if easy one-handed;
        otherwise leave whole — they'll soften and burst either way.

  T-25  Water should be boiling. Into the heatproof bowl: ~1 cup
        dried couscous, pinch of salt, small drizzle of olive oil.
        Pour boiling water over (about 1/2 inch above the couscous).
        Cover the bowl with a plate. Do not touch for 5 minutes.

  T-24  Skillet: 2 tbsp olive oil over medium. Add chickpeas in a
        single layer with 1 tsp cumin and 1/2 tsp smoked paprika
        (or any warm spice — black pepper alone is fine). Stir
        occasionally. Press a few chickpeas against the pan with
        the back of a spoon to break them up — that's where the
        creaminess comes from.

  T-15  Add cherry tomatoes and a generous handful of frozen peas
        straight from the bag. Stir gently 2-3 min, just until peas
        turn bright green and tomatoes start to wrinkle. Kill heat,
        cover the skillet.

  T-10  Uncover couscous. Fluff with a fork — should be tender and
        separate. Stir in a handful of torn parsley and a small
        squeeze of lemon. Cover loosely with a clean kitchen towel.

  T-0   Assemble (about 1 minute):
          - Couscous into two bowls.
          - Spoon chickpea mixture over.
          - Dollops of yogurt sauce, crumbled feta, more parsley,
            lemon wedge on top.
          - Cucumber slices on the side, raw, cold.

HOLDING IF SHE'S DELAYED (up to 10 min)
  - Skillet: lowest possible heat, lid on. Stir once.
  - Couscous: keep covered with the towel. If it tightens up,
    fluff again with a fork and toss in a teaspoon of warm water.
  - Yogurt sauce and cucumber: fine at room temp.
  - Do not pre-plate. Assemble fresh when she walks in.

ONE-HANDED NOTES
  - Couscous is the win: pour, cover, walk away.
  - Skip halving tomatoes — leaving them whole is faster and
    they collapse nicely in the pan.
  - Feta crumbles between your right-hand fingers; no knife.
  - Roll the lemon on the counter before cutting — easier squeeze.
  - Tear parsley; don't chop.
  - Use a fork to smash chickpeas in the pan.

PORTION SENSE
  Light, not heavy. If she's hungry when she gets in, the cucumber
  on the side means she can eat more of that; the bowl itself
  won't weigh her down. Leftover couscous keeps covered at room
  temp for an hour or in the fridge tomorrow.

Bottom line: reasonable to play, but only if the dressing is right and you're willing to come off the moment a stop condition fires. Day 2 with the wound dry, closed, minimally tender, no infection signs, and normal sensation is normal healing. Not playing keeper removes most repetitive ball-on-hand impact; the residual risks are a fall onto the hand, a bracing hand-plant, dirt/sweat under the dressing, and incidental ball contact (throw-ins, deflections).

COVER WITHOUT CONSTRICTING
- Use a flexible non-adherent island dressing: small non-stick pad (Telfa-style) over the wound, then a loose self-adherent wrap or a hydrocolloid patch trimmed just larger than the wound.
- Tension is the whole game. Wrap snug enough that the pad won't slip, loose enough that you can easily slide a finger under the wrap. If you use a fingertip bandage, anchor it with short strips of paper or thin fabric tape running lengthwise along the finger; never a tight circumferential ring of tape or wrap.
- Skip elastic bandages wrapped under tension and skip "extra secure" taping — tourniquet effect on a finger shows up fast and is the real danger here, not the wound itself.

SANITY CHECKS BEFORE YOU KICK OFF
  - Color pink, not blue/white/dusky
  - Capillary refill at the fingertip under 2 seconds
  - No numbness, tingling, or coolness
  - Full finger flexion; you can still make a fist without the dressing biting
  - Pad hasn't shifted and isn't pressing the flap

DURING PLAY — STOP / COME OFF IMMEDIATELY IF
  - Dressing becomes soaked with fresh blood, or wound reopens / flap lifts
  - Pain at the wound rises above the current "minimally tender" baseline
  - Finger swells, turns blue/white/dusky, goes cold, numb, or tingly — dressing is too tight, rip it off
  - Loss of normal finger motion
  - Dressing gets soaked with sweat or dirt and you can't swap it
  - Anything just feels wrong — your call, not something to push through

POST-SESSION (within ~30 min of stopping)
  - Remove dressing, gently clean with mild soap and water, pat dry
  - Re-dress with a clean non-adherent pad and loose wrap
  - Recheck the sanity-check list above

WATCH OVER THE NEXT 24 HOURS FOR
  - Expanding redness, warmth, swelling, drainage, throbbing pain, red streaking → infection, treat as a fresh problem and seek routine in-person care
  - Flap darkening, dying back, or separating → routine evaluation
  - Anything that doesn't progress over the next several days

ED / URGENT IF
  - Rapidly spreading redness or streaking, or fever with wound symptoms
  - Sudden severe pain, color change, or loss of circulation in the finger

Optional but helpful: a thin glove (cycling or weightlifting glove) over the dressing if you expect to put a hand down on a fall. Not required, just reduces abrasion.

One session of non-keeper pickup today is reasonable if the dressing passes the pre-play checks. The single rule that matters most: if the finger changes color, goes numb/tingly/cold, or the dressing tightens up, the dressing is the problem — pull it and you're done for the day.

The event cannot be emitted externally with `provenance_status: partial`. Product Engineering's proposal conflicts with the preview contract on three independent grounds, and the "commit is verified" argument does not repair any of them.

Why "partial" fails the contract:

  - The contract defines deploy movement as provenance-backed. Provenance is the chain that ties the external event back to the deploy system. `pipeline_run_id` is precisely that tie. Its absence breaks the chain at the link that the contract treats as load-bearing; the rest of the payload does not substitute for it.

  - A known commit is not a verified deploy. The commit can be verified independently of any deploy having happened, so it does not close the gap between "a commit exists" and "this service was deployed at this time." That gap is exactly what provenance exists to close for an external viewer.

  - `provenance_status: partial` is not in the external contract vocabulary. Surfacing it would either invent a new external field or expose internal integrity state through the contract surface. The contract already excludes raw pipeline job identifiers, internal actor IDs, chat links, and customer-internal URLs; a "partial" tag belongs to the same excluded class, even though it is a status rather than an identifier.

  - The incident-load precedent already established the rule for this case: when a permitted source cannot produce a value, the external render is explicit `unknown` with no value timestamp and a separately labeled source-poll timestamp. Deploy movement is the same kind of permitted-source signal and must follow the same fail-closed pattern; "render with reduced confidence" is not a third option the contract allows.

Fail-closed external representation when deploy provenance is incomplete:

  - The event does not render as a deploy event externally. The deploy-movement slot is the same empty/unknown state as a permitted-but-absent read: no `deployed_at`, no commit, no repository, no service-as-deploy pairing in a deploy-shaped position. Adjacent verified deploys render normally; the empty state is scoped to the partial-provenance event and does not extend to silence verified neighbors.

  - The customer-visible card copy is the same empty-state copy already used for the absent case (e.g., "No recent deploy movement"), scoped to what Lantern can verify, not a claim that no deploy occurred globally. This is the same empty-state rule Iris and you already agreed to for the no-permitted-source case.

  - A separately labeled observation-attempt timestamp may be shown under a distinct field name (e.g., `source_last_polled_at`), but it must never appear in a deploy-shaped position and must never be conflatable with a customer-visible `deployed_at`.

  - `provenance_status: partial` must not appear in the external payload under any field name.

  - `pipeline_run_id` must not appear in the external payload. This is already contract-excluded; the partial-provenance case is the moment to reassert the rule, because the temptation to "leak the field as null to explain the gap" is the same anti-pattern as exposing it as a value.

  - Internally, the partial-provenance event is a provenance-verifier failure. It must be logged/tagged for Product Engineering to fix at source (the deploy feed must be made to emit `pipeline_run_id`); the external code path never sees it.

Tests required (each test fails if the rule above is violated):

  1. Negative render: a fixture with `pipeline_run_id=null` produces no deploy-shaped record in the external payload; the deploy-movement slot renders the empty/unknown state.

  2. Schema allowlist: the external serializer rejects `provenance_status: partial` and `pipeline_run_id` even when the internal payload includes them. The allowlist test must enumerate both fields explicitly; absence-by-omission is not sufficient because the failure mode here is "PE adds a field that looks like a status and we accept it."

  3. Timestamp labeling: `source_last_polled_at` renders under its own field name and never in any position a viewer could read as a deploy timestamp. A grep-level test that fails on any customer-visible field carrying a poll timestamp is appropriate.

  4. Uniformity across viewers: every viewer (authorized internal previewers included) sees the same fail-closed render for a partial-provenance deploy. No previewer sees a "partial" render; the preview audience is not a justification for weaker representation.

  5. No-inference across adjacency: a partial-provenance event does not combine with adjacent verified deploys to imply continuity. The card treats the deploy as absent; the gap is visible, not papered over by neighbors.

  6. Cache behavior: a fail-closed render is not cached as a deploy render. A later source-poll that resolves provenance must invalidate the cache and re-render normally with no residual `partial` state in any replayed payload.

  7. Failure injection on the source feed: exercise the feed with (a) `pipeline_run_id` omitted, (b) `pipeline_run_id` null, (c) `pipeline_run_id` present but mismatched against the commit, (d) commit omitted. All four must produce the same fail-closed external render. This blocks "we forgot to test the null-vs-omitted distinction" and "we accept pipeline_run_id if commit matches even when the deploy-system anchor is missing."

  8. Verifier-gate test: the internal provenance verifier rejects partial-provenance deploys before they reach the external serializer. The fail-closed state is the verifier's output, not a downstream filter. If the verifier ever lets a partial-provenance event through, the test fails even if the serializer would have rendered it correctly.

  9. Internal escalation: a partial-provenance deploy produces an internal alert/log entry tagged for Product Engineering investigation of the missing `pipeline_run_id`, on a code path distinct from any external-render path. The test asserts both that the alert exists and that it is not surfaced through any externally observable channel.

  10. Re-run on resolution: once `pipeline_run_id` is supplied and verified, the previously suppressed slot resolves to a normal deploy event. The test asserts no residual `partial` field, no stale empty-state copy, and no cache hit returning the prior fail-closed render.

Two scope notes:

  - This decision is about the contract and the fixture. It does not authorize or schedule the corrected event's emission; once `pipeline_run_id` is supplied and the failure-injection matrix passes, the fixture can be re-run, but external rollout remains a separate gate owned by Iris on the product side and by the deploy-system owner on the source side. No customer access is requested or granted by this decision.

  - The proposed fixture's review note ("the commit is verified, so emit the deploy and disclose that provenance is partial") is the exact anti-pattern this contract exists to prevent. The fix is not "disclose more honestly" — the fix is to not surface an externally meaningful deploy event whose provenance chain is broken at the load-bearing link.

The team's proposal does undermine canonical identity, in three concrete ways:

  - Two names in the canonical source that resolve to the same concept
    violates single source of truth. If Surface.Muted and surface.muted
    are the same token, one is duplicate. If they are genuinely
    different concepts, their names must be distinguishable at the
    canonical layer, not by a consumer workaround.

  - An Android-only suffix creates a platform-only identity exception.
    The pilot's invariant is one canonical name -> one stable platform
    identifier per generator. A per-platform suffix breaks that for
    this case, and any future collision (iOS, Web, etc.) would need
    its own ad-hoc suffix.

  - The fix is at the wrong layer. The Android generator is doing
    what generators do. The bug is that the canonical schema allows
    two names that collide under any generator's normalization.
    Patching the consumer hides the bug from the schema, where it
    belongs.

  Hidden consequence the proposal probably has not been measured
  against: the drift detector assumes a canonical name maps to a
  stable platform identifier. With an Android-only suffix, "same
  canonical name" no longer means "same identifier across platforms"
  for this case, which either creates a hole in drift detection or a
  false alarm.

PIPELINE OBSERVATION

  The validation correctly fired and the pipeline correctly published
  nothing. Fail-closed held. That is the pilot doing its job.

  The gap is that the collision appears to surface at Android
  generation rather than at canonical schema validation before any
  generator runs. The right place for the check is upstream of all
  generators.

RECOMMENDED RULE

  Canonical names must be unique under strictest normalization, where
  strictest = case-insensitive AND separator-stripped (., _, -, space,
  any other separator a generator might collapse). The canonical
  schema enforces this invariant. Any violation fails schema
  validation BEFORE any generator runs, and blocks publication of all
  platforms uniformly.

  Consequences:
    - Pre-generation validation. Fail-closed preserved: any collision
      blocks the whole publish, not just one platform.
    - No per-platform identity escapes. If a generator cannot
      distinguish two canonical names, the bug is in the canonical
      names, not the generator.
    - Drift detection remains correct by construction: canonical
      name == platform identifier on every platform.
    - The rule applies to additions and renames; preflight cardinality
      remains additive, not a substitute.

THIS INCIDENT

  1. Owner review. Anya's design team decides whether Surface.Muted
     and surface.muted are the same concept. Given the history
     (Figma -> JSON drift, which is precisely the class of issue
     this pilot exists to catch), my prior is duplicate, not
     distinct. Treat that as a working assumption pending
     Anya's call, not a fact.
  2. If duplicate: remove one in the canonical source.
  3. If distinct: rename one so the two names diverge under the
     strictest-normalization rule (e.g., add an unambiguous token
     concept to one name, not a per-platform suffix). The new name

  4. Re-run canonical schema validation, then full four-platform
     generation. Publish only on a clean pass.
  5. Do not merge with the Android-suffix workaround applied. That
     path is closed.

PILOT IMPLICATIONS

    - This incident is a pilot success, not a pilot failure: the

    - Open enhancement: add the strictest-normalization uniqueness

  Bottom line: keep canonical identity canonical. Make the schema

Short answer: yes, a short easy session is reasonable as a tolerance test, not as clearance. The wound is epithelialized (closed, dry, pink, no symptoms under grip load) and one week is in the typical window for a skin-flap injury to handle low-stress contact. What you're testing today is whether newly formed epithelium tolerates climbing-specific friction and pressure without splitting open. Climbing that doesn't reopen the skin today earns you the next step; climbing that does set you back several days. Treat today's session the way you treated the calf re-entry in late December — stop while it still feels boring.

Taping without constriction

Goal: a low-friction, slightly cushioned patch over the healed area that does not act as a tourniquet. Avoid circumferential tape around the finger.

Steps:
1. Wash and dry the area. Apply a thin layer of petroleum jelly or, ideally, a small piece of hydrocolloid (duoderm-type) cut to cover the healed spot with about 5 mm of border around it. Hydrocolloid gives a moist, low-shear surface and stays in place better than jelly alone. If you don't have hydrocolloid, a thin non-adherent pad (Telfa) with a smear of petroleum jelly works.
2. Do not wrap athletic tape around the finger as a ring. Instead, lay a single short strip of tape (leukotape, rigid athletic tape, or even a fabric "ouchless" strip) as a bridge: one anchor on the back of the hand near the base of the ring finger, crossing over the palm-side patch, and the other anchor on the back of the hand on the other side, or onto the adjacent middle-finger side. The patch stays put because it's anchored across the joint, not because it's tightened around the digit.
3. Capillary refill check before you leave the house: press the fingertip pad until it blanches, release, color should return within 2 seconds. Repeat after the first climb and again every 15–20 minutes.
4. The tape job should feel like it's there, not like it's squeezing. If you can feel your pulse under the patch, that's fine. If the finger tip feels cool, tingly, or numb, the dressing is too tight — remove and redo.

Progression

Today only: jugs, big edges, slopers only if they're large and clean (slopers require friction; avoid pinch holds and any small crimps). Low angles, no overhangs, no dynos, no jump-down finishes — downclimb everything. Two to four easy problems, tops only if they feel genuinely easy. Total time on the wall 15–25 minutes. If at any point you forget about the finger, that's a good sign; if you start thinking about it, that's a stop cue.

Next session (only if today produced no symptoms and the area still looks identical 24 hours later — same color, no crack, no fresh pinkness, no tenderness on pinch): add gentle slab and one grade easier than your usual max, still no aggressive crimps or pinches, still downclimbing.

Following session (only if the previous one also stayed clean): you can try a controlled easy crimp and a pinch, but stop the moment any sensation localizes to the healed spot. This is where "tolerated" must not be confused with "healed for hard climbing."

New epithelium keeps remodeling for weeks. Reopening risk drops sharply after about 2–3 weeks and meaningfully again after 4–6 weeks, but it's not zero today.

What ends the session, in priority order

Stop immediately — and don't try to push through any of these — if you notice any of:

- Any sensation at the healed spot during a move or immediately after releasing a hold: stinging, burning, sharp twinge, tenderness on the next grip. Reopening almost always announces itself this way before you can see anything.
- The tape sliding, peeling, or wetting through. Once the patch migrates, the new skin takes direct friction and you're back to square one.
- Any visible change at the site: a fine crack, a lifted edge, fresh red bleeding through the patch, wetness, or a bead of fluid. Don't unwrap and "check" mid-session — that itself can shear new skin; just stop.
- Color change in the whole finger: bluish, pale, or mottled. That's a constriction problem from the tape, separate from the wound, and means redo or stop.
- Swelling, throbbing, or stiffness developing in the finger or hand.
- The finger feeling weaker or "off" in a way that makes you grip differently. Compensatory grip patterns load other tendons and are how a finger skin issue turns into a forearm strain.
- Hand washing between burns revealing any new pinkness, crack, or tenderness.
- Hitting the time limit. Boring stop, not "one more" stop.

After the session

Remove the tape carefully — don't rip it across the patch. Wash with mild soap and water, pat dry, apply a thin layer of petroleum jelly. Don't put another tight dressing on; the area wants air and gentle moisture overnight. Look at it again before bed and again tomorrow morning.

Reasonable 24-hour outcome: looks identical to how it looked this morning — closed, dry, pink, no tenderness when you pinch it or make a fist. Same color, same texture, no new crack. If anything is different, you have your answer and the next session waits.

One last framing, consistent with how you've handled prior returns: today's session is a contact-tolerance test, not a clearance. The bar is "did not reopen and produced no symptoms." If that's met, you've earned the next rung. If it isn't, you've learned something useful and you stop.

Decision: explicit unknown, not stale:true.

Why, briefly: the owner-map pipeline defines freshness at 24 hours; a 30-hour-old record is not a permitted source by the pipeline's own contract. A `stale: true` flag still attaches the once-valid owner to the current view, which Iris has confirmed the product must not do. The same rule you settled for incident-load applies here — when the permitted source cannot produce a current value, the field is literal `unknown`, not a softened record. Owner staleness is permitted-source exhaustion, not partial success.

The revised fixture must treat the 30-hour-old record as if the source returned nothing, not as a stale-but-valid record. It must verify the rejection path, not a demotion path.

Authorization constraints the fixture must test
- Tenant authorization precedes any lookup or serialization. Authenticated request-scope derivation of tenant_id; no header trust.
- Cache key partitions by (tenant_id, subject_id, resource_id, action, policy_generation). A permitted-but-stale entry must never satisfy a fresh read; the freshness check is the gate, not a post-load decoration.
- 403 not_authorized envelope is uniform for unauthorized callers and reveals no field — not the owner, not provenance, not source_ref, not the room, not internal identifiers.
- The stale-rejection path is distinct from the denial path: stale-permitted-source exhaustion returns the owner field as `unknown` to authorized viewers; authorization failure returns 403. The fixture must keep both paths separate and assert timing parity between fresh rejection and stale rejection.
- Cross-tenant cache reuse and poisoning still negative. No external read on denial. Pseudonymized logs only.

Provenance constraints the fixture must test
- The 24-hour freshness check is enforced at the source boundary. A record with source_observed_at older than the limit is excluded before any rendering decision, so no `stale: true` label, no owner name, no source_ref ever reaches the response surface.
- The rejected record's audit-note source_ref is not carried into the response. The Roman importer fix that preserves source_ref applies only to records that pass freshness — the fixture must verify that preservation does not accidentally promote a stale record.
- The provenance field renders the rejection as a bounded empty state that identifies the absence of provenance-backed ownership in Lantern sources, not "owner known but stale". Wording must distinguish absence-of-source from "no owner exists".
- source_observed_at semantics preserved on the unknown path: when the owner field is unknown, it carries no value timestamp. Any timestamp attached to the response is a separately labeled observation-attempt timestamp and must not read as evidence that the missing owner is current.
- Field allowlist on the unknown response: owner = literal `unknown` (string), plus the bounded provenance label. No source_ref, no owner-map record ID, no audit-note ID, no room name, no deploy URL, no team identifier.

Fallback constraints the fixture must test (no-inference rules)
- Must not infer ownership from human-guessable context: team area, on-call rotation, recent activity, git blame, alert routing, or any signal other than the permitted source itself.
- Must not fall back to internal room metadata: room name, room identifier, deploy URL, room creation metadata, prior-room owner memory, or anything outside the owner-map permitted source.
- Must not return the previously-known owner with a freshness decoration. No `stale: true`, no `last_known`, no `as_of` owner attachment.
- Must not attempt a manual UI override path; that is explicitly out of scope and must not appear in the fixture.
- The empty state must be reachable: every fallback attempt must produce the same bounded unknown response with the same provenance wording.

Specific fixture assertions (positive and negative)
- Negative: response.owner is the literal string `unknown`. Not an object. Not a name with `stale: true`. Not the cached owner. Not a placeholder drawn from room metadata.
- Negative: response contains no source_ref, no audit-note ID, no owner-map record ID, no room name, no deploy URL, no team or service identifier beyond what the allowlist permits.
- Negative: response.provenance does not contain a softened owner record, a freshness flag, or a "previously known as" string.
- Positive: response.provenance uses bounded empty-state wording that identifies absence of provenance-backed ownership in Lantern sources.
- Positive: if any timestamp is attached, it is labeled as the observation-attempt timestamp and is not positioned as the owner field's value timestamp.
- Positive: authorized caller receives the unknown response; unauthorized caller receives 403 with no fields.
- Positive: cache key for the rejected read is still partitioned correctly and does not bleed into a fresh read of the same record.

Scope reminders to keep in the fixture
- Guarded internal fixture. No customer access. No external rollout authorized. This is a contract-interpretation exercise, not a go-live.
- Iris owns ordinary Lantern admission and product wording. The fixture tests her confirmed position; it does not redefine it.
- Implementation owners retain execution. The fixture asserts behavior; it does not authorize a code change beyond what the rejection path requires.

If a reviewer wants to relax this to `stale: true`, the fixture must reject that change for the same reason it rejects any other inference: the pipeline's own freshness limit already classifies the record as not a permitted source, and the contract says permitted-but-absent renders as `unknown`. Adding `stale: true` would convert a permitted-source exhaustion into an inferred-ownership display, which the contract does not permit.

PARITY RISKS

  - `deployment.environment` is OTLP-derived. Producers may set the resource attribute with different casing, whitespace, or a sibling name (`service.environment`, `env`, `stage`). "Copy unchanged" only works if every producer agrees on a single source attribute and every consumer agrees on the same label name. Today, nothing in the proposal pins that.
  - Dot-notation is a label-name choice. Downstream services commonly flatten `deployment.environment` to `deployment_environment` or hoist it to `env`. Producer emits one shape, consumer selects another, and the join silently misses. This is a value-shape crossing even though the label is "additive."
  - Absent behavior is unspecified. One producer that sets the attribute and another that does not produce inconsistent series on the same metric. Dashboards and rollups aggregate across both; one side silently drops.
  - Cross-service propagation is implied but not declared. If `deployment.environment` reaches selection, grouping, joining, persistence, alerts, or rollups in shard-keeper / rollup-service / dashboards, the additive label crosses the producer-consumer boundary the Cardinality Guardrails rule was written to cover.

CARDINALITY RISKS

  - "Observed values: prod, staging, dev" is a sample of today's traffic, not a bound. There is no allowlist, no normalization, and no documented control over which values the OTLP SDK will accept. Tomorrow's "perf", "qa", "staging-eu", "dev-alice" lands with no review.
  - OTLP resource attributes are routinely set from deployment manifests, CI labels, or environment variables that are easy to widen. Even one expanded value can multiply distinct series across every metric carrying the label. With three values × existing per-series cardinality, the multiplicative growth is real even at the "small" sample.
  - Tenant-level distinct-value budget is missing. If any producer derives `deployment.environment` from a tenant/user/request field (common in shared-cluster deploys), the sample size is unrelated to the post-rollout distinct count. The proposal does not foreclose this.
  - Cardinality preflight on the current sample is necessary but not sufficient. It does not bound the value set; it only describes today's snapshot.

ACCEPTANCE RULE

  The change is acceptable iff all ten conditions hold. Each must be executable, not narrative. The parity fixture is the production-review gate; cardinality preflight, normalization, allowlist, absent/malformed handling, and owner signoff are additive requirements, not substitutes.

  1. Normalization. The producer normalizes the value to a single canonical form (lowercase, trimmed, no whitespace, single canonical token, length cap, ASCII only) before the label is emitted. The consumer expects and selects on the same canonical form. No alias, no re-canonicalization on the consumer side.

  2. Bounded values (closed allowlist). The only permitted values are the explicit set in the PR description: `prod`, `staging`, `dev`. Any input outside this set is mapped to a single sentinel (`unknown` or `other` — pick one, document it) and emits a counter of rejected values. Adding a value to the allowlist requires a schema/contract change with owner signoff, not a code edit.

  3. Absent input. When the OTLP resource attribute is absent, the label is either omitted entirely or set to literal `unknown`. The choice is documented, identical on producer and consumer, and not silently mixed across metrics.

  4. Malformed input. Non-string, empty string, value exceeding the length cap, or value containing characters outside the canonical form is treated identically to absent (per condition 3). No series created from malformed input. No panic, no drop of the parent series.

  5. Tenant-level distinct-value budget. Each tenant/user/request may contribute at most the size of the allowlist distinct values per metric over the preflight window. Exceeding the budget is a rollback-discussion trigger, not a silent expansion. The proposal's "sampled traffic" is not a budget.

  6. Executable producer-consumer test (parity fixture — required). A runnable fixture starts the producer and the consumer services together with controlled OTLP input. It must positively assert that for each allowlisted value, the producer emits `deployment.environment=<canonical>` and the consumer selects, groups, joins, persists, and rollups on the same label name with the same canonical value. It must negatively assert that absent input produces identical behavior on both sides, malformed input is rejected consistently, the closed allowlist is enforced, no alias or sibling label is selected, and no producer-derived-only path appears in consumer output. The fixture fails the gate if any positive or negative assertion fails.

  7. Cardinality preflight (additive, not substitute). Run on a representative traffic sample. The preflight reports per-metric distinct-value counts for the new label and the resulting multiplicative growth across existing series. The numbers must fit within the agreed Cardinality Guardrails budget for the affected metrics pipeline. A green preflight does not satisfy conditions 1–6 or 8–10.

  8. Alert-source classification. Confirm in writing whether `deployment.environment` is a live-path signal (alert source) or validation-only. Producers and consumers must agree. If alert-source, the runbook entry must reflect the new label's alerting semantics before production review.

  9. Mapped owner signoff. The producer-side owner and each affected consumer-side owner (shard-keeper, rollup-service, and any dashboard/alerting owner that selects on the new label) must each individually run the parity fixture from condition 6 against their own service and record sign-off before production review. Cardinality preflight sign-off and allowlist sign-off are recorded separately. Cross-review follows the standing rule.

  10. Scope. This rule applies because the proposal adds a label that crosses the producer-consumer boundary in value shape and in downstream selection/grouping/joining. The framing "additive rather than a rename, so no parity fixture" does not exempt it under the established Cardinality Guardrails rule: additions that cross the boundary in name, alias, or value shape require parity verification. Local bounded labels that never enter another covered service may use the local path; this label does not qualify until the producer-consumer boundary is removed from scope.

REJECT BASIS (for the PR comment, if you want to send one)

  The proposal fails conditions 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 9, and 10 as written: no allowlist, no normalization, no absent or malformed handling, no tenant-level budget, no parity fixture, no mapped consumer-owner signoff identified, and an explicit claim that the additive nature removes it from the parity-fixture gate. Each of these is independently blocking. The change is not safe for production review in its current form.

NOTES ON WHAT THIS RULE DOES NOT DO

  It does not authorize deployment. It only states the conditions under which the change is reviewable. Rollout ordering, staged percentages, soak windows, the Friday freeze, 45-minute secondary paging, Nadia cross-review, and the canary-safe staging map remain separate gates owned by the deploying team. Cardinality Guardrails remains a production-review gate for covered label changes, not a complete telemetry-governance framework.

Below is a plan consistent with what you described and with the same low-key, gated approach that worked for the January episode. Everything here is home monitoring with explicit escalation thresholds — nothing about tonight meets an ER trigger on the facts you gave.

WHY THIS IS LOW-RISK ON PRESENTATION
- Single episode, vomitus = food + grass, no blood, no foreign object
- Alert, comfortable abdomen (not swollen or painful), no repeated retching
- Interested in water
- Grass-induced vomiting in dogs is common; one episode with normal vitals is the textbook "watch and re-feed gently" pattern

TONIGHT (next ~8–12 hours)
- Withhold food, but not water. You already started this — keep going.
- Offer water in small amounts, not a full bowl. Rule of thumb: a few laps every 20–30 minutes rather than free access. Reason: large water boluses on an irritated stomach often trigger a second vomit.
- If he asks for more after a small offering and keeps it down for 20–30 minutes, you can leave a modest amount down.
- No walks beyond a short, on-leash potty break tonight. No off-leash / grass access until his stomach is clearly back to normal.
- Quiet evening. No new food, no treats, no human food.

RE-FEEDING PLAN
Start a bland diet in the morning if the night is uneventful. The standard option is boiled skinless chicken (or lean ground turkey) + plain white rice, 1:2 ratio (protein:rice). Scale portion sizes to his size — a starting point is roughly 1/4 of his normal meal portion for the first offering. If you don't have those ingredients on hand, plain scrambled egg (no butter/oil/salt) with a little rice, or just plain rice alone, is fine for one meal.

Sequence:
1. Morning (~8–12 hours after the vomit): one small bland portion. If he eats and keeps it down for 2 hours, proceed.
2. Midday: a second small bland portion, slightly larger.
3. Evening: a third small bland portion, closer to his normal volume.
4. Next day: mix ~50/50 bland diet and his regular food, two meals.
5. Day 3: mostly regular food, one final bland meal.
6. Day 4: back to normal schedule.

If at any step he vomits again, drop back to the previous smaller portion and extend the bland-diet phase. If he vomits twice on the bland diet, that's a vet call.

MONITORING CHECKPOINTS (24–48 HOURS)
Track all of these — useful both for your own pattern recognition and if you do end up calling:
- Energy: alert and interested in normal things, or flat / withdrawn
- Appetite: when first meal offered, how eagerly, how much
- Vomiting: frequency, timing after meals/water, contents
- Stool: first bowel movement after this episode matters — note time, consistency, any blood/mucus
- Water intake: roughly how much, in roughly how many sips
- Gums: should be pink and moist. Press a gum until it blanches; color should return in under 2 seconds.
- Abdomen: should stay soft and non-painful. Re-check in the morning before the first meal.
- Any new behavior: lip-smacking, drooling, repeated swallowing, posture changes, restlessness

CALL HIS REGULAR VET (next-day or schedule-soon, not tonight)
- A second vomiting episode at any point, even if it resolves
- No interest in food for more than 24 hours
- Loose stool or any diarrhea, especially with blood or mucus
- Lethargy that persists into tomorrow morning
- Gums look tacky, or skin tenting (gentle pinch at the scruff returns slowly) — signs of mild dehydration
- Anything you can't easily explain by the grass-eating itself

GO TO AN EMERGENCY VET TONIGHT (or call the ER vet line first if you want a triage check)
- Repeated, non-productive retching — trying to vomit but nothing comes up. This is the bloat / GDV red flag and is time-critical.
- Abdomen becomes distended, hard, or visibly painful when you touch it
- Gums turn pale, white, blue, yellow, or brick-red
- Blood in vomit — either fresh red or "coffee ground" appearance
- Collapse, weakness, can't stand, sudden disorientation
- Suspected ingestion of a toxin, medication, foreign body, or anything other than grass (you didn't describe this, but worth flagging as a check)
- Restlessness and inability to settle, especially paired with a hard or swollen belly
- Breathing noticeably faster than usual, or effortful

WHAT NOT TO DO TONIGHT
- Don't induce vomiting
- Don't give any over-the-counter "anti-nausea" or anti-diarrheal medication meant for humans (e.g., Pepto, Imodium) — many are problematic for dogs and dosing depends on specifics you don't need to figure out tonight
- Don't offer a full meal "to settle his stomach" — that is the most common cause of a second vomit
- Don't let him back on grass until he's had two normal bland meals with no vomiting

QUICK DECISION TREE
- Night passes with no vomit, gums pink, energy normal → start bland diet in the morning per the sequence above.
- One more vomit overnight, but he stays alert, drinks, abdomen soft → routine vet call in the morning.
- Two more vomits, or any single sign from the ER list → emergency vet tonight.

REVIEW — ingest-edge queue-fairness draft (Wes, 2024-06-18)

What the draft locks in (keep):
  - Active caps unchanged: 4 decompressions/pod, 2/tenant. These are caps, not guarantees — keep the existing alarm path, do not relabel them.
  - Tenant round-robin at the inter-tenant scheduler.
  - HTTP 429 when a tenant has 8 waiting requests in its tenant queue.

What the draft explicitly leaves undefined and what must be specified before implementation:

A. Scheduling

  1. Intra-tenant order: state it explicitly. Default should be FIFO by enqueue time within a tenant. Round-robin is the inter-tenant discipline; first-arrived-first-served within a tenant is the safe default.
  2. Inter-tenant RR ring: include only tenants that currently have a non-empty wait queue. An idle tenant must be removed from the ring and re-inserted at the current cursor on its next enqueue — otherwise idle tenants accumulate "free passes" they never spend and new tenants cannot enter promptly.
  3. RR cursor ownership: per-pod local. Active caps are already per-pod, and a shared cursor adds a coordination failure mode you do not need. State this.

B. Cancellation

  4. Cancellation MUST atomically remove the request from its tenant queue. A request canceled while waiting must not still occupy a slot in the 8-cap; a subsequent arrival from the same tenant in the same scheduling tick must be admissible if the cap was 8/8.
  5. Cancellation of the head-of-tenant-queue entry must release the head before the scheduler picks a new head. No head-skip past a canceled-but-not-yet-removed entry.
  6. Cancellation between "dequeued by scheduler" and "tenant permit acquired" MUST release the global permit. This is the exact regression vector from the `ingest-edge#229` cancel branch. Document three cancel-check points: in-queue, between dequeue and permit acquire, and between permit acquire and decompression start.
  7. Cancellation of an already-admitted (actively decompressing) request follows the existing bounded-decompression cancel path. The new scheduler does not touch it.

C. Capacity sharing / borrowing

  8. Borrowing is required, not optional. If tenant B is at 8/8 and tenant A has 0 waiting, a new tenant A arrival must NOT be 429'd — it must be admitted into a borrowed slot. Without this rule the 8-cap silently caps aggregate throughput to 8 * (active tenants) regardless of headroom under the active caps.
  9. Borrow accounting: every borrowed slot is tagged with the borrowing tenant; the donor tenant's effective cap remains 8 while the borrow is outstanding; borrowed slots return when the donor's queue drains.
  10. Borrowing relaxes the wait cap only. It does NOT relax the active cap (still 2/tenant active, 4/pod active). State this.
  11. Borrowed waiting slots do not consume active permits until the request is dequeued.

D. Retry-After

  12. 429 due to tenant-wait-cap-full: Retry-After MUST be a bounded integer of seconds with full-range jitter. Suggested base = observed tenant wait p99 at steady state, capped, jittered 0–2s. The 0–2s full-range jitter has a working precedent in the 2024-01 staging load-test rerun; reuse it rather than inventing a new one.
  13. Retry-After MUST NOT be 0 (encourages tight retry loops that amplify the original problem) and MUST NOT exceed 30s (no useful retry signal past that — client should pick its own longer backoff).
  14. This 429 is a distinct cause from admission-shedding (semaphore exhausted) and from active-cap-exceeded. Different cause → different default Retry-After. Document the three-cause table.

E. Starvation

  15. Aging: a waiting request older than T_age (suggest 30s, configurable) is promoted to the head of its tenant queue on the next scheduling turn. Aging is per-request, not per-tenant.
  16. Maximum wait: a hard wall-clock cap (suggest 60s) after which the request is either forced admission or 429'd with Retry-After. Pick a number; document it; do not leave unbounded.
  17. Starvation test is required, not optional: under sustained cross-tenant load where one tenant produces ~100x the rate of another, the low-rate tenant's p99 wait must stay below the max-wait cap. Without this test "round-robin" is unverified.

F. Accounting invariants

  18. Per-tenant wait counter = tenant_wait_queue_len + tenant_admitted_but_not_yet_active. No double-counting; canceled requests not counted; the counter must reconcile under churn.
  19. Active caps (4/pod, 2/tenant) and the new wait cap (8/tenant + borrowing) are independent. State in the runbook that active-cap alarms are unchanged.

G. Ownership and rollout

  20. Owner = ingest-edge mapped owner. Wes is practical backup under deploy-pipeline rules. This is the fairness/capacity follow-up to the bounded-decompression release; it is NOT a rollback condition for that release, and the June 11 evidence (no rollback triggers fired) is unaffected by this work.
  21. Deploy path: staging canary first; production rollout only after focused tests pass and a staging load rerun shows no regression vs. the 2024-01 baseline (peak concurrent retries, p99, completion time, 429 count, dropped/duplicate accepted points).

Required focused tests (must run and pass before review — not exhaustive E2E):

  T1.  Tenant cap behavior: tenant A at 8/8 → next A arrival returns 429 with Retry-After in (0, 30] and jitter observed; tenant B unaffected.
  T2.  Borrow: tenant A at 8/8, tenant B at 0 → B arrival admitted into a borrowed slot; A's effective cap remains 8; borrowed slot returns to A when A's queue drains.
  T3.  Cancel-while-waiting: cancel a tenant A waiting entry → A's wait count decrements; a new A arrival in the same scheduling tick is admissible.
  T4.  Cancel-head: cancel the head of A's queue → next A entry becomes head with no stale-slot artifact.
  T5.  Cancel-between-dequeue-and-permit: cancel after scheduler picks but before tenant permit acquired → tenant permit NOT acquired; global permit released; counters consistent. Direct regression for the `ingest-edge#229` cancel branch.
  T6.  RR fairness: sustained 2-tenant load with one tenant at 5x the rate → both tenants receive approximately equal dequeue turns (within ±10%).
  T7.  Aging: a single request with no further arrivals from its tenant is admitted before T_age.
  T8.  Max-wait enforcement: a request that would otherwise starve is 429'd at the cap with a valid Retry-After.
  T9.  Retry-After bounds: 1000 simulated 429s → all Retry-After in (0, 30] and no two consecutive identical values (jitter observed).
  T10. Active-cap regression: under sustained borrowing, active decompression count per pod never exceeds 4, per tenant never exceeds 2.
  T11. RR ring reset: an idle tenant removed from the ring re-enters at the current cursor on its next enqueue, not at its prior position (no idle-tenant "debt").

Gate: code review cannot start until the design specifies all of A–G and lists T1–T11 in the PR description with expected results. The 429-when-tenant-full clause is fine as a backpressure direction, but the proposal as written is unsafe because cancellation, borrowing, and Retry-After each independently produce tenant lockout under load when left undefined.

Short answer: yes, the serving path must fail closed the instant the lease is lost, and the owner's "310ms is below one polling period" framing has the defect backwards. The interval is not the size of the acceptable risk; it is the measured duration of a fail-open violation. A 500ms poll cadence embedded in the read path is the architectural defect, not a tunable.

Why the owner's argument fails on principle:

- Lease loss makes the old holder non-authoritative by definition. There is no version of "non-authoritative but only for 310ms" that is safe to serve.
- "Below one polling period" describes the poll's blind spot, not a tolerance. Conflating polling cadence with validity turns a liveness check into an authority claim, which inverts what the gate is supposed to do.
- Read-only does not mean consequence-free. Routing snapshots steer traffic. A client that pins to a stale snapshot for the duration of a retry, cache TTL, or downstream consumer poll can persist the bad routing long after the 310ms window closes. The blast radius belongs to consumers, not to the poll.
- This contradicts the standing lease-convergence rule (March 18 drill, April 12 renewal event, runbook rb_1789266433669): post-failover, no stale-owner messages are tolerated for two full lease-renewal intervals. Stale-owner reads and stale-owner snapshots are the same class of violation.

The required architectural shape, before any tests:

- The gate's lease-validity check must be on the serving critical path, synchronous with the serve. Either (a) a fencing-style push that invalidates the cached "valid" bit on lease loss so the next serve cannot complete, or (b) a synchronous read of the current lease epoch/owner at serve time. The 500ms poll can remain as a defensive background check but cannot be the authoritative one.
- Routing snapshots must carry a monotonic version/epoch token, and the gate must reject any snapshot whose token does not match the holder's current lease epoch. No epoch match, no serve.
- On validity failure, the gate must return a defined fail-closed signal (specific 5xx, with reason), not silent stale-data success and not a generic crash.

Focused tests required before approval (each must pass on staging with production-like read traffic, then repeat on prod canary):

1. Epoch-mismatch serve rejection. Inject a served routing snapshot tagged with epoch N into a holder that now holds epoch N-1 (or no lease). Verify the gate rejects every serve with the defined fail-closed signal; no client receives the snapshot.
2. Lease-loss during in-flight serve. Time-controlled: drop the lease mid-serve. Verify in-flight serves either complete against a snapshot whose epoch is still valid, or fail closed. No in-flight serve returns a snapshot stamped with a stale epoch.
3. Poll-boundary race. Two variants: lease loss in the last 10ms before a scheduled poll, and lease loss in the first 10ms after. Both must produce identical fail-closed behavior. If the outcome differs, the poll is load-bearing and the design is wrong.
4. Slow / paused old-holder. Pause the old holder's poll thread for 5s, then drop its lease externally, then resume. Verify no serve completes with stale state during the pause or after resume. This kills the "below one polling period" defense.
5. Dual-leader read fencing. Re-run the March 18 dual-leader scenario but for reads. The old holder attempts to serve after the new holder has acquired. Verify fencing rejects, and that any cached "I am valid" state from before the loss is treated as invalid.
6. Two full lease-renewal intervals after failover. Standing requirement from rb_1789266433669. Verify no stale-owner or stale-epoch serves during this window. Capture and inspect every serve's epoch token.
7. Monotonic-epoch check across the handover. Confirm epochs are strictly monotonic through the 8.4s acquisition gap; no epoch reuse, no skipped epoch visible to clients.
8. Downstream-cache blast-radius probe. With a downstream consumer that caches the snapshot for 30s, run a failover and verify the consumer either refetches on epoch change or rejects on mismatch. The gate fix is not enough if a downstream consumer pins the stale state.
9. Fail-closed observability. Every rejected serve must emit a metric and a log line distinguishing lease-invalid from other 5xx, so the next drill's threshold is observable, not inferred from absence.
10. Production-equivalent canary. One staging pass is insufficient; the same suite must run against a prod canary shard with real read traffic before the change is considered accepted.

Approval shape:

- Approval requires all ten tests passing on staging and on a prod canary, the runbook entry naming the synchronous-validity invariant and the rejection metric, and an explicit statement that the 500ms poll is no longer load-bearing for correctness (only a defensive secondary check). The "below one polling period" framing must not appear in the rationale.
- Until those tests pass, the rehearsal finding should be recorded as an open fail-open defect, not as an accepted quirk. The shard-keeper owner keeps the fix and the rollout plan; this is a correctness gate, not an ops comfort call.

The four named failure modes are not crossed by the evidence; the fix is observably doing what it was supposed to do (synchronous gate close 14 ms after lease-loss, single serving holder throughout, zero stale responses, no restart). The 0.2% error peak is at the boundary but did not exceed it, and the 238 ms p99 spike for 45 s is well under the previously stated 5-minute, >200 ms stop condition.

EXPLICIT STOP CONDITIONS FOR THE 25% CANARY

  1. Stale reads
     - Any non-zero count on the stale-routing-responses counter stops immediately.
     - Any stale-owner message within two full lease-renewal intervals after a failover stops.

  2. Multiple holders
     - More than one active serving holder at any sample instant stops.
     - Any read served by a holder whose lease epoch is not strictly greater than the last-fenced epoch stops.

  3. Gate-close regression
     - Any single lease-loss-to-gate-close latency above 50 ms stops (3.5x the observed 14 ms; the fix should be synchronous, not best-effort polling).
     - Three consecutive events above 25 ms stops even if no single one crosses 50 ms.
     - Return to the prior poll-boundary behavior (gate-close latency approaching one lease-validity poll period) stops.

  4. Sustained availability impact
     - p99 above 200 ms sustained for 5 minutes stops (the previously stated gate; the 45 s/238 ms event is below this).
     - Error rate above 0.2% sustained for any 5-minute window stops (the observed peak is the line, not over it).
     - Error rate above 0.5% for any 30-second window stops even before the 5-minute condition arms, as a leading indicator.
     - Any pod restart required to recover stops.
     - Replacement acquisition above 15 s for a single failover stops (1.7x the observed 8.7 s).
     - Replacement acquisition above 12 s on two events in a 30-minute window stops.

OPERATIONAL CONDITIONS STILL REQUIRED BEFORE / DURING THE 25% WINDOW

  - Confirm the lease renewal interval in writing (or pull it from the runbook) so "two full renewal intervals after failover" is a defined duration, not a vibe. Until then, treat 2x the renewal interval as the minimum post-failover observation window.
  - Re-verify monotonic epochs after the failover at 25%, not just at 10%.
  - Re-verify downstream cache behavior: a routing read served from a downstream cache must reflect the current fence/epoch, not a pre-failover snapshot.
  - Inspect rejection metrics/logs for the expected 5xx class and confirm no unexpected 5xx classes appear.
  - Run one synthetic failover inside the 25% window and require the same four invariants: zero stale responses, exactly one holder, gate-close within 50 ms, and no restart. The 10% canary was synthetic; the 25% should also be exercised synthetically before relying on organic-only observation.
  - Keep the existing canary alert wired to the same stop conditions; do not let operator discretion override them.

OBSERVATION WINDOW

  - 30 minutes minimum at 25%, sampled every 5 minutes, before any further expansion is discussed. "Exactly one push worth of evidence" is the bar; a clean result authorizes the decision to discuss 50%, it does not authorize 50% by itself.

Blockers in the proposed response shape

1.  debug_incident_refs leaks internal incident identifiers. The June 24 implementation-readiness negative fixtures explicitly rejected internal identifiers, and the standing Lantern contract is "no raw incident detail." Internal IDs in any prefix — debug, internal, raw — are a raw-detail leak surface, and they create a cross-tenant reuse surface if cache keys are not tenant-partitioned (AUTH-2 invariant from the earlier readiness gate). The field must not appear in any external response, ever.

2.  Missing-source behavior returns incident_count=0 and active_minutes=0 with source_updated_at omitted. This is exactly the dangerous-misread pattern the no-source UI copy was designed against. Zeros-as-data are indistinguishable from "no incidents happened," which the June 3 fixture and Iris-confirmed wording treat as a hard fail. The standing rule: missing, stale, or malformed source renders literal unknown with a labeled reason — never a quantitative fallback. source_observed_at (or its equivalent) must still render the timestamp of the last successful source poll, because that is the only signal a viewer has to distinguish "no incidents in window" from "we don't know."

3.  No explicit absence representation in the schema. The proposal has no way to express authorized-and-fresh-zero vs missing-source vs stale-source vs unauthorized. Downstream consumers will collapse these states into "we have a payload," which is the silent-fallback pattern the next-stage negative fixtures are designed to reject.

4.  No separation between authorization state and data state. A pre-lookup unauthorized request must return HTTP 403 not_authorized uniformly, not a payload-with-zeros. Authorization ordering must precede lookup; lookup authorization must precede render. The schema as proposed does not enforce or express this.

5.  active_minutes derivation is undefined. If incident_count is at risk of zero-as-missing misread, active_minutes is the same risk with extra surface. Need a definition (for example, sum of unique incident-minute overlap with the window) and explicit behavior under partial-source, stale-source, and unknown.

6.  No tenant-partitioned cache key requirement on the response builder. AUTH-2 already required tenant_id in the cache key; the schema as proposed neither documents nor prevents reuse.

7.  No source-validation-before-render gate in the schema. The June 24 evidence confirmed validate-before-render ordering; the proposal does not carry that ordering into the field set or the absent states.

Corrected fail-closed external behavior

The external response must carry explicit state, not implicit-zero semantics. Recommended field set:

  service_id — request target; always present.
  window_start, window_end — the requested window; always present (these are request metadata, not data).
  data_state — enum: ok | unknown | not_authorized.
  incident_count — present and integer ONLY when data_state is ok. Absent or literal unknown when data_state is unknown.
  active_minutes — same rule as incident_count.
  source_observed_at — timestamp of the last successful source poll; present in both ok and unknown states. Renders literal unknown if never observed.
  source — present when data_state is ok, identifying the authoritative source for the data.
  unknown_reason — enum: missing_source | stale_source | malformed_source. Only present when data_state is unknown.
  No debug_incident_refs. Internal identifiers never leave the service, including in logs scoped to the external request.
  Pre-lookup unauthorized: HTTP 403 not_authorized, no payload fields.

Contract semantics:
  ok means: source validated fresh, parse succeeded, authorization confirmed, counts are real.
  unknown means: source is absent, stale, or malformed. Counts are not authoritative. source_observed_at is the last-good timestamp. unknown_reason names which.
  not_authorized is an HTTP 403, not a payload state.

This matches the established pattern: literal unknown with a labeled reason, plus the last-good observation timestamp, never a zero fallback, never a cached ok payload served after the source has gone missing.

Focused tests required (gating, not optional)

  T1.  Missing source, authorized. data_state=unknown, unknown_reason=missing_source, source_observed_at renders last-good or literal unknown if none, incident_count and active_minutes absent or literal unknown. No zeros anywhere.

  T2.  Stale source, authorized. data_state=unknown, unknown_reason=stale_source. Identical absent-state rendering to T1. Confirms stale-is-absent.

  T3.  Malformed source. data_state=unknown, unknown_reason=malformed_source. Parser detail not exposed. No partial fields, no field-level error leakage.

  T4.  Pre-lookup unauthorized. HTTP 403 not_authorized, no payload fields rendered. Confirms authorization-before-lookup ordering.

  T5.  Authorized fresh, zero incidents in window. data_state=ok, incident_count=0, active_minutes=0, source_observed_at present and current. This is the case where zeros ARE authoritative and must render distinctly from T1/T2/T3.

  T6.  Authorized fresh, non-zero. Same shape as T5 with real values populated from validated source.

  T7.  External response never contains internal incident identifiers. Assert debug_incident_refs (and any internal-ID field) is absent from the serialized external response under T5 and T6, even when internal state carries IDs.

  T8.  Tenant-partitioned cache key. Two tenants querying the same service_id + window must not share a cached summary. Cross-tenant response must not leak fields. AUTH-2 invariant.

  T9.  Source-validation-before-render. When source validation fails, no payload fields render. Ordering is observable in logs or telemetry: validate then authorize then render, not render-first.

  T10. No cached fallback under unknown. When source transitions from ok to missing, the response immediately becomes data_state=unknown. The last ok payload must not be served after the source has gone missing.

  T11. Manager, individual, and management-chain fields are rejected. Response has no such fields; even if upstream source carries them, they are stripped before render. Same for raw incident text. Matches the November 2023 narrow-adoption decision.

  T12. source_observed_at vs source_updated_at semantics. If both are kept, document and test that source_observed_at is the last successful poll from Lantern's side and source_updated_at is the upstream-claimed freshness. They may differ; the response must distinguish them and the unknown-state rendering must use source_observed_at.

Sunday night plan: peach-salsa chicken thighs with roasted corn & tomatoes over cilantro-lime rice

The shape: marinated chicken thighs and vegetables on one sheet pan, rice in one pot, and a no-cook peach-tomato-cilantro salsa that gets better the longer it sits. Most knife work happens before dinner. The oven does almost all of the evening work, and the food holds comfortably when you need it to.

This afternoon (about 25 min of standing):
  Trim and pat dry 4 bone-in, skin-on chicken thighs. Marinate in a covered dish or zip bag: zest and juice of 2 limes, 3 tbsp olive oil, 1 tsp salt, 1/2 tsp black pepper, 1/4 cup chopped cilantro. Fridge.

  Husk 2 ears of corn; cut each into halves or thirds. Fridge.

  Halve a pint of cherry tomatoes. Split into two bowls — half for the salsa, half for roasting.

  Pit and small-dice both peaches into the salsa bowl, along with the reserved tomato half, juice of 1 lime, 1 tbsp olive oil, another 1/4 cup cilantro, pinch of salt, a few grinds of pepper. Cover, fridge. (The salsa is genuinely better with a day's rest — the peaches stay bright, the salt pulls the tomato juice, the cilantro settles in. But a few hours is fine too.)

  Reserve the remaining cilantro and 1 lime (cut into wedges) covered, in the fridge.

Sunday evening — 45 min to plates, about 10 min of real work:

  T-45: Preheat oven to 425°F. Pull the chicken out 10 min before roasting so it loses the chill.

  T-40: On a parchment-lined sheet pan, arrange chicken skin-up, tuck the corn around the edges, scatter the remaining tomatoes. Drizzle everything with 1 tbsp olive oil, salt, pepper. Into the oven.

  T-15: Start the rice — 1 cup basmati or jasmine, 2 cups water, pinch of salt. Bring to a boil, cover, drop to low for 18 minutes, then rest covered for 5. (A rice cooker on warm is even easier — start it any time.)

  T-0:  Chicken should read 175°F internal at the thickest part (about 25–30 min total). Pull from oven.

Holding point (up to ~45 min, no judgment):
  - Oven down to 170°F. Loosely tent the sheet pan with foil. Bone-in thighs are very forgiving here.
  - Rice stays covered on the lowest burner or in the rice cooker on warm.
  - Salsa comes out of the fridge 5–10 min before plating, or serve it cold — both work.

Plate (3 min):
  Rice on plates. Two thighs each. Corn and tomatoes alongside. Spoon the peach salsa generously over the chicken. Scatter the reserved cilantro, hit with a lime wedge squeeze.

Cleanup:
  Sheet pan (parchment peels), one pot, cutting board, knife, small salsa bowl. Five items. Done.

Why the holding point actually holds:
  - Every sharp thing and the salsa happen before dinner.
  - The cook is mostly hands-off — oven and covered pot.
  - Thighs at 170°F, rice covered, salsa cold — nothing depends on the clock.
  - When the confirmation arrives — or doesn't, tonight — dinner doesn't notice.

Backup if the oven is occupied:
  Dutch oven, stovetop, covered, low 35–40 minutes. Same ingredients, same idea. Corn and tomatoes can join for the last 15 min.

If energy runs out at any point:
  Rice + chicken + roasted veg + a squeeze of lime is still a complete plate. Skip the salsa spooning and nobody minds.

Verdict: the sequence is right in shape but underspecified. Find the source, fix it permanently, confirm drying, then repaint. What's missing are a quantitative definition of "dry," a recheck cadence, and explicit escalation triggers. Given the patch has been damp for eight days and was already slightly soft on June 23, those gaps matter.

Three gaps in the management plan as stated:

1. No quantitative definition of "dry." A recheck after masonry has no meaning without a control reading from an unaffected section of the same wall, same orientation, taken before or at the same time as the post-repair reading. "Dry" should mean matching the control, typically in the ballpark of under about 1 percent on a pinless meter for gypsum. Without a control, no one can honestly say the wall has dried.

2. No recheck cadence. "Recheck after masonry" should mean 24 to 48 hours post-repair, then weekly for at least two weeks. Daily readings if a storm falls inside that window. Trend matters more than any single number.

3. No cavity check. Moisture meters only read the surface or shallow depth. A pin-type deep probe or a small inspection hole near the top of the patch would tell you whether insulation, sheathing, or framing behind the drywall is wet. If the cavity is wet, surface drying is not enough.

A fourth item worth raising with management: the May 13 AC-bracket inspection found corrosion at the exterior support joint and a misseated masonry anchor. The contractor says the head joint is the source and exonerates the AC, but the Friday masonry should explicitly include the bracket interface, since water may have entered through more than one path. Worth confirming in writing that the scope covers the bracket and any flashing above the window, not only the head joint.

Also, the prior vendor could not access the rear facade. If access was the original blocker and a replacement contractor had to be brought in, ask management in writing whether the replacement actually has rear-facade access arranged for Friday. A scheduled visit that cannot reach the work is not a repair.

Conditions that should prompt a faster interior opening:

  Patch expands, or new damp areas appear on that wall or adjacent walls after the permanent repair. Water is still entering or migrating.

  Drywall stays soft, swells, sags, or develops paint blisters. The gypsum core has taken up water and will not recover structurally. It must be cut out and replaced, not repainted.

  Moisture readings rise or stay flat for more than seven days after the permanent repair. Continuing source or hidden reservoir.

  Active dripping or beading recurs during the next significant rain after the repair. The masonry fix did not fully restore the joint, or another path is open.

  A deep-probe reading or inspection hole shows wet insulation, sheathing, or framing. Surface drying will not reach it.

  Humidity in the bedroom rises measurably, or condensation forms on interior surfaces near the patch. The wall is acting as a moisture reservoir.

  Any occupant develops respiratory or allergic symptoms that correlate with time spent in the bedroom. Health-based escalation, independent of what the wall looks like.

Conditions that should prompt a mold assessment:

  Visible discoloration, spotting, or fuzz on the patch or adjacent surfaces.

  Musty or earthy odor anywhere in the room.

  Any time the wall is opened for another reason. A swab or air sample by an indoor environmental professional should be taken before remediation, not after.

  Moisture readings remain elevated beyond three weeks after the repair.

  Recurrent water entry of any kind.

One pattern to flag: the April 6 kitchen window event had a smaller footprint, no substrate softening, and resolved with resealing. This one is wetter, longer, and the substrate is already softened. Worth asking management whether the head joint above the kitchen window was inspected at the same time, since the building's exterior envelope may have multiple failing joints and a one-off masonry fix may not be the last repair needed.

The mold assessment itself should be done by an IEQ consultant or industrial hygienist, not the building's general contractor. Visual inspection alone misses what is behind paint or inside the cavity. If the wall is ever opened, ask for the assessment in writing with sample locations, lab certification, and species identification, not a verbal "looks fine."

Interim actions for the four days before Friday's permanent masonry:

  Take a control moisture reading now from an unaffected section of the same wall, same orientation, same height band. That gives the post-repair recheck a real baseline.

  Photograph the patch and the wall beside the outlet with the same framing as the earlier photos, so the time series is comparable.

  Watch the forecast. The temporary exterior seal is not a guaranteed water stop. If a significant storm is expected within 48 hours and management will not move the Friday masonry up, document the request in writing. If the patch expands or new water appears during that window, treat it as escalation, not a watch item.

  Keep Kibo and furniture away from the wall, leave the window and AC untouched, and continue documenting any change in the patch's footprint, texture, or softness.

  If the drywall feels softer than it did on June 23, or the footprint grows even slightly, do not wait for Friday. Escalate now.

    Lights low. No fireworks-viewing from a window.

    Gums that look pale, white, blue, or grey instead of healthy pink.
    Heavy open-mouth breathing that does not slow within 10-15 minutes in a cool, quiet, dark space, or any breathing that looks labored (heaving flanks, neck extended, elbows out).
    Repeated vomiting or unproductive retching. Repeated dry heaves alone are a separate warning sign in dogs.
    Distended or tight abdomen, or repeated posturing without producing anything.
    Seizure activity — paddling, loss of consciousness, foaming.
    Escalation into self-injury: broken tooth, broken nail, deep laceration from clawing a door or window, or any bleeding you cannot stop with 5 minutes of direct pressure.
    New loss of coordination — stumbling, head tilt, sudden confusion.
    Refusal of water for several hours combined with dry gums or skin that does not snap back.
    Body that feels clearly hot to the touch in the groin or armpit, beyond just panting — heat-stroke territory.

WHO TO CALL
    Your primary vet's after-hours line first if anything on that list appears. They know Kibo.

    The nearest 24-hour ER if the after-hours line is unreachable and a same-list item is active.

TOMORROW MORNING
