1. 78°F indoors is the upper edge of comfortable for most dogs. Fine for resting, but Kibo should not be panting indoors. If open-mouth breathing starts inside, the room isn't cool enough.

2. Pavement is the bigger risk than air temperature today. At 93°F ambient, exposed asphalt in direct sun commonly reaches 140–150°F. Pavement holds heat well after the air cools — even when the air drops to 85°F in the evening, sun-baked sidewalks can still burn paws.

Indoor cooling
- Keep the AC running. Close bedroom blinds during peak sun (roughly 11 AM – 6 PM) to cut solar gain.
- A second fan pointed across Kibo's resting spot helps more than it feels like it should — moving air matters.
- Fresh cool water available and refilled midday; dogs drink more in heat.
- A damp (not cold, not soaking) towel draped over his back/belly is fine if he seems warm. Skip ice packs directly on him.
- If you can lower the thermostat, 72–75°F is more generous than 78°F. If 78°F is all the unit will hold against a 93°F day, that's still acceptable as long as he isn't panting indoors.

Walk timing
- Done for the midday window. Peak pavement heat in NYC runs roughly 2–6 PM; air temperature typically peaks 3–5 PM.
- Next walk: evening, ideally after 8 PM once pavement has had two-plus hours to cool. Test before leaving (rule below).
- Tomorrow morning: before 9 AM for a longer walk; before 10 AM is the latest comfortable window.
- Cut duration. 15–20 min in heat instead of the usual 30–45. Sniff walks on grass beat distance walks on pavement.
- Carry water, offer sips every 5 min. If Kibo slows, seeks shade, lies down, or pulls toward home — he's telling you it's too much. Head back immediately.

Pavement test
- Press the back of your hand flat to the sidewalk for 7 full seconds. If you can't hold it comfortably, Kibo can't walk on it.
- Stay on grass, dirt, shaded sides of the street, or interior Prospect Park paths. Mornings and evenings in the park are the right call today.
- Avoid the Prospect Park entrance plazas and any asphalt/blacktop in direct sun, even briefly.

Panting — what's normal vs. what's not

Expected after a warm walk; should resolve within ~10 min back in the AC:
- Open-mouth panting, tongue out and wide, mild drool
- Slightly faster breathing than baseline
- Wants water, drinks normally
- Alert, responsive, walks normally once inside

Stop the walk, get inside, watch closely (not necessarily an emergency):
- Panting that doesn't slow within 10 min once in the AC
- Kibo seeking cool surfaces (tile, bathtub) and not settling
- Reluctance to drink
- Excessive drooling, or drool that's thicker/stickier than usual

Urgent vet / ER now — true heat stress or heat stroke:
- Bright red, purple, or gray gums/tongue instead of healthy pink
- Staggering, weakness, collapse, or refusal to stand
- Disorientation, confusion, or no response to your voice
- Vomiting or diarrhea during or after the walk
- Body temperature 104°F+ if you can take it rectally (heat-stroke threshold; 106°F+ is critical organ-damage territory)
- Seizure

- Don't muzzle him — he needs to pant.

Plan: sheet-pan salmon with lemon-dill orzo and yogurt sauce. The trick is that the salmon stays RAW in the fridge during the hold — it cooks last, so it can't dry out no matter how long Devika naps. Everything else waits quietly.

TIMING
  T+0 to ~30 min   active prep (orzo, sauce, veg, salt the salmon)
  T+30 to ~75 min  holding window (up to 45 min — orzo covered and warm, salmon in fridge, veg at room temp, sauce in fridge)
  T+75 to ~90 min  sheet-pan finish (~12-14 min)
  -> plates

INGREDIENTS (everything you listed, plus olive oil, salt, pepper)
  2 salmon fillets
  ~3/4 cup dry orzo
  1 generous handful green beans, trimmed
  ~1 cup cherry tomatoes, halved
  1 lemon (zest + juice)
  small handful dill, chopped (split half/half)
  ~1/2 cup yogurt
  bread, sliced
  olive oil, salt, pepper

PHASE 1 — ACTIVE PREP (~30 min)
  1. Preheat oven to 425F. Line a sheet pan with parchment (this is the cleanup win).
  2. Salt the salmon generously on both sides, pepper, place skin-side down on a small plate, back into the fridge. Do not cover tightly — let it air a bit.
  3. Boil the orzo in salted water per package (~9 min). Drain, return to the pot off heat. Toss with a glug of olive oil, the lemon zest, and half the dill. Cover with a lid. Leave on the stove — residual heat keeps it warm and moist for the hold.
  4. While the orzo cooks: trim green beans, halve the cherry tomatoes, set on a plate at room temp.
  5. Yogurt sauce: stir yogurt with a squeeze of lemon juice, the other half of the dill, a pinch of salt, a small drizzle of olive oil. Loosen with a teaspoon of warm water until pourable. Cover and refrigerate.

PHASE 2 — HOLDING WINDOW (up to 45 min, totally safe)
  Orzo:       covered pot on the stove, still warm. If it tightens, a splash of hot water before serving loosens it.
  Salmon:      plate in the fridge. Pull it out 10-15 min before cooking so it loses the chill — cold salmon cooks unevenly.
  Veg:         on the plate at room temp, ready to dump on the sheet pan.
  Sauce:       in the fridge; pull it out 5 min before serving so it's not ice-cold.
  Bread:       ready to warm.
  This is the quiet block. No alarms, no reheating. Devika naps; you do whatever. If she surfaces late, nothing has degraded — the orzo just wants a splash of water and a stir at the end.

PHASE 3 — FINAL COOK (~12-14 min, start when Devika is up)
  1. Toss the green beans and cherry tomatoes on the sheet pan with olive oil, salt, a grind of pepper. Spread them on one half.
  2. Place the salmon skin-side down on the other half. A lemon slice on top is nice.
  3. Roast 10-12 min. Target 125F internal in the thickest part — it will coast to 130F as it rests. Visually: flesh flakes but is still translucent in the very center, tomatoes collapse and just char at the edges, green beans are crisp-tender with a few brown spots.
  4. Warm the bread in the oven for the last 3 min, or in a dry pan.
  5. Rewarm the orzo: low heat, splash of water, stir. 60 seconds.

PLATE
  Orzo on the plate, veg alongside, salmon on top (skin peels off easily if you don't want it). Spoon the yogurt-dill sauce over the salmon or serve on the side. Bread for mopping the tomato-orzo juices.

WHY THIS DOESN'T DRY OUT
  Salmon is the only thing that punishes you for sitting, and it's not cooked yet. Orzo stays moist under a lid with a splash of water at the end. Veg are roasted at the end so they keep snap. Sauce is cold-held separately so it doesn't break from heat.

NOTES
  - If Devika wakes earlier than expected and you want to start sooner, the salmon only needs ~5 min out of the fridge, not 15.
  - If she sleeps past the 45-min window and you want to push it: orzo can hold another 20 min easily; just keep the lid on and add water. Salmon raw on the counter is still safe in that range (well under the 2-hr room-temp limit), but you'll want to start cooking by then anyway.
  - No second-pan stress: parchment-lined sheet pan goes in the trash, small pot gets a rinse.

ASSESSMENT

Today's checks satisfy the functional gate that was still open on 7/11 and revisited on 7/14: single-leg hops clean, lateral hops stable, and a one-foot step-off is functionally what the figure-eights and moderate cuts have already exceeded. Seven consecutive days with no swelling and no giving way is a real floor of symptom-free loading, not just a one-off good moment. A first controlled soccer session today is reasonable.

That is not the same as unrestricted clearance. This is a sport-specific re-entry after the third lateral sprain on the same side in roughly ten months. The recurrence pattern is independent of today's clean checks — the structural question doesn't go away just because today's checks passed. The non-urgent sports-medicine or orthopedic stability evaluation is overdue and should be scheduled once this episode is fully behind you. Today makes the rationale slightly stronger, not more urgent.

WARM-UP (~15 min, deliberately longer than the time you'll actually play)

1. 5 min easy jog or walk-to-jog on flat ground, even cadence.
2. Dynamic mobility, both sides: 10 straight-leg kicks, 10 lateral leg swings each direction, one ankle alphabet per side, 2x10m easy side-shuffles each way.
3. Progressive ball prep in order — do not skip steps:
   - 2 min easy passing and ball touches at conversational pace.
   - 3 min controlled dribbling in a small space with planned direction changes (cones or shoes as markers), ~60–70% of full pace.
   - 4 x ~10s progressive accelerations to ~80%, full walk-back recovery between each.
4. End with one or two easy cuts at the same 60–70% effort you'll use in play — this is the final gate. If any of this reproduces lateral ache, instability, or a catch, you stretch, ice, and call today the graded session. You do not play.

INITIAL TIME CAP

- 30 minutes total time on the field, including warm-up. Warm-up ~15 min → ~15 min of actual play.
- The 30 min is a cap, not a target. Leaving early is success, not weakness. Same framing as the 2/4 duration progression.
- If the warm-up alone eats the 30, you don't play. The warm-up *is* the gate today.

- Cuts: only the cuts you already did this morning (forward, lateral, figure eights, moderate cuts). No pivoting at full speed off a planted trail leg.
- Surface: grass or a forgiving artificial surface. Avoid hot, rock-hard turf if you have a choice.
- If you've been using an ankle brace or tape during the graded progressions, use the same thing today. Do not debut a new brace on return day.
- After the session: walk home, elevate, ice 10–15 min if the ankle feels warm or full. No same-day bouldering, no errands on the ankle.

STOP CRITERIA (any one = stop immediately, sit out the rest)

- Lateral ankle pain ≥2/10 at any point during play. Same threshold that held you out on 7/11.
- Any sense of giving way, catching, or "almost going" on a cut or landing.
- Sharp pain anywhere in the foot, Achilles, or lateral malleolus.
- New swelling, warmth, or focal tenderness that wasn't there this morning.
- Limp, altered gait, or protective stride — even if pain is below the threshold.
- Loss of push-off power on the right side that you can't immediately attribute to general fatigue.

If you stop: ice 10–15 min, walk home, elevate, and don't try to "test it" again in the session. Today's session is closed.

NEXT-DAY + 24–48H CHECK (this is what tells you whether today was actually tolerated)

- If tomorrow morning shows any ache, swelling, or instability → reset 48–72h, then return to the graded session template, not to live play.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT AUTHORIZE

- Full-intensity play, full matches, or any session where you'd be tempted to chase a result.
- Skipping the sports-medicine or orthopedic stability evaluation. Three lateral sprains on the same side in ten months is the recurrence signal; scheduling the eval is overdue, independent of how today goes.

EVIDENCE ANCHOR

  Observed during the 12-minute window:
    ingest-edge queue wait: 90-140 ms
    per-tenant waiting cap: not reached
    eligible capacity: remained in use
    accepted-point counters: continuous
    dropped-point counters: zero
    handler duration: 1.7-1.9 s
    client total deadline: 2.0 s

  Not yet observed (the gap that blocks any scheduling or limits change):
    distributed trace decomposing connection setup, auth, handler work, response delivery
    which phase(s) consumed the 1.7-1.9 s
    what the 2.0 s deadline actually bounds and where it is enforced
    per-phase deadline accounting on the client (if any)

The combination "handler duration 1.7-1.9 s vs 2.0 s total deadline, with no queueing and no drops" means the handler work itself is sitting within 100-300 ms of the client's total deadline. Anything that adds even tens of milliseconds to a non-handler phase pushes the request over the deadline and surfaces as a 504. That is the central fact; everything below is a refinement of it.

RANKED PLAUSIBLE CAUSES (most to least likely)

  1. Handler work itself approaching the 2.0 s ceiling.
     Direct match to the 1.7-1.9 s observation. Sub-causes worth keeping distinct even though they share the same shape: a downstream RPC on the handler critical path slowed; in-process serialization/compression change in the handler; an in-process cache miss storm that the handler owns; a single dependency that lives inside the handler's measurement boundary. Ranked first because the only timing we have is handler duration, and nothing in the evidence contradicts this.

  2. Authentication / token-validation path slowdown adjacent to the handler.
     Auth is often counted inside handler duration but is usually a separate call (JWKS fetch, token introspection, signature check against a remote key). A slow auth window raises handler duration without raising queue waits. Structurally a sub-case of (1), but kept distinct because it points at a different component and a different owner.

  3. A single downstream dependency on the handler critical path.
     Handler work that fans out to a write store, enrichment service, or side cache. Same shape as (1)/(2); ranking roughly tied, separated only by typical architecture. The trace alone distinguishes these three.

  4. Connection setup / TLS / keepalive anomaly at the edge or load balancer.
     Full-handshake storm after a keepalive failure, LB connection-pool churn, brief TLS resumption gap. Would not show in ingest-edge queue waits and would not necessarily raise accepted-point counters. Plausible but lower because accepted-point continuity means the request actually reached handler start.

  5. Client-side deadline accounting boundary.
     "2.0 s total deadline" is ambiguous. It may be measured from connection start, from request send, from first byte, or it may be a server-side handler timeout. If the deadline starts at connection start, even a 1.7 s handler leaves only 300 ms for setup and delivery; if it starts at first byte, the bound is looser. Not a cause on the ingest path; a measurement question that changes whether the observed 1.7-1.9 s is fatal or only close to fatal.

  6. Response-side serialization or compression.
     Unlikely primary cause; possible secondary contributor. Only matters if (5) puts the deadline close.

  7. Pod-level runtime stall (GC, runtime scheduler, cgroup throttling, brief CPU steal).
     A sustained 1.7-1.9 s handler duration with no queue-wait rise is more consistent with a slow handler phase than a stall, but a partial GC pause or cgroup stall inside the handler is still possible. Distinguishable from (1)-(3) via pod and runtime metrics, not via the trace alone.

  8. Network-level anomaly between client and ingest-edge (retransmit, brief congestion, RST).
     Possible but low: an outage-class network event would more likely surface in adjacent paths or in the load balancer.

  9. Tail-latency saturation of eligible capacity without queue-cap pressure.
     Capacity "in use" does not preclude tail spikes, but the 90-140 ms queue-wait observation argues against a capacity-saturation story.

DISTRIBUTED-TRACE EVIDENCE NEEDED

For a sample of failed requests during the 12-minute window, plus a control sample of successful requests immediately before and after the window, capture:

  Spans required, in order, with explicit start and end timestamps:
    a. client connect / TLS handshake, with a resumption indicator
    b. request send
    c. edge or LB ingress span (if present)
    d. ingest-edge admission span (when the request entered the scheduler)
    e. ingest-edge queue-wait span (must reconcile to the 90-140 ms aggregate; if it does not, the queue-wait metric and the trace disagree and the queue-wait metric is the wrong instrument to scope this by)
    f. authentication / token-validation span
    g. handler work span, with child spans for every downstream call the handler makes (write store, enrichment, cache, side RPC)
    h. response serialization / compression span
    i. response send, first byte, last byte spans

  Fields and tags required on each span:
    stable tenant identifier (or tenant hash; do not rely on raw tenant in production logs)
    pod identifier, instance, zone
    retry attempt number (so this trace is not a retry of a previously traced request)
    outcome: 200 / 504 / client-cancelled
    HTTP/2 stream id or HTTP/1.1 connection id, for connection-level correlation
    deadline fields if the client emits them: deadline_total and deadline_remaining at each phase boundary

  Derived quantities to compute from the spans:
    per-phase mean and p99 across failed samples vs control samples
    which single phase accounts for the difference between failed and control (this is the question the trace exists to answer)
    whether handler duration in the trace equals the 1.7-1.9 s aggregate metric, or whether auth or downstream work sits outside the handler's measurement boundary

CLIENT-DEADLINE EVIDENCE NEEDED

The phrase "2.0 s total deadline" is ambiguous and that ambiguity is part of the problem. Required before any change:

  1. Which deadline it is:
     client-side total budget from connect start; from first byte; from request send; server-side handler timeout only; or per-phase budget (e.g., 200 ms connect, 300 ms auth, 1.4 s handler, 100 ms delivery).

  2. Where it is enforced:
     in the SDK or client library; at an outbound proxy or sidecar; server-side via context timeout.

  3. What the client emits:
     per-phase deadline_remaining telemetry; only a wall-clock total; the deadline value attached to the outgoing request (some SDKs send a deadline header).

  4. Whether the 504 is client-generated or server-generated.
     If client-generated, the client gave up at 2.0 s and the server may have completed after; handler duration alone is not a server-side problem and the cause is a client-deadline problem, not an ingest-edge problem. If server-generated, the server (or its edge) returned 504 and the cause is server-side.

  5. Whether the deadline is the same for all tenants or per-tenant. The "affected client" framing suggests one tenant; confirm it is not a per-tenant override that recently changed.

This evidence distinguishes cause (5) in the ranking from causes (1)-(3) and is necessary before any conclusion about ingest-edge.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR INGEST-EDGE SCHEDULING OR LIMITS

  No change is warranted yet. The 90-140 ms queue waits, the unused waiting-cap headroom, the continuous accepted-point stream, the zero dropped points, and the still-in-use eligible capacity together rule out the ingest-edge scheduler, the per-tenant waiting cap, the fairness ring, and the decompression scheme as the source. Changing any of them would address a problem the current evidence does not show exists.

  Pre-change gate, in order:
    1. Distributed-trace decomposition per the span list above, with per-phase p99s for failed vs control samples.
    2. Client-deadline specification per the five items above.
    3. Identification of which phase is responsible for the 1.7-1.9 s handler duration (downstream RPC, auth, in-process work, response work).
    4. Confirmation that the 504 is server-generated if the conclusion is to act on ingest-edge at all. A client-generated 504 driven by a tight total deadline is not an ingest-edge problem in any form.

  Until those four items are in hand, the response to support is: the 12-minute burst is consistent with a handler-side slowdown approaching the client's 2.0 s deadline; the ingest-edge scheduler, caps, fairness, and decompression showed no failure modes during the window; no ingest-edge scheduling or limit change is authorized; trace and client-deadline evidence is the next required step, owned by the team that owns the affected handler path, not by ingest-edge.

The line that holds: do not convert "we have not yet seen the trace" into "therefore we should adjust the scheduler." Adjusting caps or fairness to relieve a handler-side slowdown is the kind of change that turns a transient 12-minute burst into a longer fairness regression for tenants that were not affected.

What the evidence supports and doesn't:

  Soccer last Sunday was 45 min of straight-line and cutting loads under your own endurance control. That's good evidence the ankle tolerated controlled multi-directional ground loading, but bouldering adds a different load profile that Sunday did not cover: heel hooks and high-step inversion, twisting on small footholds, fall-and-landing mechanics on the right foot, and dynamic foot moves. A symptom-free week after a controlled soccer session is evidence the ankle tolerated that specific session, not clearance for a different one. Third lateral sprain in ~10 months is still a recurrence pattern; conservative progression is the right frame, not "permission."

60-minute window (cap is the point, not the goal):

  0:00-0:10  Arrival, tape/brush shoes, easy bike or row for warmth. No standing in line cold.

  0:10-0:20  Ankle-specific warm-up on the wall. Traversing only, lowest angle, V0-V1. Easy foot swaps, slow weight transfers, single-foot matching at low height. Stop traversing early if any lateral tightness shows up. This block exists to confirm the ankle tolerates weight on small holds before you commit to any problem — if it doesn't, the night is over.

  0:20-0:35  Phase A — short V0-V1 problems, 4-7 moves, fully downclimbable, well within the fall zone. One problem, full rest, next problem. No flash attempts on anything above your top warm-up move.

  0:35-0:50  Phase B (optional, gated). V1-V2 only if Phase A was boring-clean. Stay on slab or gentle vertical. No overhangs. Still downclimbable, still well-padded.

  0:50-0:55  Easy traverse wind-down. Foot placement quality check on the way out.

  0:55-1:00  Cool down, walk out.

Hard caps regardless of how you feel: 60 min total, ~40 min actual climbing time on the wall, exit the gym at the 60-min mark even if nothing has fired.

Route selection rules (apply at the wall, not in theory):

  - Grade ceiling V1 for the first half of the session. V2 only as a gated step, not as a goal.
  - Slab and low-angle vertical only. No steep, no overhangs, no roofs.
  - Every move must be downclimbable. If you can't visualize the downclimb, don't try the move.
  - No heel hooks, anywhere, on any hold. A heel hook on a recovering lateral ankle is the single highest-risk bouldering move for your specific injury pattern.
  - No toe hooks, no high-step inversion, no figure-four or flagging that loads the lateral right ankle.
  - No small chip footholds that demand precise edging — pick problems with real foot features.
  - No dynamic or jump moves, no campus moves, no moonboard/kilter style tension.

Fall rules (this is the other half of the plan):

  - No jumping off the wall. Step down or controlled downclimb every time.
  - Stay below "no pad required" height — call it ~8 ft to the highest hand you commit from. Above that, only if pads are full coverage and well-spotted.
  - If a fall would land you on an uneven angle or twisted, don't take the fall — downclimb.
  - Spotting: ask Ren to spot the fall zone, not the catch. Pad positioning matters more than the throw.

Stop criteria (any one of these ends the session — pick the most restrictive):

  1. Any pain in the right ankle, no matter how mild. Lateral tightness, dull ache, anything.
  2. Any sensation of catching, giving way, or instability, on or off the wall.
  3. Pain ≥ 2/10 anywhere — ankle, foot, calf, knee, hip.
  4. Sharp or sudden pain anywhere.
  5. Loss of push-off strength on the right vs left, or any noticeable weakness.
  6. New swelling, warmth, or stiffness during the session.
  7. Gait change off the wall — limping, favoring, hitching.
  8. The warm-up block (0:10-0:20) produces any lateral tightness — done for the night, no Phase A.
  9. Mental state: rushed, fatigued, frustrated, distracted. Climbing when any of those is present is how "fine" becomes a re-sprain.
  10. 60 min elapsed, or ~40 min on the wall, whichever comes first.

Next-day and 24-48 hour gates (these govern what happens after, not just tonight):

  - Tonight is a duration and load test, not clearance for the next session.
  - Walk home counts as part of the test. Note any tightness or awareness in the right ankle on stairs, curbs, uneven sidewalk.
  - Tomorrow morning: stairs, single-leg calf raises, easy forward and lateral hops on the right foot. Stop the moment anything reproduces lateral tightness.
  - No new climbing or soccer until 48 hours of clean response (no pain, swelling, stiffness, instability, no next-morning tightness).
  - Three lateral sprains in roughly ten months is a recurrence pattern. The non-urgent sports-medicine or orthopedic stability eval you've been deferring is still warranted — a clean week after one controlled session doesn't change that, and bouldering-specific loads aren't covered by Sunday's soccer tolerance either.

Tell Ren the cap up front. If Ren is expecting a normal session and you bail at 40 min because the ankle got boring-clean and you've hit the gate, that's the plan working, not the plan failing. "Stopped while it still felt boring" is the right exit, same as the December 2023 slab re-entry.

One thing I want to be honest about rather than smooth over: a heel hook is the move most likely to re-injure a healing lateral ankle in a gym, and you'll see other climbers using them on routes you'll be skipping. That's not a sign you're being overly cautious; it's the specific load vector your injury pattern doesn't tolerate, and "skip heel hooks tonight" is a much smaller cost than a fourth sprain.

Based on the facts you described, this is a pressurized cold-supply leak. The drip rate (every ~8s, faster with the cold tap running) and the dry hot line / dry trap rule out the drain and hot side. The most useful single fact is that the angle stop turns normally — that gives you a real shutoff.

1) Immediate containment and shutoff

  - Close the cold-water angle stop (the small football-shaped handle on the cold supply tube, on the wall or floor of the cabinet). Turn clockwise (righty-tighty), gently, only until it stops. Quarter- to half-turn is typical. If it resists, stop — don't force it.
  - Open the cold faucet fully for 5–10 seconds to depressurize the line, then leave it open so any residual pressure vents through the faucet instead of dripping.
  - Watch the leak for one full minute with the stop closed.
      Drip stops or slows to a stop within a minute → leak is downstream (supply tube or faucet tailpiece). Fixture-side, super can fix tomorrow.
      Drip continues at the same rate → leak is at the angle stop stem or packing (building-side plumbing). Leave the stop closed, leave the faucet open, and use the building's emergency line.
  - Leave the towels and bowl in place; the cabinet is now your only moisture monitor.
  - Don't run the dishwasher or washing machine tonight. They share the cold line and can hide or worsen a leak you can't see.

2) What NOT to tighten or disassemble tonight

  - Don't crank the angle stop past hand resistance with pliers. If it won't close by hand, that's a super-call signal, not a DIY fix.
  - Don't loosen or remove the supply tube nut at either end (the compression fitting at the stop, or the coupling nut at the faucet tailpiece). The ferrule bites into the tube; once disturbed the joint won't reseal without a new ferrule and tube, and you can crack the stop outlet or split the tube.
  - Don't remove the faucet handle, cartridge, or supply elbow to "find the leak." That turns a drip into a spray.
  - Don't use Teflon tape, pipe dope, flex-seal, or epoxy on a pressurized supply joint. They don't reliably fix compression or packing-nut leaks, and tape shreds clog aerators and screens downstream.
  - Don't store anything on the cabinet floor while it's wet — bottles, bins, trash can. Wet cardboard and particle board swell and grow mold within 24–48 hours. Move them out now.

3) How thoroughly to empty and dry the cabinet

  - Pull everything out tonight. Soak standing water with towels; wring into the sink basin (cold is off but the trap still drains).
  - Wipe the cabinet floor, back panel, and underside of the countertop dry. Get the corners where the back panel meets the floor — that joint traps water.
  - Leave the cabinet door open overnight. If you have a small fan, aim it into the cabinet.
  - The bar is the same one you've been using on the bedroom window: dry enough that the back panel and floor read roughly 10% or below on a moisture meter (or feel dry and firm to a finger press by morning), with no softening, darkening, or odor.
  - Recheck in the morning before the super arrives. If the back panel is still damp, soft, darkened, or smells musty, flag that — the cabinet may need more than a plumbing fix.

4) Signs that make this an emergency rather than a tomorrow-super job

  This is the same emergency-line criterion you've already established with management for the bedroom window — active water reaching a place it shouldn't, or signs the building-side system is failing rather than a single fixture joint.

  Call the emergency line tonight if any of these appear:

  - The drip becomes a steady stream, or visibly accelerates even with the angle stop closed.
  - Closing the angle stop does not stop or slow the leak (leak is past the valve, in the wall or under the floor).
  - Water reaches the kitchen floor, migrates into an adjacent cabinet, or approaches any electrical point. You said there's no outlet in this cabinet — still check the kick-plate area, dishwasher plug, or disposal switch.
  - The supply tube bulges, kinks, shows green/white corrosion at the ferrule, or water tracks along the tube instead of dripping from one point.
  - The cabinet base or back panel softens, swells, buckles, or darkens within hours.
  - Water appears below — ceiling of the unit below, or a wet floor outside the kitchen.
  - The hot side starts dripping, or the drain trap begins leaking too. Two simultaneous failures point to pressure or back-up issues, not one bad joint.
  - You lose cold pressure anywhere else in the apartment, or the hot-side / boiler behavior changes.
  - Any discoloration or smell develops in the water when you run a tap.

  If none of those happen overnight, this can wait for the super tomorrow. Close the cold stop, leave the cold faucet open, dry the cabinet as above, and write the super note as: cold-supply fitting drip under the kitchen sink, ~one drip every 8 seconds when the stop is open, faster with the cold tap running; cold angle stop functional; hot side and trap dry. That gives them what they need to bring the right part (supply tube and ferrule, or angle-stop packing, depending on your one-minute test).

Headline: The visible `unset` legend is strong evidence of a contract violation, not a pure presentation artifact. Pure PromQL semantics cannot produce an empty-label result series unless an underlying series carries the label as an empty string. The remaining ambiguity is producer attribution, not artifact-vs-violation.

What the contract says (per Aug 6 rollout basis):
  - Only `prod`, `staging`, `dev` may be published as `deployment_environment` values.
  - Missing input omits the label entirely; no series is published with that label absent.
  - `qa`, unknown, malformed, and arbitrary raw strings are rejected pre-publication; zero resulting series.
  - Cardinality bound = three values.

Why the legend transform cannot manufacture `unset`:
  The query `sum by (deployment_environment) (rate(ingest_points_total[5m]))` requires the label to be present on each underlying series for the result to carry that label. A series that does not have the label at all cannot aggregate into a result series — it is excluded. A result series with empty `deployment_environment` can therefore only exist if an underlying series has the label set to empty string. The dashboard's "empty → unset" rename is a display-time substitution; it does not invent a series that was not in the query result. The most parsimonious read of the visible `unset` is: a series with `deployment_environment=""` exists in TSDB and is being summed.

Why that is itself a contract violation:
  The rollout spec says missing input omits the label entirely. Publishing a series with `deployment_environment=""` is not omission; it is publication of a fourth value (the empty string). This breaches the cardinality bound of 3 and is the failure mode the pre-pub rejection gate was designed to prevent.

Residual ambiguity that still needs evidence:
  - Producer attribution: who is publishing the empty-string series? The rollup-service (contract-bound producer — direct violation), or a different path (OTel collector direct export, metrics-router self-publish, sidecar)? If the latter, the cardinality breach is real but the rollup-service contract may not be the breach point.
  - Time-of-appearance: did this series exist before Aug 6, or did it appear with the rollout?
  - Whether the dashboard is doing anything beyond the stated query (e.g., a synthetic "no-label" bucket rendered from a separate count).

Raw-series evidence required:

  1. TSDB series enumeration.
       Query equivalent: `count by (__name__, deployment_environment) ({__name__="ingest_points_total"})` or the TSDB admin API listing every distinct label-value pair for `ingest_points_total`.
       Expected under contract: exactly three values — prod, staging, dev.
       If four appear including empty string: contract violation confirmed at the data layer.

  2. Underlying label value of the `unset` series.
       Print the raw `deployment_environment` value on each matching series (not the legend-rendered word).
       Empty string ("") → label is present-but-empty, which is itself the breach.
       Truly absent (no label at all) → standard query semantics cannot have produced this series; must be a separate aggregation or synthetic dashboard bucket.

  3. Producer attribution.
       Identify which path published the offending series: rollup-service output, metrics-router self-published series, OTel collector direct export, or a sidecar.
       rollup-service → direct breach of the rollout spec; owner is the mapped rollup-service owner, not Alex.
       other producer → separate path breach; expand investigation to that producer's label normalization; do not assume the rollup-service contract is the breach point.

  4. Time-of-appearance.
       When did the `unset` series first appear? Before or after the Aug 6 rollout start?
       After rollout → defect introduced by this change; revert or fix before continuing the 48h observation.
       Before → pre-existing artifact; verify the rollout did not amplify or surface new traffic into it.

  5. OTel input mapping.
       For samples feeding the `unset` rate window, inspect the originating OTel span/point attribute `deployment.environment`.
       Attribute truly absent → normalization stage should have omitted the label; empty-string output is a defect.
       Attribute present but blank → blank-handling defect.
       Attribute present as arbitrary string → that string should have been rejected pre-publication; rejection gate failed.

  6. Total reconciliation.
       Sum of `rate(ingest_points_total[5m])` across all four legend series should equal `rate(sum without (deployment_environment) (ingest_points_total[5m]))`.
       Divergence by the `unset` rate → real backend series, not synthetic.
       Match → either no `unset` series (legend artifact) or an exact coincidence (treat as real until TSDB enumeration says otherwise).

Classification gates once evidence is in hand:
  - TSDB shows four label values including empty string: CONTRACT VIOLATION. Halt the 48h observation, page the mapped producer (rollup-service owner if attribution points there), revert the producer change, treat the rollout as paused.
  - TSDB shows exactly three values and totals reconcile: PURE LEGEND ARTIFACT (the dashboard must be doing something beyond a plain `sum by`). File a dashboard bug; no production action; continue 48h observation.
  - TSDB shows three values but totals diverge with a phantom `unset`: producer outside rollup-service publishing a series with empty label; investigate that path separately; rollout remains paused until cardinality is bounded again.

What is NOT sufficient to classify:
  - The dashboard view alone.
  - Raw samples beside the chart (sample inspector may show a post-filtered subset that differs from backend scope).
  - The Aug 6 opening health check (covered the first window only; does not retroactively prove absence of drift hours later).
  - The legend text itself (it is a rendering of label values, not a distinct signal).

Required next step before classification: pull the TSDB series enumeration and the producer-side label-value map for `ingest_points_total` over the same window the chart displays. Do not advance the 48h observation to a production conclusion, and do not declare either pure artifact or violation, until both are in hand. Ownership stays with the mapped rollup-service / metrics-router / OTel owners per the rollout basis — Alex is observing, not implementing.

The remaining risk over the next 48 hours is the damp cabinet base holding moisture long enough to swell or grow mildew, plus a slow-developing leak at the new connection that wouldn't have shown up in the first 24 hours.

DRYING (next 48 hours)

  1. Keep the cabinet empty and doors open. Don't put anything back yet.
  2. Move air through it. A small fan on low, aimed into the cabinet base (not directly at the supply lines), does most of the work. Continuous low airflow beats a one-time wipe-down. If no fan, an open cabinet in a normally ventilated apartment is fine.
  3. Lay a folded dry towel on the cabinet floor directly under the cold supply line and shutoff. Replace it if it shows any wetness. This makes a slow leak visible fast instead of pooling invisibly on the base.
  4. Optional: a cheap pin-type moisture meter (~$10-15) on the cabinet floor gives you a hard number. Particle board / MDF under ~12-15% with a downward trend is the goal. Skip if you don't already have one — touch and smell are sufficient.
  5. Skip desiccants, heaters, and "drying sprays." A fan is enough; a space heater near particle board can do more harm than good.

MONITORING SCHEDULE

  Check at these moments; each one takes under a minute:
    - Morning, before first use of the cold tap
    - After the first cold-water run of the day (run ~30 seconds, then check the connection and towel)
    - Midday, quick visual
    - Evening, after the last cold-water run
    - Once overnight if convenient

  At the connection, look for:
    - Beads of water at the new ferrule, supply tube, valve, or valve stem
    - White crust or mineral deposits forming (a slow-seep signature)
    - Dampness on the towel that wasn't there at the previous check
    - Drip from the valve stem or handle base

  In the cabinet, look for:
    - Cabinet floor at the original damp patch — should trend from slightly damp to dry, not stay the same or get damper
    - Firmness under gentle finger pressure on the base and back wall — firm, not soft or spongy
    - Edges and back panel — no new darkening, tide lines, bubbling, or raised seams
    - Smell — neutral, or a faint "drying water" smell is fine; musty / earthy / mildew is not

CALL THE SUPER BACK IF ANY OF THESE SHOW UP

  Renewed leak:
    - Any drip from the new ferrule, supply tube, shutoff, or valve stem
    - Wet towel under the line that wasn't there at the previous check
    - Drip rate that increases when the cold tap is running

  Moisture not drying:
    - Cabinet floor still damp at 48h, or getting damper
    - Dampness spreading beyond the original patch
    - Moisture appearing on the cabinet walls or back panel that wasn't there before

  Material damage:
    - Any soft, spongy, or swollen spot in the base or walls
    - Particle board bubbling, flaking, or puffy edges
    - Laminate peeling or bubbling
    - Visible warping or raised seams

  Staining that suggests ongoing wetness or mold:
    - New dark spots, wet rings, or tide lines
    - Black, green, or gray spotting (mold / mildew)

  Odor:
    - Musty, earthy, or mildew smell that wasn't there before, or that persists with the cabinet open and airflow running

  Water elsewhere:
    - Water on the floor outside the cabinet
    - Water appearing below or beside the cabinet
    - Dampness on the wall behind the sink

WHEN IT'S REASONABLE TO CLOSE AND USE THE CABINET

  You can put things back when ALL of the following hold at the same time:
    - At least 48 hours have passed since the repair
    - The connection has been dry at every check, including after multiple cold-water cycles
    - The cabinet floor is dry to the touch (or matches the dry wood around the patch)
    - No soft spots, no new swelling, no new staining
    - No musty smell

  If all of that holds, close the doors and return light items. Avoid stacking heavy storage directly on the previously-damp patch for another week or two — particle board that has been wet once is weaker than new even after drying. A liner or tray under stored items is cheap insurance against a future leak.

  Borderline cases (faint residual smell, slight dampness at the back edge, very minor tide-line staining that's clearly old and fully dry): give it another 24-48 hours with the cabinet open and the fan on. Old tide-line staining from a prior, fully-dried leak is normal and not a reason to keep the cabinet open. Ongoing dampness or smell is.

Bounded note: the 12-15% moisture threshold and the 48-hour minimum are standard moisture-remediation ranges, not measurements from your specific cabinet. Treat them as guideposts, not pass/fail numbers.

Bicycle tube slow-leak diagnosis and repair. The pattern you describe — "held pressure Friday, flat Saturday morning, faint hiss I can't localize, no obvious tread damage" — is consistent with a slow leak from a small tread puncture, a valve-base leak, a spoke-hole leak (rim tape failure), or a bead/rim interface leak. Here's how to find it and verify it before riding.

0. Quick reality check before starting
- The tube is currently flat. Do not trust reinflation alone — a slow leak will re-deflate within hours. The goal below is to find and remove the cause, not to confirm the tube can briefly hold air.
- You'll need: a basin of water or a spray bottle with soapy water, a marker, plastic tire levers, a pump with gauge, and either patches (vulcanizing fluid + sandpaper) or a spare tube. A rag is useful for feeling inside the tire.

1. Valve and hiss localization (tube still in tire)
- Inflate to firm — enough to feel air, not so hard it bulges.
- Wet your bare fingertips. Slowly sweep: tread, both sidewalls, valve stem and base, rim/tire interface, and along the spokes from outside.
- Pay special attention to the valve base (where stem meets the rubber). A pinhole there is one of the most common causes of "can't localize." Soapy water there will reveal it immediately.
- Spray or brush soapy water on: valve stem and base, both tire beads all the way around, the valve hole in the rim. Bubbles appear at the leak.
- If the leak is at the bead (rim/tire interface), the cause is usually a burred rim edge, a mis-seated bead, or a tube pinched at install.
- If you still can't localize: a short piece of hose or a straw to your ear lets you sweep the tire by sound. Move slowly.

2. Tube removal and puncture location
- Fully deflate. Presta: unscrew the small locknut and push the valve through the rim from inside. Schrader: just push it through.
- Starting opposite the valve, push one bead off the rim. Plastic tire levers are fine; if the tire is tight, two levers a few inches apart is safer than one. Do not use a screwdriver — it will cut the tube and possibly the rim tape.
- Pull the tube out. Note its orientation (a small mark on the tube and tire now saves time later).
- Inflate the tube outside the tire, firm but not rock-hard.
- Locate the puncture:
  - Submerge sections in a basin of water, rotating slowly. Even a tiny leak produces a steady trail of small bubbles.
  - Alternative: hold the inflated tube near your cheek/lips and sweep slowly. Escaping air feels cool.
  - Alternative: in a quiet room, rotate the tube past your ear.
- Mark the hole with a marker. Note whether it's on the tread side, sidewall side, or near the valve base.
- Check the valve itself: try unscrewing the core (Schrader) and reseating it firmly. Inspect a Presta stem for cracks. Wet the stem-tube junction and look for bubbles.

3. Inside-tire and rim-tape inspection (this prevents a repeat flat)
- With the tube out, run a finger carefully around the entire inside of the casing — tread side and sidewall side. Use a rag if you suspect sharp embedded debris. Common offenders: glass shards (often invisible), wire, thorns, staples, even a small zip tie tooth.
- Look for: cuts, exposed casing cords, bulges, anything that punctured from outside.
- Inspect the sidewall — cuts here mean tire replacement, not patch.
- Inspect the rim tape:
  - It must fully cover every spoke hole. Any visible spoke hole means the tube will eventually be cut there.
  - Tape not torn, frayed, slipped, or wrinkled.
  - Tape width should cover the full rim well, not just the spoke holes.
  - Old narrow strip-over-spoke-holes tape compresses over time and develops gaps even if it looks intact — replace if old or visibly gapping.
- Inspect the rim:
  - Run a finger around the rim well. Any sharp edge or burr can cut a tube.
  - Check each spoke nipple for sharp edges.
  - Check the rim seam for roughness.
  - Confirm the rim is true — spin the wheel in the frame and look for hop or wobble. A bent rim can pinch the tube.

4. When patch is enough vs. when to replace

Tube
- Patch is adequate if: puncture is small (under ~5 mm, single hole), not at the valve base, the rest of the tube looks healthy (rubber pliable, no dry rot, no other thin spots), and there are fewer than ~3 prior patches.
- Replace the tube if:
  - Puncture is closer than ~2–3 cm to the valve base — patches do not seal well there.
  - It is a tear or long cut, not a puncture.
  - Multiple holes in close proximity, or many holes total.
  - Valve stem is cracked, cut, or the core will not seat.
  - Tube feels stiff, chalky, cracked when bent, or visibly aged (years, or stored in heat/cold).
  - It already has several patches — past a few, the wall is weakened.

Tire
- Keep the tire if: the puncture was from glass/thorn, the casing is intact, no cuts reach the cords, no bulge, tread still has life (check wear indicators if your tire has them), and the bead seats cleanly.
- Replace the tire if:
  - Sidewall cut exposing casing cords.
  - Tread cut deep enough to expose casing.
  - Any bulge (separated casing — failure imminent).
  - Repeated flats in the same spot (casing damaged).
  - Tire is old, dried, cracked, or the rubber feels hard.
  - Bead is damaged, will not seat, or does not match the rim type.

Valve
- Schrader: usually fixable by tightening or replacing the core (cheap, standard tool). If the stem is bent or cut, replace the tube.
- Presta: cores are usually not user-replaceable. Replace the tube if the stem is cut, the cone will not seat, or there is air at the stem-tube junction that tightening does not stop.
- If the valve hole in the rim is ovalized (wallowed out), a new tube will not help — that needs rim repair or replacement.

Rim tape
- Replace any rim tape that is torn, has gaps at spoke holes, has slipped, is wrinkled, or is the wrong width for the rim.
- Replace even if it looks okay if it is the old-style narrow strip-over-spoke-holes on a high-pressure tire — high-pressure tubes need full rim-well coverage.
- Acceptable: dedicated cloth rim tape (good), quality nylon/poly tape, or rubber rim strips. Not acceptable: electrical tape, gaffer tape, or generic tape — these compress, slip, or fail at the spoke holes.

5. What must be verified before riding

The bar is not "the tube holds air now." The bar is that the repair is sound and the cause of the original flat has been removed.

Before remounting
- The cause of the puncture is identified and removed from the tire (or the tire is replaced). Do not reinstall a tube over a sharp object you did not find.
- If you patched, the patch is fully cured per the kit instructions — typically 2–5 minutes for vulcanizing fluid, longer for cold patches.
- Tube reinserted with correct orientation; valve is straight, not angled.
- Tire bead fully seated all the way around on both sides, even distance outside the rim lip, no bulges or unseated spots. Low pressure helps seat the bead; bring it up only after both sides look right.
- Valve stem is straight; valve nut (if any) is just snug — over-tightening cuts the tube.
- Pressure is set within the tire sidewall's printed range, not above max.

Static checks (before any ride)
- Inflate to target pressure.
- Wait 10 minutes. Recheck pressure — no audible hiss, gauge reading has not dropped meaningfully. A few PSI in cool ambient is fine; a clear drop means the repair failed or the cause is still present.
- Spin the wheel in the frame. Tire tracks true, no visible hop, wobble, or unseated bead.
- Squeeze the tire in different spots — feel for anything embedded that you may have missed.

Dynamic check
- Ride a short loop (a few blocks) at low effort. Listen for hiss, feel for handling changes.
- After the ride, recheck pressure. If it is unchanged, the repair is holding under load.
- Wait 30–60 minutes (or overnight) and recheck once more. A slow leak usually shows up here, before it strands you mid-route.

Acceptance gate: pressure at target, holds across 10 minutes sitting, holds across a short ride, and holds across an hour of sitting afterward. Anything short of that and the wheel is not ready for a longer ride. If the leak recurs, do not just re-patch — either the cause was not removed or there is a second cause (rim, rim tape, or valve).

Review of the execution sheet before the internal rehearsal runs.

The August 6 instrumentation dry run cleared the instrumentation prerequisite for preparing the rehearsal, but preparation is not proof that tenant isolation passed, the data-contract stage stays closed, and customer access stays closed. One correlated dry run is evidence about that run, not a general pattern.

The sheet lists one stop condition: "stop if one tenant's rendered response contains the other tenant's fixture data." That covers a single late-cycle data leak in the response stage. It misses per-phase and per-evidence failures that would already have broken tenant isolation upstream of the rendered output.

Missing stop conditions:

  1. Authorization span correlation stop: stop if the wrapper span does not carry the synthetic-tenant correlation field for the request's tenant, carries the wrong tenant, or returns a 2xx response for a denied context. The August 6 dry run showed distinct request identifiers; the rehearsal must verify they map to the same tenant end-to-end.

  2. Cache tuple correlation stop: stop if the normalized cache tuple for a request does not contain the synthetic-tenant component, if the tuple for tenant A equals tenant B's tuple (key collision on shared service_id=checkout), or if the ordered input fields composing the tuple are not all visible in the trace. The August 2 dry run did not record deploy-card cache-key components; the August 6 run exposed the tuple, but the rehearsal sheet must require its visibility as a stop, not just a recorded field.

  3. Adapter span correlation stop: stop if an adapter span lacks the synthetic-tenant correlation field, carries only the shared service_id without the tenant, or appears without a matching wrapper attribution (orphaned adapter activity). The August 2 dry run's adapter spans contained only the shared service identifier; the sheet must require the correlation field to be present, not just the span to exist.

  4. Denied-case stop per phase: stop if a not_authorized request invokes any adapter or renders any non-403 body, or if the 403 envelope omits the not_authorized reason. Per the data-contract stage, denied paths must remain zero-adapter.

  5. Cross-stage correlation stop: stop if authorization, cache, adapter, and response traces for any single request do not all carry the same synthetic-tenant ID. This is the shared-correlation check the sheet is missing — loss of correlation in any one of the four trace types must halt, not just a leak in the response.

  6. Forbidden-field stop: stop if any rendered response contains raw incident references, room metadata, employee identifiers, individual comparisons, unpublished ownership, or internal fallback. These six categories were closed in the data-contract stage and must remain absent across deploy-card, ownership, incident-summary, and explicit-unknown phases.

  7. Customer-access flag stop: stop if the customer access flag is enabled at any point during any phase, including between phases. "Verify before setup" is necessary but not sufficient; the check must extend to during and after each phase.

  8. Per-phase isolation stop: stop the current phase on any of the above, and do not advance to the next phase with the same synthetic tenants until the cause is identified and the instrumentation is re-confirmed against the August 6 prerequisite.

  9. Rehearsal-level stop: stop the entire rehearsal if any phase fails any stop. A single successful phase is evidence about that phase; a failed phase halts, it does not accumulate.

Missing evidence ownership (mapped owners retain implementation and operational responsibility; this is not Alex's catch-all):

  1. Synthetic-tenant setup owner: who creates tenants A and B with shared service_id=checkout, confirms their fixture data is disjoint, and confirms customer access is disabled before setup. The sheet must name this person, not "the team."

  2. Customer-access verifier per phase: who checks customer access is disabled before setup, during each phase, and after each phase, and signs each check. This is the named owner the sheet is missing.

  3. Per-phase evidence recorder: who records the authorization span, normalized cache tuple, adapter span, and rendered response evidence for each of the four phases.

  4. Cross-stage correlation verifier: who asserts that all four trace types for each request carry the same synthetic-tenant ID. This must be independent of the recorder; otherwise verification collapses into implementation.

  5. Denied-case verifier: who asserts 403 + zero adapter calls + forbidden-field absence for the not_authorized run inside each phase.

  6. Forbidden-field verifier: who scans rendered output across all four phases for the six forbidden field categories.

  7. Stop-condition enforcer: when a stop fires, who halts the rehearsal. Alex does not operate the run; the enforcer must be a named mapped role with authority to stop the current phase and the rehearsal as a whole.

  8. Per-phase acceptance: who accepts each phase's evidence package before the next phase begins. The sheet does not state whether phases run sequentially with gates between them or in one continuous run. Sequential gating with named per-phase acceptance is the safer boundary, and the sheet should say so.

Until each stop condition and each named owner above appears in the execution sheet, the internal rehearsal should not run. The instrumentation prerequisite is cleared; the execution sheet is not. Customer access remains closed. The data-contract stage is not reopened by this review.

PRE-INSTALL VERIFICATION (do these before the new tube goes in):

1. Re-inspect the rim valve hole specifically. Run a fingertip around the inside and outside edges. The valve-stem split points to this area. Any burr, ridge, or sharp edge — dress it smooth with a small file or fine sandpaper, then wipe clean.
2. Check the rim tape at the valve hole. Confirm a clean, centered opening that doesn't leave a hard edge. Confirm it still fully covers every spoke hole and lies flat (no bunching, no slip toward the rim well).
3. Inspect the tire bead area, both sides, with a finger inside the bead channel. You're looking for cuts, exposed casing wire, or fraying — even though the tread looked intact Saturday, bead damage is where a future failure will come from.
4. Confirm exact size match. The new tube's printed size must match the tire's printed size on the sidewall exactly (e.g., 700x25c, 27.5x2.1, 26x1.75). Wheel diameter and tire width both have to match.
5. Confirm valve type and length. Schrader vs Presta must match the rim. Stem length must clear the rim depth plus your pump head — too short means the pump can't seat. If the tube has a stem nut, the nut goes on the outside of the rim.
6. Pre-inflate the new tube with just enough air to give it shape. Visually and by feel inspect the entire tube, especially the valve-stem junction, for any defect, blister, or thinning. Then deflate fully before installing.

INSTALLATION:

1. Insert the valve stem through the rim valve hole straight and perpendicular to the rim. Not angled. An angled valve means the tube is being pinched between the bead and the rim at the valve hole.
2. Tuck the tube into the tire all the way around the circumference. Tube should lie flat with no twists, no bunching, not pinched between the bead and the casing.
3. Seat the tire bead by hand, starting at the valve and working away in both directions. Hands-only is safest. If you must use a lever, the lever goes between the tire bead and the rim only — never between the tube and the rim, never trapping the tube.
4. As the last bit of bead goes on, recheck at the valve: the tube must be fully inside the tire, the bead fully inside the rim hook, the valve pulling straight up out of the hole.
5. Visually inspect both sides of the tire around the full circumference. The tube should not be visible at the bead line anywhere. The valve should pull straight up with no lean.

PRE-INFLATION SEATING:

1. Add just enough air to give the tire shape — about 10–20 PSI, sometimes less. The goal is to pop both beads evenly into the rim hooks all the way around. Don't go to full pressure yet.
2. With both hands, work the tire circumferentially at this low pressure: squeeze and rotate slightly side to side. This helps the beads seat evenly into the hooks.
3. Check the bead line. Many tires have a thin colored line near the bead. That line should be visible all the way around on both sides, parallel to the rim, with no section dipping below the rim edge. If a section is low, deflate, push the tube back into the tire on that side, and reseat.
4. Recheck the valve: it must pull straight up. If it's leaning, deflate, ease the tube back into the tire on the leaning side, and reseat.
5. Confirm no bulges or uneven sections in the tire profile. An uneven section means the tube is pinched or the bead isn't seated there.

INFLATION:

1. Inflate in stages: ~20 PSI, pause and recheck bead line and valve straightness; ~40 PSI, recheck; up to target.
2. Target pressure is on the tire sidewall — use that printed range. Typical ranges: road 80–130 PSI, gravel/hybrid 50–80 PSI, mountain 25–50 PSI. Pick within the range for your weight, surface, and feel.
3. Use a pump with a gauge. Don't estimate.
4. Stop and investigate any sudden pressure drop, audible hiss at the bead, or visible bubbling. That indicates a pinch or unseated bead, not a slow leak.

PINCH-AVOIDANCE (recap, in priority order):

- Hands-only seating whenever you can
- Lever only between bead and rim, never between tube and rim
- Valve in perpendicular, not angled
- Tube fully tucked inside tire before any lever work
- Low pressure for seating, then stage up
- Bead line visible evenly around before going to full pressure
- Valve still straight before going to full pressure

PRE-RIDE VERIFICATION (all of these, in this order):

1. Hold check at full pressure. With the wheel either in or out of the frame, listen and feel at the valve, around both beads, and over the tire surface for at least 60 seconds. Optional: soapy water on valve and bead, look for bubbles. Any hiss = deflate and reseat, do not ride.
2. Spin check. Wheel rotates freely, no binding, no brake rub, no grinding. Tire runs concentric with no visible wobble or hop. For rim brakes, check clearance both sides. For disc brakes, confirm the rotor sits cleanly in the caliper and pads don't drag with the brake released.
3. Axle check. Quick-release: skewer fully closed with the right resistance, wheel fully seated in dropouts. Test by trying to lift the bike with the brake applied — the wheel should not shift. For thru-axle, tightened to spec, lever fully closed. For disc-brake rear wheels, confirm the rotor is in the caliper before you close the skewer, not after.
4. Brake function. Squeeze each brake. Lever should feel firm, pads engage, wheel shouldn't rotate when fully braked. No grinding or excessive pad drag on discs.
5. Stationary bounce. Straddle the bike (or hold it) and put your full weight onto the bars and saddle. Feel for any soft, hissing, or abnormal feel. Listen for any tick or hiss.
6. Low-speed roll test. Walk the bike 10–20 m, then ride at walking pace for another 20–30 m with a finger over each brake. Check tracking straight, no pulling, no brake rub, no ticking, no hiss.
7. Short functional ride. 2–5 minutes at normal pace, including one deliberate moderate stop from speed, one easy corner each direction, and one firmer stop. Listen and feel for any hiss, drift, vibration, or soft feel. After the ride, recheck pressure with the gauge — a slow leak shows as a small drop over this period; a tube losing more than a couple PSI in 5 minutes needs investigation.

Ride only when every one of those is clean. "Tube holds air" is not a ride-clear signal — the failure mode you saw Saturday (split at the valve-stem junction) is consistent with a pinched or mis-seated tube that can hold pressure for hours before failing.

FOR YOUR SPECIFIC FAILURE MODE (valve-stem split):

- Most common causes are a sharp edge at the rim valve hole, a mis-sized or wrong-shape tube, or the valve installed at an angle. You said rim tape looked intact and you didn't see a sharp rim edge — re-check the rim valve hole specifically with a fingertip. That is the area.
- Confirm the new tube is the exact size match to the tire, not "close enough."
- Confirm the new tube's valve type and length match your rim.
- Confirm the valve goes in straight and stays straight through the full seating and inflation sequence.

DIAGNOSTIC PRINCIPLE FIRST

The single most useful test is the SWAP-SIDE TEST. It tells you whether
the rub comes from a wheel that is sitting off-center in the frame
(fixable in the bike) or from a rim that has true lateral runout (a
wheel problem, not a brake problem). Do the brake-centering work ONLY
after this test says the rim is true relative to the frame. Adjusting
the brake before that is exactly the masking move you want to avoid.

WHAT YOU ALREADY KNOW (FROM YOU)

  - Tube held pressure overnight, bead evenly seated.
  - Wheel reinstalled, rim drags lightly against one pad once per
    revolution (so the contact is rhythmic with rotation, not constant).
  - Wheel is not visibly bent, axle APPEARS seated.
  - Brake did not rub before the tube install.
  - You will not ride until the wheel spins freely.

That last point is the gate. The sequence below ends only when the
wheel spins freely AND all pre-ride checks pass.

PRECONDITIONS BEFORE YOU START

  - Bike stable. A repair stand is best. Flipped upside down on the
    bars and saddle is acceptable if the bar/saddle finish is protected.
  - Tire stays at riding pressure. Deflating is unnecessary and risks
    disturbing the evenly-seated bead you already have.
  - Brake lever NOT engaged. You want to see pad-to-rim clearance
    directly.
  - A flashlight or work lamp so you can clearly see rim-to-pad gap on
    BOTH sides as the wheel rotates.
  - A small piece of tape or a pencil to mark the rim at the contact
    point.

PHASE 1 — SWAP-SIDE TEST (the discriminator)

Goal: figure out whether the rim is laterally warped, or whether the
wheel is sitting off-center in the frame.

  1. With the wheel installed as it is now, slowly rotate the wheel by
     hand. Watch the rim-to-pad gap on both sides of the brake. Note
     which pad it approaches, and approximately where in the rotation
     (e.g. "near the valve hole at top," or "opposite the valve at
     bottom").

  2. Mark the rim contact point with a small piece of tape or pencil.

  3. Remove the wheel.
     - QR: open the lever, slide the wheel out. Note which side the
       lever was on.
     - Thru-axle: unthread fully.
     - Nutted axle: loosen both nuts.

  4. Reinstall the wheel on the OPPOSITE side from how it was mounted.
     For QR this means the lever ends up on the other dropout. You may
     need to flip the QR around. The wheel rotates 180° around its
     own axle as part of this step — that is expected and is what makes
     the test work.

  5. Re-seat the axle carefully into the dropouts BEFORE applying any
     tension. Push the axle straight up into both dropouts so it
     bottoms on both sides. Hold it there with one hand while you
     bring the QR up to tension with the other. Letting the wheel
     "hang" on one side as you tension will seat it crooked.

  6. QR tension reference: with the adjusting nut on the opposite
     side from the lever, finger-tighten until the lever just begins
     to offer resistance when closed about halfway. Then close the
     lever fully. The closed lever should require firm hand pressure
     — enough to leave a slight imprint in your palm — but you
     should NOT need a fist to close it. If you can spin the closed
     lever freely, it is too loose. If you have to gorilla-grip it,
     you are over-tensioning.

  7. Spin the wheel and observe the rub. Two outcomes:

     A) The rub is now on the OTHER pad / other side of the brake.
        The mark on the rim is now at the OPPOSITE rotational point.
        Interpretation: the rim is laterally TRUE (not warped). The
        wheel was sitting off-center in the frame. Go to PHASE 2.

     B) The rub is STILL on the SAME pad / same side of the brake.
        The mark on the rim is still at the same rotational point
        relative to the brake (because the rim's lateral profile is
        what determines contact, and the profile is attached to the
        wheel, not the frame).
        Interpretation: the rim has TRUE LATERAL RUNOUT. It is
        warped or out-of-true. Go to PHASE 3.
        DO NOT adjust the brake to compensate. A warped rim is a
        wheel problem, not a brake problem.

  8. (Useful confirmation) Reinstall the wheel back on its ORIGINAL
     side. The original behavior should return. This proves the
     test is reading wheel/frame centering, not noise.

PHASE 2 — RIM IS TRUE, WHEEL IS OFF-CENTER IN THE FRAME

This is the most common outcome after a wheel has been removed and
reinstalled. The fix is mechanical alignment, not brake adjustment.

  - Wipe both dropout faces and the axle ends clean. A small piece
    of grit on one dropout face can tilt the axle a fraction of a
    millimeter — enough to shift the rim noticeably.

  - QR skewer assembly: confirm both springs are present and
    oriented correctly. The narrow end of each spring goes IN toward
    the hub. The wide end sits against the dropout face. A flipped
    or missing spring changes effective QR length by a couple of mm.

  - Equal axle depth in dropouts: with the QR open, push the wheel
    straight up into both dropouts until the axle bottoms. Hold it
    there while you bring up the QR. Asymmetric seating is the
    most common cause of a wheel sitting off-center.

  - QR tension calibration as in Phase 1, step 6.

  - For nutted axles: tighten the non-drive side first until snug,
    then the drive side, alternating in quarter-turns so the wheel
    does not pull to one side. Final tightness firm, not violent.

  - Eyeball centering: with axle seated and tensioned, look from
    above the rear of the bike straight down the seat tube. The
    tire should be equidistant from the left and right chainstays.
    Equal gaps both sides. If one gap is visibly smaller, re-seat —
    do not "fix" it by moving the brake.

  - Spin test: wheel should now spin freely, OR with equal light
    drag on both sides (a small amount of symmetric drag is normal
    on some rim brakes). The test is whether the rub is unilateral
    and rhythmic with the wheel position. It should not be.

  - If the wheel now spins clean, go to PHASE 4 for a small
    brake-center verification.

PHASE 3 — RIM IS ACTUALLY WARPED (lateral runout)

Do not adjust the brake to mask this. The rim's profile is not flat
side-to-side as it should be. Centering the brake to compensate
produces uneven pad wear and reduced braking.

  - Confirm by feel: with the wheel out of the bike, hold the axle
    in both hands. Slowly rotate the rim past your thumb held
    about 1–2 mm from the rim surface near the pad contact area.
    You should feel no lateral deviation. If you do, the rim is
    laterally untrue.

  - Confirm by sight: lay the wheel on a flat surface with the tire
    inflated. Sight along the rim profile against a straight edge
    (a long ruler, a level, the edge of a doorframe). Watch for
    side-to-side deviation. Even 1–2 mm of deviation is enough to
    cause a rhythmic rub.

  - What likely happened: a tube install should not warp a rim.
    The candidates are a hard drop of the wheel during the work,
    a tire lever that slipped against a spoke and partially turned
    a nipple, or the wheel resting awkwardly while off the bike.
    Since the brake did not rub before removal and the rim now has
    runout, something changed during the tube install. Find it
    rather than paper over it.

  - Quick spoke check: with the wheel in hand, squeeze pairs of
    adjacent spokes near the affected area. They should feel
    evenly tensioned. An obviously loose or sloppy spoke relative
    to its neighbors is a likely culprit and can sometimes be
    re-tensioned by hand — a quarter-turn clockwise on the nipple
    at a time, checking spin and feel after each. If you are not
    comfortable doing this, take it to a shop.

  - Resolution options:
      (a) Bike-shop wheel true: usually cheap and fast.
      (b) Wheel replacement if the rim is bent beyond truing
          tolerance or multiple spokes are damaged.
      (c) Riding is not safe until the rim runs true under the
          pads.

PHASE 4 — BRAKE CENTERING (only after the rim is confirmed true)

Because the brake did not rub before the tube install, the brake's
own centering should not have changed. Most likely you will do
little or nothing here. If you do adjust, treat it as a fine
correction, not a mask for a wheel problem.

For V-brakes / cantilever / sidepull calipers (rim brakes):

  - With the wheel installed and true, look at pad-to-rim clearance
    on both sides. Each pad should sit roughly parallel to the rim
    and contact the braking surface (not the tire, not below the
    rim).

  - Squeeze the brake lever firmly once to seat the pads to their
    rest position. Release. Look again.

  - If one pad is noticeably closer to the rim than the other, the
    caliper is offset.

  - On V-brakes there is typically a small centering screw at the
    brakearm pivot; turn it a quarter-turn at a time, alternating
    sides if there are two, until both pads are equidistant from
    the rim.

  - On sidepull calipers (road), centering is via the single
    centering screw on the caliper body, OR via the spring tension
    set by the pad-height washers.

  - On linear-pull / V-brakes with separate spring adjusters, you
    can dial one side's spring tension a half-turn to shift the
    caliper laterally.

  - Re-spin after each adjustment. The wheel should spin freely
    through full rotation with the brake not engaged.

  - Confirm simultaneous engagement: squeeze the lever firmly. Both
    pads should contact the rim at the same moment. If one hits
    first, the caliper is still off; adjust and retest.

For mechanical disc brakes (only if your bike is disc, not rim):

  - Inspect the rotor for lateral runout by spinning and watching it
    pass the caliper window. A bent rotor will visibly wobble.

  - If the rotor is true, recenter the caliper: loosen the caliper
    mounting bolts a half-turn, squeeze the brake lever firmly (this
    self-centers the pads against the rotor), keep the lever
    squeezed while you retighten the bolts evenly. Release.

  - If the rotor is bent, true it with a rotor truing tool or take
    it to a shop. Do NOT loosen the caliper bolts and shift the
    caliper to compensate — same masking problem.

PRE-RIDE CHECKS — ALL MUST PASS

Do not ride until every one of these is satisfied.

  1. Wheel spins freely through full rotation with brake NOT
     engaged. No rub, no ticking, no clicking. Listen AND watch.

  2. Pad-to-rim gap is symmetric on both sides (rim brakes). For
     disc, rotor sits centered in the caliper slot.

  3. Brake lever pull: both pads (or both pistons, on disc)
     engage at the same moment. Lever does not bottom out on the
     bar.

  4. Brake lever release: lever returns fully, pads retract
     fully, no residual drag when the lever is released.

  5. Axle / QR: axle fully seated in both dropouts. QR lever
     closes with firm hand pressure, leaves a slight palm
     imprint, you can twist the closed lever slightly but cannot
     freely spin it. For nutted axles, both nuts firm.

  6. Wheel centered between the chainstays (eyeball from above
     the saddle, looking down the seat tube). Equal gaps both
     sides.

  7. No visible vertical wobble when spun (a different problem
     from lateral runout — a vertical hop means a rim dent or
     flat spot, also grounds for not riding).

  8. Spokes feel evenly tensioned (no obviously loose spoke pair)
     on a quick squeeze-check.

  9. Tire: bead still evenly seated, pressure holds, no hiss on
     a 60-second listen at the valve and along the bead.

 10. Walk-speed roll: walk the bike forward 10–20 feet while
     listening for rub, ticking, or wobble. None acceptable.

 11. Slow roll in a quiet area: low speed, apply each brake
     independently then both together. Bike tracks straight,
     brakes firmly, releases cleanly.

If any check fails, do not ride. Diagnose, fix, recheck.

WHAT TO BRING TO A SHOP IF YOU DEFER

If the swap-side test points to a warped rim, or any check above
fails and you cannot isolate it, the diagnosis you bring to a shop
is enough on its own:

  - The wheel rubs one pad once per revolution.
  - The rub does not change pad side when the wheel is flipped
    in the frame, so the rim has lateral runout.
  - The brake did not rub before the tube was replaced.
  - Please true or replace the wheel.
