Bottom line: this is a client-interpretation problem, not accounting loss. Sphere's counters close exactly: 11,760 accepted + 240 rejected = 12,000 attempted. There is no gap and no point is unaccounted for on the server side. The "240-point discrepancy" exists only because the client is conflating "submitted in the HTTP body" with "delivered into the pipeline."

Why the dashboard is wrong

The OTLP/HTTP partial-success response is the contract. When ingest-edge returns HTTP 200 with a body whose `partial_success` field reports `rejected_data_points: 240`, the spec is telling the client that 240 points in that exact payload were refused at the edge. The client has three obligations on receipt:

  - Read `partial_success.rejected_data_points` and the associated `error_message`.
  - Drop those 240 points from its local buffer. They are not deferred, not queued for retry, not "in flight."
  - Not retry them. Retrying the rejected slice would fail again for the same reason (the rejection was deterministic — invalid attributes, not transient backpressure), and would risk duplicate submission of points that were already accepted if the client re-sent a wider window than the rejection indices named.

The reason the client's dashboard says 12,000 is that it is counting "points put on the wire," not "points the server acknowledged as accepted." That metric was always going to diverge from server-side acceptance the moment the SDK started producing any rejected points. The SDK upgrade is the proximate cause: something it now emits does not satisfy the server's attribute validation, so 240 points per ~12,000 are being refused at parse/validate time.

How the client should represent the three counters

Three counters, all client-side, all derivable from this single response:

  attempted  = 12,000
              The size of the request payload the client assembled and sent.

  accepted   = 11,760
              Read from the partial-success body's accepted count, or computed as
              attempted - rejected when only rejected is reported. These are the
              points Sphere has ingested and will store/process.

  rejected   = 240
              Read from partial_success.rejected_data_points, with the rejection
              reason captured separately as a labeled attribute or log line so the
              client can attribute the loss to the SDK upgrade and to the
              specific attribute that fails validation.

The invariant the dashboard should enforce and surface is:

  accepted + rejected == attempted, per request, per batch, per export.

Any time that invariant does not hold, the client is misreading the response. The "missing" 240 in this case are not missing — they are in the rejected bucket, and the dashboard needs a rejected bucket.

Practical follow-ups for the client

  - Surface the rejection reason (invalid attributes) as a first-class signal in the client's own telemetry, labeled with the SDK version that introduced it. This is how the client proves to itself that the loss is bounded and explainable rather than mysterious.
  - Do not retry the 240. The rejection is deterministic. Retry would only burn capacity and risk duplicating accepted points if the retry window is broader than the rejection set.
  - File the root cause at the SDK upgrade: diff the attribute schema the new SDK emits against the validation contract, identify the attribute(s) the server now rejects, and either correct the SDK to emit valid attributes or carry an exporter-side filter that drops the offending points before export.
  - Keep the per-export accepted/rejected counters in the client's send-path metrics so the next partial-success event is visible in the dashboard without a manual reconciliation against Sphere.

What this is not

It is not a duplicate-request problem (no duplicate request IDs were observed), not a retry-induced double count (no retries), not a server-side accounting gap (the counters close), and not a lost-in-flight problem. The server received all 12,000, processed all 12,000, and reported on all 12,000. The only thing that went wrong is that the client treated the HTTP 200 as a blanket acceptance and ignored the partial-success body.

When he settles on the bed, reward with a calm "good" and a treat; when he drifts back toward the entry, just wait without comment — he's choosing the bed again if you don't follow him to the door.
  A long-lasting chew or a lick mat (peanut butter without xylitol, plain yogurt, or his wet food pressed in) once he's on the bed does the same work as the freeze/lick activity from the fireworks night — gives him something to do with his mouth that isn't alert-barking.

Two symptom-free weeks of low-load activity is not the same as return-to-soccer clearance, especially given how often in past cycles the "flat-ground tolerance" feeling has set up a recurrence when acceleration, hard cuts, or repeated push-offs were layered back in. Below is a staged field test and the conservative play/modify/stop/evaluate criteria.

RECOMMENDED SEQUENCE
- Saturday Nov 2 afternoon (~22-26 hours before Sunday pickup): graded field test session
- Saturday evening and Sunday morning: observation window
- Sunday Nov 3 morning: capped pickup, only if the field test and overnight response are both clean
- Sunday Nov 3 afternoon with Devika: independent of the soccer decision. Do not let the morning outcome reshape it either way.

WHY SATURDAY, NOT SUNDAY MORNING
- A Saturday test gives you a 16-24 hour window to see whether the calf stiffens back up overnight, feels "tight" on stairs the next morning, or reproduces on a re-check. Sunday-morning-only testing has no delayed-symptom window, so a same-day go-ahead is more permissive than the pattern supports.
- The Devika afternoon is not a backstop and not a recovery plan for soccer. A clean pickup Sunday morning does not obligate continued play on future weeks. A stopped field test or a stopped pickup does not require canceling or modifying the Devika plan.

GRADED FIELD TEST (Saturday, on forgiving surface — turf preferred over concrete; softer shoes and grass-cut corners between reps if only concrete)
Start with a 10-12 minute easy jog as warm-up. If at any point during warm-up you feel anything (tightness, pulling, "awareness"), the day's field test is over.

Stage A — Push-off load (your recurrent trigger zone)
- 4 x 30-second easy-to-moderate tempo runs with 60 seconds walking between. Effort capped around 60-65% — conversational pace, no breath hold.
- Pass: no tightness, no pulling, no side-to-side asymmetry.
- Stop the day on any reproduction.

Stage B — Lateral load
- 3 x 20-meter lateral shuffle each direction, controlled, upright posture.
- Pass: no tightness, no grabbing at end range, no delayed tightness on the walk back.
- Stop the day on any reproduction.

Stage C — Acceleration
- 4 x 10-second accelerations from a jog start, building to roughly 80% (not all-out, not a sprint). Full stop between each. Walk back as recovery.
- Pass: no tightness at push-off, no calf "grab" or cramp, no after-pull within the next minute.
- Stop the day on any reproduction. Anything resembling a "pop" or sudden sharp pain is a same-day stop AND an evaluation flag.

Stage D — Repeated push-off and light bounding
- 5-6 easy alternating-leg bounds over about 10 meters, landing soft, no max height.
- 10 easy two-foot hops in place.
- Pass: no tightness, no feeling of "weakness" or hesitation on landing.
- Stop the day on any reproduction.

Stage E — Controlled direction change
- 3-4 controlled cuts at roughly 75%, not sharp deceleration, planted foot staying under the hip. Each direction.
- Pass: clean. No tightness on the plant leg, no after-pull.
- Stop the day on any reproduction.

Stage F — Walk-down cool-down
- 5-8 minutes easy walking. During and after, the calf should feel neutral or better than at the start. A calf that is "tighter than it was" by the end of the test is a same-day stop.

Between stages, walk and shake out for at least 2 minutes. If a stage passes cleanly but the calf feels "off" during the recovery walk before the next stage, the day is over.

OBSERVATION WINDOW (Saturday evening through Sunday morning)
- Saturday evening: stairs, walking, getting up from a chair should all remain neutral. If anything tightens, the field test has effectively failed and Sunday pickup is off by default.
- Sunday morning on waking: 10 slow single-leg calf raises on the right plus stairs. Any tightness, asymmetry, or after-pull means pickup is off by default. A normal resting morning does not, by itself, replace Stages A-F.

SUNDAY MORNING PICKUP — IF AND ONLY IF EVERYTHING ABOVE IS CLEAN
This is a duration and intensity cap, not a return to form.
- Arrive 10-15 minutes early. Do your own 10-12 minute easy jog warm-up before joining play. The warm-up is part of the test, not something to skip to "save" the calf.
- First 10 minutes: easy jog and short passes only. No sprinting yet.
- Next 15-25 minutes: easy-to-moderate play. Short distances, first-step only, no long sprints, no fully-committed 50/50s, no hard tackles, no contested jump headers.
- Final 5-10 minutes: cool down with walking and easy jog. No "one more sprint" to test it.
- Total on-field time: roughly 30-40 minutes of play. Treat as a duration progression, not as clearance for unrestricted play on a future Sunday.

MODIFY (dial back, keep playing) CRITERIA
- A faint awareness of the calf that resolves within about 60 seconds of walking.
- Mild fatigue in the calf without pulling, tightness, or pain.
- A pump-feel that is symmetric to the left and matches overall exertion.
- These are not stop-the-day signals, but they should pull intensity to walking and jogging, and end any plan to add sprints or cuts in this session.

STOP (leave the field this session) CRITERIA
- Any pulling, grabbing, cramping, or tightness in the right calf during play.
- Any popping sensation.
- Any new focal tenderness you can point to with one finger.
- Any sense of hesitation on push-off because the calf feels off.
- Any limp or altered gait, even subtle.
- Calf feels "tighter" at mid-session than it did at warm-up.
- A minor symptom that does not resolve with 2-3 minutes of walking.
- Stop means stop — finish the cool-down walk and leave. The Devika afternoon is unaffected.

MEDICAL EVALUATION CRITERIA (do not self-treat through these)
- A "pop" or sudden sharp pain during the field test or pickup, especially followed by inability to push off.
- Swelling, bruising, or a visible or palpable defect in the calf.
- Focal tenderness over the high calf (the original tightness region) that persists past 24-48 hours after the test, or that worsens rather than improves.
- Pain at rest, or pain that disrupts sleep.
- Calf pain with swelling, warmth, and redness together — same-day evaluation regardless of how the test felt.
- Recurrence of tightness with the same low-load activities (walking, stairs) that had been clean.
- Symptoms persisting past 3-4 weeks of relative rest without a clear improving trend, even at low load.
- A second stopped field test in a row where the same trigger keeps reproducing.

SUNDAY AFTERNOON WITH DEVIKA — INDEPENDENT
- Not a recovery plan for soccer and not a substitute for it. Do not shorten, lengthen, or cancel based on how the morning went.
- If the calf feels off after the morning session, the long-walk portion of the 3-6pm block should be the shorter option (or replaced with a seated plan at home). That is a sensible same-day adjustment, not a soccer decision.

EXPLICIT NON-CLEARANCE
- A clean Saturday field test is not clearance for Sunday. It gates the Sunday pickup only.
- A clean Sunday pickup is not clearance for unrestricted play on a future Sunday. Each future session still gates itself on its own warm-up and stop criteria.
- Each "clean" is a result of that session only. The flat-ground-tolerance = cleared pattern is exactly what this staged protocol is designed to break.

If you want, after the Saturday session I can help you write up what actually happened — what reproduced, what didn't, what the next decision should be — without treating "felt fine" as more than that.

What's already observed is the textbook signature of microwave leakage into 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi, so you don't need to move anything or buy anything to test it — the room layout you described is the test.

WHY THE PATTERN FITS WITHOUT FURTHER EQUIPMENT

Microwave ovens radiate at ~2.45 GHz, which sits directly on top of Wi-Fi channels 1–11. Even an oven that meets the FCC leakage limit can momentarily desense a nearby 2.4 GHz radio when it starts or runs. The consequences are exactly what you see: 2.4 GHz throughput or association collapses during the cycle and recovers within a second or two after it ends; 5 GHz is far enough away from the magnetron fundamental to be unaffected; wired Ethernet has no radio and is unaffected; the modem and ISP path are bypassed entirely. The fact that the modem status page is clean and the provider has no outage confirms the failure is RF, not link-layer or upstream.

A SHORT, NO-EQUIPMENT VERIFICATION

Treat it as a two-arm, before/during/after test on the work-room laptop. Total time about five minutes. Pick whichever target you can already reach without installing anything: the router's gateway IP (commonly 192.168.0.1 or 192.168.1.1), or a stable external address such as 1.1.1.1.

  Arm A — on 2.4 GHz (the failing link):
    1. Quiet baseline (~60 s): start a continuous ping or a long speedtest; record typical latency/loss or throughput.
    2. Microwave on (~60 s): start a normal kitchen cycle (a minute or more is ideal so the magnetron actually runs, not just the timer).
    3. Recovery (~60 s): microwave off; confirm the link settles back.

  Arm B — control, same window:
    Repeat the three steps on 5 GHz (same laptop if it sees the 5 GHz SSID) or on a wired Ethernet connection. This is what tells you the interference is local to 2.4 GHz and not, say, a brownout or upstream hiccup that just happens to coincide.

If Arm A shows clear loss/disconnect only while the microwave runs and Arm B is steady across the same window, the hypothesis is confirmed and you can stop looking. If Arm A is already steady without the microwave, the original narrative needs revisiting — the cause isn't the microwave. If both arms drop, you've localized the problem somewhere other than 2.4 GHz RF and should look at the router, the modem, or the upstream link first.

Two cheap pieces of evidence you can capture in parallel without any tools: time-stamp the laptop's Wi-Fi association state at the start, middle, and end of each minute (Windows `netsh wlan show interfaces`, macOS Option-click on the Wi-Fi icon, Linux `iw dev wlan0 link`) and photograph the microwave's door-seal area once — a visibly worn or food-stained gasket is enough to make "microwave leakage" plausible even if you can't measure it.

WHAT TO ACTUALLY CHANGE AFTER VERIFICATION

The stable choice is whichever of these you can already do without new hardware. In order of least disruption:

  1. Wire the work-room laptop during any session that can overlap with cooking. Ethernet to that room already runs cleanly along the baseboard, no walking-route crossing. Wired is immune to RF interference and is the most robust default for sustained work.

  2. If the laptop also supports 5 GHz, point it at the 5 GHz SSID (or set its preferred band to 5 GHz in the adapter's advanced properties) and stop using the 2.4 GHz SSID on that machine. This is a one-time preference change, costs nothing, and removes the failure mode entirely for that client.

  3. Leave the 2.4 GHz network in place for the rest of the household — phones, smart-home devices, Kibo's devices — until/unless they show the same problem.

WHAT NOT TO DO YET

  - Don't change the 2.4 GHz channel expecting a fix. Channel 1 vs 6 vs 11 does not help against a strong, broadband in-apartment source a few meters away on the same wall; you'd be tuning around a sledgehammer.
  - Don't replace the router, add a mesh node, or buy a USB Wi-Fi adapter. Premature.
  - Don't move the modem or the router. The kitchen is the source, not the living-room shelf.
  - Don't open a ticket with the ISP. The modem and the upstream link are demonstrably healthy.

STOP / ESCALATE CONDITIONS

Reopen the question — and consider the router itself — if: 2.4 GHz drops persist with the microwave off; the drops also affect 5 GHz or wired in the same window; the laptop shows a falling RSSI on 2.4 GHz over days independent of microwave use; or rebooting the router no longer restores 5 GHz when it would have before. None of those are happening today, so the current picture is interference, not hardware failure, and the work-room laptop is best served by either a cable to the existing Ethernet run or a one-time switch to the 5 GHz SSID.

Classification of the queue event

The 82% local queue episode for eleven minutes is the client-side backpressure the experiment was designed to capture, not a fault or regression. The signals line up with the intended design rather than against it:

- The queue that filled was the client's local send queue, not ingest-edge. The temporary 2,000-point maximum and one-second flush held throughout — the client released at or under the per-flush limit, so the queue filled because sustained arrival rate during the burst exceeded the release rate. That is client-side backpressure surfacing visibly under bounded limits.
- The queue drained without dropping points once the burst subsided. No data loss.
- The client's p99 over the interval was 1.08s. Elevated against the run aggregate of 0.97s, but consistent with normal short-burst queuing delay at the client, and not extreme.
- Overall errors stayed at surrounding baseline. Accepted-versus-rejected point accounting reconciled with no unexplained discrepancy. Duplicate request identifiers remained zero — meaning the client did not retry during the burst, just queued and waited. Ingest-edge admission behavior is unchanged.
- "Client-side backpressure" is one of the five recording items the second run was scoped to capture. The event matches that scope exactly: bounded duration (11 minutes), self-resolving (drained), visible at the client, no server-side or data-loss signal.

This is the experiment working. The limits are doing their job — pushing bursts back to the client where they can be observed and absorbed, rather than letting them propagate to ingest-edge and risk dropped points or admission changes.

Recommendation for the final two days

Keep the temporary 2,000-point maximum and one-second flush unchanged for the final two days.

Reasons not to change:

- Only two days remain. Changing parameters mid-run would invalidate comparison against the prior twelve days and reduce the evidence value of the closing window.
- The observed event is consistent with the experiment's intent, not evidence of miscalibration. There is nothing in the report to suggest the limit was set too high or too low.

The two options the poll worker offered are the standard remedies when a scanner rejects with an ambiguous-mark warning in NYC: spoil the current ballot and get a clean replacement, or cast it through the site's emergency-ballot (sealed-envelope) process.

Safer ordinary option: spoil and replace.

Why:
- It keeps you on the scanner's normal path. Once your marks are unambiguous, your ballot is counted through the same procedure as everyone else's, with no extra handling steps.
- The emergency-ballot process is the fallback for when the regular machinery can't accept your ballot. It involves a sealed envelope, a separate review path, and additional administrative steps, which means a small risk of the ballot being set aside or rejected for an envelope or signature issue rather than for the marks themselves.
- The poll worker is offering the replacement, which means you're still entitled to one. Take it.

Before marking the replacement:
- Ask for the posted sample ballot and the marking instructions. The poll site has them on the wall or at the marking booth; you don't need your ballot to look at them.
- Common reasons a scanner flags "ambiguous mark": the oval isn't fully filled (hollow center, stray inside), marks stray outside the target, checkmarks or X's instead of a filled oval, or a pen the scanner can't read well.
- Use the pen/stylus the site provides. Fill the oval completely and stay inside it. No stray marks.

Preserving ballot secrecy while asking for help:
- You never have to show your marked ballot to a poll worker, and you never have to say which contest or which selection triggered the warning. That's your right and it isn't needed for them to help you.
- Ask procedural questions in general terms only. Phrases that work without revealing anything:
  - "What counts as a clear mark on this scanner?"
  - "Can I see the sample ballot with proper markings?"
  - "Is there a different pen or stylus?"
  - "Is there a way to see what the scanner flagged, on its own screen?"
- The marking booth exists exactly so you can fill out your ballot away from poll workers and other voters. Use it.
- If a poll worker asks you to point out or describe a specific mark, you can decline. They can answer your general question without you identifying which contest was involved.

If, after a replacement, the scanner flags it again, the emergency-ballot process is the right next step at that point — but don't preemptively choose it now. The ordinary scanner path is the simplest, lowest-handling route, and you still have a fresh ballot available.

One last practical note: when you hand the spoiled ballot back, the poll worker should mark it "spoiled" and set it aside in the sealed spoiled-ballot envelope. You don't need to disclose anything to do this — just hand it over and ask for the replacement.

SUMMARY

  The patch is the right response to the diagnosed root cause, and the staging evidence is sufficient to open a bounded 5% production canary — not to skip the canary, not to expand past it, not to treat the rollout as resolved. Hold the safeguards and rollback signals above as the operational contract for the window. Cyrus's team retains the decision.

EVALUATION OF THE PROPOSED CROSS-SERVICE ALERT
================================================

1. Does `unless` suppress an independently actionable rollup backlog?

Yes — and it does so more completely than the annotation implies.

PromQL `A unless on() B` is a label-set subtraction, not a time-window guard. With `on()` carrying no labels, the matcher treats the empty label tuple as a subset of every series' label set, so it matches every series on the RIGHT against every series on the LEFT. Practical effect:

  - When `up{job="metrics-router"} == 0` returns ANY series (metrics-router scrape target down), the RIGHT side is non-empty and EVERY series on the LEFT — across all rollup partitions, all tenants, all rollout labels — gets stripped.
  - When metrics-router scrape is healthy, the RIGHT side is empty and the LEFT flows through.

Net result: the rollup backlog signal is silenced wholesale whenever metrics-router scrape is absent. Two concrete failure modes:

  (a) Independent rollup incidents during a metrics-router outage are missed entirely. Rollup workers fail for reasons unrelated to metrics-router (own deploys, own dependencies, own on-call).
  (b) Joint incidents are half-observed. Infra gets paged for metrics-router down; data platform gets paged for nothing; the operator has to manually cross-reference, which is what this rule was apparently trying to automate.

2. Why the ownership framing is wrong, not just the syntax.

"Infra supplies upstream boundary evidence" and "data platform owns the alert" reads as a clean split. The `unless` clause makes infra's scrape state a HARD GATE on data platform's primary signal. That is not context — it is a suppression switch controlled by a service data platform does not own. The alert effectively says "data platform's rollup backlog only matters when infra's target is up," which inverts the ownership model.

There is prior precedent on this exact routing trap: in August 2024 an internal rollup-service freshness alert was routed to the infra channel despite rollup-service belonging to data platform. The proposed rule would embed a similar mis-routing into the alert itself — harder to spot and harder to unwind than a routing misconfiguration.

3. Bonus issue with the breach condition.

`max_over_time(rollup_queue_age_seconds[5m]) > 300` means "any sample in the last 5 minutes exceeds 300s" — a single instantaneous spike trips it. With no `for:` clause, this is too twitchy for a page. Add `for: 2m` to require sustained breach (roughly 7 minutes wall-clock).

4. What "context, not suppression" should look like.

  - Drop the `unless` clause. The rollup backlog alert fires on its own evidence.
  - Make upstream health a SIBLING alert owned by infra, with joint routing/grouping in Alertmanager if correlation matters operationally. Do not encode the dependency in PromQL.
  - Where manual correlation is acceptable, surface upstream health as a templated dashboard link in the description so the on-call can click through to context without the alert itself depending on that signal.
  - Document data-platform ownership explicitly in labels (team: data-platform, service: rollup-service, runbook link to the ownership entry) so ownership is unambiguous on the firing page.

5. Concrete safer formulation.

  - alert: RollupQueueBacklog
    expr: max_over_time(rollup_queue_age_seconds[5m]) > 300
    for: 2m
    labels:
      severity: page
      team: data-platform
      service: rollup-service
    annotations:
      summary: "rollup-service queue age exceeds 5 minutes"
      description: >
        rollup-service queue age has been above 300s for at least 2m
        (observed peak in last 5m window above 300s). Owner: data platform.
        Check rollup workers, downstream consumers, and compaction health.
        Correlated upstream signal (CONTEXT, NOT a suppression):
        {{ $externalURL }}/graph?g0.expr=up%7Bjob%3D%22metrics-router%22%7D

  - alert: MetricsRouterTargetDown
    expr: up{job="metrics-router"} == 0
    for: 2m
    labels:
      severity: page
      team: infra
      service: metrics-router
    annotations:
      summary: "metrics-router scrape target down"
      description: >
        metrics-router target unreachable for 2m. Owner: infra.
        Note: this may reduce visibility into any metrics-router-dependent
        series; treat as joint context, not a substitute for downstream alerts.

If joint routing is wanted, configure Alertmanager to co-route these two when both are firing (e.g., a higher-priority notification or joint channel), not to suppress one when the other is active.

6. Summary for Cyrus.

  - `unless on()` is a hard global suppression, not a context gate. It silently strips the entire rollup backlog signal whenever metrics-router scrape is down — including backlog conditions that are independently actionable.
  - Upstream health belongs in a separate infra-owned alert plus an annotation/dashboard link, not in a PromQL suppression of a data-platform-owned alert.
  - Rollup backlog fires on its own evidence; metrics-router scrape fires on its own; Alertmanager handles joint routing if correlation is operationally needed.
  - Ownership stays with data platform throughout. Infra owns the metrics-router scrape alert and nothing more.

The wet-only squeal pattern you describe is consistent with normal disc-brake behavior. Here is the breakdown.

WHY WET SQUEAK HAPPENS

A thin water film on the rotor-pad interface briefly changes friction. The pad slips microseconds, sticks, slips again — that stick-slip vibration is what you hear. Once the interface dries and regains steady dry friction, the vibration mode disappears and braking goes quiet. This is especially common on recently replaced rotors and pads because the pad transfer layer on the rotor is still maturing. Your rotor was replaced on Oct 26 and bedded in per the manufacturer procedure, so the system is roughly two weeks into that maturation. The behavior you described — squeal while wet, quiet when dry, lever firm, no pulse, no scrape, no discoloration, no debris — matches benign wet-mode friction rather than contamination, warping, or a mechanical fault.

CLEANING SEQUENCE BEFORE THE NEXT RIDE

Do this when the rotor is fully cool, not right after the wet ride.

1. Visual check first: pads (even wear, no oily sheen, adequate material — typically at least 1.5 mm including backing plate), rotor (no crack, no deep gouge, no large blue or black heat tint), caliper area (no fluid seep).
2. Clean the rotor only if you see residue, water spots, or a faint gray film. Use a clean lint-free cloth or paper towel lightly moistened with 90%+ isopropyl alcohol. Hold the cloth against the rotor and slowly rotate the wheel backward by hand so your hand never passes the pad path. Wipe both sides. Let it dry fully before any braking.
3. Do not use soap, degreaser, spray lubricant, chain lube, WD-40, or any petroleum product anywhere near the pads or rotor. If pads are contaminated, replace them; cleaning contaminated pads is unreliable.
4. Re-spin the wheel: no rub, no pulse, free rotation.

TEST SEQUENCE BEFORE THE NEXT RIDE

Pick a dry, flat, traffic-free area. Each step is a gate — do not proceed if it fails.

- Pre-roll walk-bike check: lever firm and consistent with prior rides, no pulsing, caliper and axle visually seated.
- Low-speed stop check: three or four gentle stops from walking pace up to a few mph. Lever should feel smooth and the bike should stop straight. Any squeal here on a dry rotor is a stop signal.
- Moderate-effort verification: three to five progressive firm stops from about 12–15 mph down to about 5 mph, with a brief coast between each to bleed heat. Each stop should be firm, straight, and quiet. Do not lock the wheel and do not hold the brake clamped while stationary.
- Cool-down: let the brakes cool for several minutes before parking or any descent.

STOP-RIDING SIGNS

Stop immediately — walk the bike if needed — if any of these appear.

- Lever goes soft, spongy, or bottoms out. Suggests air in the hydraulic system, a leak, or contaminated pads.
- Bike pulls strongly to one side under braking.
- A new once-per-revolution pulse or thump through the lever. Rotor warp, hub, or caliper alignment issue.
- Visible rotor crack, deep scoring, or thickness below the stamped minimum (commonly 1.5 mm).
- Pads below the wear indicator, unevenly worn, or with an oily or glazed sheen.
- Persistent squeal, scrape, or grinding on a fully dry rotor after the cleaning sequence and moderate-effort stops.
- Burning smell, smoke, or any visible fire from the brake area.
- Hydraulic fluid on the rotor, caliper, pads, or lever.
- Rotor dragging noticeably when the wheel is spun freely with the brake released — caliper piston may be sticking.

If none of these appear during the test sequence and dry braking matches your prior baseline, the bike is ready to ride and the wet squeal can be treated as expected behavior. Re-check only if it recurs on a dry day.

Sum of nameplate loads:
  Monitor         120 W
  Laptop adapter  140 W
  Network switch   30 W
  Desk charger     10 W
  Task light       90 W
  -------------------
  Total           390 W

Current draw:
  At 120 V: 390 W / 120 V = 3.25 A
  At 125 V: 390 W / 125 V = 3.12 A

Strip rating
  15 A × 120 V = 1,800 W (or 1,875 W at 125 V)

Comparison
  Headroom against the 15 A nameplate: roughly 11.75 A, or about 1,400 W.
  Utilization: about 22% of the strip's stated watt rating, about 27% of the
  commonly applied 80% continuous-load limit (1,440 W on a 15 A branch
  circuit).

Verdict
  The stated load is comfortably within the strip rating. The task light
  adds about 1 A (90 W on 120 V), which is a small fraction of the
  available margin. The physical checks you already performed (cool strip,
  plug, and outlet; no buzzing or odor; no daisy-chained strip or
  extension cord) line up with a healthy installation.

Notes on what the numbers do and do not prove
  - Nameplate watts are upper bounds; real draw from the laptop adapter
    and monitor is usually lower. The calculation is therefore
    conservative.
  - The strip itself only protects against overload if its internal
    breaker (if any) trips; many 15 A strips are passive and rely on the
    wall circuit. A 15 A branch circuit is the actual upstream limit.
  - Adding the light does not change the conditions you checked. Keep
    those conditions true as you add or move equipment.

Warning signs that require unplugging immediately
  - Heat at the strip body, any receptacle on the strip, the plug, or
    the wall outlet. Warm is acceptable during use; hot to the touch is
    not.
  - Any odor, especially a hot-plastic, vinyl, or "fishy" electrical
    smell.
  - Buzzing, crackling, popping, or sizzling from the strip, plug, or
    outlet.
  - Discoloration, scorching, melting, warping, or any deformation of
    the strip housing, plug blades, or outlet face.
  - Sparks, arcing, or a visible flash when plugging in or operating a
    device.
  - Plugs that feel loose, fall out, or sit crooked in the strip.
  - Breaker tripping or any GFCI / AFCI on the circuit tripping while
    the strip is in use.
  - Lights on the same circuit dimming or flickering when a device
    turns on, or any device behaving erratically.
  - Any sign of moisture on or near the strip, or the strip lying on a
    wet or damp surface (rug spill, plant leak, window condensation).
  - Mechanical damage to the strip, cord, plug, or wall outlet cover.
  - Repeated breaker nuisance trips even after removing devices.

If any of those appear, stop using the strip, unplug it from the wall,
and identify the cause before further use. Heat, odor, discoloration,
or repeated tripping are reasons to retire the strip or have the
outlet and circuit inspected; an electrician is the right call for any
sign of damage at the wall outlet or the circuit breaker.

Routine practices that keep this load safe
  - Plug the strip directly into the wall outlet, never into another
    strip or an extension cord.
  - Keep the strip visible and ventilated; do not bury it under paper,
    fabric, or a closed desk enclosure.
  - Periodically feel the strip and plug during use; warmth that
    increases over time is a red flag.
  - Treat the laptop adapter and the task light as the two largest
    contributors and the most likely sources of any future change in
    heat or smell.
  - If you ever add a higher-draw device (printer, space heater,
    kettle, vacuum), recompute the total before leaving it plugged in.

The light-brown cold water is typical disturbed sediment from the valve work (iron/manganese oxides from the building mains). It's not a health hazard on its own, but it can clog aerators, showerheads, appliance inlet valves, and drinking-water filters. The goal is to push the sediment OUT of the apartment's pipes before sensitive equipment sees it.

What you described — both cold taps clearing within seconds to 20 seconds, no sediment after clearing, no odor, no leak, no boil notice — is on the normal end of post-shutdown conditions. The sequence below is precautionary, not a response to a red flag.

SAFE FIXTURE-FLUSHING SEQUENCE

Phase 1 — Cold side (apartment sediment clearing)
  1. Remove the aerators from the kitchen and bathroom cold taps (and the showerhead if you have a wrench). Set them in a cup; rinse and reinstall at the end.
  2. Kitchen cold tap: open fully, run 2-3 minutes past when it cleared.
  3. Bathroom cold tap: open fully, run 2-3 minutes past clear.
  4. Shower, cold handle only: run 1-2 minutes until clear.
  5. Toilet: flush 2-3 times to clear the supply line.
  6. Rinse aerators, reinstall. Reinstall showerhead.

Phase 2 — Hot side (verify and move existing water-heater tank content)
  1. Bathroom hot tap, full hot, until clear, then 2-3 minutes more.
  2. Kitchen hot tap, same.
  3. Shower, hot only, 1-2 minutes until clear.
  The tank itself is full of pre-shutdown water; it's not contaminated, but the brief flush confirms the hot system is intact.

Phase 3 — Appliance return to service (in this order)
  1. Washing machine: empty cycle on the hottest setting (old towels optional, to see what comes out). Clears inlet hoses and pump.
  2. Dishwasher: empty cycle on the heaviest/hottest setting. A cup of white vinegar on the top rack is fine if you want.
  3. Drinking-water filter: replace the cartridge now — the old one has almost certainly caught sediment and is no longer effective. For under-sink filters, replace the sediment pre-filter and run 2-3 gallons to waste before drinking.

Phase 4 — Drinking water and refills
  - Cold tap water that ran clear is fine for drinking and cooking. No boil notice is in effect, so boiling is not required.
  - Refill Kibo's water bowl from the flushed cold tap only — not from pre-shutdown stored water.
  - If you have a fridge ice maker, discard the first batch of ice.

STOP CONDITIONS — contact management before continuing

The findings below mean the situation is no longer normal post-shutdown sediment and warrants reporting:

  1. Discoloration persists beyond ~5 minutes of full-open flow at any tap — sustained brown, yellow, or red. A few seconds is normal; minutes is not.
  2. Visible particles or grit in the water after the initial clear.
  3. Sewage odor from any tap or drain. (Absent now; if it appears, possible cross-connection or back-siphonage from the valve work.)
  4. Chemical, petroleum, gasoline, or strong metallic odor that doesn't fade within the first minute of running. Mild chlorine is normal.
  5. Sputtering or air that doesn't resolve after several minutes — brief air is normal; sustained air suggests a system issue.
  6. Pressure problem — sudden drop, no water, or a trickle at any fixture after others were opened.
  7. Any visible leak — under sinks, around the water heater, around toilets, on ceilings or walls, or a water meter that keeps turning when all fixtures are closed.
  8. Hot water is discolored after cold is fully clear — the water heater has substantial sediment and should be flushed by maintenance.
  9. Management issues a boil-water notice at any point after restoration. Until lifted, boil drinking and cooking water for 1 minute (rolling boil) or use bottled water.
 10. GI symptoms (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, cramps) in any household member or pet after water use — possible contamination, worth reporting even if another cause seems likely.

BOTTOM LINE

Your current observations fall inside the normal post-shutdown range: clear within seconds, no sediment, no odor, no leak, no notice. The four-step sequence above (cold flush, hot flush, appliances in order, then refill) gets everything back to routine without exposing sensitive equipment to sediment. None of the ten stop conditions are present, so there's no reason to hold off on the sequence or escalate to management before starting it.

The 30-day distribution is bounded evidence, not a general license. Three self-selected clients participated, so the 99.6% / 0.4% split describes that cohort, not the entire ingest-edge population. Non-participating clients may burst more or less often, and we have no comparative sample. Any permanent disposition inherits this sampling gap unless the participating cohort is treated as the working assumption rather than the universe.

The 30-day analysis also does not give us, and the comparison cannot assume:

  - the sub-distribution inside the 0.4% burst band (how many points sit in 2,001-4,000, 4,001-8,000, 8,001-9,600)
  - per-tenant peak concurrency or burst-time correlation across tenants
  - whether the "burstiest client" in Option A is the same entity that drove the October 4 latency path
  - SDK behavior on partial-success responses or on rejection-driven retry
  - whether the 0.4% rate is steady or clustered in identifiable windows

OPTION A — Hard 2,000-point client cap

Failure modes:
  - 88% peak local queue utilization leaves roughly 12% headroom. Combined with the runbook's existing 4-active/pod and 8-request waiting cap per tenant, the burstiest client sits one transient away from a stall on its own tenant lane.
  - Splitting a 9,600-point burst into 2,000-point sub-batches multiplies request count. We do not know how many sub-batches each burst creates, or whether the sub-batch stream collides with the 8-request waiting cap.
  - The cap is client-side, so a non-participating client can still produce the October 4 pattern.
  - "Preserves point accounting" depends on implementation: a hard reject at 2,001 drops the entire batch; silent truncation breaks accounting. The phrasing is an intent, not a verified implementation.

Evidence gaps:
  - no measurement of split-induced sub-batch counts per burst
  - no measurement of the burstiest client's queue saturation under the 7-day experiment — peak utilization was observed, but runbook waiting-cap and 5xx behavior at saturation were not separately reported
  - no comparison to burst rates of the non-participating client base
  - no recording of which implementation shape (truncate vs. reject) the 2,000-point cap actually used

OPTION B — Documentation-only guidance

Failure modes:
  - No enforcement means the previously reproduced latency path remains possible. The 30-day analysis covers three clients; any other client retains the freedom to make the same batch-size change the October 4 client made.
  - There is no stop condition, no rollback trigger, and no observable signal that distinguishes "documentation worked" from "no one has yet reproduced the issue." Future regressions cannot be attributed to a missing guardrail because no guardrail was committed to.
  - The 0.4% burst rate is the participating cohort under the temporary cap. It is not evidence that documentation alone would hold the line.

Evidence gaps:
  - no evidence the October 4-affected client has committed to a permanent batch-size discipline after the 7-day experiment closed
  - no evidence other clients have read, understood, or will follow the documentation
  - no measurement of pre-existing burst behavior without the temporary cap in place

OPTION C — Ingest-edge soft rejection above 8,000

Failure modes:
  - 0.03% rejection is small in aggregate, but the failure mode concentrates in the 8,001-9,600 region of the burst band. Without the sub-distribution of the 0.4% burst band, we do not know whether the threshold is in a sparsely-used region or near a peak. If a tenant regularly batches near 8,000, the threshold is a small reduction in their headroom, not a distant guard.
  - Soft rejection requires explicit client retry and partial-delivery semantics. If clients retry without jitter, the load-test sawtooth pattern (peak concurrent retries 94 → 19 with jitter) recurs. The runbook's randomized Retry-After 1-3s covers server-side backpressure; client-side retry behavior is the dominant factor and is not part of the 30-day analysis.
  - Partial-delivery semantics depend on every relevant SDK correctly parsing a multi-status response and persisting only the accepted points. SDK 2.6.0 had a similar-shaped defect (immediate retry on 429 before application receipt) — we have no equivalent audit for partial-success parsing. A defect here turns 0.03% rejections into either retry storms or silent point loss, both worse than the steady-state rejection rate suggests.
  - The per-tenant quota (120,000 samples/second, 1-second window, no burst credits) interacts with retry behavior. A rejected client that retries against a tight quota may hit 429s in addition to the soft rejection, stacking two backpressure mechanisms on the same tenant.
  - "Soft rejection" is undefined as an HTTP/code contract. HTTP 413, custom 4xx, or 200-with-body are different operational shapes; the 30-day analysis does not specify which.

Evidence gaps:
  - no SDK coverage audit for partial-success handling
  - no measured client retry behavior after rejection (back off, jitter, drop, or storm?)
  - no sub-distribution of the burst band to confirm 8,000 is well above the steady-state ceiling
  - no quota interaction analysis under post-rejection retry
  - no decision on the HTTP/code contract the soft rejection will use

CROSS-OPTION OBSERVATIONS

  - A and C both rely on assumptions about client behavior. A assumes the burstiest client can absorb sub-batch multiplication and 88% utilization without crossing runbook thresholds. C assumes clients correctly implement retry-with-jitter and partial-success parsing. The 30-day analysis supports neither assumption; it only records the request-count distribution under the temporary setting.
  - B is the only option that does not require client cooperation, because it asks for none. It is also the only option that adds no defense against the previously reproduced latency path. Choosing it means accepting that risk explicitly.
  - The 30-day analysis does not establish a permanent disposition. It establishes that, under the temporary client cap, three participating clients produced the 99.6% / 0.4% split. The disposition question is what to do once that setting is removed.

WHAT THE COMPARISON DOES NOT ESTABLISH

  - whether the October 4-affected client is one of the three participating clients, or whether their behavior has changed since the temporary experiment closed
  - the aggregate behavior of non-participating clients (the cap and the rejection threshold only matter to clients whose bursts exceed them)
  - whether the runbook's existing queue caps (4-active/pod, 8-request waiting/tenant) are themselves the right ceiling under any of these options, or whether they should be revisited independently
  - the cost of any option to legitimate burst patterns that sit just below the chosen threshold
  - whether the 0.4% burst rate reflects client-side behavior change or just the temporary cap's effect

The disposition remains bounded by what the 30-day analysis proves (request-count distribution under the temporary cap for three clients) and what it does not prove (client-base-wide behavior, sub-band distribution, SDK coverage, retry semantics, burst correlation across tenants, post-experiment state of the October 4 client). Permanent disposition requires filling those gaps before choosing, not after.

- Facial, lip, tongue, or throat swelling — even mild, especially if progressing
- Stridor, noisy breathing, increased respiratory effort, gums that look pale/blue/grey
- Repeated retching or vomiting (more than once), or vomiting with blood or "coffee-ground" appearance
- Persistent drooling that doesn't taper after the first 30–60 minutes — suggests inability to swallow comfortably
- Sudden refusal of water after initially drinking, or pawing/rubbing the face against surfaces
- Collapse, severe lethargy, or agitation out of character
- Any seizure

When to call animal poison control instead (no drive needed yet)
Call if you want case documentation, a specific dose/risk read, or guidance on whether the bite-and-drop pattern needs in-person exam. Both charge a consultation fee but give a case number your regular vet can reference later:

- ASPCA APCC: 888-426-4435 (24/7; fee applies)
- Pet Poison Helpline: 855-764-7661 (24/7; fee applies)

Have ready: approximate weight of Kibo, time of exposure, what he did (bit and dropped), your current symptoms list (lip-lick only, otherwise normal), any concurrent medications or conditions.

When to call your regular vet (next business day, non-urgent)
- He ate his full normal dinner and drank water but you want it on the record
- Mild, self-resolving drooling that stopped and didn't recur
- A single soft stool overnight without other symptoms

Realistic best case and honest uncertainty
Best case: brief oral irritation only, fully resolved within an hour, normal dinner and sleep. That's the most likely outcome for a bite-and-drop without confirmed swallow and matches the March 30 history.

Honest uncertainty: we can't see inside the mouth without him letting you look, can't know if a fragment lodged in a tonsil crypt or under the tongue, and can't predict individual sensitivity. The monitoring plan above covers the realistic range from "no effect" to "developing irritation."

What would change my recommendation right now
- Visible swelling anywhere in the mouth or face
- Drooling that starts or persists past the first hour
- Any breathing change, including faster rate at rest
- A second vomiting episode
- Any sign he is guarding his mouth or refusing water he previously took

If none of those appear by morning, this resolves the same way the March event did, and the case is closed without vet contact.

One non-clinical item: the plant is now a known hazard. Pothos and dogs aren't a safe combination long-term. Worth a separate decision about rehoming the plant to a room Kibo cannot enter, hanging it, or removing it entirely. Don't conflate that decision with tonight's handling — secure it tonight either way.

Heat-retention plan for ~90-minute boiler-tech window

Current state: apartment 64°F, falling ~1.7°F/hr, so without action you'd reach ~61°F by 10:00 PM. The plan is to slow loss and add safe small heat, with explicit thresholds.

Setup (next 15 minutes)

1. Pick one warm room. Bedroom is usually best — smaller volume, mattress retains heat, Kibo's bed is already there. Close all interior doors to other rooms. Roll a towel and tuck it under the door to reduce drafts.

2. Block window drafts in the warm room. Hang a blanket or fitted sheet over each window. Leave the bedroom window's exterior cover alone unless it has clearly shifted — you have that under bounded monitoring.

3. Heat the bed now. Boil water on the stovetop for filling bottles only — not for space heating. Fill hot water bottles, a thermos, or a glass bottle wrapped in a sock. Place covered bottle at the foot of the bed under a blanket, not directly against skin (use the cover or a towel). A second bottle if you have one.

4. Layer for sleep. Long underwear, fleece/sweater, socks, hat. Head and feet account for disproportionate loss. Keep a dry change of socks by the bed.

5. Consolidate bodies. Alex, Devika, and Kibo in the same room. Single large shared blanket is warmer than three separate ones. Kibo's familiar bed goes in that room.

6. Kibo specifics. If he has a sweater for cold weather, use it. Let him choose to be near you or on his bed. Don't confine. Watch for: persistent shivering, whining, lifting paws, refusal to settle — those are his early signals.

7. Optional warm shower/bath. Warm (not hot), 10-15 min, before bed. Raises core temp; residual steam adds humidity, which holds heat better than dry air. Ventilate briefly after to avoid condensation on cold windows.

What NOT to do

- Gas stovetop or oven for space heating. CO and fire risk even briefly.
- Outdoor grill, patio heater, or propane heater indoors. CO.
- Candles for heat. Fire.
- Hair dryer as a space heater. That's what tripped your bathroom GFCI last time.
- Daisy-chained heaters on one outlet. Already off the table.

Re-checks every 30 minutes

- Warm-room thermometer reading
- Cooling rate (compare to ~1.7°F/hr baseline)
- Kibo's posture and behavior
- Fingers/toes/nose — cold-and-pink is fine, white/blue or numb is not
- Technician ETA — call management back if no update by 9:45 PM

Escalation thresholds

Indoor temp at the warm-room sensor:
  ≥ 62°F: hold plan, re-check in 30 min
  60-62°F: tolerable but uncomfortable; if technician ETA slips past 10:30 PM, move to Plan B
  < 60°F: Plan B now, regardless of ETA
  < 55°F: leave the apartment now

Kibo-specific leave trigger (independent of thermometer): persistent shivering or lifting paws in the warm room is your earliest signal that the apartment is too cold for him. Don't wait for the thermometer.

Symptom thresholds — leave immediately, don't wait for temp

Adults: persistent uncontrollable shivering, confusion, slurred speech, fumbling hands, drowsiness beyond normal, clumsiness walking.
Kibo: persistent shivering in the warm room, nonstop whimpering, lifting paws, refusal to move, pale gums, uncharacteristic lethargy.
Anyone: wet clothing that can't be changed immediately (accelerates heat loss dramatically).

Plan B (when temp threshold trips OR ETA slips > 30 min)

1. Confirm with management: technician en route, or reschedule. Do not accept "we'll send someone tomorrow" if it's already below 62°F and falling.
2. Identify a heated alternative, in priority order:
   a. Building common areas if heat is on — lobby, lounge, gym. Ask management.
   b. Nearby 24-hour business — pharmacy, hotel lobby.
   c. Friend/family with heat and a pet-friendly space.
   d. Pet-friendly hotel.
3. Pack: phones/chargers, IDs, Kibo's leash and his bed or a familiar-smelling blanket, water bottles (warm from tap), any medications.

Hour-by-hour target

  8:30 PM  64°F  plan starting
  9:00 PM  aim ≥ 62°F after warm-room setup + bottles
  9:30 PM  technician update expected
 10:00 PM  technician arrival; if no heat restored within 30 min after they leave, escalate
 11:00 PM  if still no heat and temp < 60°F, Plan B

One last note: your February 2024 outage resolved at 68°F after a boiler pressure-switch reset, so a single fix is plausible tonight. The plan above is built for that outcome but doesn't depend on it.

The read is right: she's named what she needs (shower, quiet hour, not alone), and the job tonight is to honor that without turning the hour into a "support conversation." Presence without questions is the offering.

A few practical moves that usually land on nights like this:

Before she walks in, or while she's in the shower:
  - Have the bathroom warm. Towel out, anything she likes for after the shower (lotion, robe, clean sleep clothes) ready and visible.
  - Pick food that's easy to eat or skip. Things she can graze from the fridge standing up, or a small plate she can ignore without guilt. Soup, yogurt, fruit, bread, something with salt if she's had little. No cooking-with-attention; no plating effort she'd have to acknowledge.
  - Water within reach wherever she lands. A glass, a bottle, doesn't matter.
  - If Kibo is the kind of company she wants, let him be near. If not, gate him out gently. She gets to choose.

During the quiet hour:
  - You don't have to narrate. "I'm in the other room if you want me" once, said normally, then actually be in the other room. Reading, scrolling, something boring. Close enough that the apartment doesn't feel empty.
  - Don't ask what happened. Don't ask if she's okay. Don't offer a reframe or a coping strategy. If she comes out and wants to talk, she'll come out. If she doesn't, the night still counts as supported.
  - No "at least." No silver-lining. No "you did everything you could." Those all ask her to do more emotional work right now.

The morning after:
  - Don't lock anything in. Coffee and breakfast normal, no plan. If she wants to talk then, fine. If she wants a walk, fine. If she wants a completely ordinary Sunday, that's also fine.
  - You can, gently and once, name that you're glad she's home. Don't make it a moment.

The hard part is the temptation to do something — to fix, to comfort with words, to make the night meaningful. Tonight the meaningful thing is that the shower is warm, the food is easy, the apartment is quiet, and you're nearby without being asked anything.

MEAL PREP PLAN — Nov 17 (Sun) into Devika's Tue–Thu hospital stretch

What this produces (8 servings across the week):
- Sun dinner: lentil stew + lemon-yogurt sauce (eaten Sun; no rice/eggs on the table)
- Mon: lentil-rice bowl w/ roasted veg (refrigerated)
- Tue at-home, pre-hospital: lentil-rice bowl + 2 hard-boiled eggs (refrigerated)
- Tue hospital (portable, 4h in insulated bag + ice packs): lentil-rice salad + sauce on the side
- Wed hospital: lentil-rice bowl (frozen; thaw Tue PM in fridge)
- Thu hospital: lentil-rice bowl + 2 hard-boiled eggs (frozen; thaw Wed PM)
- Fri+ (1–2 servings): leftover lentil stew or rice bowl (frozen; thaw morning of)

Estimated quantities from what you listed:
- Dry lentils (green or brown): 2 cups
- Rice (basmati or jasmine): 3 cups dry
- Eggs: 10
- Cauliflower: 1 large head
- Carrots: 6–8 medium
- Spinach: 1 5–6 oz bag
- Onions: 2 large
- Lemons: 3–4
- Plain yogurt: ~1.5 cups
- Olive oil, salt, pepper; any other spices are optional

Why no rice or eggs at Sunday dinner: it sidesteps the room-temperature concern entirely, keeps the evening simple, and frees the stove for batch cooking right after you eat. Stew rewarm and freezer tolerance are both forgiving.

PHASE 1 — Sunday dinner (6:05–7:45 PM)

6:05  Rinse 2 cups dry lentils; combine in a large pot with 6 cups water (or broth) and 1 tsp salt. Bring to a boil, then simmer 25–30 min.
6:10  Dice both onions. Slice 4 of the carrots. Cut half the cauliflower into florets (save the other half for the week's bowls).
6:20  In a separate skillet, sauté one diced onion in olive oil 5 min; add the sliced carrots, cook 5 min more.
6:30  Stir the onion/carrot mix and the cauliflower florets into the lentils. Season with salt, pepper, and any spices you like.
6:55  Wilt 2–3 handfuls of spinach into the stew. Squeeze in juice of 1 lemon. Taste and adjust.
7:00  Stir yogurt sauce: 1 cup yogurt + juice of 1/2 lemon + pinch salt (and minced garlic/cumin if you have them).
7:15  Ladle 2 bowls; pass the sauce at the table. Nothing rice- or egg-based is on the table, so nothing is cooling at room temperature while you eat.
7:45  After dinner: portion the leftover stew into 2–3 shallow containers for the fridge (next-day use) and freezer (Fri+).

PHASE 2 — Batch cooking (8:00–9:00 PM)

[All rice and eggs are cooked after dinner so neither sits out during the meal.]

8:00  Rice: rinse 3 cups dry rice; combine with 5.5 cups water + 1 tsp salt; bring to boil, cover, reduce to lowest heat, cook 18 min; off heat, rest covered 5 min.
8:05  Eggs: place 10 eggs in a saucepan, cover with cold water by 1 inch, bring to a boil, cover, remove from heat, rest 12 min.
8:15  While both cook: dice the remaining 4 carrots and remaining 1/2 cauliflower into small bite-size pieces for the week's bowls.
8:30  Drain eggs; plunge into ice water.
8:35  Uncover rice; fluff with a fork and turn out onto a rimmed sheet pan, spread in a thin even layer (this is the rapid-cool step below).

PHASE 3 — Rapid cooling (8:35–9:30 PM)

Cooked rice is the most sensitive item here (Bacillus cereus spores survive cooking and germinate as rice cools in the danger zone 40–140°F). Lentils, eggs, and roasted veg have similar rules but more tolerance.

- Rice: thin layer on the sheet pan should drop from ~180°F to ~70°F in ~15 min. Stir once at 10 min. Do not leave it on the counter after that — move it into containers or the fridge.
- Eggs: 5 min in the ice bath, then peel and pat dry.
- Lentils/veg already in shallow containers: leave uncovered in the fridge until they reach ~70°F, then cover. (Don't seal hot food tightly; condensation drips back and slows cooling.)
- Active rule during 8:35–9:30: keep rice on the sheet pan, eggs in ice bath, and stew in shallow containers — none of it sits loosely on the counter.

9:15  Peel the eggs; set aside.

PHASE 4 — Portion, label, store (9:30–10:00 PM)

Use leak-proof containers; label each with contents + day. Build each bowl at ~1.5 cups rice + 1 cup lentils/veg + roasted carrot-cauliflower, with lemon zest stirred through.

  C1  Mon — refrigerate (eat within 48h of cooking).
  C2  Tue at-home — refrigerate; tuck 2 peeled hard-boiled eggs in a side compartment or on top.
  C3  Tue hospital — refrigerate (packed in the morning, see Phase 5). Pack the yogurt sauce in a separate small sealed container; tuck in a lemon wedge.
  C4  Wed hospital — freeze. Thaw Tue evening by moving from freezer to fridge.
  C5  Thu hospital — freeze with 2 peeled hard-boiled eggs added. Thaw Wed evening.
  C6  Fri+ — freeze 1–2 servings (stew or rice bowl). Thaw morning-of in fridge.

Storage rules:
- Refrigerated: use Mon and Tue within 48h of cooking.
- Frozen: best within 2–3 weeks; thaw overnight in fridge; do not refreeze once thawed.
- Peeled hard-boiled eggs keep 5 days refrigerated; store with a damp paper towel in the container to keep whites from getting rubbery.
- Yogurt sauce: hold in fridge; do not freeze (it splits).

PHASE 5 — Tuesday morning insulated-bag pack (7:00–7:30 AM Tue)

7:00  Pull C3 + sauce container from the fridge; keep them cold until the last moment.
7:05  Place both into a small insulated bag with 1–2 fully frozen gel packs (freeze them overnight Sun–Mon). Smaller, fully frozen packs outperform larger half-frozen ones.
7:10  Add a fork, napkin, optional lemon wedge. Zip the bag.
7:20  Hand off on Devika's way out.

This holds the food below 40°F for ≥4h as long as the bag stays closed. Don't include anything hot — cool/cold components travel safely; hot food in an insulated bag without active heating can spend too long in the danger zone.

The 600/600 numbers are accurate and are not the source of the four-minute gap. Edge-gateway forwarded 600 requests, the collector received 600 requests, and the collector returned HTTP 200 for every one. Transport succeeded end to end. There is no transport-layer fault to investigate.

The loss happened one layer later, at the collector's point-acceptance stage, where each OTLP request is unpacked and every data point is validated individually. The collector rejected 240 points across those requests for timestamps seven minutes in the future, beyond its future-timestamp tolerance. OTLP is designed to do exactly this: when a request is mostly valid but some points fail validation, the collector returns HTTP 200 and embeds a partial_success block in the response body listing the rejected points and their reasons. The HTTP status reflects request acceptance; the body reflects point acceptance. They are deliberately not the same thing, and conflating them is what hid the gap.

The rejected points have client-side timestamps seven minutes ahead of the collector clock, so they never enter storage or rollup. The dashboard therefore sees the most recent portion of client clock time that exceeds the collector's future-timestamp tolerance as missing data. With a roughly three-minute tolerance and a seven-minute skew, that window is about four minutes of client time, which matches the reported gap exactly. The gap length is not transport-derived; it is the skew minus the tolerance, expressed in client time. This is not an ingest transport failure. The transport layer did its job. The collector did its job by refusing to write points timestamped in the future relative to its own clock, which would otherwise create out-of-order artifacts and a different integrity problem.

Smallest server-side diagnostic correction:
  The collector should be emitting a per-rejection metric labeled by reason, for example rejected_points_total{reason=...}. The 240 rejections for timestamps too far in the future should already appear there; if they do not, that is the smallest server-side addition. A second small addition is to keep partial_success counts and reasons visible at the gateway tier so the gateway's accepted-forwarded count can be cross-checked against per-request partial_success counts when needed.

Smallest client-side diagnostic correction:
  Read the response body, not just the status line. The client's exporter must parse partial_success and count rejected points per request, ideally exposing a per-reason counter. Logging only the HTTP status is exactly why 240 points disappeared from the client's view while the request appeared successful.

Smallest client-accounting correction:
  Count accepted points, not successful requests. "600 requests returned HTTP 200" is not equal to "all points accepted" in OTLP. Treat any response with a non-empty partial_success block as a partial send, not a success. Subtract rejected points from the "successfully ingested" total and surface them under a separate counter tagged by reason.

Underlying cause worth verifying separately: a seven-minute offset between client clock and collector clock is large enough to be an NTP problem on the client side, not ordinary drift. Until that is fixed, every request will continue to drop the most recent skew-minus-tolerance minutes of samples.

What this incident is not: not a transport outage, not a gateway failure, not a collector crash, not data loss in the storage or durability sense, and not evidence that the gateway or collector dropped anything. It is the OTLP partial-success protocol operating as designed, combined with a client that ignored the body and a clock skew large enough to push samples past the future-timestamp rejection threshold.

Scope: this classification is bounded to this client's four-minute gap driven by the 240-point rejection. It is not a claim about ingest reliability, gateway accuracy, or collector partial-success behavior in general.

Simple Paw Plan — Right Front, Post-Pebble

1. Clean once, gently, then leave it alone
   - Lukewarm water on a damp cloth or a quick rinse. Wipe between the pads and around the toes on that paw.
   - Pat dry thoroughly, especially between the pads. Trapped moisture there is what turns a clean removal into next-day irritation.
   - One recheck of pads and webbing for any cut you may have missed in low light, residual redness, a tiny puncture mark, or grit still in place. If you don't see any of those, stop looking.

2. Walking for the next 24-48 hours
   - Shorter loops, clean and dry surfaces.
   - Avoid hot pavement, gravel, sand, and salted or grit-treated sidewalks. Late November in the city often means treated curbs, so stick to clean asphalt or grass where you can.
   - Quick rinse and dry of that paw after any walk on a dirty surface.

3. What to watch over the next 1-2 days
   - Brief licking right after removal is normal. Licking that keeps recurring or gets more focused is not.
   - Gait on the next one or two walks: any return of a head-bob or shortened stride on the right front.

4. Call the vet if any of these appear
   - Limp returns and lasts more than 24 hours, or worsens at any point.
   - Swelling, heat, or spreading redness in the paw or between the pads.
   - Bleeding, discharge, or a bad smell from the paw.
   - A visible wound, puncture, or anything still embedded.
   - Paw becomes painful to touch — pulling away, snapping, or refusing to bear weight.
   - Persistent licking or chewing that doesn't settle within a day.
   - Appetite loss, lethargy, or any other behavior change along with the paw.

5. Routine (non-urgent) vet call is fine for
   - Mild redness that is not clearly better after 48 hours.
   - Licking that reliably returns after walks without any of the above signs.

Given Kibo's track record with this paw, I'd treat the 24-hour and 48-hour thresholds as firm rather than generous — if anything in section 4 starts to show, it's a same-day or next-business-day call rather than a wait-and-see.

INSPECTION SEQUENCE (do in order, stop and resolve any failure before the next step):

  1. Magnified visual — phone camera zoom or a magnifier on the cut, both from outside and (after step 3) inside. Look for: embedded glass shards (often clear, easy to miss), casing threads (look like fine fabric weave or steel belt wires), and any daylight showing through.

  3. Inside view — dismount the tire from one bead on the rear wheel (no need to fully remove). Reach inside and look at the cut from the inner surface. For a tire cut you want a patch-style boot on the INSIDE of the tire spanning the cut — Park Tool TB-2 is the standard; a piece of tough material (scrap tire, heavy patch, even a folded dollar bill in a pinch) cut larger than the cut and seated between tube and tire works.

  - Low to moderate speed
  - No curbs, potholes, jumps, hard braking, or loaded cargo
  - Carry a phone and a way to walk home
  - Do not start the ride if the static check shows any anomaly

IMMEDIATE STOP CRITERIA

  Stop riding the moment any one of the following is observed or suspected. Walk the bike home; do not ride on a soft tire:
    - Any drop in tire pressure, felt or measured, during the ride
    - Any hissing, ticking, or new air sound
    - Any visible bulge, "knot," raised edge, or deformation at or around the cut, either while riding or at any stop
    - The cut visibly growing, edges lifting, or the inner surface becoming visible
    - Boot shifting, lifting, peeling, or partially ejecting
    - Any handling change attributable to the rear wheel: thumping, vibration, rear-end instability, pulling to one side under braking, or unusual noise
    - Tube contact felt through the rim or pedal feedback (suggests extrusion through the cut)
    - Any brake or rim anomaly
  If in doubt, stop. A wrong call here costs a walk home; the wrong call the other way costs the tire, the rim, or a fall.

POST-RIDE INSPECTION (BEFORE THE NEXT RIDE)

  - Deflate, break the bead on one side, and inspect the cut and boot from inside
  - Cut must not have grown; edges must not be lifting; inner surface still smooth
  - Boot must be intact, centered, fully covering the cut, and still seated
  - Tube must show no abrasion mark, bulge imprint, or cut opposite the boot area
  - Reinflate and check static hold for at least one more hour

REPLACE THE TIRE, DO NOT BOOT AND RIDE AGAIN, IF ANY OF THE FOLLOWING OCCUR

  - Any immediate-stop criterion triggered during the ride
  - Post-ride inspection shows cut growth, lifted edges, exposed casing, shifted boot, or tube marking
  - Static hold after the ride no longer meets the pre-ride two-hour result
  - The boot has shifted, partially ejected, or is no longer fully covering the cut

LONGER VIEW

  A booted tire with a 4 mm tread cut is a bounded-risk interim measure, not a permanent repair. Plan replacement on the next convenient service window regardless of how the test ride goes.

Numbers first, then a sequence that fits your 40-minute window.

Where you are
- Breast 162°F is essentially done. A whole bird carries over 5–10°F during rest, so 162°F pulled now will land 167–172°F after a 15–20 minute rest, which is the safe window for white meat without going badly dry.
- Thigh 151°F needs another 12–15°F of climb to reach 165°F. Without help, that will take a long time at the temperature the breast can tolerate.

Don't carve yet. Keeping the bird whole is your main lever right now: the breast and thigh finish on different curves, and carving turns the breast into a flat piece of meat that dries out the moment you add more oven heat to chase the thigh.

Finish the dark meat without nuking the breast
1. Heat the oven up to 425°F (or 450°F if your roasting pan is dark/thin — go higher because the thighs are what you want to drive). The point is hotter-than-before to move the thigh quickly through the danger zone while the breast is insulated.
2. Shield the breast with a loose tent of foil, shiny side out, just covering the breast and the wing tips. Leave the thighs and drumsticks fully exposed. Crimp the foil to the carcass or pan edges so it doesn't slide and touch the thighs. A second small piece tucked around the upper breast near the neck end is fine.
3. Return the bird to the hot oven. If you have pan juices or melted fat, baste the thighs once when you put it in and again at the 10-minute mark — direct fat on exposed dark meat is the fastest way to add heat to the thigh without raising the breast temp.
4. Probe only the deepest part of the thigh, in the meatiest spot away from bone. Take a reading every 5 minutes. Pull the bird at 162–163°F in the thigh. Don't chase 165°F in the oven — carryover will do that for you during the rest.
5. If the thigh stalls below 160°F after 12–15 minutes at 425°F, that is your stop signal: pull anyway and accept a longer tented rest. Do not keep cranking the oven; that path overcooks the breast into chalk.

Rest and carve
- Move the bird to a warm spot (a trivet on the counter or a 200°F oven door cracked open is fine). Loosely tent the whole bird with foil — looser than the breast-only shield, so the skin doesn't steam and go soft.
- Rest 15–20 minutes. The breast will coast from ~162 to ~167–172°F and the thigh from 162–163 to 167–170°F. Both end above 165°F, which is the instant-read target the USDA uses for whole poultry.
- Carve at the table or in the kitchen after rest. Save the pan juices for the gravy if you haven't already combined them.

Holding the sides for 35–40 minutes
You're holding already-hot, already-cooked food. Two different holds are best because each side behaves differently.

Potatoes and carrots (already cooked, ready)
- Best hold: covered roasting dish or their pot with a tight lid, in a 200°F oven, with a tablespoon or two of water or stock in the bottom of each vessel to keep steam around them. They will be perfect at serving and you don't have to stir.
- Acceptable alternative: covered pot on the smallest burner setting, lowest possible flame. Add the liquid, lid on, stir once midway.
- Stop / fix-it signs: dry edges, fond on the bottom, or a starchy skin on the potatoes. Stir gently and add another tablespoon of hot liquid; recover.

Gravy (already made)
- Hold on the stove in a small saucepan on the lowest setting your burner has. Stir every 8–10 minutes. If it tightens up, whisk in a splash of stock or hot water — not cold, so it doesn't lose shine.
- Don't put gravy in the warming oven. The surface dries, the skin cracks, and you end up with a lumpy mess.
- If your stovetop runs hot, pour the gravy into a thermos or insulated carafe that you've pre-warmed with hot water. It will hold 40 minutes cleanly with no attention.

Green beans (waiting)
- Don't start them yet. Aim to drop them into salted boiling water (or a hot pan with butter) at T+30 minutes — that's during the bird's rest. They'll be ready exactly when you carve.

Putting it on the clock from 4:22 PM (your now)
- 4:22 — tent breast only with foil, oven to 425°F, bird back in, baste thighs.
- 4:32 — first thigh probe; baste thighs again.
- 4:42 — second thigh probe; if 160–163°F, pull. If still under 158°F, give it 5 more minutes and reassess, then pull regardless.
- 4:42–5:02 — bird rests loosely tented. Potatoes/carrots in 200°F oven. Gravy on lowest burner.
- 4:52 — start green beans.
- 5:02 — carve, finish gravy with any collected juices, serve.

Two safety boundaries worth naming explicitly, since you tend to think in these terms
- Don't carve early to "speed up" the thigh. A carved breast in a 425°F oven is a dried-out breast in under 10 minutes, and the thigh still won't move faster.
- If at any point the breast climbs above 170°F before the thigh is at 160°F, pull the bird, tent it loosely, and accept the longer rest. A 170°F breast with a 160°F thigh is recoverable; a 180°F breast with a 158°F thigh is not.

Friday portion (refrigerated)

Surplus (freeze today — Friday)

- Cool to fridge-cold before moving to the freezer (your shallow-container cooling already gets you most of the way; if anything still feels warm at the center, refrigerate 30 more minutes, then freeze).
