Practical plan below. Draws on the same cautious-rinse approach used in your Feb 2024 and Dec 2023 episodes, plus the explicit "short walks on clean surfaces" guidance from the July 30, 2024 vet visit.

  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  1. PRE-WALK (barrier + setup)
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  Apply a thin layer of plain paw balm to the pads and between the
  toes of all four feet. Plain pet paw balm is fine; petroleum
  jelly is a backup if you run out. This acts as a sacrificial
  barrier so the salt dissolves into the balm instead of the pad.

  Walk out with a damp microfiber or small towel in your coat
  pocket (or a damp paw-wipe pouch). That lets you do a quick
  in-loop wipe if Kibo stops and starts licking mid-walk.

  Do NOT apply balm right between the toes if Kibo's interdigital
  skin is at all damp — that traps moisture, which is exactly what
  you don't want. Pads and outer edges only if there's any
  residual dampness.

  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  2. ROUTE (keep the quiet loop, salt-aware detours)
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  Goal: same quiet side-street loop, but reduced salt contact.

  - Do a one-time eyeball of the loop. Note which segments had
    visible granules today. Treat those as "salt-loaded" until
    weather washes them away.
  - Default rule: walk the unsalted or lightly salted segments.
    Cross salt-loaded segments briskly rather than letting Kibo
    sniff/paw at them.
  - Stay closer to the building edge or plowed curb-cut edges
    where salt is less concentrated than the middle of the
    sidewalk. Avoid the slushy puddle zones at corners.
  - If the salt-loaded segment is short, lift Kibo over it OR
    carry a towel to wipe paws at the next clean surface.
  - Shorten duration by ~20–30% on salted days. Loop is already
    quiet; faster pace + shorter time = less contact.

  No need to abandon the quiet route. You're localizing the
  exposure, not eliminating the route.

  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  3. PAW CLEANING (after the walk)
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  Do this within 5–10 minutes of getting home, before Kibo
  starts his post-walk lick routine.

  - Lukewarm water rinse. A shallow dish or low sink works. Dip
    each paw for 5–10 seconds, or pour water over them.
  - Gently separate the toes and rinse between pads. Salt hides
    there and is the most common irritation site.
  - Pat dry with a clean towel. Do not rub — friction on a
    softened pad can abrade. Get between the toes.
  - Quick visual check: any redness, cracks, swelling, debris
    stuck between pads, cuts, or dampness left over.
  - Apply a thin layer of paw balm after paws are fully dry.
    This restores the barrier for the next walk.

  Supplies you're using: lukewarm water ✓, clean towels ✓, plain
  paw balm ✓. Booties noted as not-yet-fitting — don't force them.
  A loose, ill-fitting bootie holds moisture and grit, which is
  worse than the salt alone.

  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  4. MONITORING PLAN (today through the next week)
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  Daily quick check (10 seconds per paw, in daylight if possible):
  - Pads: any new redness, cracking, peeling, blanching, or
    discharge.
  - Between toes: any redness, swelling, odor, or visible grit.
  - Nails / dewclaws: any debris packed at the base.
  - Gait: walk Kibo a few steps on a flat indoor surface. Any
    new hesitation, head-bob, or weight shift.

  Behavioral cues (during and after walks):
  - Licking frequency: a couple of post-walk licks normal;
    sustained licking, chewing, or paw-lifting is a signal.
  - Mood: any reluctance to start the walk, slowing on a
    familiar segment, or stopping to attend to a paw.

  Frequency: daily visual check this week, since today is the
  first salted walk of the season and the pads haven't built up
  any callus yet. Once you have a clean week, you can drop to
  every-other-day spot checks.

  Log it lightly — date, weather, how salted the loop was,
  any paw notes. Two lines is enough. Helps you see a trend if
  something does flare.

  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  5. END THE WALK NOW (turn for home, mid-loop)
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  Any of these during the walk:
  - New limp or favoring a leg.
  - Repeated stopping to lick or chew a paw.
  - Lifting a paw and refusing to put it down.
  - Whining, yelping, or a sudden behavioral shift
    (snapping at the leash, sitting down, refusing to move).
  - Visible cut, bleeding, or pad flap.
  - Kibo shaking a paw vigorously as if something is stuck.

  If any of those happen: short loop home, immediate lukewarm
  rinse + visual check, then go to the monitoring section.

  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  6. WHEN TO CALL THE VET
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  ROUTINE (call your regular clinic, next business day or
  within 24–48 hours) if you see:
  - Redness between pads or on pads that doesn't resolve within
    24 hours of rinse-and-dry.
  - Mild swelling of a toe or pad.
  - Cracking, peeling, or noticeable dryness that doesn't
    improve after a couple of days of balm + reduced exposure.
  - Recurring limp after rest, or Kibo shifting weight off a
    foot on a flat indoor surface.
  - Persistent licking/chewing that resumes right after each
    post-walk rinse.
  - Any new discoloration of pad tissue (gray, white patches,
    darkening).

  URGENT / SAME-DAY (ER or urgent vet visit) if you see:
  - Active bleeding from a pad, cut, or between toes that
    doesn't stop with gentle pressure in a couple of minutes.
  - Open wound, ulcer, or raw exposed tissue.
  - Hot to the touch, especially with swelling — early
    infection sign.
  - Pus or foul discharge.
  - Refusal to bear weight on a leg at all.
  - Systemic signs: lethargy, refusal to eat or drink, vomiting,
    fever-like behavior (panting at rest, warm ears), or any
    severe pain response when you touch the paw.

  If Kibo ingested salt (ate granules, drank puddle slush):
    drooling, vomiting, or unusual lethargy within hours is also
    urgent — that's GI / salt toxicity, not a paw issue, and
    needs the vet.

  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  CLOSING NOTE
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  Today is a "no signs yet" day, which is the cheapest moment
  to put a routine in place. Barrier + rinse + dry + balm covers
  ~90% of salt paw issues before they start. The plan above
  keeps the quieter loop as the default and treats salting as
  a temporary variable, not a route change.

  If you do want booties later, a properly fitted set (snug but
  not tight, breathable or waterproof, walkable gait) is the
  only thing that beats the balm + rinse routine for salt-heavy
  days. Don't substitute ill-fitting ones.

The pattern you're describing — message from a legitimate domain plus a portal link that lives on a separate, unfamiliar domain — is one of the more common ways vendor-onboarding phishing works. The W-9 request itself is plausible (vendors do ask for them below the $600 1099-NEC threshold), so the request alone isn't the red flag. The red flag is the domain mismatch and the fact that North Pier has never sent Anya to a third-party portal in prior correspondence.

Below are the steps I would take, in this order.

1. Independent verification — do this before touching the link

   a. Do not click the link in the email. Do not log in to the linked page even if Anya is curious.
   b. Re-read the email and confirm the sender's actual domain (the part after @, not the friendly display name). Look at the full message header if available — the "Return-Path" and "Received" lines show where it really came from. If "From" is northpier.com but "Received" chain ends at a vendor-services domain, the message was relayed through or spoofed.
   c. Open a fresh browser tab and navigate to North Pier's real website by typing the address Anya already knows (the one from prior workshop emails, the contract/invoice thread, or her own saved bookmark). Do not copy the address from the email.
   d. From that real North Pier site, look for any mention of a vendor portal, AP onboarding, or a "submit W-9" link. If North Pier's own site doesn't reference the vendor-services domain, treat the request as unverified.
   e. Phone or message North Pier's AP or the workshop lead using a contact method from the existing legitimate thread — not any phone number or address inside the new email. Ask directly: "Did your AP team send me a W-9 request via a vendor-services portal, or was that message something you didn't send?"
   f. Only proceed to the portal if North Pier confirms in writing (through the original thread or in person/phone) that they actually use that portal for AP onboarding.

2. What a W-9 actually requires for Anya's situation

   For an individual independent contractor paid for a one-off workshop, the only lines Anya must fill in are:

   - Line 1: Legal name (must match her SSN/ITIN record or her business tax-return name)
   - Line 2: Business name, only if different from Line 1 (leave blank if she's operating under her own name as a sole proprietor)
   - Line 3: Federal tax classification — check "Individual/sole proprietor or single-member LLC" (her case)
   - Line 4: Exemptions — only if applicable to a 409A or FATCA exemption; almost certainly leave blank
   - Line 5: Mailing address
   - Line 7: Account number(s) — optional; only used by the payer to match payments. She can leave blank unless North Pier has assigned her a vendor ID she wants recorded.
   - Line 8: Taxpayer Identification Number — her SSN, OR an EIN if she has one (most sole proprietors use SSN)
   - Line 9: Backup withholding — leave blank. She is not subject to backup withholding if she provides a correct TIN.
   - Signature and date at the bottom.

   Lines she does not need to fill in for a $350 one-off workshop:
   - Line 6 (foreign address) — N/A unless she is not a U.S. person
   - Line 4a/4b exemption codes — N/A
   - Any "account number" she doesn't already have
   - Driver's license, date of birth, bank account, or routing number — none of these are W-9 fields. If anything else is asked for on the linked portal, that's a separate red flag.

   The W-9 contains one piece of highly sensitive data — the SSN/TIN on Line 8. Everything else is ordinary business contact information.

3. What Anya must NOT send by ordinary email

   - A completed W-9 as an attachment (PDF, image, or otherwise). Ordinary email is unencrypted at rest on every server it traverses; once sent, she cannot recall it.
   - The SSN or EIN in the body of an email, even partially, even with redactions.
   - Any combination of name + SSN + signature in the same unencrypted message.
   - Banking details, voided checks, or anything financial — not asked on a W-9, so any request for those via the suspicious portal is itself disqualifying.

4. How to submit securely once the portal is independently verified

   If North Pier confirms the vendor-services portal is real:

   - Use the portal's web form with TLS (the browser should show a valid certificate for the verified domain).
   - Confirm the submission acknowledgment contains a reference number and the W-9 image/PDF she uploaded.
   - Save that confirmation email in a folder; it is her proof of submission if a 1099 issue ever needs to be reconciled.

   If North Pier says they did NOT send the email or do NOT use that portal, or if she cannot reach a human to confirm:

   - Do not submit through the unverified portal.
   - Reply on the original legitimate North Pier thread only (or call) and ask for an alternative method — fax, encrypted email, mail, or upload through North Pier's own main domain.
   - If they want a fax number or mail address, get it from the verified channel, not from the suspicious email.

5. Stop conditions (treat as confirmed phishing if any of these are true)

   - The linked portal asks for fields beyond a real W-9: bank account, login credentials, MFA codes, driver's license image, date of birth, payment to "release" the W-9, or a link to "verify" her SSN.
   - The vendor-services domain has a recent registration, a misspelled North Pier name, or doesn't match what North Pier's own website references.
   - North Pier's real AP contact does not recognize the request.
   - The portal's certificate doesn't match its displayed domain, or the browser warns about the certificate.

   If any of those hold, treat the email as a phishing attempt: do not reply to it, do not click anything in it, forward it as an attachment to North Pier's real AP/security contact through a channel she already trusts, and report it through whatever reporting address her own email provider supports.

6. Practical summary for Anya

   Verify before filling. Call North Pier on a number she already has from the original workshop thread, ask whether they really use a vendor-services portal for AP, and only then decide where to submit. If verification is clean, submit directly through that portal's HTTPS form. If verification is not clean — or she can't reach a human — the safest move is to ask North Pier's AP for a fax number, an encrypted email option, or a mailed envelope, and to withhold the W-9 entirely until she has confirmation. She should never email the completed W-9 as an attachment through normal email, even to a confirmed North Pier address.

Failure boundary

The failure sits inside the new client wrapper, on the OTLP/HTTP wire. It is not in the collector, the edge-gateway, or any other ingest path. Three independent observations pin it there:

  - 120 gzip OTLP/HTTP -> 120 x HTTP 415 (Unsupported Media Type)
  - 120 uncompressed OTLP/HTTP -> 0 errors
  - 120 OTLP/gRPC -> 0 errors

Only the gzip OTLP/HTTP path broke. The collector is reachable (uncompressed HTTP and gRPC both reached it). The edge-gateway logged the failed requests, so it forwarded them. The collector then refused them with 415, which is the response it returns when the request advertises a Content-Encoding it cannot accept.

The decisive clue is `Content-Encoding: gzip, gzip` in the edge-gateway logs. RFC 9110 section 8.4 lists content codings as a comma-separated list of tokens, with each token listed at most once. A duplicated token is malformed. The OTLP/HTTP receiver is reading `gzip, gzip` as either a request to apply gzip decoding twice (the body is only compressed once, so the second pass fails) or simply a repeated-token rejection. Either way it returns 415 and does not consume the body.

The wrapper is therefore emitting two `gzip` tokens on the request. The most likely shape is a wrapper-level "set Content-Encoding if compressed" step layered on top of an underlying SDK / HTTP client that was already setting `Content-Encoding: gzip`, producing the duplicate via string concatenation (`, gzip` appended to an existing `gzip`) or via two header writes both firing. The wrapper version on production is the prior build without that step, which is why production stayed healthy.

Why this is not a collector or general ingest outage:

  - The collector accepts the same payload class when Content-Encoding is well-formed (uncompressed pass).
  - The collector accepts the same logical data over gRPC, which uses a different wire and is unaffected.
  - The edge-gateway accepted and forwarded the malformed requests; it does not validate Content-Encoding.
  - Production, on the prior wrapper, is healthy with no analogous 415s.
  - The 415 count equals the gzip OTLP/HTTP request count exactly (120 of 120), which is the signature of a wire-level encoding rejection, not a downstream capacity or auth issue.

Smallest wrapper correction

Make the wrapper emit exactly one `Content-Encoding: gzip` token on compressed OTLP/HTTP requests. The diff is one line of intent: idempotent single-write.

  - Locate the code path that produced the second `gzip` (a header append, a middleware that called `Header().Set("Content-Encoding", "gzip")` on a request whose underlying transport already sets it, or a `Set("Content-Encoding", v+", gzip")` concatenation).
  - Change it so that if the underlying transport / SDK already advertises gzip, do nothing; otherwise set `Content-Encoding: gzip` once.
  - Leave the body compression alone: one gzip pass is correct, and the body is fine.

No collector change, no edge-gateway change, no SDK upgrade. One wrapper diff, scoped to the wrapper that shipped to PE staging.

Bounded staging replay before any production movement

Scope: PE staging only, with the corrected wrapper. Production stays on the prior wrapper throughout this replay; production is not part of this decision.

Replay matrix (identical to the failed run):

  - 120 gzip OTLP/HTTP
  - 120 uncompressed OTLP/HTTP
  - 120 OTLP/gRPC

Pass criteria, all of which must hold:

  - All 360 requests return 2xx. Zero 415, zero 5xx, zero non-2xx.
  - Edge-gateway logs for the gzip OTLP/HTTP run show `Content-Encoding: gzip` exactly: single token, no `gzip, gzip`.
  - Collector receipt count equals edge-gateway accepted-forward count for each class. Exact accounting, no unexplained gap.
  - Partial-success (if any) reconciles honestly: accepted plus rejected equals sent, no orphan rejections, no silent drops.
  - p99 latency for each class within ~10 ms of the pre-wrapper-change staging baseline.
  - Memory within baseline.
  - Zero dropped series, zero reload failures, zero restarts on the collector.

Stop conditions, any one halts and reverts:

  - Any 415, any 5xx, or any non-2xx on the replay matrix.
  - Any duplicated Content-Encoding token in edge-gateway logs.
  - Edge-gateway accepted-forward != collector receipt for any class.
  - Dropped series, reload failure, or restart on the collector.
  - p99 above ~10 ms of pre-wrapper staging baseline, or any memory regression.
  - Any malformed-request crash or forwarding loop on the collector.

What still has to happen before any production movement, and is not in this replay:

  - A clean replay does not authorize production. Promotion requires a fresh, explicit approval after at least 24 hours of clean observation of the staging replay traffic and metrics, with the pass criteria held continuously.
  - A separate decision is needed on whether the corrected wrapper also gets its own narrow production canary (suggested: a small percentage of the wrapper-emitting PE clients first, with the same stop conditions, owned by whoever owns the wrapper). That canary is its own ask, not bundled with the wrapper fix.
  - The wrapper diff, the replay numbers, and the pass-criteria evidence must be recorded before any production approval is requested.
  - Production movement does not happen in the same change as the wrapper correction.

Summary: one wrapper regression on one wire path in one replay. Bounded fix, bounded replay, no production movement without a fresh decision.

Bottom line: the freezer itself crossed the 40°F safety threshold (43°F at close) for up to 2h 40min, which puts the higher-risk items in the danger zone above the 2-hour rule. Discard chicken, milk, and ice cream. Keep and refreeze the peas. Nothing leaked, so cleanup is light.

Per-item decisions

Raw chicken (44°F at the surface, no ice crystals)
- Discard. Raw poultry is the highest-risk item in the freezer (Salmonella, Campylobacter). Surface temperature tracking the freezer air at 44°F means it had been in the danger zone. We cannot rule out that the package was above 40°F for the full window, and you have asked me not to use smell or taste as a secondary check, so there is no second signal to lean on. Do not "cook it off" as a rescue; that only works when you can verify the food was below 40°F the whole time, which we cannot.

Milk in the fridge compartment (43°F)
- Discard. Pasteurized but perishable; 43°F is in the danger zone and the exposure window exceeded 2 hours. Without smell or taste as a backstop, temperature and time are the only evidence, and both point to discard. Seal the container in a bag before it goes in the trash.

Ice cream (liquid around the edges)
- Discard, on two grounds. Safety: the container tracked freezer ambient above 40°F for a window past 2 hours. Quality: ice cream that has fully melted and is refrozen develops severe ice-crystal texture and is poor even when it would be technically safe. Not worth keeping.

Frozen peas (still hard, visible ice crystals)
- Keep. The item itself never crossed 40°F; ice crystals are the clean signal that it stayed frozen. Peas are low-risk for pathogens, and a refreeze with this state of product is normal. Return them to the freezer promptly once it is back at 0°F.

Anything else in the freezer not listed
- Same rule, no exceptions: if an item is above 40°F and has been for more than 2 hours, discard. If it still contains visible ice crystals or measures at or below 40°F, it can be refrozen once the freezer is back to 0°F.

Freezer recovery steps

1. Confirm the door is fully latched. Open and re-close it deliberately so the latch engages; a partly-shut door was the root cause and re-closing by feel is not enough.
2. With the door open, inspect the gasket all the way around for food debris, frost buildup, or warping. Wipe the gasket with warm soapy water, rinse, and dry. Any crack, hardening, or gap that does not seal with a dollar bill slid along it is a gasket problem.
3. Engage a fast-freeze, quick-freeze, or power-freeze setting if the freezer has one. This runs the compressor continuously and pulls the temperature down faster.
4. Do not open the freezer again until it is back at 0°F. Every opening slows the recovery. The peas can wait.
5. Recheck the appliance thermometer at 1 hour, 4 hours, and 24 hours.
   - 1 hour: a noticeable drop is expected (a full freezer drops faster than a partly full one).
   - 4 hours: should be moving toward 0°F.
   - 24 hours: should be at or below 0°F and stable.
6. Read the result at 24 hours. Two cases:
   - Returns to 0°F and holds: the unit is fine, the cause was the door. Refreeze the peas.
   - Stays above 0°F with the door closed: an appliance fault (compressor, sealed system, thermostat, or a failed gasket you cannot see). Do not rely on this freezer for long-term storage until it is serviced or replaced; it is no longer trustworthy for raw meat, dairy, or anything you would want to keep for weeks.

Cleanup steps

Nothing leaked onto ready-to-eat food, so this is light.

1. Wipe up any condensation or frost melt inside the freezer with a clean cloth or paper towels.
2. Where the chicken package and the ice cream sat, clean with hot soapy water, then a food-safe sanitizer (1 teaspoon unscented liquid bleach per quart of water, or white vinegar), then dry. There was no leak, so this is precautionary, not a contamination response.
3. Bag the discarded chicken, milk, and ice cream in sealed plastic bags before putting them in the trash. This is household hygiene, not food safety.
4. Wipe the refrigerator compartment at 43°F as well, even though the only known affected item is the milk.
5. Sanitize the instant-read thermometer probe with isopropyl alcohol before reusing it on other food.
6. Wash hands and any surface that touched the discarded items with hot soapy water.

One pattern note worth keeping: this is the fourth door-ajar event this year (Feb 24 freezer about 3h, internal 28°F; Aug 28 freezer drawer about 3h, internal 24°F; Oct 9 fridge about 2h 40min, display 50°F; today about 2h 40min, internal 43°F). The earlier three stayed under 40°F and items were kept; today is the first where the freezer crossed 40°F, which is why the outcome changes. When the unit is back at 0°F, a deliberate check of gasket condition, door alignment, and whether anything inside is sitting against the door is worth doing before restocking, since the recurrence pattern suggests the cause is not random.

  - Confirm every part on the manual's parts list is present: rear plate, clamp body, bolt(s), washers, VESA plate, VESA screws, cable clips, tension-adjust hex key. Missing hardware is a stop until you obtain it.
  - Note the manual's torque value for the desk-clamp bolt and for the VESA screws. If a number is given, that number overrides any generic guidance below.

DESK AND CLAMP INTERFACE PREP
  - Wipe the underside of the desk where the rear plate will sit. A single grain of debris prevents flush contact and lets the clamp rock.
  - By hand, confirm the full rear plate fits flat against the underside with no cable, beam, frame member, drawer slide, or trim in the way. Any obstruction is a stop until the location is changed.
  - Decide final arm position now: depth from desk edge, side offset, pivot side. Repositioning later can leave witness marks on the desk.

CLAMP INSTALLATION
  - Slide the rear plate into position from the front of the desk.
  - Confirm the rear plate is flush along its entire contact area. A gap at the rear means the front edge is bearing all the load.
  - Hand-thread the bolt until it contacts the rear plate, then confirm the clamp body and rear plate are parallel to each other and to the desk top. Skewed is a stop and reposition.
  - Torque to the manual's value. If the manual gives no number, use the lower end of typical range (around 5–7 Nm for most M6/M8 bolts on a 28 mm solid-wood top) and stop the moment the clamp body stops rotating against the desk.
  - Do not continue tightening past spec. The arm is rated for the clamp's grip, not for crushing the desk. Over-torque can split the top or strip the clamp threads.

CLAMP-ONLY PROOF TEST (no monitor mounted)
  - With the arm in its lowest or folded position, press firmly downward on the clamp body. No flex, rock, or creak.
  - Pull outward on the empty arm extension with a steady, controlled force well below anything that could damage a sound clamp. No movement, no sliding sound, no gap opening at the rear plate.
  - Try to twist the clamp body around the desk axis. No movement.
  - Lift on the empty arm. The clamp should hold silently and without shifting.

This is a tight, well-bounded replay of the deterministic 8,000-point rejection path. Here is what it proves and what it does not decide.

What this proves about the deterministic rejection path

  1. Determinism. 25,000 of 25,000 requests above the 8,000-point threshold received HTTP 413. There is no observed escape, race, partial-acceptance, or threshold drift in the replay window. The rejection is reproducible on size alone.

  2. Total rejection with exact accounting. For every oversized request, accepted = 0 and rejected = exactly the submitted point count. There is no silent drop, no fractional acceptance, and no off-by-one. The accounting math closes cleanly inside each response.

  3. Stable reason code. Every 413 carries `oversized_batch`. Clients can distinguish this rejection from other failure modes programmatically rather than inferring it from status or body shape.

  4. No overhead on the compliant path. Control batches at or below 8,000 points stayed near baseline latency and error rate. The rejection logic is not measurably penalizing in-spec traffic in this window.

  5. No destructive loss of valid data. After splitting the same payload into compliant requests, every point was accepted with no accounting discrepancy. The replay therefore proves the rejection is terminal for that attempt but the points themselves remain valid — they fail only on sizing, not on content.

  6. The deterministic semantics are independent of retry. The test client made no unchanged retries, which is test discipline rather than proof, but combined with the size-only determinism in (1), an unchanged retry of an oversized payload would be rejected identically. There is no implicit credit or absorption on resubmission.

What this does not prove and what remains in the owners' permanent-disposition decision

  1. Which rejection strategy is the right permanent contract. This replay validates exactly one option — deterministic HTTP 413 above 8,000 points. The owners still have the live menu of options on the table:
       - hard cap at a lower size (the 2,000-point option remains rejected on local-queue grounds)
       - documentation only (rejected as unenforced against the latency path)
       - soft rejection above 8,000 (the 11/21 proposal: HTTP 429, retryable)
       - the deterministic 8,000-point 413 path just tested

  2. The 413 vs 429 choice. 413 is a terminal, non-retryable signal ("Payload Too Large"). 429 is a rate-limit signal that implies backoff and retry. Both would reject the batch; they communicate different contracts to clients. The replay does not adjudicate which contract is correct.

  3. Client-side contract impact. Whichever HTTP status is chosen, the owners still owe verified behavior from SDKs, retry libraries, and the high-volume client whose batches exceeded 8,000 points in the original 30-day distribution. Specifically, how each library treats 413 (terminal) vs 429 (retry with Retry-After), and whether any library would silently retry unchanged oversized payloads against a 413 contract.

  4. Quota, jitter, partial-success, and backpressure interactions. If the owners land on 429, retry/jitter/partial-success/quota semantics still need verified behavior. If they land on 413, they need confirmed terminal handling.

  5. Customer-facing communication. Any change to the HTTP contract above 8,000 points requires coordinated rollout to clients, particularly the one client whose payloads drove the 0.03-0.4% of batches in the 8,001-9,600 range.

  6. Coverage scope of the evidence. The replay is bounded to the client mix and traffic pattern used. Full client population, burst sub-distribution, concurrency correlation, and post-experiment behavior remain outside this window.

  7. Operational policy at the boundary. Alerting on 413 rate, per-tenant allowances or exceptions, threshold value (8,000 fixed vs sized), and ownership of the permanent contract are owner decisions, not replay outputs.

In short: the replay proves the deterministic 413 rejection path behaves correctly on its own terms — total, exact, reason-coded, non-leaky, and non-disruptive to in-spec traffic. It does not prove that deterministic 413 is the right permanent contract versus the soft 429 option, nor does it settle any of the client-contract, communication, or operational-policy questions that sit above the path itself. Those remain the owners' call.

Safest sequence — duplicate $34 transit-wallet charge

The shape here (same timestamp + merchant descriptor, two posted charges, only one load on the wallet side, neither pending) matches the authorize-twice / duplicate-posting pattern you've handled before (Feb 2024 Marriott, Mar 2024 MOS-7721).      - Screenshot the transit-wallet transaction history showing the single $34 load, with the load's transaction ID, timestamp, and funding method.
     - From the card side, capture for BOTH charges: authorization code, posted date, transaction reference / processor ID, and the masked card-number tail.
     - Capture the wallet's load-confirmation ID (usually in the load receipt or activity log).

  2. FIRST CONTACT — TRANSIT-WALLET OPERATOR, not the card issuer
     - This matches your established preference: vendor-issued reversal avoids competing-claims risk between operator and card issuer.
     - Open a support case referencing: the wallet load-confirmation ID, the load timestamp, both card-charge identifiers, and the request that ONE of the two $34 charges be reversed.
     - Ask the operator to identify which charge corresponds to the wallet load (likely the one sharing the internal payment-intent ID) and to reverse the other.

  3. WRITTEN GATES YOU NEED FROM THE OPERATOR BEFORE THEY TOUCH ANYTHING
     - Acknowledgment that the duplicate is under investigation.
     - Written confirmation that NONE of the following will apply while the case is open: late fee, account suspension, wallet freeze, balance adjustment, or adverse ledger entry against your account or wallet.
     - Confirmation that any refund will be issued to the SAME card and will not reduce or reverse the legitimate $34 wallet load.
     - Case reference number and a stated resolution timeframe.

  4. DO NOT DO YET
     - Do not file a card-issuer chargeback / dispute. Doing so before the operator resolves creates two competing claims and complicates the operator's refund — you've hit this exact pattern before.
     - Do not reverse or refund the load from inside the wallet app. That would erase the legitimate load and leave you with neither the load nor a clean duplicate reversal.
     - Do not label either charge as fraud on either side. "Duplicate posting under investigation" is the precise framing.
     - Do not accept an automated refund without verifying it targets the duplicate line.

  5. AFTER THE OPERATOR ACTS
     - Verify on the card statement that the refund is a posted CREDIT of exactly $34 from the same merchant descriptor, and that one $34 debit remains as the only $34 debit.
     - Verify on the wallet that the single $34 load is still intact and unmodified.
     - Save the closure note from the operator.

  6. STOP / ESCALATE TRIGGERS
     - Operator reverses the wrong charge (refunds the legitimate one) → request immediate re-posting of the legitimate load and reversal of the duplicate; pause any card-issuer action until that's settled.
     - Either side applies a fee, adverse entry, or wallet restriction during the investigation → cite the written confirmation from step 3 and escalate to operator supervisor; only then consider a narrowly scoped card-issuer dispute as a parallel track.

     - Wallet still shows the single $34 load, unmodified.
     - No fee, suspension, freeze, or adverse ledger entry applied at any point.

The order matters: evidence → operator → written gates → operator action → verify. Card-issuer dispute stays in reserve unless the operator path stalls or mishandles the reversal.

Why this is still salvageable: the red dye is mostly still loose in the fiber and in the water. Direct dyes (the usual red sock dyes on cotton) only bond permanently once they are heated. Wet + cool + no dryer = maximum reversibility window. Anything you do from here must keep them wet, cool, and unheated until the pink is gone.

Salvage sequence (all water cool or cold — never warm or hot until the pink is fully gone):

  1. Keep everything wet. Do not let anything drip-dry, towel-dry, or enter the dryer. Pull the red sock out and set it aside in a separate basin.

  2. Flush first. Re-run the shirts alone in the washer, plain cold water, no detergent. Repeat 2-3 cycles. Goal is to physically wash out the loose, unbound dye before any chemistry. The water should run visibly clearer each time.

  3. Oxygen-bleach soak. This is what the labels permit (sodium percarbonate, sold as OxiClean or generic "oxygen bleach"). Use a basin or the washer tub. Cool water per the package — typically 1-2 scoops per gallon. Submerge the shirts, push out air pockets, then soak 6-8 hours or overnight. Stir or gently agitate once or twice.

  4. Drain and rinse thoroughly in cold water.

  5. Inspect. Hold each shirt flat against a white background in good light.
       - Pink gone: jump to step 8.
       - Faint pink remains: one more oxygen-bleach soak (step 3 again), then re-inspect.
       - Pink still strong after a second soak: stop aggressive treatment (see stop conditions below).

  6. Optional vinegar follow-up — only if a faint cast persists after step 5: soak 30-60 min in 1 cup white vinegar per gallon of cool water. Rinse well in cold.

  7. Final detergent wash — once shirts look acceptably white: normal cold-water wash with regular detergent, no fabric softener. Do not add other items that could re-deposit dye.

  8. Dry only after the pink is fully gone:
       - Preferred: air-dry flat or on hangers, out of direct sun.
       - If machine-drying is needed: lowest heat or air-fluff, and check at 10 minutes. If any pink shows, stop the dryer, air-dry, and reconsider before any further heat.

Hard don'ts:
  - No chlorine bleach (labels prohibit, and on transferred direct dye it can yellow the cotton or fix the color further).
  - No hot water at any point until step 8 — heat is what permanently bonds the dye.
  - No dryer, no ironing, no radiator-drying until the pink is gone.
  - No "color-run" sheets as a substitute here; they only catch loose dye in the wash, they don't lift what's already on the fabric.

Stop conditions — when to quit and accept the result:
  - Two full oxygen-bleach soaks with no visible improvement: additional chemistry is unlikely to lift more. Stop.
  - Any fabric weakening, yellowing, or roughness at any point: stop that treatment immediately.

Small amounts of polyester stuffing or tiny fabric fragments, if any were swallowed, usually pass on their own. The rare outcome to watch for is a gastrointestinal obstruction, and the symptoms below are designed to catch that early.

Escalation criteria, with timing matched to severity:

Go in now or call on the way (urgent):
  - Repeated unproductive retching or abdominal heaving
  - Bloated, firm, or painful-looking abdomen
  - Inability to keep water down for more than a few hours
  - Pale, white, or tacky gums
  - Collapse, sudden weakness, or unusual lethargy
  - Persistent choking, gagging, or pawing at the mouth
  - Visible distress, restlessness that won't settle, or a "prayer position" / hunched posture
  - Blood in vomit or stool, or stool that looks black and tarry

Same-day call to his regular vet:
  - A single vomit, especially if it contains stuffing, fabric, or unusual material
  - Loose stool or diarrhea that persists beyond one or two trips
  - Skipped interest in food across one full meal
  - Energy that drops below his baseline at his next normal active period
  - New or persistent drooling
  - Straining to defecate without producing stool
  - Any change you can't quite place

Continue observation if none of these appear. His next meal and his next normal walk are reasonable first checkpoints.

Monitoring plan for the next 48 hours:
  - Keep his normal routine. Don't change food or skip meals preemptively; normal intake supports normal GI motility.
  - Each meal: confirm normal interest and that he finishes. Note early departure or picking.
  - Water: he's already accepting it, which is reassuring. Normal intake is the signal.
  - Energy and behavior: check at his usual active periods (walks, play). Less engagement than baseline is the marker.
  - Abdomen: a relaxed visual check at rest. Don't press firmly. Stop checking if he shows discomfort when you approach the area.
  - Stool: normal consistency and color. Don't sift through it; just glance. Note any straining or absence of stool over a normal day.
  - Vomit or retch: count episodes. One isolated vomit is informational; repeated retching is escalation.
  - Mouth: brief glance if he yawns or eats. No need to pry open. Drooling or pawing is the trigger to look closer.

Timing note: most concerning signs from a swallowed foreign body, if any are going to appear, tend to show within the first 24 hours. The 48-hour mark is a reasonable boundary for "no longer acutely concerning from this episode." If something is going to pass through, it usually does within 24 to 72 hours, and most often you won't see it in the stool.

  - Discard the damaged toy now. Don't repair and reissue it; the seam failure shows the construction didn't hold under his chewing.

  - Don't induce vomiting at home. If anything was swallowed, retrieval by vomiting isn't reliably safer than passage and induction carries its own risks. Leave that decision to a vet if symptoms develop.

  - Inability to fully extend the fingers (late sign of compartment syndrome — rare but serious)
  - Pain that radiates up past the elbow or down into the palm or fingers
  - Symptoms that worsen rather than improve over the next 48–72 hours


Graded self-check (next day or two, before the next session)

Run these in order. Stop and downgrade at any step that reproduces the ache above 2/10 or feels worse than baseline. Do not repeat the full sequence multiple times — once is enough.

  1. At rest — sitting quietly, any forearm ache? Target 0/10. Any resting pain: skip the next session and re-check the following day.
  2. Full range of motion — make a fist, open fully, rotate the wrist, extend the wrist palm down. Target: pain-free through entire range.
  3. Light finger flexion — curl fingers against the other palm as light resistance, or squeeze a folded towel. Target: under 1/10, no sharp twinge.
  4. Resisted wrist flexion — palm up, resist with the other hand while curling the wrist. Target: under 1/10.
  5. Hook grip hang — hang from a large jug (doorframe pull-up bar, or a real hold if available) with fingers only, open hand. 10 to 15 seconds, body weight only. Target: under 1/10, no cramping.
  6. Open-hand hang — same hold, flat open crimp. 10 seconds. Target: under 1/10.
  7. Half-crimp hang — last four fingers at 90 degrees, thumb free. 5 to 10 seconds. Target: under 1/10. Clear reproduction of the ache here: stop, skip the session.
  8. One easy pull on a large hold (home wall or pre-session) — target pain-free.


Decision for the next bouldering session

Skip the session if any of the following:

  - Resting pain above 1/10 at the morning check
  - Pain on light finger flexion or resisted wrist flexion
  - Any new red-flag symptom developed overnight
  - The graded check reproduces the ache above 2/10 at any step
  - Morning forearm stiffness above your baseline

Modify (significant downgrade) if the morning checks pass but the session still feels tight:

  - Warmup only on large holds (jugs, big open-hand slopers, no full grip)
  - Easy routes only — at least 2 grades below your usual max
  - Vertical or slab only — no steep overhangs (overhangs load the flexors much more)
  - Open-hand grip only — no full crimps
  - Cap at 30 to 40 minutes, or end of warmup rounds, whichever comes first
  - Stop on the first sign of returning ache, not at 2/10
  - No dynamic moves, no highballs, no stick-repeaters
  - Downclimb everything
  - Avoid slopers that demand a death-crimp

Climb normally only if all of these are true:

  - Pain-free at rest and on the graded check through step 7
  - Pain-free walk to the gym
  - Pain-free first 15 minutes of warmup (large holds, easy routes)
  - No symptom increase during warmup


After a successful modified session

Step back up one notch per session in this order: route difficulty → angle (vertical before overhang) → grip type (open hand before crimp) → volume. If the ache returns at any point, drop back two notches and hold there for two sessions before re-attempting.


Boundary to preserve

Same rule as April 16: easy controlled climbing being tolerated is not the same as the grip intensity of a normal session. Do not let a clean modified session justify jumping straight back to max-effort crimps on steep slopers. The grade has to be earned one step at a time.

Principle: you can't silence or cover any alarm. The tools are (1) physical/audible distance between Kibo and each device, (2) sound masking inside the work room, and (3) keeping his arousal low before and between tests. The technician testing one alarm at a time, sequentially, is your main structural advantage — you just have to set it up.

WEDNESDAY NIGHT / THURSDAY MORNING (Dec 12)
- Normal evening walk and normal breakfast. Don't add a brand-new long walk right before — fatigue backfires into restless settling.
- Note roughly where the work-room alarm sits on the ceiling/wall. You'll place his bed as far from it as the room allows.

BY 8:45 AM — WORK ROOM SETUP (before the technician arrives)
- Door: closed. If it's hollow-core, pin a folded towel along the bottom gap — no obstruction to any alarm, just dampens airborne hallway sound and removes the light/draft cue at floor level.
- Sound masking on: a fan, the AC, a white-noise machine, or low-volume talk radio. Continuous broadband sound blunts the startle of intermittent sharp alarm tones. It needs to be on before Kibo goes in.
- Furnishings: bed against the interior wall farthest from the alarm, with a blanket under and around it.
- Familiar scent: an unwashed t-shirt of yours on or near the bed.
- Water: filled, on the opposite side of the room from the bed so he doesn't knock it.
- Long-lasting chew/lick item (frozen Kong, lick mat, bully stick — whatever he already does well with): have it ready in your hand, not in the room yet.

8:50–8:55 AM — KIBO PLACEMENT
- Walk him in calmly with a treat.
- Hand him the chew/lick item as he settles on the bed.
- Step out, close the door. Don't linger, don't repeatedly reassure, don't make the goodbye a moment.

9:00 AM — BRIEF THE TECHNICIAN (highest-leverage step of the morning)
Keep it short and matter-of-fact:
- "Dog's secured in the work room. Couple of things that would help:
  1. Quick heads-up before each test.
  2. If your tester has a hush/quiet-test mode, please use it where supported.
  3. Some inspectors carry a wireless tester that doesn't actually trigger the alarm at all — if you have one, even better.
  4. Work room last, if your sequence allows — the closest/loudest exposure comes after he's already been settling through the others."

9:00–11:00 AM — DURING THE INSPECTION
- Move with the technician. Keep hallway traffic normal.
- Do not crack the work-room door between tests. Each crack is a fresh alarm blast plus the visual of you leaving again.
- If you hear sustained distress (prolonged barking or door scratching) for more than a couple of minutes, step into the hallway outside the work room and speak once, low and short, through the door — then move on. Don't open it.
- Have a couple of high-value treats ready in your pocket for the reunion.

11:00 AM — REUNION (only after the technician has left and alarms are silent for at least 60 seconds)
- Open the door calmly. No excited greeting.
- Straight out for a walk. The walk is the reset.

POST-INSPECTION NOTES
- Record any failed or marginal device and the technician's contact info. That's a separate decision point — don't conflate it with Kibo handling.
- If the technician's tester was wireless (didn't actually trigger the alarms), the entire sound-exposure question turns out to have been moot — worth knowing.

SIGNS THAT'S MORE THAN ORDINARY STRESS (vet call, not management)
- Distress that doesn't settle within ~30 minutes after the reunion
- Refusal of food, treats, or water for the rest of the day
- Destructive door behavior, escape attempts, aggression unusual for him
- Housetraining regression
- Panting at rest, trembling, or GI upset lasting more than an hour

THINGS NOT TO DO
- Don't disable, cover, remove, or pre-test any alarm yourself
- Don't crate him if he's not crate-trained for sustained stays — the closed work room is your containment
- Don't repeatedly open the work-room door to soothe him
- Don't use medication without your vet's standing guidance

Let me verify the numbers by hand:

- attempted_points = 4,000,000
- accepted_points  = 3,996,000
- rejected_points  = 4,000
- request_count    = 190,000

Accounting check:
- accepted + rejected = 3,996,000 + 4,000 = 4,000,000 = attempted. **Reconciled exactly. No data loss.**
- (attempted − accepted − rejected = 0.)

Per-request arithmetic:
- avg points per request = 4,000,000 / 190,000 = 400 / 19 ≈ 21.053 points/request
- dashboard's "rejection_rate" = rejected_points / request_count = 4,000 / 190,000 = 4/190 = 2/95 ≈ 0.02105… → 2.1% (matches what the dashboard printed).

Diagnosis
- This is a **unit mismatch**, not data loss. The dashboard divides *points* by *requests*. Points and requests have different denominators (points are per-data-point, requests are per-batch/transport call). The 4,000 rejected points are real; they're simply being expressed against the wrong base.
- True point-level rejection rate = rejected_points / attempted_points = 4,000 / 4,000,000 = 1/1000 = 0.1%.
- True accepted-point rate = 3,996,000 / 4,000,000 = 99.9%.
- The "2.1%" figure is a *rejected-points-per-request* density (≈0.021 rejected points per request), which is a legitimate diagnostic but it is **not** a rejection rate and should never be labeled one.

Why the framing matters here
- "0.1% of points rejected" and "2.1% rejection rate" describe the same underlying event (4,000 rejected points out of 4,000,000 attempted) with very different psychological weight. Both numbers must coexist, but each must be named by what it actually measures.
- The 4,000 rejected points must not be hidden by re-labeling the dashboard. Whatever fix is applied has to preserve the absolute count and surface its meaning at the correct grain.

How to fix the dashboard query and annotation
1. Change the metric's name and definition.
   - Replace `rejection_rate = rejected_points / request_count` with `point_rejection_rate = rejected_points / attempted_points`.
   - Keep `rejected_points` and `attempted_points` as separate, labeled panels so the absolute 4,000 is visible at a glance.
2. Make the units explicit in the panel titles and legends.
   - Panel title: "Point rejection rate" with subtitle "rejected_points ÷ attempted_points".
   - Axis label and tooltip: "fraction of attempted data points rejected (0–1, or %)" — never "rejection rate per request."
3. Add the reconciled-identity line so the reader can audit the math.
   - Show: `accepted_points + rejected_points = attempted_points` (here 3,996,000 + 4,000 = 4,000,000). If this identity ever breaks, it's a real data-loss signal — currently it holds exactly.
4. If the per-request density is worth keeping (it's a useful "how much damage per offending batch" signal), keep it as a *separate* panel with a correct name.
   - Suggested name: `rejected_points_per_request` or `rejected_point_density`.
   - Value: 4,000 / 190,000 ≈ 0.0211 rejected points per request. Do **not** call this a "rate" — it's a per-batch density.
   - Pair it with `avg_attempted_points_per_request ≈ 21.05` so the reader sees the same event expressed at both grains.
5. Annotation for this specific release window.
   - Headline: "0.1% of attempted data points rejected (4,000 of 4,000,000)."
   - Side panel: "Per-request rejected-point density: ≈0.021 rejected points/request across 190,000 requests. This is not a request-rejection rate; 100% of requests were accepted at the transport layer."
   - Footer: "Accounting: accepted + rejected = attempted exactly. No data loss observed in this window."
6. Guardrails to prevent regression.
   - Add a unit assertion in the query: `assert(rejected_points <= attempted_points)` and `assert(accepted_points + rejected_points == attempted_points)`. Surface a banner if either fails.
   - Add a comment on the panel JSON/query explaining why the old `rejected_points / request_count` formula is wrong (units), referencing this incident so the next person doesn't reintroduce it.
   - In the panel description, include the corrected formula in plain text so it's discoverable from the dashboard UI, not only from the query source.

Bottom line
- The counters reconcile (accepted + rejected = attempted, exactly). There is no data loss.
- The "2.1%" was a unit error: points divided by requests. The correct point-rejection rate is **0.1%** (4,000 / 4,000,000). The 4,000 rejected points remain real and must remain visible.
- Fix: rename and redefine the metric to `point_rejection_rate = rejected_points / attempted_points`, keep the absolute rejected-points panel prominent, show the accounting identity, and if the per-request density is retained, give it an honest name (`rejected_points_per_request`) so it cannot be mistaken for a rejection rate again.

## shard-keeper: rollback procedure (post-Apr-14 hardened path)

### Rollback (label-map rollback path)

1. Re-push prior label map.
2. Confirm rollup-service consumer is reading it.
3. Pre-coordinate with Nadia on label-name parity.
4. NEVER deploy from laptop, even on staging.

This is the single tested command path that replaces the prior three-coordinated-command sequence. It is invoked only after the consumer inventory is verified end-to-end and the parity fixture is green.

---

### Lagging follower recovery (lease-safety first, not timer-driven)

A replication-lag warning on a follower is not, by itself, a restart trigger. Do not restart a lagging replica on a timer. Treat host health and lease safety as separate signals, and only restart after the lease-safety checks below have been satisfied and forward progress has stopped.

1. Remove the affected replica from follower reads immediately. Take it out of the read pool before any further diagnosis; do not wait on a threshold window. This bounds the blast radius of stale reads while the host and lease state are evaluated.

2. Verify lease holder and epoch stability on the affected replica and on the shard it serves:
   - Confirm a single, stable lease holder.
   - Confirm lease epochs are monotonic (no regression, no gap).
   - Confirm the lease has not flipped during the lag window.

3. Confirm the absence of acquisition or relinquishment events on the affected replica for at least two full lease-renewal intervals. Any acquisition or relinquishment event invalidates the assumption of a quiet lease and must be investigated before reentry.

4. Confirm the absence of stale-owner messages on the affected replica for at least two full lease-renewal intervals. A stale-owner message means the replica observed an owner it should not have, and is a lease-safety signal, not a host-health signal.

5. Confirm the absence of overlapping leadership on the shard. There must be exactly one recognized leader for the duration of the evaluation window.

6. Confirm the absence of write errors on the affected replica during the lag window. Replication lag combined with write errors is a different failure mode than lag alone and is not addressed by this procedure.

7. Confirm forward catch-up progress: the replica's applied position is advancing toward the leader's position over time, not flat. A replica that has stopped progressing after satisfying checks 2-6 is the only case in which restart is appropriate.

8. Reentry conditions (all must hold continuously for 15 minutes before the replica returns to the follower read pool):
   - Host disk latency at baseline (not merely "below the warning threshold" - at baseline).
   - Replication lag below one second.
   - Checks 2-6 remain clean across the full 15-minute window.

9. Restart only as a last resort, and only after checks 2-6 have passed and then failed: if the replica stops progressing (applied position flat, no catch-up) while lease safety remains clean, a restart is permitted. A timer-based or threshold-based automatic restart is not permitted; restart is a deliberate decision made after the lease-safety checks above.

10. Do not close the alert on host disk latency alone. Close the alert only after the replica has been returned to the follower read pool and checks 2-6 plus the reentry conditions in step 8 have held. If the replica was restarted, the post-restart catch-up and reentry gates still apply; a restart does not by itself close the alert.

---

### Notes

- Separation of host health and lease safety is deliberate. Disk-latency recovery does not authorize closing a lag alert if lease safety is still being evaluated, and lease-safety cleanliness does not authorize reentry if the host is unhealthy.
- The "five-minute warning threshold then restart" guidance previously associated with this entry is superseded by this procedure. Do not apply that guidance to current incidents.
- Coordinate with Nadia on any replica where acquisition/relinquishment events, stale-owner messages, overlapping leadership, or write errors are observed; these are out of scope for a host-side recovery and may indicate a lease or quorum issue requiring owner-level escalation.
