    repair, not a slow leak. Treat any mid-ride softness as data, not
    noise.

  Warm-up behavior:
    Friction will warm the tires over the first few minutes of riding
    and pressure will creep up. Do not add air before riding on the
    basis of "they look low."

  Verdict: pressures are safe for a short local ride in current
  conditions. Front is the one to keep an eye on if temp drops
  further or the ride runs long.


PRE-RIDE — TIRE / WHEEL

  1. Re-measure both tires cold just before mounting. Write the
     numbers down or remember them — they're your reference.
  2. Valves seated straight, caps finger-tight.
  3. Spin each wheel slowly. Look again for bulge, exposed casing,
     embedded debris, or any cut you may have missed at the gauge.
  4. Palm-squeeze each tire. Firm, not spongy. Soft = stop, recheck.
  5. Front axle / QR fully seated, lever firm (you've done this
     recently — confirm it's still where you left it).
  6. Rear axle / QR same check.
  7. Wheel true: spin and watch the brake pad gap. Even, no hop.
  8. If temp drops below ~28°F during the ride, plan a mid-ride
     re-measure on the front.


PRE-RIDE — BRAKES / DRIVETRAIN

  9. Squeeze both levers at standstill. Firm, no pull, no pulse.
     Rotor is bedded and was quiet on the Nov 9 dry ride; any new
     continuous squeal or grinding in dry cold is a stop signal.
  10. Chain visual — lube shouldn't be gummy at 33°F; if it is,
      short ride is fine, plan a re-lube after.
  11. Quick-release / thru-axle indicators all seated (you know
      what "fully seated" looks like on this bike).


PRE-RIDE — RIDER (cold-specific)

  12. Helmet on. Glasses clear (no fog/ice). Gloves on; confirm
      fingers can operate shifters and brake levers well.
  13. Plan the first 5 minutes as warm-up: flat, dry, low-traffic,
      gentle inputs only. Rubber is stiffer cold; traction is
      reduced until the tire warms.
  14. Layered, bright-visible jacket. December sun is low — anyone
      in a driver's blind spot is at higher glare risk this month.


ROUTE — SURFACE / ICE (separate from tire concern)

  Default route shape:
    Start on sunny-side streets; favor south- and east-facing
    blocks where solar gain has been longest. Cross to shadier
    streets later, never first.

  Avoid:
    - North-facing blocks still in building shadow at 9-10 a.m.
    - Bridges, overpasses, underpasses (freeze first, stay frozen).
    - Metal: manhole covers, grates, streetcar tracks, expansion
      joints.
    - Painted lines, crosswalks, bike-lane chevrons.
    - Leaf piles over pavement (they hide ice, not just damp).
    - Patches that look freshly wet on otherwise dry pavement —
      could be black ice or brine.
    - Anything that looks "cleaner" than the surrounding salt
      staining (often a thaw refreeze).

  Prefer:
    - Recently salted/sanded arterials.
    - Wide streets with sun exposure and room to recover from a
      surprise patch.
    - Streets you've ridden recently and remember.

  Pace:
    Ride at a speed where an unseen ice patch is brakeable, not
    panic. Longer following distance. No sudden lean changes.
    Treat the first shaded block as a walk-pace recon, not a
    cruise.

  Bail-out plan:
    Pick a turn that returns you to a sunny, familiar, well-salted
    street at the halfway point. If conditions are worse than
    expected at the bail-out, you shorten without improvising.


STOP CONDITIONS — TIRE / WHEEL

  - Felt or heard pressure loss (thump, hiss, soft feel through
    saddle).
  - Visible bulge, new cut, or embedded object in tread.
  - Wheel hop or wobble on smooth surface.
  - Mid-ride pressure check on either tire drops more than ~3-4
    psi from the pre-ride reading (slow-leak indicator).


STOP CONDITIONS — TRACTION / SURFACE

  - Front wheel slips on level ground (not a lean slide).
  - Rear steps out under normal pedaling.
  - Shaded ice patch longer than a bike length — walk across, do
    not ride across.
  - Salt/sand coverage disappears mid-block.
  - Snow line appears on shoulders or in gutters.
  - Surface conditions visibly worse than when you started.


STOP CONDITIONS — RIDER

  - Fingers too numb to safely modulate brakes.
  - Glasses fogging or icing.
  - Wind picking up sharply, temp dropping, or precipitation
    starting.
  - Any symptom (shivering you can't control, slurred speech,
    confusion) — stop immediately, get indoors.


STOP CONDITIONS — BIKE / SYSTEM

  - Brake lever goes soft or pulls to one side.
  - New continuous grinding, scraping, or dry squeal (wet-only
    squeal is normal for you; dry is not).
  - Wheel true issue surfaces.
  - Any rattle or noise that wasn't there pre-ride.
  - Chain skip under normal pedaling.


CLOSING

  Pressures are safe. Front is the thin margin — keep an eye on it
  if temp falls or ride runs long. Ice is a separate problem; the
  route plan and traction stop-conditions are the levers for that,
  not the tire pressure. The two checklists are deliberately split
  so a pressure question doesn't get conflated with a surface
  question mid-ride.

  Enjoy the ride.

ASSESSMENT: ordinary charger warmth, consistent with normal 65 W USB-C operation.

Why the readings fit normal operation
- 104 F (40 C) on the brick surface is well within typical 65 W USB-C charger operating range. Reputable 65 W bricks commonly measure 40-55 C (104-131 F) on the housing under normal load. UL 60950-1 / IEC 62368-1 user-accessible surface limits during normal operation sit much higher than 40 C, so there is thermal headroom.
- The heat source is AC-to-DC conversion loss. A 65 W brick at roughly 88-92 percent efficiency dumps roughly 5-8 W as heat through the housing; that is what you are feeling.
- The outlet face and plug body at 76-77 F, only 6-7 F above the 70 F room, is the reassuring reading. It says the wall-side connection is sound, not overloaded, and not dissipating meaningful heat. If the outlet were the problem, that face would climb.
- Separately routed outlet means it is its own receptacle (and likely its own circuit). 65 W is about 0.54 A at 120 V; even a 15 A circuit has 30x margin. Building wiring is not the variable here.
- Every absence check passed: no discoloration, odor, buzz, spark, looseness, cable damage, breaker trip, and the laptop is actually accepting charge. Those are the signs that would tell you the brick or outlet is failing.

If you want a single rule of thumb: warm-but-comfortable-to-hold is normal; too-hot-to-hold-for-more-than-a-few-seconds is not.

Safe monitoring (while Devika keeps using it)
- Quick touch test on the brick every so often during a charging session. Warm and tolerable is fine; a clear step up in temperature within the same session is a signal.
- Glance at the outlet face and plug body once per session. They should stay within a few degrees of room temperature.
- Listen for any new buzz, hiss, or crackle from the brick or outlet with the room quiet.
- Smell check the area near the brick and outlet. No odor at all is the expectation.
- Confirm the laptop still reports "charging" normally. Intermittent charging, charging only at certain angles, or rapid connect-disconnect is a plug or cable symptom, not a thermal one.
- Once after the laptop reaches full charge, recheck the brick. Load drops sharply at full charge; a healthy brick cools noticeably within 10-15 minutes. A brick that stays just as hot at idle is still probably fine but is worth a closer look.
- Keep the brick on a hard, open surface while charging. Do not bury it under papers, a pillow, a blanket, or pile clothing on it; that is the one easy way to push a normal-warm brick into a hot one.

Unplug immediately if any of these appear
- Brick too hot to hold comfortably for more than a brief touch (rough threshold: surface above roughly 130-140 F / 54-60 C). "Warm and tolerable" continues; "hot enough to want to put it down" stops it.
- Any odor: burning, hot plastic, sweet/electrical, fishy, or chemical. Even faint.
- Visible discoloration, yellowing, browning, or scorch marks on the brick housing, the plug prongs, or the outlet face.
- Buzzing, hissing, crackling, or popping from the brick or the outlet.
- Any visible spark when plugging or unplugging, or a visible flash inside the outlet.
- The plug becomes loose, wobbly, or falls out of the outlet without you holding the cord.
- Any cable damage: cracked, brittle, or melted jacket; exposed conductor; a kink point that has hardened or discolored.
- Outlet face becomes noticeably warm or hot (well above the current 76-77 F), or shows any darkening around the socket.
- Breaker trips or GFCI trips on that circuit.
- Laptop stops charging while plugged in, or charging becomes intermittent only at certain cord angles.
- Brick housing swelling, bulging, or deforming.
- Any liquid near the brick, cable, or outlet.

For any of the above, unplug the brick from the wall (pulling by the plug body, not the cable). Let it sit on a hard surface away from anything flammable until it cools. Do not reuse it until the cause is identified. If the symptom involves the outlet itself rather than the brick, do not use that outlet again until an electrician has looked at it.

Electrician escalation criteria (the outlet, not the brick)
- Outlet face runs warmer than ambient during normal use, or shows any discoloration, darkening, or melting near a socket.
- Repeated breaker or GFCI trips on that circuit, even after unplugging the brick.
- Buzzing or crackling coming from the outlet (not the brick) with nothing plugged in.
- Plug will not stay seated, feels loose in the outlet, or the outlet face is cracked, missing a cover, or visibly damaged.
- Outlet feels hot to the touch on its face plate.
- A burning or electrical odor localized at the outlet rather than at the brick.

Most of the unplug criteria above point at the brick; the items in this list point at the outlet or the building wiring and need an electrician, not a new charger.

Management escalation criteria
- Anything in the electrician list above, since the outlet is part of the building.
- Any incident involving smoke, scorch marks, or a tripped breaker, even if it self-cleared, so there is a dated record.
- A request to identify which circuit the separately routed outlet is on and confirm it is properly rated (not strictly necessary for a 65 W load, but useful to have on file).
- Do not need to contact management for ordinary warmth, normal operation, or a charger replacement that Devika handles on her own.

Bottom line for right now
- 104 F on the brick, 76-77 F at the plug and outlet, no other symptoms, charging working: leave it alone and use the monitoring list. The brick is doing what a 65 W brick does. The decision points above are the triggers; none of them are present.

PRECONDITION — do not delete anything until a fresh, verified backup exists. The Nov 5 backup is ~6 weeks stale and does not protect anything added or changed since then.

PHASE 1 — PRE-FLIGHT (5–10 min, no changes yet)
1. Identify the OS and the update target (e.g., macOS Sonoma vs Ventura, Windows 11 23H2 vs 24H2). The target determines the free-space floor.
2. Open the built-in backup app and confirm it sees the external drive as a destination. Do not assume.
3. On the laptop, check the external drive's free space in Finder/Explorer. The safe rule for a first full backup: external free ≥ laptop used (≈500 GB on a 512 GB drive with 9 GB free). If the external drive is borderline, note it before starting.
4. Plug the laptop's charger in. Backups run longer than expected and updates fail or stall on low battery.

PHASE 2 — BACK UP FIRST (before any cleanup)
1. Connect the external drive.
2. Start the backup. Time Machine / File History will show progress — let it run uninterrupted.
3. Verify the "Last successful backup" timestamp is today, with the "successful" qualifier. "In progress" or interrupted is not verification.
4. Open the backup from Finder/Explorer and confirm a few recent items are present (a folder edited this week, recent photos). This proves the backup is readable, not just "completed."
5. Stop condition: if the backup fails, stalls, or throws a permissions/disk error, do not proceed to cleanup. Resolve the backup first.

PHASE 3 — FREE-SPACE TARGET
- 25 GB free is the realistic floor for most current OS updates.
- 40 GB free is a comfortable buffer, especially for a major version update.
- If the update is major (macOS major, Windows feature update), aim for 40 GB.
- If 25 GB cannot be reached without touching personal files she has not reviewed, the update should not be started today.

PHASE 4 — DO NOT DELETE MANUALLY
Items that look deletable but break things or lose data if removed:
- Anything in Documents, Desktop, Downloads, Pictures she has not personally reviewed.
- Mail database (~/Library/Mail on macOS; .pst/.ost on Windows).
- Browser bookmarks, history, saved logins, extensions, and cookie stores.
- Keychain / Windows credential vault.
- Photo Library originals — only the Library's caches subfolder is safe.
- iCloud Drive placeholder files. They are tiny on disk but represent real cloud data; deleting can remove them from her iCloud account.
- Time Machine local snapshots (macOS prunes these automatically; manual deletion can break future backups).
- Virtual machine disk images (.vmdk, .vdi, .vbox, .img) — these are large but recreating the VM is not a few-click process.
- Boot Camp partition, if present.
- .app bundles in /Applications — use the app's own uninstaller, not Trash.
- Anything that prompts for an admin password — pause and verify before entering it.
- Anything she does not recognize — leave for review, do not force-delete.

PHASE 5 — CLEANUP, BIGGEST SAFE WINS FIRST

Tier 1 — definitely safe
- Empty Trash / Recycle Bin. Often surprisingly large.
- Downloads folder: remove old installers (.dmg, .pkg, .exe, .iso) she no longer needs. Keep installers for apps she still uses.
- Old iOS/iPadOS device backups. macOS: ~/Library/Application Support/MobileSync/Backup/ — each backup is commonly 5–30 GB. Verify the folder date and device name before deleting; do not delete the backup of a device she still uses.
- Browser caches (Chrome: Settings → Privacy → Clear browsing data → Cached images and files; Firefox: similar; Safari: Develop → Empty Caches).

Tier 2 — likely safe
- Mail cached attachments and downloaded messages (Mail → Mailbox → Erase Attachments on macOS; in Outlook, compact the .ost data file).
- Application caches for apps she no longer uses: ~/Library/Caches on macOS, %AppData% on Windows.
- Spotify, Messages, Teams cached media.
- Old .dmg/.pkg installers left in /Applications.

Tier 3 — only if Tier 1 + Tier 2 are not enough
- Unused applications. Use AppCleaner (macOS) or Revo Uninstaller (Windows), not just Trash, to remove leftover support files.
- Old Documents/Desktop items she has confirmed she has elsewhere.
- Large videos with copies elsewhere.

After each tier, empty Trash and recheck free space.

PHASE 6 — RE-VERIFY BEFORE UPDATING
1. Confirm free space ≥ 25 GB (ideally 40 GB).
2. Re-run the backup so the post-cleanup state is captured. This is the snapshot that protects the OS update if something goes wrong.
3. Confirm charger is connected and battery is charging.
4. Confirm internet is stable for the download + install.
5. Begin the OS update via the OS's own flow.
6. Stop conditions for the update: free space drops below threshold mid-install, battery drops, install errors, or repeated restarts without progress. Pause rather than push through.

PHASE 7 — AFTER THE UPDATE
1. Confirm the OS boots normally and the update shows as installed.
2. Reconnect the external drive and let one more backup run so the updated state is captured.
3. Verify the backup schedule is actually active (Time Machine "Back Up Automatically"; File History toggle "On"). Do not assume — open it and look.
4. Do not start further cleanup or reorganization on the same day. Let the update settle.

SEPARATE ITEMS — flag for Anya, not for today
- The backup drive is only useful when connected. The Nov 5 → today gap will repeat every time unless the routine changes (an always-attached drive, a scheduled cloud backup, or a recurring plug-in reminder).
- 9 GB free on a 512 GB drive is a recurring-accumulation pattern, not a one-off. A quarterly 30-minute pass through Tier 1 + Tier 2 prevents this from becoming update-blocking again.

This sequence is bounded: backup, verify, hit the free-space floor using only clearly safe cleanup, then update. It does not require her to sort personal files.

Two readings drive the answer, and only one of them is on the bill:

  1. The Dec 12 actual ending reading. Stated on the current bill as actual.
  2. The actual reading on Nov 11. NOT on the prior bill, because the prior bill said "ending reading estimated November 11." The 252 kWh it billed was based on a guess, not a meter read.

The 286 kWh on the current bill was computed from some starting reading to the Dec 12 actual. The key unknown is whether that starting point is the November estimate (in which case any estimate error is baked into the 286 kWh) or a later-obtained actual reading (in which case 286 kWh is the true Nov 11 to Dec 12 usage).

How to separate real increase from estimate reconciliation

  Step 1. Verify the Dec 12 actual. Photograph the meter now. If the current dial matches what the bill says for Dec 12, the ending is correct. If it differs, the bill may have used an older actual.

  Step 2. Recover the actual Nov 11 reading. Options:
    - Utility account portal: some utilities post a corrected actual once obtained.
    - Any photo you (or the utility) have of the meter on or near Nov 11.
    - Ask the utility directly for the actual Nov 11 reading and the starting reading used to compute this bill's 286 kWh.

  Step 3. Compute actual period usage = (Dec 12 actual) - (Nov 11 actual).

  Step 4. Compare to the billed 286 kWh. The gap is the reconciliation component.

  Three scenarios:
    - Billed 286 ≈ actual period usage → the 34 kWh jump is real.
    - Billed 286 > actual period usage → the Nov 11 estimate was too high. This bill over-collected and you may be owed a credit.
    - Billed 286 < actual period usage → the Nov 11 estimate was too low. Some of this bill is catching up underbilling from the prior period.

Calculations to make before contacting the utility

  Per-day usage:
    Current: 286 / 31 = 9.23 kWh/day
    Prior:    252 / 30 = 8.40 kWh/day
    Delta:    +0.83 kWh/day, or +9.9% on a like-for-like daily basis.

  Per-kWh rates on this bill (current):
    Supply:    $34.32 / 286 = $0.1200 / kWh
    Delivery:  $56.20 / 286 = $0.1965 / kWh
    Total:     $90.52 / 286 = $0.3165 / kWh

  Pull the supply and delivery dollar amounts from the prior bill and divide by 252 kWh. Compare per-kWh figures. If supply and delivery per-kWh are essentially unchanged, the higher total is from higher kWh, not a rate change. If either per-kWh jumped, that explains part of the increase and is a separate question (you've said you aren't disputing rates, but worth confirming so you don't conflate the two effects).

  Weather and occupancy check:
    - NYC daily mean temperature: early-to-mid December is materially colder than early-to-mid November. Heating load plausibly explains part of a single-digit-to-low-double-digit percent kWh increase.
    - Any new loads between the two windows: space heater, holiday lights, extra cooking, a new appliance, longer lighting hours.
    - Occupancy: same number of people, same work-from-home vs out pattern.

What to ask the utility before deciding whether to dispute

  1. The actual meter reading on or closest to Nov 11 (not the estimate).
  2. The starting reading they used to compute this bill's 286 kWh.
  3. Whether the 286 kWh includes any reconciliation from the prior estimated period, or whether the prior estimate will be trued up separately (sometimes it shows as a one-time "estimated read adjustment" line).
  4. Confirmation that the Dec 12 reading on the bill matches a fresh meter read, not a carried-forward figure.

When the answer would justify a dispute

  - Starting reading for 286 kWh was the Nov 11 estimate and the actual Nov 11 reading is materially lower → bill has over-collected.
  - Stated Dec 12 actual does not match a fresh photo → ending is wrong.
  - Supply or delivery per-kWh changed without notice → rate issue, separate from usage.
  - The bill shows an "estimated read adjustment" or "true-up" line you weren't expecting → ask for the math.

When the answer would not justify a dispute

  - Starting reading was an actual obtained after Nov 11 and per-kWh rates match the prior bill → the +34 kWh is real, and a colder December plus normal use explains it.

Photos to take now

  - Meter face showing the full reading, with timestamp.
  - Same shot showing the meter number (74-118-620 if it matches the prior account record).
  - Date the photo.

That gives you a defensible record if you later need to provide evidence, the same pattern that worked on the November 7 photo on the prior South Slope bill (utility accepted the photo and adjusted from $214.38 to $126.74 by replacing the estimated ending with the actual reading).

One small wording note: the bill says "Ending meter reading: actual, December 12." If the bill's usage line is 286 kWh and the period is 31 days ending Dec 12, the implied starting reading is (Dec 12 actual - 286). That's the single number to pin down with the utility, because it tells you which of the three scenarios you are in without needing the separate Nov 11 actual.

ASSESSMENT (proposal not endorsed, not rejected):

The proposal layers three mechanisms:
  A. SDK pre-flight: client rejects batches >8,000 points before transmission, instructs caller to split
  B. ingest-edge HTTP 413: zero accepted, submitted-count rejected (whole-batch)
  C. `oversized_batch`: server backstop for clients that don't adopt SDK validation

What this changes versus the prior soft-rejection proposal:
  - Status code shifts from 429 to 413 (semantically correct for size)
  - Counter semantics become deterministic (0 accepted, N rejected) — addresses the earlier ask for deterministic whole-batch rejection
  - Adds a client-side guardrail that pushes enforcement off the server
  - Adds an explicit backstop for non-adopting clients
  - Introduces a transition period with mixed client behavior (2 of 3 adopting immediately)

The layering changes the failure surface, not just the threshold. Each layer can fail independently; failures compose. Three categories warrant separate analysis.

PER-LAYER FAILURE MODES:

A. SDK pre-flight:
  - Threshold alignment: SDK and server thresholds must match including off-by-one. Proposal says "above 8,000" (strict >). Server must use the same; otherwise valid batches may be rejected client-side or invalid ones accepted server-side. Boundary at exactly 8,000 needs explicit definition on both sides.
  - Caller behavior on rejection: "instruct callers to split" is design intent, not verified outcome. Automated callers that don't read the split instruction will either silently drop, loop on retry, or escalate. Need caller contract (error code, response shape, recommended action) and evidence each of the two adopting clients actually splits.
  - Adoption asymmetry: during transition the production mix is uneven. SDK-rejected batches never reach ingest-edge, so server-side accounting only reflects the older backstop client's traffic. If 91% of historical >8,000 traffic came from one client and that client adopts SDK pre-flight, the residual server cohort shrinks sharply; if the 91% client is the older backstop, the residual does not. Per-client share is not specified in the proposal.
  - SDK release-cycle dependency: a defective SDK pre-flight requires a coordinated release. Rollback for SDK pre-flight must be independent of ingest-edge.
  - Quota interaction: client-side rejected batches should not count against tenant quota; verified behavior needed.

B. ingest-edge HTTP 413 whole-batch:
  - Determinism: zero accepted, submitted-count rejected must hold across all pods and paths. The replay validated this ("retain the validated"); permanent disposition needs continuous validation, not only during the replay window. A regression test for partial-rejection (any partial batch landing in accepted-side accounting) is needed.
  - Retry contract: 413 with caller-side retry of the same batch rejects it again. Caller must split before retry. The response body or headers need to carry guidance, not just status — otherwise callers can't distinguish "size rejected, retry smaller" from "transient failure, retry same."
  - Quota policy: do rejected batches count against per-tenant per-second or per-day quota? If yes, oversized batches consume quota unfairly; if no, quota accounting must distinguish. Policy is undefined in the proposal.
  - Concurrency: a burst of oversized batches across connections could still cause admission pressure. Evidence that the post-rejection path itself does not contribute latency is missing.

C. `oversized_batch` backstop:
  - Definition ambiguity: the proposal says "backstop for older or nonconforming clients" but does not specify whether `oversized_batch` is a server flag, a metric/label, a distinct response code, or a distinct log line. If it's only a label, observability is straightforward; if it's a separate code path with a different response shape, observability and client behavior diverge from the primary path.
  - Distinguishability: operator dashboards need three distinct counters — SDK-rejected (not visible at ingest-edge), server 413 (primary path), and `oversized_batch` (backstop path). Without that, on-call cannot tell expected post-experiment behavior from a latency regression during transition.
  - Rollback: can the backstop be turned off independently of the primary 413 path? If `oversized_batch` involves a behavior change beyond a config flag, toggling it is more involved.

COMPOSITION FAILURE MODES:
  - The proposal moves enforcement to SDK where possible, but the 0.4% (2,001–9,600) and 0.03% (>8,000) replay evidence does not break down per-client. Whether the backstop client carries most of the residual server-side load or a small fraction depends on which client is the older one — unspecified.
  - The 8,000 threshold is replay-validated for normal traffic. It is not validated for burst sub-distribution or concurrency correlation across tenants. If the backstop client produces correlated bursts, server-side latency pressure may persist even with the 8,000 cap.
  - The proposal doesn't address non-8,000 boundary cases. The original latency issue was concentrated above 8,000 (91% from one identifier), so 8,000 is well-placed; but catastrophic sizes (e.g., ≥100,000) and their response-time profile are not characterized.

COMPARISON VS. OPTIONS A, B, C:

Option A (hard 2,000-point client cap on the affected client, no ingest-edge change):
  - Failure: forces a single-client structural decision; addresses one client's contribution but not the broader pattern. Simpler. If the 30-day distribution already shows 99.6% ≤2,000 across the other two clients (per-client share unverified), Option A may be redundant for them.
  - New proposal vs. A: more general (covers all three clients), more complex (three layers vs. one config). A's simplicity is its main advantage.

Option B (ingest-edge soft rejection above 8,000, no SDK change):
  - Failure: still pays server-side admission cost for batches that should never be sent. Doesn't reduce ingest-edge load; only changes response style.
  - New proposal vs. B: B is a strict subset. New proposal adds SDK pre-flight (moves cost off server) and explicit backstop. B alone leaves caller instruction and backstop undefined.

Option C (documentation only):
  - Failure: leaves the reproduced latency path unenforced; no operational signal that the threshold is honored.
  - New proposal vs. C: strictly more enforcement, with the cost of more release surface and coordination.

EVIDENCE NEEDED BEFORE PERMANENT DISPOSITION:

1. Threshold boundary:
   - Exact point count at which SDK pre-flight triggers vs. server 413 triggers (8,000 inclusive or exclusive on each side)
   - Behavior at extreme sizes (≥100,000 points): does ingest-edge reject quickly or process slowly? Response-time profile for catastrophic oversized batches

2. Caller behavior:
   - For each of the three clients, what does the caller do on SDK rejection (split-and-retry, drop, hang)?
   - For the older backstop client, what does the caller do on 413? Has this caller ever seen 413? Will it recognize the response?
   - Sample caller code paths (production or representative) confirming the contract

3. Determinism:
   - Across all ingest-edge pods and paths, regression test confirming 0 accepted, N rejected when N is the submitted count
   - Test for partial-rejection: confirm no partial batch lands in accepted-side accounting

4. Quota and accounting:
   - Whether oversized batches (SDK- or server-rejected) count against per-tenant quota. Policy needed.
   - Counter consistency: SDK-rejected batches are not visible at ingest-edge; aggregate "rejected" metric needs a definition that doesn't double-count or mis-attribute

5. Adoption and transition:
   - Timeline for SDK adoption for each of the three clients
   - Expected fraction of traffic from the older backstop client during transition
   - Whether backstop is permanent "just in case" or temporary until full SDK adoption

6. Operational:
   - Definition of `oversized_batch` as a metric/label — distinct from the general 413 counter?
   - Dashboard representation: how on-call distinguishes SDK-side rejection, server 413, and backstop
   - Rollback paths for each layer independently

7. Burst and concurrency (not yet captured):
   - Within-batch spike pattern of the 0.4% cohort
   - Concurrent oversized batches across tenants: do they affect each other at admission?
   - Post-experiment behavior after the temporary 2,000 cap was lifted: did the 0.4% pattern return, persist, or evolve?

8. Ownership:
   - Which team owns SDK pre-flight release for each client
   - Which team owns ingest-edge 413 path and `oversized_batch` flag
   - Rollout and rollback authority

DECISION POSTURE:

The proposal is plausible. Three specific gaps block permanent disposition:

a. Caller contract is undefined. Until the actual behavior of each client (especially the older backstop-only one) on rejection is verified, the proposal's effect on end-user behavior is unverifiable. "Instruct callers to split" is intent, not outcome.

b. The 8,000 threshold is replay-validated but not burst-validated. Replay covered normal traffic; spike pattern and concurrency of the >8,000 cohort are not characterized. If the backstop client produces correlated bursts, server-side latency pressure may persist.

c. Per-client breakdown of the 0.4% is missing. Without it, the operational metric definition (when does `oversized_batch` count spike?) is unanchored, and the impact of mixed adoption cannot be predicted.

Hot-electrical smell after a stall with an obvious cause (stone in the burrs) is most likely the motor windings heating briefly under stall current in the seconds before you unplugged. That is recoverable in most cases, but the whole point of the inspection below is to rule out the cases where it isn't. Working hypothesis: a foreign object caused the stall, the windings heated briefly, you cut power, the system cooled cleanly. The job now is to verify that hypothesis with a bounded sequence, not to hope. Do all of the following while the grinder stays unplugged.

============================================================
1. PRE-REMOVAL INSPECTION (unplugged, sitting still)
============================================================

Give the grinder at least 5 minutes to fully cool before you touch the burr-chamber area.

Check, in this order:

  a. Outlet, plug, and cord.
     - Outlet face cool, no discoloration.
     - Plug prongs straight, not darkened, no pitting.
     - Cord flexible along its full length. No stiff spots, no flat
       or shiny sections, no bulge near the plug or where the cord
       enters the housing.
     - Strain relief at the housing entry intact.

  b. Housing exterior.
     - Cool to the touch all over (top, sides, base).
     - No odor anywhere on or around it.
     - No discoloration, brown or yellow scorch marks, bubbled or
       warped plastic, hairline cracks near motor vents.

  c. Burr chamber, visible through the hopper opening.
     - Note the color and condition of any plastic you can see.
     - Look for a brown or dark patch near the burr base or the
       motor-housing seam. That alone is a stop signal before you
       touch anything else.

STOP HERE AND DO NOT TEST if any of the following are present:
warm housing, scorch or discoloration, melted plastic, persistent
odor, stiff or damaged cord, darkened plug, or a tripped breaker
or GFCI during the original event. In any of those cases the
grinder stays out of service pending replacement or authorized
service.

============================================================
2. REMOVE THE OBSTRUCTION (still unplugged)
============================================================

Consult your model's manual for the exact steps; the consumer
burr-grinder pattern is:

  a. Remove the hopper and any beans.
  b. Remove the top burr per the manual — usually a counterclockwise
     twist and lift, or a release lever. Do not force it. If it
     won't move normally, stop.
  c. Lift out the stone with fingers or a soft brush. Do NOT use
     metal tools inside the chamber — a slip can chip a burr tooth
     and turn a recoverable event into a junked grinder. A wooden
     chopstick or a plastic pick is acceptable; a small soft brush
     is best.
  d. Inspect both burrs:
       - All teeth present, none chipped or bent.
       - No metal-to-metal scoring marks (shiny arcs).
       - No visible warping.
       - Burrs sit flat against each other with no rocking.
  e. Inspect the chamber:
       - No stone fragments left behind.
       - No discoloration of the plastic walls.
       - No other foreign debris.
  f. With the top burr removed, gently rotate the lower burr carrier
     (which is the visible end of the motor shaft) one full turn
     by hand.
       - Should turn smoothly, with no scraping, grinding, or buzzing.
       - Should have no excessive play. A small amount of axial play
         is normal on most consumer grinders.
       - Should not feel gritty.

Do NOT open the motor housing. It is not user-serviceable, opening
it will not give you useful information, and it will void any
warranty.

============================================================
3. INSPECTION CRITERIA — TEST ONCE vs. LEAVE OUT OF SERVICE
============================================================

You may do a single brief test ONLY if ALL of the following hold:

  - Housing is fully cool to the touch after the 5-minute wait.
  - No scorch, discoloration, or melted plastic anywhere on the
    housing, inside the chamber, on the cord, or on the plug.
  - Cord and plug are undamaged, cool, and flexible.
  - No residual odor after 10 minutes of airing out.
  - The stone looked like an ordinary pale pebble (not metallic,
    not magnetic if you happen to have a magnet handy).
  - Both burrs look intact: no chipped or bent teeth, no scoring.
  - The motor shaft turned smoothly and silently by hand.
  - No breaker or GFCI tripped during the original event.

Leave the grinder out of service (replace or send for authorized
service) if ANY of the following are true:

  - Any scorch mark, brown or yellow discoloration, or melted
    plastic on the housing, chamber, cord, plug, or outlet.
  - Cord is stiff, has a flat spot, or shows any heat damage.
  - Plug prongs are darkened or pitted.
  - Housing is warm to the touch after 10 minutes.
  - Any residual odor persists after 10+ minutes of airing out.
  - The stone was metallic, magnetic, or had sharp angular edges
    suggestive of something other than a pebble.
  - A burr tooth is chipped, bent, or shows scoring.
  - The motor shaft is hard to turn, gritty, has excessive play,
    or makes scraping, buzzing, or any non-silent noise when
    turned by hand.
  - The breaker or GFCI tripped at the time of the original event.
  - You had to use force to free the top burr or to extract the
    stone.

There is no "probably fine" category. Each item above is binary,
and any one failure means out of service.

============================================================
4. IF YOU PROCEED TO TEST (one shot only)
============================================================

  - Keep the grinder unplugged until the test moment.
  - Empty chamber: top burr reinstalled, no beans, hopper off or
    empty, lid open so it cannot jam on first spin.
  - Plug directly into a wall outlet. Do not use an extension cord
    or a power strip for this test.
  - Run for 5 to 10 seconds maximum.
  - Listen for any grinding, scraping, buzzing, or hum that is
    louder or different from the normal no-load sound.
  - Smell immediately. Any electrical or hot-insulation smell
    stops the test and the grinder goes out of service.
  - Unplug, then within 30 seconds touch the motor housing. It
    should be cool or only just barely warm from a 5–10 second
    no-load spin.
  - If anything is off: unplug, do not retry, leave out of service.

A clean empty test is a necessary gate, not a full clearance.
The follow-on loaded test with a small amount of beans is a
separate decision: a loaded test that stalls, smells, or trips
also means out of service.

============================================================
SUMMARY
============================================================

The stone explains the stall. The brief hot-electrical smell is
consistent with the motor working against that stall for the few
seconds before you unplugged. Most grinders survive a single
short stall with an identified foreign-object cause cleanly, but
the inspection list above is the test of whether yours did. Any
single anomaly on the inspection list means the grinder stays
out of service. If you want, tell me the make and model and I
can tailor the burr-removal steps to that specific grinder.

The pattern — pain-free ordinary use, comfortable on open-hand holds, recurrence only on the undercling — is classic for an incompletely resolved forearm flexor strain / early tendinopathy rather than a new injury. The 11 days of rest clearly lowered baseline irritability (Dec 10's 2/10 ache is gone in daily life), but today's test exposed that the tissue still isn't ready for the wrist-flexed + active-finger-extension load that an undercling creates. That is informative, not alarming. It also matters: the rest you did has real value, but it isn't finished. Rest alone rarely restores tendon capacity; graded loading is what does. Today's session counts as a test, not a regression.

Here is a bounded plan with explicit gates. Treat each stage as a separate decision; do not advance on optimism.

CONSERVATIVE LOADING PAUSE (now through ~5 days of being pain-free at rest and during ordinary use)
  - No climbing, including easy open-hand sessions. Warmups that "felt boring" before still reproduced the issue last time, so don't use "felt fine" as proof of readiness.
  - Avoid loaded wrist-flexed gripping in daily life for a few days: carrying heavy grocery bags or a suitcase by the handles, pull-ups, dead-hangs, levering a stuck jar, heavy backpack on one shoulder strap.
  - Ordinary daily gripping — kettle, doorknob, mug, steering wheel — is fine and useful. Ordinary use being clean is the gate to advance, not the goal.
  - Heat or ice per preference; whatever you normally tolerate for forearm soreness. Topical NSAID gel is reasonable if you want it; oral NSAIDs are optional and not required.
  - Sleep, hydration, normal protein. Nothing exotic needed.

RETURN PROGRESSION (each stage must be pain-free during the session AND the morning after; any ache >1/10 or pattern-recurrence returns you to the previous stage and adds 2–3 rest days before retrying)

Stage 1 — Pain-free isometric loading in neutral wrist
  - Rice-bucket squeezes or a soft-grip hand exerciser at low force, neutral or palm-down wrist.
  - 30–45 second holds × 4, twice daily. No wrist flexion against resistance.

Stage 2 — Wrist-flexion isometrics, short lever only
  - Light isometric wrist flexion against your opposite palm, fingers mostly straight, elbow tucked.
  - 20–30 second holds × 5, twice daily. Stop short of any pinch.

Stage 3 — Light concentric/eccentric wrist curls
  - 1–2 kg (a soup can is fine), palm up, slow tempo through the full pain-free range.
  - 3 × 12, once daily. Add a light eccentric by lowering with the off-hand.

Stage 4 — Climbing re-entry, slab and traversing only
  - 15–20 minutes of easy slab and low traversing.
  - Open-hand grips, slopers, big jugs only. No crimps, no pinches, no underclings.
  - Downclimb everything. No jump-downs.
  - Hard rule: stop while it still feels boring. No "one more."

Stage 5 — Add vertical jugs and moderate movement
  - Still no crimps, no pinches, no underclings.

Stage 6 — Open-hand crimp on large edges only
  - Avoid full crimp. Single attempts, not reps.

Stage 7 — Undercling reintroduction, last
  - Wide, comfortable underclings on low-angle walls, 2–3 attempts max, then return to neutral holds.
  - Bail plan set before you start. A single undercling that brings back familiar discomfort means stop for the day; two such attempts on different days means pause the undercling line for a week and reassess.

Important framing, preserved deliberately:
  - Open-hand climbing being tolerated is not the same as undercling tolerance, and easy tolerated is not the same as sports-cleared. Each stage is a separate test of a separate capacity.

CRITERIA FOR SPORTS-MEDICINE OR PHYSICAL-THERAPY EVALUATION (book a non-urgent appointment, but don't delay the booking)
  - Pain does not fully clear at rest within 2–3 weeks of this pause.
  - Pain recurs at progressively lower loads across return attempts — a sign of cumulative tissue irritability rather than transient overload.
  - Pain persists >24 hours after a return-stage session, or shows progressive next-day worsening rather than morning-of mildness that fades within an hour.
  - New focal bony tenderness, especially at the medial epicondyle or along the forearm muscle-tendon junctions.
  - Palpable thickening, nodule, or tender band that wasn't there before.
  - Objectively reduced grip strength compared with the other side (a cheap hand-grip dynamometer reading is enough).
  - Pain at rest, with ordinary unweighted activities, or pain that wakes you from sleep.
  - Any numbness, tingling, or nerve-pattern referral into the hand or fingers.
  - Visible swelling, bruising, or skin color change.

SAME-DAY URGENT EVALUATION (urgent care or ER — not PT, not sports medicine)
  - Sudden sharp "pop" or tearing sensation during any activity.
  - Acute compartment-syndrome signs in the forearm: rapidly increasing pain, severe pain on passive finger extension, visible tenseness or swelling of the forearm, pallor, paresthesia, pulselessness or weak pulse. These are rare but emergent.
  - Suspected tendon rupture — sudden loss of grip strength with a visible or palpable change in the muscle or tendon.

If none of those thresholds trigger, the right next step is the pause and the staged return above, with Stage 7 deliberately last and gated. Recurrence at a specific provocative load on day 11 is a signal to change the loading strategy, not a reason to declare the forearm broken — but it is also not permission to keep testing it every few days. Give it the pause, run the progression honestly, and use the gates.

A side note, low-priority: today is in your Friday window. Save the progression start for Monday so you're not testing new forearm loading the same week. If you want to use the weekend for a flat walk with Kibo or Devika instead, that's a clean use of the time and keeps the forearm quiet.

The 126°F reading is meaningfully under the 145°F serving guidance for fish, and 133°F is close but not there. Carryover rest alone won't bridge 126°F → 145°F (a thick piece typically climbs only 8–10°F under foil). You need active, gentle heat applied to the thick sections while shielding the already-finished thin one. Here's the bounded plan.

Finish the salmon — safest path:

1. Separate the sections now. Slice the thick portions away from the thin tail. The thin 145°F section goes onto a warm plate, tented with foil, off-heat. The two thick sections stay on the cooking surface or move to a small sheet pan, skin side down.
2. Low-oven finish at 225°F, not higher. Higher heat will jump the outer layers past 145°F before the center catches up. At 225°F the gradient is gentle enough that the center can climb while the outer edge stays near target.
3. Target the 126°F section first — it's the longest path. Plan on roughly 4–6 minutes at 225°F for a ~1.5-inch thick portion pulled at 126°F. The 133°F section will finish sooner.
4. Check with the instant-read at the 3-minute mark in the geometric center of the thickest piece. Recheck every 60–90 seconds after that.
5. Pull each thick section the instant its center hits 143–144°F. Carryover during the 1–2 minute rest under foil will carry it to 145°F.
6. Stop conditions: if the outer edge of a thick section climbs past 150°F while the center is still under 140°F, drop the oven to 200°F or pull and tent — the gradient is too steep and you're heading toward overcooked-outside / under-inside.

If you don't want to separate, the fallback is: tent just the thin section with a doubled foil sleeve, return the whole fillet to 225°F, and check the thick center every 2 minutes. It's a wider window and easier to overshoot, so the separated version is the more controlled choice.

Vegetables during the delay (roughly 5–10 minutes):

- Turn the burner under the vegetables off, slide the pan off the hot element, and put a lid on. Covered residual heat will keep them at a safe serving temperature for 10 minutes without overcooking or drying out.
- If the pan is shallow and you're worried about cooling fast, set it on a warm (not hot) burner that you just used — the residual element warmth is usually enough.
- Don't put the vegetables in the 225°F oven with the salmon. Veggies over-dry at low-oven hold and you don't need to expose the salmon's finishing window to anything else.

Order of operations: vegetables off-heat and lidded first, then start the salmon finish. That way the salmon lands at target just as the vegetables are still hot.

Practical lost-badge sequence. Two phases: TONIGHT (containment + verify nothing happened) and MONDAY MORNING (replace + verify new badge works). The badge carries no keys, medication, or patient info, so the data-at-rest risk is essentially zero — the real risk is an unauthorized scan before you block it, so the call is the first move, not the search.

Reference points from prior verified experience: on the March 22 incident, hospital security took the call, verified her identity, temporarily blocked the badge, and a nurse found it near the locker-room sign-out station. On April 22, the credentialing office accepted government photo ID plus coordinator confirmation. Use the same channels here.

TONIGHT — Sunday 12/22

1.  Containment call to hospital security (now, before Monday)
    -   Call the hospital security/operator line — same path as the March 22 incident. Do not wait for Monday morning to report.
    -   Report: badge lost; last verified use was her 7:05 AM Friday scan-out. Confirm that timestamp directly.
    -   Request: temporary deactivation/block pending replacement, so a found or stolen badge cannot be used over the weekend.
    -   Capture: incident/ticket number, officer name, time of call, and what they actually did (block applied now, block pending, etc.). Write these down — you'll need them Monday.

2.  Account and remote-access checks to ask security (or IT) to run tonight
    Ask security/IT to pull and confirm the following before Monday:
    -   Badge scan history on her badge ID from 7:05 AM Friday through the current time. The expected outcome is zero scans after 7:05 AM Friday; anything else is an access-control incident, not a routine loss.
    -   EHR / clinical-system login history tied to her badge or identity since Friday morning. Badges often front EHR sessions even when no physical door is involved.
    -   SSO and authentication-app sessions. The hospital SSO and the phone authentication app are separate from the badge, but they share the identity. Ask whether any session has been opened under her identity that she did not start.
    -   VPN or remote-access sessions under her identity since Friday. Confirm whether the badge is even part of that path (it usually is not) and whether any remote session is open or has been opened.
    -   Pharmacy, controlled-access, or supply-dispensing logs under her ID.
    -   Manager-facing systems: any attempt to view schedules, payroll, or contact info under her identity.
    Important framing for the call: she is not asking them to investigate a breach, she is asking them to confirm the badge has been idle since 7:05 AM Friday. That is a routine audit pull, not an alarm.

3.  Bounded apartment search tonight — do not tear the place apart
    Concentrate on surfaces and Friday-morning paths:
    -   Coat: inner breast pocket, lining pocket, sleeve pocket, hood.
    -   Work bag: pen/pencil loops, inner mesh, side pockets, bottom compartment, key clip.
    -   Entry area: key hook, shoe rack shelf, umbrella stand, doormat (lift and shake), coat-closet floor.
    -   Friday-morning path: re-walk mentally and physically wherever she set the badge down before leaving Friday. That is the highest-yield apartment search.
    -   Car (if applicable): footwells, door pockets, trunk, between seats.
    Do not move furniture, pull out appliances, or empty closets tonight. The higher-yield path is the workplace search by security on Monday (per the March 22 precedent — badges turn up near locker-area sign-out stations).

4.  If found tonight
    -   Call security back to lift the temporary block or mark the badge recovered.
    -   Confirm no scan occurred between Friday 7:05 AM and recovery.
    -   No Monday credentialing visit is needed unless security requires one.

5.  If not found by bedtime
    -   Stop searching. Lock in the Monday plan. Going past a reasonable stop time does not improve the odds and breaks sleep before a clinical day.

MONDAY MORNING — 12/23

6.  Pack before leaving
    -   Government photo ID.
    -   Hospital employee number (if she has it on a paystub or ID portal).
    -   The incident/ticket number and officer name from tonight's call.
    -   Charged phone with the hospital authentication app working.
    -   Any credentialing/security appointment confirmation from tonight's call (time, office).
    -   A payment method, in case there is a replacement fee — typical hospital policy, but do not assume a specific amount; ask security tonight what the fee is so it is not a surprise at the desk.

7.  Arrive early enough to clear credentialing/security before her shift starts
    -   Go to the hospital security / credentialing office. Per the April 22 re-verification pattern, the credentialing office accepts government photo ID plus a confirming reference — here the equivalent is tonight's lost-badge ticket plus ID.
    -   Sign any required lost-badge affidavit or statement. Hospitals vary on whether a statement, a manager signoff, or both are required; do not skip this step, because it closes the audit trail.
    -   Pay the replacement fee if asked.
    -   Receive the replacement badge.

8.  Test the new badge before patient contact
    -   Scan in at one staffed/secure door and confirm the read is hers.
    -   Test each door on her normal Monday route — unit/ward entry, locker, supply, medication room if she uses one.
    -   Confirm EHR/SSO login works with the new badge or replacement identity.
    -   Confirm the authentication app on her phone still works and is linked to her account.

9.  Confirm closure, not just issuance
    -   Ask security to confirm the old badge is fully deactivated in the access-control system, not just blocked. A block can be reversed; a deactivation cannot.
    -   Keep the ticket number. Some hospitals run a 30-day audit on lost badges and may follow up.
    -   If her unit has a charge nurse, coordinator, or attending she routinely checks in with, give that person a brief heads-up before patient contact — it is operationally cleaner than letting them find out from a delay.

Stop and escalation triggers (do not improvise past these)
-   If security reports any scan on her badge between Friday 7:05 AM and the block, that is an access-control incident, not a routine replacement. Escalate to IT and her supervisor; do not treat it as "probably nothing."
-   If replacement requires a supervisor approval she didn't anticipate, ask whether she can work in a non-secured role (charting, phone triage within policy, etc.) or float until cleared. Do not use someone else's badge or a workaround.
-   If the authentication app or SSO is also affected, do not log into clinical systems until IT confirms a clean state.
-   If she cannot reach security tonight by phone, leave a voicemail plus a written report through whatever after-hours channel the hospital publishes (operator page, intranet form). Do not let the report sit until Monday morning — the whole point of the tonight call is to close the window between Friday 7:05 AM and Monday.

8. Replaced-node catch-up and follower-read-pool behavior. Confirm the new node converged before any replica reentered follower reads; no replica reentered before convergence.

9. No reload failures, restarts, or dropped series during the interval. Standard guards.

10. Replacement provenance and shard-set mapping. 11. Alert-vs-reality reconciliation. Why did the alert fire on 12 of 480 specifically? Check the alert's threshold and sampling so we know whether other shards could have shown the same behavior without alerting. The alert is coarse; verification reads logs.

OVERVIEW
  Strategy: cook chicken and potatoes at the same temperature (425°F) on different
  oven racks, stagger their start times so the chicken finishes 20 minutes before
  the potatoes, rest the chicken while the potatoes finish, then sauté the green
  beans in the last 8 minutes. Nothing sits longer than 25 minutes covered.

  Oven is 425°F the entire time. Probe-thermometer verification drives the pull
  decision, not the clock.

TIMED SEQUENCE (clock times anchored to 6:30 PM service)

  3:30 PM  Chicken out of fridge. Remove giblets/neck, pat bone-dry inside and out
           (paper towels; this is the single biggest factor for crisp skin).
           Salt generously all over and inside cavity. Set breast-up on a rack
           in the roasting pan. Leave on the counter — 60 min of chill-off
           evens out the cook.

  3:45 PM  Lower rack in place. Preheat oven to 425°F.

  4:00 PM  Scrub and cut potatoes into uniform 1.5-inch pieces. In the separate
           pan, toss with 2–3 Tbsp oil, salt, pepper. Hold at room temp.

  4:15 PM  Optional aromatics in cavity (halved lemon, garlic, thyme). Tuck wing
           tips behind the back, tie legs loosely. Pat skin dry one more time,
           lightly oil, sprinkle with salt.

  4:30 PM  Chicken on lower rack. Close oven. (75-min expected cook.)

  5:15 PM  Potatoes on upper rack. (They'll share the oven with the chicken
           for the next 30 minutes.) (50-min cook from here.)

  5:40 PM  First temp check — see verification section below. Plan to pull
           chicken no later than 5:50 PM regardless, to allow 15-min rest and
           25-min buffer for veg.

  5:45 PM  Pull chicken if probes hit target. Move to cutting board or warm
           platter. Tent LOOSELY with foil (loose = skin stays crisp; tight
           foil steams it).

  6:05 PM  Pull potatoes. Cover the pan TIGHTLY with foil. They'll hold above
           150°F easily for 25 minutes this way.

  6:10 PM  Wash and trim green beans. Have garlic/oil/butter ready by the stove.

  6:15 PM  Large skillet, medium-high. Oil or butter, sliced garlic, 30 sec.

  6:16 PM  Green beans in, toss to coat, salt and pepper.

  6:20 PM  Splash of water or broth, lid on, 90 sec to steam-crisp.

  6:22 PM  Lid off, heat up, 60–90 sec to drive off moisture and char edges.

  6:24 PM  Off heat. Taste, adjust salt, optional squeeze of lemon or knob of
           butter.

  6:25 PM  Uncover potatoes, toss, taste. (Covered 20 min — still hot.)

  6:27 PM  Carve chicken: legs off, thighs separated from drumsticks, breast
           sliced against the grain. Arrange on warm platter.

  6:28 PM  Beans and potatoes into serving bowls.

  6:30 PM  Serve.

TEMPERATURE VERIFICATION (the gate, not the clock)

  Probe placement — two distinct sites, both probed:
    1. Thickest part of the THIGH, taking care the tip does NOT touch bone.
       Bone contact reads falsely high and you'll undercook the meat.
    2. Thickest part of the BREAST, same rule — tip in the meat, not against
       bone or cartilage.

  Targets (USDA safe minimum is 165°F everywhere; pull earlier and let
  carryover finish the job):
    Breast:  160–163°F at pull  →  rests to 165–168°F
    Thigh:   172–175°F at pull   →  rests to 175–180°F, dark meat is tender

  If breast is at target but thigh is still under 170°F: tent just the breast
  loosely with foil and return the bird 5–8 minutes. Re-probe.

  If thigh is at 175°F but breast is climbing past 165°F: pull now. The breast
  is already at safe temp; further roasting only dries it out.

WHY THE VEGETABLES STAY HOT

  Potatoes: covered tight 6:05 → 6:25 (20 min). A foil-sealed pan retains heat
  far better than a tented one; they come off the heat at ~200°F and will be
  well above serving temp at 6:25.

  Green beans: finished at 6:24, plated 6:28, served 6:30 — only 6 minutes from
  pan to plate. No holding needed.

  Chicken: tented LOOSELY 5:45 → 6:25 (40 min on the board, but only the last
  ~25 min matters for serving; the first 15 min is the rest, the rest is fine
  at warm-room-temp while you carve). Cutting board or warm platter, not a
  cold surface.

FAIL-SAFE ADJUSTMENTS

  If chicken is running 10 min behind at the 5:40 check: pull potatoes at
  6:05 anyway (they can hold covered); let chicken run to 5:55. Start green
  beans at 6:20 instead of 6:16 — they'll still be done with 4 min to plate.

  If chicken is running 10 min ahead (breast already 165°F at 5:30, thigh
  already 175°F): pull now. Start potatoes immediately. Green beans at 6:20.
  You'll be early, which is the correct kind of problem on Christmas Eve.

Yes, the combined load alone fully explains the trip; nothing in what you've described points to a wiring fault yet.

The math
  15 A × 120 V = 1,800 W breaker rating.
  NEC continuous-load practice (loads expected to run >3 hr) caps sustained draw at 80% of that, i.e. ~1,440 W.
  1,500 W kettle + 1,450 W toaster = 2,950 W, or roughly 24–25 A at 120 V.
  That is ~1.6× the breaker's rating and ~2× the continuous limit, so an instantaneous trip is exactly what an overload of that size produces. Either appliance alone (about 12.5 A and 12.1 A respectively) is within rating.

What your reset tells you
  You unplugged both before resetting, the breaker held set, and there is no heat, odor, discoloration, buzzing, sparking, looseness, or repeat trip with the loads off. That sequence is consistent with a pure overload on a healthy circuit. The absence of any warmth at the breaker face, the plug, or the receptacle after the trip is the key negative finding — overload trips often leave the wiring cool because the breaker opens before the conductor insulation gets meaningfully hot.

Safe reuse on this circuit
  Run the kettle and the toaster one at a time, not simultaneously. Either alone is fine on a 15 A circuit, including for normal cycle lengths (kettle 2–4 min, toaster a few minutes). Kettles and toasters are short-duty by design and won't push the continuous-load envelope.
  If you want both running at once in the future, the right move is to test a different kitchen receptacle on a different circuit, not to push more load through this one. NEC 210.11(C)(1) generally requires two small-appliance branch circuits serving kitchen counters, so a second receptacle is often on a separate 15 A or 20 A circuit. Try the other counter outlet with only one appliance first; if it holds with one appliance, you can reasonably run kettle on one receptacle and toaster on the other. Label which outlets share which breaker at the panel so you don't have to guess.

Things not to do
  Do not swap the breaker for a higher rating — that's a fire hazard and a code violation, and it masks the real constraint.
  Do not use an extension cord, power strip, or "cheater" adapter to draw the two appliances from the same receptacle.
  Do not tape, hold, or otherwise defeat the breaker.
  Do not reset repeatedly without identifying the cause; each reset on a real fault adds heat to the weakest joint.

Escalation triggers — leave the circuit off and call someone if any of these appear
  Trip with a single appliance running (kettle alone, or toaster alone) on this circuit.
  Trip that reoccurs the moment you reset, before any appliance is plugged in.
  Breaker face, plug, receptacle, or cord feels warm or hot to the touch at any time.
  Buzzing, crackling, sizzling, or any odor from the breaker panel, receptacle, or appliance plug.
  Discoloration, scorch marks, melted plastic, or a loose/burning-smelling plug.
  Flickering lights or other appliances losing power on the same circuit when the kettle or toaster runs.
  Repeated nuisance trips even with one appliance, especially after the appliance has run fine elsewhere.
  Breaker that won't reset at all, or that resets but won't stay set.

Who to call and when
  Building management first is appropriate when the issue is in the building's wiring — for example, a receptacle that feels warm, a panel that buzzes, a breaker that won't hold set with no load, or any suspicion that the circuit is mislabeled or shared in a way the panel directory doesn't reflect. Management owns the panel and the wiring in the walls; they're also the right contact if you want a licensed electrician brought in, because most leases require landlord coordination before tenant-arranged electrical work.
  A licensed electrician directly is appropriate when you've ruled out appliance behavior — each appliance runs fine alone on a known-good outlet elsewhere, the breaker won't hold with no load, or there are physical signs of damage at the receptacle or in the cord. An electrician can also do a one-time circuit audit: identify which receptacles share which breaker, measure actual loaded voltage, and check terminations at the panel if you want certainty before relying on this circuit for breakfast routines.
  If you smell burning, see smoke, or the breaker area is hot, treat it as an active electrical fault: leave the breaker off, do not reset, and call management or an electrician the same day. 911 / fire department is appropriate only for active fire or smoke you can't isolate by switching the breaker off.

Bottom line
  A 1,500 W kettle and a 1,450 W toaster on one 15 A, 120 V circuit will trip that breaker by overload every time; your reset held and no damage signs appeared, so the circuit is behaving normally. Use them one at a time on this circuit, or split them across two receptacles if your kitchen is wired with two small-appliance circuits. Any of the escalation triggers above flips this from a routine overload into a wiring or breaker issue that warrants management or an electrician before further use.

The 1.67% (7/420) crossing is real but statistically uninformative at that sample size. Three things make it a low-signal page rather than a production incident:

  - 420 decisions in 5 minutes is dramatically below the usual tens of thousands. At that volume, a single synthetic probe suite failing 7 times is enough to clear 1%.
  - All 7 share one synthetic identifier. That is the dominant signal: a probe-specific failure, not a correlated real-user regression.
  - Surrounding intervals are clean, latency is normal, egress reconciles. The pipeline is healthy; the rule is paging on noise around an isolated test probe.

Interpretation: this is most likely a probe-side failure (fixture drift, infra flakiness in the synthetic generator, or a probe whose expectations no longer match the current router behavior after a recent change). It is not a routing regression, not a dependency failure, and not a customer-visible issue based on the data given.

Immediate evidence checks, in order:

  1. Resolve the shared synthetic identifier to its probe owner and probe type. Pull its fixture, run schedule over the prior 24h, and request_type. If it runs every 5 minutes and only failed this once, the working hypothesis is intermittent probe flakiness. The page belongs to the probe owner, not the metrics-router oncall.
  2. Pull the 500 cause on the 7 requests: timeout, panic, upstream dependency error, missing config, validation failure, or fixture mismatch. A probe-specific error class (e.g., fixture validation, expected-vs-actual schema) confirms the test-side root cause.
  3. Check whether real tenant traffic in the same window produced any error under a different identifier. Expected: zero. If non-zero, the picture changes and the synthetic finding is incidental.
  4. Check customer-facing channels (support inbox, status page mentions, internal Slack escalation channels) for the same window. Expected: nothing.
  5. Cross-reference the probe against any release, config push, or dashboard change in the prior 30 minutes. If a canary or config landed recently, the probe may now mismatch expected behavior. Still a probe issue, but worth flagging to the canary owner so the probe can be updated or pinned.
  6. Confirm rollup/egress accounting is still exact (it is, per the data given) and that no other canary panel tripped.

Safer alert formulation:

The current rule treats "1% error rate over 5 minutes" as a fixed threshold. The signal-to-noise ratio of that rule depends entirely on N, so the rule is too sensitive on near-idle traffic and roughly correct at steady state. Three layered changes fix it without losing sensitivity to real failures.

  A. Minimum sample size guard. Only treat the rate as meaningful above a traffic floor:

       (rate(500s[5m]) / rate(decisions[5m])) > 0.01
       AND rate(decisions[5m]) > 1000
       for: 2m

     This is the single highest-value change. At N=420 there is no page. At N=10,000 with a true 1% rate there still is. The 2m `for` window prevents a single-interval blip from clearing.

  B. Absolute burst detection. Real failures usually look like an absolute count jump, not a ratio. Add a sibling rule:

       rate(500s[5m]) > 50
       for: 1m

     where 50 is set from the historical 99th percentile absolute 5m count with headroom. This catches a 1% rate at 100k rps (1,000 errors/5m) and also catches an unusual spike at moderate traffic that the ratio rule might miss if it is still under 1%.

  C. Synthetic / non-production identifier separation. If synthetic traffic is labelable (e.g., `source="synthetic"` or a known identifier prefix), exclude it from the production error rate and alert on synthetic failure rate separately, routed to the probe owner. This isolates probe health from router health so a failing probe cannot page the metrics-router oncall.

  D. (Optional) Multi-window burn confirmation for sustained conditions:

       (rate(5m) > 1% AND rate(1h) > 0.5%)

     This catches drift that the fast window alone cannot, and rejects single-window spikes. Less critical if A and B are in place.

Combined, A + B + C give:
  - Real production failure -> B fires (absolute burst), or A fires if traffic is sufficient
  - Synthetic probe blip on holiday -> only C's synthetic alert fires (or nothing, if probe team has its own page path)
  - Single-window statistical noise -> A's `for: 2m` and B's `for: 1m` require sustained signal

The current alert fails because it conflates "error rate" with "errors." A is the targeted fix for this specific failure mode; B and C cover the cases a ratio-based threshold structurally cannot see. None of these changes suppress detection of real failures - they only suppress detection of noise that, by construction, the ratio threshold cannot distinguish from real failures at low N.

CLINICAL READ (where you are on 2024-12-28)

What you have is a low-grade right forearm flexor / flexor-tendon strain, still in the healing window. The picture is mostly reassuring — no swelling, bruising, numbness, tingling, focal bony tenderness, full motion, normal grip, pain-free ordinary use, and only 1/10 on resisted wrist flexion at rest. But the undercling-specific reproduction at 2/10 is the part that matters most, because:

  - it has now reproduced on two separate occasions,
  - it is the same movement pattern each time,
  - it specifically loads the wrist and finger flexors through range,
  - and the load is small.

That combination argues the tissue is not yet back to tolerating the very pattern that provoked it, and points more toward a flexor-tendon strain (which heals more slowly than pure muscle) than a one-off muscle pull. Honest framing: easy open-hand climbing being tolerable is not the same as the flexor tendon tolerating an undercling.

GRADED LOADING PLAN

Phase 0 — Relative rest + symptom baseline (this week, through ~2025-01-04)
  - Keep the full pause on climbing and undercling-type loading.
  - Ordinary daily use is allowed and is your rehab signal — stay 0/10 in real life.
  - Self-check daily: open-hand grip, resisted wrist flexion, light undercling simulation.
  - Optional: hot/cold contrast or warmth before the self-check, never through it.

Phase 1 — Sub-pain-threshold isometrics (start 2025-01-04 if Phase 0 criteria met)
  - Wrist-flexion isometric against light resistance, ~5–7 s hold, several reps, 1–2x/day.
  - Stop at the first hint of discomfort; do not chase 1/10.
  - Forearm extensor isometrics for balance (same time, similar effort).
  - Gentle finger-flexor isometrics (light rubber-band finger extensions, or a soft ball hold-and-relax).
  - No loading the day before a re-check of the undercling simulation.

Phase 2 — Isotonic and eccentric loading (only after Phase 1 cleared)
  - Light wrist curls (very low weight, full pain-free range).
  - Eccentric wrist extension (reverse wrist curls) — important for tendon health.
  - Eccentric finger flexion with a rubber band or finger-extension hangs on a low edge, slow tempo.
  - Continue extensor work to keep flexor/extensor balance.

Phase 3 — Climbing re-entry (only after Phase 2 cleared, and never on the same day as a flexor-loaded session in Phase 2)
  - Easy open-hand jugs only, large holds, no pinches, no crimps, no underclings.
  - Short sessions, 15–25 min, downclimb everything.
  - Stop while still boring. No "one more try."
  - Volume cap: if you can't repeat the same session cleanly two days in a row, drop a grade.

Phase 4 — Progressive loading, including undercling (the last thing you reintroduce)
  - Step 1: small open-hand crimps, easy angles, then larger slopers and pinches.
  - Step 2: small undercling on a large hold, very low intensity, single move, walk-off.
  - Step 3: undercling sequences, short, easy grades.
  - Step 4: undercling at session intensity, with strict rep/time cap.
  - Stop and return to the previous step for any 1/10 or higher in-session or the next morning.

UNDERCLING-SPECIFIC GUIDANCE

  - Treat the undercling as a separate, later-stage exposure, not a normal climbing move.
  - Prefer open-hand undercling grips (less finger flexion) before finger-flexed underclings.
  - First reintroduction: single move, large undercling jug, walk-off downclimb, no chain.
  - Avoid undercling in a hangboard or repeater context for several cycles after first tolerance.
  - If undercling reproduces pain at any step, drop back one step for a full week before retrying.

CRITERIA TO DELAY (do not start Phase 3 climbing yet)

  - Open-hand grip at rest is not 0/10 in ordinary use.
  - Resisted wrist flexion reproduces >0/10.
  - Light undercling simulation reproduces >0/10.
  - Any new swelling, bruising, focal bony tenderness, numbness, tingling, or grip loss.
  - Grip strength is reduced versus your normal baseline.
  - Self-check is trending worse over two consecutive days, not stable or improving.
  - You had any recurrence during Phase 1 or Phase 2 loading — treat that as the same pattern returning and reset one phase.

CRITERIA FOR SPORTS-MEDICINE / PT EVALUATION

I'd actually recommend being proactive on this one given the pattern. A reasonable trigger list:

  - Same-pattern recurrence has now happened twice in roughly 18 days — that is a real signal even at low intensity.
  - Light undercling simulation is still >0/10 after 2 more weeks of Phase 0 + Phase 1.
  - Phase 1 loading reproduces the pattern in the same location.
  - Any undercling simulation at 2/10 or higher at the end of next week (before Phase 3 starts).
  - Any in-session or next-morning pain during Phase 3 or Phase 4.
  - Any new red flag: rest pain, night pain, swelling, bruising, focal bony tenderness, numbness, tingling, progressive weakness, or mechanical symptoms (clicking, catching, crepitus).
  - Functional limit: ordinary grip, opening jars, or carrying a bag becomes symptomatic.
  - Pain that begins to spread proximally (toward elbow/upper arm) or distally into the hand.

A sports-medicine clinician or a climbing-experienced PT can distinguish flexor muscle strain, flexor-tendon strain / early tendinopathy, and any referred or nerve-related contribution, and can hand you a loading program matched to your tissue rather than to the population average. Given the recurrence, "wait and see through one more cycle" is a defensible choice but not the conservative default — a single evaluation now is a small cost relative to letting a flexor-tendon strain become a recurring season-long issue.

REASSESSMENT CHECKPOINTS

  - 2025-01-04 (1 week): self-check all three levels; decide Phase 1 vs continued Phase 0.
  - 2025-01-11 (2 weeks): same self-check; if undercling simulation still >0/10, book PT/sports-medicine before considering Phase 3.
  - 2025-01-18 onward: same self-check weekly before each climbing re-entry.
  - Stop the entire plan and seek same-week evaluation for any red-flag item above.

If it helps, treat the next two weeks the same way you treat a metered canary window: hold the criteria, do not advance on intuition, and stop and re-evaluate the moment any single signal trips. The fact that you caught this on the second recurrence, with no red flags and clean baseline function, is the best moment in the timeline to either resolve it conservatively or hand it to someone who can read the tendon directly.
