The macOS-flavored terminology in the prior storage-cleanup context ("application-support folders", "old device backups", "Caches" as a category) makes macOS the working assumption. If this is actually Windows, the structure below is still right; the platform-specific tools become BitLocker recovery key instead of FileVault, WinRE instead of Recovery Mode, and a system-image or File History backup instead of Time Machine. The principles (verify the backup, secure the recovery credential before you start, disconnect the backup drive during install, escalate recovery in order from least to most destructive) are the same.

============================================================
PRE-UPDATE CHECKLIST
============================================================

Final readiness gate is at the end of this section. Do not start the install until every item in the gate is true.

1. BACKUP — THE RECOVERY ANCHOR

  - Re-run backup verification RIGHT NOW. "Still verifies" from earlier is not the gate; the gate is a fresh verification immediately before the update.
  - Time Machine: right-click the backup disk icon in the menu bar (or in System Settings → General → Time Machine → Options) → Verify Backup Disk. Wait for completion. Do not proceed if any error appears.
  - Open the backup browser and read ONE current workshop file from it. Verify-only checks can miss a "backup succeeded but corrupt" case; an actual file open catches that.
  - Note the timestamp of the most recent snapshot. It should be after the cleanup finished, not before.
  - Confirm the backup destination still has free space.
  - DISCONNECT the backup drive physically after verification. The installer can be confused by attached external volumes, and you do not want a partial snapshot overlapping the update window.

2. POWER AND INTERRUPTIONS

  - AC adapter plugged in AND seated. Gentle wiggle-test: if the MagSafe / charging light flickers or the battery indicator drops, fix the connection before continuing. A mid-update power loss is one of the few ways to corrupt the boot volume.
  - System Settings → Battery → confirm "Wake for network access" / Power Nap is OFF. The updater must not be paused by sleep.
  - Confirm "Prevent computer from sleeping automatically when the display is off" is ON.
  - Enable Focus / Do Not Disturb so Slack, Mail, calendar, and other alerts don't pop dialogs over the installer.
  - Cancel or disable any scheduled backups, virus scans, sync jobs, or backup-vault maintenance that would start during the install window.
  - Confirm automatic logout / screen-saver password is set to a long interval or off, so the installer is not interrupted by a lock screen.

3. DISK SPACE

  - 41 GB free, 28 GB shown by the updater. That is healthy headroom, but the install phase can transiently need a small amount more. Re-check the updater's stated requirement immediately before starting (it can drift if Apple has published a different version since the last check).
  - Activity Monitor → Storage tab. Confirm no app is holding a suspiciously large cache. If something unknown is using >5 GB, quit it.

4. RECORD CURRENT STATE — THE ROLLBACK TARGET

  - Apple menu → About This Mac → note EXACTLY: macOS version, macOS build, chip (Apple Silicon vs Intel), and storage size.
  - In Software Update, note the target update's version + build.
  - Note FileVault status (System Settings → Privacy & Security → FileVault).
  - Record these on paper or in a note on another device, not on this laptop. The laptop is the thing that may not come back.

5. FILEVAULT RECOVERY KEY — THE CATASTROPHIC-RISK GATE

  - If FileVault is ON: a failed boot will require the recovery key to access data. The key must be retrievable from OUTSIDE this laptop — because if the laptop won't boot, you cannot get the key from it.
  - Confirm the key is in one of: iCloud (reachable from another device or icloud.com), a printed / written record in another physical location, or an institutional escrow.
  - If you cannot confirm the key is retrievable from outside this laptop: STOP. Do not proceed with the update. There is no recovery path for a FileVault-locked boot failure without the key.

6. CREDENTIALS AND ACCESS FROM ANOTHER DEVICE

  - Apple ID password (for the account signed into this Mac) — known, retrievable.
  - 2FA trusted device working (your phone or another Apple device).
  - Password manager (1Password, iCloud Keychain, etc.) — sync status confirmed as of today.
  - App Store / vendor credentials for any must-restore app — recorded outside this laptop.
  - License keys / install media / installer files for any non-App-Store app — recorded outside this laptop or on a second external drive that is NOT the Time Machine backup drive.

7. NETWORK

  - Wi-Fi signal stable. If marginal, plug into Ethernet or move closer to the router.
  - Confirm no planned ISP outage / router reboot in the next several hours.
  - A weak link during a macOS install can hang the installer in a way that requires Recovery to repair.

8. PERIPHERALS

  - Disconnect all external displays, drives, hubs, dongles, and printers. Keep only: AC power, built-in keyboard/trackpad, and the built-in or already-attached primary display.
  - Reason: the installer can target attached external volumes in some failure modes, and fewer peripherals means fewer failure modes.
  - Reattach after the post-install verification is fully complete.

9. RECOVERY MEDIA — OPTIONAL BUT CONSERVATIVE

  - If a spare USB stick (16 GB+) is available, creating a bootable macOS installer matching the version currently installed gives the deepest rollback: even if the internal Recovery partition is corrupted, a USB installer can boot the Mac and reinstall.
  - Skip this if no spare USB is available, or if creating it would risk confusing the Time Machine backup drive. The internal Recovery partition is sufficient for the common failure modes.

10. TIME AND ATTENTION

  - Block 90-180 minutes of uninterrupted time. First boot after a major update can take 30+ minutes before the login screen appears.
  - Stay physically present. The install itself does not require input, but a hung installer that needs force-shutdown is best diagnosed in person.
  - Do not start right before a meeting, an outage window, or right before leaving the apartment.

FINAL READINESS GATE — start the install ONLY when all of these are true:

  - Backup freshly verified, current workshop file opened from backup, backup drive physically disconnected.
  - AC connected and stable, sleep/Power Nap disabled, Focus on.
  - Updater's stated requirement is still ≤28 GB right now.
  - FileVault recovery key is retrievable from outside the laptop (or FileVault is confirmed off).
  - macOS version, build, chip, and FileVault status recorded on paper or another device.

INSTALLATION SEQUENCE
============================================================

  - Do NOT press the power button.
  - Do NOT touch the trackpad or keyboard unless the installer asks for a click.
  - Do NOT assume the installer is hung if the progress bar pauses or disappears. macOS installer phases include multi-minute "preparing" stages with no visible progress. Anything under 90 minutes of no progress is normal.
  - If you smell smoke, hear the fan at maximum for >30 minutes with no progress, or see an error code on screen: do not power off. Note the exact error / symptom and take a photo.

STEP 4 — First automatic reboot
  - The Mac will reboot itself into the new OS. The Apple logo and progress bar may appear multiple times; that is normal.
  - Wait at least 30 minutes from the first Apple-logo appearance before declaring the install hung.

STEP 5 — First login
  - Enter the FileVault password (if FileVault is on; the first login after the update may ask again).
  - Enter the user account password.
  - Complete any first-login setup (Apple ID, Siri, location, etc.) but defer "Move data from another Mac / iCloud" prompts until after the verification in the next section.

3. Wi-Fi connected and a normal page loads in Safari. If Wi-Fi will not connect, the install may have wiped a network setting; networking must work before any cloud-restored data can flow.

4. Finder works, dock works, basic UI responsive. Open Disk Utility and confirm the boot disk shows Healthy.

5. Open the most-used app and confirm it launches. Open ONE current workshop file from the LOCAL disk (not the backup) and confirm it opens correctly.

6. Reconnect the backup drive. Confirm the backup app sees it and that a backup will run (or trigger one manually). Open the backup browser and confirm one current workshop file still opens from backup.

7. App Store → Updates and Software Update both report the OS is up to date. If a new update is offered that you did not expect, do not apply it now.

8. Console.app → System Reports. Scan for install-time errors. Do not deep-dive; just confirm the install-phase logs look clean (no panic, no "install failed" entries with the update timestamp).

9. Time Machine creates a fresh post-update snapshot. This is the recovery anchor for whatever comes next.

10. Sleep / wake works. Close the lid briefly, reopen, log back in. This catches a class of post-update power-management bugs.

============================================================
RECOVERY STEPS IF INSTALLATION FAILS
============================================================

Listed from least to most destructive. Only escalate when the prior step fails.

MODE A — Installer reports an error and aborts (visible error message)
  - Note the exact error code and message text.
  - Reboot normally if possible → retry the install from Software Update. Many installer errors are transient (network blip during a re-fetch, disk-write hiccup).
  - If retry fails with the same error: boot to Recovery (Apple Silicon: shut down → hold power → release on "Loading startup options" → Options → Recovery. Intel: shut down → hold Command-R at boot). In Recovery → "Reinstall macOS" → reinstalls the OS over the current install WITHOUT erasing user data.

MODE B — Mac won't boot past Apple logo or progress bar (no login screen)
  - Wait at least 30 minutes. First boot after a major update can be slow.
  - If still stuck: force shutdown (hold power 10 seconds), then power on. Sometimes the second boot completes.
  - If second boot also fails: boot to Recovery → reinstall over.
  - If Recovery reinstall fails: erase and reinstall, then restore user data from Time Machine. This destroys installed apps (you reinstall them after) but user data and documents survive.

MODE C — Mac boots but FileVault asks for a recovery key you don't have
  - This is the catastrophic case. Without the recovery key, data on the encrypted disk is unrecoverable.
  - This is exactly why Section 5 (key retrievable from outside the laptop) is the pre-update gate that is non-negotiable. If the gate failed, the recovery path does not exist.

MODE D — Account login fails or Apple ID password not accepted
  - Reset Apple ID password from another device (iforgot.apple.com).
  - If FileVault recovery key is needed for the disk-unlock step, this becomes Mode C.

MODE E — Boot loop or repeated kernel panics after first login
  - Boot to Safe Mode: shut down → hold power → release on "Loading startup options" → select Macintosh HD → hold Shift → confirm "Safe Mode" in the menu bar.
  - Safe Mode disables most third-party launch items. If the Mac boots in Safe Mode, the problem is a third-party login item or extension, not the OS itself.
  - From Safe Mode: System Settings → General → Login Items → disable recently-added items one at a time. Reboot normally between each removal.
  - If Safe Mode also fails: Recovery → reinstall over → restore from Time Machine.

MODE F — Install succeeded but apps or settings are broken
  - Do NOT immediately clean install. Most post-update breakage resolves with: reboot, sign out and back in to the affected service, reinstall the affected app, or wait for a vendor update.
  - Time Machine restore is a last resort and only if breakage is pervasive across many apps.

============================================================
RECOVERY-PATH PRINCIPLES
============================================================

- The backup is the rollback target. Everything in Section 1 is built around preserving it and verifying it under this laptop's nose, not from memory.
- Recovery Mode "reinstall over the existing install" is the first action for any boot failure. It does not erase user data.
- Erase and reinstall is the last action. It erases installed apps; reinstall them after; user data and documents are restored from backup.
- The FileVault recovery key must be retrievable from outside the laptop BEFORE the install starts. No key, no recovery path. This is the one gate that, if missed, has no workaround.
- A bootable USB installer is the deepest rollback; only needed if the internal Recovery partition is corrupted. Optional and conservative.
- Do not re-run Software Update from Recovery unless you have first confirmed normal boot works.

STATUS: stable but elevated-risk; treat as a fire starter, not a battery. Cell is cool, not charging, not punctured, seam ~2 mm, no other warning signs. Current state can hold safely for days while you arrange disposal — no panic, no rushing, just disciplined isolation.

IMMEDIATE RESPONSE (NOW)

Do now:
1. Stop using it. Already done — good.
2. If it is currently on a soft/flammable surface, near a heat source, in direct sun, or in Kibo's reach, move it ONCE, gently, to the isolation spot below. Do not press the seam closed while moving.
3. Put a visible note on or beside it ("swollen Li-ion — do not touch, charge, or move") so you, Devika, or guests do not disturb it.

Do not:
- Press the case closed
- Charge, discharge, or "test" it
- Puncture, bend, drop, or compress it
- Submerge in water or any liquid
- Put it in a freezer — modern Li-ion thermal runaway is self-sustaining once started, freezing will not stop an internal short
- Tape the seam shut
- Throw it in trash, recycling, fire, or sink
- Let Kibo sniff, bat, or chew it

ISOLATION IN THE APARTMENT

Pick one spot that meets ALL of these:
- Hard, non-flammable floor or surface (concrete, ceramic tile, metal)
- Cool, dry, room temperature, no sun, no radiators, no heat vents, no stove/oven nearby
- Away from flammables: paper, books, bedding, curtains, wood furniture, plastic bins, gas range
- Out of walkways so it can't be kicked or have something set on it
- Out of Kibo's reach
- Somewhere you walk past often enough to glance at it

A commonly recommended setup that ticks every box:
- Clean metal trash can (galvanized or steel) on a tile floor, lid LOOSE (not airtight — pressure must be able to vent if the cell goes)
- Line the bottom with 1–2 inches of sand, dry kitty litter, or vermiculite if you have any
- Place the bagged battery ON the absorbent layer (not buried)
- Note on the can

Acceptable alternatives: ceramic planter on tile floor; inside a metal pot with loose lid; on top of an unused, cool major appliance (washer, dryer, oven that is off and cool). A balcony is usually a poor choice because NYC winter temperatures (and summer sun) swing outside the stable range, and weather exposure is uncontrolled.

Leave it there. Glance at it when you pass by. No need to hover.

EMERGENCY SIGNS — EVACUATE AND CALL 911

ANY ONE of these changes the response from "monitor" to "leave now":

- Sudden warming or heat (without it being on a charger)
- Hissing, whistling, popping, crackling
- Smoke of any color (white, gray, black)
- Sweet chemical or solvent smell (electrolyte venting — distinct, not "hot electronics")
- Visible liquid leaking from the seam
- Swelling accelerates — gap visibly grows within minutes
- Discoloration, charring, or scorch marks on the case
- Sparking or arcing
- Open flame

Action if any appear:
1. Do NOT move the battery. Moving a venting or igniting cell is worse than leaving it.
2. Evacuate — people and Kibo out, door closed behind you.
3. Call 911 from outside or a neighbor's apartment. State: "swollen lithium-ion battery, possible thermal runaway."
4. Do not re-enter until FD clears it.

If a very small fire has JUST started at the cell and has not spread, you can attempt a dry-chemical (ABC) extinguisher for a few seconds, but the moment it spreads beyond the cell itself, evacuate. Do not stay in the room fighting a lithium battery fire.

PREPARING IT FOR TRANSPORT

Do this when you are ready to drive it to a drop-off. No urgency — the cell can sit in isolation for a week or more without issue.

1. Tape over the USB ports and any exposed metal contacts with electrical tape (masking or packing tape also works). This prevents shorts during handling. Do NOT tape the swollen seam itself.
2. Place the taped battery in a heavy-duty zip-lock or plastic bag as secondary containment in case of leak.
3. Get a rigid container:
   - Best: a 1–2 gallon metal can or plastic bucket with a LOOSE-fitting lid
   - Line with 1–2 inches of sand, dry kitty litter, or vermiculite if you can find any
   - Battery sits ON the liner, not buried, not stacked under anything
4. Close the lid loosely. Tape can be used to hold the lid on but not to seal it airtight.

Do not transport it in a backpack, tote, purse, paper bag, or loose on a car seat. Do not stack items on it.

DURING DRIVE

- Container goes on the floor of the car (front passenger footwell or trunk well), wedged with a bag or towel so it cannot slide or tip
- Drive directly to the drop-off — no errands or detours
- Climate control on, windows up, to avoid temperature swings
- If you smell anything unusual at any point: pull over in a safe open area, stop, get out with Kibo and people, call 911. Do not try to retrieve belongings.

DISPOSAL — NOT HOUSEHOLD TRASH

Do not put it in:
- Kitchen/regular trash
- Curbside recycling (Li-ion causes fires in sorting facilities and compactor trucks)
- Standard battery bins unless explicitly labeled for rechargeable/Li-ion (most alkaline drop-offs will not accept it)
- Anything that goes in a hot garbage truck or compactor

Verified-style options (call ahead before driving over — policies and hours change):

1. Call2Recycle — call2recycle.org drop-off locator. Filter for Li-ion or rechargeable. Many participating retailers. Free.
2. Best Buy — most US stores accept rechargeable Li-ion power banks at the customer service desk. Call to confirm they accept a swollen/damaged cell specifically, and ask about any per-visit quantity limit.
3. Home Depot / Lowe's — store-by-store variation; service desk sometimes accepts rechargeable batteries. Call ahead.
4. NYC Department of Sanitation (DSNY) — Special Waste Drop-Off sites and events accept Li-ion batteries. Confirm current location, hours, and what's accepted before going: nyc.gov/dsny "Special Waste" page, or call 311.
5. Some NYC fire stations accept Li-ion drop-off — call ahead, do not just walk in.
6. Mail-back through Call2Recycle or similar services if transport is hard for you. Follow their packaging rules.

At the counter, simply say: "Swollen 10,000 mAh lithium power bank, not punctured, currently stable, want safe disposal." Bring the whole container if you want — most places will accept the rig as-is.

WHAT TO RECORD

- Photograph the swollen seam, the brand, model, and any lot/serial number
- Note where and when you bought it, approximate age, charging habits
- This is enough to file a quality report with the manufacturer and/or the CPSC at saferproducts.gov if you want — the CPSC database exists for exactly this. Optional, not required for safe disposal.

WHAT I HAVE NOT VERIFIED (so you don't act on assumptions)

- I have not checked current DSNY schedules, current Best Buy / Home Depot / Lowe's acceptance rules, or any specific NYC drop-off address. Please call ahead.
- I have not looked up the brand/model of your power bank for active recalls. If you share it, I can check.
- I have not contacted building management. If your only viable isolation spot is in a shared building area (laundry room, hallway), let me know and we can think through that — but a spot inside your own apartment is preferred.

TIMELINE

- Today: isolate, label, take the photo for your records
- This week: drop it off
- No need to rush. The current state is stable. The plan's purpose is to keep it that way until it leaves your home.

Kibo's situation as described — two loose stools hours apart after a small amount of fatty skin, with no vomiting, normal drinking, alert, wants food, no pain or swelling, no blood, no weakness — is most consistent with a mild, self-limiting dietary indiscretion. That's a "watchful waiting with a bland diet" situation, not a "call the clinic now" situation. The plan below is conservative and assumes that interpretation.

Note: I'm not a vet. If anything below conflicts with what Kibo's regular clinic has told you for him specifically, the clinic wins.

FOOD (next 24-48 hours)

Don't fully fast him. Go straight to small, frequent, bland meals.

  - Base recipe: boiled skinless chicken breast (no skin, no fat, no salt) plus plain white rice, roughly 1 part chicken to 2-3 parts rice.
  - Acceptable swaps: boiled extra-lean ground turkey (drained of fat) plus rice, or low-fat plain cottage cheese plus rice.
  - Optional support: 1-2 tablespoons of plain canned pumpkin per meal (NOT pie filling). Helpful if you have it; not required.
  - Portion: start at about 1/4 to 1/3 of his normal meal volume, split into 3-4 small meals through the day.
  - If those go well, gradually work back toward his normal volume over 24-36 hours.
  - Total bland-diet duration: 2-3 days, then transition back to his regular food over another 1-2 days by mixing increasing amounts of his normal food into the bland base.

Avoid during this period: treats, table scraps, fatty food, dairy beyond the small amounts above, rich or flavored food, and anything else he might steal.

HYDRATION

  - Keep fresh water available at all times. Do not restrict.
  - He should drink on his own; don't force.
  - If he gulps a lot at once, that's fine — just refill and let him sip on his own pace.

Dehydration checks, once or twice today:

  - Gum moisture: slick, not tacky or dry.
  - Skin tent: gently lift the scruff over his shoulders; it should snap back within 1-2 seconds. Slower than that is a flag.
  - Eyes: not sunken.
  - Energy: not markedly duller than his baseline.

MONITORING (next 48 hours)

Track without overreacting to a single data point:

  - Stool: frequency, consistency, color, presence of blood or mucus.
  - Appetite: still interested in food across meals.
  - Vomiting: any new vomiting is a meaningful data point.
  - Water intake: roughly normal.
  - Energy and alertness: matches his baseline.
  - Abdomen: soft and non-tender on gentle palpation; no visible swelling.
  - Gums: pink and moist.

Expected course if this is mild dietary indiscretion: stool firms up over 24-48 hours, energy and appetite stay normal, no vomiting, no blood. Slight worsening in stool within the first day before it improves is common and not by itself a reason to escalate.

WHEN TO ESCALATE — THE GATE YOU ASKED FOR

Call your regular vet, same day:

  - Stool has not improved by the 48-hour mark, or is worsening after 24 hours on the bland diet.
  - Loose stool continues beyond 48 hours total.
  - Mucus, very foul smell, or unusual color (yellow, grey, pale) appears.
  - Mild appetite drop that persists beyond one skipped meal.
  - Mild lethargy that doesn't resolve with rest.
  - Mild abdominal discomfort on palpation.

Seek urgent or emergency care now (ER if your regular clinic is closed):

  - Repeated vomiting, or vomiting that prevents him from keeping water down.
  - Blood in the stool — bright red or, more concerning, black and tarry.
  - Escalating abdominal pain: hunched posture, "prayer position" (front down, back up), guarding, vocalizing when touched, or visible abdominal distension or swelling.
  - Sudden weakness, collapse, pale or white gums, rapid or labored breathing, shivering.
  - Refusal to drink for more than 12 hours, or clear dehydration (sunken eyes, tacky gums, skin tent >2 seconds).
  - Gums turning yellow, blue, grey, or very pale.
  - You remember or find evidence he got into something else — bones, chocolate, raisins, grapes, onion, garlic, xylitol products, medication, marijuana, etc. That changes the picture immediately.

Not a reason to call or escalate right now:

  - One or two soft or loose stools in an otherwise bright, drinking, eating dog with no other signs. That's where Kibo is.

THINGS TO AVOID WITHOUT VET GUIDANCE

  - Human anti-diarrheal medicines. Imodium/loperamide and Pepto-Bismol are not uniformly safe for dogs; both need a vet's call.
  - Sudden food switches to richer foods.
  - "Wait and see" beyond 48 hours if anything is still trending worse.
  - Inducing vomiting at home. The fat was eaten ~13-15 hours ago and is past the stomach; inducing now risks aspiration without helping.

PRACTICAL

  - Brief, familiar walks for the next 24 hours. Easy cleanup matters more than distance.
  - If stool looks abnormal, a photo is useful in case you end up needing to show your vet.
  - If this does escalate to a vet visit, a fresh stool sample (within ~12 hours of the appointment) is helpful to bring.

If Kibo's other signs hold and the stool firms up across today and tomorrow, this is the kind of mild, self-resolving episode that doesn't need professional input. The cleanest gate is 48 hours: if it's not trending better by then, even without red flags, that's the right time to call the clinic for a non-urgent appointment.

Classification of the evidence (preliminary, pending verification below)

The pattern matches bounded maintenance behavior under active compaction, not an incident:

  - Scope: 3 of 480 shards (~0.6%). Breach magnitude: 4 to 6 minutes over
    the 15-minute warning line.
  - Plausible causal mechanism: snapshot age is a lagging indicator of
    compaction throughput. While a compaction worker is mid-flight on a
    shard, snapshot production waits for the latest compacted tier, so
    age can briefly drift above warning and recover without operator action.
  - Direction: positive. Snapshot age is declining for all three shards.
  - No integrity signals: zero read/write errors, lease convergence complete,
    no stale-write, no split-generation, no generation inconsistency.
  - No serving impact: client latency at baseline, disk under 61% (ample
    headroom, so this is not a capacity or IO-exhaustion story).
  - Structural analog in memory: the 12/23 node-replacement case
    (12/480 shards, two observed generations for 22 s, zero write errors,
    baseline latency) was classified as a node-replacement artifact, not an
    incident. This case is structurally similar — brief, narrow, no
    integrity signal, recovery in progress, with a clear maintenance
    cause — though here the trigger is routine compaction rather than a
    one-shot node swap.

  The key thing that has to be confirmed before the call holds is that
  compaction is actually progressing on those three shards. "Compaction
  workers are active" is necessary but not sufficient; if compaction is
  stalled, looping, or wedged on those specific shards, the same surface
  symptoms would be an incident. The classification stands or falls on
  that single check.

Verification conditions (must all hold before treating as bounded maintenance)

  Causal confirmation
    - Identify the affected shard IDs and their assigned compaction workers.
    - Confirm compaction is actively progressing on those three shards
      (state advancing, not pinned at the same key).
    - Compaction backlog is bounded and draining, not growing.

  Recovery confirmation
    - Snapshot age is monotonically declining for all three shards
      (not oscillating, not flat).
    - No additional shards have joined the breach during the window.
    - Snapshot production has resumed or is actively resuming on the
      affected shards.

  Integrity confirmation (fresh, not stale from before convergence)
    - Lease convergence is current.
    - Zero read/write errors across all client classes during the breach
      window (not just a sampled subset).
    - No stale-write, split-generation, or generation-inconsistency signal
      anywhere in the alert set or in shard-keeper logs.
    - No pod restarts or reload failures during the interval.

  Capacity confirmation
    - Disk utilization is sustained under 61% and not rising toward
      warning/critical.
    - Compaction throughput within the expected band for the worker pool.

  Cross-signal confirmation
    - Client latency at baseline across all client classes, not just
      the obvious ones.
    - rollup-service and other downstream consumers showing no impact.

  Evidence preservation (same shape as the 12/23 handling)
    - Affected shard IDs, old/new generation numbers, node logs,
      compaction worker logs, and the alert interval retained so this
      stays auditable.

Escalation conditions (any one flips to incident handling)

  Recovery stalls or expands
    - Snapshot age stops declining or reverses direction on any of the
      three shards.
    - A fourth shard joins the breach.
    - Any of the three crosses a meaningfully higher threshold (e.g.,
      30+ minutes), or the breach window stretches rather than closes.

  Integrity signals appear
    - Any non-zero read or write error.
    - Any stale-write, split-generation, or generation-inconsistency signal.
    - Lease divergence, non-monotonic epoch, overlapping holder.

  Serving impact
    - Client latency regression beyond baseline on any class.
    - Error rate movement on rollup-service or any downstream consumer.

  Capacity pressure
    - Disk utilization climbing toward warning/critical rather than
      holding under 61%.
    - Compaction backlog growing rather than draining.

  Operational instability
    - Compaction worker restart or reload failure during the window.
    - Stalled or looping compaction on any of the three shards.
    - A second breach episode repeating the same pattern within a short
      interval (suggests the first wasn't actually bounded).

Premium increase

  Current annual: $168
  Renewal annual (effective Jan 5): $204
  Dollar increase: $36/year
  Percentage: $36 / $168 = 21.43%
  Monthly equivalent: +$3/month
  Daily equivalent: ~$0.099/day

  Note on the stated reason: "building-area rate revision" is a category-level rate action — the insurer has revised its rate for the building/area classification, not your individual policy. With claim surcharge: none, the increase is not driven by your claim history; it's a market or underwriting-rate action that likely affects all carriers writing the same building class. Worth asking whether the revision is uniform across carriers in your ZIP/building, but the answer shouldn't change the substantive questions below.

Most important like-for-like questions

  Coverage

    1. RCV vs ACV basis for personal property. This is the single most consequential line on the policy. Replacement Cost Value pays to replace at today's prices; Actual Cash Value deducts depreciation. A three-year-old laptop paid at ACV is a fraction of its replacement cost; at RCV it pays for a comparable new one. Confirm which basis applies, and confirm it for every category (property, loss-of-use, liability doesn't apply here).

    2. Personal-property limit adequacy against a current inventory. $40,000 is reasonable for typical contents but verify against what you actually own: clothing, kitchenware, books, electronics (laptop, monitors, task lighting), Devika's clinical-essentials box, climbing gear, bikes, dog supplies. A rough inventory is enough to confirm whether $40K is over- or under-insured.

    3. Loss-of-use limit realism. $12,000 against the cost of a comparable temporary rental in your area for the time it takes to make the unit habitable. $12K covers roughly 2–3 months at modest NYC-area rental rates; if displacement runs longer, this caps out. Confirm it tracks actual fair rental value, not a flat percentage.

    4. Personal-liability limit. $300,000 is a common floor; many recommend $300K–$500K. Ask whether the renewal narrows any liability peril or quietly changes the defense-cost treatment.

    5. Sub-limits on categories you actually own. Jewelry, watches, art, furs, firearms, bikes, and electronics are often capped at $1,000–$2,500 inside the policy. Confirm the dollar sub-limits for any category where you hold items above the cap. A new bike or laptop can exceed that cap.

    6. Anything that changed besides premium. Confirm by side-by-side declarations page, not just the bill. A "rate revision" can coincide with a quietly narrowed peril list or removed endorsement.

  Deductible

    1. Per-claim vs per-incident vs per-coverage-type. Confirm $500 applies per occurrence, not cumulatively across categories, and confirm it applies to property only (liability typically has no deductible).

    2. Category-specific deductibles. Some policies carry separate, larger deductibles for wind, hail, hurricane, named storm, or water/sewer backup. A $500 base doesn't mean $500 applies to a water-damage claim. Ask for the full deductible schedule.

    3. Silent deductible change. Confirm $500 is the same number from last year. A "rate revision" sometimes moves the deductible up by a hundred dollars without highlighting it on the renewal notice.

    4. Whether the deductible applies before or after depreciation. ACV policies can leave a small claim below the deductible once depreciation is applied; RCV policies apply the deductible to replacement cost.

  Exclusion

    1. Dog/animal liability for Kibo. With a dog in the household, this is the single highest-priority exclusion to verify. Some carriers exclude certain breeds, impose a per-incident cap, or require a pet endorsement. Confirm by name/breed that Kibo is in scope and that bite-related and non-bite-related incidents are both covered. The renewal notice doesn't state pet liability treatment — that gap is a flag, not a confirmation.

    2. Water/sewer/backup coverage. Often excluded or sold as an add-on. Given a multi-floor unit and aging plumbing, this is worth pinning down.

    3. Mold/fungus. Standard mold coverage is usually capped low. Ask for the dollar limit and whether it's an aggregate or per-claim cap.

    4. Home-office or business property. Given the work-room setup (desk, monitors, lighting, any clinical-essentials contents), confirm business-use contents are in scope. Some policies exclude or sub-limit business property; an explicit endorsement may be needed.

    5. New exclusions added this renewal. Ask directly. "Rate revision" can include a tightening of the exclusion list.

  Replacement-cost

    1. RCV vs ACV. (Re-stated because it's the most consequential single question.) Confirm in writing and confirm for sub-limited categories too — some policies give RCV on general contents but ACV on jewelry.

    2. Like-kind-and-quality guarantee. At RCV, the carrier can in principle substitute a functionally similar but lower-quality item. Confirm the policy requires replacement of like kind and quality, not functional equivalent.

    3. Replacement-required condition. Some RCV policies only pay the full replacement cost if you actually replace the item; otherwise they pay ACV. Confirm which model applies and over what time window.

    4. Pair-and-set clause. If one item in a set is damaged (a matched set of luggage, a camera-and-lens kit), some policies pay only the damaged piece, not the full set's replacement. Confirm whether this clause exists and how it's enforced.

    5. Loss-of-use calculation basis. Confirm that "loss of use" is paid against actual additional living expense with the $12K as a cap, not a flat $12K regardless of need.

    6. Replacement-cost geography. Confirm replacement cost is calculated against your specific market, not a national average that could understate local prices.

Decision frame

  The renewal reduces to four checks: (1) is the premium increase buying the same coverage or quietly narrowing it; (2) is pet liability for Kibo confirmed in writing; (3) is the property basis RCV or ACV; (4) are sub-limits and deductibles stable or quietly tightened. If the renewal is genuinely like-for-like and the rate action is uniform across carriers in your building/area, the decision becomes whether the 21.43% is worth accepting or worth shopping. If shopping, the same six questions (RCV/ACV, pet, deductible structure, sub-limits, exclusions, replacement-cost treatment) should be answered by every competing quote before comparison — premium alone isn't a like-for-like comparison.

The stated terms are not symmetric: the competing quote is more specific on a few items (RC basis stated, water backup explicitly excluded) but silent on others (sublimits, dog liability) where the renewal is also silent.

2. Does the $18 savings compensate?
------------------------------------------------------------

In expected-value terms, no — not on its own. The math:

  Extra deductible exposure per claim      +$500
  Stated annual savings                    -$18
  -------------------------------------------
  Net on a single claim-year               -$482

  Ratio:  $500 / $18  ≈  27.8x

You would need to file ~28 deductible-only claims in one policy year before the savings turned net-positive against the deductible change alone. For any realistic one-claim year, you lose money on the deductible trade.

Loss-of-use delta ($4,000 less coverage) is conditional — displacement is rare but high-impact. At ~$200-$300/night for a NYC short-term rental, $4,000 buys roughly 13-20 additional nights of temporary housing. A typical fire/sewer/major-water displacement runs 30-90 days, so $8,000 on the competing quote may not even cover the full displacement window, while $12,000 on the renewal gets you closer. This is a real exposure but one you might never collect against.

Net read on the stated savings alone:
  - Zero-claim, zero-displacement year:  you are +$18, but with materially
    less coverage if anything happens.
  - One claim at the deductible, no displacement:  -$482 net.
  - One claim + displacement event:        -$482 - (uncovered loss-of-use
                                            above the $8,000 cap).

The $18 only "compensates" if you attach positive value to deltas the comparison has not yet established — replacement-cost basis, water-backup treatment change, dog-liability treatment change, sublimit differences, or carrier quality differences. Those need to be confirmed before the trade can be evaluated honestly.

3. Exact questions to resolve before deciding
------------------------------------------------------------

A. Cost basis and endorsements (biggest unknown block)

  1. On the renewal: is the $40,000 personal-property limit on a
     replacement-cost basis, actual cash value, or hybrid? If ACV, the
     competing RC quote may be the materially better deal even at $186,
     and the $18 savings is not the right comparison.
  2. On both: list every endorsement currently attached (replacement-cost
     endorsement, water backup / sewer backup, identity theft, loss
     assessment, earthquake, equipment breakdown, etc.) and the dollar
     amount each adds to the premium.
  3. On the competing quote: can water backup be added back, and at what
     premium and limit? (Often $30-$50/yr for $5,000-$10,000 of coverage.)
  4. On the renewal: is water backup currently included, and at what limit?

B. Sublimits (silent on both, but the competing quote's silence is more
   concerning because it usually means the default cap applies)

  5. What is the electronics / computer sublimit on each policy? (Often
     $1,000-$2,500 default for items like laptops, cameras, tablets —

  6. What is the jewelry, watch, and furs sublimit on each policy?
  7. What is the bicycle sublimit on each policy, on-premises and

  8. What is the off-premises coverage for personal property generally —

C. Loss-of-use mechanics

  10. On the renewal: does the $12,000 cap include both additional living
      expenses and fair rental value, or just one? Is there a time limit

  11. On the competing quote: same three questions for the $8,000 cap.
  12. On both: is loss-of-use measured as a percentage of the personal-
      property limit or as a flat dollar amount? (If percentage-based on

      flat, the dollar number is the only cap.)

D. Deductible specifics

  13. On the competing quote: is the $1,000 deductible per incident or
      per policy year? Some carriers apply a single annual deductible;
      most apply per claim.
  14. On both: are there separate, named deductibles for specific perils
      (wind/hail, water backup, earthquake, dog bite)? A $500 base
      deductible can sit on top of separate $1,000 or $2,500 peril
      deductibles you never see in the headline number.
  15. Does the deductible apply to liability claims, or only to property

E. Dog liability — material because Kibo is in the household

  17. On the competing quote: does the policy cover dog bite / dog-related

      questionnaires, or required inspections?
  18. Is the $300,000 liability limit inclusive of legal-defense costs, or

      by legal fees; some don't. Big practical difference.)

F. Binding mechanics, continuity, and switching risk

  20. Does the renewal auto-bind if no action is taken, or does it lapse?

Because the renewal terms are silent on RC basis, water backup, and

  - Dim lights in the bedroom; hallway light off.

Don'ts during setup
  - Don't coax him out to "check on him" repeatedly.
  - Don't rearrange things after he's settled.
  - Don't crating him in an unfamiliar crate.
  - Don't pick him up if he's tensing; let him choose contact.

EVENING TIMELINE (Devika leaves at 7:00 PM)

  - 5:15–6:30 PM — finish retreat setup, keep the apartment routine. Normal dinner is fine; serve it in or near the retreat area so he doesn't have to leave it.
  - 6:30–6:45 PM — pre-Devika-departure walk. Short loop near the building, on leash. Goal is potty, not exercise. If he freezes, refuses treats, or pulls toward home, turn back immediately.
  - 7:00 PM — calm goodbyes. Don't make the departure dramatic.
  - 7:00–10:00 PM — settle in the same room as the retreat. TV or music at moderate volume is fine on top of the white noise. Stay reachable; he can hear where you are.
  - 10:00–10:30 PM — last brief bathroom trip if he asks, accepts the leash, and the bursts between now and midnight aren't at peak. Skip it otherwise. Don't force a midnight walk; the risk-to-benefit doesn't justify it.
  - 11:00 PM–12:30 AM — peak window. Stay calm, stay near. White noise on, lights dim, no loud reactions to bangs.
  - 12:30 AM onward — bursts taper but can run into 1:00–2:00 AM. Same setup. You can begin turning lights up slightly if he's calm.

FOOD, WATER, AND OCCUPATION

  - Normal dinner, normal timing. Don't withhold food or water preemptively.
  - Water available in the retreat area. Refill if he drains it; don't make him come out to the kitchen.
  - Lick/chew activity once he's settled: xylitol-free peanut butter on a lick mat, a frozen wet-food Kong, or a safe long chew. Licking and chewing lower heart rate.
  - Treats only if he actively seeks you. Don't repeatedly offer reassurance treats — that pairs noise with reward and can keep him alert.
  - No table scraps, no new foods, nothing risky tonight.

WHAT YOU'RE AIMING FOR

A dog who is breathing normally, willing to settle, taking water, accepting a lick/chew, and showing normal interaction between bursts. Panting, pacing, clinginess, and ears-back are expected at peak — that's manageable at home if he returns to baseline between bangs and is still eating/drinking/responding.

CALL YOUR REGULAR VETERINARIAN (next-day or same-week appointment, not ER) IF ANY OF THESE APPEAR

  - Housetraining regression tonight.
  - A scrape, broken nail, or limping that shows up tomorrow.
  - Trembling or hiding that does not ease between bangs.

URGENT OR EMERGENCY VETERINARY CARE — GO TONIGHT IF YOU SEE

  - Repeated vomiting or any retching without producing vomit.
  - Collapse, weakness in the legs, or inability to stand.
  - Any seizure-like event, loss of consciousness, or disorientation that doesn't resolve in seconds.
  - Bloated or distended abdomen, especially with restlessness and unsuccessful retching.
  - Pale gums, heavy drooling, or rapid breathing that doesn't slow between bangs.
  - Self-injury — broken tooth, cut paw, broken nail to the quick, scraped nose from pawing.
  - Active destruction of doors, windows, or crates with bleeding or risk of escape.
  - Sudden aggression that breaks his normal pattern (snapping, growling, biting when handled).

HAVE READY (pull these up now, before the peak window)

  - The nearest 24-hour ER. In the South Slope / Park Slope area, BluePearl Brooklyn and Veterinary Emergency Group (VEG) are the usual options — confirm address and that they're open before you need them.
  - ASPCA Animal Poison Control 888-426-4435 only if a toxin is involved (not expected tonight).

WHAT NOT TO IMPROVISE

  - No human medication. None. Acetaminophen, ibuprofen, diphenhydramine, melatonin, CBD — all carry risk without dosing guidance specific to him.
  - No essential oils, no aromatherapy diffusers in the retreat room.
  - No tight "thunder shirt" if he's never worn one — that's a new stressor.
  - No punishment for any distress behavior.
  - No opening the door or window to "show him" the source.

A FEW REMINDERS

Diagnostic sequence to distinguish stale generated output (A), generator-version drift (B), and canonical-package problem (C) without touching the iOS artifact. This is what Anya runs; you interpret the branches.

Framing of the three hypotheses (so the branches are mutually exclusive):

  A — write side: iOS file was not actually overwritten during the clean run (excluded target, dry-run, write blocked, cache returning prior artifact, wrong output path).
  B — transform side: generator read the right value from canonical but emitted the old one (iOS template/transform/unit-conversion bug, hardcoded override, iOS emitter pinned to a version predating this spacing semantic).
  C — read side: generator did not actually see the new value from canonical (stale read cache, wrong pinned package version, the new value lives at a key path the iOS generator does not traverse, or the file inside the package that the iOS generator reads is stale).

The web/iOS asymmetry is the key clue: web matches canonical, iOS does not. Whatever differs between the two generators is the locus. So the diagnostic must localize the divergence along the read → transform → write axis before any rebuild.

Step 1 — Establish canonical baseline (read only).
  - Resolve the pinned version of the versioned machine-readable package from the same source the generator uses (same version-pin registry entry, same artifact hash). Do not re-derive "intended" value from intent; read the artifact.
  - Record: the spacing token's exact key path, raw value, unit, and the artifact hash.
  - Compare against what Anya believes is in there. If the value, key path, or unit does not match what the iOS generator is expected to consume → C at the package level (wrong version pinned, or new value added under a different path than the iOS generator reads). Stop and surface this before continuing — Step 3 cannot disambiguate if Step 1 already shows the canonical does not carry what the iOS generator needs.

Step 2 — Confirm the iOS generator actually wrote during the clean run (no edits, only observation).
  - From the existing clean run, capture: iOS target's invocation status, the run manifest's recorded canonical-package hash, and iOS file mtime / size / hash before vs after the run.
  - Branch:
    - iOS file was NOT rewritten → A. Sub-causes to walk through without editing: iOS target excluded from this run's target list, dry-run flag still set, output path not writable, partial-overwrite suppressed, or a cache layer returning the prior artifact instead of writing. Resolution is one re-invocation forcing the iOS target on, cache invalidated, write enabled — read-only of the resulting iOS artifact. Confirm whether iOS now matches canonical.
    - iOS file WAS rewritten → proceed to Step 3.

Step 3 — Re-invoke the iOS generator with cache invalidated, verbose/debug on (no edits to iOS file; only observe what the run produces).
  - Capture four values from this instrumented run:
    (a) canonical-package version/hash the generator actually loaded
    (b) exact key path the iOS generator resolved for the spacing token
    (c) value the generator intended to emit (post-transform, pre-write)
    (d) value actually present in the iOS artifact after the run
  - Branch:
    - (a) or (b) differs from Step 1's canonical record → C. The divergence is on the read side. Most likely: stale canonical read cache, wrong file inside the package (e.g., iOS reads a derived subset that wasn't regenerated), or the spacing token lives at a path the iOS generator does not traverse. Fix is to refresh the cache / repin the correct file inside the package / extend the iOS generator's read path to the new key — none of which require editing the iOS artifact.
    - (a) and (b) match Step 1, (c) is the new value, but (d) is the old value → B. The divergence is on the transform/emit side. Most likely: iOS transform handles an older spacing semantic, hardcoded override for this token, unit-conversion bug, or the iOS emitter's pinned version predates support for this token path. Fix is in the generator/iOS template, not in the iOS artifact.
    - (a), (b), (c) all match Step 1 and (d) is the new value → the prior "clean run" was actually A in disguise; the canonical and generator are sound, and the iOS file on disk before this diagnostic was stale. No workflow change needed.

Step 4 — Cross-check (one read).
  - Compare the iOS artifact hash produced by Step 3 against the canonical hash + generator version recorded in the run manifest. Confirms Step 3 produced a fresh artifact and is not itself reading through a stale layer.

Acceptance criteria for the diagnostic itself:
  - Every step is read-only against the iOS artifact. No manual edit, no patch, no "fix the iOS file and reconcile later."
  - Canonical-source authority preserved: every comparison is against the pinned version of the versioned machine-readable package. No second source of truth introduced.
  - Anya's lane preserved: the diagnostic runs inside her existing generator invocation, with her existing version pins. Nothing is added, removed, or rewired.
  - Outcome is a single mutually exclusive root cause — A, B, or C. No "regenerate and see what happens" hand-off; a fresh regenerate alone cannot distinguish B from C, which is why Step 3 exists.

Explicit out of scope (so the diagnostic does not silently expand):
  - Does not change the generator, the canonical package, the version pins, the drift check, or the workflow.
  - Does not patch the iOS artifact, even temporarily.
  - Does not collapse B and C into "regenerate again and compare." The web/iOS asymmetry is what makes the run informative; the second run is informative only because Steps 2 and 3 have already localized the divergence.
  - Does not propose a redesign (deterministic emit ordering, semantic drift comparison, packaging-metadata vs content hashing). Those are separate questions and were already resolved in prior cycles.

If Anya wants, the same sequence applies to Android for parallel verification — Android previously showed byte-differences from map traversal order, so a matching instrumented run there would either confirm the divergence is iOS-specific or show that the read/transform issue affects Android too. Run only after the iOS branch resolves, to keep the lane narrow.

PRE-FLIGHT
  Bike in a stand if you have one; otherwise invert it resting on saddle and bars with a rag under the hood. Good light, clean rags, a flashlight, a chain checker (or ruler), and a cassette lockring tool + chain whip only if you're prepared to go that far. The chain is on, no obvious crash damage, and indexing is otherwise clean — so the suspect set is small.

INSPECTION ORDER — lowest-cost / lowest-risk first

Step 1 — Visual scan (no contact)
  Cog teeth: look at the smallest cog first, then each other cog. New teeth are symmetric with parallel sides and blunt tops. Worn teeth look hooked, asymmetric, leaning forward ("shark fin"). A single broken or bent tooth is a separate, sharper symptom — call it out and stop.
  Chainring teeth (front): the chain also passes through these. Look for a missing, bent, or hooked tooth.
  Cassette: gaps, dirt packed between cogs, any visible rock between cogs.
  Derailleur hanger: sight down the back of the bike. The hanger face should sit roughly in plane with the cassette. A visibly bent hanger is a shop job and a likely cause.
  Chain: rust, kinked links, visibly misaligned plates.

Step 2 — Wheel security
  Grab the top of the tire and rock fore-aft and side-to-side. Any play in the dropouts = wheel is loose, even if the QR feels closed.
  Quick release: lever should close with firm palm pressure and leave an imprint; should point back along the stay, away from the drivetrain. Re-close if it fails either check.
  Thru-axle: should be fully torqued, not just snug.

Step 3 — Cassette and freehub
  With the bike on the stand, try to rock the largest cog counter to the drive direction against the freehub. It must not move at all. If it does, the cassette lockring is loose or the splines are damaged.
  Spin the cassette briskly by hand in the freewheel direction. Listen and feel for immediate, clean ratchet engagement. A delayed engagement, silence-then-catch, or coasting past the pawls = freehub pawl/spring wear. Shop.
  If anything felt off, pull the wheel and look at the splines on both the cassette and freehub body: missing, rounded, or shiny-worn splines are not safe to reuse.

Step 4 — Stiff link
  Shift to a middle cog so chain tension isn't extreme.
  Rotate cranks slowly backward and watch the chain pass over the pulleys and cassette. A stiff link shows as a visible hop or kink at one consistent spot in the chain's rotation — same position each turn, independent of cog.
  With chain slack, manually flex suspect links laterally. They should articulate freely. A stiff link resists flex and often looks slightly bent. It can be confirmed by noting the position and watching for the same hop on the next rotation.

Step 5 — Chain wear measurement
  Chain checker: 0.5% = replace soon. 0.75% = replace now and inspect cogs.
  No tool: 12 full links should measure exactly 304.8 mm. At 0.5% stretch it reads ~306.3 mm; at 1% ~307.8 mm.

Step 6 — Cog wear confirmation
  Good light on each cog, especially the smallest. Compare a suspect cog against a less-used cog in the same cassette. Worn teeth look obviously different from less-worn neighbors.

Step 7 — Indexing
  Shift crisply to the smallest cog with no load. The upper derailleur pulley should sit directly under the cog and ~5–6 mm below it.
  Try to push the derailleur outward past the cog by hand. The high limit screw should stop it firmly with no further travel.
  Cable tension at the smallest cog should be taut; obvious slack in the housing or visible derailleur movement under no load = cable tension issue.

WHAT EACH TEST CONFIRMS OR RULES OUT

  Indexing — confirms if pulley misaligned, limit allows over-travel, cable tension visibly off, or skip disappears with a 1/4–1/2 turn of the barrel adjuster. Rules out if pulley aligned, limit firm, skip persists after barrel adjustment.

  Stiff link — confirms if a kink/hop repeats at one consistent chain position across multiple rotations regardless of cog, and that link resists manual flex. Rules out if the chain articulates uniformly.

  Worn chain / cog — confirms if chain measures >0.5% AND smallest cog teeth look hooked while other cogs look less worn. Rules out if chain <0.25% and all cog teeth look symmetric.

  Loose wheel or cassette — confirms if wheel has play in dropouts, cassette rocks on the freehub, or freehub engagement is delayed or silent. Rules out if wheel is solid, cassette is solid on the freehub, and the freehub engages immediately.

WHAT IS IN SCOPE OFF-BIKE
  Re-closing a QR that wasn't fully seated.
  Working a confirmed stiff link free by hand flex and re-lubing.
  A quarter-turn at a time on the rear barrel adjuster, with a controlled re-test between turns.
  That is the list.

SHOP CRITERIA — DO NOT RIDE UNTIL A SHOP HAS LOOKED
  Skip recurs on a controlled low-load re-test after any adjustment.
  Cassette rocks on the freehub, or freehub splines look worn or damaged.
  Freehub engagement is delayed, silent, or slips under hand-spin.
  Wheel has any play in the dropouts.
  Any cog teeth look visibly hooked or asymmetric, especially combined with a chain past 0.5%.
  Chain measures >0.75% — replace as a chain + cassette set, requires tools you may not have and cogs need to be inspected at the same time.
  Derailleur hanger is bent.
  Chainring has a missing, bent, or hooked tooth.
  Diagnosis is unclear after all seven steps.

CONTROLLED RE-TEST BEFORE RESUMING RIDING (only if the cause is identified and the fix is in your scope)
  Bike in a stand: load the smallest cog by feathering a brake against the wheel while turning the cranks at moderate effort. No skip, no hop, no chatter.
  Test ride in a traffic-free area, low speed, gradually increasing load in the smallest cog for 2–3 minutes. Then a similar pass through each other cog.
  Stop and return to inspection if you see any skip, hesitation, chain bounce, or new noise. Re-test is a gate, not a confidence vote — one miss means back to the bench.

The renegotiation from 1 Gbps to 100 Mbps is a copper-Ethernet physical-layer symptom: gigabit needs all four pairs clean, so when one or more pairs degrade (loose connector, marginal cable, oxidation, EMI), the PHYs fall back to 100 Mbps, which only uses two pairs. The optical LED staying normal and reseating fixing it both point to the patch cable / connector joint as the leading hypothesis, not the fiber, ONT, or upstream provisioning.

The least-disruptive sequence below is ordered so that every step changes exactly one variable, preserves router configuration, and produces a screenshot/log artifact before the next change. Nothing here requires a factory reset, firmware change, or ISP contact until the evidence supports it.

1. Capture the current stable state before touching anything
   - Screenshot the router admin WAN page showing negotiated link speed (should read 1000 / 1 Gbps / "Full") and link state.
   - Screenshot or export the full router system log. Note the timestamp of the most recent WAN renegotiation event relative to "now."
   - Open the Arris S33 status page (192.168.100.1 from a wired client) and capture the Downstream/Upstream optical Rx levels (dBm) and any Recent Event Log entries. This is the only customer-visible signal that the fiber side is healthy even when the visible optical LED looks normal. Typical DOCSIS Rx range is roughly -8 to +8 dBm; values outside that band are an ISP-side trigger even with a green LED.
   - Do not reboot, reset, or change any setting. This step is zero-disruption and gives a defensible "before" baseline.

2. Physical inspection of the short patch cable (zero-disruption)
   - Both RJ45 ends: latch intact, no kinks or tight bends along the run, no strain, no visible jacket damage.
   - Look at the contacts for greenish oxidation or pushed-in pins. If any are visible, that's already evidence that the cable is the failure mode.
   - Confirm the WAN-port LEDs on both devices are steady (link up) rather than blinking in an irregular pattern.

3. Cable substitution, the highest-yield single test
   - Replace the short modem-to-router patch with a known-good Cat5e or Cat6 cable of the same or shorter length. Do not power-cycle either device; do not touch router config.
   - After the swap, re-capture the router WAN link speed and a fresh log snapshot. If renegotiation events stop appearing and the link holds at 1000 Mbps, the original cable is implicated and the case is closed at the customer side. Keep the suspect cable labeled; don't throw it away until 24-48 hours of clean operation.
   - Observation window: the original symptom was intermittent and reseating gave only one hour of stability before the conversation. Treat one hour as encouraging but not conclusive; two to four hours of clean router log, plus a sustained 1000 Mbps negotiated speed, is the bar for "cable was the cause."
   - If the link renegotiates again on a known-good cable, the suspect shifts to the router WAN port or the modem's Ethernet port.

4. Port isolation, only if step 3 fails
   - Move the cable to a different WAN-capable port on the router, if one exists. This is still a single-variable change with no config edit.
   - The Arris S33 has a single Ethernet port, so the modem side of the joint is not port-swappable without extra hardware. If the link still renegotiates after a clean cable on a different router port, the failure is most likely the modem's Ethernet PHY. That's a customer-hardware issue (Arris S33), not an ISP-line issue, even though the ISP sold you the modem historically; since you own it outright, replacement is on you unless you're still inside a manufacturer warranty path.

5. Evidence that would actually justify contacting the ISP
   Any one of the following, captured in the modem's status page or event log, is a defensible ISP trigger. Until you have one of these, the symptom is not ISP territory:
   - Optical Rx power outside the spec band (-8 to +8 dBm is the usual range; verify against the exact Arris S33 spec for your firmware).
   - Modem event log entries showing T3 / T4 timeouts, ranging retries, or upstream signal alarms, even if the visible optical LED reads normal.
   - Optical LED behavior change (flicker, color change, going dark during a renegotiation event) — at that point the failure is on the fiber drop or ONT, which is ISP-owned.
   - Modem reboots or freezes coincident with the WAN-link renegotiation, where the modem is the device that initiates the event rather than the router.
   - Sustained inability to maintain >100 Mbps link after a known-good cable, known-good router port, and a clean modem restart, especially if the modem's own diagnostics report its Ethernet port as degraded.

6. Evidence that does not justify an ISP ticket
   - A single 1G-to-100M event that cleared on reseat and has not recurred.
   - Marginal, kinked, or oxidized customer patch cable.
   - Router WAN-port failure.
   - Modem Ethernet-port failure on a customer-owned Arris S33.

7. What to keep on file regardless of outcome
   - The "before" screenshots from step 1.
   - The post-swap screenshots from step 3, with timestamps.
   - The Arris S33 optical levels and event log at the time of any future renegotiation, if one recurs.
   - A short note of what changed and when (cable swap at HH:MM, port swap at HH:MM, etc.) so that any later renegotiation can be correlated to a specific variable.

If nothing in steps 3 and 4 produces a renegotiation event in the next several hours of normal use, no ISP action is warranted. The fix is a replacement patch cable and an eye on the router log over the following week. ISP contact should wait until one of the documented triggers in step 5 is actually observed.

A clasp whose spring gate does not return fully on its own is not a clasp you can trust on a dog walk. The spring gate exists specifically to fail closed: every other part of the snap can be fine and the gate still has to seat flush against the hook body without your hand on it. When you can't verify that at a glance and a tug, the cost of being wrong is Kibo going where you can't follow. So: yes, any incomplete automatic closure at any point in the sequence below means retire it from Kibo use. Cleaning may restore function, but a restored result becomes a demotion, not a restoration — see the decision rule at the end.

Before you start: put Kibo in another room or with Devika. You'll be pressing the gate with your thumb; a curious dog at your elbow is a pinch risk, and a dropped clasp pinging across the floor is exactly the kind of thing Kibo will investigate.

Cleaning sequence (unloaded, no dog attached):

1. Visual inspection, more thorough than what you've already done. Confirm:
     - hook body straight, no bend or twist
     - gate straight, no kink and no chip at the tip
     - spring coils evenly spaced, no stretch, no gap between coils
     - no green or white corrosion, no packed grit at the hinge
   Stop here and retire if any of those are present. Cleaning won't fix bent metal.

2. Lukewarm (not hot) tap rinse. Hot water can soften spring temper. If the leash has fabric or leather stitched above the clasp, keep water away from that joint and wipe the webbing with a damp cloth instead. The goal is to dissolve salt residue off the clasp, not to soak the leash.

3. Mild dish soap and a soft toothbrush. Scrub the gate hinge, the gate tip, and inside the hook mouth. While you scrub, work the gate open and closed with your thumb — the motion helps work grime out of the spring pivot. About 30 seconds is plenty.

4. Clean water rinse. Shake out the excess.

5. Dry thoroughly. Pat with a lint-free cloth. Then either air-dry, use a hair dryer on cool, or a short blast of canned air into the hinge. Any moisture left in the pivot will either flash-freeze on the next walk or attract the next round of grit.

6. Lubricate sparingly with a dry lubricant only — dry silicone or PTFE. One short spray, work the gate ten times, then wipe the outside of the clasp. Do not use oil, grease, or WD-40 as a "fix." They attract and hold grit, which is what started this.

Unloaded test sequence (still no dog):

7. Hook onto a fixed steel D-ring or carabiner with an opening similar in size to Kibo's harness D-ring (about 3/4 inch / 19 mm). A chair-frame loop, a fence ring, or a fixed-eye bolt works.

8. Let go. Look at the gate. Run a fingernail along the seam where the gate meets the hook body. There should be no daylight, no step, no gap. If you can feel the gate sitting proud of the body, it has not closed.

9. Five open/close cycles by hand. Each cycle should produce a clean tactile "snap" and a fully seated gate on release. No stickiness, no hesitation halfway.

10. Load tests, all with the clasp still on the fixed D-ring:
     a. Slow steady pull along the leash axis (the direction a dog walks). Clasp holds, gate does not creep.
     b. Sudden moderate tug (mimics a lunge). Holds, no audible click of the gate popping.
     c. Lateral pull perpendicular to the gate plane — this is the worst-case direction for the gate. Holds. Most snap-hook failures show up here.
     d. Rotate the clasp on the D-ring. Should spin without binding, and the gate should not walk open during the rotation.
   After each load test, re-check the gate is still fully seated.

11. Open the clasp once more and watch the spring return. It should be a single, immediate motion to fully closed, with the gate landing flush without you nudging it.

Pass criteria: every gate check at every step shows a fully seated, flush closure with no daylight, no step, no hesitation. Spring return is immediate on every cycle.

Decision rule for Kibo:

  - If any single step shows an incomplete automatic closure (gate not flush, gate returning partway, gate sticking, gate creeping open under lateral load): retire this clasp from Kibo use. One rerun is reasonable if you suspect residual moisture, but if it fails twice the spring is fatigued and that's the answer — no third attempt.

  - If cleaning restores full, immediate automatic closure and every test passes: this was a slush-grime failure, not a spring failure. The conservative choice, consistent with how you handled the September 2023 near-backout and the subsequent harness replacement, is to retire it from Kibo walks anyway and keep the backup as primary. Demote this one to car or travel-bag status, or discard. A snap hook whose spring has been observed to fail in real conditions is not a primary safety component, even after a successful recovery. The cost of a replacement clasp is trivial relative to the cost of Kibo going loose near traffic.

  - Softer middle ground if you want one: use the restored clasp only as a secondary connection alongside a primary one (a short loop tied through the harness), never as the sole connection, and only in low-distraction environments. That's a reasonable compromise if you want to extend its life for non-critical uses.

What not to do:

  - Do not bend the spring to "tighten" it. You'll either change its travel or snap it.
  - Do not bend the gate back into shape with pliers. Bending work-hardens the metal and creates a future snap point.
  - Do not tape, zip-tie, or otherwise bind the gate shut. That removes the only thing that was still working.
  - Do not swap in a random carabiner without confirming the gate closes fully and the gate gap is no larger than the D-ring it's meant to sit on.
  - Do not use any oil, grease, or WD-40 as a fix. The next walk will pack it with grit and you're back where you started.

One last check while you're looking at this: look at the leash body and the splice where the clasp meets the webbing. If the leash shows any fraying, broken stitches, or webbing separation near the clasp, retire the whole leash regardless of how the clasp cleans up. A good clasp on a failing splice is the same outcome as a bad clasp.

For Kibo's next walk, use the backup. The backup's gate will close or it won't, and you'll have your answer about whether this whole class of failure is one-off or pattern before you commit to buying a replacement.

Your restraint so far is exactly right. Hold it. Do not type anything into the recovery screen, do not visit any recovery-key site, do not reset, do not bypass, do not follow any instruction that appears on that screen. Each of those moves has real downside: a recovery key handed to the wrong party decrypts the entire disk, and "recovery key" pages on the open web are a known phishing trap.

What you are likely looking at

  On a Sphere-managed device showing that asset tag, a screen asking for a disk recovery key is almost certainly the legitimate BitLocker recovery prompt. A firmware update can alter TPM state, which is exactly what triggers BitLocker to demand the 48-digit recovery key on the next boot. That is the boring and most likely explanation.

  The reason you should still be cautious is that a fake recovery prompt looks identical to a real one. The test is what the prompt is doing, not how it looks:

    Legitimate: asks ONLY for a 48-digit recovery key. Nothing else.
    Suspicious: shows a phone number, URL, QR code, or instruction beyond "Enter recovery key."
    Worst case: asks for a Sphere password, MFA code, or any personal credential. Real BitLocker recovery never asks for those.

  If the screen shows anything other than a clean 48-digit entry field, hold the power button to force-shutdown and treat the prompt as compromised until a verified Sphere contact says otherwise.

What to do next, in order

  1. Leave the laptop at the recovery screen. Powering it on and off at that screen does not damage it, but repeated reboots are not useful and will not clear the prompt on their own.

  2. From a different, trusted device, find a verified Sphere IT channel. Do not use any contact information shown on the recovery screen itself. "Verified" means one of:

  4. While you wait, the laptop being out of service is the correct state. Nothing more for you to do on the device.

What not to do

  Do not search the web for "BitLocker recovery key" or "Sphere disk recovery."
  Do not click any link in any email, Slack DM, or chat that claims to be from IT about this. Verify out-of-band first.
