PROPORTIONATE ACCOUNT-CONTAINMENT SEQUENCE
Single old online-retail account. Unique password. MFA on. No unfamiliar orders, payment changes, recovery changes, or active sessions observed. Alert link not followed. Independent navigation available.

The current evidence is consistent with "password exposed, account not yet misused." The sequence below is sized to that. Stop and re-evaluate at any acceptance gate that fails, and treat anything in Phase 6 as a separate decision.


PHASE 0 — PRE-FLIGHT (do once, before any change)

  - Navigate to the retailer by typing the URL yourself, using a bookmark, or via your password manager entry. Do not use the alert link, "go to breach," or any URL embedded in the alert email or SMS.
  - Confirm the certificate and exact domain in the address bar before entering anything. Close the tab if anything looks off; reopen from the saved entry.
  - Open a fresh note or text file to timestamp what you observe (account activity page, sessions, MFA, recovery, payment methods) before and after each change. This becomes your rollback receipt and your evidence file if the situation changes.
  - Have your password manager unlocked and your MFA second factor ready.


PHASE 1 — INDEPENDENT SIGN-IN AND CURRENT-STATE SNAPSHOT

  - Sign in with the existing credentials. Expect and complete the MFA prompt. The prompt itself is evidence MFA is still working.
  - Capture and record what you currently see, in this order, before any change:
      a. Order history and any "recent activity" page
      b. Saved payment methods (last-4, issuer, expiry)
      c. Saved addresses (billing, shipping)
      d. Login / session list, if exposed
      e. Account email and recovery email
      f. Recovery phone number
      g. MFA factors enrolled
      h. Backup codes status (unused / remaining count)
  - Acceptance gate: every item above is recorded, and each item matches what you expect. Any unfamiliar entry, unfamiliar order, unfamiliar payment method, unfamiliar address, or unfamiliar MFA factor is an immediate stop — see Phase 6.


PHASE 2 — PASSWORD REPLACEMENT

  - Open Account / Security / Change Password.
  - Generate a new password with the password manager. Do not derive it from the old one, do not type a related word, and do not store it anywhere except the manager.
  - Save the new entry. Confirm the manager now shows the new password for this account and no longer offers the old one.
  - Submit the change. If the site requires re-authentication or MFA confirmation, complete it.
  - Sign out of the current session, then sign back in with the new password from the manager. This is your independent proof the change took.
  - Acceptance gate: sign-in succeeds with the new credential from the manager; old password is rejected; manager entry is updated.


PHASE 3 — SESSION REVOCATION

  - Locate "Active sessions," "Sign out of all devices," "Devices," or equivalent. If the retailer exposes a per-session list, record what is shown (device, OS, browser, IP, last activity, current city/region) before revoking.
  - Choose the appropriate scope:
      - If you see only this device and want to keep it signed in: revoke everything else.
      - If the list shows anything unfamiliar: revoke everything and re-authenticate this session fresh from a clean browser profile.
  - If "Sign out everywhere" is the only option, take it and re-sign-in on this device.
  - Acceptance gate: after revocation, only the session you just re-authenticated is present, or no sessions are present and your fresh sign-in works.


PHASE 4 — MFA AND RECOVERY CHECKS

  - MFA factors: confirm each enrolled method is yours (authenticator app entry name, hardware key serial, phone number, etc.). Remove any factor you did not add.
  - Recovery email: must be an inbox you control. If the recovery email is unfamiliar, changed, or was modified during a window you cannot account for, stop and escalate per Phase 6.
  - Recovery phone: same check. If unfamiliar or recently changed, stop and escalate.
  - Backup codes: regenerate. Treat the existing set as exposed — the credential was in a breach, so anything an attacker could derive from the account is in scope. Save the new set to the password manager or to a separate secure note, not in the same record as the password.
  - Acceptance gate: every factor, recovery email, recovery phone, and the new backup codes are accounted for and belong to you.


PHASE 5 — SAVED-PAYMENT REVIEW

  - For each saved card on file, record last-4, issuer, expiry, and whether it is a default / backup card.
  - Verify each one is yours and still expected. No unfamiliar card, no unfamiliar billing address, no unfamiliar PayPal / wallet link.
  - If you intend to keep the cards on file, no action is required at this step. The exposure model is "retailer breach contains your password," which does not by itself expose the stored card numbers — most retailers store tokens, and the payment data sits with the processor. Do not preemptively delete cards unless one of the Phase 6 triggers fires.
  - Acceptance gate: every card and address matches what you expect.


PHASE 6 — POST-CHANGE HYGIENE AND DOCUMENTATION

  - In the password manager, mark the entry as rotated-on-<date> after a breach exposure (or equivalent note field). This is so future audits of the manager can find it.
  - Confirm via the manager's audit / reuse / breach tools that this password was unique to this account. If the manager reports reuse elsewhere, treat that as a separate containment scope and rotate those other accounts independently.
  - Save the alert artifact (date, source, breach name, the password record that matched) for your records. Do not click any remediation link in it.
  - Optional but useful: enable any sign-in / new-device email or push alerts the retailer offers, and confirm you receive a test one.


ESCALATION TRIGGERS — CONDITIONS THAT JUSTIFY BROADER ACTION

Treat the following as automatic stops to the routine above. Each is a separate decision with its own evidence requirement; do not bundle them.

A. Account-takeover evidence found in Phase 1 or 4
    - Unfamiliar order, even a small test charge
    - Saved payment method or address you did not add
    - Recovery email, recovery phone, or primary email changed
    - MFA factor you did not add, or backup codes regenerated by someone else
    - Session in a location, device, or browser you do not recognize

    → Action: stop the routine sequence. Preserve the snapshot from Phase 1. Contact the retailer's support through a channel you reach by typing the URL yourself or via a phone number on a prior statement / your card issuer's site, not via anything in the alert. Request account lock, audit of recent activity, and removal of unauthorized changes. Open a dispute only for unauthorized charges.

B. Reuse found by the password manager
    - The breach exposure is no longer single-scope. The same password is on another account.
    → Action: rotate each reused account independently, in order of blast radius — primary email first, then financial, then everything else. Email first because it is the recovery vector for almost everything else.

C. Card on file was actually used in an unauthorized transaction
    - The card PAN may have been exposed through the account, or used while the attacker had access.
    → Action: request the issuer to reissue the card with a new number. Do not close the account unless the issuer recommends it; a reissue preserves the history and any auto-pays tied to the old number if the issuer can port them.

D. You suspect the alert itself was a phishing lure and you may have typed credentials somewhere
    - Even if the breach report and the account are both real, the path matters. If you ever entered the password on a page reached through the alert's link, treat the alert as the attack vector, not just the breach source.
    → Action: rotate, revoke sessions, review MFA, then contact the retailer independently to confirm no unauthorized changes. The retailer-side steps are the same as A.

E. MFA fails or is unexpectedly challenged during the sequence
    - If your MFA code is rejected, the second factor may have been intercepted or rotated by an attacker.
    → Action: stop. Use a known-good backup code or out-of-band recovery. If those also fail, contact the retailer's fraud line directly.

F. Anything you cannot verify
    - A page that does not load, a setting that is missing, a recovery option that is grayed out, a session list that is empty when you expect entries — leave it as-is and continue with what you can verify. Do not infer a clean state from absence. Mark the gap in your notes and resolve it via support.

WHAT IS NOT NEEDED, GIVEN YOUR STATED FACTS

  - Cross-account password rotation: not warranted. You said the password is unique.
  - Card replacement on stored cards: not warranted in the absence of unauthorized transactions or unfamiliar payment methods.
  - Closing the retail account: not warranted as containment. Closing before the alert is resolved can lock you out of your own audit trail.
  - Following the alert's remediation link: do not, even if it appears legitimate.


CLOSURE CRITERIA

The sequence is complete when all six acceptance gates above have passed and your notes record the before / after state. Re-check the account in 24 hours and again in 7 days for unfamiliar activity; most attacker use of breached credentials either happens quickly or not at all. If those re-checks are clean, the containment is closed.

PRESERVATION-FIRST SEQUENCE: ENCRYPTED LOCAL PHONE BACKUP

Principle: do not change anything that could reduce your recoverable state until a backup exists and has been verified as recoverable. The cloud backup has not completed since December 26, but the December 26 snapshot is still in iCloud and has not been overwritten — that is your current fallback. The local backup below is intended to be more recent and not share the cloud-storage constraint.

PHASE 0 — Record four things BEFORE you plug in

  - The encryption password you will set (set at the start of the backup; cannot be added afterwards)
  - Where the backup will live on the computer (a folder the OS will not touch, NOT inside a cloud-sync folder like iCloud Drive, OneDrive, or Dropbox)
  - Today's date and the phone model / iOS version
  - The phone passcode (you will need it to trust the computer)

  Password rule: the encryption password is the only thing standing between you and your backup. iOS / iTunes / Finder cannot reset it. If you lose it, the backup is unrecoverable. Store it somewhere that is NOT only on the computer holding the backup (password manager, paper in a separate place, or both).

PHASE 1 — Preconditions (verify before starting; abort if any fail)

  - Computer free space comfortably exceeds the expected backup size (your phone's prior iCloud backup size is a reasonable proxy; the 49.7 GB of account usage is dominated by Photos, which are synced via iCloud Photos and are NOT in this backup)
  - USB cable is known-good (frayed or loose cables are the silent failure mode; substitute if in doubt)
  - Computer on AC power, not battery
  - Phone charged (50%+ recommended; on the charger is better)
  - Finder (macOS Catalina or later) or iTunes (Windows / older macOS) is up to date
  - No other backup or sync currently running on the computer
  - You can keep the phone and computer undisturbed for 30–90+ minutes

  Stop conditions (do not start if any are true): free-space margin too thin, cable suspect, computer on battery, phone low charge with no outlet access, or the timing window is constrained.

PHASE 2 — Create the encrypted backup (one uninterrupted run)

  a. Connect the phone by USB. Wired is strongly preferred for the initial backup.
  b. On the phone, tap "Trust" when prompted and enter the passcode.
  c. In Finder / iTunes, select the phone.
  d. Under Backups, choose "Encrypt local backup" and set the password from Phase 0. Confirm the password.
     — "Encrypt local backup" is the choice that captures Messages, Settings, Keychain, Health, call history, visual voicemail, and most app data.
     — Do NOT choose "iCloud" here.
  e. Click "Back Up Now."
  f. Leave both devices alone until completion: do not disconnect, do not close the app, do not let the computer sleep, do not switch networks, do not start another backup.

  Stop conditions during the run:
    - Any error dialog (record the exact text; do not blindly retry)
    - No progress change for 30+ minutes without explanation
    - Phone disconnects, computer sleeps, app closes
    - Backup completes but with a warning indicator

  If any stop condition fires, abort this run, diagnose (cable, port, free space, app version), and start a fresh run.

PHASE 3 — Verify (the step most people skip; treat it as a separate phase)

  A backup that exists is not a backup you can restore from. Verification is what turns a file into a backup.

  Required read-back from the Finder / iTunes UI:
    1. "Last backup" shows today's run, not an older entry
    2. No error or warning indicator on that entry
    3. The on-disk backup folder size is plausible (multiple GB typical; years of messages plus app data can push this into the 5–15 GB range)

  Strongest verification (if you have a spare or borrowed device): restore the backup to that device and confirm that messages, recent conversations, and key settings appear. This is the only way to prove the backup is actually restorable rather than merely written.

  If no spare device is available, record (a)–(c) above and label the backup "verified-present, not yet verified-restorable." Treat upgrading to restore-on-spare as a follow-up rather than declaring full verification.

  Acceptance gate to move to Phase 4: today's timestamp, no error, plausible size, password recorded in a separate location. Until all four are true, do not proceed.

PHASE 4 — STOP HERE. Do not yet do any of the following:

  - Delete the stale cloud backup from iCloud settings (it is your current fallback until the local backup is verified)
  - Reduce iCloud Backup scope by unchecking Messages or specific apps
  - Toggle "Messages in iCloud" on or off
  - Free space on the phone by deleting apps, messages, or attachments
  - Upgrade or downgrade the iCloud storage tier

  Reasoning: every item above reduces what is currently being protected somewhere. Until the local backup is independently verified, narrowing cloud coverage would leave Messages, Settings, or app data with no verified copy.

PHASE 5 — Record the artifacts, in writing, somewhere independent of the backup computer

  - Date and time the backup completed
  - Phone model and iOS version
  - Absolute path to the backup folder on the computer
  - Approximate size
  - Where the encryption password is stored (and confirmation it is NOT only on the computer holding the backup)
  - One sentence stating what you verified (read-back timestamp, size, error-free) and what you did NOT verify (e.g., restore on a spare device)

PHASE 6 — Out of scope for this turn, available as a follow-up once the local backup is verified

  These each deserve their own decision on their own evidence; do not bundle them:
    - Deleting the now-redundant stale cloud backup(s)
    - Whether to leave iCloud Backup enabled at all, narrow its scope, or disable it
    - Whether to enable Messages in iCloud as a redundant, continuously-synced store for messages (separate from iCloud Backup)
    - Whether the long-term answer is more iCloud storage rather than scope reduction
    - Whether to upgrade to restore-on-spare verification

That is the full preservation-first sequence. The single most common failure mode is treating "backup completed" as the same thing as "backup verified" — Phase 3 exists specifically to keep those two separate.

Short assessment: this is a defect, not a working staged-enablement.

What the description shows
  - Validator returns `oversized_batch` for >8,000 points. Fine — this is the SDK-side
    validation path Alex previously asked for, and the programmatic code is unchanged.
  - The catch block then puts the *original, unchanged* request on
    `genericTransientRetryQueue`. Not fine.
  - The test asserts zero immediate sends + one later send of the unchanged object.
    The test is encoding the bug as the contract.

Why the catch-block retry is wrong
  1. `oversized_batch` is a permanent client-side validation failure, not a transient
     server condition. The 8,000-point cap is a hard client limit; re-sending the same
     payload cannot make it smaller. Putting it on a transient queue is a category
     error.
  2. `genericTransientRetryQueue` is the wrong home even if retry were acceptable.
     Mixing permanent validation rejections with timeout/5xx retries will pollute the
     queue, starve legitimate retries under load, and contaminate retry-exhaustion
     metrics (the retry is guaranteed to fail every cycle).
  3. The server-side backstop is HTTP 413 with zero accepted points, so every retry
     burns bandwidth and CPU and inflates the `oversized_batch` rejection counter
     with no new information. If ingest-edge behavior ever drifts (e.g., quota or
     limit changes), a previously-rejected batch could be accepted on retry and
     produce duplicate-accepted points — the exact failure mode Alex blocked earlier
     (reject-only retry, not whole-batch retry).
  4. It directly contradicts the split-before-retry instruction that was the
     explicit acceptance criterion for the SDK text fix. The validator tells the
     caller to split; the SDK then retries the unsplit batch anyway. The two halves
     of the contract disagree with each other.
  5. It contradicts the prior correct observation — "the test client made no
     unchanged retries for the oversized requests." That property is being lost.

What the right behavior looks like
  - The catch block should not enqueue the unchanged object. Two acceptable shapes:
      a. Surface the `oversized_batch` (and the human-readable limit + split
         instruction) up to the caller and stop. Caller decides.
      b. Drop with a metric/log line tagged `oversized_batch` and stop.
  - Either way, no retry, no re-send. The staged-enablement flag should gate only
    the validation-error return, not a retry-loop that has no recovery path.

What the test should assert
  - Zero immediate sends (already correct).
  - Zero later sends — the unchanged object must not be transmitted again.
  - The caller-visible error carries `oversized_batch` and the 8,000-point limit.

Scope note
  - The validator + error-text half of the staged enablement is the part that
    resolves the SDK text issue Alex already approved. The catch-block retry
    enqueue is a separate, unjustified behavior change and should be removed from
    this PR, not bundled into it. If the implementer wants a retry path here, it
    is a fresh change with its own justification, its own flag, and its own
    acceptance criteria — not a side effect of enabling the validator.

Nothing in the description supports shipping the retry enqueue as-is. The PR is
not mergeable in this shape; the test is the load-bearing evidence of the bug and
should change, not the validator.

PRESERVATION-FIRST CLOUD-CLEANUP SEQUENCE
January 17, 2025

Goal: remove ONLY the obsolete 8 GB device backup from the replaced phone, verify the resulting headroom, then refresh the current phone's encrypted cloud backup. Nothing else in your backup scope changes. Photo Library, current phone's stale backup, settings, messages, and the verified local encrypted backup all stay intact.

PRE-FLIGHT — verify before you delete anything

A. Re-verify the local encrypted backup is still good before touching the cloud.
   1. Reopen the local backup file in Finder/iTunes.
   2. Confirm the device summary still opens (proves structural validity).
   3. Confirm the recovery metadata still opens with your encryption password (proves the password works and the key set is intact).
   4. Note and screenshot: filename, size, completion timestamp, device name, iOS version.
   Stop condition: if any step fails, ABORT the cloud cleanup entirely. The local backup is your only offline recovery copy. Do not weaken it.

B. Snapshot the current iCloud state into a fixed note you can compare against later.
   Write down BEFORE deletion:
   - Storage used: 49.7 of 50 GB (~0.3 GB free)
   - Photo Library status: sync complete
   - Backups present (device name, model, size, last successful date):
       Current phone — STALE, last backup Dec 26, 2024 — KEEP
       Old phone (replaced last year) — ~8 GB — DELETE TARGET
   - Current state of: iCloud Drive, Messages in iCloud, Keychain, Health, Advanced Data Protection.

C. Positively identify the obsolete backup.
   On the phone: Settings → [Apple ID] → iCloud → Manage Storage → Backups.
   The obsolete backup must show ALL of:
   - device name ≠ current phone
   - model ≠ current phone
   - last backup date is from BEFORE you replaced the phone
   - size ≈ 8 GB
   If any of those four checks is wrong, STOP. Do not delete. Local backup and cloud both stay.

D. Acceptance gate. Proceed only if A, B, and C all pass.

PHASE 1 — DELETE ONLY THE OBSOLETE 8 GB BACKUP

1. In iCloud → Manage Storage → Backups, tap the obsolete backup.
2. Confirm the screen shows the OLD device name, OLD model, OLD date, ~8 GB.
3. Tap Delete Backup → confirm the prompt.
4. Do not tap any other backup. Do not toggle iCloud Backup off. Do not sign out. Do not touch Photo Library, Messages in iCloud, or any other data toggle.

What is being deleted: one obsolete device backup from the replaced phone.
What is being preserved: Photo Library, current phone's stale cloud backup, Messages in iCloud, iCloud Drive, Keychain, Health, settings, messages on the device, and your verified local encrypted backup.

PHASE 2 — VERIFY THE RESULTING FREE SPACE

1. Wait ~30–60 seconds for the storage display to refresh.
2. Reopen Settings → Apple ID → iCloud → Manage Storage.
3. Expected after deletion:
   - used ≈ 41.7 GB
   - free ≈ 8.3 GB
   - Photo Library size unchanged
   - current phone's stale backup still present, size and date unchanged
   - obsolete backup: gone
4. Walk down your Phase 0 inventory line by line. Every item other than the obsolete backup must be present and unchanged.
5. Stop conditions:
   - Free space is meaningfully less than ~8 GB → something unexpected was removed or accounting is off. Do not proceed to Phase 3.
   - Free space is meaningfully more than ~8 GB → something other than the obsolete backup was removed. Investigate immediately.
   - Photo Library, current phone backup, or any other expected item is missing → STOP.
   - Any error or "could not delete" state appears → STOP.

Rollback note: iCloud keeps deleted backups recoverable for 30 days in Recently Deleted. If you discover the wrong backup was deleted, recover it from Settings → Apple ID → iCloud → Manage Storage → Backups → Recently Deleted within that window. The verified local backup remains your offline rollback if cloud recovery fails.

PHASE 3 — RERUN THE CURRENT ENCRYPTED CLOUD BACKUP

1. On the current phone: Settings → [Apple ID] → iCloud → Backup.
2. Confirm "Back Up This iPhone" / "iCloud Backup" is ON.
3. Confirm the phone is on Wi-Fi and either plugged in or has sufficient battery. iOS will not run a reliable backup over cellular or at low battery.
4. Tap Back Up Now.
5. Watch the progress. Do not lock the phone. Do not toggle other settings during the upload.
6. When it finishes, reopen Settings → Apple ID → iCloud → Manage Storage → Backups and verify:
   - current phone's backup shows a fresh Last Backup timestamp dated today
   - size is reasonable (typically at least the stale size, often larger)
   - status reads Successful, not Stale or In Progress
7. Light sanity check on the phone: open Messages and confirm the latest conversations are still there; confirm a couple of representative settings (Focus, Wi-Fi networks, Mail accounts) are still configured. The backup process does not alter on-device state, but verifying now is cheap.
8. Stop conditions:
   - Backup stalls, fails, or ends Stale → do not retry more than once; the Dec 26 stale backup is still in the cloud and still recoverable. Stop and decide separately.
   - An unexpected prompt for your local-backup encryption password during an iCloud backup → STOP. iCloud Backup does not normally ask for that password. If it does, something is off.
   - Backup completes but size or timestamp does not look right → do not assume success; re-check after 5 minutes before trusting it.

PHASE 4 — STOP. DO NOT CHANGE ANY OTHER BACKUP SCOPE.

After the fresh cloud backup is verified, freeze the configuration. Do NOT touch:

- Photo Library settings or sync
- Messages in iCloud toggle
- iCloud Drive sync settings
- Keychain, Health, or any other iCloud data toggle
- iCloud Backup on/off
- Advanced Data Protection settings
- Retention, "Delete All", or deletion of any other backup
- The verified local encrypted backup on the computer

End state:
- Local verified encrypted backup — kept, offline, encrypted with your password
- Fresh encrypted iCloud backup of the current phone — kept, online, dated today
- Photo Library — kept, complete, untouched
- Obsolete 8 GB backup from the replaced phone — gone
- All other iCloud data toggles and contents — unchanged

The sequence ends here. Any further backup-scope decisions (turning on Advanced Data Protection, changing retention, an additional offline copy, scheduled cadence, etc.) belong in a fresh decision window, not bolted onto this one.

$1.00 NORTHSTAR DIGITAL pending auth — proportionate response

Two competing explanations for a single small unfamiliar auth, indistinguishable right now:

  H1 (most common): a merchant card-verification hold. Subscription trials, prepaid card activations, transit systems, and account-verification flows frequently place a $1.00 (or sub-$1) auth that drops within 1–7 business days. If this is H1, the auth disappears on its own and no action beyond monitoring is warranted.

  H2 (less common, more serious): a card-testing probe. Parties holding breached card numbers often validate them with tiny charges before attempting larger fraud. The fact that the physical card is with you, login and MFA still work, and there has been no phishing interaction is consistent with EITHER hypothesis — it does not distinguish them.

What follows is the smallest response that respects both, with explicit gates to escalate.

1. Preserve evidence now (in the next few minutes):

  - Screenshot the pending $1.00 NORTHSTAR DIGITAL line including timestamp, merchant descriptor, amount, and any transaction/reference ID the app shows.
  - Screenshot the full recent-activity list so the "no other unfamiliar activity" snapshot is on record.
  - Note the screenshot date/time in one place (text file, notes app).
  - Do not delete, dispute, or "remove" the pending entry. Leave it in place until it either drops on its own or you have a decision to make.

2. Observation window — 5 to 7 business days from today (through roughly Jan 24–27):

  - Check the app or online banking at least daily for: any new pending or posted unfamiliar activity, the original auth changing status, or any login/MFA prompts you didn't initiate.
  - If the $1.00 auth drops off on its own during this window, that is H1 confirmed. No further action needed; keep the screenshots for ~90 days in case of a late dispute window.
  - Do not call NORTHSTAR DIGITAL, do not email them, do not click any link in a text or email about this charge.

3. Independent issuer contact — verification only, not a dispute:

  - Use the phone number on the back of the physical card or the in-app messaging feature. Do not use a number from a text, email, or web search result.
  - Ask: (a) whether this is an authorization expected to settle or a hold expected to drop, (b) what transaction-level detail they have on the merchant (descriptor MID, MCC, terminal location, channel — in-person/online/recurring), (c) whether they can flag the card for enhanced monitoring on their side, (d) whether they see any other recent activity from unfamiliar merchants.
  - Record the call: date, time, rep name/ID, the answers, and any case or reference number. This becomes part of the preserved evidence.
  - You are NOT opening a dispute yet. Opening a dispute before the auth resolves creates competing-claim friction (cf. the Metro Office Supply / Marriott / transit-wallet patterns) and is unnecessary if the hold drops.

4. Criteria to lock the card NOW (do not wait for the window):

  - A second unfamiliar pending auth appears.
  - The original $1.00 auth posts as a charge instead of dropping.
  - Any posted charge from NORTHSTAR DIGITAL or any other merchant you don't recognize.
  - Login alert or MFA prompt from a device/location you didn't initiate.
  - Any change to account email, phone, mailing address, or saved payment methods.
  - Anything from the issuer or a "fraud team" arriving via text/email that asks you to call a number or click a link.

5. Criteria to replace the card (replacement, not just lock):

  - Any of the trigger conditions in step 4.
  - The issuer recommends replacement after they review the transaction-level detail.
  - A pattern appears (multiple small auths, auth + immediate decline pattern, recurring microcharges from unknown merchants).
  - Two or more of the criteria in step 4 hit within the observation window, even if mild.

  Replacement is a bigger step than lock because it cascades: every autopay, subscription, transit-reload card, and saved payment method on this card needs to be updated, and rushed updates on unfamiliar flows create their own fraud surface. Hold replacement behind evidence, not the auth alone.

6. Criteria to close with no further action:

  - The $1.00 auth drops off during the 5–7 day window.
  - No other unfamiliar activity appears.
  - Issuer confirms normal merchant pattern on their side.
  - Keep the screenshots for ~90 days in case of a late dispute window, then retire.

On the lock-while-pending question

Do not lock yet. The evidence pattern (single $1.00 unknown auth, card in hand, working MFA, no phishing interaction, no other unfamiliar activity) is consistent with H1, and locking now cascades into every recurring charge on the card without buying you information you can't get from a 5–7 day observation window plus the issuer verification call. Lock is the right tool for the trigger conditions in step 4; the pending auth alone isn't one of them.

One-line rule: preserve evidence today, call the issuer once tomorrow on a number from the back of the card, watch the auth for 5–7 business days, lock or replace only on the triggers above.

Note (2024-06-17, accepted resume boundary — encodes the rule the infra review asked to live here before configuration pushes resume): the pause criteria above (retired objects > 4 per pod OR any STW cleanup pause > 100 ms) and the rollback floor above (active-generation inconsistency, route divergence beyond the existing bar, or any non-zero dropped-series increment attributable to the canary) are now the operational stop / repause / rollback rule for configuration pushes. This note is the boundary the responder enforces between pushes; it does NOT declare the underlying retirement-delay cause resolved, and it does NOT authorize laptop deploys, skipping the canary slice, or relaxing the existing rollback bar (sustained out-of-band p99, error-rate movement, dropped writes firing, rollup-service lag) for true user-visible regressions.

Stop condition (further pushes are paused):
- Retired generation count crosses above 4 per pod, OR
- Any stop-the-world cleanup pause crosses above 100 ms.
Either crossing alone is sufficient. Pushes are paused as soon as either is observed; do not wait for both, do not wait for a second sample, and do not attempt a compensating push in the same window.

Bounded single-push resume (exactly one push may be attempted, with full observation, only when ALL of the following hold together):
- Retired generations have drained to 1 or fewer per pod.
- Request p99 has returned to its pre-canary baseline.
- Heap has returned to its pre-canary baseline.
- Active-generation consistency holds across pods.
- Route parity holds within the existing divergence bar.
- Dropped series are at zero (or at the pre-canary baseline if non-zero).
- No reload failures.
- No restarts.
The resume is exactly one configuration push to exactly one canary pod, observed in full against the existing checks (p99-by-pod, generation snapshot, heap, route parity, dropped series, reload, restarts). No next push is attempted until the target pod drains back to 1 or fewer retired generations and the checks above remain clean. This is a resume boundary, not a fix announcement; the retirement-delay cause remains open.

Immediate re-pause (any single threshold recrossing pauses pushes again):
- Retired generation count recrosses above 4 per pod.
- Any STW cleanup pause recrosses above 100 ms.
- p99 leaves baseline.
- Heap leaves baseline.
- Active-generation inconsistency appears.
- Route parity breaks the existing divergence bar.
- Dropped series move off zero (or off the pre-canary baseline if non-zero).
- A reload failure occurs.
- A restart occurs.
A re-pause is an operational signal, not an automatic rollback. After a re-pause, the bounded single-push resume above must be re-satisfied from scratch before any further push is attempted.

Rollback conditions (unchanged and still authoritative — these remain rollback, not pause):
- Active-generation inconsistency across pods (split-brain, or a pod stuck on a retired generation that will not drain).
- Route divergence beyond the existing bar.
- Any non-zero dropped-series increment attributable to the canary.
- A reload failure.
- A restart.
Any one of these is sufficient for rollback via the pipeline. They are not softened by a recovered p99, a drained retired count, or a returned-to-baseline heap; they are the floor. The existing rollback bar (sustained out-of-band p99, error-rate movement, dropped writes firing, rollup-service lag) is unchanged and still applies alongside them.

Interaction with prior notes:
- The 2024-05-30 generation/cleanup guidance above remains the underlying triage layer; this note formalizes its pause thresholds into the operational stop / repause rule and adds the bounded single-push resume above.
- The parser-cleanup warmup rule (2023-09-27) and the CPU-only warmup rule (2023-09-07) still apply on their own facts; this note does not relax either of them.
- This note does NOT authorize laptop deploys, skipping the canary slice, dropping the staging-quiet precondition, or relaxing the existing rollback bar for true user-visible regressions.

Scope and ownership: this note exists so the next on-call enforces the accepted resume boundary — stop on threshold crossing, attempt at most one bounded push with full observation when the resume conditions all hold, re-pause immediately on any recrossing, and roll back on any of the rollback conditions above. Ownership of this runbook is unchanged (alex / wes). Do not open a separate generation-lifecycle project in response to this pattern, and do not treat resume under this rule as confirmation that the retirement-delay cause has been fixed.

ingest-edge tenant-fair queue behavior — 2024-07-05 [reference, production behavior]

This section is the authoritative record for the ingest-edge tenant-fair queue behavior, layered on top of the existing bounded-decompression and randomized 1–3s Retry-After production behavior. Tenant-fair queueing is now production behavior on the ingest-edge path at 100%. ingest-edge stays at 100% on the tenant-fair path; it is not rolling back to the prior global FIFO ordering.

What changed (and what did NOT)
Preserved verbatim and not relaxed:
- Four active decompressions per pod (unchanged).
- Two active decompressions per tenant (unchanged).
- Bounded decompression — per-pod and per-tenant active caps continue to bound accepted concurrency; fairness only governs who gets the next eligible slot (unchanged).
- Eight waiting requests per tenant cap (unchanged). When a tenant hits 8/8 waiting, new requests for that tenant receive HTTP 429 with a randomized 1–3s Retry-After — same contract documented under v2.19.4.
- Randomized 1–3s Retry-After on queue-cap responses (unchanged).
- Cancellation removes the queued request and releases the permit at every race point (unchanged).
- Separation between waiting (≤ 8 per tenant) and active (≤ 2 per tenant, ≤ 4 per pod) limits (unchanged).
- Aging / hard maximum wait bounds on queued requests to prevent starvation (unchanged).

Adds only:
- Per-pod round-robin ring contains only tenants with at least one queued or active request — empty tenants are not in the ring.
- Newly enqueued tenant is inserted into the ring immediately on enqueue (no waiting for next one-second ring rebuild).
- Scheduler wakes immediately when a tenant is inserted so the new tenant can claim the next eligible slot.
- During Next(), empty tenants are skipped; round-robin order is preserved among tenants with work.
- When cancellation empties a tenant's queue, the tenant is evicted from the ring.
- Work-conserving dispatcher uses otherwise idle capacity — an eligible slot is not left idle when work exists. Borrowing uses idle waiting capacity; tagged and reversible when the donor drains; does not relax the four-per-pod or two-per-tenant active caps.

Explicit stop boundaries (authoritative for this rollout)
- More than 4 active decompressions on a single pod at any moment.
- More than 2 active decompressions for any single tenant at any moment.
- Any tenant exceeding 8 waiting requests.
- Any queue-cap 429 response without a Retry-After header, or with a Retry-After outside the 1–3 second randomized range.
- Any accepted point dropped after acceptance.
- Any idle decompression slot lasting more than 100 ms while queued or active work exists (work-conservation failure).
- First-request wait for a newly enqueued tenant exceeding 250 ms when an eligible slot is available.
- Pod restart on any ingest-edge pod during the rollout window.
- Any 5xx increase on the ingest-edge path.

Existing v2.19.4 boundaries (peak retry attempts ≥ 130,000/s, p99 latency ≥ 190 ms, queue depth ≥ 76%, accepted-throughput loss ≥ 3% vs baseline) remain in force and are not relaxed.

- More than 2 active decompressions for any single tenant at any moment.

- Any idle decompression slot lasting more than 100 ms while queued or active work exists for the scheduler (work-conservation failure).

- Pod restart on any ingest-edge pod during the rollout window.
- Any 5xx increase on the ingest-edge path.

Short version: yes to continued rinsing plus short route, yes to a dog-safe paw balm, and here are the specific triggers and time window that should move you from monitoring to a vet call.

Current read of the trajectory
  - The between-pad pinkness from five days ago is gone, and Kibo is otherwise normal, no limp, no pain on handling, no foreign body, no broken nail. That is real improvement, not just absence of worsening.
  - The shallow 4 mm rough patch is a new minimal finding on a single pad. It is not the same as the August 31 flap. It is consistent with mild chemical irritation or superficial roughening from repeated contact with treated sections, but it could also be the very early stage of something that does not stay superficial. The right stance is treat it as mild and monitor with explicit triggers, not assume it will resolve.

Rinsing and a short route are still reasonable
  - Lukewarm water rinse after every walked-on-treated-surface outing, including the quieter route. Cool or warm, not hot. Pat dry between pads and on the pad surface; do not rub the rough patch.
  - Keep walks short and on the cleanest stretch available. The quieter route still has scattered treated sections, so the goal is fewer exposures per walk, not a perfect surface.
  - Wiping paws at the door with a damp cloth is a reasonable supplement to a full rinse if a full rinse is not practical after a very short walk.
  - Continued licking is a useful signal. If licking returns to the same paw after a walk, that walk is effectively too much exposure and should be shortened further or replaced with a very short, clean-surface loop.

Dog-safe paw balm
  - Appropriate as a barrier and as a mild protectant over a non-bleeding, non-swollen rough patch. It is not a treatment for an infection and it is not a substitute for the rinse-and-dry step.
  - Use a balm specifically labeled for dogs, or a simple beeswax-and-plant-oil balm. Avoid zinc oxide and any petroleum-jelly-based product with zinc, since zinc is toxic to dogs if licked off and ingested in quantity. Avoid lanolin-heavy or heavily fragranced products.
  - Timing matters. A thin layer before a walk can reduce contact with residue on treated sections. A thin layer after the rinse and dry can help the rough patch stay protected overnight. If Kibo licks it off immediately after application, reapply and briefly distract him so it sets, or skip the pre-walk layer and use only the post-walk layer.
  - Do not apply over a wet or dirty paw, and do not apply over any area that is bleeding, hot, swollen, or has discharge. If any of those appear, skip the balm on that spot and call the vet.

When persistence justifies the vet
  Same-day or urgent vet call if any of these appear at any point:
    - Bleeding from the rough patch or any new split
    - Swelling, heat, or spreading redness around the pad
    - Discharge or odor from the paw
    - Limp, favoring the paw, or pain on gentle handling
    - Visible foreign object, broken nail, or anything embedded
    - Behavioral change: marked lethargy, appetite loss, or feverish behavior

  Routine vet call (within 24 to 48 hours, do not wait it out) if:
    - The rough patch is not clearly smaller and less rough by 5 to 7 days from today, so roughly by Wednesday or Thursday of next week
    - Licking of the same paw keeps recurring after walks despite shorter, cleaner routes, or increases in frequency or duration
    - The rough patch enlarges, deepens, or develops a flap or crust
    - A second paw starts showing similar findings

  Routine vet call at the next available appointment if:
    - The rough patch gradually resolves but the same paw keeps re-flaring after every treated-section walk. That pattern is the signal to ask about a formal plan for walks during the rest of the deicer season, including whether a more protective routine or a vet-recommended balm is warranted.

One operational note consistent with your pattern: keep the symptom timeline running. Date, what the paw looked like, walk length and route, rinse done yes or no, licking observed yes or no. If you do end up calling, that timeline is exactly the kind of evidence your clinic has found useful in the past.

Short answer: yes, retire the shorter leash now, don't trim or tape it. The longer leash can be used safely near the Prospect Park entrances, but only with a controlled-length technique and a quick pre-use inspection.

On retiring the shorter leash

  - The handle-end webbing is the highest-stress zone on a leash — that's where grip force and any lunge or redirect load converge. Several cut fibers in that zone mean the remaining fibers are carrying load they weren't designed to carry alone.
  - Tape (electrical, duct, self-amending wraps) is cosmetic. It doesn't restore tensile strength, it hides the damage from your eyes going forward, and it can mask a tear that grows under load.
  - Trimming only removes the visibly bad section. The real failure mode is internal — adjacent fibers are usually compromised even when they look intact, and the cut propagates under sudden load (the exact scenario a passing bike or scooter near the curb creates).
  - The leash hasn't failed yet, but the relevant question isn't "has it held?" — it's "would I trust it under an unexpected lunge at the curb?" If the answer is no, retire it.
  - Don't repurpose it as a tie-out, a "quick errand" leash, or a backup in a bag. Partial-strength webbing either holds Kibo or it doesn't.

This matches the precedent from the January 5 clasp-return issue: you stopped using the shorter leash rather than continuing with a compromised closure. Same principle applies here.

On using the longer leash safely near the Prospect Park entrances

  1. Inspect the longer leash first, before relying on it. With Kibo out of the picture, check:
       - Handle loop and the stitching that joins the webbing to the handle (same zone you just found damage on the short leash)
       - Webbing the full length for cuts, fraying, discoloration, or stiffness
       - Stitching at any seams or junctions
       - Clasp spring action — it should snap closed fully and lock under thumb pressure, not sit partway open
       - Clasp gate alignment (no bent or twisted gate)
     If anything on the long leash raises the same kind of concern, retire it too and the question becomes a different one.

  2. Replicate the short-leash working length, don't just clip and go. The reason the short leash is the default at the entrances is close control when bikes cut close. A longer leash at full length recreates the exact risk the short leash was adopted to address. Use one of these controlled-length techniques:
       - Thumb-loop hold: pass the handle loop over your thumb, gather the slack in your palm with the working end (clasp side) held short, and let the excess coil in your grip. This keeps the effective length short while leaving the full leash intact.
       - Half-hitch shorten: pass the clasp end through the handle loop and back through itself to create a temporary choke that shortens the working length to roughly the short-leash distance. Test the hitch with a firm pull before attaching to Kibo.
       - Wrist wrap: only as a secondary control, not the primary hold — wrap the excess once around the wrist, but keep the working end pinched in the hand. The wrist wrap is a backup if Kibo lunges, not the active grip.
     Whichever you use, the active grip should leave Kibo at roughly the same distance from your hand as the short leash did.

  3. Keep the front-clip harness. The harness fit you confirmed on January 5 is unchanged, and front-clip + close control was the working combination near the curb. Don't switch to a back-clip or collar attachment just because the leash is longer.

  4. Walk posture stays the same. Treat the long leash as if it were the short one — short effective length, hand close to the clasp end, no slack on the ground near the curb, body between Kibo and the road at entrances.

  5. Time and entrance choice. If a particular entrance is especially busy with bikes or scooters cutting close at certain hours, either shift the time a few minutes or use a different entrance until the shorter leash is replaced. This is a temporary workaround, not a permanent route change.

On replacement

  When you do replace the shorter leash, the replacement criteria worth matching are: similar short length, the same handle-and-clasp-end construction (so your shortening habits transfer), a clasp with a positive spring-return and lock (not just a snap-shut), and webbing that's the same thickness you're used to handling. If you want, tell me the specific replacement you're considering and I can sanity-check it against those criteria.

A small note on the short leash itself

  Since it isn't being used again, bagging it and setting it aside (rather than putting it back in the rotation) makes the "don't accidentally grab it" decision automatic. If you want to return it under warranty or to the maker, keep the receipt and the leash intact; don't cut into it.

Bounded verification sequence for Anya, plus the asymmetry argument. Frame this as her lane — she's the pilot owner, and the answer here is "diagnose the generator, don't invert the source."

The asymmetry (why iOS → canonical is wrong without source-level evidence)

The iOS file is a downstream artifact of (canonical package) × (generator version) × (runtime/locale). If it disagrees with the canonical package, the disagreement is itself a signal about the generator or the generation environment — it is not evidence about what the canonical values *should* be. File timestamps on a generated artifact record when it was written, not whether its values are correct; newer-looking timestamps are explained by generator re-runs, cache invalidation, build metadata, or generator-version drift, none of which constitute a source-level rationale. Writing iOS-derived values back into the canonical package would:

  - Invert the data flow. A consumer becomes the source. Future regenerations can never reproduce what was just written, because nothing in the canonical history says those values are right.
  - Destroy the audit trail. The canonical package is versioned, reviewed, and diff-able. A bulk overwrite from a generated file carries no per-key rationale and no reviewable commit.
  - Lock in whatever the generator produced, including any generator bug, stale cache, nondeterminism, or runtime variance (Linux/macOS ZIP divergence is already in this pilot's history).
  - Break the drift-check invariant. The drift check exists precisely to surface divergence between canonical-derived output and committed generated output. Overwriting canonical from generated output makes the drift check unfalsifiable — divergence can no longer mean "generator is wrong," because canonical now inherits the generator's output.
  - Hide the real defect. The same symptom (timestamp, hash, value drift) will recur on the next regeneration, with no signal left in the system to locate it.

The rule: a canonical change must originate from a source-level decision — a reviewed edit to the versioned machine-readable package, with intent, attribution, and a regenerable trail. Anything else is a generator/cache/environment problem to diagnose, not a canonical problem to "fix" by overwriting.

Bounded verification sequence (run in this order; stop and reassess if any step changes the picture)

  1. Generator version check
     - Identify the generator version that produced the iOS file in question (build stamp, CI artifact metadata, generator commit SHA in the iOS header, or the pinned version in the generation pipeline).
     - Compare it against the generator version used for the last known-clean regeneration that the drift check accepted.
     - Confirm the generator binary/commit has not been modified, repinned, or run from a different checkout since the last accepted run.
     - Outcome: a generator version is either consistent with the accepted baseline, or it has drifted. Drift here is sufficient explanation for output divergence; no canonical change is warranted.

  2. Canonical package commit check
     - Record the commit SHA of the canonical versioned machine-readable package that was fed into the generation run that produced this iOS file.
     - Confirm it matches the canonical HEAD at the time of generation (i.e., no in-flight branch with intended-but-unmerged changes).
     - Confirm the canonical package itself has no uncommitted local edits, no unmerged PRs, and no review-in-progress changes that the iOS file might be partially reflecting.
     - Outcome: the canonical input to the generator is identified and pinned. If canonical HEAD has moved since generation, the divergence is a stale-output problem; regenerate from current canonical and re-check.

  3. Generation logs check
     - Pull the CI run log for the iOS generation: start, end, exit code, warnings, retries, partial runs.
     - Look for skipped steps, post-generation formatter passes, locale/environment substitutions, dependency-resolution noise, or any transform that touches the file after generation.
     - Confirm the generator consumed the canonical commit identified in step 2, with no intermediate mutation.
     - Outcome: a clean, traceable generation from a pinned canonical input. Any anomaly here is the divergence's actual cause; the iOS file is a symptom, not a source.

  4. Drift check (run explicitly, do not skip)
     - Trigger the drift check against the current canonical package and the committed generated outputs.
     - Read the result: pass means canonical and generated agree; fail means the drift check produces a key-level diff identifying exactly which keys differ.
     - A failing drift check with a key-level diff is the system's own determination of divergence. It is the signal to investigate, not a directive to overwrite canonical with whichever side happens to be newer.
     - A passing drift check after step 1–3 means the apparent timestamp asymmetry is packaging/build metadata, not a content divergence; the canonical package is fine and the iOS file's timestamps do not represent a substantive problem.

Decision rule after the four checks

  - Generator version drifted, or generation logs show an anomaly, or runtime/locale produced a divergent output: regenerate from current canonical using the pinned baseline generator version; re-run the drift check. Canonical is not touched.
  - Canonical HEAD has moved since the iOS file was generated: regenerate from current canonical; re-run the drift check. Canonical is not touched.
  - Drift check fails with a key-level diff and steps 1–3 are clean: this is the only path that legitimately surfaces a canonical-question. Even then, the response is not "write iOS values into canonical." It is: stop, name the keys that diverged, determine whether the canonical or the generated side reflects the intended design (a source-level review against the design intent, the Figma source of truth if relevant, and the version history of those keys), and make an intentional, reviewed edit to the canonical package — followed by regeneration, not the other way around.
  - All four checks clean: the timestamps are not evidence of a canonical defect. No canonical change. Document the finding in the pilot log so the next regeneration re-verifies the same baseline.

What to tell the engineer proposing the script

  - The script inverts the contract. It reads from a downstream artifact and writes to the upstream source.
  - "The generated file is newer" is not a source-level reason to change canonical; it is exactly the kind of signal the drift check is designed to surface and route to the generator side.
  - The correct remediation for any perceived staleness is regenerate-from-canonical, not overwrite-canonical-from-generated.
  - If, after the four checks, there is a real canonical defect to address, the change goes in as a reviewed edit to the versioned machine-readable package, with a per-key rationale, and the regenerated outputs follow.

Given what you've described (slow drain, stopper works, no odor, no gurgling elsewhere, no backups, no cabinet leak, visible hair and residue at the stopper), the picture is consistent with localized hair and soap accumulation right at the stopper, not a main line or trap problem. That is renter-fixable with mechanical removal and mild, non-chemical flushing.

Cleaning sequence (lowest-risk first)

Step 1 — Remove and clean the stopper
- Lift the stopper in the normal way and look at how it sits in the drain opening.
- Many pop-up stoppers unscrew counterclockwise by hand once lifted, or release from the pivot rod under the sink. If anything resists, stop — that is a stop sign, not a reason to force it.
- Bag and discard the hair and residue. Wipe the stopper with a paper towel and a small amount of dish soap.
- Shine a flashlight into the open drain. If you can see hair at the mouth, pull it out with a gloved finger or needle-nose pliers. Do not push anything down.

Step 2 — Mechanical pull just below the stopper
- Use a plastic barbed drain tool (Zip-It style) or a straightened wire with a small bent tip. Insert slowly 2–4 inches, twist gently, pull straight back out. Repeat 2–3 times.
- Wipe the tool between passes. The goal is to snag hair sitting just below the opening, not to chase a deep clog.
- Stop if the tool meets firm resistance, will not withdraw easily, or feels like it is catching on something other than hair.

Step 3 — Hot water and dish soap flush
- Plug the drain, fill the basin partway with the hottest tap water, add a small squeeze of dish soap, then release the stopper so the full volume goes through at once. This carries loosened residue down without chemicals.

Step 4 — Optional mild flush (only if Steps 1–3 did not restore full flow)
- 1/2 cup baking soda down the drain, let sit 10–15 minutes, then 1 cup white vinegar. After the fizz subsides, flush with a kettle of hot (not boiling) water.
- Skip this step if the drain is already emptying promptly.

Step 5 — Verify
- Run the tap at a normal flow for a full minute. The basin should empty continuously without standing water. If the basin still empties in roughly 90 seconds or longer, repeat Step 2 once. If it is still slow after that, escalate.

Do not do
- Chemical drain cleaner (corrosive to pipes and finishes, and most leases require professional clearing)
- Disassemble the P-trap or any plumbing under the sink (renter boundary without approval)
- Plunge the sink (rarely effective on pop-up stoppers, and it can splash contaminated water)
- Pour boiling water into the basin or onto PVC components

Stop and contact management if any of the following appears
- The drain stops clearing at all, or water rises instead of falling
- A sewage odor develops from the sink or any other drain
- The tub, shower, or toilet starts gurgling, slow-draining, or backing up
- Water appears under the sink cabinet, around the drain flange, or at the wall
- The stopper mechanism is stuck, stripped, or shows visible corrosion when you try to remove it
- The clog returns within a few days despite the cleaning sequence
- You see any damaged, displaced, or corroded component you did not intend to disturb

If you want, tell me which style of stopper you have (lift-and-turn, push-pull, toe-touch, or a visible rod behind the faucet) and I can give you the exact removal motion for it before you start.

Smallest non-destructive sequence. Each step changes exactly one variable. Stop as soon as the image is restored.

0. Pre-check (2 seconds, no moves)
   Look at the monitor's OSD / input indicator. After the direct-HDMI test, the monitor may have auto-switched inputs and is now listening on HDMI-1 while the dock is outputting on HDMI-2 or DisplayPort.
   - If the dock's output is on a different input than the one selected, select the right input.
   - If image appears, you were done before you started. Stop.

1. Identify what the OS sees (~30 seconds, no moves)
   Settings → System → Display.
   - External monitor listed → OS sees the dock/display but is not drawing on it (output/format or downstream issue).
   - External monitor not listed → OS has lost the display topology entirely (stakeholder-level handshake failure, or upstream cable/port disconnected at the OS level).

2. Reset the graphics stack (~10 seconds, no moves)
   Press Win+Ctrl+Shift+B. Screen flashes once. Wait 5 seconds.
   - Image restored → confirmed stale graphics-stack state from wake. Handshake issue. Done.
   - No change → continue.

3. Cycle the projection mode (~30 seconds, no moves)
   Press Win+P, then Enter, stepping through PC screen only / Duplicate / Extend / Second screen only. Pause 2–3 seconds on each. Watch the external monitor.
   - "Second screen only" lights it up → stale projection-mode state after wake. Still a handshake issue. Done.
   - No change on any mode → continue.

4. Substitute the USB-C upstream cable (one physical move)
   Swap the dock's USB-C cable for a known-good USB-C cable that is confirmed to support DisplayPort alt mode (same model, or one previously used for video). Reconnect, give ~10 seconds to enumerate, check display.
   - Image restored → the original cable's high-speed pairs are degraded even though its power and USB data lines work. Confirmed cable problem. Done.
   - No change → cable is exonerated; fault is downstream of the cable.

5. Move the video load to a different path (one physical move)
   Pick exactly one:
   - Plug the monitor into the dock's other video output (HDMI-out vs DP-out, second USB-C downstream, etc.) with a known-good display cable, OR
   - Move the dock's USB-C upstream cable to the laptop's other USB-C / Thunderbolt port (if one supports DP alt mode).
   - Image restored on the alternate path → confirmed dock video-path issue on the original path (specific output or specific upstream port). Done.
   - Still no image → the dock's video pipeline itself has failed, independent of output and upstream port. Stop diagnostic; next step is hardware-side.

6. Optional last step (only if 1–5 inconclusive) — cold boot instead of wake
   Shut down, reconnect dock, boot cold. Wait for full login.
   - Image present after cold boot → dock has a wake-from-sleep firmware bug. Workaround: shut down rather than sleep when using the dock; escalate with the wake-vs-cold-boot evidence.
   - Still no image → hardware fault inside the dock. Escalate.

Stop conditions:

  - Stop at the first step that restores the image. Record what fixed it. Do not keep going "to be thorough" — additional steps re-introduce variables and obscure the cause.
  - After Step 5 fails, the diagnostic has isolated the fault to the dock itself. The next action is a hardware ticket (RMA or IT), not more laptop-side testing.
  - Do not modify BitLocker, MDM, or any device-management policy. None of the above steps touch security settings. If a future step would (for example, reinstalling a display driver through a managed channel), stop and confirm the policy path first.
  - Do not rapidly unplug/replug the dock during a single fault window without rebooting the laptop between attempts. The dock can enter a half-state that only a host reset clears, and rapid reconnects will mask that.

  - It does not prove the laptop's USB-C port is bad. Step 5 narrows it, but a true port-isolation needs a second USB-C host (another computer, or a USB-C video adapter plugged directly into the laptop's port, bypassing the dock). The signal shape — one tenant at 7/8 waiting, p99 queue-wait 14× higher while accepted points, dispatch errors, and the other tenants are all clean — is consistent with this tenant's queue draining slower than its arrival rate. Given the runbook invariants (4 active/pod, 2 active/tenant, 8 waiting/tenant, work-conserving dispatch, randomized 1–3s Retry-After), and the 1/29 cancellation-regression fixture you already validated (500 empty + 1 nonempty; nonempty served next eligible turn), only one of three things matches this signature. Two of them are not server changes.

Three hypotheses, ordered by how often this exact pattern is one of them:

  1. Client hold-open (most common cause of this signature). The tenant's 2 active slots are occupied by requests the server has finished dispatching but the client hasn't finished reading or acknowledging. Decompression can't free up, the 7 waiting can't be promoted, p99 queue-wait climbs while dispatch errors stay clean (nothing is actually failing server-side) and accepted-point accounting stays clean (no lost work). Server change does not fix this — the bottleneck is upstream of dispatch.

  2. Per-tenant active cap doing its job under a rate spike. 2 active + 7 waiting = the tenant is at its cap and the cap is enforcing. p99 queue-wait is set by how fast this tenant's own active requests finish. If they finish normally, queue-wait is sub-second; if they're slow, the cause is upstream of the scheduler, not the scheduler itself. Not a defect, not a server change.

  3. Scheduler fairness failure (least common, and your "I don't see evidence empty tenants are sticking in the ring" already weakens it). Dispatcher ring pointer or empty-tenant skipping is broken, and the affected tenant is being passed over despite a non-empty queue and decompression slots available. Would produce this signature, but the 1/29 fixture was designed to surface exactly this, and your read of the ring is consistent with (3) not being the cause — not conclusive, but pointing away.

Smallest discriminating evidence set, all on the affected tenant's pod for the current 5-minute window, no server change yet:

A. Per-request trace (this is the dispositive check). For each of the 2 active requests: capture `dispatch_start` → `dispatch_complete` (server-side work), `dispatch_complete` → `response_sent` (server write), and `response_sent` → either `response_acked` or last `socket_recv_window_update` (client read), plus the TCP socket state (ESTABLISHED / half-closed / RST) and `bytes_sent` vs `bytes_acked` if the kernel exposes them. If `dispatch_complete → response_sent` is fast but the gap to client ACK is large or absent and the socket is still ESTABLISHED with the receive window full, that confirms (1). If `dispatch_start → dispatch_complete` itself is long, that's server-side slow — a different investigation, neither (1) nor (3). For each of the 7 waiting: `enqueue_time`, `current_age_seconds`, and `dispatch_decision_count` (how many times the dispatcher passed over each entry).

B. Dispatch-decision log for the pod (the fairness check). Last 100 `dispatch_decision` events on this pod. For each, classify the skip of the affected tenant as: (i) skipped because the tenant's 2-active cap was full — that's expected, not a fairness defect; (ii) skipped because the ring pointer reached it but no decompression slot was available elsewhere on the pod — also expected; (iii) skipped because the pointer advanced past the tenant while its queue was non-empty and a slot was free — that's (3), and is the only outcome that justifies a server change. The 1/29 fixture's invariant is the reference: when cancellation empties a tenant.queue, the tenant is removed from the active ring before dispatch resumes.

C. Client deadline / timeout configuration (the upstream-cause check). Read timeout on the tenant SDK side (commonly 5–30s, sometimes 60s+ on long-poll or streaming configs), overall request timeout, and whether the client reuses persistent connections across the 2 active sockets. If the client's read deadline materially exceeds the server's decompression budget, the server cannot free the active slot even though the work is done — and that produces exactly this signature. (1) confirmed, configuration-driven; no server change.

D. Queue-age distribution on the 7 waiting (the rotation check). Are they the same set aging in place, or rotating (some served, new arrivals replacing)? Same set aging = dispatcher not draining at all = (1) or (3). Rotating = dispatcher is draining but rate of drain < rate of arrival = (2), head-of-line blocking behind the tenant's own 2-active cap. A stable per-request age list across two consecutive samples is the simplest visual discriminator.

Decision gate before any ingest-edge change:

  - (1) confirmed → no server change. The fix lives in the tenant's SDK read-timeout / socket-reuse config. ingest-edge cap and dispatch stay as-is.
  - (2) confirmed → cap is working as designed. No defect, no change, unless product revisits the 2-active-per-tenant policy, which is a separate decision with its own authorization.
  - (3) confirmed → server change is justified, but only with: the specific dispatch-decision events, a reproducer trace, the pod build/sha, and a tested rollback. The waiting cap stays at 8.

Until one of those three is confirmed by A–D, the default is the precedent already on record: queue-side behavior is preserved, the 8-waiting cap and 2/4 active limits are unchanged, and no scheduling or limit change is authorized by current evidence.

Short answer: the old in-city address on the 1099 does not affect your New York residency allocation, and it does not require an issuer correction before you file.

Why residency is unaffected
- 1099s and W-2s are federal information returns. The address printed on them is the issuer's mailing/contact address on file, not a residency declaration. The IRS and NY tax administration match income to your TIN, not to the address line on each form.
- New York City residency is binary at the city level: you are either a full-year NYC resident or not. Moving from Park Slope to South Slope in late September is a within-NYC move. You were physically present in NYC every day of the year, so you are a full-year NYC resident, and the full-year NYC resident tax rate applies. There is no NYC/NYS split to allocate and no part-year allocation triggered.
- Even if the 1099 address were treated as a residency signal, Park Slope is in NYC, so the result would be identical: full-year NYC resident.

Why no issuer correction is required before filing
- The substantive tax data on the 1099 is correct: name, TIN, payer, income, and withholding. Those are the fields the IRS and NY actually use.
- The address is administrative. A mismatch between the 1099 address and the address on your return (South Slope, matching the corrected W-2) is a verification item, not a substantive error. You file the return with your current correct address; the 1099's reported income and withholding still flow in unchanged.
- You can request a corrected 1099 from the issuer for tidy records if you want, but it is optional and not a prerequisite to filing.

Practical notes (proportionate)
- Worth flagging the address mismatch to your tax preparer so they aren't surprised when software cross-checks W-2/1099 addresses against the return.
- If the IRS later sends an identity-verification letter referencing the Park Slope address, it's routine and resolved by confirming your current address and TIN — not by reissuing the 1099.

The current picture is consistent with mild post-bath irritation on the outer ear flap, and with no debris, discharge, odor, swelling, bleeding, foreign object, or canal findings, plus normal behavior, home monitoring for a defined window is reasonable. The plan below is low-risk only — it does not replace an otoscopic exam if any of the listed signs appear.

SAFE HOME CARE

Do
  - If water is the suspected cause, gently dry the visible outer ear and the part of the canal opening you can see with a soft, dry cloth or cotton ball. Do not probe.
  - Let Kibo shake his head normally; that is a clearance mechanism, not a problem.
  - Keep the routine normal — appetite, walks, settling, behavior. Behavior normality is one of the more useful negative signals here.

Do NOT
  - Insert Q-tips, swabs, fingers, or any object into the ear canal, even gently. Probing can push material deeper or damage the canal lining.
  - Apply over-the-counter ear cleaners, hydrogen peroxide, alcohol, vinegar mixes, essential oils, or human ear products without veterinary direction. Pre-emptive cleaning on a non-inflamed ear is itself an irritant.
  - Apply any topical ointment, hydrocortisone, or antibiotic without vet direction.
  - Re-bathe or allow water into that ear for the next 48–72 hours if possible.

MONITORING WINDOW

Actively observe for 48–72 hours from now, with quick checks at rest, walks, meals, evening, and the next morning:
  - Pink area: unchanged, fading, or growing?
  - Scratching/shaking frequency: same, less, or more?
  - Any new discharge, odor, swelling, or handling sensitivity?

A small, non-progressing pink area on the outer flap alone is consistent with mild local irritation. Improvement or stable findings across 48–72 hours is reassuring.

CALL THE REGULAR CLINIC (routine, non-urgent) IF:
  - Scratching or head-shaking persists or increases over the next 48–72 hours, even without other findings.
  - The pink area enlarges, becomes more vivid red, or develops a scab, crust, or pimple-like bump.
  - Any new debris or discharge appears — waxy brown, black "coffee-ground," yellow, green, or bloody.
  - A new odor develops from the ear.
  - Mild discomfort or flinching on gentle handling of the ear or the ear base.
  - The pink area is not clearly improved by ~Tuesday morning (~72 hours from now).

URGENT / SAME-DAY VISIT IF:
  - Visible swelling of the ear flap itself (possible aural hematoma — often warm, soft or firm, fluid-filled swelling on the pinna).
  - Bleeding from the canal or flap.
  - Sudden, clear pain response when the ear is touched or the head is moved.
  - Head tilt (ear held lower, or head consistently angled to one side).
  - Balance change, stumbling, circling, or rapid eye movement (nystagmus). These suggest middle/inner ear involvement and warrant prompt evaluation.
  - Repeated strong head-shaking that does not settle.
  - Marked lethargy, appetite loss, or feverish behavior alongside any of the above.

WHAT THIS PLAN DOES NOT REPLACE
An otoscopic exam and cytology — the vet looking down the canal and swabbing any discharge — is the only way to distinguish simple irritation from early otitis externa or a missed foreign body. The plan above is appropriate only because current findings are minimal and behavior is normal. Early ear issues are much easier to treat than late ones, so the threshold for contacting the clinic is low: if anything in the lists above appears, do not wait for it to worsen.

Classification: counter-reset artifact, not real accounting loss.

Mechanism
- Edge-gateway's monotonic cumulative counter is unaffected by a collector restart, so its panel shows the full window.
- The restarted collector's cumulative receipt counter resets at 4:21 PM, so its panel shows only receipts accumulated after restart.
- A panel comparing the two across the restart shows the pre-restart accumulated value as an apparent "delta." That is the 14,208.
- This is the same artifact pattern already documented: pre-restart cumulative ~18,442, post-restart ~37, no real loss.

Why the evidence rules out real loss
- Pre-restart split: forwarding = receipts (matches).
- Post-restart split: forwarding = receipts (matches).
- No rejected-point change means nothing was filtered.
- No forwarding loop means nothing was duplicated or rebroadcast.
- No collector error means no mid-stream failure.
- No customer-visible gap means users saw continuous delivery.
- All four "real-loss" indicators are absent; only the cumulative-reset signature is present.

Dashboard annotation (proposed)
"Counter-reset artifact: collector restart at 2025-02-10 16:21 ET reset the cumulative receipt counter inside the panel window. The 14,208-delta equals the collector's pre-restart accumulated value, not data loss. Pre-restart and post-restart sub-intervals each reconcile (forwarding = receipts). No rejected-point change, no forwarding loop, no collector error, no customer-visible gap. Scope: this 5-minute panel only."

Verification still required before closing
1. Cumulative-match check (the smoking gun). Pull the restarted collector's cumulative receipt value in the instant before 4:21 PM. It should equal, or sit within tight drift of, 14,208. If it does, the "delta" is fully accounted for by the reset and no data is unaccounted.
2. Rate-based continuity. A `rate(receipts[5m])` or equivalent derivative panel for the same metric should remain flat across 4:21 PM. Rate panels are immune to cumulative resets; flat rate confirms traffic was continuous.
3. Per-collector isolation. Confirm the 14,208 is fully attributable to the one restarted collector. No other collector's receipts should be missing from the comparison.
4. Re-confirm clean indicators (already reported by Alex): rejected-point counter flat, no forwarding loop, no collector error in window, no customer-visible gap or alert.

- Add a restart-time annotation/filter on the panel.
- For dashboards that must use cumulative counters, document the restart-aware reconciliation procedure.
