Two hypotheses to distinguish, plus one to keep in reserve:

  H1 retention — route-table snapshot objects accumulate in some long-lived reference path during replay; the live set grows.
  H2 allocation pressure — snapshot objects are short-lived but allocation rate outruns minor-GC reclamation during replay; live set is roughly stable, RSS is elevated because young-gen plus uncollected garbage dominates.
  H3 profiler-misdirection — the heap allocation profile points at snapshot serialization but the actual retention lives in a different code path the same call touches. Hold in reserve; the comparison below either confirms H1/H2 cleanly or motivates a heap dump to test H3.

SMALLEST BOUNDED STAGING COMPARISON

  Single staging replay, single pod, single version. Reuse the existing 25-minute replay fixture and the flat route count. No config changes, no deploys, no new traffic, no feature flag, no code change. The whole experiment is read-only observability on a replay that is already isolated to staging.

  Two parallel continuous captures run side-by-side during the same replay window:

    Capture 1 — live-set / retention signal. Continuous pprof heap (inuse_space) sampled every 10 seconds for 40 minutes: 5 min pre-roll, 25 min replay, 10 min cooldown. inuse_space is what GC has not yet collected. If the snapshot-class trend rises during replay and stays elevated at cooldown end, retention. If it returns to the pre-roll level within the cooldown window, pressure.

    Capture 2 — allocation-rate / pressure signal. Continuous pprof alloc_space sampled every 10 seconds over the same 40 minutes. alloc_space is bytes allocated per sample window. If alloc rate spikes during replay but inuse stays flat, that is pure pressure. If both spike, both are happening and the magnitudes separate them.

  Why one replay, not two. Toggling the snapshot path (feature flag or staging-only build) would isolate the snapshot hypothesis cleanly, but it requires either a code/config change or a separate staging-window authorization. That expands scope beyond observability. The dual-capture design answers the original question (retention vs pressure, and at what magnitude) using only read-only measurements on the replay already in motion. The follow-up if H1 is confirmed is a heap dump at peak, which is still read-only.

SET OF MEASUREMENTS

  Pair the two continuous captures with four fixed-timestamp ground-truth snapshots:

    T0 — 5 min before replay starts (baseline)
    T1 — replay minute 25 (peak)
    T2 — replay stop + 0 min
    T3 — replay stop + 10 min (after the observed 6-min cooldown has elapsed; this is the window where the 1.9 GiB residual lives or does not)

  At each timestamp, capture:

    RSS — container metric or /proc/<pid>/status. This is what Wes actually saw climb 1.8 → 2.6 GiB; it must stay in the record even though we are breaking it down below.
    jcmd <pid> GC.heap_info — heap used, old-gen used, young-gen used, metaspace. Breaks RSS into its JVM components.
    jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram | grep -i <snapshot-class> — live count and live bytes of the snapshot class and its referenced child classes. Direct answer to the snapshot-hypothesis question.
    jstat -gc <pid> 1000 60 — sixty one-second samples around the timestamp. Captures young-gen occupancy trend and minor-GC frequency, which is where H2 shows up.

  From the continuous captures, plot two lines per timestamp window:

    inuse_space for the snapshot class at T0, T1, T2, T3 — and the delta between T3 and T0.
    alloc_space rate (bytes/sec) at the same four points — and the delta between T1 and T0/T3.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA

  H1 retention supported if, at T3 vs T0:
    inuse_space for the snapshot class is elevated by an amount consistent with the 0.8 GiB climb (or a meaningful fraction of it);
    old-gen used is elevated at T3 vs T0 (objects survived minor GC);
    RSS is elevated at T3 vs T0 (the observed 1.9 vs 1.8 GiB residual, if repeatable, lives here);
    GC.class_histogram shows N times more live snapshot instances at T3 than at T0.

  H2 pressure supported if, at T3 vs T0:
    inuse_space returns to within sampling noise of T0;
    old-gen used returns to within sampling noise of T0;
    RSS returns to within sampling noise of T0;
    alloc_space rate at T1 is materially above the T0/T3 baseline;
    young-gen occupancy and minor-GC frequency spike at T1 and normalize by T3.

  Mixed (partial retention, partial pressure) supported if:
    inuse partially returns (e.g., the 100 MiB residual the original observation hints at);
    old-gen residual matches the inuse residual;
    the result that would justify a follow-up heap dump at T1 to identify the residual reference path.

STOP CONDITIONS

  Bounded read-only staging observability, but the same comparison discipline applies:

    If pprof overhead exceeds budget (heap profiling typically 1-3 percent CPU; alloc_space more), throttle sample interval from 10s to 30s and continue — do not abandon the comparison.
    If staging replay crashes during measurement, abort and reopen under a fresh staging-only window. Do not retry against production.
    The four jcmd snapshots are blocking on the JVM for sub-second each; safe to repeat.
    No production traffic, no config push, no deploy, no route change. This stays inside Wes's existing non-production practical-backup scope; no owner-map or production change implied.

INPUTS WES WOULD NEED TO CONFIRM BEFORE STARTING

    The exact class name (or fully-qualified symbol) for "route-table snapshot serialization" so GC.class_histogram greps target the right class. The allocation profile usually surfaces the call site; the histogram needs a class.
    Continuous pprof overhead budget approval for the 40-minute window. If that is a problem, fall back to the four-timestamp jcmd snapshots only, which cost almost nothing and still answer H1 vs H2 — just with coarser time resolution.
    Confirm T0 capture happens before any replay traffic so the comparison is clean.

  None of these reopen the experiment. They are inputs to running it once.

First-use inspection (before leaving the apartment)

  Hardware
    - Clasp closes fully with an audible/spring-confirmed snap; reopen and close three times.
    - Trigger guard returns flush — no sticky or half-released position.
    - Gate is centered when closed, no sideways drift or wobble.

  Webbing & handle
    - Run the full length through your fingers — no cuts, abrasion, pulled stitches, or soft spots.
    - Handle stitching is even and tight; no loose thread at the load-bearing seam.
    - Tail/end stop is sealed; no frayed loose strands.

  Harness fit (re-check on first wear with the new leash)
    - Two-finger rule at the chest and neck straps — snug, not tight.
    - Front-clip D-ring sits at the breastbone centerline; chest plate sits flat, not twisted.
    - Tug test: gentle forward pressure, harness should not ride up toward the throat or shift sideways.
    - Quick back-out check in the hallway: gentle rearward pressure; straps stay put, no slack for a shoulder to pop out.

Safe handling near the Prospect Park entrances

  No-wraps rule
    - Loop only goes over your thumb, like a grocery-bag carry.
    - Never around the wrist, fingers, or palm — a sudden lunge can sprain or break a finger before you can release.
    - If you need a shorter hold, gather slack in your free hand and let it run; do not coil it.

  Treat the 6 ft as a maximum, not a working distance
    - Near entrances, bike/scooter conflicts, curb cuts, crosswalks, and dog clusters, gather the leash to roughly 2–3 ft.
    - At open, low-traffic stretches, let it lengthen — but never let it go fully taut; a tight line transmits every startle as a yank both ways.
    - Keep your hand at your hip, not above it; an elevated hand pulls Kibo's head up and shifts the harness off-axis.

  Position and footing
    - Stand on the building/curb side of Kibo at entrances; you are the barrier between Kibo and the street side.
    - Wait for bikes and scooters to pass before stepping off the curb; do not startle Kibo into the roadway.

    - Clasp fails to close fully, gate drifts, or trigger sticks.
    - New webbing wear, pulled stitch, or soft spot on the leash.
    - Kibo freezes, refuses treats, lip-licks, whale-eyes, or shakes — retreat to a quieter block as before.

Cleanup sequence — tomato sauce jar break, kitchen tile + cabinet toe-kick

Kibo stays behind the closed door for the entire sequence plus the verification pass. Re-entry is a separate gated step at the end.

Phase 0 — PPE and supplies (before you touch the tile)
- Closed-toe shoes. Socks alone are not acceptable; a shard through a sock is a common cut pattern.
- Nitrile or rubber kitchen gloves if you have them; otherwise dry, intact hands are fine for the wet-pass steps.
- Supplies within reach before you start:
  - Sturdy paper towels (folded into pads for rigidity) and a damp cloth
  - A roll of painter's tape or masking tape (low-tack is fine, duct tape works but is messier)
  - A trash bag, ideally inside a small cardboard box or rigid bowl so shards cannot pierce the bag from below
  - A phone flashlight or a strong flashlight
  - Optional: a slice of plain soft bread, or a few sheets of plain white paper towel (for the fine-shard pass)
  - Optional: a chopstick, plastic knife, or wooden skewer for the toe-kick gap

Phase 1 — Sauce first, glass second (visible area on open tile)
- Wipe up the bulk of the sauce with dry paper towels before any wet wipe. Sauce dries quickly on tile and becomes a film that hides shards; removing it now exposes the field.
- Place sauce-only paper towels straight into the trash bag.
- Then do a single damp-cloth pass over the same area to lift the remaining sauce film. This is the most important visual-recovery step — once the film is gone, the residual shards glint under raking light.
- Discard the damp cloth into the bag; do not reuse it on anything else.

Phase 2 — Visible shards on open tile
- Continue with the tongs, or with folded paper-towel pads (the pad lets you pinch a shard without fingers touching it).
- Drop each piece directly into the rigid container/bagged box, not loose into a bag.
- Do not sweep yet. Brooms launch fine shards and the sauce residue still on the floor will smear them rather than collect them.
- If a vacuum is your only option, use a hose-attachment shop vac or a bagged canister vacuum, then immediately remove and bag the vacuum bag or empty the canister into a sealed bag. Do not use a bagless cyclonic vacuum on fine wet glass.

Phase 3 — Fine shards near and inside the cabinet toe-kick
The toe-kick is a recessed gap; shards sit in the shadow where the eye misses them. Treat this area as the highest-risk spot in the kitchen.
- Rake-light scan: hold the flashlight nearly flat against the floor, aimed across the toe-kick line from the side, not from above. Fine glass sparkles only at a low angle. Do this before touching anything in the gap.
- Pick out what you can see with folded tape (sticky-side-out loop around two fingers, or a strip pressed onto a shard and lifted). Drop straight into the rigid container.
- For shards you can see but not reach: wrap a damp paper towel around the tip of a chopstick or plastic knife and use it as a swab to pull the shard out. The dampness holds the shard to the towel.
- For shards sitting inside the recess you cannot see: press a small piece of soft bread (or a folded damp paper towel) firmly against the toe-kick floor and the front lip, then lift. Repeat with a fresh surface until the bread/towel comes up clean. The bread trick is reliable for shards under a couple of millimeters.
- Finish the toe-kick line with one more tape pass along the front lip where the recess meets the tile — shards get caught on that seam and are easy to miss.

Phase 4 — Final pass on the open tile around the spill
- Slow raking-light walk-through of the original spill footprint, plus a 2–3 ft perimeter (sauce splashes travel).
- One more folded-tape swipe across the perimeter, especially along the cabinet base and any grout lines. Grout lines hold tiny shards that a cloth misses.

Phase 5 — Verification before Kibo re-enters
Three independent checks. Re-entry is gated on all three passing.

5a. Visual at low angle
- Darken the kitchen (close blinds, kill overhead lights) and sweep the flashlight at floor level across the original spill area, the toe-kick line, and the perimeter. Anything that glints is a missed shard. Repeat until a full sweep produces no new sparkles.

5b. Tactile sweep
- Press a clean, lightly damp white paper towel flat across the tile in the spill area and drag it slowly toward you. Lift and inspect under light. Any shard will be visible against the white and may have made a tiny scratch. Repeat with a fresh sheet across the toe-kick face.
- If the towel comes up with even one shard, repeat Phase 3 and 4 on that spot before continuing.

5c. Foot-path check
- Wipe your shoes (or whatever you wore during cleanup) with a damp paper towel. Shards walk out of the spill area on soles; if they did, they'll re-deposit on the tile later and on Kibo's paws now.
- Wipe the path from the spill to the door you'll use to release Kibo.

Stop conditions — do not let Kibo into the kitchen if any of these are true
- You have not done all three verification checks.
- The damp-towel sweep picked up any shard, no matter how small, on its first pass.
- You have not yet cleared the toe-kick recess (the gap itself, not just the tile in front of it).
- Any sauce residue remains on the floor — dried film hides shards from a casual glance.
- Your shoes, the trash bag path, or the path to Kibo's door still has visible wetness from the spill.

Re-entry
- Open Kibo's door and watch his first 4–5 steps into the kitchen. Glass cuts on paw pads often show as a sudden limp, a lifted paw, or stopping to lick a foot. If you see any of those, stop him, re-check the floor, and contact the vet.
- Keep him out of the kitchen while you take the trash bag and any vacuum bag straight out of the kitchen in one trip; do not stage them in a hallway he'll later walk through.

Disposal
- Double-bag the rigid container or the original bag, seal it, and put it in an outside trash bin, not an indoor one. Fine shards in a kitchen trash bag are a repeat-hazard for whoever next takes the garbage out.

Three concrete risk areas Anya can raise inside her own lane. Framed as questions the proposal must answer, not as Alex's review.

DRIFT
- The automated drift check is the existing safety net. If a platform-local override is allowed for up to 7 days, the check either fires daily against an approved state (operators learn to dismiss drift alerts) or has to be suppressed for the overridden token (operators learn to ignore gaps). Either outcome erodes the signal the canonical workflow was built on.
- During the window, two platforms can each carry a different "temporary" value for the same token. The current strength — one canonical truth, N generated outputs — is gone for every active override, and the reconciliation step has to pick a winner without a defined rule.
- Reconciliation direction is unspecified. Either the platform's value gets pushed upstream (canonical bends to a platform workaround) or the regenerated value overwrites the local one (the workaround that may have been load-bearing disappears). The proposal needs to say which, who decides, and what happens if canonical rejects the override.
- A generated artifact rebuilt during the window can silently overwrite the override, or freezing regeneration blocks other tokens from flowing. Either side effect needs an explicit answer.

ROLLBACK
- "Up to 7 days" is a calendar deadline, not a CI/build/release gate. Nothing in the system prevents a 7-day override from becoming a 30-day or 90-day override; the expiry is process-tracked, not enforced.
- By the time reconciliation runs, the platform has usually shipped the overridden value to users. Rolling back then is no longer a token revert — it's a separate platform release on its own schedule.
- If reconciliation fails (canonical rejects the override, the platform team disagrees, the underlying problem isn't fixed), there is no described fallback state. The platform is left holding a value that isn't canonical and isn't approved.

AUDITABILITY
- There is no single registry of active overrides. A designer or release manager cannot currently answer "what tokens are divergent across platforms right now?" — exactly the question the canonical workflow made answerable. The proposal needs that registry, in the canonical package's review trail, not scattered across per-platform PR comments.
- Git history is not durable audit: rebases, force-pushes, squash-merge, and engineer turnover all erode it. "The engineer temporarily changed token X for 6 days" has to land in the same review record that Anya's approvals live in.
- The drift check has to rerun after reconciliation and confirm the divergence actually closed. Without that step, "reconciled" can mask an active gap the original check didn't surface.
- The deadline needs an enforced stop condition: build fails, merge blocked, override auto-expires, or on-call paged. Without one, "temporary" means "until someone remembers," and that someone is usually whoever is on call when the next incident lands.

One cross-cutting note Anya already has context on and can decide whether to flag herself: this proposal is structurally similar to the Figma-only color change and the Android-only suffix pattern that were already resolved inside the canonical package without platform-specific exceptions. If the engineer is asking for it now, the proposal should explain what changed about the canonical workflow that makes the same shape of exception acceptable this time.

Classification: allocation-pressure optimization, not a leak fix.

Discriminating evidence in the Feb 17 comparison:

    - Identical replay input controlled the workload, isolating the variable to the serialization toggle.
    - Forced post-replay GCs returned resident memory to 1.88 GiB — below the 2.0 GiB peak observed with serialization off. A leak would not be recoverable below the no-change baseline.
    - Retained heap drifted less than 2% from baseline across the run. A leak would show retained-heap drift proportional to the peak growth, not a near-zero delta.
    - Allocation flame graphs attributed the temporary growth to snapshot buffers, not to retained object paths.
    - No monotonic growth; peak then recovery on traffic stop.
    - No production effect.

This is the textbook signature of allocation pressure: working-set growth during the workload, full recovery after GC, near-zero retained-heap delta, attribution to transient buffers. None of the leak indicators (monotonic growth, retained-heap drift, GC non-recovery, retained-object attribution) are present.

Concretely, the Feb 13 staging replay (resident 1.8 to 2.6 GiB over 25 minutes, recovered to 1.9 within 6 minutes of replay stop) plus the Feb 17 controlled comparison together establish bounded warm-up behavior, not retention. The earlier 90-minute soak pattern (retained 420 to 910 MiB) is the leak-shaped comparison; the Feb 17 numbers are not on that trajectory.

Ticket scope for the metrics-router owner:

    Title: metrics-router snapshot-serialization allocation-pressure mitigation
    Type: small code change (toggle or buffer-budget bound) inside a single PR
    Owner: Alex primary, Wes backup
    Linked: Feb 13 staging replay record, Feb 17 bounded comparison record, existing metrics-router runbook, sibling runbook for the comparison methodology if separate

Evidence package to attach or reference:

    1. Identical replay input hash or fixture id for both arms.
    2. Off-arm peak (2.0 GiB) and on-arm peak (2.55 GiB) resident memory, same replay.
    3. On-arm post-replay GC trace showing 1.88 GiB recovery.
    4. Retained-heap delta vs baseline (under 2%) over the full comparison window.
    5. Allocation flame graph naming the snapshot buffer path as the source.
    6. Note that production was untouched during the comparison.
    7. Reference to the Feb 13 replay and the earlier 90-minute soak to show the comparison closes the warm-up-vs-leak ambiguity.

Pre-production acceptance criteria (must all be true before opening any owner-led window):

    - Sustained 90-minute steady-load soak with the change applied: retained heap delta vs baseline stays within +/-2%.
    - No monotonic resident-memory growth over the soak window; curve plateaus or recovers during the run.
    - Forced post-soak GC returns resident memory to within +/-2% of pre-soak baseline.
    - No new route-parity failures, dropped series, restart events, reload failures, or alert-source misclassifications during the soak.
    - p99 within the established threshold; no new alerts fire.
    - Allocation profile continues to attribute transient growth to snapshot buffers, not to any retained-object path.

In-window criteria during the owner-led rollout (per push):

    - Retired generations per pod stay at or below 4.
    - Cleanup pauses stay at or below 100 ms.
    - Full health set returns to baseline after each push (p99, heap, retired generations, route parity, dropped series, restarts, reloads).
    - Either threshold crossing stops the window immediately.

Post-rollout acceptance criteria (must all be true before declaring complete):

    - Sustained production observation across at least one full traffic-shape cycle with the change at 100%.
    - Retained heap drift vs pre-change baseline stays within +/-2%.
    - Peak resident memory does not exceed the pre-change baseline peak by more than the buffer headroom agreed in the ticket (suggest 5% as a starting bound, lock the exact number in the ticket).
    - No monotonic growth across the observation window.
    - Full health set clean across the observation window.
    - No alert regressions tied to the change.

Stop conditions and rollback triggers:

    - All existing triggers stay active: generation inconsistency, route-parity failure, dropped series, reload or restart failure, true user-visible regression.
    - New stop conditions specific to this change:
        * Retained heap drift greater than 2% from baseline during any window of the watch.
        * Forced post-window GC fails to return memory to within +/-2% of baseline.
        * Monotonic resident-memory growth observed over any 30-minute window.
        * Allocation profile attributes growth to a retained-object path rather than snapshot buffers.

Recovery push rule:

    - A stop permits exactly one fully observed recovery push, not a reopened multi-push window. Another window requires another fresh opening decision from Alex.

Explicit non-goals (so the ticket cannot drift):

    - Not a leak fix. Do not describe, title, or label it as one.
    - Not a broader memory-tuning change. Adjacent memory-limiter, cache-size, or queue-depth changes are out of scope.
    - Not a config-window policy change. The existing owner-led window rules and rollback triggers apply unchanged.
    - Not a justification for weakening the Friday-afternoon production-deploy rule or any other rollout guardrail.
    - Not a closing of the prior staged-enablement work on the SDK oversized-batch path or any other in-flight lane.
    - Scope is bounded to the snapshot-serialization path on the metrics-router; no cross-service implications.

Recommended first move: lock the pre-production acceptance numbers and the buffer headroom in the ticket body before opening any owner-led window, and link the Feb 13 and Feb 17 records as the controlled evidence that distinguishes this from the leak-shaped 90-minute soak pattern. The classification holds, and a tightly bounded ticket is the right vehicle.

Short answer: no. A producer with no `deployment.environment` value must not be coerced into publishing `deployment.environment=prod` on the strength of destination context. Destination context cannot invent a source value, so the contract treats missing input and unsupported input as two distinct states that must remain distinguishable downstream.

Correct producer behavior, by input class:

  1. Allowed input — `prod`, `staging`, `dev` (any mixed case).
     The producer sends the literal it actually has. The contract normalizes mixed case to the canonical lowercase form and attaches the result as `deployment.environment`. This is the only path that produces a `prod` label on a series. There is no other way to legitimately get `deployment.environment=prod` into the system.

  2. Missing input — producer has no environment value at all.
     The producer omits the label. The label key is simply not attached to the series. This is intentional in the contract: omission is the prescribed handling for missing input, and the resulting series is a valid series with one fewer label, not a series with an "unset," "missing," or "qa" label. A dashboard that renders absent keys locally as "unset" is a presentation artifact, not a fourth published value.

  3. Unsupported input — `qa`, `unknown`, malformed strings, arbitrary raw strings, anything that is not `prod`, `staging`, or `dev`.
     The producer must not publish these. The contract rejects them before publication, so there are zero resulting series. Rejection is the pre-publication disposition; it does not become a published fourth label value. Rejection counters track the probe, not a published state.

Why the release owner's proposal breaks the contract:

  - It asks the destination to infer a source value. The contract does not authorize that. Source-side environment context is what the label represents; destination-side "this is going to prod" is a separate fact and cannot substitute for the source value the producer has or lacks.
  - It would collapse two distinct states. Omission (missing source) and rejection (unsupported source) must remain distinguishable so the dashboard, rollup-service consumer, and rejection counters continue to behave correctly. A producer silently coercing to `prod` makes missing-input series look like legitimate production series and erases the rejection signal entirely.
  - It violates the cardinality bound. The contract caps published `deployment.environment` values at the three normalized ones, with a per-tenant ceiling of three distinct values and zero published `qa`/`unset`/unknown/malformed/arbitrary values. Inventing `prod` for a producer that did not assert it does not change the cardinality math, but it does corrupt provenance — the series would carry a label value that the source never asserted.
  - It masks a real instrumentation gap. A producer that knows it is running in production but has no environment value is missing source-side instrumentation. The correct fix is for that producer to attach `prod` from its own configuration (the deployment, the env var, the runtime context it already has), not for the pipeline to invent the value.

What the producer should actually do:

  - If the producer has `prod` in its source-side environment context, send `deployment.environment=prod`. Mixed case is fine; the contract normalizes it.
  - If the producer has no environment value, omit the label and ship the series without it.
  - If the producer has `qa` or some non-canonical string, do not publish it; either fix the source to emit one of the three allowed values, or stop sending the label.

Net rule for the release owner: destination context never writes the label. Only the source may assert it, and the only assertions the contract accepts are `prod`, `staging`, `dev`, or absent.

Symptom profile: shock-triggered cutoff, fully reproducible with body tap, no thermal/moisture signs, sealed case. That pattern is consistent with an internal solder joint, battery tab, or board-to-board connection opening under vibration — the kind of fault that does not heal on its own and tends to worsen with thermal cycling. Without opening the sealed pack, you can characterize the fault well enough to decide repair vs. retirement, but you will almost certainly not be able to fix it. The diagnostic below is ordered so each step either narrows the failure or rules out a confounding cause, and so you can stop at any point with a decision already in hand.

Non-destructive diagnostic sequence (no case opening, no bending or prying, no chemicals, no submersion)

  1. Visual external inspection, light off and on
     - Look at the lens, button, USB/charging port cover, and the case seam with the light on and off.
     - Watch for: any hairline crack around the lens or seam, fogging or condensation inside the lens (warm breath test — breathe on the cold lens, then look for interior mist that does not clear), a port cover that no longer seats, a button that sits high or rocks.
     - Decision point: any visible crack, fogging, or moisture inside means retire regardless of other findings — the sealed environment is compromised.

  2. Charging-port mechanical check (light unplugged, room temp)
     - With the cover open, inspect the port for bent or recessed pins, debris, or a loose feeling.
     - Plug the OEM cable in and gently wiggle in the vertical axis only — does the charge indicator flicker or drop out?
     - Decision point: wobbly port or wiggling drops the indicator means the charge path is intermittent, but this is not yet your cutoff cause (the cutoff is on the output side, not the input). Note it as a secondary issue; it does not explain what you saw on the road.

  3. Full charge–discharge–charge cycle on a known-good cable and charger
     - Charge to full per the indicator. Discharge on a steady medium mode until the light auto-dims or shuts off; record run time. Recharge to full.
     - Decision point: a battery that sags early, never reaches full indicator, gets noticeably warm on the case near one spot, or runs substantially shorter than its original spec points to a cell with high internal resistance. That cell can also voltage-sag under vibration-induced inrush and is not safe to leave on a bike at night.

  4. Mode and switch isolation
     - Cycle through every mode (steady, flash, eco, off). Confirm the cutoff is reproducible by tap in at least two different modes, including with the button untouched after the initial mode change.
     - Decision point: if the cutoff only happens immediately after pressing the button, suspect the switch. If it happens with the button untouched in any mode, the fault is downstream of the switch (joint, cell tab, or LED board) — which is what your road symptom already points to.

  5. Tap mapping (the most informative step)
     - Hold the light firmly in one hand on a soft surface (towel on a table). With a fingertip of the other hand, tap each region once: lens, body near LED, body near the button, body near the charging port, body near the mount base, the mount clip itself.
     - For each region, note: no effect, brief flicker only, or full cutoff.
     - Decision point: a cutoff that maps to the button area suggests the switch or its solder pads. A cutoff that maps to the LED end suggests the LED board or its interconnect. A cutoff that maps to the mount/base end suggests the cell-tab side or the main PCB-to-bus joint. Anywhere it cuts out, the unit has an internal mechanical fault and is not reliable.

  6. Thermal observation during a 10-minute steady run
     - Place the light on a non-flammable surface, room temp, steady-on mode. Every two minutes, hover your hand (do not touch) over each region and feel for warmth.
     - Decision point: any region that is distinctly warmer than the rest, or any warmth that increases with time on a region that should be cool (cell area), indicates either a high-resistance joint heating up or a cell with rising internal resistance. Either way, do not charge or run unattended. This alone is a retire signal.

  7. Controlled off-road vibration test, daytime, no traffic
     - Mount the light on the bike, ride a known rough surface (brick, cobble, rough asphalt seam) at low speed during daylight.
     - Reproduce the exact symptom you saw, then continue past it. Note: does the light recover on its own after the bump, or does it stay off until you power-cycle it? Does it come back at a lower mode? Does it flash a low-battery indicator after recovery?
     - Decision point: a light that stays off until power-cycled is not safe for night use under any circumstance. Even if it self-recovers, a road-induced cutoff in active traffic is a safety failure.

  8. Final ruling, with the light off and cool
     - Cross-check the findings from steps 1–7 against the criteria below.

Replacement or retirement criteria (any one is sufficient)

  - Visible case crack, lens crack, or fogging/moisture inside the sealed lens.
  - Any region of the case that runs distinctly warm during a 10-minute steady-on test, or any warmth that grows over time on the cell end.
  - Charge that does not reach full, or runtime materially shorter than original spec on a full charge.
  - Tap on the body reproduces a full cutoff (you already have this — that alone meets the bar).
  - Light stays off after a road bump and only returns after a manual power cycle.
  - Light self-recovers but flashes a low-battery indicator afterwards, even briefly.
  - Charging port is mechanically loose, pins are bent, or wiggle drops the charge indicator (separate fault, but it removes any safe path to a reliable charge).
  - Any swelling, odor, discoloration, hissing, or leakage (immediate retire; isolate from charger and other flammables).

A light that fails step 5 in any region, or step 7 with a stay-off-until-reset behavior, is not a candidate for repair without opening the sealed pack. It is a retire-and-replace. The case stays closed for two reasons that are independent of each other: (a) the battery is a sealed lithium cell whose casing is part of its safety design — prying it open risks cell puncture and thermal runaway, and (b) even if you opened it safely, the typical failure mode for this symptom is a cold solder joint or a broken board interconnect, which is a board-level rework, not a household fix.

What the diagnostic adds if everything else passes except the body-tap reproduction

  - You have confirmed the fault is shock-induced and reproducible without touching the button.
  - That is enough to retire the unit for night-riding duty. You may keep it as a daytime-only be-seen light (steady, low mode, short rides) until replacement arrives, provided it shows no warmth, holds a full charge, and never cuts out without a power cycle. The moment it cuts out on a bump and stays off, stop using it even in daytime.

A practical short version, if you want to skip the full sequence: do step 1 (look for cracks/fog), step 3 (charge/discharge/charge), step 5 (tap mapping), and step 6 (thermal). If tap mapping reproduces the cutoff anywhere on the body, or if any region runs warm, retire the light. If both are clean, the unit is probably still serviceable and step 7 will be the deciding test.

Your decision not to ride this light at night until it is repaired or replaced is the correct one given what is already known. The diagnostic above is for narrowing whether "repaired" is even a realistic option (it almost certainly is not for this sealed unit) versus proceeding straight to "replaced."

SECTION 1 — WHAT YOU'VE DONE RIGHT
  Shutting the equipment down through normal OS shutdown, then unplugging the UPS rather than silencing the alarm or opening the case, is the correct first move. You preserved evidence (date code 2018, symptoms, environmental state), avoided creating a new hazard path, and have not yet created a waste-handling problem because the old battery is still inside the unit.

SECTION 2 — IMMEDIATE SAFETY VERDICT FOR THE CURRENT STATE
  A "replace battery" chirp on a 2018-dated battery, with no swelling, odor, smoke, heat, leakage, discoloration, or cord damage, is consistent with normal end-of-life of a sealed lead-acid (SLA / VRLA) battery. SLA service life is typically 3–5 years; 7 years is past nominal end-of-life but not by itself an emergency. The unit may stay where it is, cool and dry, while you decide on replacement or disposal, provided none of the urgent signs in Section 6 appear. The wall receptacle being normal rules out an external cause; you have already ruled out the unit-side red flags you can see.

SECTION 3 — IDENTIFYING WHAT YOU ACTUALLY HAVE
  Before any work, you need three facts from the unit's rear or bottom label and the manual:
    a. Manufacturer + model number (e.g., APC Back-UPS Pro 1500, CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD, Tripp Lite OMNI1500LCDT, Eaton 5S, etc.). The label usually also lists the input/output VA rating and the input voltage.
    b. Battery type. Most consumer/SOHO UPS units from this era use sealed lead-acid (SLA / VRLA) — labeled "sealed lead-acid", "valve-regulated lead-acid", "VRLA", or by a chemistry like "AGM". A smaller and growing subset uses lithium-ion (Li-ion / LiFePO4), usually labeled as such on a separate battery sticker or in specs.
    c. Whether the unit is "user-replaceable" or "internally sealed". User-replaceable units have a dedicated battery access door (rear or bottom) held by one or two screws, and the manufacturer sells a replacement battery SKU for end-user swap. Internally sealed units have no service door — the case must be pried or unscrewed to reach the battery, and the manufacturer directs you to an authorized service center.
  Model + battery type + serviceability determines everything that follows. If you no longer have the manual, the manufacturer website's product page for the exact model lists the OEM replacement battery part number; the presence of that SKU at retail (battery manufacturers like RBC, CSB, Power-Sonic, or the UPS maker's own brand) is the strongest signal that the unit is user-replaceable.

SECTION 4 — USER-REPLACEABLE SEALED LEAD-ACID vs. INTERNALLY SEALED — HANDLING DIFFERENCE
  User-replaceable SLA:
    - Designed for end-user swap. Battery door opens without breaking warranty seals. Capacitor discharge risk exists but is small if you wait.
    - Replacement battery is a standard SLA part (commonly 12 V, capacities from 5 Ah to 18 Ah per brick, sometimes two in parallel). Match voltage exactly, capacity at or above original, and connector type (Faston F1/F2 tabs or Anderson connector).
    - Procedure in Section 7.
  Internally sealed (no service door) SLA:
    - Even though the chemistry is the same as above, the manufacturer did not design this for end-user access. Opening the case (a) breaks the warranty, (b) exposes internal capacitors that store mains-derived energy after the unit is unplugged and can deliver a shock if touched before discharge, and (c) may expose the main board to mechanical damage.
    - Recommended path: contact the manufacturer's support line or an authorized service center, or replace the whole UPS if the unit is older than the battery (often the case — a 2018-battery UPS with a 2018 battery is at end-of-life on both axes; the electronics may be near end-of-life too).
  Internally sealed lithium-ion (newer compact UPSes):
    - Do not open. Li-ion cells pose thermal-runaway, fire, and electrolyte-venting risk if punctured, shorted, or charged when damaged. They also retain a charge for months and cannot be safely discharged by shorting the terminals.
    - Service is manufacturer-only. Disposal path is Section 8.

SECTION 5 — SAFE STORAGE WHILE YOU DECIDE
  Whole UPS, unplugged:
    - Keep upright on a hard, non-combustible surface (shelf, concrete floor, metal table — not carpet, not on top of wood furniture, not near bedding).
    - Cool, dry, indoor. Avoid direct sun, radiators, and any temperature swings near freezing or above ~95°F.
    - Do not stack anything on top of the unit.
    - Do not place flammable material (paper, fabric, cardboard) on or against it.
    - The chirp will continue for some time after unplug because the unit can still self-test briefly on residual capacitor charge; this is not a hazard and will stop. If it persists more than a few hours, the battery is shorted internally and you should treat it as in Section 6.
  Removed SLA battery (only if you opened a user-replaceable unit to inspect — do not open otherwise):
    - Keep upright. Terminals up.
    - Place in a non-conductive container (cardboard box, original battery packaging, plastic bin). Do not use a metal tray.
    - Tape over the terminals with electrical tape to prevent accidental shorts during handling.
    - Do not let it sit discharged for weeks; SLA batteries sulfate permanently below ~12 V. If you must wait more than a couple of weeks before disposal or replacement, top it up with a small SLA float charger if you have one; otherwise, recycle it promptly.

SECTION 6 — SIGNS REQUIRING URGENT ISOLATION (read this once now and once before any future handling)
  Treat any one of these as a stop-the-line, evacuate-the-area, do-not-investigate-further event:
    - Case swelling, bulging, or any deformation of the UPS housing or of a removed battery
    - Heat when the unit is unplugged and has been idle (touch-test the case with the back of your hand; the whole unit, not just near the outlet)
    - Sulfurous / rotten-egg / sour-acid / burnt-plastic odor at any point
    - Any visible liquid, wetness, residue, or white/blue-green crust on the battery or near vents
    - Smoke, hissing, crackling, popping
    - Discoloration, charring, or melting of the case
    - Sparking when the unit is plugged in or unplugged
    - Bulging or deformed battery terminals, or a raised / domed battery top
  If any of these appear:
    - Do not open the unit. Do not move it more than necessary. Do not pour water on a lithium UPS; a Class ABC fire extinguisher or large amounts of water are appropriate for SLA. For a lithium-ion UPS that is smoking or on fire, evacuate, call 911, and do not attempt to move it once it is actively venting — that is the moment a fire extinguisher is appropriate.
    - If the unit is plugged in, unplug it only if you can do so without crossing the hazard zone (no smoke between you and the plug).
    - After the event, the unit and any removed battery go to a hazardous-waste handler, not to retail drop-off and not to municipal trash.

SECTION 7 — REPLACING A USER-REPLACEABLE SLA BATTERY (only if Section 4 confirmed this applies)
  Pre-work:
    1. Confirm the replacement battery SKU matches voltage exactly and capacity at or above the original. Using a higher-capacity battery is fine; using a lower-capacity one is not.
    2. Confirm the connector type (Faston F1 = 4.75 mm, F2 = 6.35 mm blade width) and polarity. Take a phone photo of the existing wiring before disconnecting.
    3. Tools: Phillips screwdriver, replacement battery, electrical tape. No metal jewelry on hands or wrists.
    4. Clear a dry, non-carpeted work surface. Have a non-conductive container ready for the old battery.
  Procedure:
    1. UPS off, unplugged from wall, all connected equipment already powered down as you did.
    2. Wait at least 5 minutes for internal capacitors to discharge through the unit's bleed resistors. Do not skip this.
    3. Open the battery access door per the manual. For most units this is one or two screws on the rear or bottom.
    4. Slide the battery out far enough to see the connectors. Do not pull on the wires.
    5. Disconnect one terminal at a time, noting color (red = positive, black = negative on virtually all SLA UPS batteries; if colors differ, your photo is the authority). Do not let the loose connector rest on the battery terminals or on the chassis.
    6. Lift the old battery out and place it in the non-conductive container, terminals taped.
    7. Connect the new battery: positive first (red to red, or per your photo), negative second. Make sure each connector seats fully and is not stressed.
    8. Seat the new battery, dress wires so the door closes without pinching them, close and fasten the door.
    9. Plug the UPS into the wall, leave connected equipment detached, power the UPS on, and let it charge for the manufacturer-specified absorption time (typically 4–24 hours depending on model and capacity).
    10. Initiate a self-test from the front panel or the manufacturer's management software. Confirm "replace battery" indicator clears and the unit passes self-test.
    11. Only after the self-test passes, reconnect the desk equipment.
  Common mistakes to avoid: reversing polarity (can destroy the UPS on first power-up — check twice), using a non-OEM-equivalent battery with a different connector (forcing a connector is a sign you have the wrong SKU), closing the door on a pinched wire, and skipping the charge cycle before loading the unit.

SECTION 8 — DISPOSAL OF OLD SLA BATTERY AND/OR WHOLE UPS
  Old SLA battery (whether removed or still inside a UPS you're retiring):
    - Never put in regular household trash. Sealed lead-acid is one of the most recycled battery chemistries but is also classified as hazardous waste in most US jurisdictions.
    - Acceptable drop-off channels: Call2Recycle site locator (call2recycle.org), Home Depot and Lowe's battery recycling (most stores, no purchase required), Best Buy (most stores, both battery and whole UPS), Staples (battery only, most stores), municipal household hazardous-waste facility, the UPS manufacturer's own take-back program.
    - Transport: upright, terminals taped, in a non-conductive container (cardboard box is ideal). Do not carry loose in a bag. Do not stack batteries. Keep the receipt or drop-off record until you confirm the unit's "replace battery" state has cleared, in case a warranty exchange ever becomes relevant.
    - If the battery is swollen, leaking, or otherwise in the urgent-isolation state from Section 6, do not bring it indoors through shared spaces or on public transit. Contact the household hazardous-waste facility for guidance; some will pick up.
  Whole UPS at end of life:
    - Retailers (Best Buy in particular) and e-waste recyclers accept whole UPSes. The battery will be removed and recycled by them.
    - Manufacturer take-back: APC, CyberPower, Eaton, and Tripp Lite all run recycling programs for their own equipment; check the support section of the manufacturer's site for an RMA or shipping label.

SECTION 9 — ITEMS I CANNOT ANSWER WITHOUT MORE INFORMATION
  - I cannot identify your specific model or battery SKU. The replacement-battery lookup is best done on the manufacturer's site using the model number from the rear label.
  - I cannot tell from the description whether the chirp was triggered by a true failed self-test, a battery past its date code, a recent long outage that deeply discharged the battery, or a bad connection. If the chirp started only after a recent extended outage, charging for 24 hours and re-running self-test is a legitimate diagnostic before buying a replacement — but only if the unit is user-replaceable and you can isolate it from the desk equipment during that 24-hour charge.
  - I cannot tell whether your UPS uses SLA or Li-ion without the label. The handling paths in Section 4 diverge at that point.

If you can share the manufacturer and model number (label photo or the text printed on the rear sticker), I can narrow Sections 3, 4, and 7 to your specific unit, including the OEM replacement-battery SKU and the manual's self-test procedure.

# Review of the Infra OTel collector memory-limiter PR

## What you actually have on the PR
- Container memory limit: 4 GiB (4096 MiB).
- Proposed limiter settings: `limit_mib: 4608`, `spike_limit_mib: 4096`.
- The PR adds a configuration-parsing test. It does not run a bounded load and does not observe whether the limiter activates.

## The fundamental problem
The proposed values are inverted relative to the container limit and incompatible with how `memory_limiter` is meant to work.

- `limit_mib: 4608` exceeds the 4096 MiB container limit. When the process RSS approaches the container's OOM threshold, the kernel will kill the collector before the limiter ever sees the pressure. The limiter is supposed to be a soft ceiling well *below* the hard ceiling so it can shed load gracefully. With `limit_mib` set above the container limit, the limiter is configured to be irrelevant — its enforcement point sits above the kill threshold, so the first response to pressure is a SIGKILL from the kernel, not a `Refused` from the limiter.
- `spike_limit_mib: 4096` is the high-water mark the collector allows itself between GC/check cycles. Setting it equal to the container limit means the spike allowance lives right at the kernel's hard ceiling, leaving zero headroom for the runtime, allocator fragmentation, queue growth in other processors, or the Go runtime's own heap metadata. The whole point of `spike_limit_mib` is to be *below* `limit_mib`, with the gap representing the room the collector can absorb in a single check interval before the limiter forces a `Refused`.
- The direction is also inverted from the prior cleanup you accepted (the 82% / 25% percentage-based config in the ingest-edge collector). That one expressed `limit_percentage` and `spike_limit_percentage` of the container limit, with `spike` strictly below `limit`. The proposal here expresses both as MiB and puts `spike` at the container ceiling and `limit` above it.

## What the new test actually demonstrates
A configuration-parsing test confirms only that the YAML is structurally valid and that the collector process loads the file without erroring. It does not show:
- The limiter ever firing under load.
- What error rate, p95, or p99 look like with the limiter active versus inactive.
- That the proposed MiB values map to the intended behavior relative to a 4 GiB container.
- Any relationship to the prior baseline memory profile from the 0.95.x / `0.96.2-sphere.7` work.

So the PR does not establish evidence for the values it picks, and the values it picks don't make sense for a 4 GiB container.

## What I would require before this is approvable

1. Values that respect the container ceiling. Concretely, `limit_mib` must be below 4096, and `spike_limit_mib` must be below `limit_mib`. The percentage-based form (`limit_percentage` / `spike_limit_percentage`) is the more defensible shape here because it tracks the container limit rather than a hard-coded number that will silently drift the next time the deployment bumps the cgroup. If MiB is kept, both numbers need an explicit derivation from the container limit and a comment recording it.
2. A bounded load run that actually exercises the limiter. Replay or generate enough concurrent traffic at the configured batch size to force RSS upward into the spike band, and capture: (a) the point at which the limiter starts emitting `Refused`, (b) the impact on valid-request error rate and p99 during the pressure window, (c) recovery to baseline after the burst ends, and (d) no `OOMKilled` events at the pod level.
3. A clear rollback signal in the PR description. The current material lists none. At minimum: pod OOM/restart count, valid-request error rate delta versus baseline, p99 delta, and a stop-and-revert threshold for any of them.
4. A reference back to the baseline memory profile used to derive the values — the prior ingest-edge rollout established a "p95 memory around 5% above the pre-bump collector baseline" criterion; the derivation for these MiB values should be anchored to a comparable baseline, not chosen in isolation.
5. Justification for switching from the percentage-based form that already shipped on ingest-edge to absolute MiB here. Either form can be correct, but the divergence needs a reason — different collector sizing model, different processor order, different downstream queueing — recorded in the change note, otherwise the next reader will assume one of them is wrong.

## Bottom line
Do not merge as proposed. The numbers are inverted against the 4 GiB ceiling, the only test added covers parsing rather than behavior, and the change has no rollback signal. Send it back with: corrected values (both below the container limit, spike strictly below limit, or convert to the percentage form), a bounded load observation showing the limiter firing and recovering cleanly, and an explicit rollback trigger list.

Recommendation to Nadia on the proposed release score

Core objection: a single red/yellow/green that averages live metrics-router error movement with replay-fixture mismatch movement collapses two signals with orthogonal semantics. It turns a designed control (the replay pipeline catching an adversarial fixture) into a rollback trigger, which is the opposite of what the existing dashboard legend and Cardinality Guardrails work already require.

Semantic anchors that already exist (do not need to be reinvented):
  - Live-path signals drive rollback discussion.
  - Validation / replay / mirror signals drive mismatch investigation and controls work.
  - Alert-source classification is required so a validation or replay panel is never read as a live rollback criterion.

Recommended representation: replace the single combined score with two parallel, explicitly labeled scales. Do not aggregate, do not average, do not AND-gate.

  Live-Path Release Health   (drives rollback discussion)
    Inputs (already accepted elsewhere):
      - live metrics-router error rate vs the 0.03% baseline
      - dropped writes on the canary slice (must stay at zero)
      - p99 vs existing thresholds (≈145 ms, or ≥134 ms sustained >25 min)
      - rollup-service lag on the live label set
      - parser-cache miss movement, if inexpensive to check
      - metrics-router canary alert
    State:
      green  = all inputs within thresholds
      yellow = any single input approaching threshold
      red    = any threshold crossed OR canary alert fired
    Action:
      red/yellow opens rollback discussion; green does not.

  Validation / Replay Coverage Health   (drives investigation and controls work)
    Inputs:
      - expected-fixture pass/fail
      - adversarial-fixture detection (caught vs silently passed)
      - alert-source classification result
      - coverage of the Cardinality Guardrails check slice
    State:
      green  = expected fixtures pass AND adversarial fixtures correctly caught
      yellow = expected fixtures pass but adversarial classification is ambiguous, or a coverage gap is identified
      red    = an unexpected mismatch — a fixture that was supposed to pass failed (this is a control gap, not a rollback trigger)
    Action:
      red/yellow opens mismatch investigation and controls work; never opens rollback.

Display rules:
  - Render the two scales side-by-side; never collapse them into one color.
  - Each carries its own legend line stating which action it drives.
  - A combined "release status" line is allowed only as a derived narrative, e.g.
      "Live-path: green. Validation: green — release candidate."
      "Live-path: green. Validation: red on fixture X — controls work, no rollback."
    and must never reduce to a single red/yellow/green.
  - Keep the alert-source classification check intact; any panel near the alert copy must be labeled live-path or replay/mirror validation before rollback language is used.

How this handles the sample you described:
  - Live traffic at baseline          -> Live-Path Release Health = green.
  - Adversarial Guardrails fixture mismatches and the validation pipeline catches it
                                      -> Validation/Replay Coverage Health = green.
                                        (An adversarial fixture is supposed to mismatch;
                                         detecting that mismatch is the control working
                                         as designed.)
  - Net result: no aggregated red, no implied rollback, both signals visible.
  - Counter-case worth stating explicitly: if the adversarial fixture had been silently
    classified as passing, that would be Validation/Replay Coverage Health = red — still
    not a rollback trigger; still controls work, still controls work only.

Things I am deliberately not choosing for you:
  - The exact yellow-band definition on the validation scale (ambiguity vs coverage gap is a judgment call that belongs to you and Roman, not me).
  - Whether the two scales live publicly on the release doc or stay inside the release review thread.
  - Whether the deprecated combined score is retired immediately or kept as a shadow view for one cycle.

Scope note: this is a review of the representation, not approval to change an alerting rule. Whatever representation you and Hema adopt, the rule change still goes through the normal review path with alert-source classification preserved, and Cardinality Guardrails remains additive rather than replaced.

60-MINUTE BOULDERING SESSION PLAN
Wed Feb 26 2025, evening (with Ren)

Premise: the Feb 20 reassessment cleared you to return with longer
warmup + progressive loading. Pain-free tonight is the baseline you're
protecting, not an upgrade. The new moderate circuit being undercling-
heavy is a constraint, not a reason to slide into the excluded
categories.

EXCLUDED TONIGHT
- Hard underclings (the heavy part of the new moderate circuit)
- Hard gripping: full crimps, pinches, pockets, single-finger locks
- Steep overhangs, dynamic moves, highballs, uncontrolled falls

  tolerance, even on a "moderate" grade

USE INSTEAD (Ren's read of the gym)
- Easy open-hand slabs
- Vertical footwork problems
- Low traverses

STRUCTURE (60 minutes)

1. Longer forearm warmup — 18-20 min
   a. General warmup — 4-5 min
      Easy cycling, jumping jacks, or stair work until warm and slightly
      breathing. Goal: blood flow, not fatigue.
   b. Wrist and forearm mobility — 4-5 min
      Wrist circles both directions; gentle prayer stretch and reverse
      prayer; forearm extensor stretch (elbow straight, palm down, gentle
      pull); light band-resisted wrist EXTENSION only (not flexion yet).
   c. Finger and tendon prep — 4-5 min
      Open-hand hangs on a large jug, gradually lessening hold size down
      to a comfortable open-hand edge. Slow eccentrics on a large edge
      if available. Stop well short of any crimp or pinch.
   d. On-wall warmup — 5-6 min
      Low traversing on the largest holds in the gym. Open-hand only,
      footwork-led. End while it still feels boring.

2. Progressive loading — 32-35 min, in three blocks
   Block A — Easy open-hand slabs (10-12 min)
     2-3 problems well below your max grade on slab. Open-hand only,
     deliberate feet, never let grip demand exceed easy open-hand
     comfort. Movement quality, not grade.
   Block B — Vertical footwork problems (10-12 min)
     Technical sequences that reward balance, flagging, drop-knees,
     heel hooks, and weight transfer rather than grip. If a "footwork"
     problem turns out to need a hard pull at the top, downgrade.
   Block C — Low traverses (10-12 min)
     Sustained horizontal movement kept low enough to step off or
     downclimb comfortably. Continuous movement; no individual move
     should spike forearm demand.

   Keep total attempts modest. If forearm pump is forcing form
   breakdown, end early — time on the clock is not a goal.

3. Cooldown — 5-7 min
   Light walking, gentle forearm extensor stretch, hydrate. No
   maximal gripping after the session.

- Any reproduction of right-forearm flexor-pronator discomfort, especially

- Grip quality declining mid-problem (slipping, holds suddenly feeling

- Forearm pump forcing form breakdown before a planned rest
- Any pop, swelling, bruising, numbness, grip loss, or focal bony

- The problem demanding a hard undercling or hard grip — pick a

The plan as described has three structural defects that compound, plus missing elements that should be explicit.

Problem 1: Combined 5-minute window across two services with separate owners. A shard-keeper compaction-holder move and a rollup-service worker restart touch different services, have different owners (you + Nadia coordination for shard-keeper; Data Platform for rollup-service), and have different rollback procedures. Bundling them in the same interval removes the isolation you'd want if either side regresses. If queue-age spikes during the window, you cannot tell whether to push the prior shard-keeper label map or restore the prior rollup worker config. Those are different actions by different responders.

Problem 2: Combined watch defeats cause attribution. One queue-age + request-error watch for two services means an alert that fires is ambiguous. shard-keeper compaction changes are known to push rollup-service queue age without moving metrics-router or ingest-edge (the October 25, 2024 and April 17 patterns both fit). If a worker restart happens in the same window, a queue-age rise is uninterpretable: is it the compactor move, the restart, or their interaction? The watch needs to be split, or at minimum the alerting must clearly tag which service produced the signal.

Problem 3: Friday timing. March 7, 2025 is a Friday. The plan does not specify time-of-day. Friday production-state changes are off-norm for you regardless of morning vs afternoon. If this work has to happen this week, the safer cadence is Monday March 10.

IND-031-04 — what this means

IRS rejected the federal e-file because the prior-year AGI or prior-year e-file PIN you entered for the primary taxpayer doesn't match what they have on file. This is their identity-verification step, not a calculation problem with the 2024 return itself.

Good news first. The payment screen shows no withdrawal initiated. The federal rejection happened before any debit was attempted, and the NY return is held in lockstep with federal — so no erroneous federal debit and no NY debit either. The bank is clean.

Common causes

- Prior-year AGI entered with a small error — off by $1, $100, a rounding artifact, or pulled from a draft/amended copy rather than the accepted return.
- Total income, taxable income, or Line 12 entered by mistake instead of AGI (Line 11 on Form 1040).
- Prior-year e-file PIN entered when no PIN was actually used (or wrong PIN) — PIN vs. AGI are two different verification methods; mixing them produces IND-031-04.
- Filing-status mismatch the IRS can't reconcile across years (e.g., 2023 MFJ but 2024 MFS, or vice versa).
- Primary taxpayer SSN/identity doesn't match what IRS has on the prior-year return.
- Rare: IRS records not yet updated for that prior year.

What I know vs. what I don't know

What I have from records:
- 2023 federal return was e-filed and accepted.
- $1,184 federal debit posted April 10, 2024.
- IRS account transcript showed the $2,000 January 15, 2024 estimated-tax payment recorded against 2023.

What I do not have and need from you before any re-transmit:
- The exact dollar AGI on Line 11 of the accepted 2023 Form 1040, to the cent. This is the single number that resolves most IND-031-04 cases.
- Filing status used on the 2023 return (Single / MFS / MFJ / HoH).
- Filing status being used on the 2024 return.
- Whether a 5-digit PIN was actually used to sign the 2023 return, or whether AGI was the verification method.

Resolution paths, in order of preference

1. Re-enter the exact Line 11 AGI from the accepted 2023 return and retransmit. IRS typically allows multiple e-file attempts per return within the filing window.
2. Pull the AGI straight from IRS — IRS "Get Transcript" online (immediate) or Form 4506-T (paper, ~5–10 days). This is the authoritative source and bypasses any local draft mismatch.
3. Use the e-file PIN path only if the 2023 return was actually PIN-signed and you have that PIN. Do not switch method from AGI to PIN (or vice versa) without confirming the prior-year return used that method.
4. Form 1040-X is not the right vehicle — it handles post-filing changes, not identity verification.
5. Paper-file Form 1040 as a last resort if e-file attempts exhaust.

NY status

The NY return is held because federal rejected. On most software, once the federal transmission is corrected and accepted, NY flows through automatically on the same submission. No separate NY fix, no separate debit. Don't refile NY independently — either it clears with federal or it stays held.

The one-pager should give leadership three things they can read in under five minutes: what actually changed at the handoff moment, what evidence shows it changed, and what is still open. Anya's three raw assets — adoption, drift checks, fewer exceptions — are inputs, not the categories themselves. Here are six candidate categories she can pick from and trim to fit one page.

1.  Adoption footprint, per team. For each of the three teams: which surfaces moved to the canonical package, when, who owns the pull request, and which surfaces are still on the prior workflow. Per-team facts read as evidence. "Adopted across all three teams" by itself reads as a claim.

2.  Drift catches as concrete cases. One or two named examples — what diverged, who caught it, when, and what would have reached production without the check. The earlier Figma-only rename that reproduced downstream is the kind of exemplar that lands. Counts without examples feel thin; examples without counts feel anecdotal. Pair them.

3.  Exception reduction, before and after. What categories of platform-specific override used to exist, which collapsed once the canonical package generated downstream representations, and which still require manual handling. Naming a category that is still manual is a strength, not a weakness — it tells leadership the work isn't oversold.

4.  Handoff-mechanism changes. What is actually different at the moment design hands off to engineering. Examples: design changes now flow through one source, drift is caught before review rather than at QA, fewer "is this the latest" threads, generated outputs replace hand-translation in a specific repo. Each item should be tied to an observed behavior, not a claimed benefit.

5.  What's still open or unresolved. Surfaces not yet on canonical, teams still partial, exceptions still required, gaps in drift-check coverage. Anya's earlier work shows she values unresolved-blocker visibility — naming what isn't done yet is the strongest defense against the note being read as overselling.

6.  Boundary line. Explicitly what the workflow does not claim. It does not claim engineering implementation ownership, it does not replace design judgment, and it does not eliminate the human handoff conversation. A one-line boundary prevents the note from being read as "Anya owns engineering output."

Six is more than one page. The strongest pairing for a one-pager is usually adoption footprint (per team) plus one named drift example plus exception reduction plus the boundary line. Mechanism changes and open items can be condensed into a single line each if she has room.

Two listening questions to ask while she outlines:

Q1 — the evidence check. "For each line you put on the page, can you point to a specific person, surface, or date — or is it a generalization?" This is the spine of the note: it forces observation-versus-inference separation, which is what makes the note read as evidence rather than another deck. If a line has no grounding, either she finds one or the line comes off.

Q2 — the skeptic check. "What would you want a skeptical reader to challenge first, and is that item on the page or held back?" This surfaces the soft spot in the note while she still has time to either defend it, soften it, or move it out of the lead. It also keeps the decision in her hands — she chooses what stays.

The two questions cover both directions: each line has grounding (Q1), and the weakest line is named and handled (Q2). Neither tells her what to write; both help her decide what survives.

Given the facts you've established — 18 psi drop over ~20 hours (≈0.9 psi/hr), no visible tread/sidewall/bead damage, valve straight and capped, both tires otherwise normal except the rear — the leak is slow and consistent with a small puncture, slow valve leak, or something embedded against the tube that you can't see from outside. The sidewall range you noted (50–75 psi) means 50 psi is at the floor but the tire isn't flat; that's useful, it means the leak is small enough that you'll have time for each test.

NON-DESTRUCTIVE LEAK-CHECK SEQUENCE

Run these in order. Stop and step out only when a step produces a positive finding.

1. Confirm the reading and the leak rate, not just the snapshot.
   - Measure both tires cold now with the same gauge.
   - Inflate the rear back to 68 psi (or whatever target you ride at) and record the time.
   - Re-measure at 1 hr, 6 hr, and 24 hr. A drop of roughly 0.9 psi/hr steady over 24 hr confirms a real, persistent leak (vs. a one-time event like a temp swing or a recent bead reseat). Note that temperature swings over a 20-hour window can move pressure a few psi, but 18 psi is outside that band.

2. Audible/feel test at the valve first, before anything wet.
   - Inflate to ~60 psi.
   - Cap off. Put a clean finger or your cheek close to the valve opening (don't press on it). Listen for hiss and feel for moving air.
   - For Presta: open the locknut fully, then verify it isn't leaking at the stem base while open. If the locknut is loose, snugging it (only finger-tight plus a small nudge with a wrench if you have one — do not force) sometimes cures a slow stem leak. Skip if Schrader.
   - Soapy swab at the stem-to-rubber joint and at the valve base: small dab, watch 60–90 seconds for bubbles.

3. Soapy-water spray over the entire inflated tire.
   - Mix dish soap and water in a spray bottle. Inflate to ~60 psi.
   - Spray the tread across the full circumference; then both sidewalls; then both beads (rotate the wheel slowly so you cover the whole bead on each side).
   - Wait 60–90 seconds per zone before moving on — pinhole leaks can take that long to grow a visible bubble. A headlamp or flashlight raked across the surface makes bubbles much easier to see.
   - If bubbles appear anywhere on the tread/sidewall: that's the leak's general area — mark the position on the tire with a piece of tape so you know where to look inside if you eventually pull the tube.
   - If bubbles appear only at the bead, that's a bead/rim-tape interface leak — which generally cannot be fixed without dismounting the tire.

4. Inside-tire feel test (no dismount).
   - Deflate the tire (or just lower it to ~10 psi).
   - With the wheel off the bike and the tire still mounted, push one hand inside the tire between the tube and the casing (deflating first makes this safer; even at low pressure there's enough room). Rotate slowly and run your fingers along the inside of the casing.
   - You're feeling for: a thorn, glass sliver, wire, staple, or any hard point protruding inward. Even a 1 mm shard can pierce the tube each time you inflate.
   - Also feel around each spoke hole from inside for a sharp rim edge or a missing/damaged rim-tape edge — but full rim-tape assessment requires dismounting, so note this as "to verify later" rather than a hard check.

5. Re-inflate and re-test the leak rate at the end.
   - Inflate back to 68 psi, wait 1 hr, re-measure. The rate should match step 1. A faster rate after the spray test means you may have displaced a small object or stressed the bead — stop riding until step 6.

Acceptance criteria for the sequence to be considered complete: you have either (a) located the leak zone, (b) confirmed the leak rate is steady at ≈0.9 psi/hr with no visible source, or (c) eliminated the valve as the source. After step 5, if the leak is still unlocated, you have done everything non-destructively that is reasonable.

CRITERIA FOR THE THREE OUTCOMES

Patch the tube (do not take to a shop):
- Soapy spray located bubbles on the tread or sidewall, OR a small object was found inside the casing and removed.
- The puncture is small (typically ≤2 mm, sometimes up to ~3 mm) and is in the tube body, well away from the valve stem and away from any prior patch area.
- Tube is otherwise sound (no brittleness, no long slit, no multiple punctures).
- After reinstallation and inflation to riding pressure, the tube holds with no measurable drop over 24 hr (gauge re-check at 1, 6, and 24 hr).
- Rim tape inspection (which requires dismounting) shows no exposed spoke hole, no torn tape, no rim-edge burr at the puncture location. If this can't be verified, the patch is conditional and the wheel stays out of service.

Replace the tube (do it yourself):
- No bubbles found in step 3, but a small object was found and removed in step 4 → tube almost certainly punctured; replace.
- Leak persists at the valve-stem-to-rubber joint even after snugging the locknut → stem interface, not patchable reliably (this matches what you found in August 2024 at the same joint).
- Tube is more than ~5 years old, or has been patched before in the same general area.
- Multiple small leaks or any single slit ≥3 mm.
- Once the tube is out, if the rim tape is torn, displaced, or missing at any spoke hole, replace the rim tape as part of the same job — not a separate trip.

Take it to a shop:
- Step 3 bubbles appear only at the bead and won't stop with re-inflating and bead-reseat attempts → likely rim tape, rim edge, or tire-bead mismatch, which is shop territory.
- Inside feel test finds nothing, soapy spray finds nothing, valve test is clean, leak rate is still ≈0.9 psi/hr after 24 hr → un-located slow leak. A shop has a submersion tank with more volume, a valve-core tool, and the ability to dismount and inspect rim/tape/tire without losing the leak.
- After replacement, a NEW tube also loses air → confirms rim/tape or spoke-hole issue, not tube.
- Any tire damage you missed in the visual inspection becomes visible after dismount (embedded wire, casing bulge when flexed, exposed threads). Tread cuts like the ~4 mm one you inspected in November 2024 were fine because no casing showed; if this time you see casing threads through a cut, or a sidewall bulge appears when you flex the tire by hand, the tire itself needs replacement and a shop is the right call for tire-mounting if you don't have tire levers you're comfortable with.
- Brake or wheel re-installation check: your shop visits in the past have included axle, hub, caliper, and pad checks; given this wheel will come off and on for the tube swap, consider having the shop re-verify the rear brake alignment and rotor runout (your front rotor measured above the 0.20 mm service threshold in the prior episode — worth confirming the rear is in spec at the same time, not as a separate visit).

STOP CONDITIONS (don't keep diagnosing, take it in):
- Soapy spray bubbles appear at the bead and you can't stop them with a bead reseat.
- You find casing threads, exposed casing, or a bulge inside the tire during step 4.
- After step 5 the leak rate has increased, not held steady.
