- On the PR (once a verified identifier exists), block until the summary is corrected to report the maximum and the stop rule is re-keyed to it; do not merge the mean-only change.

Classification of 108 ms under the owner-led-window rule

108 ms exceeds the 100 ms cleanup-pause ceiling. The window is STOPPED. It is not a completed safe push, not a clean single-push result, and not a reopened window. The hard maximum fires the moment any single cleanup-pause observation crosses 100 ms; an average computed across the push or across the window does not gate that check.

Rule references that fix this reading:
  - Cleanup pauses must remain at or below 100 ms during an owner-led configuration window.
  - Exceeding the 100 ms ceiling stops the window immediately.
  - Existing rollback triggers (generation inconsistency, route-parity failure, dropped series, reload/restart failure, true user-visible regression) remain active alongside the ceiling and are not replaced by it.
  - After a stop, the window stays stopped. Fresh authorization permits exactly one fully observed recovery push, not a reopened multi-push window; another window requires another fresh decision.

Why the average is not the stop signal

The ceiling is a per-observation maximum, not a per-window mean. A summary may retain averages, medians, p50/p90/p99, and counts because those are useful for trend visibility, but only if the reporting preserves the rule's actual decision surface — the maximum single observation. Once any sample crosses 100 ms the window is stopped regardless of how the surrounding samples sit.

How a summary retains averages without letting them replace the hard maximum stop check

  - Surface the maximum, not the mean, as the stop signal. Any line of the form "mean pause X ms" is context only; it must never be cited as "within threshold." Within-threshold is a property of the maximum.
  - Pair every average with the full distribution shape: min, p50, p90, p99, max, and the count of pushes or samples. The sample that triggered the stop has to be visible in the same view as any average.
  - Report the per-push max alongside any window-level average. A 108 ms observation is, by construction, an out-of-threshold observation; an average computed across pushes that includes a 108 ms sample is not a within-threshold result, even if the average itself is below 100 ms.
  - Keep the stop flag and the triggering observation preserved in the record. The window is marked stopped, the observation timestamp and value are retained, and later rows or automatic retries are suppressed.
  - Restrict trend averages to clean windows only. A summary that mixes a stopped window into a clean-window average corrupts the average's meaning and risks implying the ceiling was respected when it was breached.
  - Label the stopped window separately. Distinct fields or rows for stopped vs clean keep the average honest: a clean-window mean of 64 ms with max 88 ms is a real within-threshold reading; the same mean with a 108 ms max is a stopped window.

Recovery path after the stop

  - Window remains stopped; no further pushes inside it.
  - The full health set must return to baseline before any recovery authorization is even considered.
  - Alex opens exactly one fully observed recovery push under fresh decision, not a multi-push window.
  - If the recovery push's cleanup pause exceeds 100 ms, or any rollback trigger fires, the window stops again and a new window requires a new fresh decision.

The 108 ms case is therefore a stopped window with the triggering observation preserved, averages retained only as descriptive context, and the next action gated on a fresh decision rather than on any average that happens to sit below 100 ms.

Cardinality Guardrails assessment — `parity_fixture_failure_total{producer_value=<raw>,consumer_value=<raw>}`

Cardinality concern
- 2,706 distinct combinations from fuzzing alone is high for a metrics-pipeline counter, and the value set is caller-controlled and unbounded (new malformed shapes add more). This is the label-cardinality class Cardinality Guardrails preflight is supposed to catch on label changes touching metrics-router / shard-keeper / rollup-service.
- The retained April 17 `shard_region` → `storage_region` mismatch is the case the rule exists for; raw caller-supplied value labels in a producer/consumer parity counter reproduce that failure mode in the metric layer.

Redundancy with existing evidence
- The fixture report already records, per failing record: expected key, observed producer key and value, observed consumer key and value, and failing record index.
- The counter as proposed re-emits that same per-record detail as metric labels with no bounded value set and no additional semantic content. Per-record detail already lives in the fixture report; the metric needs an aggregated view, not a re-export.

Recommended path (pick one)
1. Bounded mismatch-type label — replace raw `producer_value` / `consumer_value` with a small enum (e.g., `key_mismatch | value_mismatch | missing_producer | missing_consumer | parse_error`). Single counter, ≤10 label values, cardinality stays flat post-publish.
2. Aggregate-only — drop both value labels; emit `parity_fixture_failure_total` as a monotonic count plus a small bounded label for fixture name or test class. Per-record detail stays in the fixture report.
3. Log + alert — keep option 2 for the metric, and route per-record mismatch details to a structured log or alert source already covered by alert-source classification, not into the metric label set.

Gate outcome
- As proposed (raw producer_value + raw consumer_value, 2,706+ unbounded combinations): fails label-cardinality preflight for a label change touching the metrics pipeline. Even if preflight is waved, the value set is caller-controlled and unbounded, so it also fails the post-publish Cardinality Guardrails intent.
- With any of the three bounded alternatives: passes label-cardinality preflight, additive to the existing fixture report, no duplication of per-record detail in metric labels, alert-source classification stays applicable.

Want me to draft the review comment along these lines, recommending option 1 (bounded enum) as the primary path and option 2 as the fallback?

Recommendation: bounded mismatch classes for the production metric

Mismatch classes (proposed bounded set, 7 values):

1. name_mismatch — producer label key differs from consumer label key. Example: storage_region vs storage_zone. This is the class the shard-keeper / rollup-service fixture caught and the class that maps to the April outage pattern.

2. value_mismatch — keys match, but the per-record value differs for the same series. Same key, different real-world value.

3. cardinality_violation — producer emitted a value outside the agreed bounded set for that label. Example: a fifth tenant_size_class beyond small / medium / large / unknown.

4. missing_producer — consumer expected a label the producer did not emit at all. Producer omits the field entirely.

5. unexpected_producer — producer emitted a label the consumer did not declare or consume. Producer has a field the consumer does not read.

6. type_mismatch — keys match, but the value types differ. Example: string vs integer, or integer vs boolean.

7. encoding_mismatch — same logical value, different normalization. Example: case difference, whitespace, locale-formatted number, leading zeros.

Where the raw producer and consumer values must remain available:

A. Per-record debug logs. The raw label key, raw producer value, and raw consumer value for the mismatched record, with trace_id and series identity. This is the same channel that currently holds the raw tenant_hash and the raw replay_source_id. The metric never carries these.

B. The parity fixture's key-level export. The fixture already produces a structured mismatch report; that export is the authoritative record of which key, which producer value, and which consumer value disagreed. rollup-service#389 should be lifted from aggregate-count equality to key-level parity, and that export is where the raw disagreement lives.

C. Trace context attached to the specific mismatched record. A responder pivoting from the metric series to one record should reach the trace without scanning logs by hand. Trace carries raw producer and consumer values, not the metric.

What the metric must NOT carry:

- Raw label keys or values as label dimensions. Cardinality is unbounded and the prior posture (raw identifiers out of production metric labels) holds.
- The mismatched value itself. The class label is enough to drive routing and the first-check decision; the value belongs in the per-record channel.
- Any field that varies per-record. The metric is per-class and per-series-identity at most. tenant identity, request_id, pod UID, and similar unbounded identifiers stay in logs and traces.

Why this shape:

- It matches the established precedents. tenant_size_class is bounded to four values. replay_source_id stays raw in logs and is reduced to a bounded class in the metric. The refusal-string work treated the raw refusal string as unsafe as a metric label and required a bounded classification instead. The same shape applies here.
- It preserves the 24-hour rule. The metric answers "what kind of mismatch happened"; the log answers "what were the actual values." The two signals stay separate.
- It is actionable. Each class maps to a different first check (label rename, fixture join, schema change, normalization pass) without exposing unbounded values. Cyrus's input-classification-or-fixture-join question is the diagnostic tree this metric supports; the bounded class is the entry point, the raw values in the log are the next hop.
- It does not weaken the parity gate. The bounded set on the metric is the alerting and routing layer; the key-level fixture export is still the gating artifact before any production deployment that crosses a producer-consumer boundary.

Stopping conditions stay intact. Any of the seven classes crossing the agreed alert threshold routes through the existing producer-consumer label-set-difference path. Raw values remain reachable in logs and traces, never in the metric.

Confirmed. The dashboard formula is mixing units, which is what produces the apparent 39,996-point gap while the underlying request flow is internally consistent.

What the formula currently computes:

  attempted_points - received_points - refused_requests
  = 1,000,000 - 960,000 - 4
  = 39,996 (the apparent gap)

What the underlying accounting actually shows:

  attempted_points: 100 requests × 10,000 points  = 1,000,000
  received_points:  96 requests × 10,000 points  =   960,000
  refused_points:    4 requests × 10,000 points  =    40,000
  received + refused                         = 1,000,000  ✓  (zero gap)

The "39,996-point gap" is exactly the cost of treating 4 refused requests as 4 refused points instead of 40,000 refused points (1,000,000 − 960,000 = 40,000; 40,000 − 4 = 39,996).

Two bounded fixes:

1. Subtract refused points, not refused requests:

     attempted_points − received_points − refused_points
     = 1,000,000 − 960,000 − 40,000 = 0

   This requires the metric to carry refused_points (or refused_requests × a known per-request point count). If point counts per request are not uniform, this still lies.

2. Reconcile in request space:

     attempted_requests − received_requests − refused_requests
     = 100 − 96 − 4 = 0

   This is robust to non-uniform point counts per request and doesn't depend on the memory limiter reporting a per-request point figure.

Option 2 is the safer reconciliation form. Option 1 only holds if every refused request is known to have carried the same number of points, which the memory-limiter refusal path does not by itself guarantee.

Net: the request-handling layer is internally consistent; the dashboard revision is the source of the discrepancy, and the fix is to subtract in the same unit space the metric is denominated in — preferably request space, since point counts per request are not a safe assumption here.

Request-level and point-level accounting

REQUEST LEVEL (one row per HTTP request, regardless of payload size):

  requests_received  = requests_accepted
                      + requests_denied_expected   (policy, budget, eligibility)
                      + requests_rejected_invalid  (oversized_batch, schema, malformed)
                      + requests_errored           (transport, timeout, 5xx after accept)

  requests_accepted  -> these requests entered point accounting
  requests_denied_*  -> 0 adapter calls, 0 points recorded downstream
  requests_rejected_invalid -> for oversized_batch this is 1 request, N points rejected, 0 accepted
  requests_errored   -> depends on stage; classify by where the failure occurred

POINT LEVEL (per request that entered point accounting, summed across requests):

  points_submitted_r  = points_accepted_r + points_rejected_r
  points_submitted    = sum_r points_submitted_r
  points_accepted     = sum_r points_accepted_r
  points_rejected     = sum_r points_rejected_r

Invariant that must hold if accounting is clean:

  points_accepted  +  points_rejected   ==  points_submitted
  requests_accepted (from request layer) == count of requests that contributed points

Cross-stage counters (must remain separable, never summed into one panel):

  edge_forwarded      -- what edge-gateway sent downstream
  collector_received  -- what the collector accepted from the wire
  validation_accepted -- what passed schema/size/tenant checks and was stored
  stored_series_count -- what is queryable

Expected relationship when nothing is lost:

  edge_forwarded  ==  collector_received  ==  validation_accepted + collector_rejected
  validation_accepted  contributes 1:1 to  points_accepted  at the point layer

Counters the dashboard must NOT mix

  1. Points and requests. Units differ. Adding points_accepted to requests_accepted is meaningless; dividing one by the other as a ratio hides partial-batch behaviour (e.g. one 8,000-point request rejected as oversized shows up as 1 rejected request but 8,000 rejected points).

  2. Accepted and rejected points. For oversized_batch the correct row is 0 accepted + N rejected. If a panel shows only accepted_points and drops to baseline while rejected_points is unchanged, that is the oversized-batch pattern, not loss.

  3. Edge_forwarded vs collector_received vs validation_accepted. Each is a distinct stage. A gap between edge_forwarded and collector_received is transport; a gap between collector_received and validation_accepted is policy/validation. A single "throughput" panel hides which gap exists.

  4. Expected denials and unexpected rejections. requests_denied_expected (tenant budget, eligibility, per-tenant waiting cap) is a normal control-plane outcome; requests_rejected_invalid (oversized_batch, schema) is a data-plane outcome. Mixing them in an alert threshold turns routine budget denials into incidents.

  5. Per-tenant and aggregate counters. Aggregate can mask a single-tenant stall or burst; per-tenant panels must be read with the same reset-aware math, never derived by subtraction from aggregate (loses the reset signal).

  6. Live traffic and replay/mirror-validation samples. Replay traffic and mirror-validation samples must carry a separate label so on-call can read p99, CPU, and throughput panels without replay load looking like production. This is the label split you already approved for the metrics-router rename.

  7. Pre-stop and post-stop windows. A panel that spans a stop boundary will show nonzero over the window even when writes are stopped, because the rate includes the pre-stop segment. The stale six-hour panel was exactly this artefact.

  8. Raw counter value and raw 5-minute delta. This is the dashboard bug. A monotonic counter that reset (pod restart, scrape gap, exporter reconnect) produces a negative raw delta even when no points were lost. The correct primitive is the reset-aware increase/rate function, not delta = sample_t - sample_{t-5m}.

Classifying the current discrepancy as reset vs real loss

Given the evidence on record -- no change in rejected_point counts, no forwarding loop, no collector error, no customer-visible gap, and the dashboard using raw 5-minute delta -- the pattern is consistent with a counter-reset artefact, not accounting loss. The discriminating checks, in order, are:

  a. Recompute the panel with reset-aware counter math (increase() / rate() with counter-reset handling). If the negative delta disappears, it was a reset.

  b. Reconcile edge_forwarded vs collector_received vs validation_accepted over the same window. If all three match, no data was lost in transport or validation; only the metric system observed a discontinuity.

  c. Confirm requests_accepted count over the window equals the count of requests that contributed to points_accepted. A match confirms the request-to-point join is intact.

  d. Confirm rejected_points is unchanged across the window, and that any oversized_batch events are accounted for as 0 accepted + N rejected.

  e. Annotate the dashboard panel to use reset-aware math, label live vs replay/validation samples, and mark the stop boundary so pre-stop segments do not bleed into post-stop reads.

Only after (a)-(d) all reconcile may the alert be closed. If any of them shows a real gap, classify it by stage (transport vs validation vs join) before paging -- that classification determines which runbook applies.

Assessment: this convenience change conflicts with the deployed layered design on the retry path after partial transport success. It is not just a stylistic concern — it encodes a behavior the design explicitly does not authorize, and the fixture is validating the wrong invariant.

1. The split-before-send half is fine

  Splitting a 9,000-point batch into an 8,000-point chunk A and a 1,000-point chunk B before transmission is consistent with the documented participating-SDK contract: locally reject above 8,000, instruct the caller to split, then transmit each chunk within the limit. Chunk A succeeding and chunk B timing out is, by itself, unremarkable — each chunk is below the threshold and treated as an independent request.

2. The retry half is the violation

  The generic retry path is storing the original logical batch and resending both chunks. After chunk A has already transmitted successfully and its 8,000 points have been accepted, resending it on retry produces a second transmission of the same 8,000 points. That is duplication after partial transport success. The design principle stored in the runbook and the staged-enablement record is explicit: oversized callers must split before retrying, deterministic whole-batch rejection is preserved for older clients, and duplication after partial transport success is not authorized. A retry that replays an already-accepted chunk falls squarely inside that prohibition, regardless of whether the original batch was oversize or not.

  The right retry shape is per-chunk: resend only the chunks that did not produce a success response, using the per-chunk request identifier, and do not replay chunks whose response was already accepted. If chunk A was accepted, the retry path has nothing to do for chunk A; it only needs to handle chunk B (and any subsequent chunks that failed). That keeps the transmitted-points accounting equal to the unique stored-points accounting.

3. The fixture encodes the bug

  Expecting 18,000 total transmitted points (9,000 original + 9,000 retry) treats transmission count as the success metric. That is the wrong invariant. The invariant under the deployed design is: after the retry sequence completes, the count of unique accepted points equals the count of points in the original logical batch, with no duplicates stored and no points lost. A fixture that asserts 18,000 transmitted points will pass even when the system has silently duplicated 8,000 stored points, which is exactly the failure mode the design was tightened to prevent. The fixture needs to assert unique-accepted-points against the original logical batch size, not transmitted-points against the retry-loop count.

  Marking the logical batch successful after the retry is also wrong as stated, because the success criterion here is "all 9,000 unique points are accepted," not "the retry loop completed." Under the correct per-chunk retry, the logical batch is successful when chunk A's prior acceptance plus chunk B's new acceptance together account for 9,000 unique points.

4. Two related points worth flagging

  - If the team wants to keep the "retry the whole logical batch" shape for any reason, they need to pair it with a server-side deduplication mechanism keyed on a stable per-chunk identifier that survives the retry, and the runbook / staged-enablement record has to be updated to authorize that deduplication path. As the design stands today, that authorization has not been granted, and a fixture that does not assert deduplication is not evidence that deduplication is in place.

  - The "logical batch" framing in the convenience change is doing real work here — it is what causes the retry to resend chunk A. The deployed design's split-before-retry rule implicitly requires the retry layer to operate on chunks, not on logical batches. Any fix should remove the logical-batch handle from the retry path or scope it so it cannot trigger a replay of an already-accepted chunk.

Net: the convenience change should not ship in its current form. The pre-transmission split is acceptable; the retry path and the fixture both need to be rewritten so that retry after partial success is per-chunk, the success criterion is unique-accepted-points, and the design's no-duplication-after-partial-success rule is honored rather than worked around.

Duplication defect under automatic splitting

The defect is not that automatic splitting creates two transmissions of the same logical batch. It is that automatic splitting creates multiple sub-batches, each of which must independently satisfy the same retry contract that a single batch currently satisfies — and any failure of that per-sub-batch contract produces duplicate stored points, not merely duplicate attempts.

Concretely, if the SDK auto-splits a 10,000-point logical batch into two 5,000-point sub-batches before transmission, the receiving service now has two distinct ingestion units where it used to have one. The dedup window that suppresses a duplicated attempt for a single batch has to suppress a duplicated attempt for each sub-batch, on the same horizon, with the same margin. Three failure modes produce duplicate stored data:

  - Unstable sub-batch identity on retry. The SDK re-derives sub-batch identifiers per attempt (or per split). The server cannot tell a retry from a new submission. Each point in the overlap is stored twice.
  - Dedup retention shorter than the retry horizon. The server forgets the first sub-batch before the retry arrives. The retry is treated as new and the sub-batch is written again.
  - Non-deterministic split boundary. The SDK splits 10,000 points into (5,000, 5,000) on attempt 1 and (4,500, 5,500) on attempt 2. Sub-batches no longer align. The partial overlap writes duplicate points; the rest is silently lost.

This is the duplication defect. It is distinct from a duplicated batch attempt (two transmissions, dedup catches it). It is duplicate stored data, which dedup cannot catch once any of the three failure modes above has occurred.

Retry-state guarantees required

These are the conditions the SDK and receiving service must hold for automatic splitting to remain safe:

  a. Stable per-sub-batch retry identity. Once the SDK assigns an identifier to a sub-batch on first transmission, that identifier must be reused for every retry of that sub-batch within the supported retry horizon. Re-derivation on retry is prohibited.
  b. Server-side deduplication retention. The receiving service must retain dedup state for each sub-batch identifier for at least the documented retry horizon plus an explicit safety margin. The margin is a documented value, not a default; a five-minute retention against a fifteen-minute horizon is unsafe.
  c. No retry of validation failures. Oversized or otherwise permanently-invalid sub-batches must not enter the retry path. They must remain unsent until the caller corrects the input. This is the defect in `sphere-sdk-java#734`.
  d. Split before first transmission. Splitting is a pre-transformation of the logical batch, not a retry strategy. The SDK must not split on retry in a way that changes the sub-batch partition relative to the original attempt.
  e. Sub-batch size bound preserved under retry. Retried sub-batches must still satisfy the documented size limit. A retry that would itself be oversized is a defect, not a transient failure.
  f. Durable commit before ack visibility. The server must commit the sub-batch durably before the ack is emitted, so a retry after a lost ack returns the same committed result rather than re-applying.

Caller-visible-result guarantees required

These are the conditions the caller must be able to rely on:

  g. Identical committed result on retry. A retried sub-batch identifier returns the same committed result as the original attempt: same accepted-point count, same batch identifier, no second application. This is the existing single-batch contract extended to sub-batches.
  h. Logical-batch either-or-nothing. From the caller's perspective, a logical batch is either fully delivered (all points stored exactly once) or failed (no duplicate storage; caller can identify which sub-batches did not commit).
  i. No silent duplication. The caller must never observe stored point count exceeding attempted point count for a logical batch under any retry pattern. Any code path that can produce that outcome is a defect.
  j. Stable error classification. The caller must be able to distinguish validation errors (do not retry unchanged), transient errors (retry eligible within horizon), and committed-and-acked (do not retry). Auto-splitting must not collapse these categories.
  k. Ack as durability boundary. The documented ack is the durability boundary. Beyond it, retries do not change stored state. Before it, retries may return either the in-progress or committed result, but must not duplicate.
  l. Failure isolation between sub-batches. A failure in one sub-batch must not silently mark the whole logical batch as failed at the caller, and must not cause already-committed sibling sub-batches to be retried as part of the same logical-batch retry.

What this does not require

  - The server does not need to know that sub-batches were produced by client-side splitting. From its perspective, each sub-batch is an independent ingestion with its own identity, dedup window, and ack. The "logical batch" is a client-side concept.
  - The SDK does not need to commit all sub-batches atomically to satisfy these guarantees; per-sub-batch dedup plus the logical-batch either-or-nothing rule at the caller is sufficient.
  - The retry horizon does not need to be universal; it is a documented, per-service value with a stated safety margin.

In short: if the SDK keeps automatic splitting, it accepts responsibility for stable per-sub-batch identities and deterministic split boundaries, and the receiving service accepts responsibility for per-sub-batch dedup retention across the documented retry horizon plus margin. Anything less reintroduces the duplication defect that the 8,000-point local rejection was chosen to avoid.

This is a parser correctness bug, not a stylistic or cosmetic issue. The current behavior violates three reasonable invariants at once, and the "successful reload" return value is actively misleading because it does not reflect the route table that was actually loaded.

Three things make it serious:

  1. Silent data loss. Two entries with ID `payments-primary` mean one entry's definition is discarded without warning. The loader reports success because it measures "did the parser return without panicking," not "was the parsed route table internally consistent." The operator who wrote both entries almost certainly did not intend for one of them to vanish.

  2. Order-dependent behavior. Reversing file order changes which target is active for the same logical input. That is non-deterministic from a configuration-intent standpoint. Whether priority 10 (current target) or priority 40 (fallback) wins should not depend on which line came last in the file. Any reliance on map insertion order for selection is a structural problem in the parser, not a property of the config.

  3. Validation runs after the fact. Inserting into a Go map keyed by route ID and then "checking uniqueness" against that same map is too late — by the time you check, the first entry has already been overwritten and is gone. The duplicate has to be caught either with a parallel seen-set during insertion, by detecting an existing key on insert, or by a pre-insert sweep over the parsed entries. Once it sits in a map, the evidence of the duplicate is structural, not visible.

Suggested fix shape:

  - Reject (or surface as a hard error) on duplicate route ID at parse time. Do not let the map overwrite hide the conflict.
  - The error should name both entries' source positions (file + line or offset) so the operator can resolve it without guessing.
  - If the project intentionally supports priority-based selection among entries with the same ID, that has to be an explicit, documented merge step — not an accident of map insertion order. Either way, the duplicate has to be visible to the operator, not silent.

Test gaps this exposes:

  - No test for duplicate route IDs, or the test only asserts last-seen-wins rather than surfacing the conflict.
  - No test asserting the route table is deterministic across file orderings for the same logical config. Given the prior priority-and-canonical-form work (the metrics-router#506 shape — sort by configured integer priority and normalized pattern, hash the canonical byte sequence), there should already be a fixture that proves repeated reloads of an identical config produce one digest and one active generation. That fixture does not currently cover the duplicate-ID case, because dropping an entry from a map still produces a stable digest for the entries that remain. Determinism of the surviving set is not the same as correctness of the full set.
  - The "successful reload" signal should distinguish "load completed" from "load completed without conflicts" if conflicts are intended to be non-fatal, and the current test collapses those two cases.

Connection to prior memory:

  The closest prior bug I have on file is the merge behavior where overlapping label predicates let an alphabetically-later rule win over a more-specific one. The fix for that one was to sort routes by configured integer priority and normalized pattern and hash a canonical form. That fix is correct for its scope — it makes the surviving route set deterministic and the digest reproducible — but it is orthogonal to this gap. Sorting and canonicalizing only helps if both entries actually make it into the sorted set, and here the map drops one before sorting ever sees it. The duplicate-ID case is a separate invariant, and the current parser change has not addressed it.

What I would require before approval:

  - A duplicate-ID test that fails on the current code and passes after the fix, with a fixture that exercises the specific `payments-primary` shape you described (two entries, distinct targets, distinct priorities).
  - A determinism test asserting that reversing the file order either produces identical route tables or produces a parse error naming both source positions — not a silently different active target.
  - A clear answer to whether duplicate IDs are intended to be a parse error or an explicit priority-based merge. The current code accidentally implements "last writer wins by file order," which is neither.

If you can share the PR ID or a link to the diff, I can check whether the parser change actually adds the duplicate-ID check or only the priority/digest determinism — those are different invariants and only one of them is broken by the scenario you described.

DUPLICATE-IDENTITY AND ORDER-DEPENDENCE DEFECT

The defect arises when a candidate routing-rules configuration can be observed in two ways that should be the same logical entry but produce different downstream effects depending on how the input was parsed. There are two failure modes that combine into the actual risk.

  1. Duplicate identity. Two entries in the same candidate generation resolve to the same canonical identity (same key tuple, same normalized rule expression, same effective route signature) but were constructed from distinct inputs (different key ordering, different whitespace, different label separators, missing-label defaults applied at different points). If the pipeline treats them as one entry, downstream matchers see fewer routes than the source intended. If the pipeline treats them as two entries with a shared identity, the registry contains a logically duplicated matcher and one of them is silently authoritative. Either way, the candidate's identity no longer uniquely identifies its matchers.

  2. Order dependence. The same set of source entries, presented in two different orders, produces a candidate generation whose observable identity, default-fill behavior, or per-generation normalization diverges. The matcher captures per-generation defaults for missing labels and normalization, so identical rule-expression strings can carry different effective semantics across generations. If order affects what gets registered, validated, or activated, the candidate's identity is no longer a function of the input alone; it is a function of input AND iteration order, which makes equality, drift checks, and rollback targets unstable.

Combined: a candidate can pass validation while carrying an identity that is neither unique within itself nor stable across reorders. The active-generation pointer can then reference a generation whose observable behavior drifts across reloads even with byte-identical input, and a duplicate inserted under one identity can outlive its sibling under another across generations.

VALIDATION GUARANTEES

  - Candidate identity is a pure function of the validated, normalized input. Two byte-identical inputs produce identical candidate identity regardless of source order, parser internals, or worker partition.
  - Within a single candidate, identity is unique. Any entry whose canonical identity duplicates an earlier entry in the same candidate is rejected at validation, with the duplicated identity and the conflicting source positions reported; duplicates are not silently coalesced.
  - Validation runs to completion on the full candidate before any matcher, key, or default-fill is exposed to the live registry. A candidate that begins inserting into the process-wide registry and then fails a later step leaves no partial registration visible to readers.
  - Validation outcomes are partitioned into three observable classes: syntax failure (rejected without semantic evaluation), semantic failure (rejected with the failed rule and reason), and validation success (advanced to apply). Partial outcomes are not represented as success.
  - Default-fill, normalization, and missing-label resolution are deterministic per generation and documented as part of the generation's identity contract, so identical rule-expression strings cannot silently acquire different effective semantics across generations.

FAILED-RELOAD GUARANTEES

  - The previously active configuration is unchanged by any failed reload attempt. A reload that fails at syntax, semantic validation, or partial worker-apply leaves the active generation pointer, the active matcher set, and the active default-fill contract exactly as they were before the attempt began.
  - A failed candidate is fully retired: no matcher, identity, or registry slot survives past the cleanup window. Cleanup is bounded in time and resource use so that a flood of failed reloads cannot exhaust the registry.
  - During the failed-reload interval the health endpoint distinguishes three states without conflating them: attempted (parsed but not validated), validated (passed validation but not yet activated, or activated and rolled back), and active (the currently serving generation). The previously active generation remains reportable as active throughout the interval.
  - No pointer to a failed candidate's matchers, defaults, or identity is reachable from active readers or from new validation paths before the candidate's resources are released.
  - Restoration of the previously active configuration on reload failure is unconditional; the failure path does not require an additional rollback signal to restore prior state.

ACTIVE-GENERATION GUARANTEES

  - At any observable instant, at most one generation is active. There is no interval during which two generations serve simultaneously or in which the active pointer is undefined for active readers.
  - The active generation is immutable for its serving lifetime. Matchers, default-fill, normalization, and identity are fixed at activation; in-place mutation of an active generation is not permitted.
  - A reader that has acquired a reference to the active generation retains a stable view for the duration of its query, even if the active pointer has advanced to a successor generation. Successor activation does not invalidate in-flight readers on the prior generation.
  - Concurrent readers see the same active generation for the same identity within a query. Two readers querying the same key during the same window observe the same generation instance; cache identity is preserved across concurrent acquisitions.
  - A generation is retired only after all acquired readers have released. Retired generations remain queryable by identity for diagnostics, drift checks, and rollback reference, and are cleaned up on a bounded schedule.
  - The active generation's identity is stable across reloads of byte-identical input, so drift checks, parity fixtures, and rollback targets remain meaningful.

These are the invariants the owner needs the system to satisfy. They are stated without prescribing parser, registry, or pointer-acquisition implementation; any implementation that meets all of them is acceptable, and any implementation that fails any one of them re-introduces the defect.

Review of the SDK-facing ingest-edge change

This is a wire-contract bug, not a style question.

What the implementation writes
  random int in [1200, 3000] as `Retry-After: <integer>`

What RFC 7231 §7.1.3 / RFC 9110 §10.2.3 say
  integer Retry-After = delay-seconds = 1*DIGIT
  No unit. Integer form is seconds. There is no milliseconds syntax.

So on the wire, 1200-3000 means 1200-3000 seconds = 20-50 minutes. That is what every spec-compliant SDK, browser, and generic HTTP library will do. The fixture is non-standard (it parses the integer as milliseconds), so the unit test passes while the contract is broken. The test does not validate production behavior; it validates a second, parallel, non-standard interpretation.

What the implementation intends
  1-3 second randomized backoff.

What the implementation actually delivers on the wire
  20-50 minute backoff for any compliant client.

What the standing record says production Retry-After is
  Randomized 1, 2, or 3 seconds, written as integer seconds. Multiple direct confirmations:
    "response builder selects Retry-After values of one, two, or three seconds"
    "queue-cap responses carried randomized Retry-After values of one, two, or three seconds"
    "all queue-cap responses retained randomized Retry-After values"
    "customer was receiving Retry-After values between one and three seconds"
    SDK 2.6.0 post-release queue-cap test: "retries follow the 1/2/3-second Retry-After delays"
  The 72-hour production report also describes "randomized Retry-After responses ranging from one to three seconds."

So the change does not preserve the existing behavior. It moves the retry delay from 1-3 s to 20-50 min on the wire, with a fixture that masks the move. If this ships, every compliant SDK that hits a 429 backs off for 20-50 minutes per request. That is a regression in latency, in retry-induced load (clients giving up and re-issuing later in much larger waves), and in fairness (low-volume tenants now blocked on the same long backoff as everyone else).

Two correlated problems
  1. Implementation domain is wrong: it must be {1, 2, 3}, not [1200, 3000].
  2. Fixture domain is wrong: it must parse the integer as integer seconds, not milliseconds.

Minimum fix that preserves the documented 1-3 s randomized retry on the wire

No RFC-compliant way to send sub-second precision via integer Retry-After exists; the HTTP-date form is the only standard alternative and is not appropriate for 1-3 seconds. So the right answer is integer seconds, not milliseconds, not fractional, not HTTP-date.

If yes, I want to see that evidence before considering the milliseconds interpretation viable; if no, the milliseconds interpretation is purely a fixture artifact and the wire is unambiguously 20-50 minutes.

The unit contract is set by RFC 9110 §10.2.3 (formerly RFC 7231 §7.1.3): the `Retry-After` header field carries either an HTTP-date or a non-negative decimal integer of seconds. The unit is seconds; there is no provision for milliseconds, fractional seconds, or unit suffixes. "Decimal integer" in the RFC means base-10 digits, not a fractional value.

Why millisecond integers break the contract

  A spec-compliant client parses `Retry-After: 1500` as 1500 seconds (~25 minutes), not 1500 ms. The parser uses the documented unit; it does not guess. So if a server change emits the intended delay in milliseconds but inside the seconds-shaped field, every compliant client backs off roughly 1000× longer than intended — `1000` ≈ 16.7 min, `2000` ≈ 33.3 min, `3000` = 50 min. The result is not a slow client; it is a server lying about the unit.

  A non-compliant client that "helpfully" assumes milliseconds would do the opposite — back off 1000× shorter than the server intends, producing the thundering-herd condition the header is supposed to prevent. Either way the unit is wrong on the wire. The randomization can stay; only the unit must match the contract.

Compliant wire-format for a randomized 1–3 second delay

    HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
    Retry-After: 1
    ... or ...
    Retry-After: 2
    ... or ...
    Retry-After: 3

  Constraints the server must honor:

    - Value is a non-negative integer of seconds (1*DIGIT).
    - No fractional seconds (`1.5` is non-conformant).
    - No unit suffix (no `ms`, no `s`).
    - No leading zeros beyond a single `0` (no `01`, no `+1`).
    - No mixing with HTTP-date in the same field.
    - All three values (1, 2, 3) must appear in the observed distribution; the randomization must remain intact.

Interoperability tests required before the change can proceed

  1. Wire-format conformance. Every 429 response carries exactly one `Retry-After` header whose value is an integer in {1, 2, 3}. Assert: no decimals, no units, no negatives, no zero, no HTTP-date variant.

  2. Distribution test. Over a representative sample window, all three values (1, 2, 3) appear at non-trivial counts. Catches both "always 1" regressions and any accidental collapse to a fixed value.

  3. Cross-client parser test. The response is fed to a battery of compliant HTTP clients — `curl`, Python `requests`, Go `net/http`, Node `axios`, Java `HttpClient`, Ruby `Net::HTTP`, plus a bare-spec parser — and each is observed to interpret the value as 1, 2, or 3 seconds, never as 1000 / 2000 / 3000 ms.

  4. Negative-space test. Scan production responses for any value outside {1, 2, 3}: `0`, `4+`, decimal forms, scientific notation, ms-suffixed strings, leading `+`, and HTTP-date format. Zero hits required.

  5. Retry-loop test. A compliant client that honors `Retry-After` and nothing else is driven through a 429 burst. The observed inter-retry delays are ≥ 1 s and ≤ 3 s, and each retry starts no earlier than the header value.

  6. Anti-pattern test. Reproduce the previously observed "three immediate retries in the same second, before the application code could inspect the header" client behavior to confirm the header-inspection fix still binds against the new wire format — i.e., the client no longer fires before reading the value.

  7. Regression test for unchanged semantics. Error rate and p99 stay within 2 % of baseline during the canary; no series dropped; no pod restarts; the existing 250 ms → 30 s full-jitter exponential-backoff / 5-attempt client behavior still passes its 96-injected-failure acceptance check.

  8. Runbook and cutover alignment. `rb_ingest_edge_cutover` records that randomized 1–3 s `Retry-After` is the production behavior, and the canary summary records the observed value distribution (1 s, 2 s, 3 s counts) at the checkpoint so a future reader can verify the unit stayed seconds and the randomization survived.

The change can proceed when tests 1–8 all pass and the ingest-edge build emits the seconds-shaped header on every overflow path while preserving the randomized 1–3 s distribution — i.e., the wire-format change is a no-op relative to today's behavior, and the ms-form is rejected at the server boundary before it reaches the response.

Review of the ingest-edge graceful-shutdown change as described.

What's wrong
  The shutdown sequence you described is: readiness false → listener close → dispatch loop exit. That order stops accepting and starts tearing down, but it does NOT drain accepted work. The dispatch loop exits while per-tenant queues still hold items, so those items never reach a terminal state.

Why the 37 count matters
  For a service that uses 202 to mean "durably accepted, downstream pending," a silent exit with accepted work in memory is not just a metric gap — it's a contract break. The client believes the batch is durably queued; the server records no success, no rejection, no cancellation, and no refused-point. From the client's view those 37 are safely in. From the server's view they were never finished. If WAL durability is on the request path before the dispatch loop hands off, the WAL record is there but the server never returned a final response. Either way, the missing terminal record is the bug.

What a correct graceful shutdown needs
  Readiness false and listener close are necessary but not sufficient. The accepted-and-queued tail has to reach a terminal state before the loop exits. Two acceptable shapes, and the choice should be explicit:

    1. Drain to completion. Loop keeps running until every per-tenant queue is empty and every in-flight handler has returned. Then exit. Test: every accepted request has a terminal record matching its acceptance.
    2. Refuse-with-retry. After readiness false and listener close, the loop walks the queues and produces a refused-point / retryable-rejection terminal for each remaining item before exiting. Test: every accepted request has a terminal record, and the terminal class for the drained tail is "refused" or equivalent, not absent.

  Mixed or implicit behavior is what's there now: readiness and listener close say "graceful," but the loop exit says "abandon." That mismatch is what produced 163 of 200.

Fixture verdict
  The 200 / 163 / 37 split is the right diagnostic. It cleanly partitions: 163 reached a terminal on their own (handlers finished before loop exit), 37 did not (queue abandonment). The fixture is reproducing the bug, not a flake.

What I would block on before any further promotion
  - Pick a shape: drain to terminal, or refuse-with-retry to terminal. State it in the PR.
  - Add a regression that asserts every accepted request produces exactly one terminal record across the full SIGTERM lifecycle (including the queued tail), and fails on any missing terminal.
  - Re-run the 200-request fixture. Pass criterion is 200/200 terminal records, with the tail class explicit and matching the chosen shape.
  - Production remains unchanged, which is correct — do not promote until the above passes.

One thing I am not asserting: I don't have a PR number for this change in front of me, so I'm reviewing the described behavior, not a specific diff. If you want a comment on the actual PR, send the ID and I'll anchor the review there.

Why changing readiness cannot abandon accepted queued work

An acceptance is a commitment the system has already extended to a caller. Once the system has acknowledged the work — by durably accepting it, returning a positive receipt, taking a queue slot, or recording it as its own responsibility — the caller is justified in treating it as no longer their concern and acting on that assumption (closing out the request, freeing caller-side resources, moving to the next item).

A subsequent readiness flip that silently discards or drops accepted work breaks that contract in three concrete ways the owner must prevent:

  1. Invisible data loss. Accepted items vanish without the caller ever learning. The caller cannot recover, retry, or escalate because no signal was returned. In the metrics-router context specifically, an accepted point is an observation the system has taken responsibility for; dropping it leaves a hole in the series that downstream alerting, billing, or reconciliation cannot distinguish from a genuine gap in source data.

  2. Retry ambiguity. Without a terminal signal, the caller does not know whether to retry, give up, or escalate. Retrying risks double-counting accepted work that may still complete; not retrying loses work that was in fact abandoned. Both outcomes corrupt accounting on the caller side and on the system side.

  3. Unprovable accounting. If accepted work can disappear without a corresponding terminal event, the system's view of accepted-minus-completed can no longer be reconciled from outside. The operator cannot prove that no abandonment occurred, and any "no points dropped" claim becomes unfalsifiable.

The readiness signal is a contract about future acceptance, not a permission to revoke past acceptance. The owner must therefore guarantee that every item already accepted reaches one of two observable terminal states before the readiness change takes effect on that item.

---

The five guarantees the owner must meet

These are deliberately implementation-agnostic. They define what must be true, not how to achieve it. Any implementation that satisfies all five — HTTP drain, gRPC drain, queue-side prefetch termination, lease-based handoff, or anything else — is acceptable.

  1. Quiesce.

     Before the readiness signal changes state, the system must stop accepting new work. Quiesce defines the frontier: after it, no additional item enters the accepted set, so the owner knows the boundary of in-flight and queued work that must later be drained or rejected.

     Quiesce is a precondition, not a resolution. It bounds the problem; it does not solve it.

     Owner-visible evidence: a timestamp or sequence boundary after which no new acceptances occurred. From that boundary forward, the set of accepted work is closed.

  2. Drain-or-explicit-rejection.

     Every item accepted before quiesce must end in exactly one of two terminal states:

       a. Drained — the item is processed to completion and the normal completion signal is delivered.

       b. Explicitly rejected — the system returns a terminal response to the caller indicating the work was not done and giving the caller enough information to act (a retry-after, a rejection reason class, or equivalent). The wire format is not specified here, but the response must be a real response, not a connection drop, a timeout-by-silence, or a swallowed error.

     Neither path is acceptable for items that were already accepted. Both paths are acceptable as long as every item follows one.

  3. Terminal-response.

     Explicit rejection must be terminal in the protocol sense: the caller can observe it, distinguish it from "still in flight" and from "completed", and act on it. A terminal response carries:

       — a semantic class sufficient to drive correct caller behavior (for example, "retryable later" versus "do not retry");
       — observability to the operator, so accounting can prove what happened;
       — durability sufficient that a retried item is not double-counted as both rejected and accepted.

     What the response says is implementation-defined; that it is a real, observable, terminal event is not.

  4. Accounting.

     The owner must be able to prove, from external observation, that no accepted work was abandoned. The accounting invariant is:

         accepted  =  completed  +  rejected (terminal)

     where "rejected" counts only items for which a terminal rejection response was delivered. Items accepted but neither completed nor terminally rejected are forbidden — they are the abandonment the readiness change must not produce.

     The accounting must be reconcilable from the operator's view: the operator can read accepted, completed, and rejected counts and verify the equation holds across the readiness-change window. A claimed-zero "abandoned" is unfalsifiable without this reconciliation.

  5. Regression-test.

     There must be an automated test that exercises the readiness-flip path and verifies the other four guarantees. The test must, at minimum:

       — drive work into the accepted state under normal readiness;
       — flip readiness while accepted work is still pending;
       — verify quiesce: no new acceptances occur after the flip;
       — verify drain-or-rejection: every accepted item reaches completed or terminally rejected;
       — verify terminal-response: the caller can observe the rejection, classify it, and act on it without ambiguity;
       — verify accounting: the invariant accepted = completed + rejected holds across the window, and zero items are unaccounted.

     The test runs on every change to readiness, drain, rejection, or queue-handling code. It must fail loudly and block rollout if any guarantee breaks.

---

How the guarantees compose

Quiesce closes the new-acceptance frontier so the obligation set is bounded. Drain-or-explicit-rejection closes every obligation inside that set. Terminal-response makes the rejection branch observable and actionable. Accounting proves, externally, that nothing leaked. Regression-test proves the system will continue to satisfy all four on every future change.

A readiness change that does not satisfy all five is a contract violation by the owner, regardless of how cleanly the underlying shutdown procedure ran.

The proposed predicate `lease_owned == true` is insufficient and would reintroduce a serving defect during the lease-acquisition-to-snapshot-catch-up window.

Why it fails:

  lease_owned becomes true at 14:03:11, but the new holder cannot
  actually serve until the serving gate opens at 14:03:23 when
  snapshot catch-up completes. The 12-second gap is exactly the
  window in which:

    - Readiness reports 200
    - The serving gate is closed
    - Routed requests receive 503

  This is not split-brain (the old holder's gate is already closed,
  as you note), but it is a user-visible serving defect that the
  readiness signal hides rather than surfaces. A readiness predicate
  that reports "ready" while the gate is closed defeats the purpose
  of readiness, since load balancers route traffic on that signal.
  The defect is on the new-holder side: lease acquisition is a
  transition, not a steady serving state.

The right predicate:

  Readiness must reflect whether the pod can serve, not just
  whether lease ownership has transferred. The minimum sufficient
  predicate is the conjunction:

    lease_owned == true AND serving_gate_open == true

  (or the equivalent post-snapshot-catch-up state; the exact
  internal name depends on the implementation). Both conjuncts
  are necessary; neither alone is sufficient. Readiness should
  flip to true exactly when the serving gate opens and flip to
  false atomically when lease is lost.

Distinguishing this from prior fixes:

  - shard-keeper#197 corrected the old holder to atomically close
    its serving gate on lease-loss notification before any routing
    read could respond. That covers the old-holder side of the
    failover and remains valid; the staged rollout evidence showed
    cache readiness preceding routed-request admission in every
    sampled trace, and the supervised verification showed the
    old-holder gate closing in 13 ms.
  - The current proposal addresses the new-holder side but stops
    too early, at lease acquisition rather than at serving-gate
    open. The lease-acquisition event is not a steady state; the
    post-snapshot-catch-up state is.

What the predicate should NOT do:

  - It should not be tightened to require zero in-flight work or
    zero lag. Those are separate capacity gates, not basic serving
    safety, and over-restricting readiness can reintroduce the
    kind of stuck-not-ready defect this work is meant to prevent.
  - It should not depend on a poll interval. The historical 310 ms
    serving-after-lease-loss pattern on the old holder (its
    500 ms lease-validity poll) showed exactly why polling for
    lease validity fails under failover.

Bottom line:

  Reject `lease_owned == true` as the readiness predicate. Require
  the conjunction with the post-snapshot-catch-up state so readiness
  becomes true exactly when the serving gate opens and becomes false
  atomically on lease loss. This preserves the fail-closed serving-
  gate behavior on both sides of the failover and eliminates the
  12-second 503 window without introducing split-brain or poll-
  based lag.

Readiness defect

The serving path was treating lease ownership as a poll-detected signal rather than as a synchronous serving-eligibility input. The observed symptom was that an old lease holder continued serving read-only routing snapshots for 310 ms after its valid lease had ended, because the serving-gate's lease-validity check ran on a 500 ms periodic poll. For that 310 ms window the instance was no longer the lease owner but its gate was still "open," so it kept issuing routing responses sourced from a snapshot that a new owner had already taken responsibility for.

The defect is not "we polled too slowly." It is that serving eligibility was derived from cached lease state, not from current lease state. Lease ownership at time T does not entitle an instance to serve at time T + poll-interval, and any optimization that retains the poll as the primary detector — or that pushes notification alongside an unchanged poll cadence without changing the close-before-next-response invariant — leaves that gap intact. A correct optimization makes lease-loss notification close the serving gate synchronously, before any subsequent routing response, with the periodic poll only as a backup detector.

Why "lease ownership alone" is the wrong frame

Lease ownership is a prerequisite for serving, but it is not equivalent to serving eligibility. A holder must also (a) know it is the current owner at the moment of each response, (b) have a usable route table installed, (c) have cache readiness preceding routed-request admission, and (d) not be in a quarantine state such as host-maintenance rejoin isolation. Readiness that flips to true on lease acquisition and only checks ownership again on the next poll confuses "I own the lease" with "I am eligible to serve right now." The optimization is approvable only when readiness is a function of all four conditions evaluated synchronously on the serving path, not a function of the last poll.

Serving-gate tests required before approval

  1. Lease-loss synchronous close. When the lease-loss notification arrives, the gate must close before the next routing response is issued. Verify under load that no response after the notification timestamp carries a snapshot from the prior generation.

  2. In-flight race. A response that was already being constructed at the instant of lease loss must either complete on the still-valid snapshot with the very next request refused, or be aborted with a clean error envelope. The test must show no response sourced from a stale snapshot issued after the notification, and no silent partial response.

  3. Notification-path failure mode. With the notification channel deliberately broken, the 500 ms poll must still close the gate within one poll cycle, and the test must record the latency bound (target: ≤ poll interval + small constant). This bounds the user-visible worst case when the primary detector fails.

  4. No spurious rejection after transient loss. If lease is regained between a notification loss and the next poll, the gate must not latch closed. A bounded transient-loss-then-regain scenario must show continuous eligibility once ownership is restored, with no gap wider than the documented latency bound.

  5. Snapshot-absence readiness. Readiness must remain false while the route table is absent (`TestReadinessFailsWhileRouteTableAbsent`-style assertion). The proposed `if currentRouteTable() == nil { return Ready }` branch, if present anywhere, must not exist in the merged change.

  6. Cache-readiness precedes routed-request admission. In sampled traces, every routed response must be preceded by a cache-readiness signal from the same instance. Any response without a prior readiness signal fails the test.

  7. Negative call-order acceptance. The shared readiness wrapper must evaluate ownership, snapshot presence, cache readiness, and quarantine state in a defined order, with a regression test asserting each negative ordering (e.g., snapshot-present but ownership lost → not ready; cache-ready but quarantined → not ready).

Routing tests required before approval

  1. No split-brain. Across a controlled failover in staging, at no observed instant do two instances both serve a routing response. The test samples both holders during the handover window and asserts at most one serves.

  2. Snapshot integrity on the new holder. The new holder's first 100 served responses in staging must reference a route table whose generation matches the generation it reported as active. Any mismatch fails.

  3. External-field containment. Sampled external response fields contain no internal-only metadata. No internal room links or other internal identifiers leak through the new holder's responses.

  4. Accepted-forward / receipt parity. Edge-gateway accepted-forward counts match collector receipt counts across the failover window, with no unexplained gap.

  5. Handoff latency is not interpreted as staleness. A slow handoff that completes correctly must not be flagged as evidence of stale serving; the alerting path must classify it as a separate availability investigation, not as a readiness regression.

  6. Tenant-authorization and permission-denial envelope remain enforced. Tenant-authorization enforcement and the permission-denial response envelope must hold on both old and new holders throughout the handover. No customer access is requested or granted by this change.

  7. Bounded rollout numbers. Canary error rate and p99 stay within 2% of baseline; accepted, dropped, and restart counts remain clean; cleanup pauses stay inside the existing owner-led window hard stop.

Handoff tests required before approval

  1. Quiesce before readiness=false. The graceful-shutdown path must drain accepted queued work or explicitly reject each in-flight request with a terminal response before flipping readiness to false. The staging fixture showed 37 of 200 accepted requests with no terminal record when the dispatch loop exited with queued work remaining; the merged change must reduce that to zero, and a regression test must fail on any non-zero count.

  2. No abandonment of accepted work. Readiness=false must not be permitted while accepted work is still queued in memory. The owner must meet quiesce, drain-or-explicit-rejection, terminal-response, accounting, and regression-test guarantees as a single bundle — a change that satisfies some but not all is not approvable.

  3. Rejoin isolation. A rejoining instance (e.g., after host maintenance) must remain isolated until it reports the current active generation. A missing generation report does not count as healthy. After it reports the current generation, the ordinary consistency, parity, dropped-series, route, and health checks must all pass before isolation is released. The rejoin rule does not change ownership, open an owner-led window, or authorize a configuration push.

  4. Classify clean serving safety and degraded availability independently. The supervised checklist for any additional session must allow the system to be classified as having clean serving safety and degraded availability simultaneously — these are not mutually exclusive, and a test that conflates them cannot stand.

  5. Boundary conditions preserved. Validated value, omission, rejection, and tenant-budget conditions remain the gates for any rollout gated by this change; none of them is relaxed by the optimization.

Framing for the review

The reviewer response should describe the readiness-review result as bounded: the serving-gate closes synchronously on lease loss, the new holder cannot serve until cache readiness and current-generation report are both present, no accepted work is abandoned at shutdown, and the slow-handoff path is treated as availability, not staleness. The remaining execution gate is the staged canary with the seven routing tests above run against the staging fixture before any production movement. The response must not imply that tenant isolation passed or that customer access may open; no customer access has been requested or granted by this change.

WHY THE CURSOR MUST BE BOTH CRYPTOGRAPHICALLY AND SEMANTICALLY BOUND TO THE AUTHORIZED TENANT

The cursor is a stateful token that, by itself, encodes enough information to drive a subsequent preview lookup. Two independent binding layers are required, and each guards a different failure mode:

1. Cryptographic binding (HMAC or signature over the cursor payload) prevents a tenant from tampering with cursor fields (tenant_id, service identifier, lookup family, record position, issuance context) and prevents a tenant from forging a cursor that did not originate from the authorization wrapper. Without it, the cursor is just opaque bytes the application trusts on faith, and a tenant can rewrite tenant_id to any value.

2. Semantic binding (cursor payload explicitly carries tenant_id and lookup family, and the server interprets these as authorization-bearing fields, not as opaque metadata) ensures that even if the cryptographic layer were bypassed (key leak, version mismatch, replay across rotation), application logic still rejects cross-tenant usage because the cursor's meaning, not just its bytes, names the authorized tenant.

A cursor that is only cryptographically bound is still vulnerable if application code interprets it generically ("give me the next page") without checking tenant identity inside the payload. A cursor that is only semantically bound is vulnerable to tampering because a tenant can rewrite tenant_id and re-submit. Both layers are necessary, and both must be checked before any adapter call.

Why missing generation evidence cannot satisfy the fail-closed rejoin gate

The rejoin gate is fail-closed by design. Its purpose is to keep a stale-generation instance from re-entering the active fleet and contaminating the metrics-router's view of the world. The gate is a precondition chain — every required input must be present and verified before isolation is released, and any missing or unverified input defaults to the safe state (isolation maintained). The April 15 runbook-clarification scope explicitly covers this rejoin check; the April 12 incident is treated here only as background showing what a clean gate looks like when evidence is present, not reopened.

Missing generation evidence breaks the chain at its foundation:

1. The current-generation report is the only signal that proves the instance has actually loaded the expected generation. Without it, there is no way to confirm the instance is not still holding retired state, an older config, or a partially-applied change.

2. The downstream checks (consistency, parity, dropped-series, route, health) are evaluated against an implicit baseline that assumes a known current generation. Without that baseline the checks cannot distinguish "everything is fine" from "we have no idea what state this instance is in." A passing health check on an instance of unknown generation is not evidence of safety.

3. Missing evidence is not equivalent to negative evidence. The monitor not having observed a generation report could mean the instance is fine but reporting on an unexpected path, the report was lost, the instance is partitioned, or the instance is genuinely stuck. The fail-closed posture refuses to guess — it treats absence as a stop condition.

4. The April 12 evidence pattern (all instances on generation 612, consistency, parity, dropped-series, route, and health checks clean) is exactly what "all conditions met" looks like. The monitor correction specifically addresses the gap that existed before that evidence arrived. Releasing isolation without that evidence would invert the lesson.

5. The contract is conjunctive, not disjunctive: isolation remains until a valid current-generation report arrives AND all five checks pass. "Valid" means a report tied to the expected current generation, not any report of any number. Partial completion of the chain is still "not released."

Tests proving isolation remains until both conditions hold

These tests treat the rejoin gate as a state machine and exercise its boundary conditions. Each has a defined setup, action, and expected outcome. They validate monitor-correction logic; none of them is a deployment authorization.

T1 — No generation report received
  Setup: instance is isolated; no generation report arrives within the expected window.
  Action: rejoin evaluation runs.
  Expected: isolation maintained; alert "no current-generation report"; other checks either not evaluated or evaluated with results insufficient to release.

T2 — Stale generation report
  Setup: instance reports a generation number older than the expected current generation.
  Action: rejoin evaluation runs.
  Expected: isolation maintained; alert "stale generation report"; shape-valid but content-invalid.

T3 — Generation missing, other checks would pass
  Setup: no generation report; consistency, parity, dropped-series, route, and health are synthetically set to pass.
  Action: rejoin evaluation runs.
  Expected: isolation maintained; passing other checks do not compensate for missing generation.

T4 — Valid generation, consistency fails
  Setup: instance reports the expected current generation; active-generation consistency check fails (reported generation does not match the active fleet's view).
  Action: rejoin evaluation runs.
  Expected: isolation maintained; alert "consistency failure despite current-generation report."

T5 — Valid generation, parity fails
  Setup: current generation reported; parity check fails.
  Action: rejoin evaluation runs.
  Expected: isolation maintained; alert "parity failure."

T6 — Valid generation, dropped-series regression
  Setup: current generation reported; dropped-series count is non-zero or has increased versus baseline.

55 minutes, fridge air 44°F, freezer 4°F, items still felt cold

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. PER-ITEM TRIAGE (conservative defaults, not forced discards)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

MILK (assume unopened pasteurized fluid milk)
  Default: KEEP. Use ahead of normal rotation (1–2 days).

EGGS (assume shell eggs, intact)
  Default: KEEP. Normal rotation.

  Default: USE PROMPTLY TODAY, FULLY REHEATED, then discard
  any leftover portion. Most conservative path is to discard
  outright.
  Rationale: Bacillus cereus spores survive cooking and the
  toxin is heat-stable. Reheating does NOT make unsafe rice
  safe. Even in favorable conditions, this is the item where
  conservative guidance diverges.

  the same day, do not re-refrigerate the reheated portion.

RAW CHICKEN — HIGH-RISK ITEM
  Default: KEEP. Cook within 1 day, to 165°F internal.
  Rationale: still cold to touch and 55 min is well under the

  room-temperature rather than cold, or you have an instant-
  read thermometer showing >40°F in the thickest part.

CUT VEGETABLES
  Default: KEEP. Normal rotation, soonest-expiring first.
  Rationale: lower pathogen load than animal products; cut
  surfaces dry quickly which limits growth.
  Lower the bar if: any item is slimy, off-smelling, or

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2. IMMEDIATE COOLING STEPS
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

a. Stop opening the door to "check." Each opening adds warm

b. If your fridge has an external temp display, watch that.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

55 minutes at 44°F air with all items still cold and freezer

Three separable concerns in this reload path:

1. Failure-path lock-hold is wasteful and possibly unbounded.

  A malformed candidate still blocks serving for the full compile window because routeMu.Lock() is taken before parse/compile. The 284-337ms benchmarks are valid-compile numbers; an invalid compile can be faster or slower with no upper bound (regex backtracking, deep recursion, allocation pressure under malformed input). For 12,000 routes, every failed push attempt is a ~300ms serving cliff by default, and there's no cap on the worst case.

2. Successful compile also runs under the lock.

  Every reload, success or failure, holds serving for the full compile duration. If reload attempts are more than rare (push windows, autoscaler-driven refresh, repeated attempts against a misconfiguration), this contributes to steady-state p99. The 100ms cleanup-pause ceiling under the owner-led window is a separate surface, but cumulative reload-lock time during a push window is adjacent and worth measuring together.

3. Compile-under-lock is an architectural choice, not a constraint.

  The standard alternative is copy-on-write:

    - Build the new generation off-lock. The write mutex protects against concurrent reloads (probably via single-flight), not against readers.
    - Run parse, compile, and validation against the side-built structure. Failure returns and the lock is never taken.
    - Take routeMu.Lock() only to swap the activeGeneration pointer.
    - Release. Previous generation stays live for any in-flight readers until cleanup.

  Under this design, the write-lock-held window is microseconds regardless of compile cost, and the failure path can't lock up serving. 12,000 routes is small enough to double-buffer in memory; the live generation is presumably read-only once published, so a fresh build has no synchronization problem.

What I'd want to verify before sign-off:

  - Worst-case bound on failure-path latency, including catastrophic-backtracking shapes of route patterns.
  - Memory budget for an off-lock build alongside the live table.
  - Reload attempt frequency in normal operation and during push windows. Drives steady-state vs burst impact.
  - Whether single-flight on concurrent reloads is intended (otherwise you can thrash building multiple candidate generations and pile up retired generations, which is exactly the axis the owner-led window caps).
  - Whether the 284-337ms benchmarks were measured cold or warm. First-load allocator cost may not match steady-state reloads.

Connections to prior context:

  - metrics-router#506: identical-config produces one digest across 1,000 reloads and retains one active generation. Preserved by swap-on-success semantics. Off-lock build doesn't disturb the digest invariant because the swap is still the only place activeGeneration changes.
  - metrics-router#433 was blocked after six requests were admitted against an absent route table and all six failed. Different shape — here active generation stays valid throughout the compile, so requests aren't admitted-with-failure. But the write-lock window is a different kind of serving impairment: requests are delayed, not failed. Worth flagging the same awareness about reload-path windows and serving.
  - Cardinality Guardrails parity rules apply to label renames, not this directly, but the principle holds: validation runs against the side-built structure before the pointer swap, the same way the failure path rejects a candidate without replacing active generation.
  - Owner-led window caps cleanup pause at 100ms and retired generations at 4. Compile time is a separate surface. If a push window can trigger multiple reload attempts, both surfaces scale together and the effective serving impairment per push is the sum.
