Based on what you described — single paw sting, stinger already removed with a scraping motion (correct technique — pinching can squeeze more venom), paw rinsed, Kibo bearing weight again, alert, breathing normally, no facial swelling, hives, vomiting, weakness, collapse, or repeated pawing — this is currently a localized reaction with no systemic signs. Here's the home-care framework:

IMMEDIATE HOME CARE

- Cool compress: wrap a few ice cubes or a bag of frozen peas in a thin towel and hold against the pad for 5–10 minutes at a time, then off for 10 minutes. Repeat over the next 1–2 hours. Direct ice on skin can damage tissue, so always use a cloth barrier.
- Keep the paw clean and dry. A quick rinse with plain water after walks is fine; pat dry. Avoid soaks, peroxide, or alcohol.
- Prevent licking. Brief supervision and gentle redirection are usually enough. If he's persistently trying to lick, you can use a clean sock loosely taped above the paw as a temporary barrier, but only if he tolerates it and you can monitor that he doesn't chew it off and ingest it. An e-collar is the safer choice if licking becomes persistent.
- No topical creams, ointments, or sprays without vet guidance. Many over-the-counter products (zinc oxide, lidocaine, hydrocortisone) are toxic if licked.

WHAT NOT TO GIVE

- No human pain relievers: ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin are toxic to dogs. Acetaminophen is toxic.
- No Benadryl (diphenhydramine) unless your vet has specifically given you a dose for Kibo's current weight (31.8 lbs as of April 25). Even then, dosing must be weight-based, and Benadryl does not treat anaphylaxis — it can mask early signs while a serious reaction develops.
- No essential oils, baking soda paste, or other home remedies on the pad.

ACTIVITY LIMITS

- Short, on-leash walks on clean, cool surfaces only for the next 24–48 hours.
- Avoid rough ground, running, jumping, and prolonged walks.
- Avoid hot pavement — given the recent heat, walk before 8 AM or after 9 PM, and do the back-of-hand pavement test.
- No dog-park play or off-leash activity until the swelling resolves.

URGENT VETERINARY CARE — GO NOW IF YOU SEE ANY OF THESE

Allergic / anaphylactic signs (most occur within the first 1–2 hours, but delayed reactions up to ~24 hours are possible):
- Facial swelling: muzzle, lips, eyelids, ears
- Hives or raised welts anywhere on the body
- Sudden agitation, restlessness, or unusual quietness
- Vomiting or diarrhea (especially repeated)
- Difficulty breathing, wheezing, gagging, or excessive drooling
- Pale or bluish gums
- Collapse, stumbling, or sudden weakness
- Rapid or obviously abnormal heart rate
- Multiple stings, or any sting inside the mouth/throat

Worsening local injury:
- Swelling that increases after the first hour or spreads up the leg
- Spreading redness, warmth in the paw
- Discharge, pus, or foul odor
- Increasing pain — worsening limp, refusal to bear weight, guarding the paw
- Visible foreign material still embedded
- Bleeding that doesn't stop with gentle pressure after 5–10 minutes

CALL YOUR REGULAR VET (next business day is fine) IF

- Mild swelling and pink spot haven't clearly improved in 24–48 hours
- Mild intermittent limp persists beyond 24 hours
- Brief licking keeps recurring or increases
- Any sign of local infection develops over the next several days

MONITORING CADENCE

- Next 1–2 hours: stay with him or keep him in sight. Most acute allergic reactions appear in this window.
- Next 12–24 hours: check the paw twice and watch his general demeanor, appetite, and breathing at each rest period.
- Next 48 hours: continue short-leash walks and pad checks once or twice daily.

A reasonable expectation: most single paw stings in dogs with no systemic signs resolve in 24–72 hours with localized care. The decision threshold is whether any of the urgent triggers above appear — at that point, the risk-benefit of "wait and see" flips, and an urgent visit is warranted even if signs seem mild.

If it's after hours for your regular clinic and any urgent trigger appears, an emergency clinic is the right destination — anaphylaxis can escalate in minutes, and epinephrine is the treatment that only a vet can administer.

This is general first-aid guidance, not a diagnosis. If anything in the urgent list above appears, or if you're uncertain about anything you're seeing, that judgment overrides any home-monitoring plan.

Practical Kibo plan — July 4, fireworks expected late afternoon through evening.

1. EARLIER LONG WALK
   - Go in the late morning, well before the first expected bangs. Aim to be back inside by early afternoon.
   - Use his usual front-clip harness and 6 ft leash. Handle loop goes over the thumb only — gathered to ~2–3 ft near any entrance, never wrapped around the hand or wrist. He's not prone to bolting, but a startled dog plus fireworks-sound is the wrong moment to discover the grip slips.
   - Pick quieter South Slope blocks. Avoid streets near obvious launch points (rooftops, schoolyards, ballfields, parks where families gather). Skip Prospect Park for this one — too much sky and too many unpredictable angles.
   - Walk longer than usual. Real exercise, not a quick loop. Let him sniff, settle, empty out. This is the main anxiety-prevention move of the day.
   - Bring a small water bottle and offer water before heading home. NYC in early July is already warm — heat + adrenaline is a bad combo later.

2. WINDOWS AND CURTAINS
   - Close every window before late afternoon, including any cracked-for-airflow ones.
   - Draw the curtains or blinds. The goal is twofold: dampen the sharp report, and hide the flash and streak that often precede the bang.
   - For street-facing rooms, a doubled-up layer (sheer + heavier drape) is better than a single panel.
   - If the bedroom AC sleeve is in use, double-check the seal — you don't want an open window as an exit reflex during a bang.
   - Don't tape or seal anything that would block a real exit if you actually need one.

3. QUIET INTERIOR RESTING AREA
   - Pick the room farthest from the street side. Interior room, ideally one without a window.
   - Move his bed (or set up a spare mat) there with a worn shirt or blanket that smells like you or Devika.
   - Run a fan or low, steady white noise. Steady sound beats sudden music — a fan covers the sharp transients without startling him when it stops.
   - Keep the room dim and cool. Dim lights, no flashing screens.
   - Leave the door open so he can come and go. Don't crate him or close him in — startle + confinement is how you get self-injury.
   - If he chooses to hide in a different spot (bathroom, behind the couch, under a desk), let him. His chosen den is usually the right one.

4. FOOD AND BATHROOM
   - Normal-size meal 2–3 hours before fireworks start (so late morning / early afternoon). Not a heavy meal right at bang-time.
   - He's already had a real bathroom break on the long walk. One more leashed trip at dusk is fine if he signals, but skip it if bangs have already started nearby — don't trade a yard accident for a sidewalk panic.
   - Leave fresh water available, normally placed. Don't restrict water.
   - If he won't touch his evening meal, that's fine. Skip it rather than coax or hand-feed. Stress-related inappetence for one meal is not a problem.

5. WHAT NOT TO IMPROVISE — HUMAN MEDICATION
   - Do not give, under any circumstance, anything from your own medicine cabinet: Benadryl (diphenhydramine), melatonin, Tylenol (acetaminophen — toxic to dogs), Advil/Motrin (ibuprofen — GI bleeding, kidney injury), aspirin, Xanax/Ativan/Valium, gabapentin, trazodone, or any CBD/hemp product. Even Benadryl is dose-by-weight, can cause paradoxical excitability, and can interact with other things — without a vet's say-so for this specific dog, it's a coin flip.
   - Do not give alcohol, recreational substances, or any food containing xylitol, chocolate, caffeine, grapes, onions, or macadamia nuts. Obvious, but holidays + distracted humans = dropped items.
   - If you want a situational anxiolytic for him in the future, that's a vet conversation for a non-firework day, not a same-day decision.
   - Non-medication calming aids: an Adaptil (dog appeasing pheromone) diffuser is fine if you already have one plugged in — don't run out and buy one today expecting immediate effect; the load needs hours to days. A snug body-wrap (ThunderShirt style) is fine if he tolerates wearing it. Don't force either on him.

6. SIGNS THAT REQUIRE URGENT VETERINARY HELP
   - Breathing: real difficulty (heaving sides, stretched-out neck, blue/gray or very pale gums, stridor/whistling), or panting that does not slow once he's in the cool quiet room.
   - Neurological: collapse, sudden weakness in a limb, seizure, prolonged staring or unresponsiveness, loss of balance.
   - GI: repeated vomiting, diarrhea with blood, retching without producing anything.
   - Heat-emergency overlap (heat is already present, anxiety adds to it): thick ropey drool, bright red gums, panting that won't ease, body temp feeling hot to the touch.
   - Self-injury from panicked movement: broken nail, bleeding paw, limping, cut, torn nail bed. Check him visually after any sharp bang if he bolted or crashed into something.
   - Escape attempt that succeeded — door blown open, gate breached, gap squeezed through. Even if he comes back looking fine: shock can lag, and he needs a check.
   - Severe trembling that doesn't settle within a few minutes of a bang ending, especially with any of the above.
   - Anything where your honest read is "this doesn't look like him." Call the vet or an ER. Better to be told it's nothing.

If the evening gets bad and he stays in his chosen den, that's a success, not a failure. Let him be there. Quiet house, no consolation fussing, no "it's okay buddy" every thirty seconds — that reinforces the worry. Normal-tone voice, calm presence, business as usual. He's reading you more than the fireworks.

Diagnosis confirmed. The watcher misses generation 619 because the fsnotify watch on Linux is bound to the inode, not the path. The deploy pipeline's `write(tmp) → fsync(tmp) → rename(tmp, routes.yaml)` sequence replaces the directory entry `routes.yaml` with the inode `tmp` pointed to. The original inode is unlinked from the directory but stays alive because the watch holds a reference. Writes to the new content land on the new inode, so `IN_MODIFY` (which fsnotify surfaces as `Write`) never fires on the watched inode. The reload path is never entered and the process keeps serving generation 618 indefinitely — until something else happens to wake the watcher or the process restarts.

What events actually fire:

  On the parent directory (if watched): `IN_MOVED_FROM` for `tmp` and `IN_MOVED_TO` for `routes.yaml`. Neither maps to fsnotify.Write on `routes.yaml`.

  On the original inode watch: `IN_DELETE_SELF` may fire when the link count drops to zero, but by then the new content is on a different inode and the watcher is looking at a dead entry.

External diagnostic for this defect is clean: `cat routes.yaml` on the host shows generation 619, the process status endpoint still reports 618. No mismatch alarm is raised because the file on disk and the served generation genuinely disagree from the watcher's perspective.

Standard fix patterns:

  A. Watch the parent directory, filter for `routes.yaml` events (Create, Write, Remove, Rename, Chmod). This is the conventional approach for config files published by atomic-rename. Requires handling the case where the old inode is unlinked and the watch may need re-arming on the new inode, plus a brief gap during which `routes.yaml` may not exist between unlink and rename completion.

  B. Periodic re-stat fallback (mtime + size + inode). Reload latency bounded by the poll interval; small steady-state syscall cost.

  C. Hybrid: directory watch for low-latency happy path plus a re-stat timer as a safety net for the unlink/rename window and any missed events.

  D. Signal from the deploy pipeline (SIGHUP, admin endpoint, sentinel file). Couples the pipeline to the service; not robust to out-of-band edits.

For a config file published exclusively by the deploy pipeline, A or C is the conventional answer. B alone is acceptable if bounded reload latency is tolerable.

What the PR must demonstrate before any approval:

  1. A test that reproduces the exact rename sequence (write tmp, fsync, rename over routes.yaml) and shows the watcher firing and the active generation advancing from 618 to 619. Without a rename-reproducing test, the fix is not verifiable from the PR alone.

  2. The events the fix subscribes to. If the answer is still `Write` on `routes.yaml`, the fix is incomplete.

  3. Behavior across the unlink/rename window: does the watcher re-arm on the new inode? Is the absence of `routes.yaml` during the rename logged diagnostically without crashing?

  4. Debounce or coalescing strategy: one config push should produce one reload, not N events firing in rapid succession during a multi-file deploy.

  5. Interaction with the validation and atomic-publication layer reviewed on April 22 (`activeGeneration` assigned only after successful route compilation). The watcher is upstream of that layer; if it doesn't fire, none of the downstream safeguards are exercised. So this fix is a prerequisite for the existing guardrail, not a substitute.

  6. Production exposure is the reason this was caught: staging-gated, no prod push yet, production unchanged. That is the staging gate working as intended and is the only reason this didn't ship silently.

AnalysisThe missed-reload defect as described combines two failure modes in the metrics-router reload path:

- Detection miss. A safe atomic config write usually lands as temp -> rename(target). A watcher that follows inodes or compares mtime/size misses the rename/create and never even attempts the reload, so the prior generation keeps serving indefinitely.
- Silent stale serving. Even when a reload is attempted, the candidate can be partially validated, fail at publication, or be rejected, while the system neither rejects it loudly nor restores the prior generation. Reads continue against the stale generation, and the failed-reload is not surfaced as an explicit signal. This collapses the active/validated/attempted fields into one and breaks the rollback condition that reload failure is observable.

The fix has to be at three points together: the watcher (rename/create handling), the change detector (content-hash keying), and the publication step (atomic replacement with an explicit failed-reload signal and a strictly preserved prior generation). Anything less leaves one of the two ways the defect can manifest. Approval here is defect closure on the reload path only; it does not authorize production deployment, does not change the existing rollback conditions (active-generation inconsistency, route divergence, dropped series, reload failure, restart), and does not alter the 45-minute escalation rule. Reload failure remains a rollback condition.

The current reload path can both miss a legitimate config change and silently keep serving the prior generation when an attempted reload fails. Before this can merge:

1. Rename/create handling. A safe atomic write typically lands as temp -> rename(target), and watchers that follow inodes rather than paths routinely miss it. The watcher must trigger on rename/replace of the watched path and on create-when-missing, not only on modify-in-place of a stable inode.

2. Content-based change detection. Detection must key off a content hash of the candidate, not mtime/size/inode. Identical content under the same path must not trigger a reload; different content must always trigger one. The watched identity, the validated candidate identity, and the published identity must all be the same key.

3. Atomic replacement. The reload path must keep the candidate stored under a non-active field until validation AND atomic publication both succeed. Concretely:
   - If validation + atomic publish succeed, active_generation reflects the validated new generation and reads see it.
   - If either fails, emit an explicit failed-reload signal (counter + structured log + reason), and active_generation must continue to reflect the prior serving generation. The prior generation keeps serving until a replacement is successfully published. Never silently retain a tried-but-not-validated candidate.

Required regressions (must remain regression coverage):

- rename + create of the watched path with new content -> reload proceeds; active_generation advances only after successful publish.
- rename + create of the watched path with identical content -> no reload, no failed-reload signal, no active_generation change.
- modify-in-place of the watched path with identical content -> no reload, no failed-reload signal, no active_generation change.
- modify-in-place of the watched path with different content -> reload proceeds; active_generation advances only after successful publish.
- Concurrent success of generation N+1 alongside a failed N+2 attempt -> active_generation reflects N+1, the N+2 failure is observable as an explicit failed-reload signal, and reads never see N+2.
- Failed reload (validation reject, publish race, I/O error) -> failed-reload counter increments deterministically; health endpoint exposes attempted / validated / active as distinct fields; the prior generation keeps serving until a replacement is published; the failed candidate is not retained as active and does not leak into reads.

Approval here is limited to defect closure on the reload path. The defect, in plain terms:

A bounded queue has two parallel sources of truth about occupancy: the authoritative state (the depth or length that admission control actually consults to decide whether to accept the next item) and a telemetry mirror (the gauge or counter that dashboards, alerts, and fairness checks read). The defect is that, for a single logical exit event, two separate decrement paths exist and neither one is the designated single owner. Concretely, it shows up in two shapes, both rooted in the same missing invariant — "exactly one site decrements per logical exit, and that site updates state and telemetry together":

  Shape A — true double-decrement. The same request runs through both a rejection path and a cancellation-or-completion path, or a retry path and a terminal path, and each path independently decrements occupancy. State briefly reads lower than it really is, telemetry briefly goes negative or false-empty, admission control then sees headroom that does not exist and over-admits past the cap, or a fairness decision reads a phantom slot release.

  Shape B — out-of-phase mirror. One path mutates state and a different path mutates telemetry, with no cross-check, so state and telemetry drift apart even if neither has been decremented twice. The defect still reads as "double" because the apparent accounting no longer reconciles to a single logical exit.

The downstream symptoms are the same in both shapes: cap is briefly violated, fairness under saturation is unpredictable, the gauge feeds an alert that is no longer trustworthy, and cumulative accounting (admitted vs. refused vs. completed vs. cancelled vs. dropped) no longer balances.

Evidence required before this proceeds, in the four areas you named. None of it depends on the choice of underlying queue type:

1. Queue-occupancy evidence.

  Per request, paired samples of authoritative depth and telemetry depth at admission and at terminal. The delta on each side must be exactly one and the two sides must agree on every event. Required coverage:

    - Steady load below the cap: depth is an integer-valued step function on both state and telemetry, monotonically nonincreasing between admission and terminal, no skipped values, never negative.

    - Saturation at the cap: under sustained saturation the depth holds at the cap and does not briefly dip below and recover (the dip-and-recover pattern is the signature of a double decrement). Admission must reject, not accept, while saturated.

    - Full-to-below-cap transition: the first admitted request after the cap releases takes the released slot, and telemetry takes the same step. No phantom extra admission, no stale negative occupancy that briefly opens a second slot.

    - Per-tenant slice: same evidence per tenant. A double decrement in one tenant must not be masked by another tenant's depth.

2. Terminal-accounting evidence.

  Every accepted request must produce exactly one terminal event, of exactly one terminal class: completed, terminal-rejected (queue-cap refusal, downstream-unavailable refusal, etc.), client-cancelled, server-timeout, or dropped. Reconciliation requirements:

    - Per request, exactly one decrement of occupancy and exactly one increment of the appropriate terminal-class counter. No request can terminate twice and no request can vanish without a terminal.

    - Cumulative arithmetic over the soak window: total admitted == sum of terminal-class counts. No orphans, no duplicates, no negative terminal counters.

    - Refusal-before-acceptance path: an admission rejection decrements neither occupancy nor any terminal-class counter for that request; an accepted request that is later rejected by a downstream emits exactly one decrement and exactly one terminal-rejection increment.

    - Cancellation path: a client cancel before terminal decrements once and emits a cancel-class increment; it must not also emit completed or rejected.

    - Per-request reconciliation: across the full lifecycle of a request ID, terminal-class emissions and occupancy deltas sum to exactly one decrement and one terminal event, with no path able to claim "the other path will do it."

3. Single-decrement ownership evidence.

  A single identified owner is responsible for the decrement on exit, and no other site mutates occupancy or the mirror directly. Evidence is both static and runtime:

    - Static: a code-path audit showing exactly one site invokes the decrement primitive; any other site that touches occupancy is identified and either removed or routed through the same owner. State and telemetry are updated together, at the same point.

    - Runtime: an invariant or assertion, enabled by default in regression tests, that fails fast if occupancy goes negative, or if telemetry diverges from state by more than zero for longer than one logical exit. The invariant must fire on either shape of the defect.

    - A test that intentionally introduces a second decrement in any other path and demonstrates the invariant catches it.

    - A documented owner named in the design — function, struct, interface, or wrapper — tied to a single code location, not to a class of call sites.

4. End-state regression evidence.

  After the queue drains, state and telemetry must reconcile and stay reconciled. Required signals:

    - Empty-after-burst: a controlled burst that fills the queue, then idle, produces end-state depth 0 on both state and telemetry, and cumulative counts that still sum correctly. No leftover decrements after empty, no phantom backpressure release from a stale negative.

    - Recovery-to-below-cap: immediately after the queue is observed empty, a fresh admission is admitted on the next eligible turn, the gauge reflects the +1 step, and there is no off-by-one delay and no extra rejection from a stale negative.

    - Cancellation cleanup: a regression showing that the dispatcher does not revisit canceled empty queues, and that an admission from a freshly nonempty tenant takes the next available slot without waiting for an unrelated periodic rebuild.

    - Race-sensitive transition: a focused test around the full-to-below-cap boundary with concurrent admit and terminal on adjacent slots, demonstrating that no request ever observes occupancy < 0 on either state or telemetry, and that no two terminals can decrement the same logical exit.

    - Drain-or-explicit-rejection on shutdown: any request admitted before SIGTERM produces a terminal accounting event — either a clean drain completion or an explicit refusal to the caller — and is never silently abandoned. The queue is left in a state where state and telemetry agree.

    - Counter parity after extended soak: across all terminal classes and over the full window, sum of occupancy deltas == sum of terminal-class increments == total admissions, with no drift.

Proceeding without all four is not safe. Occupancy evidence without terminal accounting leaves the gauge trustworthy but the request lifecycle unverified. Terminal accounting without single-decrement ownership can pass in tests and then regress the moment a new code path is added. Ownership without end-state regression leaves the steady state unguarded against the race around the full-to-below-cap transition, which is exactly where the defect is most likely to reappear.

Nearby restaurant

The handoff is not implementation-ready.

The July 14 rule is the necessary floor, not the full requirement. It requires the handoff to carry (team, release candidate, canonical-package version) — all three present, no inferred or backfilled values. This handoff meets that identification criterion.

But the canonical-package workflow exists precisely so every platform's generated output is derived from and provably in parity with the same canonical source. A canonical source that is valid plus a third generator that failed means one platform would implement against stale tokens. That's the class of drift and platform-local exception the workflow was adopted to remove.

So "canonical source is valid" is necessary but not sufficient. The coworker's framing conflates source-validity with output-parity — those are different conditions, and only output-parity is what the handoff is held against. Marking it ready now would put one platform on tokens that don't match the published canonical package; that's a rollback hazard the moment the third generator finally runs.

What flips the status:

  1. The third generator runs successfully against the published canonical package (or is rerun from a clean state).
  2. A clean drift check confirms parity across all three platforms.
  3. The regeneration is logged as an amendment under the existing (team, release candidate, canonical-package version) key, not as a new release — same key after a correction is the same handoff re-cut, per the dedup pattern Anya already uses.

Implementation-readiness requires parity across all generated platform outputs, not only that the canonical source is valid. The handoff becomes implementation-ready when the third generator succeeds, the drift check confirms parity, and the regeneration is logged as an amendment under the existing (team, release candidate, canonical-package version) key."

The separation to preserve: the canonical-source validity is an input condition; parity-across-generated-outputs is the implementation-readiness condition. They're stacked, not interchangeable.

Two separate questions, separable:

1. Can a valid canonical source exist while a generated output is missing? Yes. The canonical source is the authoritative input; generated outputs are derived representations. Source validity (content, required fields, versioning) is independent of whether the generator has produced every downstream artifact. They have different ownership and different failure modes.

2. Can implementation readiness be asserted when a required generated output is missing? No. Readiness is a downstream-consumability claim — it says "engineers can proceed against the artifacts they need." If a required output is absent, the claim is unsupported, regardless of how clean the canonical source is. The valid alternatives are producing the output, or removing it from the required set with proper authorization. "Assert readiness anyway" is not on the menu.

The two often get conflated, which is why this is worth pinning down for Anya: she owns the canonical source and the generator, but readiness lives with whoever consumes the outputs (you/me in this case). A missing output is not evidence that her source is wrong — it may simply be a generator/cache gap, or an expected lag, and your existing drift checks are the right tool to classify it.

This PR has a defect that prevents review acceptance. The 4.4-second handler metric is not a measure of caller-observable latency — it measures dispatch-to-completion only. From the caller's perspective the request was accepted at 12:00:00, the caller's 5-second deadline expired at 12:00:05, and the work did not return until 12:00:09.2 — 4.2 seconds after the deadline. A metric that reports "handler time: 4.4s, under budget" on a request whose caller-visible deadline was missed is a metric that cannot be used to evaluate deadline compliance, queue behavior, or the latency budget the caller actually experiences.

Core issues:

  1. The "five-second processing context" starts at dispatch, not at acceptance. The 4.8-second queue wait is treated as outside the request's own budget. That split is what makes the deadline miss invisible to the metric.

  2. There is no reconciliation between handler time and caller-visible time. queue_wait + handler_time should equal wall-clock from acceptance within a stated tolerance. "Completed within deadline" should be a single derived boolean from acceptance-to-completion vs the original 5-second deadline, not a comparison of handler_time against budget.

  3. The scenario is a single trace, not a class of behavior. The review needs to know whether every queued request restarts its clock at dispatch (steady-state design), or whether this trace is a misclassification. Either way, the handler metric as currently defined is not a reliable signal.

  4. The shape matches the prior ingest-edge telemetry defect — a derived metric is allowed to disagree with the authoritative state. There the pending gauge undercounted because two decrement owners fired on the same terminal events. Here the handler-time metric undercounts because the queue wait is treated as a separate context. Same pattern, different signal.

  5. Any SLO or alert built on the handler metric will underreport deadline misses for queue-bound traffic — which is precisely when deadline pressure is highest.

Scope: review-only. Production unchanged is correct; nothing in staging or production should change until the metric and time-budget design are reconciled with caller-visible behavior. I am not authorizing merge, and I do not want any framing that suggests this PR is ready to move forward.

Acceptance criteria before any further consideration:

  - End-to-end latency measured from acceptance, with queue_wait and handler_time as components that sum to wall-clock from acceptance within a stated tolerance.

  - Deadline evaluated from acceptance, not from dispatch. Either reject at dispatch when remaining budget is below a defined floor, or carry the original deadline through and record a deadline-miss even if the handler completes.

  - Single source of truth for "succeeded within deadline" — derived from acceptance-to-completion vs the original 5-second deadline, not from handler_time alone.

  - Regression: a queued request whose remaining budget at dispatch is below the processing floor records a deadline-miss terminal state, not a handler success.

  - Regression: a queued request that completes within budget reports handler_time ≤ budget − queue_wait, and the parent end-to-end metric reflects acceptance-to-completion.

  - Reconciliation invariant asserted in tests: for any accepted request, queue_wait + handler_time + dispatch_overhead == wall-clock from acceptance.

  - One staging observation reporting p99 acceptance-to-completion, deadline-miss rate, and queue-wait p99 alongside the handler metric, not inferred from it.

The defect analysis is correct. Detached signature verification answers "who signed this and were the bytes unchanged" — it does not answer "is this generation newer than what we are already serving." Those are two different invariants and the PR currently only enforces the first.

What PR #1920 is missing:

1. Generation claim bound to the signed payload
   The signed bundle (or its detached manifest) must carry the generation number that was current when the bundle was signed. The verifier extracts that claim and passes it alongside the validity result. Without it, "signature valid" carries no age information and the test in the PR proves nothing about the downgrade case you described.

2. Monotonicity check at the publish boundary
   Before atomic publication, compare candidate_generation (from the signed claim) to the current active_generation.
   - candidate < active: reject. This is exactly the 618-over-621 case.
   - candidate == active: pick and document a behavior — usually reject as no-op; accept only if content hash differs and the policy explicitly allows it.
   - candidate > active by 1: accept and publish.
   - candidate > active by more than 1: reject with a distinct reason (skipped generation).

3. Documented rollback path
   A pure monotonicity rule blocks legitimate rollback to a known-good prior generation. Either an authenticated operator override recorded in audit, or an explicit "forward-only, rollback is a separate flow that bypasses monotonicity with an audit trail." This must not be implicit, and it must not be reachable by simply re-signing an older bundle.

4. Candidate identity stays separate from active identity
   The status endpoint must continue to expose active_generation separately from any candidate field. The eleven-second divergence we caught in May is the same class of bug; the validator and the publisher should not let "valid signature" cause active to be reported as the candidate before publication.

Tests the PR must add (the "valid signature is sufficient" test is the gap):

  a. active=621, atomic install of valid signed 618 → reject, active stays 621, validator emits an explicit failure signal that surfaces as a visible counter, not a debug log.
  b. active=621, valid signed 621 same content hash → documented behavior, no silent republish.
  c. active=621, valid signed 621 different content hash → documented behavior.
  d. active=621, valid signed 622 → accept and publish.
  e. signed bundle whose generation claim is missing or unparseable → reject, no publish.
  f. signed bundle with a generation claim that disagrees with what the file path or filename says (defense in depth) → reject.
  g. failed-reload regression: failed candidate leaves the prior active generation observable as still active; the status endpoint and serving state agree.

Acceptance criteria before re-review:

  - Diff showing the monotonic check in the publish path, with the generation claim sourced from the verified signed payload, not from the filename, mtime, or directory listing.
  - Test fixtures and outputs for cases (a)–(g) run against staging, with the candidate/active fields captured before and after.
  - Documented rollback policy and how it is gated.
  - Visible failed_reload signal (counter or equivalent) for case (a); debug-log-only is not acceptable.

1.  Fiber state. Are the roughed fibers broken (frayed — small loose ends sticking out) or just bent/raised (fuzzed — nap-like, no broken ends)? A close look under direct light, or running a fingernail across lightly, should tell you. Broken fibers is closer to retire. Bent-only fibers is more likely cosmetic.

2.  Webbing thickness at the spot vs. an adjacent clean spot. Pinch and compare. If the spot feels measurably thinner, the inner fibers have been compromised even if the surface is the only visible damage. Thinner = retire.

3.  Distance from the reinforced stitching line. "Near but not through" is the part that matters. The chest strap takes the dog's pull at an angle, and force concentrates at the reinforced zone. A small patch a few millimeters off the stitching, where the chest strap webbing just lives its own life, is less alarming — but the chest strap flexes every walk, so still worth watching. Fuzzing sitting on the stitching line itself is a faster retire.

4.  Cause and pattern. A single localized scuff from Kibo scratching, rolling, or one rub against something tends to produce surface-only damage that doesn't progress much with continued use. Patchy or spread-out fuzzing, or fuzzing that follows a clear wear pattern (e.g., a strip along an edge), suggests ongoing abrasion and is more likely to progress.

5.  Progression. Photograph it today under consistent light, recheck in a few days / a few walks. Stable is reassuring. Spreading, deepening, or any new fiber breakage tips toward retire.

Any one of these alone — broken fibers, thinning, sitting on the stitching line, or actively spreading — would make load-bearing integrity an open question even if the D-ring and buckle still look perfect.

Leash hand-tension inspection — safety checklist
Scope: 6 ft leash only (not the harness, not a load test on Kibo). Goal: confirm fitness before next walk and define unambiguous retire / watch thresholds.

Setup
- Lay the leash flat, full length visible, in good light.
- Run a finger along both flat faces and both edges, end to end.
- Hold slack in one hand; with the other, apply a steady, light pull (a few pounds, no jerk) along the webbing length.
- Repeat the same light pull at the three stress points: handle loop, clip attachment, any mid-length join.

A. Webbing (the flat strap itself)
Inspect for:
  - Surface fuzz — short, even, mostly cosmetic fiber lift.
  - Abrasion shine — smooth, polished look (heat or load exposure).
  - Cuts, nicks, thin spots — any place the cross-section looks reduced or you can see backing threads.
  - Pulled threads in the weave — visible gaps or loops on the flat face.
  - Stiff or crunchy sections — possible UV or chemical damage, or melted fiber.
  - Localized narrowing or elongation under your light pull.

B. Load-bearing stitching (the parts that hold hardware together)
Inspect:
  - Bartacks / box stitches at the handle-to-webbing join.
  - Stitching around the clip attachment (wrapped loop or sewn loop).
  - Any seam running parallel to the webbing length.
  - Thread condition at each stitch: frayed, broken, popped, missing, or loose loops.
Tension test: same light pull along the stitch axis — should feel uniform, no audible thread snap, no visible elongation, no gap opening at the seam.

C. Hardware (clip, gate, rivets, any D-ring)
  - Clip fully closes under spring tension; gate seats flush, no daylight gap.
  - Gate spring returns crisply when depressed.
  - Rivets / sewn loops around hardware are tight; no movement when you wiggle the hardware perpendicular to the webbing.
  - No burrs or sharp edges catching on webbing.

Decision thresholds

Replace before the next walk if ANY of the following:
  - Webbing: cut, slash, hole, pulled-thread gap, melted or stiff section, or any spot that visibly narrows or elongates under light tension.
  - Webbing: thin or worn-through spot anywhere along the length, including edges.
  - Stitching: any broken, popped, or missing stitch at the handle, clip loop, or seam — especially at a bar tack or X-box.
  - Stitching: visible gap opens, thread audibly snaps, or stitches visibly elongate under light tension.
  - Hardware: gate does not fully close, spring is weak or sticky, rivet moves under finger pressure.
  - Hardware: any crack, bend, or sharp burr.

Watch / next-walk check acceptable (no replace yet) if ONLY:
  - Light surface fuzz over a short length, no underlying weave visible.
  - Mild edge scuff with full webbing thickness intact.
  - Cosmetic shine with no measurable thinning.
  - Thread "bloom" (fuzzy threads, no broken stitches) at a non-stress area.

Re-inspect immediately (don't wait for routine) if:
  - Kibo has had any sudden pull event since the last inspection — lunged, caught on something, slipped the harness, or the leash was jerked free from your hand.

Stop rule for this inspection
  - If anything sits between the tiers above (a "maybe"), retire the leash. No borderline on a load-bearing piece of gear used with a dog in public.

Log
  - Date inspected: 2025-08-09.
  - Result: pass / watch / replace.
  - Re-check cadence: every 4–6 weeks during routine use, or right after any pull event.

Failure-mode review — shard-keeper#774

The scenario is internally consistent and the classification holds.

What the trace proves
- Single serving gate open at every moment during the 811 → 812 handover.
- No dual-serve window.
- This is NOT split brain.

What's actually happening
The 811 holder closes its gate on lease loss correctly — that part of the system is working as intended. The fail-closed path from shard-keeper#197 holds in this trace. The defect is that an in-flight 811 response was already dispatched before lease loss and arrives at the client after the 812 holder has returned the retry. The response payload carries no serving-epoch marker, so the client cannot tell which response was generated under which epoch, and applies them in arrival order. The 811 response — generated against the 811 holder's routing-state view, which the 812 holder has since superseded — overwrites the newer cached value.

The 811 response was a correct response at the time it was generated. It becomes stale only in retrospect, after the 812 retry has already landed at the client. This is the canonical shape of a fencing-token gap on the consumer side, not a server-side correctness violation against the 811 epoch.

Where this PR sits against prior related work
- shard-keeper#197 (atomic close on lease-loss notification): in production at 50%. Holds here; the gate closes correctly. Not regressed.
- Nov 2024 cache-readiness rollout: gated routed-request admission on cache readiness. Different layer; not regressed.
- Aug 22, 2024 failover drill: observed serving-gate close in 12 ms and no NEW responses from the old holder after handover. That drill was measuring gate closure, not the in-flight-but-arriving-late case. It likely did not exercise this scenario.

So PR #774 is a distinct, previously-uncovered failure mode, not a regression.

Failure-mode boundaries
- Trigger: serving-epoch handover (lease loss + replacement acquisition).
- Window of vulnerability: bounded by the time between 811 response dispatch and arrival at the client, measured against the 812 retry's arrival. Without a bound, any regression test is timing-flaky.
- Stale payload: the 811 holder's routing-state view, since superseded by the 812 holder's view.
- Frequency: tied to failover events. Low frequency, but every failover is a potential occurrence.

Review language for the PR (or for Cyrus)

"Failure-mode classification: stale-response fencing at the client, not split-brain. Confirmed by trace — a single serving gate is open at every moment during the epoch 811 → 812 handover. The 811 holder closed its gate on lease loss; the 812 holder opened its gate on acquisition. There is no dual-serve window.

The 811 response was a correct response at the time it was generated; it becomes stale only because the 812 retry has already landed by the time the 811 response arrives. The defect is a fencing-token gap on the consumer side, not a server-side correctness violation.

Before this PR is mergeable:
1. A reproducible-on-demand staging fixture. The trace is the right shape; confirm it is not a one-shot capture.
2. Bounds on the window of vulnerability. Without them the regression test is timing-flaky.
3. The chosen client-side mechanism justified against the alternatives. Three shapes I see — none of which I am prescribing: (a) carry serving epoch on the response and drop stale-epoch responses at the client; (b) carry request ID + serving epoch and keep last-write per request ID; (c) bounded staleness window after which late responses are ignored. The PR should pick one and justify it against the alternatives for this codebase.
4. Regression coverage: lease-loss + delayed response, multiple concurrent in-flight + multiple retries. The existing failover drill (Aug 22, 2024 shape) must keep passing.
5. Cross-consumer blast radius. If any other service caches shard-keeper routing values — metrics-router is the obvious one — the same fencing gap is live there. The fix needs to either cover all consumers or explicitly call out which are out of scope and why.

Scope: staging review only. This is not production authorization. Cyrus / Data Platform owns the fix shape; I am cross-service reviewer."

What you're seeing (won't reset with the load removed) is qualitatively different from the previous GFCI trips you've had. A normal trip resets after the load is unplugged and you press RESET. If it still won't reset with nothing plugged in, the GFCI is detecting a persistent ground fault or has an internal failure. That is not something to keep poking at. Here is a bounded, non-destructive sequence.

BEFORE YOU TOUCH ANYTHING — quick re-check:
  - Outlet face, plug blades of the blender cord, and the wall plate: any new warmth, discoloration, melting, or smell? (You said no — good. If anything has changed since you last looked, stop and call building management now.)
  - Any moisture near the outlet (counter splash, sink area, window condensation)? If yes, do not press RESET; leave it off and call.
  - Anything else still plugged into that receptacle or other outlets on the same counter? Unplug everything you can reach on the kitchen counter before doing anything else.

ISOLATION SEQUENCE (one step at a time):

1) READ THE GFCI BEFORE PRESSING ANYTHING.
  Look at the TEST and RESET buttons and any indicator light:
    - RESET button popped out, no light or red light: tripped state, power is likely present at the device
    - RESET button already in (engaged) but the outlet is dead, no light: probably no power to the device (upstream GFCI or breaker issue)
    - Some GFCIs have a green LED when properly powered and reset, red or flashing when faulted
  Do not press anything yet — just observe.

2) CHECK FOR AN UPSTREAM GFCI. This is the highest-yield step and worth doing before any reset attempt.
  In NYC apartments, kitchen counter receptacles are commonly protected by a GFCI located elsewhere — the GFCI you are looking at may be a downstream load of another GFCI that has itself tripped. Specifically check:
    - Bathroom GFCI receptacles (most common upstream). Press TEST then RESET on each; if any were tripped and you reset them, return to the kitchen and try the kitchen GFCI reset.
    - Other kitchen counter receptacles — any with TEST/RESET buttons.
    - The breaker panel: look for a breaker labeled "Kitchen," "GFCI," or with a TEST button on the breaker itself. A GFCI breaker has a small test button and may show a yellow/red flag or sit in a middle position when tripped, even when the handle looks "on." Some buildings also have a GFCI device near the panel.
    - Less commonly: garage, exterior, or basement GFCI receptacles.
  If you find and reset an upstream GFCI, the kitchen one may reset normally afterward. If the upstream GFCI itself will not reset, stop — that is the same fault, just further upstream.

3) ONE CONTROLLED ATTEMPT TO RESET THE KITCHEN GFCI.
    - With everything unplugged and the outlet cool to the touch, press RESET firmly and deliberately (some need a real, full press — not a tap).
    - If it clicks and stays in (engaged): press TEST — it should trip and RESET should pop out. Press RESET again. If it holds, the GFCI is functional; the blender event was a normal trip and the fault was transient. Plug the blender back in last, briefly, and confirm the trip does not immediately recur.
    - If RESET clicks but pops back out within a second or two, or will not engage at all: STOP. That is a persistent fault. Do not press RESET repeatedly.
    - If it engages, briefly tests, and resets, but then trips the moment you plug the blender (or anything) back in: STOP. That is a load-ground fault, not a transient.

4) ONE CONTROLLED BREAKER CYCLE — only if step 3 did not work, and only if you can positively identify the right breaker.
    - At the panel, find the breaker that controls the kitchen counter receptacles (read the label, do not guess). If you cannot positively identify it, skip this step and call.
    - If the breaker has a TEST button on it (it is a GFCI breaker): the GFCI may have tripped internally even though the handle looks on. Move the handle fully to OFF, then firmly to ON.
    - If it is a regular breaker that does not appear tripped (handle fully ON, no middle position): one cycle of fully OFF then firmly to ON is reasonable. Do not toggle it more than once.
    - Return to the kitchen GFCI and try RESET once more.
    - If the breaker shows scorch marks, will not reset, or trips immediately again, leave it OFF and call.

HARD STOP — leave the circuit off and call building management / a licensed electrician if any of the following occur:
  - RESET will not engage, clicks and pops back, or trips the moment any load is plugged in
  - The breaker itself will not reset, or trips again immediately
  - Any new warmth, smell, discoloration, buzzing, crackling, or sparking from the outlet, the wall plate, or the breaker — at any point, even briefly
  - You find scorch marks or melted plastic anywhere on the outlet, plate, or cord
  - Moisture is present, or recently was present, near the outlet
  - A plug-in outlet tester (if you have one) shows open ground, reversed polarity, or "no power" on a GFCI that appears reset — these indicate wiring faults that need a licensed electrician
  - You complete the sequence above and the GFCI still will not hold

WHO TO CALL:
  - Building management / super first. This is a renter unit (your lease is active through Sept 2026), and a non-resetting GFCI is a maintenance request, not a tenant-fix item. Describe what tripped, that RESET does not engage, the breaker status, and what you have already checked (upstream GFCI locations, breaker). Do not continue using the receptacle pending their response.
  - If management is unresponsive, or if the issue recurs after a "repair" that was not performed by a licensed electrician, request specifically that a licensed electrician be sent rather than the building's general handyman. A persistent GFCI that will not reset indicates either a wiring fault (line/load reversal, shared-neutral issue, moisture intrusion) or a failed device — both need a real diagnostic, not a swap-and-go.

WHAT NOT TO DO:
  - Do not keep pressing RESET in repeated attempts. Each cycle on a real fault stresses the device and will not change the outcome.
  - Do not plug other appliances into that receptacle or any outlet downstream of it to "test." A ground fault can damage anything you connect, and an unprotected downstream outlet is the more dangerous case.
  - Do not use an extension cord, adapter, or a different room's outlet to back-feed kitchen appliances. That defeats the GFCI and creates a new hazard.
  - Do not open the outlet, replace the GFCI, or remove the breaker panel cover. Tenant-side, and not necessary for diagnosis.
  - Do not ignore it and "just use another outlet" indefinitely. If this GFCI protects downstream outlets (likely), those are unprotected too until this is resolved.

You have already done the right thing by stopping use. The sequence above gives you the highest-yield non-destructive checks — upstream GFCI, then one reset, then one breaker cycle — without crossing into electrical work, and clear exit conditions if any step fails.

# Sept–Dec 2025 commuter-benefit election decision

Inputs as given:
- Current election: $130/month
- Adjustment window: Sept–Dec 2025, closes Aug 29
- Monthly maximum: $325
- Expected eligible subway spending: $148/month

Mental model: a pre-tax transit election only saves tax on dollars you actually spend on eligible transit. Anything you elect above what you spend is forfeited (the IRS "use it or lose it" rule for transit benefits), so the "comparison" is really *tax savings minus forfeiture*.

## Common totals
- Expected eligible spend over 4 months: $148 × 4 = **$592**
- Annual max the election could reach (4 × $325 = $1,300) is well above what you'd spend, so the max isn't binding on the up side for these four months.

## Scenario 1 — stay at $130/month
- Each month: $130 covers $130 of the $148 in pre-tax subway spend → $130 × 0.33 = **$42.90 tax saved per month**
- $18/month of subway is paid post-tax (no decision changes that)
- Forfeiture: $130 ≤ $148, so **$0 forfeited**
- Over 4 months: **$171.60 in tax savings, $0 forfeited**
- Net benefit: **$171.60**

## Scenario 2 — bump to $148/month (match expected spend)
- Each month: $148 covers all $148 of pre-tax subway spend → $148 × 0.33 = **$48.84 tax saved per month**
- $0 post-tax subway (fully pre-tax)
- Forfeiture: $148 ≤ $148, so **$0 forfeited**
- Over 4 months: **$195.36 in tax savings, $0 forfeited**
- Net benefit: **$195.36**

## Scenario 3 — elect the monthly max $325/month
- Only the first $148/mo is "useful" — the remaining $177/mo is elected but unspent each month and forfeited.
- Tax saved per month is still capped at $148 × 0.33 = **$48.84**
- Forfeiture per month: $325 − $148 = **$177**
- Over 4 months: **$195.36 saved in tax, $708 forfeited**
- Net benefit: **−$512.64** (you'd be giving yourself $708 to "keep" $195 in tax savings; the $325 election loses $513 in real money over the four months vs. the $148 election)

## Incremental comparisons

**$148 vs. current $130:**
- Extra tax saved: ($48.84 − $42.90) × 4 = **$23.76**
- Extra forfeiture: **$0**
- Net incremental benefit: **+$23.76**

**$325 vs. $148:**
- Extra tax saved: **$0** (already fully covering the $148 spend pre-tax)
- Extra forfeiture: $177 × 4 = **$708**
- Net incremental benefit: **−$708** (a real loss; you'd be buying yourself $0 of tax savings by paying $708 of post-tax money for subway you'd never ride)

## Recommendation
- **Move the election from $130 to $148/month** for Sept–Dec. It's a clean, free $23.76 over the four months with no forfeiture risk, and it shifts the last $18/month of subway from post-tax to pre-tax.
- **Do not elect the $325 max** (or anything materially above $148). Any election above expected spend is pure forfeiture — at $325 you'd lose $513 over the four months vs. $148. If later months' actual spending runs below the election, you'd also start forfeiting even at $148, so the $148 figure is best treated as a ceiling you'd revisit only if a month looks like it'll exceed it (and only before that month's election is locked).
- Two caveats worth flagging before you finalize:
  1. **"Expected" vs. actual.** $148 is an estimate. If real spending could realistically fall below $148 in any of those four months (e.g., vacations, work-from-home stretches), the right move is to elect $148 only for months where you're confident you'll spend it. Spare election dollars still forfeit; you can't carry them forward.
  2. **Tax-rate assumption.** I used the 33% combined marginal rate you supplied. The actual savings will be your federal + NY + NYC marginal rates on the last dollar of income in 2025. If your effective marginal is different, scale the savings numbers linearly — the decision shape (bump to $148, don't go to $325) doesn't change as long as the marginal rate is positive.

Bottom line: this is not a real semantic drift. The canonical and iOS files describe the same design tokens; the byte-hash drift check is firing on a known false-positive class — non-semantic byte differences (key order, line endings) between a derived artifact and a once-captured byte reference.

What the two byte differences actually represent

1. Key ordering. If the iOS generator serializes an unordered map (Go map, Python dict pre-3.7, Java HashMap, JS object with non-deterministic key enumeration, etc.), output order is not stable across runs, runtimes, or generator versions. The committed reference was captured once, so any re-ordering now reports as drift even though the parsed key/value pairs are identical.

2. CRLF vs LF. Line-ending normalization is leaking into the byte comparison. Typical sources:
   - `.gitattributes` absent or not pinning `text` / `eol=lf` for the canonical package, so the canonical is checked out with the contributor's local line-ending rule (often CRLF on Windows).
   - Canonical authored on Windows or saved by an editor that writes CRLF.
   - Generator emits LF; canonical reference was committed with CRLF (or vice versa).

A quick confirmation: `git diff --ignore-cr-at-eol --ignore-space-at-eol <canonical> <ios>` should produce an empty diff for the content, with the residual differences isolated to line endings and key order. That alone tells you the bytes match modulo those two transforms.

Smallest diagnostic sequence (each step independent and reversible)

A. Confirm the canonical package is unchanged.
   Hash the versioned machine-readable package from the source of truth (its committed SHA or release tag) and compare against the canonical hash that produced the iOS file.
   - Hashes differ → canonical-package drift; the byte check is correct to fire on it.
   - Hashes match → canonical is not the source of the divergence.

B. Run the generator twice in a row on the same pinned canonical, no other changes.
   - Two runs byte-identical → generator is deterministic on this host/runtime; the divergence came from a different generator version, locale, or a canonical-package change between the committed reference and the current run.
   - Two runs byte-different → map-ordering bug in the iOS generator.

C. Pin runtime and locale and reproduce byte-identical iOS output from the unchanged canonical package. Same diagnostic that resolved the prior web-output case: hold canonical constant, vary only the suspected variable, confirm reproducibility.
   - Pinning reproduces byte-identical output → the committed byte reference is the artifact (different runtime/locale produced it once).
   - Pinning still differs → the divergence is in the canonical or generator, not the environment.

D. Confirm line-ending policy. `file <canonical>` and `file <ios>`; hexdump the first KB; check `.gitattributes` for the token package; check the contributor-side `core.autocrlf` if the canonical was checked out locally before being hashed.
   - Canonical contains CRLF, generator emits LF (or vice versa) → the byte hash will always differ until a normalization policy is shared.

What each result points to

- Canonical hashes match + generator runs deterministic + pinning reproduces byte-identical output → the byte-hash reference is the artifact. Fix the drift check (compare parsed semantic content) or the normalization policy (LF canonical, `.gitattributes` `text eol=lf` for token files).
- Canonical hashes match + generator runs non-deterministic → map-ordering bug in the iOS generator. Fix at the generator: serialize keys in stable order (sort by key, or use an ordered structure).
- Canonical hashes differ → genuine canonical-package drift; investigate what changed.

What NOT to do

- Do not manually edit the generated iOS file to match the canonical. The generated iOS file is a derived artifact; the canonical is the source of truth. Editing the generated file treats a symptom and leaves the underlying drift-detection flaw in place.
- Do not amend or bump the canonical version to match the generator output. No token name, value, type, or package version actually differs.
- Do not open a token-change ticket on the assumption this is a design-token change. It is not.

Recommended fix locations, in order of likelihood

1. Add a line-ending normalization policy for the canonical package: LF canonical, `.gitattributes` `text eol=lf` for the token files, and/or a normalization step in the drift check that strips CRLF before hashing.
2. Make the iOS generator emit keys in a stable, deterministic order (sorted by key, or via an ordered structure).
3. Tighten the drift check to compare parsed key/value maps rather than raw bytes, with a separate byte-hash check reserved for canonical-side changes the semantic compare cannot see (comment drift, whitespace drift inside values).

This is consistent with the established North Pier governance: the versioned machine-readable package is canonical, generated outputs are derived, and drift detection should distinguish canonical-side changes from generator-side non-determinism. Non-semantic byte differences are a normalization/serialization concern at the generator/CI boundary, not a design-token concern, and the fix belongs there.

The right line: canonicalize the comparison INPUTS to a stable, declared form, byte-compare that form, and keep the original artifacts (raw producer output, raw consumer output, fixture source, run context) at a different layer as evidence. The metric label carries only the bounded structural outcome of the comparison, never the raw values or unbounded fixture identity.

WHAT GETS CANONICALIZED FOR PASS/FAIL:
  - Producer output and consumer output each reduced to ONE stable canonical encoding, declared up front:
    - Sorted keys, one canonical form per type.
    - Numbers normalized to a declared precision and representation (so 1 / 1.0 / 1e0 collapse only when the type system says they should).
    - Strings normalized under a declared trim and case policy.
    - Lists/sets order-normalized only where the type semantics say order is not significant; otherwise preserved.
  - The comparison is then byte-equal between the two canonical forms.
  - The result of that comparison maps to EXACTLY ONE of the four bounded mismatch classes:
    missing_key, wrong_key, unsupported_value, unequal_bounded_value.
  - That class is the only structural fact the metric label exposes about the failure.

WHAT STAYS AS EVIDENCE (NOT IN THE METRIC):
  - Raw producer value, as it actually appeared.
  - Raw consumer value, as it actually appeared.
  - Expected key for the failing record.
  - Failing-record index inside the fixture.
  - Fixture source: file path, content hash, rule_set_version, fixture inventory id.
  - Run context: run id, timestamp. (Commit SHA alone is not sufficient, per the key=(sha, fixture, rule_set) point already on record.)
  - These belong in the fixture report (which already retains expected/observed keys, values, and index) and in structured logs keyed by the same bounded correlation id used in the metric.
  - They do NOT get promoted into the metric label.

WHY THE LINE FALLS HERE:
  - Byte-equal of the RAW producer/consumer output is too strict. Any whitespace, ordering, encoding, or formatting drift fails even when the semantic content matches, which floods the failure signal with non-defects.
  - Pure semantic comparison without a declared canonical form is too loose. It can mask real divergence (e.g., "values within tolerance" hides the actual gap) or treat non-canonical encodings of the same value as different without a rule.
  - The middle is: declare the canonical encoding once, byte-compare that, and treat any divergence as one of the four bounded mismatch classes. The raw artifacts remain available to explain WHY a given class fired, without leaking cardinality into the metric.

ON THE fixture_name LABEL (the active cardinality issue):
  - 417 caller-supplied fixture_name values from fuzzing is exactly why this dimension cannot stay as free-form.
  - The label should carry a BOUNDED fixture identity, not caller-supplied strings:
    - rule_set_version (small, declared), AND
    - Either a fixture inventory id from a controlled set, or a fixed-width content hash of the fixture.
  - Free-form fixture_name (file paths, names read from the fixture metadata) belongs in the fixture report / structured log, not in the metric label.
  - That keeps label cardinality bounded AND keeps evidence fully recoverable: metric -> bounded id -> fixture source -> raw producer/consumer values.

ONE-LINE BOUNDARY:
  - Canonicalize structure + declared encoding before comparing.
  - Byte-compare the canonicals.
  - Expose only the bounded mismatch class and a bounded fixture identity in the metric.
  - Preserve raw values, fixture source, run context, and failing-record index in the fixture report and structured logs.
  - Evidence recoverability via the bounded id is the contract; raw artifacts are never promoted to labels.

**The two states, separated**

1. **Unavailable** — A row exists from the permitted source, but it lacks a stable `source_event_id`. Without that ID, Lantern cannot confirm whether the row is a new deploy movement or a duplicate of an earlier delivery attempt. So it isn't *heuristically deduplicated* and isn't rendered as a deploy card. This is an **identity** problem, not a freshness problem.

2. **Explicit unknown** — The permitted source itself is stale or missing for the selected window. Lantern has the authorization to read it, but the data isn't current (or isn't there). It renders as an explicit "unknown" rather than a guess or a fabricated value. This is a **freshness / presence** problem at a permissioned source.

**Why "Unavailable means Lantern has stale data" is wrong on three points**

- It misattributes *unavailable* to staleness when it's actually a missing stable identifier.
- It collapses *unknown* into the same bucket, blurring a state that's specifically meant to say "we don't know" without lying.
- It risks implying Lantern has the underlying data but is just slow to refresh it — which sounds like a broader or more complete access than the read-only two-account preview actually has.

> "Unavailable" means Lantern can't confirm a unique deploy event — the permitted source row doesn't carry a stable identifier we can verify, so we don't render it as a deploy movement rather than risk showing a duplicate.

**Blocking follow-up — atomic-replacement burst handling**

The atomic-rename watcher must detect a normal burst of replacements from a single publish run (write(tmp) → fsync → rename repeated N times in quick succession), not just the first swap. Required:

1. **Prompt burst detection.**
   - Rearm the watch on the *parent directory* (rename + create events) *and* on the candidate file's parent, so a write(tmp)+rename sequence that doesn't touch the watched inode is still seen.
   - On each detected replacement, perform content-hash validation against the previously active generation. A rapid N-event sequence where each candidate is a valid superset/replacement of the prior one is a **burst**, not drift; collapse it into one observed "generation advanced N→M" event and re-validate once at the end.
   - Equivalent-behavior note is acceptable only if it can prove (a) no event in the burst is dropped, (b) the post-burst generation equals the final on-disk generation, and (c) reconciliation runs on burst end.

2. **Explicit failure signal when prompt detection fails.**
   - If the watcher misses one or more replacements in a burst, or if reconciliation cannot confirm the post-burst generation, emit `failed_reload{reason}` and keep the **last known good** generation active. Do **not** silently rearm on a partial read; do **not** advance `active_generation` to a candidate that wasn't validated end-to-end.
   - Logging is bounded: reason enum, expected vs. observed generation, burst length, and a short hash. No raw config bodies in logs.
   - The failure signal must be visible to the existing reload-failure alert path — no new silent failure mode.

3. **Executed burst-replacement regressions (must run, not just exist).**
   - Burst of N valid replacements ending on a good generation → active == final on-disk, no failed_reload, one validation per burst (not N).
   - Burst of N where an intermediate candidate is invalid (bad content hash, missing fields, weight total ≤ 0) → active remains the last good generation pre-burst, failed_reload{reason=invalid_candidate} emitted, final good candidate after the bad one is *not* auto-advanced without a fresh explicit load.
   - Burst where the watcher misses ≥1 event → failed_reload{reason=burst_undetected} or equivalent, active unchanged, on next reconcile the active generation equals the latest validated one.
   - Concurrent burst + authorized rollback attempt → rollback grant is still bound to current/target generation and single-use; burst does not consume or invalidate the grant.
   - Shuffle-the-deck case (bad N+2 leaves good N+1 active) from the prior blocker remains in scope.

The two canonicalization steps you described are appropriate; the third is not.

Sorting token keys and normalizing CRLF to LF both address non-semantic differences — they bring both sides to the same parsed-map representation so the byte-for-byte check can ask the right question. Anya's earlier characterization of the divergence was exactly those two things, so the fix should be confined to them.

Trimming leading and trailing whitespace from every string value rewrites the values being compared, and that is a different category of normalization. It is not on the non-semantic list, and the `" 12 px"` vs `"12 px"` fixture is direct evidence that it is not safe:

- The fixture's purpose is to assert that a leading space inside a token value is a real semantic difference. Trimming both sides collapses that pair to equal and silently passes a fixture whose job is to surface the difference.
- It expands the canonicalization surface beyond what was characterized as non-semantic. If trimming were always harmless, it would have been part of Anya's earlier description of the gap; it wasn't. Any normalization that touches string values needs an explicit non-semantic argument grounded in the token model, not a "looks harmless" intuition.
- It defeats the purpose of the check. The generated iOS file is what gets shipped. If that file actually contains `" 12 px"` while the canonical package contains `"12 px"`, that is a real divergence between shipped output and canonical source, and the drift checker should report it. Suppressing it makes the check quieter, not more correct — and a drift checker that quietly green-lights whitespace drift is exactly how the original byte-for-byte divergence would have been masked in the first place.

If there is a class of values where incidental leading or trailing whitespace should not survive into generated outputs, that belongs in generation (where the canonical value is rewritten into the platform output), not in comparison. Comparison should report what each side actually contains; generation should be where the canonical shape is enforced.

So the fix should ship as: parse both artifacts, sort token keys, normalize CRLF to LF, then compare. The string-value trim should be removed. If Anya wants whitespace handling to be non-semantic for North Pier, that needs to be argued and agreed as a token-model decision and reflected in the canonical package and generators — not introduced through the drift checker.

Three-part engineering boundary, framed so Anya owns the design half and the comparison machinery owns the rest:

1. What engineering may safely normalize for a semantic comparison
   Engineering can normalize anything that is purely a transport or structural artifact of the serialized container:
   - key traversal order (sort once, compare as maps, not as ordered lists)
   - line-ending policy (CRLF vs LF)
   - inter-token whitespace inside the JSON/YAML container
   - encoding BOMs and trailing-newline differences
   - file-level metadata that is not part of the token map
   Anything *inside* a token — the key string, the value string, numeric precision, list order, unit suffixes, color-case, default-value folding — is part of the semantic contract. The comparison tool does not get to redefine it. If a consumer normalizes later, that is a consumer-side decision that should be visible in the consumer, not pre-applied in the comparison.

2. Why token-value whitespace must not be silently normalized unless the schema declares it insignificant
   Three reasons, in order of consequence:
   - Semantics. Surrounding or interior whitespace is load-bearing in many real token values. "Roboto, sans-serif" becomes invalid CSS the moment the space after the comma is stripped. "8px" and " 8px" compose differently under interpolation, calc(), and template-string consumers. Inner whitespace inside a multi-word string token is content, not formatting.
   - Hidden contract change. If the schema does not declare a field whitespace-insignificant, normalizing it makes the comparison tool the de facto authority on token semantics. That is a design-system decision, not a tool decision. The tool either preserves byte-exact values or it gates the normalization on an explicit schema statement that this specific field is insignificant.
   - Evidence loss. Normalizing before compare destroys your ability to tell "same value, different representation" (a serialization bug worth fixing) from "genuinely different value" (a real drift), and it discards the raw bytes that prove what was actually shipped. Comparison should preserve the original artifact and report the difference, not paper over it.

3. Original artifacts to retain as evidence
   Kept in fixture reports or structured logs scoped to a single comparison run — never in metric labels, because labels carry cardinality and the guardrail blocks unbounded caller-supplied strings:
   - raw producer output (byte-exact, with content hash)
   - raw consumer output (byte-exact, with content hash)
   - canonicalization policy in effect on this run (which normalizations were applied: sorted keys, line endings, BOM handling, nothing-value-level)
   - declared expected key set from the schema
   - failing-record index or token path (which entry triggered the diff)
   - fixture source identity (commit, generator version, content hash of inputs)
   - rule-set version
   - run ID and timestamp
   - the schema declaration that defines which fields are insignificant and which are not
   These are local evidence for one run, not aggregated signals. The bounded metric on top of them stays one of `missing_key`, `wrong_key`, `unsupported_value`, or `unequal_bounded_value`, with a controlled fixture identity rather than free-form `fixture_name`.

The handoff boundary for Anya is just this: she owns the schema declaration — required keys, value types, which fields are whitespace-insignificant, which lists are order-insignificant, what the canonical serialization form is — and engineering can refuse to run a comparison until those declarations are explicit. Engineering does not fill in those answers, and engineering does not get to relax them inside the comparison tool. Everything above is the boundary; everything inside it is her call.

Short answer first: requesting the wheelchair or cart at LGA is not excessive at all. It's a service the airline offers for exactly this kind of situation — a traveler who can walk independently but wants to skip long terminal distances and standing in lines. There's no medical gatekeeping, no "you're only allowed this if you're really hurt" threshold. If it reduces standing and preserves energy for the days that matter, it's a reasonable choice.

Practical comparison, non-medical

Using the gate-to-curb wheelchair or cart
  - What happens: an airline staff member meets you at the jet bridge or gate with a chair or motorized cart, pushes you through the terminal, often via a shorter or staff-only route, drops you at baggage claim (assistant may retrieve checked bags or hand them off), and continues to the curbside pickup area, usually closer to where a car can pull up than the regular exit.
  - Standing time: near zero after deplaning. You stay seated through baggage claim and the curb handoff.
  - Walking distance: jet bridge only. The rest is seated.
  - Time cost: usually 5 to 15 minutes of waiting at the gate for the chair or cart to arrive, then transit time similar to or shorter than walking. Total gate-to-curb is often close to walking, sometimes faster.
  - Energy cost: very low. You arrive at the curb rested.
  - Independence: the choice stays yours the whole time. You can walk any segment you want, change your mind at any point, or stand to board. The staff adapts to you, not the other way around.
  - Logistics for Nov 9: flights landing around 1:20 PM are mid-day, so staffing and cart availability are usually fine. Curbside pickup at LGA works well with this — Alex meets you at the curb, you don't have to navigate the terminal together.

Walking the terminal on your own
  - What happens: deplane, walk the jet bridge, walk the concourse, stand at the baggage carousel (often several minutes, sometimes longer if bags come out slowly), walk from baggage claim out to the curb.
  - Standing time: real, mostly at the carousel and any lines. LGA concourses are long; even with moving walkways, you're on your feet for most of it.
  - Walking distance: depends on the gate, but at LGA it's commonly 10 to 20 minutes of mostly continuous walking plus the carousel wait.
  - Time cost: comparable or slightly faster than the chair when there are no lines, slower when there are.
  - Energy cost: noticeable, especially after a flight. The knee aggravation you've described tends to show up in the second half of the walk, not the first.
  - Independence: full autonomy over pace and route.

The relevant trade-off isn't independence versus care — it's energy spent in the terminal versus energy saved for the ceremony and the family dinner. Walking the terminal doesn't really gain anything; it just front-loads fatigue into the first hour of the visit. The assisted route gives you the same arrival, just with a rested start.

One small thing worth knowing: even with the chair, you still walk the jet bridge and stand briefly at the curb for the car. So this isn't "being wheeled everywhere" — it's skipping the long, low-value middle of the terminal.

Hey Mom — quick note on the wheelchair thing. It's not excessive at all. The airline offers it for exactly this situation: a traveler who can walk fine but wants to skip a long terminal and the standing around at baggage claim.
