DEFECT — UNBOUNDED CARDINALITY FROM RAW TRACE IDs AS LABEL VALUES

Prometheus creates one time series per unique (metric_name, label_set) tuple, and every active series carries fixed overhead in the head block and the TSDB index (rule of thumb ~3 KB per series in memory plus on-disk cost). Cardinality is therefore a hard resource bound, not a soft preference: cost grows linearly with active series, query cost grows faster.

A trace_id is by definition a high-entropy unique identifier — 16 or 32 hex chars depending on the W3C trace-context variant — drawn from a keyspace so large that collisions are not expected inside any realistic window. Treating it as a metric label turns every traced sample into a brand-new series. The fixture already shows this: 5,000 distinct values in 10 minutes ≈ 8.3/s. Sustained for a day that is ~720k series from this one metric; sustained for a week it is ~5M+, before any cross-product with the other labels already attached to it. At those numbers the failure modes are concrete, not theoretical:

  - Prometheus head block grows until OOM or scrape stalls; missing scrapes produce silent gaps.
  - TSDB compaction and query latency rise with active series; any aggregation that touches this label becomes unusably slow or hits query-time limits.
  - Ingest-edge already enforces a 128-character cap on exemplar label values (prior fixture had a 142-char trace_id that breached it). A 32-hex-char W3C trace_id fits, but any vendor prefix or alternate format truncates or drops samples silently.
  - The cost is paid continuously by every consumer of the metric, including dashboards that never need the trace, to deliver a debugging affordance the trace backend already provides.

The intended debugging path is the one OTel and Prometheus already designed. Keep the trace_id in logs and in exemplar metadata: an exemplar links a metric sample to a trace by reference (the trace_id is the exemplar's identifier, not the metric's label). Metric labels should carry only the bounded classification the dashboard actually needs — a small, closed enum (e.g. trace_present ∈ {true,false}, trace_source_class ∈ {live,staged,replay}, trace_status_class ∈ {2xx,4xx,5xx}, trace_outcome ∈ {ok,error}) — which does not grow with traffic.

VERIFICATION-TO-USE GAP — EXPLANATION

The proposal performs two decoupled operations:

  1. Owner sync: digest D1 of bundle B1 is verified against an owner-signed manifest M1.
  2. Restore: the runbook follows a mutable "latest" pointer to a bundle filename, then loads and re-verifies whatever bundle that name currently resolves to.

The defect is structural, not a signing bug. Bundle B2 (substituted into the "latest" slot between sync and restore) is independently validly signed. The signature on B2 verifies cleanly. What decouples verification from use is not the signature — it is the pointer. The signed manifest binds a digest; the pointer does not. Any actor with write access to "latest" between sync and restore can swap B1 for B2 without invalidating B2's signature. Owners reviewed B1. Restore loads B2. The "what was reviewed" object and the "what was used" object are not bound.

This is a TOCTOU (time-of-check, time-of-use) gap. Verification establishes integrity at one moment. Use depends on a mutable, separately-addressed handle resolved at a later moment. Re-verifying B2's signature at restore only proves B2 is well-formed and authorized by the same key set — it does not prove B2 is the bundle owners reviewed.

In staging, the gap surfaced because the pointer was rewritten between sync and restore and recovery loaded a different validly signed bundle than the one whose digest was in the verified manifest. Production is unchanged; this remains review-only / staging-only until the acceptance criteria below are evidenced.

Two parts below: (1) what the defect is and why it breaks the bounded review, and (2) a draft blocking response you can send once you've confirmed the channel.

============================================================
1. The retry-overwrite defect
============================================================

The storage optimization upserts evidence keyed on the (expected_generation, observed_generation) pair. That key treats every attempt sharing the same gen-pair as the same logical evidence slot. A retry that runs against the same gen-pair therefore writes through the prior record instead of appending alongside it.

In the staging run you described:
  - Attempt A: gen-pair (E, O) → unexpected downstream key → mismatch, recorded
  - Attempt B: same gen-pair (E, O) → passed, recorded

Because the upsert key is the gen-pair, attempt B overwrote attempt A. The 7-day retention window still contains exactly one row for (E, O): the passing one. The original mismatch has been erased from the very surface the review is supposed to read.

Why this is a defect, not an instrumentation gap:
  - The retention contract was "signed expected_gen + signed observed_gen + bounded-value class for seven days." That contract is now silently per-gen-pair, not per-attempt. A reviewer cannot tell from the retained evidence whether (E, O) ever mismatched, or whether it was always-passing.
  - The corrected fixture's signature verification (signed generations checked before any key/value comparison) is intact — that's not the issue. The issue is that storage collapses attempts after verification has succeeded.
  - A mismatch that "resolved on retry" is now indistinguishable from "never mismatched." For a bounded provenance review, that distinction is the whole point: the reviewer is supposed to see mismatches even when downstream behavior recovered.

Root cause: missing attempt identity in the storage key, and upsert semantics that destroy prior rows on a matching gen-pair. Equivalent framing: storage is doing logical deduplication on a key that is meant to identify a *comparison*, not an *attempt*. Comparisons are reusable; attempts are not.

Production is unchanged, so this is a staging-only, review-only defect. It is still a block for promotion of the optimization because the retention it claims to provide is not the retention it actually provides.

The corrected fixture's signature verification is unaffected; the defect is in storage collapsing attempts after verification.

Acceptance criteria for promotion past this review.

The rule for Wes (design-only, not a deployment update):

The problem
  Per-element validation (weight is a finite number in [0,1], inclusive lower bound) is necessary but not sufficient. Two individually valid zero weights sum to zero, giving normalization a 0/0 denominator. Per-element checks pass; the group is unsendable.

The rule — two-stage group validator, order matters
  Stage 1, before normalization — group total:
    - Sum the group's weights.
    - Require the sum to be finite (no NaN, no Inf) AND strictly positive (> 0, not >= 0).
    - On failure, reject with a stable, group-specific diagnostic (e.g. `route group <name> has non-positive or non-finite total weight`).
    Strict positivity is what excludes the all-zero case. Finiteness is what blocks NaN/Inf leaking in from bad inputs.

  Stage 2, after normalization — outputs:
    - Every normalized weight must be finite.
    - The normalized weights must sum to 1.0 within a documented tolerance (match the existing router's tolerance; do not introduce a new one).

Why the order
  You cannot meaningfully normalize against a zero or non-finite denominator. The check has to fire first so the diagnostic is the correct "group total" condition, not a downstream symptom like "normalized weight is NaN" or "outputs do not sum to 1."

Acceptance for the validator change
  - Stage 1 fires for: all-zero group, group containing NaN, group containing Inf, group containing a missing or non-numeric entry.
  - Diagnostic names the offending group and states the failing condition.
  - Regression: a valid group with mixed positive and zero weights (sum > 0) normalizes correctly — outputs finite, sum within tolerance.
  - Stages are independent — Stage 2 does not silently mask a Stage 1 failure.
  - Existing per-element checks (finite numeric, in [0,1]) remain in place; this is additive, not a replacement.

Boundary

Defect:
The sequence validates generated-artifact metadata (step 2) against whatever object sits behind the mutable `current` URL at that moment, then replaces that object (step 4), then sets `implementation_ready=true` (step 5) using the prior validation result. Validation and the artifact actually served at readiness refer to different bytes. The manifest-listed output presence check, the metadata-presence check, and the canonical-package-version match check all pass against the validated object, but they do not bind to the bytes that will be served. A replacement with independently valid metadata (matching canonical_package_version, complete metadata, manifest-listed) still produces `implementation_ready=true` against bytes that were never validated. This is a TOCTOU defect through the mutable `current` URL.

Safety requirement:
The validation result used to set `implementation_ready=true` must be bound to an immutable artifact identity that survives any `current` swap between validation and readiness publication. Any change to that identity between step 2 and step 5 must invalidate the prior validation result, regardless of whether the replacement's metadata is independently well-formed.

Acceptance criteria for staged evidence:
  1. Validation reads metadata from an immutable reference (content digest, signed manifest entry, or equivalent), not from whatever happens to be at `current` at the time.
  2. The validated artifact identity is carried forward as a binding constraint to `implementation_ready=true`; identity mismatch at readiness publication prevents the flag from being set.
  3. Replacing the object behind `current` after step 2 does not allow `implementation_ready=true` to be set against a different artifact identity, even when the replacement's canonical_package_version, manifest presence, and metadata fields are all individually valid.
  4. A valid handoff with no swap still completes and sets the flag.
  5. An immutable identity that survives an attempted swap (e.g., digest pinned at validation, pointer swapped to a different validly-signed bundle) still permits normal flow only when the served bytes match the pinned identity.
  6. Coverage fixtures include: no swap, swap to different bytes with matching metadata, swap to identical bytes, swap after readiness but before consumer fetch, concurrent swap during validation.

Handoff process owner retains implementation, release, and rollback. This response is review-only; I am not approving or designing the production change, and I am not the owner of the fix path.

Production status:

Pattern note:
This is structurally the same class of defect as the staff-only shard-keeper rollback bundle issue: identity is verified against a digest, but restore / readiness uses a mutable pointer that can substitute a different validly-identified artifact. The same defense pattern applies here — pin the immutable identity at validation, carry it through to readiness, re-verify at the publish step.

  2. Confirm whether the `current` swap between step 2 and step 4 is intentional (e.g., a staging-to-canonical promotion step) or accidental, since the fix differs slightly between the two.

EXPLANATION OF THE DEFECT

The defect is a TOCTOU (time-of-check to time-of-use) gap between artifact validation and readiness publication, with readiness bound to a mutable pointer instead of immutable artifact identity.

Sequence that produced it:
  1. Release-candidate manifest and canonical-package version pinned.
  2. Generated-artifact metadata validated per manifest-listed output.
  3. Validation result captured (digest computed over the bytes reachable via URL at that instant).
  4. Object behind the mutable `current` URL replaced — different bytes now serve at the same pointer.
  5. `implementation_ready=true` set using the earlier validation result, which described the pre-replacement bytes.

18-A — the "?" is your tell. The clue is doing double duty: "cutting" works both physically (a blade) and verbally (a sharp remark). You're looking for the 6-letter agent-noun form (one who ____s) of a verb that names a sharp verbal jab — and that same verb also names a literal action done at a distance. S?I?E? is tight; there's basically one answer.

33-D — straight definition. What 7-letter verb means to keep something (an animal, a feeling, a secret) from getting out? C_N_A_N is extremely constraining — should click fast.

52-A — G_A_C_ is so tight it almost gives itself away. The most common 6-letter verb for a brief look, ending in -E.

33-D (Keep from escaping, 7, C_N_A_N): CONTAIN — C_O_N_T_A_I_N lands C at 1, N at 3, A at 5, N at 7. To contain is literally to keep (something) from escaping.

52-A (Quick look, 6, G_A_C_): GLANCE — G_L_A_N_C_E lands G at 1, A at 3, C at 5. A glance is the canonical quick look.

18-A (One making a cutting remark?, 6, S_I_E_): SNIPER — S_N_I_P_E_R lands S at 1, I at 3, E at 5. To snipe is to make sharp, cutting remarks (the figurative sense that gives the clue its question mark); a sniper is the one doing it.

Apple Crisp - 8" square, not-too-sweet

Before the walk (~10 min):
1. Turn the oven on to 375 F now, or set it when you walk back in.
2. Peel, core, and slice the 6 apples about 1/4 inch thick straight into the pan. Toss with:
   - 1 Tbsp brown sugar
   - 1 tsp cinnamon
   - 1 Tbsp flour
   - pinch of salt
3. In a small bowl, mix:
   - 3/4 cup old-fashioned oats
   - 1/2 cup flour
   - 1/3 cup packed brown sugar
   - 1/2 tsp cinnamon
   - pinch of salt
4. Cube 5 Tbsp cold butter and work it into the dry mix with your fingers or a fork until it looks like coarse crumbs with a few pea-size chunks left.
5. Scatter the topping evenly over the apples. Cover the pan loosely (foil or a clean towel) and head out.

After the walk:
6. Bake at 375 F for 35-40 minutes, until the topping is golden and the apples bubble at the edges. Let it rest 10 minutes before serving.

The four controls compose as separate stages. A single request can pass one and fail another; nothing was replaced.

1. Decode-admission cap (NEW)
   72 active decode admissions per pod. Above this, the client receives a retryable pre-acceptance result with a 1–3 second Retry-After. Nothing is accepted, nothing is enqueued, no slot is held.

2. Decoded-attribute byte cap (NEW)
   1,048,576 bytes aggregate across all gzip members of the request. Above this, the request is rejected before acceptance and enqueue. Not retryable on this basis alone.

3. Whole-batch point cap (PERMANENT, unchanged)
   8,000 points per batch. Above this, ingest-edge returns HTTP 413 with error code `oversized_batch`, zero accepted points, and the rejected count. Requires explicit client retry with partial-delivery semantics. Stays in place as the backstop for older or nonconforming clients.

4. Per-tenant waiting cap (PERMANENT, unchanged)
   8 accepted waiting requests per tenant. Above this, the request gets retryable backpressure in the queue. Separate from the decode-admission cap — a request can be admitted to decode and still hit this cap when it tries to enqueue.

Composition
  - Controls 1 and 2 fire before acceptance.
  - Control 3 fires after decode and admission, on the accepted batch.
  - Control 4 fires after acceptance, in the waiting queue.
  - The byte and admission controls are additive. They did not replace the whole-batch or tenant-waiting rules; both of those still apply to anything that gets through.

  Min 0–5:  conversational, 5–10% slower than summer easy. Cold masks effort — do NOT chase the opening 5 min.

Duration: 15 minutes (six prompts × ~2.5 min). Scope: rehearsal only.
Roles: Wes teaches responder path. Nadia owns postmortem section. Alex contributes only bounded failure case.

1. Durable acceptance
   Prompt: A request sits in the admission queue and the client socket closes. What is its state?
   Expected move: Identify durable acceptance first — server-side record on disk before classifying any outcome. Treat socket close, retry, or timeout as downstream of that record.
   Failure signal: Calling it "accepted" or "cancelled" without locating the durable record, or treating the in-memory admission slot as acceptance.

2. Cancellation vs caller disconnect
   Prompt: Durability shows one attempt; the trace shows the client TCP closed before any server write completed. What does the responder say?
   Expected move: Distinguish server-initiated cancel from client disconnect by reading server-side state, not client behavior. Disconnect before server durability is not a cancel and not a publish.
   Failure signal: Reporting "cancelled" because the socket dropped, or "disconnected" when the server actually issued a cancel, or fusing the two.

3. Process recovery
   Prompt: The metrics-router process crashes and is restarted mid-request. What does the responder look up first?
   Expected move: Resume by recovering the one durable attempt identity from persistent state and classifying from that record. Restart is an event, not an outcome.
   Failure signal: Treating the restart as acceptance, minting a new attempt identity, or losing the original durable identity across the boundary.

4. Exactly one terminal result
   Prompt: Same attempt identity surfaces two terminal markers — `cancelled` and `published`. What does the responder do?
   Expected move: Refuse to proceed. Insist on exactly one terminal outcome (cancelled OR published, never both, never neither) bound to the one durable attempt identity. Escalate rather than pick.
   Failure signal: Choosing the "later" marker, suppressing one, or declaring a third hybrid state. Counts of zero or two terminals are both failures.

5. 45-minute secondary boundary
   Prompt: T+38 minutes, cause still unisolated, primary is still paging metrics-router logs. What does the responder do at T+42?
   Expected move: Note observable clock, failed-isolation evidence, and page the secondary (Wes, mapped implementation/release/rollback owner) before T+45, not at T+45. Refer to Wes, not Alex.
   Failure signal: Waiting for the boundary, paging Alex as fallback, or declaring "isolated" without logs/metrics/test evidence.

6. Friday staging preparation vs production change
   Prompt: A responder proposes a staging run on Friday at 3 PM, with a config flag flip in prod "to validate end to end." Is that in scope?
   Expected move: Classify the staging run as Friday preparation — no production-state change. Reject the prod flag flip. Production cutovers remain Monday morning. Tabletop authorizes no deploy, release, rollback, review closure, ownership change, or production-state change.

WINTER PREP — AT-HOME ONLY
Current state assumed: front brake recently serviced and normal; rear brake, tires, lights currently sound.

INSPECTION (one-time baseline before salted streets start, then a 60-second check after each ride)
  Tires
    Sidewalls: no cuts, bulges, cracks, exposed casing.
    Pressure: cold, before riding. Sidewall max is the upper limit; cold drops pressure ~1 PSI per 10°F, so recheck weekly. A slow leak after sitting = tube/valve/rim-tape, not weather.
    Spin: no hop, rub, or sideplay. Quiet and true = baseline.
  Brakes
    Lever feel: firm, full stop without sinking to the bar. Lever that sinks = hydraulic leak or stretched housing → shop.
    Pads (rim or disc): ≥ 1.5 mm of material; even wear; pad pulls straight in the caliper.
    Rotor (disc): wipe with isopropyl alcohol if it squeals; deep grooves or persistent rub = shop.
    Rim (rim brake): clean track, no shiny groove; wipe after every wet ride.
    Walk test: fully squeeze each brake and push forward — wheel must lock.
  Lights & reflectors
    Front and rear: confirmed working; lens clean, mount tight, fresh batteries (cold shortens battery life).
    Reflectors: present and intact on front, rear, both wheels (or pedals), both sides.
  Drivetrain
    Chain: wipe, no rust, no stiff links.
    Wear check: chain checker at 0.5% = plan to replace; 0.75% = replace now.
    Cassette/chainring: hooked or shark-fin teeth → shop.

SALT PROTOCOL (within an hour of every salted or wet ride)
  1. Low-pressure rinse + mild soap. Avoid pressure spray at hub, bottom-bracket, and headset bearings.
  2. Brush chain, derailleurs, brake surfaces with an old toothbrush.
  3. Dry fully before storage — salt sitting on wet steel is the failure mode, not the salt alone.
  4. Lube the chain: one drop per roller, wipe off the excess. Wet lube for winter streets, not dry lube.
  5. Recheck tire pressure the next morning before the next ride.

STOP RIDING — TAKE TO SHOP
  Brakes: lever sinks, walk test fails to lock the wheel, hydraulic fluid leak, rotor cracked or deeply scored, pad material under 1.5 mm, uneven pad wear.
  Tires or wheels: sidewall bulge or cut exposing casing, persistent flat after one repair, broken or loose spoke, rim dent, hub play, wheel hop.
  Frame or fork: any crack, bent dropout, steering play.
  Drivetrain: chain skips under load, crank play, cassette or freewheel loose or skipping.
  Lights: intermittent failure after a fresh battery, cracked mount or wiring.
  Anything that recurs or deviates from the baseline you just confirmed.

If borderline (slow leak, occasional skip, faint rub, intermittent light): ride straight to the shop rather than "see how it goes."

Critical failure mode - log.Fatal in an HTTP handler

log.Fatal calls os.Exit(1) after writing the log line. A single malformed request body terminates the entire metrics-router process, not just the failing request. Concrete consequences on the publish path:

  - Every in-flight request loses its connection with no response.
  - Durable state held only in memory - in-flight retries, journal records, partial publishes - is lost mid-operation. On the publish path this is worse than on a read-only path.
  - Any caller (legitimate or test) that sends a body decodeAndValidate rejects crashes the process for every other caller. A request-scoped error is being treated as a process error.

Other failure modes in the same handler

  - No HTTP response on success. After publish(policy) returns, the handler exits without writing to w. The client hangs until timeout. Callers commonly retry on timeout, which can duplicate the publish if publish is not idempotent.
  - r.Body is not closed. Slow leak under load.
  - No panic recovery. A panic in decodeAndValidate or publish kills the process with no log line.
  - decodeAndValidate likely distinguishes decode errors (caller error, return 4xx) from policy-rule errors (could be a learning signal, return 4xx with structured log). Both currently log.Fatal; the latter is not a process-killer.
  - No request id in the error log. No correlation to caller, body, or tenant.
  - No bound on r.Body size or read deadline. Slow-loris / oversize-body exposure during decode.
  - publish has no context, no cancellation. A blocked downstream call ties up the goroutine.

Not in this review

  - Not proposing an implementation. The minimum fix for log.Fatal is small (return 4xx with a structured log line; 5xx if you want policy-rule violations flagged as server-side), but error-class mapping, status codes, retry guidance, and observability choices belong to Wes.
  - Not authorizing release. This is review of the failure surface of the pasted snippet, not approval.

Right now (~5:27 PM): you're inside the safe carryover/rest window. Don't carve yet, don't put it in the fridge, don't leave it on the counter uncovered for long. The plan below keeps it above 140°F for the next ~95 minutes without drying it out.

REST (now → ~5:40 PM)
  - Let it sit on the counter ~10–15 min, uncovered or loosely tented.
  - Carryover will push the internal from 165°F to roughly 170–175°F in the thickest part, and the juices redistribute. This step matters more than it looks — skipping it is the main reason carved turkey leaks juice onto the cutting board instead of staying in the meat.

HOT HOLD (5:40 PM → 6:50 PM)
  Pick one. Both keep it safely above 140°F for 90+ minutes:

  Option A — whole breast in a low oven (less work, very reliable):
    - Wrap the breast tightly in two layers of heavy-duty foil. Wrap a clean kitchen towel around the foil for extra insulation.
    - Oven at its lowest setting, target 170–200°F ("warm" / "keep warm"). On a rack or in a roasting pan.
    - At ~6:15 PM, verify with an instant-read thermometer in the thickest part. You want ≥155°F. If it's climbing past 180°F, drop to "warm" only.
    - Pull at 6:50 PM.

  Option B — slice now, hold in broth (best insurance against drying):
    - After the 10-min rest, carve the breast into ~1/4" slices against the grain.
    - In a wide covered dish, warm ~3/4 cup turkey drippings or low-sodium chicken broth with a small pat of butter — hot, not boiling.
    - Lay the slices in a single layer, press a sheet of parchment directly onto the surface (prevents skin formation), cover tightly.
    - Hold on the stove over the lowest possible burner OR in the oven at 170°F.
    - Bring to a brief simmer for ~60 seconds right before plating so the gravy is hot.

  Rule of thumb: if the breast felt on the edge of done when you pulled it at 165°F, pick Option B. If it had plenty of give and juices ran clear at pull, Option A is fine.

CARVING & PLATING (~6:50 PM → 7:00 PM)
  - Option A: unwrap, rest 5 min, carve, plate. Target internal at service ≥165°F in the thickest slice.
  - Option B: already carved — just ladle a little of the hot holding liquid over each portion at the table, or serve the rest in a small pitcher.
  - Re-confirm 165°F in the thickest slice going out, not just at pull — it's the number the FDA/UDSA guidance and your thermometer routine both key on.

SIDES (so they meet 7:00 PM)
  - Mashed potatoes + stuffing: hold covered in the oven at 170°F alongside the turkey (or on the lowest burner). Stir potatoes once. Stuffing must also hit 165°F before hold.
  - Green beans: start at ~6:25 PM, plate at 6:55 PM.
  - Gravy: keep at bare simmer or hold in a pre-warmed thermos/carafe.

LEFTOVERS (after dinner)
  - Refrigerate within 90 minutes of plating — so by ~8:30 PM. This is the rule you already used last year.
  - Slice any remaining breast into portions; store in a shallow container with a spoonful of broth/drippings so it doesn't dry out in the fridge.
  - Potatoes, stuffing, beans, gravy — separate shallow containers. Shallow matters: a deep hot container cools too slowly and re-enters the danger zone.
  - Cooling targets if you want to be explicit: 70°F within 2 hours of plating, 40°F within 4 hours after that.

THINGS NOT TO DO
  - Don't carve and leave slices uncovered on a platter at room temp — that's the fastest path into the 40–140°F danger zone for an hour and a half.
  - Don't seal the foil airtight immediately after pulling — let the initial steam vent for a minute, then seal, otherwise the meat stews and the skin (if any) goes soggy.

---

**Blocking review — `Content-Encoding` validation accepts ambiguous composite headers**

The current staging candidate splits the header on commas, trims whitespace, and uses only the first token. That silently accepts `gzip, identity` as `gzip`, even though the header advertises both encodings. This is an ambiguous interpretation — a composite header could mean a chained decode sequence, a negotiated fallback, or a single encoding, and "first token only" is none of those — and it means every token after the first is never checked against the allowlist. The reversed chain (`identity, gzip`) following a different path makes the same point from the other side: behavior depends on which token happens to land first, not on what the header actually says.

**Required before this can be re-reviewed**

1. **Exact singular allowlist.** The full, trimmed `Content-Encoding` header value must equal exactly one explicitly permitted encoding (e.g., `gzip` or `identity`). No comma-splitting, no first-token acceptance, no case-folded synonyms unless enumerated. The comparison must run before any decode work, before request acceptance, and before enqueue.

2. **Executed tests proving every non-allowlisted form fails closed before decode admission or acceptance.** Each test must show the rejection occurs before decode starts, with no partial decode, no slot consumed, and exactly one terminal result returned to the caller. Coverage required:
   - **Chained:** `gzip, identity`, `identity, gzip`, `gzip, deflate`, `deflate, gzip, br`
   - **Duplicated:** `gzip, gzip`, `gzip, gzip, gzip`, `identity, identity`
   - **Empty:** `""`, `,`, ` , `, `, gzip`, `gzip, `
   - **Unknown:** `br`, `zstd`, `deflate`, `compress`, `unknown`, `gzip2`

3. **Explicit handling of a missing `Content-Encoding` header.** Either an enumerated default is permitted and tested, or absence fails closed — but the choice must be stated, consistent with the singular allowlist, and covered by tests.

**Authority unchanged.** Implementation, release, and rollback remain with Yuki. Production is unchanged. The request-wide decoded-attribute limit, 72-request admission cap, exactly-one-terminal-result, exactly-once slot release, and existing 8,000-point / eight-waiting-per-tenant controls remain as previously approved and are not the subject of this comment. This is a review comment, not a release or production authorization.

Walk-in checklist — rear-tire sidewall split (~9 mm), pressure currently held, no riding, no air added

1. Avoid loading the damaged tire
   - Walk the bike beside you, hand on the saddle or top tube; do not ride, push-mount, or coast.
   - Keep the rear wheel off the ground as much as practical. If you must cross a curb or step, lift by the frame, not the wheel.
   - Avoid potholes, storm grates, speed bumps, and any surface that would force the split to bear load or deform.
   - When stopped, rest the bike on the kickstand or lean it against something at the front wheel — do not rest it on the rear wheel.
   - Do not strap, clamp, or hang the bike by the rear wheel for transport.

2. Stop the trip and re-route if you observe
   - Visible pressure loss, tire visibly deflating, or a new low/soft spot on the rear.
   - The split lengthens, opens wider, or a bulge/"blister" appears next to it (casing is bulging through).
   - A hiss, ticking, or any audible air escape.
   - Wheel goes untrue, develops visible play, or a spoke goes slack.
   - Rim tape exposed, bead unseated, or any damage to the rim under the split.
   - Conditions turn icy, slushy, or pooling-water — surface slip-load on a sidewall-compromised tire is not worth the risk; come back another day.

3. Ask the shop before authorizing a replacement
   - Is the split in a replace-only zone per the manufacturer (sidewall vs. tread), and can they show you the specific criterion?
   - Is a patch an option here, or is sidewall location a hard no? Get their reasoning, not just the verdict.
   - Same tire model/size/compound as currently installed, and is the front tire the same age/tread — replace as a pair or not?
   - Do you need a new tube and fresh rim tape as well, and is that included in the quote?
   - Itemized cost: tire, tube, rim tape, labor, disposal; warranty on the new tire; turnaround time.
   - Will they show you the removed tire so you can see the failure mode (useful for the next tire decision)?
   - Anything they found during the inspection beyond the split (brakes, trueness, spoke tension) that should be addressed now vs. deferred?

MAINTENANCE NOTE

Subject: Request for inspection — bedroom window, lower sash (South Slope)

Hello,

Requesting an inspection of the lower sash on the bedroom window. Overnight wind produced a steady cold draft and audible whistle along the lower sash. The window is fully latched and secure.

Observations:
- No broken glass and no visible frame damage.
- No water intrusion and no wall moisture around or below the window.
- No smoke, no burning odor, no electrical concern.
- The room remains usable.
- The radiator and its access path are unaffected.

This is a comfort and energy issue rather than an emergency, and we wanted to report it promptly. Please inspect the lower-sash seal and weatherstripping at your convenience, and let us know the timing. Happy to coordinate.

Thank you,
Alex

TEMPORARY DRAFT REDUCTION

All of the following are removable, do not block the window or the radiator, and keep Kibo's space clear. Apply along the lower sash only; leave the latch and any egress path unobstructed.

1. Removable foam weatherstrip tape (1/2" or 3/4" closed-cell foam). Apply to the lower sash stops or the sill, not to the glass. Press the sash against it when latched; peel off later without damaging paint. Skip if it would interfere with the latch.

2. Rope caulk (window seal cord). Press a length into the seam where the lower sash meets the frame on the room side. Removable, reusable, leaves no residue. Best match for a whistle that tracks a specific seam.

3. Fabric draft snake. A weighted fabric tube laid along the interior sill against the lower sash. Does not seal, but breaks the convective loop and dampens the whistle. Choose a weighted or wall-tucked version so Kibo cannot drag it; keep it well clear of the radiator and the access path.

4. Weighted curtain. A curtain with weights sewn into the hem, hung on a rod that pulls aside. Reduces the convective draft without sealing the window and does not block egress. Confirm the rod bracket is rated for the weight and does not sit over the radiator.

What to avoid, given your constraints:
- Do not seal the window shut. No shrink-film kits, no permanent caulk, no foam-in-place. The bedroom window is likely a fire-egress path and you want it able to open in seconds.
- Nothing on or in front of the radiator. No towels, fabric, or paper on the floor there; the access path needs to stay clear.
- No small loose objects on the floor in Kibo's reach. Favor weighted or wall-tucked options over anything he could pick up.

If the whistle is still audible after foam tape + rope caulk + a draft snake, the remaining cause is usually sash fit rather than just seal, which is exactly what the inspection should evaluate.

Short answer: yes, retire the whole string. Your read of the situation is correct — and the unplug-and-out-of-Kibo's-reach action was the right immediate step.

Why retire rather than repair:

The symptom — a section going dark when the cord near the molded plug is moved — is the classic signature of an intermittent open at a high-flex point. The most common cause is broken copper conductor strands inside the cord, right where it enters the molded plug body. That's mechanical fatigue: it doesn't heal, it progresses, and the next move can be a momentary re-make under load rather than a clean open. Internal arcing at an intermittent plug connection is a known fire precursor, and the molded body conceals any heating until it doesn't. You correctly noted the absence of heat, smoke, odor, spark, discoloration, exposed conductor, and effect on other apartment power — none of those red flags are present, so this is not an emergency, but the underlying fault is in a sealed, non-user-repairable assembly. Light strings are inexpensive, so cost-benefit is clearly on the side of replacement.

What to check on a replacement:

Certification mark (any one of these is sufficient; UL is the most common in the US):

  - UL "LISTED" mark with a category identifier such as "HOLIDAY OR DECORATIVE LIGHTING" or similar
  - ETL "LISTED" mark by Intertek
  - CSA mark (Canada)

The mark should be on a permanent tag, on the cord, or molded into the product. A paper-only sticker with no permanent mark is a red flag.

Indoor rating:

  - Should say "Indoor" or "Indoor/Outdoor" on the package or the permanent tag. "Outdoor only" works but is overkill; no rating at all is a skip.

Cord and plug features:

  - Wire gauge: 20 AWG is the standard and preferred; 22 AWG is acceptable for shorter LED strings. Lower number = thicker wire. Avoid anything thinner.
  - Insulation: flexible thermoplastic, not brittle, not tacky, no exposed copper or visible thinning at the plug or socket transitions.
  - Molded plug: single-piece body, not screwed together, with a visible strain-relief boot where the cord enters the plug. The strain-relief boot is exactly what your old string lacked at the failure point.
  - Plug blades: solid, firm in the body, not loose or wobbly.
  - Polarized plug: one blade wider than the other. Standard on modern listed strings and ensures correct polarity — a good sign, though not a strict requirement.
  - Fused plug: many UL-listed strings have a replaceable fuse accessible via a small sliding cover on the plug body, typically rated 3A. This is a desirable safety feature and easy to verify in-store before purchase.

Bulbs:

  - LED is the practical default now. Much lower current, far less heat, longer life, and more resistant to the flex and shock that breaks incandescent filaments. For indoor decorative use, there's no real reason to choose incandescent anymore.

Sanity checks before each season's use, to avoid repeating this:

  - Visual inspection of the cord, plug, and every socket
  - Brief plug-in test before decorating to confirm the full string lights
  - Don't run under rugs, furniture cushions, or through doorways where the cord gets pinched or walked on — that's the same flex-fatigue pattern that just failed
  - Respect the manufacturer's stated maximum end-to-end connection count (typically 3-5 strings for LED); don't daisy-chain beyond it
  - Out of Kibo's reach, as you've already done this time

Same-day post-salt clean — no pressure washer, all products kept off brake surfaces. Disc-brake protocol throughout.

1. Pre-rinse (dissolve bulk salt)
   Gentle lukewarm water — hose on shower setting or a watering can — over the lower frame, chainstays, seatstays, fork lowers, and drivetrain. No jets. Keep the stream off hub/bottom-bracket/headset bearings and off the brake calipers and rotors.

2. Wash frame
   Mild bike wash or dilute dish soap + soft brush or sponge on lower frame, dropouts, fork lowers. Old toothbrush for derailleur pulleys and chainring teeth. Soap stays away from rotors, pads, and calipers.

3. Degrease drivetrain
   Bike degreaser (or diluted citrus/simple green) on chain, cassette, chainrings, derailleur cage. Stiff brush. If using a chain-cleaner tool, position it and a drip rag so rinse can't reach the rotors.

4. Rinse
   Low-pressure rinse on cleaned areas only. Water still stays off calipers and rotors.

5. Wipe rotors (defensive baseline)
   Even if no splash reached them: wipe each rotor with isopropyl alcohol (≥90%) and a clean lint-free cloth. Clean surface before any lube work.

6. Dry
   Microfiber on frame and components. Wipe the chain link by link until visibly dry. A few minutes of air-dry helps; gentle compressed air on the drivetrain is fine if you have it.

7. Quick brake-pad check
   Visual: no oily sheen, no embedded grit. Lever pull: firm, not spongy. If a pad looks contaminated, replacement is the only fix — flag it, do not ride.

8. Lubricate chain
   Wet-condition lube suited to salt/winter — one drop per roller while slowly back-pedaling the full loop. Let it sit ~5 minutes.
   Do not apply lube to: rotors, pads, cassette, chainrings, or derailleur jockey-wheel contact faces. If your pulleys have serviceable bushings, a single tiny drop on the pivot only — never on the running surfaces.

9. Wipe excess
   Lightly squeeze a clean rag around the chain while back-pedaling. Remove surface lube so it doesn't grab tomorrow's grit.

10. Post-clean inspection
    a. Rear tire (Nov 27 replacement): sidewall intact, no cuts, pressure feels right.
    b. Front tire: same — it wasn't separately re-inspected at the Nov 27 visit, so look it over now after today's salted ride.
    c. Wheels: spin true, no loose spokes, QR or thru-axle levers tight.
    d. Brakes: rotor clean and dry, pads clean, lever firm.
    e. Shifting: clean click through every gear front and rear, no sticky cable pull.
    f. Lights: front and rear still functional.
    g. Frame and bolts: no new cracks at dropouts, cable guides, or salt-prone seams; seatpost, stem, bottle-cage bolts visually seated.

11. Low-speed test ride (flat)
    Two firm brake checks from walking pace to confirm lever feel and stopping power, then a short shift run through all gears. If anything feels off, walk it back — don't ride through it.

12. Tomorrow, before the next ride
    If salt was heavy, a 60-second wipe of the lower frame and a light re-lube of the chain. Salt wicks moisture overnight; a quick dry wipe prevents the corrosion cycle from restarting.

The four terms, in plain language:

- Billed amount — what the provider charged for the service. This is their full list price. It is almost never what you actually owe.
- Allowed amount — what your plan agrees the service is worth for payment purposes. In-network providers usually accept this as the maximum, even though they billed higher. The difference between billed and allowed is a write-off; you do not owe it.
- Plan payment — what your insurer actually paid the provider on this claim, after applying your benefits (deductible, coinsurance, copay rules).
- Patient responsibility — what the plan says you owe for this claim: your copay, coinsurance share, or any deductible portion not yet met. This is the only number from the EOB that should line up with what the provider bills you.

Important distinction: an EOB is not a bill. It explains how the claim was processed. The actual bill comes from the provider, and the two should agree on patient responsibility. If they don't, that's worth contesting.
